## ⟦S0025⟧ ux-guidelines.csv — UI/UX Pro Max — lookup databases
- **What it is:** A lookup table of 119 UX rules across 20+ categories (Navigation, Animation, Layout, Touch, Interaction, Accessibility, Performance, Forms, Responsive, Typography, Feedback, Content, Onboarding, Search, Data Entry, AI Interaction, Spatial UI, Sustainability, Security/Accessibility); each rule has a description, a Do, a Don't, good and bad code examples, and a severity.
- **How it looks:** What the table lets a builder produce: pages that behave correctly under the visitor's hands — a sticky nav that never covers content (body padding equal to nav height), a visible focus ring on every control including inside modals, an error message under the exact field that failed plus a focusable error summary at the top of the form, and text that still fits at narrow widths and user spacing overrides.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion as a table. Its Animation rows govern motion: animate 1–2 key elements per view maximum; easing matched to purpose (deceleration/ease-out when arriving, linear only for constant-rate progress such as spinners); the prefers-reduced-motion query is mandatory; auto-rotating content must provide previous/next and play/pause and stop on focus or hover.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Columns: No, Category, Issue, Platform, Description, Do, Don't, Code Example Good, Code Example Bad, Severity. Key values: smooth scroll via `scroll-behavior: smooth` on html; z-index scale 10 / 20 / 30 / 50 (never z-[9999]); use dvh, not 100vh, for full-screen mobile layouts; text measure 65–75ch; touch targets 44pt iOS / 48dp Android / 24 CSS px on web (WCAG), minimum 8px gaps; `touch-action: manipulation` to remove tap delay; contrast minimum 4.5:1 for normal text; body line-height 1.5–1.75; toasts auto-dismiss after 3–5 seconds; breakpoint testing at 320 / 375 / 414 / 768 / 1024 / 1440; `font-display: swap` against invisible-text font loading; form errors inline below the field, referenced with aria-describedby, plus a top summary (`role="alert"`, tabindex −1) whose items link to each invalid field. WCAG 2.2 rows (100–119): Focus Not Obscured, minimum AA / enhanced AAA (offset sticky UI with `scroll-padding-top: var(--header-height)`); Focus Appearance AAA (indicator at least a 2 CSS px perimeter, 3:1 state contrast); Dragging Movements (single-pointer alternatives such as Move up / Move down buttons); Target Size (Minimum) 24×24 CSS px; Consistent Help; Redundant Entry (reuse confirmed data instead of re-asking); Accessible Authentication (allow paste, password managers, passkeys — no cognitive-test-only login); compact-label and chip semantics (badges are static state, chips are values/actions; interactive chips need a native button role, state and visible focus); cancellable state transitions (cancel the prior transition and set the final state directly — never depend on transitionend). The table's Critical-severity rows cluster on accessible authentication, text reflow/spacing, essential-text truncation and compact-control semantics.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max — lookup databases; WCAG 2.2 criteria are named inside the rows (focus obscured, focus appearance, dragging movements, target size, consistent help, redundant entry, accessible authentication).
- **Best for:** The QA/rules layer for every section — forms, navigation, call/CTA and proof blocks especially; this is the checklist a finished build gets audited against.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0025⟧
## ⟦S0026⟧ stacks/angular.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 50-row lookup table of current Angular (22.x) build rules — each row gives a category, the guideline, a plain description, a Do and a Don't, a good and a bad code snippet, a severity (High/Medium/Low) and an official docs link. Categories: Components (8 rows), Routing (6), State (6), Forms (6), Performance (8), Testing (6), Styling (5), Architecture (5).
- **How it looks:** The table itself produces nothing visual; it governs how an Angular app is put together so the visitor gets a clean, fast app — pages that lazy-load feature screens on demand instead of one heavy first load, forms that only show an error message under a field after the visitor has touched that field, content below the fold that appears with a skeleton placeholder when scrolled into view (@defer on viewport), and hero images served through NgOptimizedImage with declared width/height and priority so they do not shift the layout.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (The table prescribes no animation system; its only time-based rules are performance ones: preload lazy route modules in the background after first load, and set form validation to run on blur or submit instead of on every keystroke.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Signal-based reactivity throughout — signal() for local state, computed() for derived values, effect() only for side effects; standalone components as the default (no NgModules for new code); built-in @if/@for/@switch template control flow with track item.id in @for lists (never track $index for dynamic data); input()/output() signal component APIs; extract a sub-component when a template exceeds 50 lines; typed reactive forms with FormBuilder generics and ValidatorFn functions; OnPush change detection plus zoneless-readiness (signals, markForCheck, AsyncPipe); loadComponent() lazy routes with functional canActivate guards and ResolveFn resolvers; tree-shaking by importing only the Angular features used; @angular/ssr for SEO-critical public routes. Every row is marked active and verified 2026-08-13.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; every row links to official Angular documentation at angular.dev (plus ngrx.io for the Signal Store row, material.angular.io for CDK harnesses, github.com/ngneat/spectator, tailwindcss.com for the Tailwind-in-Angular row).
- **Best for:** Reference only when a build is actually an Angular app — not applicable to the single-file HTML trade sites this bank mainly builds. Useful rows if Angular ever applies: quote/contact form behaviour (typed reactive forms, errors shown after touch, updateOn blur for expensive validators), lazy-loading discipline for heavy sections, and image sizing/priority rules for heroes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0026⟧

## ⟦S0027⟧ stacks/astro.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 53-row lookup table of Astro (7.1.6) build rules in the same format as S0026 (category, guideline, Do/Don't, good/bad code, severity, docs link). Categories: Architecture (5 rows), Routing (5), Components (5), Styling (4), Data (5), Performance (5), ViewTransitions (4), SEO (5), Integrations (4), TypeScript (3), Markdown (3), API (3), Security (3), Build (3).
- **How it looks:** It shapes a content site that feels instant: static pages shipped with zero JavaScript by default, where only genuinely interactive islands wake up — a comment block hydrates when scrolled into view (client:visible), a non-critical widget waits for browser idle (client:idle) — and images arrive optimised and responsively sized through the built-in Image/Picture components instead of one heavy file for every screen. Between pages, shared elements such as the header can carry a transition:name so they morph/persist across navigation instead of the page flashing white, and a playing video marked transition:persist keeps playing while the visitor moves to another page.
- **Frame by frame:** Mostly static — no prescribed easing or duration values. The one motion behaviour the data describes is Astro's ClientRouter page transitions: click an internal link → the client-side router swaps the page without a full reload → elements with matching transition:name animate/morph between their old and new positions and transition:persist elements (e.g. a media player) stay alive untouched → end state is the new page with those elements continuous. The table also requires a no-JS fallback so content still works if the router never runs. No durations or easing curves are given.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Islands architecture with client directives chosen by timing (client:load / client:visible / client:idle); file-based routing with [param] dynamic routes and getStaticPaths() for build-time generation; per-route `export const prerender = false` for on-demand rendering (the old output:'hybrid' is removed); Zod-schema content collections with getCollection() preferred over Astro.glob; data fetched by top-level await in frontmatter, never in client useEffect; PUBLIC_ prefix for any env var exposed to the client; Tailwind 4 integrated through the official @tailwindcss/vite plugin (the @astrojs/tailwind integration is deprecated); built-in prefetch turned on with `prefetch: true` or data-astro-prefetch; astro:assets <Image /> for all local images; strict TypeScript with typed component Props interfaces; set:html only for sanitised content.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; rows link to the official Astro documentation at docs.astro.build. Several rows (colocate styles, is:global sparingly, CSS variables, some performance/canonical rows) record no docs URL.
- **Best for:** Directly relevant if a trade site is ever built as a static Astro site: hero and gallery image handling (astro:assets, responsive Picture, lazy below-fold), the zero-JS discipline that keeps a brochure site fast, prefetching so town/service pages open instantly, sitemap + RSS + canonical SEO rows for local-search pages, and the ClientRouter transition rows for smooth page-to-page movement.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0027⟧

## ⟦S0028⟧ stacks/avalonia.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 38-row lookup table of Avalonia 12 (cross-platform .NET desktop UI) build rules, same table format as S0026. Categories: XAML (4 rows), Styling (6), Controls (3), Data Binding (4), Cross-Platform (4), Performance (4), Architecture (4), Accessibility (3), Testing (3), Navigation (3).
- **How it looks:** This governs a desktop application window, not a web page: a Fluent- or Simple-themed app whose buttons visibly react to the pointer (a :pointerover style drops a button to 0.8 opacity, :pressed and :focus have their own looks), data grids and tree views for tabular/hierarchical data, a native menu bar that follows each operating system's own convention, and a light/dark switch done by flipping the app's theme variant rather than repainting every control. Long lists stay smooth because only the visible rows are rendered (virtualization).
- **Frame by frame:** The table describes one named motion: page/view switching with built-in transitions — a RoutedViewHost PageTransition such as PageSlide (horizontal) with Duration 0:0:0.3 (0.3 seconds) or CrossFade, so on navigation the old view slides/fades out as the new one slides/fades in, replacing an abrupt content swap. Everything else is static styling/state rules with no motion values.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Avalonia's own XAML namespace (https://github.com/avaloniaui — never the WPF namespace); compiled bindings with x:DataType, on by default in Avalonia 12 (AvaloniaUseCompiledBindingsByDefault = true, trim-safe for Native AOT), with the #name shorthand for element-to-element bindings because ElementName does not resolve under compiled bindings; CSS-like style selectors including pseudoclasses and child/descendant combinators; styles split into StyleInclude files instead of a 1000+ line App.axaml; DataGrid requires the separate Avalonia.Controls.DataGrid package plus its theme StyleInclude or it renders unstyled; TreeView uses TreeDataTemplate (HierarchicalDataTemplate does not exist in Avalonia); MVVM with ReactiveUI or CommunityToolkit.Mvvm ([ObservableProperty]), ObservableCollection for bound lists, ViewLocator convention resolution, and a Microsoft DI container built before any view is constructed; AutomationProperties.Name on icon-only controls and full keyboard navigation; Avalonia.Headless for CI UI tests; F12 DevTools for layout/binding inspection.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; every row links to the official Avalonia documentation at docs.avaloniaui.net.
- **Best for:** Desktop .NET apps only — no direct use for the web trade-site builds. The transferable ideas are the state-style discipline (named styles for pointerover/pressed/focus rather than ad-hoc effects) and the rule that only visible list rows should render.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0028⟧

## ⟦S0029⟧ stacks/html-tailwind.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 59-row lookup table of Tailwind CSS (4.3) utility-first build rules, same table format as S0026 — the stack this bank's single-file HTML builds actually use. Categories include Animation (4 rows), Z-Index (3), Layout (many, spread through the table), Images (5), Typography (6), Colors (6), Spacing (3), Forms (4), Responsive (3), Buttons (4), Cards (3), Accessibility (3), Performance (4), Plugins (2), Interactivity (1), Customization (1).
- **How it looks:** Applied well it produces the standard clean trade-site look with exact numbers: content held in a centred max-w-7xl container with px-4 / md:px-6 / lg:px-8 breathing room; cards as rounded-lg (or rounded-2xl) shadow-md panels with p-6 padding and space-y-4 inside, lifting to a bigger shadow on hover; images locked to aspect-video or aspect-square boxes with object-cover so galleries never distort or shove the page around while loading; body text at leading-relaxed (1.625 line height); headings balanced across lines with text-balance; buttons at px-4 py-2 or px-6 py-3 with a minimum 44px touch target (min-h-11 min-w-11) on mobile; overlays dimmed with bg-black/50; gradients written in the v4 bg-linear-to-r form; brand colours used as semantic tokens (bg-primary) declared once in @theme instead of raw palette classes everywhere; dark: variants available for a dark theme.
- **Frame by frame:** This table's own Animation/Interactivity rows describe the motion: (1) Hover/focus changes never snap — elements carry transition classes (typically transition-colors or transition-shadow) so a hover background or a card's shadow eases between states. (2) Built-in animate utilities supply the moving elements — animate-pulse, animate-spin, animate-ping — instead of hand-written keyframes for simple effects. (3) animate-bounce is rationed: sparing use only, and paired with motion-reduce:animate-none so it stops entirely for reduced-motion visitors. (4) All UI transitions run at duration-150 to duration-300 (150–300 ms); duration-1000 or longer on UI elements is explicitly banned. (5) Every animation/transition is cancelled for reduced-motion users via motion-reduce:animate-none / motion-reduce:transition-none. (6) Parent/sibling state styling (group-hover, peer-checked) replaces JavaScript for simple hover-driven changes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The fixed z-index scale z-0/10/20/30/40/50 only — z-50 for modals and fixed navigation, -z-10 for decorative backgrounds, never arbitrary z-[9999]; spacing strictly on the Tailwind scale (p-4 = 1rem, gap-4/6/8), arbitrary values like p-[15px] or text-[17px] banned in favour of the scale (text-sm/base/lg/xl); negative margins (-mt-8) reserved for deliberate card overlaps; mobile-first breakpoints (base styles, then md:/lg:/xl:), with testing required below, at and above each breakpoint up to 2xl; focus always visible — focus:ring-2 with ring-offset, focus:outline-none with no replacement is banned, focus-visible:ring-2 for keyboard-only rings; form inputs standardised at h-10 px-3, placeholders placeholder:text-gray-400, disabled at disabled:opacity-50 + disabled:cursor-not-allowed; long text handled with line-clamp-2/truncate, wrap-anywhere + min-w-0 so URLs cannot blow out a flex row; chips/labels as flex flex-wrap gap-2 with min-w-0 truncate labels and shrink-0 icons; square elements with size-* (size-6 etc.); SVGs given explicit width/height (24×24) to reserve space; Tailwind v4 specifics — classes auto-detected from source, @source only for ignored/external paths, class names must stay complete static tokens (bg-${color}-500 interpolation breaks detection), custom tokens via @theme { --color-primary: oklch(...) }, custom utilities via @utility, built-in @container queries with @lg: variants, prose/prose-lg from @tailwindcss/typography for article text, official plugins only (@tailwindcss/forms, @tailwindcss/typography). One row (JIT mode) is marked deprecated/legacy 3.x.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; most rows link to the official Tailwind CSS documentation at tailwindcss.com (including the v4.3 release blog for container queries). A few rows (hover transitions, negative z-index, responsive padding, flexbox alignment, input sizing, disabled/placeholder styling, button/card sizing, focus-visible) record no docs URL.
- **Best for:** The everyday rulebook for every section of a single-file HTML build — hero (container width, priority image space, balanced headings), work/gallery (aspect-ratio + object-cover discipline), proof/reviews (card structure and hover), forms (focus rings, input sizing, disabled/loading states, 44px targets), navigation (fixed bar stacking at z-50), and any CTA button. Check any Tailwind build against its Animation rows before adding custom keyframes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0029⟧

## ⟦S0030⟧ stacks/javafx.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 75-row lookup table of JavaFX 26 desktop-application rules — the largest table in this chunk — same format as S0026. Categories span Application, Threading (3 rows), FXML (4), CSS (3), Layout (4), Controls (5), Binding (3), Events (2), Accessibility (4), Validation (2), Dialogs (2), Images (2), Animation (2), Performance (3), Architecture (4), Modules, Packaging, Testing (2), Theme (8), Icons, Components (2), Navigation (2), Workflow, TableView (3), Forms (2), Tasks (2), Audit, Configuration, Deployment (2), Dependencies.
- **How it looks:** It describes a dense enterprise desktop app: a BorderPane shell with toolbar on top, navigation at the left and a central workspace; high-density data tables with compact rows, sorting, filtering and a selection summary; long forms broken into titled sections (TitledPane) with a validation summary at the top plus an error marker beside each bad field; status shown as semantic badges and row styles (e.g. a "blocked" row state) instead of cryptic one-letter codes; the AtlantaFX PrimerLight theme as the neutral default skin (PrimerDark for dark mode), brand colour layered on top as named looked-up colours (-app-primary #2563eb, -app-danger #dc2626), and consistent Ikonli font icons instead of emoji. Subtle shadow is rationed — one specified drop shadow for dialog cards: dropshadow(gaussian, rgba(0,0,0,.18), 16, 0, 0, 4) — and banned on ordinary table rows.
- **Frame by frame:** Deliberately restrained: the Animation rows cap desktop transitions at 150–250 ms (worked example: a FadeTransition of 180 ms fading a pane to opacity 1) for reveal, hover and selection changes, forbid multi-second timelines (a 2-second Timeline is the named bad example), and require a reduced-motion setting that skips decorative animation and sets final state directly. Background work shows motion as feedback: a ProgressBar and status label bound live to a background Task's progress/message properties rather than polling. Navigation swaps the shell's centre content instead of rebuilding the window, so there is no flicker.
- **Mechanism & key values:** All UI mutation on the FX Application Thread, background work in Task/Service with results delivered via bindings or Platform.runLater; FXML for declarative layout with @FXML fx:id injection and fail-fast loading; layout by constraints (BorderPane shell, GridPane forms, hgrow/vgrow, percent column widths) — hard-coded pixel positions are the named anti-pattern; spacing via shared constants (example form: hgap 12, vgap 10, padding Insets 16); controls backed by ObservableList, TableView/ListView virtualization for hundreds of rows, explicit placeholder nodes for empty tables; property binding for derived UI state (e.g. a save button's disabled state bound to form validity); TextFormatter filters that reject invalid characters as typed; modular apps declaring requires javafx.controls/javafx.fxml and opening controller packages; delivery via jlink/jpackage so users never install Java themselves; theming centralised in a ThemeService; workflow actions logged through services (user, action, entity, result, timestamp) for audit.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; rows link to the official OpenJFX javadoc (openjfx.io), the AtlantaFX documentation (mkpaz.github.io), Ikonli (kordamp.org), ControlsFX, TestFX on GitHub, and the WCAG 2.2 contrast guidance (w3.org) for the status-colour contrast row.
- **Best for:** Enterprise desktop Java applications only — no direct use for web builds. The portable lessons are the density/validation/table conventions if a trades business ever needs an internal desktop tool, and the 150–250 ms animation ceiling as a sanity check on UI motion generally.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0030⟧

## ⟦S0031⟧ stacks/laravel.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 50-row lookup table of Laravel 13.x front-end build rules, same format as S0026, covering the three Laravel UI stacks. Categories: Blade Templates (8 rows), Livewire (8), Inertia.js (6), Styling (5), Components (6), Forms (6), Performance (5), Security (5).
- **How it looks:** It shapes a server-rendered site with SPA manners: pages share one master layout (header/footer defined once via @extends/@section), reusable pieces — cards, badges, modals with named header slots — render identically everywhere as x-* components; forms keep the visitor's typed input after a failed submit (old() repopulation) and put a red per-field error message under the exact field that failed (@error, text-red-500) instead of a dump of errors at the top; a flash success banner appears in the layout after actions; Livewire buttons disable themselves and show loading state while a server action runs (wire:loading), and Alpine.js handles purely local behaviour like opening a dropdown with x-data/x-show/x-transition; on Inertia pages the header and sidebar never remount between navigations (persistent layouts), so moving around feels instant rather than a full page reload.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no prescribed animation durations or easings. The only motion-adjacent behaviour named is Alpine x-transition availability for local show/hide elements, and Livewire/Inertia's no-full-reload navigation feel; no values are given for either.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Blade components with @props defaults documenting each component's API, @class for conditional classes, {{ }} escaping for all dynamic text ({!! !!} never on user data), @vite for asset loading with HMR/cache-busting; Livewire wire:model binding, wire:model.live + #[Validate] for validate-as-you-type, wire:click actions, mount()/updated() lifecycle discipline, lazy attribute for heavy components, WithFileUploads for uploads; Inertia Inertia::render() page endpoints, global auth/flash shared once in HandleInertiaRequests middleware, <Link> for internal navigation, useForm for form state, optional SSR for public pages; Tailwind via the Vite plugin with content scanning of Blade/JS files (no content config = shipping ~3MB of CSS is the named failure), class-strategy dark mode, @theme brand tokens (--color-brand: oklch(0.6 0.2 250) is the worked example), @apply only for genuinely repeated patterns; forms validated in FormRequest classes (make:request), @csrf in every mutating form, @method('PUT') spoofing; performance — eager-load relations with with() to kill N+1 queries, paginate lists (paginate(20) is the example), queue anything over 200 ms, cache slow partials (sidebar cached 3600 s in the example), Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 for static pages; security — @can/Gate policies instead of inline role checks, upload validation (image, mimes:jpg,png, max:2048) stored outside the public root, signed URLs expiring in 30 minutes for private downloads, a strict CSP header (default-src 'self'; script-src 'self').
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; rows link to the official Laravel documentation (laravel.com/docs), the Livewire documentation (livewire.laravel.com), Inertia (inertiajs.com) and Tailwind CSS docs.
- **Best for:** Only relevant if a project is a Laravel app — e.g. a trade firm's booking/quote portal: its Forms rows are a solid checklist for a quote-request form (per-field errors, old input preserved, CSRF, flash confirmation), and the Livewire loading-state rows for any form that submits to a server. Not applicable to the static single-file HTML builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0031⟧

## ⟦S0032⟧ stacks/nextjs.csv — Part 03B, UI/UX Pro Max lookup databases (stack guidelines)
- **What it is:** A 61-row lookup table (60 active rows plus closing legacy/migration rows) of Next.js 16.2 build rules, same format as S0026. Categories: Routing (6 rows), Rendering (5), DataFetching (5), Images (5), Fonts (3), Metadata (3), API (4), Middleware/Proxy (5), Environment (3), Performance (4), Link (3), Config (3), Deployment (2), Security (3), Caching (6).
- **How it looks:** It produces a React site that paints fast and never jumps: the hero image is marked priority and given explicit width/height (or fill inside a sized parent) so text does not shift when it lands; slow parts of a page stream in behind Suspense boundaries with skeleton placeholders (an h-48 skeleton is the worked example) while the static shell is already on screen; fonts are self-hosted through next/font so there is no external-font flash or layout shift; internal navigation is client-side via <Link> with prefetching, so moving between service pages feels instant; route-level loading.tsx and error.tsx (with a reset) mean a slow or failed page shows a designed loading/error state instead of a blank screen; social shares carry proper OpenGraph images.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion design, durations or easings are prescribed. The described behaviour is loading choreography only: navigate → static shell renders immediately → suspended sections show skeletons → each section replaces its skeleton as its data resolves → end state is the complete page with no layout shift.
- **Mechanism & key values:** App Router with file-based routing (page.tsx/layout.tsx, [slug] dynamics, (group) folders that do not affect the URL, colocated _components); Server Components by default, 'use client' pushed down to leaf interactive components only; rendering chosen per route (SSG / ISR with `export const revalidate = 3600` as the example / Partial Prerendering's static shell + Suspense holes); data fetched with await directly in async Server Components, request deduplication automatic; the Next.js 16 cache model is explicit — Cache Components enabled with cacheComponents: true, 'use cache' directive at file/component/function scope, cacheLife profiles (cacheLife('days') is the example), cacheTag for targeted invalidation, updateTag after Server Action mutations for immediate read-your-own-writes, and revalidateTag(tag, 'max') for stale-while-revalidate (the one-argument form is deprecated); Server Actions for mutations with mandatory input validation + authorization (they are public endpoints); middleware renamed to proxy.ts in v16 (export function proxy, nodejs runtime, path matchers like ['/dashboard/:path*']) — middleware.ts and export function middleware are legacy/deprecated; next/image for all images with remotePatterns whitelisting (never domains: ['*']); NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix for client env vars, validated at startup; reactStrictMode: true; dynamic() imports for heavy components and @next/bundle-analyzer (ANALYZE=true) for bundle checks; output: 'standalone' for Docker self-hosting; CSP headers configured in next.config.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; rows link to the official Next.js documentation (nextjs.org/docs) and the Next.js 16 release notes (nextjs.org/blog/next-16) for the Cache Components and proxy changes. A few rows (route colocation, fetch deduplication, priority images, font application, OpenGraph, API responses, strict mode, prefetch/scroll options) record no docs URL.
- **Best for:** Only if a build is a Next.js/React site. The transferable rows for content sites: priority + dimensioned hero images, skeleton/streaming discipline for slow sections, self-hosted fonts to kill layout shift, metadata/OpenGraph setup for local service pages, and the explicit-cache rules if pages mix static marketing content with dynamic data.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0032⟧
## ⟦S0033⟧ stacks/nuxt-ui.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 76-row guideline table for building with Nuxt UI v4 (the Vue/Nuxt component library), one row per rule with Category, Guideline, Description, Do, Don't, good/bad code, Severity, Docs URL and Applies To. Categories: Installation, Components, Icons, Theming, Forms, Overlays, Dashboard, Tables, Navigation, Feedback, Color Mode, Customization, Performance, Accessibility, Content, AI/Chat, Editor, Links, Loading, Data, Layout, Composables, i18n, Motion, Security.
- **How it looks:** The table is a selection menu for a complete Nuxt UI interface: U-prefixed components (UButton, UInput, UModal, UTable, UTabs) styled by meaning-based colour props (primary, success, error) and built-in variants (solid, outline, soft, subtle, ghost, link), in five steps of size (xs, sm, md, lg, xl). Following it produces dashboard shells with a collapsible resizable sidebar and top navbar, data tables powered by TanStack Table, form fields with labels and error text under them, modal/slideover/drawer overlays with real title-and-description headers, toast notifications, skeleton placeholder bars while data loads, and a light/dark colour-mode toggle — all themed from one runtime config instead of per-component colour classes.
- **Frame by frame:** Mostly static data — but two rows describe actual motion the builder can select. (1) UMarquee (row 60): a band of logos or testimonials scrolls sideways in an endless loop; the content repeats (repeat prop, example value 3) and the band pauses while the pointer hovers it (pauseOnHover). (2) Motion row 74: all of the library's enter, exit and movement transitions are retimed at once by overriding a single theme token, `--ease-out`, so overlays and moving elements across the whole app share one easing curve.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Applies to nuxt-ui 4.11.1. Custom palettes must define every shade 50 through 950 in `@theme static`; motion token example `--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`; form validation defaults to the `['blur', 'change']` events via `validateOn`, with `eager` as the opt-in; icons use the Iconify `i-{collection}-{name}` format (e.g. `i-lucide-home`) and the collections must be installed locally for SSR; overlays are controlled with `v-model:open` or the `useOverlay` `create().open()` API (which returns a promise for confirmation results); large tables take the `virtualize` prop; component detection (`experimental.componentDetection`) generates CSS only for used components; CommandPalette XSS fix requires Nuxt UI 4.11+ (row 76, High severity).
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; every row carries its own Docs URL to ui.nuxt.com (e.g. https://ui.nuxt.com/docs/components/button, https://ui.nuxt.com/docs/getting-started/theme/design-system#motion). All rows verified 2026-09-21, status active.
- **Best for:** Any Nuxt/Vue build — dashboards, docs/content sites (UContentToc, UContentSearch), forms, tables, chat UI (UChatMessages/UChatPrompt), and page layout (UHeader/UFooter). Little direct use for the single-file HTML trade previews, but the marquee, skeleton, toast and overlay patterns are the reference when a Vue/Nuxt stack is chosen.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0033⟧

## ⟦S0034⟧ stacks/nuxtjs.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 67-row guideline table for the Nuxt 4 framework itself (no component library): Routing, Rendering, DataFetching, Lifecycle, Server, State, SEO, Middleware, ErrorHandling, Link, AutoImports, Plugins, Environment, Performance, Configuration and Migration — each row with Do/Don't, good/bad code, severity and a nuxt.com docs link. Applies to nuxtjs 4.5.
- **How it looks:** The table lets a builder assemble a server-rendered Vue site whose pages arrive as finished HTML: file-based routes from an `app/pages` folder (including `[id].vue` dynamic pages and `[...slug].vue` catch-alls), social-share previews set through `useSeoMeta` OpenGraph tags, internal links that prefetch and swap pages without a full reload, loading and error states shown while data is pending, and below-fold sections that hydrate late instead of blocking the first paint. What the visitor sees is a fast SSR site with correct meta previews and no blank loading screens on primary content.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The data governs structure, data flow and rendering order, not animation (the only time value in the table is a caching example, `routeRules: { '/blog/**': { isr: 3600 } }` — a one-hour incremental-static-regeneration window).
- **Mechanism & key values:** SSR on by default (`ssr: true`); `.client.vue` / `.server.vue` suffixes split rendering; `useFetch` for URL data, `useAsyncData` for custom sources, `$fetch` only inside event handlers and server routes; `lazy: true` / `useLazyFetch` and `Lazy` component prefix plus `hydrate-on-visible` for deferred interactivity; `pick`/`transform` to shrink payloads; `useState` only for serializable values under unique keys, Pinia for complex state; `runtimeConfig` split into private root keys and `public`, with every key declared before a `NUXT_` environment override can fill it; `useCookie` with `sameSite: 'lax', secure: true`; errors via `createError` with short generic `statusMessage`; link prefetch tunable with `prefetch-on="interaction"`; Nuxt 3 is end-of-life — row 67 (deprecated) says migrate with `future: { compatibilityVersion: 4 }`.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to nuxt.com/docs/4.x (e.g. https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/getting-started/routing, https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/api/composables/use-fetch). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** Scaffolding any Nuxt 4 site or app — page structure, SEO head management, API routes under `server/api`, auth middleware, and performance work (lazy hydration, payload trimming). Framework plumbing only; it prescribes no visual design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0034⟧

## ⟦S0035⟧ stacks/react.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 66-row guideline table for React 19.2.x: State, Effects, Rendering, Components, Props, Events, Forms, Hooks, Context, Performance, ErrorHandling, Testing, Accessibility, TypeScript, Patterns, Tooling, Concurrency and Security — each row a rule with Do/Don't, good/bad code, severity and a react.dev link.
- **How it looks:** The table is how a builder keeps a React interface feeling instant and correct: lists longer than 100 items windowed instead of thousands of DOM nodes, search boxes that stay responsive because filtering is deferred (`useDeferredValue`), forms that submit through Actions with a pending state on the button (`useFormStatus` in a child of the form), optimistic UI that shows the expected result while the save runs (`useOptimistic`, only inside an Action), error boundaries that contain a crash to one section instead of blanking the app, real `<button>`/`<nav>` elements with labels tied to inputs and `aria-live` regions announcing updates.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The rows govern rendering behaviour, responsiveness and state timing (batched updates, transitions via `startTransition`), not visual animation.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Compiler-first memoization — enable React Compiler and keep `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`React.memo` only for measured hotspots; hooks only at top level; custom hooks named with the `use` prefix; `ref` passed as a normal prop — `forwardRef` is deprecated in React 19 (row 59, legacy); `useEffectEvent` for non-reactive effect logic; `use()` only with cached/stable promises; lazy initial state `useState(() => …)`; `flushSync` is a rare escape hatch, not a batching tool; security floor: React 19.2.1+ on any React Server Components path (row 60, Critical — 19.2.0 had an unauthenticated RCE); lint via eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended preset (the old eslint-plugin-react-compiler package is legacy).
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs mostly to react.dev (e.g. https://react.dev/reference/react/useState, https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/07/react-compiler-1) and testing-library.com. Verified 2026-08-13, with Forms/Hooks rows re-verified 2026-09-21.
- **Best for:** Any React or Next.js build — component structure, form handling, list performance, accessibility checks. It is the correctness layer under a React implementation, not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0035⟧

## ⟦S0036⟧ stacks/shadcn.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 68-row guideline table for shadcn/ui on CLI v4: Setup, Theming, Components, Dialog, Sheet, Form, Select, Command, Table, DataTable, Tabs, Accordion, Toast, Popover, DropdownMenu, Tooltip, Skeleton, AlertDialog, Sidebar, Chart, Blocks, A11y, Performance, Customization, Patterns and Registry — each row with Do/Don't, code, severity and a ui.shadcn.com docs link.
- **How it looks:** Selecting from this table produces the shadcn look: components copied into your own codebase and styled with semantic OKLCH CSS variables, so a button is `primary` with a paired `primary-foreground` text colour in both light and dark schemes; dialog boxes with a proper header (title + description) and trapped focus; slide-in side sheets for filters and settings; tab bars and one-open-at-a-time accordions for FAQ-style content; Sonner toast notifications stacked from the root layout; skeleton bars exactly the size of the content they replace; sidebar app shells with a mobile trigger; charts themed from one `chartConfig` object instead of inline hex fills.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The data specifies component choice and structure (which control opens, slides or expands is named — Dialog, Sheet, Accordion, Popover — but no durations, easings or keyframes are given anywhere in the table).
- **Mechanism & key values:** CLI v4 workflow — `npx shadcn@latest init` first (sets up components.json and globals.css, with an explicit `--base`: Base UI is the new-project default, Radix and React Aria are the other bases), then `npx shadcn@latest add <component>`; inspect before writing with `--dry-run` / `--diff`; theming via `:root` and `.dark` semantic OKLCH variables exposed to Tailwind v4 through `@theme inline` (dark background example `--background: oklch(0.145 0 0)` — legacy space-separated HSL snippets are explicitly wrong); variants via cva (`variant`, `size` props), overrides via `className`, never by editing sizing into the component source; forms use React Hook Form `Controller` or TanStack Form field adapters with the `Field`/`FieldLabel`/`FieldError` primitives and Standard Schema validators such as Zod; composition differs per base — Radix uses `asChild`, Base UI uses the `render` prop, React Aria keeps real anchors styled with `buttonVariants()`; registries are namespaced in components.json (`registry:base`, `registry:font`, `registry:ui` item types) and public GitHub registries install as `owner/repo/item`; prebuilt layouts come from blocks (`npx shadcn@latest add dashboard-01`, `login-01`).
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to ui.shadcn.com (e.g. https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming, https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/components/dialog, https://ui.shadcn.com/blocks). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** React/Next.js product UI — dashboards, settings, data tables, forms, command palettes, FAQ accordions and dialogs. For the trade-site previews it is a component-pattern reference (accordion FAQ, sheet, dialog) rather than a stack we ship.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0036⟧

## ⟦S0037⟧ stacks/svelte.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 55-row guideline table for Svelte 5 (runes mode) with the Svelte ≤4 legacy rules kept alongside and marked deprecated: Reactivity, Props, Bindings, Events, Lifecycle, Stores, Slots, Styling, Transitions, Actions, Logic, SvelteKit, Performance, TypeScript and Accessibility — each row with Do/Don't, code, severity and a svelte.dev link.
- **How it looks:** The table steers a builder to a Svelte interface whose updates are fine-grained: values declared with `$state` re-render exactly the text or attribute that uses them, `$derived` values recompute on their own, lists render through keyed `{#each}` blocks so rows keep their identity when the list changes, async content swaps between the `{#await}` block's loading, success and error branches, and forms use two-way `bind:value` so the input and the data never disagree. Styling stays scoped to the component that declares it, with CSS custom properties passed in for theming.
- **Frame by frame:** The data does describe motion — Svelte's built-in transition directives (rows 31–33). An element entering with `in:fly` and leaving with `out:fade` plays two different animations: it flies in on mount, then only fades when removed; `transition:fade` (or slide) plays the same effect both ways. Adding the `|local` modifier (e.g. `transition:slide|local`) stops a parent change from retriggering the transitions of everything inside it — important in lists. No durations or easings are specified in the table; the directive names and modifiers are the prescribed values.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Runes are the current contract — `let count = $state(0)`, `$derived(...)` for computed values, `$effect` only for external side effects (never for derived state), `let { name } = $props()` with destructured defaults, event handlers as plain properties (`onclick={...}`), snippets (`{@render children()}`) instead of slots; legacy `$:`, `export let`, `on:` directives, `createEventDispatcher`, `$$slots`/`$$restProps` and `$app/stores` are all marked deprecated and kept only for maintaining ≤4 code; stores remain `writable`/`readable`/`derived` with `$`-prefix auto-subscription and mandatory unsubscribe cleanup; SvelteKit conventions: `+page.svelte` routes, `load` in `+page.js`, secrets only in `+page.server.js`, server form actions, app state from `$app/state` (not `$app/stores`); `{#key}` forces a fresh component instance; TypeScript via `<script lang="ts">` and an `interface Props` on `$props`.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to svelte.dev and kit.svelte.dev (e.g. https://svelte.dev/docs/element-directives#transition-fn, https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/$props). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** Any Svelte/SvelteKit build — reactive components, route data loading, form actions. Its transition-directive rows are also the quick reference for how Svelte's fly/fade/slide enter-exit pairs behave when a Svelte stack is chosen.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0037⟧

## ⟦S0038⟧ stacks/threejs.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 53-row guideline table for Three.js 0.185.1 — the most motion-heavy table in this range: Setup, Camera, Geometry, Materials, Lighting, Raycasting, Animation, GSAP, Performance, Particles, Responsive, Accessibility and Production, each row with detailed Do/Don't, full good/bad code, severity (many Critical) and a threejs.org docs link. It is effectively a checklist for a WebGL scene that renders correctly and stays at 60fps.
- **How it looks:** Followed properly, the table produces a transparent WebGL canvas (`alpha: true`, clear colour alpha 0) composited over the page's own CSS background, holding a lit 3D scene: PBR objects shaded by an ambient fill plus a directional key light with real shadows (2048px shadow map), exponential fog dissolving distant objects into the background colour, thousands of points-based particles drifting, and a camera the visitor can drag to orbit — or that glides along a fixed path as they scroll. Interactive objects answer the pointer: hover raycasts once per frame and the cursor switches to a pointer over anything clickable.
- **Frame by frame:** The Animation and GSAP rows specify the motion system step by step. (1) The render loop runs only on `requestAnimationFrame`/`renderer.setAnimationLoop` — never `setInterval` — and pauses entirely when the tab hides (`setAnimationLoop(null)` on `visibilitychange`). (2) Each frame starts with one `timer.update(timestamp)` call (THREE.Timer; THREE.Clock is deprecated since r183); `dt = timer.getDelta()` is read once and reused, so a spin written as `rotation.y += dt * 0.8` runs at the same speed on 60Hz and 120Hz screens. (3) Pointer follow is a per-frame lerp, `value += (target - value) * alpha` with alpha 0.03–0.1 — the camera eases after the mouse instead of snapping. (4) Dragging orbits in spherical coordinates (theta/phi, drag sensitivity 0.005, phi clamped 0.1 to π−0.1) so vertical drag works; moving `camera.position.x` directly is called out as the classic broken version. (5) Scroll-driven scenes tween camera properties with GSAP ScrollTrigger at `scrub: 1` — the camera trails the scroll position with a 1-second lag instead of snapping at thresholds. (6) Particles mutate their Float32Array positions per frame (example: `pos[i+1] += Math.sin(t + i) * 0.001`) and only move on screen because `needsUpdate = true` re-uploads the buffer. (7) If `prefers-reduced-motion` is set — checked live via a MediaQueryList `change` listener, not a one-time read — all auto-rotation, particle and camera motion is gated off.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pin `three@0.185.1` on npm (or an exact-version import map; core and `three/addons/` on the same release); one WebGLRenderer per page (browsers allow only 8–16 GPU contexts); `renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2))`; camera FOV 45–75 — 75 for general interactive scenes, 45–55 for product close-ups — with aspect + `updateProjectionMatrix()` on every resize, sized from `canvas.clientWidth/clientHeight` (ResizeObserver on the container, not window resize); geometry created once, shared across meshes, disposed explicitly with its material and textures; segment budget: hero objects 32–64, background 8–16, particle stand-ins 6–8; MeshBasicMaterial (no lights) for flat/UI elements, MeshStandardMaterial only where light should land, with `renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true` set before any `castShadow`, selective shadows on hero meshes and ground only; one shared Raycaster, mouse stored in NDC (`x = (clientX/width)*2−1`, `y = −(clientY/height)*2+1` — Y negated), `intersectObjects(targets, true)`; InstancedMesh at 50+ identical objects; particles as BufferGeometry + Points, starting count 1,000–3,000, frame drops beyond 50,000 on mid-range mobile; `THREE.LOD` detail swaps at 0 / 15 / 50 units; FogExp2 example density 0.02 for view distances over 100 units; output `SRGBColorSpace` with `ACESFilmicToneMapping`, exposure 1.0; GSAP loaded separately (CDN 3.12.2 example) and `gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger)` before any scrollTrigger config; canvas gets `role="img"` and a descriptive aria-label; touch handlers mirror mouse with `{ passive: false }`.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to threejs.org docs/manual, gsap.com and MDN (e.g. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/renderers/WebGLRenderer, https://threejs.org/manual/en/color-management.html). Verified 2026-08-13, with the Timer/shadow rows re-verified 2026-09-26.
- **Best for:** Any 3D/WebGL section — product viewers, orbitable models, particle fields, scroll-driven camera reveals in heroes. This is the correctness-and-performance gate to run before shipping a Three.js scene on any page, trade sites included (e.g. a rotating roof/product visual), because most rows are Critical-severity failure preventions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0038⟧

## ⟦S0039⟧ stacks/uno.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 59-row guideline table for Uno Platform — building one C#/XAML codebase on the WinUI 3 API surface (Uno.WinUI via Uno.Sdk) that runs on iOS, Android, WebAssembly, and desktop (Windows/macOS/Linux). Categories: XAML, Conditional (platform code), Navigation, Renderers, Performance, Data Binding, Styling, Architecture, Accessibility, Testing, WASM, Controls, Lifecycle. Native desktop-app technology, not web design.
- **How it looks:** What the table lets a builder produce is one Fluent-styled app rendered everywhere: a NavigationView shell (side menu of items with icons), CommandBar toolbars of icon-plus-label AppBarButtons, ContentDialog modal confirmations, ToggleSwitch rows for settings, and theme brushes that follow light/dark automatically — drawn by the Skia renderer so the same pixels appear on every platform, or by native controls where a target uses them. On WASM the first paint is a branded splash overlay in index.html instead of a blank white page while the runtime boots.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The rows cover structure, binding, rendering targets and lifecycle; no animations, durations or easings are specified.
- **Mechanism & key values:** New projects use `Uno.Sdk` with features declared once (`<UnoFeatures>Material;Hosting;Toolkit;Logging;MVVM</UnoFeatures>`) instead of hand-matched PackageReferences; `Microsoft.UI.Xaml` namespaces only (Uno.WinUI, not the legacy Uno.UI/UWP surface); targets `net10.0-desktop` (single Skia shell, Uno 5.2+) and `net10.0-browserwasm`; platform code isolated behind `#if __IOS__ / __ANDROID__ / __WASM__ / __DESKTOP__` partial classes and interfaces; compiled `x:Bind` preferred over `{Binding}`; `XamlControlsResources` must be merged in App.xaml or Fluent controls render unstyled; leave `Application.RequestedTheme` unset to follow the system (`"Default"` is not a valid value and throws); theme variants via `ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries` keyed Light/Dark/HighContrast (example brand brush `#005A9E` light, `#3A96DD` dark); WASM needs the IL linker, AOT (`InterpreterAndAOT`) and an extended splash; `PublishAot` only in a TFM-and-Release-conditional PropertyGroup for net10.0-desktop; never block on `.Result`/`.Wait()` (deadlocks the UI thread) — async `[RelayCommand]`s disable their control while running; UI updates from background work go through `DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue`; desktop apps save state on `Window.Closed` because `Application.Suspending` never fires there; `SystemNavigationManager.GetForCurrentView()` crashes on WinAppSDK desktop — guard BackRequested by platform.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to platform.uno docs and learn.microsoft.com (e.g. https://platform.uno/docs/articles/features/using-skia-desktop.html, https://platform.uno/docs/articles/features/working-with-xaml-hot-reload.html). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** Cross-platform .NET app development only — one codebase shipping native apps plus a WASM web version. No use for the HTML trade-site builds; indexed because it sits in the same stack-database series.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0039⟧

## ⟦S0040⟧ stacks/uwp.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 55-row guideline table for UWP (Universal Windows Platform) XAML apps — and every row is marked deprecated: UWP is maintenance-only and the table itself directs new work to WinUI 3 / Windows App SDK. Categories: XAML, Controls, Styling, Navigation, Data Binding, Performance, Threading, Adaptive, Accessibility, Architecture, Lifecycle, Testing. Kept in the bank as the legacy reference for maintaining existing UWP apps.
- **How it looks:** The table describes the classic Windows 10 app surface: a NavigationView hamburger shell, CommandBar app bars, ContentDialog system dialogs, AutoSuggestBox search with a suggestion dropdown, PersonPicture circular avatars with initial fallbacks, acrylic translucent panels (Fluent material) floating over the window, and layouts that reflow between phone, tablet, desktop, Xbox and HoloLens forms. ThemeResource brushes mean the same screen restyles itself under light, dark and contrast themes without hardcoded hex.
- **Frame by frame:** One row describes real motion: ConnectedAnimation (Navigation, row 20) — when the user taps an item in a list, that item's image is prepared with `ConnectedAnimationService.GetForCurrentView().PrepareToAnimate("image", sourceImage)` before navigation, and on the detail page the same image animates continuously from its list position and size into its place in the new layout instead of the page cutting abruptly. The rest of the table is static data — no other durations or easings are specified.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Compiled `x:Bind` throughout (and `Mode` must be stated — x:Bind defaults to OneTime, not OneWay); `x:Load=False` defers hidden panels; `x:Phase` renders list-item templates in priority phases; AdaptiveTrigger breakpoints are MinWindowWidth 640 (small) and 1008 (medium) inside VisualStateManager state groups; ListView/GridView virtualize by default (a non-virtualizing ItemsPanel silently kills it), `ISupportIncrementalLoading` loads more as the user scrolls; all IO async/await with `CoreDispatcher` for UI-thread access and `IProgress<T>` for progress; suspend saves state with `SuspendingOperation.GetDeferral()` because the OS grants only about 5 seconds before termination; prelaunch opt-in via `CoreApplication.EnablePrelaunch(true)` (Windows 10 1607+) with heavy init skipped when `PrelaunchActivated`; accessibility via AutomationProperties.Name, XYFocus keyboard/gamepad navigation, Accessibility Insights FastPass; UI tests via WinAppDriver/Appium 2 (Coded UI Test deprecated in VS2019; WinAppDriver v1 in low-maintenance mode).
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to learn.microsoft.com windows/uwp docs (e.g. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/uwp/design/motion/connected-animation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/uwp/design/layout/screen-sizes-and-breakpoints-for-responsive-design). Verified 2026-08-13; Applies To "uwp legacy", status deprecated on all rows.
- **Best for:** Maintaining legacy UWP apps and planning their migration to WinUI 3 (rows 53–54). Not a source for new builds or for any web work.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0040⟧

## ⟦S0041⟧ stacks/vue.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 49-row guideline table for Vue 3.5.x with the Composition API: Composition, Reactivity, Watchers, Props, Emits, Lifecycle, Components, Composables, Templates, State, Routing, Performance, TypeScript, Testing, Forms and Accessibility — each row with Do/Don't, good/bad code, severity and a vuejs.org link.
- **How it looks:** The table steers a builder toward a Vue interface that updates precisely: `ref` for single values and `reactive` for object state, `computed` values that cache and refresh themselves, two-way `v-model` bindings (with `.lazy`, `.number`, `.trim` modifiers doing the parsing) so inputs and data stay in step, lists keyed with `:key="item.id"` so rows reorder without losing their internal state, async components and lazy routes so heavy modals and pages load only when opened, and browser-only widgets wrapped in `<ClientOnly>` so the server and client markup match and nothing flickers or jumps on hydration.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The rows govern reactivity, rendering and loading behaviour; no animations, durations or easings are specified.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<script setup>` is the default component form; `defineProps`/`defineEmits` typed in TypeScript, `withDefaults` for optional props, props never mutated — changes go up via `emit('update:modelValue', …)`; `shallowRef`/`shallowReactive` for large or flat data to skip deep reactivity; watchers return cleanup (`onCleanup`) and unmount removes listeners in `onUnmounted`; composables named `useX`, return refs (not reactive objects that lose reactivity when destructured), and accept ref-or-value inputs via `toValue()`; never put `v-if` on the same element as `v-for` (v-if wins and breaks); Pinia is the state library (setup stores via `defineStore`, destructure only through `storeToRefs`); `v-once` for never-changing content, `v-memo="[item.id]"` for expensive lists, `defineAsyncComponent` for heavy components; template refs typed (`ref<HTMLInputElement>(null)`), complex props via `PropType<User>`, generic SFCs with `generic="T"`; forms validated with VeeValidate/FormKit rather than hand-rolled logic; SSR through Nuxt, with hydration mismatches treated as High severity.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to vuejs.org, pinia.vuejs.org, router.vuejs.org and test-utils.vuejs.org (e.g. https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/reactivity-fundamentals.html, https://pinia.vuejs.org/core-concepts/#destructuring-from-a-store). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** Any Vue 3 build — component structure, state, routing, forms and SSR hygiene. The plain-Vue counterpart to the Nuxt tables (S0033/S0034); correctness guidance, not visual design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0041⟧

## ⟦S0042⟧ stacks/winui.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 59-row guideline table for current WinUI 3 desktop apps on the Windows App SDK: XAML, Controls, Styling, Navigation, Data Binding, Performance, Threading, Packaging, Accessibility, Architecture, Testing and Lifecycle — each row with Do/Don't, code, severity and a learn.microsoft.com link. This is the current-platform successor to the deprecated UWP table (S0040).
- **How it looks:** Selecting from this table produces a modern Windows app: a NavigationView shell with left/top/compact pane modes and footer items, InfoBar status strips (success/warning/error) instead of home-made coloured panels, TeachingTip bubbles anchored to a control for onboarding, BreadcrumbBar paths for hierarchical screens, NumberBox fields with inline spin buttons, Expander sections that open to reveal settings groups, and Fluent surfaces chosen by lifetime — Mica texture on the long-lived main window, Acrylic blur on transient flyouts — with a custom title bar whose content extends into the window chrome while the caption buttons keep working.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The rows name controls that open, expand or slide (Expander, TeachingTip, flyouts) but prescribe no durations, easings or keyframes anywhere.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Compiled `x:Bind` everywhere it fits (Mode stated explicitly — default is OneTime), including inside DataTemplates with `x:DataType`; `x:Load=False` defers hidden panels; `x:Phase` staggers list-item rendering; responsive layout via VisualStateManager AdaptiveTrigger (example `MinWindowWidth="720"` moving a sidebar from hidden to visible); back navigation through `NavigationView.BackRequested` (not UWP's SystemNavigationManager); UI-thread work via `DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue` (not CoreDispatcher); theme via ThemeResource brushes (`TextFillColorPrimaryBrush`, `CardBackgroundFillColorDefaultBrush`) so light/dark/high-contrast all hold; backdrops set directly with `Window.SystemBackdrop` (`<MicaBackdrop Kind="Base"/>`, WinUI 3 1.3+) instead of hand-wired MicaController code; `ExtendsContentIntoTitleBar = true` plus `SetTitleBar(element)` for custom chrome; packaging through the `Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK` package with single-project MSIX (`<EnableMsixTooling>true</EnableMsixTooling>`); MVVM with CommunityToolkit `[ObservableProperty]`/`[RelayCommand]`, AsyncRelayCommand exposing `IsRunning` and cancellation for IO; single-instancing via `AppInstance.FindOrRegisterForKey`; KeyboardAccelerator (e.g. Ctrl+S) instead of manual KeyDown switches; Accessibility Insights FastPass per page.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to learn.microsoft.com windows/apps docs (e.g. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/develop/ui/controls/navigationview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/signature-experiences/materials). Verified 2026-08-13; Applies To "winui current windows app sdk", all rows active.
- **Best for:** New Windows desktop apps (WinUI 3) and UWP migrations. Native-app guidance only — no direct use for the web/trade-site builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0042⟧

## ⟦S0043⟧ stacks/wpf.csv — PART 03B — UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup databases
- **What it is:** A 56-row guideline table for WPF (Windows Presentation Foundation) desktop development: XAML, Data Binding, Layout, Styling, Commands, Performance, Threading, Accessibility, Architecture and Testing — each row with Do/Don't, good/bad code, severity and a learn.microsoft.com link. Applies to "wpf current".
- **How it looks:** The table steers a builder to declarative XAML windows instead of code-built UI trees: Grid layouts with proportional star-sized columns (a `2*` main column rather than a fixed 350px one), DockPanel shells with the menu docked top, sidebar left and the last child filling the rest, long forms wrapped in a ScrollViewer instead of clipping, one implicit Button style (padding `12,6` in the example) restyling every button at once, and named BasedOn style variants (a PrimaryButton) instead of ten copied setters. On .NET 9+ the whole app can take the Windows 11 Fluent look through a single `ThemeMode="System"` instead of the legacy Aero2 theme.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Layout, binding, command and threading rules only; no animations, durations or easings are specified anywhere in the table.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Root elements carry `x:Class`; `x:Name` only on elements code-behind actually touches; layout via attached properties (`Grid.Row`, `DockPanel.Dock`) instead of margin arithmetic; routed events handled once at a parent (`Button.Click="OnAnyButtonClick"` on a StackPanel) with `e.Handled = true`; binding sources implement INotifyPropertyChanged, lists use ObservableCollection, `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged` for search-as-you-type, validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo/ObservableValidator with DataAnnotations instead of error-string properties; resources centralized in App.xaml dictionaries (example `PrimaryBrush` `#0078D4`), StaticResource preferred over DynamicResource, embedded assets via `pack://application:,,,` URIs; actions are ICommands — RelayCommand/AsyncRelayCommand from CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, `CanExecute` driving the disabled state, `CommandParameter` for item context, Ctrl+S via `Window.InputBindings` KeyBinding; lists virtualize (ListBox/ListView by default; TreeView needs `VirtualizingStackPanel.IsVirtualizing="True"` with Recycling mode), static Freezables frozen, custom-control binding targets must be DependencyProperties; background work via async/await and Task.Run with `IProgress<T>` reporting, UI access through Dispatcher, and a global `DispatcherUnhandledException` handler that logs and sets `e.Handled = true`; DPI via a PerMonitorV2 app.manifest entry; app startup overridden in `App.OnStartup` with the Generic Host resolving the MainWindow when constructor injection is needed.
- **Reference / source:** UI/UX Pro Max (uupm.cc) lookup database; per-row Docs URLs to learn.microsoft.com dotnet/desktop/wpf docs (e.g. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/controls/grid, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/communitytoolkit/mvvm/relaycommand). Verified 2026-08-13.
- **Best for:** WPF desktop application work — window layout, MVVM structure, command wiring, list performance. Native Windows development only; not a web or trade-site source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0043⟧

## ⟦S0044⟧ web-design-guidelines — PART 04 — Vercel
- **What it is:** A tiny procedural skill (about 1 KB, no reference files) that turns the agent into a UI code reviewer: when the user asks to "review my UI", "check accessibility", "audit design", "review UX" or "check my site against best practices", it fetches Vercel's current Web Interface Guidelines and checks the named files against every rule.

If the user names no files or pattern, the skill asks which files to review before doing anything.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The workflow is a fixed four-step sequence: fetch the latest guidelines from the source URL → read the specified files → check against all rules in the fetched document → output findings in its specified format. The guidelines are fetched fresh before every review, so the rule set is whatever the source holds that day, not a frozen copy in the bank.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Single source URL: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md`, retrieved with WebFetch at review time. No parameters, thresholds or rule text are stored in the skill itself — the fetched `command.md` contains all the rules and the output-format instructions.

## ⟦S0045⟧ vercel-react-view-transitions — PART 04 — Vercel
- **What it is:** Vercel Engineering's complete guide (version 1.0.0; SKILL.md plus five reference files — implementation workflow, patterns, troubleshooting, CSS recipes, Next.js — also compiled into one AGENTS.md, ~116 KB in total) for animating between UI states with React's native View Transition API: declare what animates with the `<ViewTransition>` component, trigger it with `startTransition`/`useDeferredValue`/`Suspense`, and control how it moves with CSS classes on the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements. No third-party animation library; browsers without support simply skip the animation.
- **How it looks:** The page never hard-cuts. Going from a list into a detail page, the tapped photo itself grows and travels from its grid cell into its large slot at the top of the detail view while the rest of the page slides sideways; going back reverses it. Switching tabs cross-fades the panel while a solid underline bar slides from the old tab to the new one. While data loads, a skeleton block slides down and away and the real content slides up into its place. Filtering a grid makes the surviving cards glide into their new positions instead of blinking out and reappearing elsewhere, and the section below a growing list is pushed down in one smooth glide rather than jumping. Header and other persistent chrome stay pinned and still throughout — only the content moves.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger is a navigation or state change wrapped in `startTransition` (a plain `setState` never animates). (1) Shared element morph — click a thumbnail: the browser snapshots the old and new versions of the element with the same `name`; over the move duration the snapshot pair travels and rescales from the thumbnail's box to the hero box, passing through a brief blur (the `via-blur` keyframe hits `blur(3px)` at 30%) so the raster stretch doesn't shimmer; end state is the live full-size element. For text, the `text-morph` class instead hides the old snapshot and shows the new text at full resolution, top-left anchored, so headlines don't ghost. (2) Directional page slide — on a `nav-forward` navigation the old page fades out while sliding 60px to the left and the new page fades in sliding from 60px right to rest; `nav-back` mirrors it exactly. (3) Suspense reveal — the skeleton exits sliding down with a fade while the loaded content enters sliding up 10px (`--slide-y-offset` default) with a fade, the enter delayed until the exit has run. (4) List reorder — keyed items are snapshotted in their old slots and their groups animate to the new slots, so cards visibly swap places; content displaced below glides as one block (layout displacement morph). (5) Tab indicator — the single underline element rendered under the active tab morphs position: its group slides over 220ms with `cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.2, 1)` while old/new snapshots are disabled so the bar stays solid. (6) Scale enter/exit — a panel scales from 0.85 with opacity 0 up to full size on entry, and back down on exit. (7) Collapse — a toggled section expands/collapses through `expand-in`/`collapse-out` enter/exit classes, optionally composed with React `Activity` so its scroll and form state survive being hidden.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Global timing variables: `--duration-exit: 150ms`, `--duration-enter: 210ms`, `--duration-move: 400ms`. Prescribed duration bands: direct toggle (expand/collapse) 100–200ms, route slide 150–250ms, Suspense reveal 200–400ms, shared-element morph 300–500ms. Slide offset 60px; vertical reveal offset 10px; scale floor 0.85; tab-underline 220ms at `cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.2, 1)`; fade keyframes are opacity-only (blur is scoped to morphs that ask for it); imperative events example animates scale 0.8→1 with opacity over 300ms `ease-out` via `onEnter`. Four triggers: `enter`, `exit`, `update`, `share` — `share` beats enter/exit; `addTransitionType` tags a transition (`nav-forward`/`nav-back`) and type maps on `enter`/`exit`/`share` pick the class, with a mandatory `default` key; `default="none"` disables a boundary (including update and share) and is required on named and page-level VTs so they don't cross-fade on every transition. Critical placement rule: `<ViewTransition>` must appear before any DOM nodes or its enter/exit never fires; a VT wrapping `{children}` in a layout kills page-level enter/exit; names must be globally unique (`photo-${id}`); `router.back()`/browser back carries no types, so directional slides resolve to `default` (untyped morphs still play). Persistent and floating elements are isolated with a real `view-transition-name` plus `animation: none` on their group (z-index 100 for chrome, 200 for toasts) — `view-transition-name: none` is a no-op; backdrop-blur elements hide their old snapshot instead. Live-root recipe: `::view-transition-old(root) { display: none }` and `::view-transition-new(root) { animation: none }` keep unnamed content rendering during transitions; `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` restores clicks through the overlay for unnamed content. Reduced motion: under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, all `::view-transition-old/new/group(*)` get `animation-duration: 0s !important; animation-delay: 0s !important` — mandatory in the global stylesheet. Availability: stable React/react-dom 19.3+ outside Next.js; Next.js App Router bundles it (never install react@canary there, no `experimental.viewTransition` flag); browsers Chromium 125+, Firefox 144+, Safari 18.2+; Next.js `<Link transitionTypes>` shipped in Next.js 16.2.0.
- **Reference / source:** PART 04 — Vercel (Vercel Engineering). The skill names the official React `<ViewTransition>` reference (https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) and the Next.js view-transitions and prefetching guides (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/view-transitions) as the API authorities, and links the csswg issue #10930 for the named-element hit-testing limitation and React PR #36690 for experimental parentEnter/parentExit.
- **Best for:** React/Next.js interfaces — route changes between list and detail pages (work/gallery → project page), tab and segmented-control switching, skeleton-to-content loading reveals, filterable/searchable grids, expandable cards and drawers. The shared-element morph is the standout pattern for a portfolio: a project thumbnail that grows into the project hero. Not usable in the plain single-file HTML previews (it needs React 19.3+/Next.js), but its timing bands and slide/blur values are a sound reference for hand-rolled page transitions anywhere.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0045⟧
## ⟦S0046⟧ vercel-composition-patterns — PART 04 — Vercel
- **What it is:** Vercel's React Composition Patterns (v1.0.0, January 2026): 8 rules in 4 priority categories for building flexible, maintainable React components without boolean-prop proliferation — using compound components, lifted state, and dependency-injected context instead.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen changes by itself — this is a code-structure skill, not a visual one. What the visitor sees is the same interface (the worked example throughout is a message composer: a header, a text input, and a footer row holding Attachments, Formatting and Emojis buttons plus a Send button), but each variant is a complete, explicit assembly of shared parts: the channel composer shows the standard footer, the thread composer adds one extra "also send to channel" field above the footer, the edit composer swaps Send for Cancel/Save buttons. No variant is the same component with pieces switched on and off.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Categories by priority: 1 Component Architecture (HIGH), 2 State Management (MEDIUM), 3 Implementation Patterns (MEDIUM), 4 React 19 APIs (MEDIUM). The 8 rules: `architecture-avoid-boolean-props` (impact CRITICAL — each added boolean doubles the possible states); `architecture-compound-components` (HIGH — subcomponents read shared state from context, not props); `state-decouple-implementation` (the provider is the only place that knows whether state is useState, Zustand or server-synced); `state-context-interface` (a generic context interface of exactly three parts: `state`, `actions`, `meta`); `state-lift-state` (HIGH — state lives in a provider so siblings outside the component's visual frame, e.g. a dialog's Forward button, can read and submit it); `patterns-explicit-variants` (one named component per variant); `patterns-children-over-render-props` (children for static structure; render props only when the parent must pass data back, e.g. a list's renderItem); `react19-no-forwardref` (React 19+: ref as a regular prop, `use()` instead of `useContext()`, and `use()` may be called conditionally). 45 KB, 11 reference files.
- **Reference / source:** Vercel (PART 04 — Vercel). References named inside: react.dev, react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context, react.dev/reference/react/use.
- **Best for:** Structuring reusable React component sets — message composers, quote/estimate form variants, any component that would otherwise grow boolean mode props (`isThread`, `isEditing`…). Only relevant when the build is React/Next.js; no direct use in single-file vanilla HTML builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0046⟧

## ⟦S0047⟧ vercel-react-best-practices — PART 04 — Vercel
- **What it is:** Vercel Engineering's React and Next.js performance optimization guide (v1.0.0, January 2026): 70 rules across 8 categories ranked by impact, each rule with an explanation and incorrect-vs-correct code, written to guide automated refactoring and code generation. 214 KB, 73 reference files.
- **How it looks:** The visitor sees the same pages, but they paint sooner and stay responsive. On navigation the page chrome — sidebar, header, footer — appears immediately while only the data-dependent block shows a skeleton and streams in when its fetch resolves. Heavy components (a chart, an editor) are absent from the first paint and load only when the feature is activated or hovered. Long lists and galleries render their off-screen rows lazily instead of all at once.
- **Frame by frame:** No prescribed visual animation. The perceivable sequence on load: static shell renders at once → skeleton fallback sits where data is pending → real content swaps in as each independent fetch resolves (fetches run in parallel, not one after another). During typing or filtering, non-urgent re-renders are deferred (startTransition / useDeferredValue) so the input never stutters waiting for the expensive list below it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** 1 Eliminating Waterfalls (CRITICAL): check cheap sync conditions before awaiting remote flags; defer `await` into the branch that uses it; `Promise.all()` for independent operations — 3 sequential round trips become 1, claimed 2–10× improvement; `better-all` for partial dependencies; start promises early in API routes and await late; Suspense boundaries so wrappers are not blocked by data. 2 Bundle Size Optimization (CRITICAL): import directly, never barrel files; `next/dynamic` for heavy components; defer analytics/logging until after hydration; load modules conditionally on feature activation; preload on hover/focus. 3 Server-Side Performance (HIGH): `React.cache()` for per-request deduplication; cross-request LRU cache (worked example: `new LRUCache({ max: 1000 })`); hoist static I/O (fonts, logos) to module level; minimize data serialized to client components; parallelize fetches by component composition; `after()` for non-blocking work; authenticate server actions like API routes. 4 Client-Side Data Fetching (MEDIUM-HIGH): SWR for automatic request deduplication; deduplicate global event listeners; `{ passive: true }` on touchstart, wheel and scroll listeners; version and minimize localStorage data. 5 Re-render Optimization (MEDIUM, 15 rules): extract expensive work into memoized components; primitive dependencies in effects; subscribe to derived booleans, not raw values; derive state during render, not in effects; functional setState; pass a function to useState for expensive initial values; use refs for transient frequent values (e.g. pointer position); never define components inside components. 6 Rendering Performance (MEDIUM): animate a div wrapper, not the SVG element itself; `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size: 0 80px` for long lists; reduce SVG coordinates to 1 decimal place; inline script for client-only data to avoid hydration flicker; ternary instead of `&&` for conditionals (prevents stray 0/false rendering); `defer`/`async` on script tags; React DOM resource hints for preloading. 7 JavaScript Performance (LOW-MEDIUM): Set/Map for O(1) lookups; index maps for repeated lookups; cache property access and function results; combine filter/map passes into one loop; loop for min/max instead of sort; hoist RegExp creation out of loops; `toSorted()` for immutable sorting; `requestIdleCallback` to defer non-critical work. 8 Advanced Patterns (LOW): keep `useEffectEvent` results out of effect dependency arrays; store event handlers in refs; initialize app-level state once per load, not per mount.
- **Reference / source:** Vercel Engineering (PART 04 — Vercel). Tools named inside: better-all (github.com/shuding/better-all), SWR, lru-cache, next/dynamic.
- **Best for:** Any React/Next.js build, review or refactor — data-fetching pages, long work/gallery lists, dashboards. For the trade-site builds it matters when a site is built in React; the waterfall/Suspense rules and `content-visibility` for long lists are the ones that change what the visitor actually perceives.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0047⟧

The rules themselves are not embedded in the skill — they are fetched fresh every time.
