- **What it is:** A quantified design-quality scorer: reads a UI file and returns 0–100 across seven weighted categories with per-line deductions, a letter grade, and a "fix first" list ordered by score gain — plus a Gate mode that loops fix-and-rescore until the file clears the floor.
- **How it looks:** A terminal-style scorecard: a bar (e.g. `████████████████░░░░░░  C-`), one row per category with its fraction and the offending lines, then the top fixes with their expected point gains and a projected re-score ("Re-score after: ~92 / 100").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The gate loop is the sequence: score → if < 80, apply fix-first list → re-score → repeat up to ~3 times → present with the final score.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Weights: Color discipline 18, Hierarchy & typography 18, Layout & rhythm 14, Cards & elevation 12, States & a11y 18, Motion & interaction 8, Coherence 12 (total 100). Letter bands: 90+ A, 80–89 B, 70–79 C, 60–69 D, <60 F. Signature deductions: any `#000`/`text-black` −4 each (cap −8); a second decorative accent hue −5; emoji as UI icons −5; a normal/OK state shown in a status colour −4; content on bare background instead of cards −6; 1px borders doing separation work −4; shadows over ~8% opacity −4; missing empty/loading/error state −5 each (cap −10); contrast under 4.5:1 −6; touch target < 44px −4; no visible focus −5; ad-hoc fades instead of a named motion seed −3; scroll-linked/parallax is forbidden in this system (−5). Gate rule: ≥ 80 is a floor before showing the user, not a target to polish past — shipping a clean 85 beats delaying for 95.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-score); categories read from the project's DESIGN-LANGUAGE and VISUAL-CRAFT documents (not bundled).
- **Best for:** QA discipline — the weighted-scorecard shape (and especially "fix in gain order, stop at the floor") is a reusable audit format; the rubric itself scores StyleSeed conventions, so don't apply its numbers blindly to a trade homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0242⟧

## ⟦S0243⟧ ui-setup — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** An interactive, one-question-at-a-time setup wizard: app type → brand colour → optional famous-brand style → font → app name, then it writes the tokens, scaffolds the first page from a composition recipe, and locks every choice into a `STYLESEED.md` design-lock file.
- **How it looks:** A chat conversation of five short multiple-choice questions, ending in a "Setup Complete!" summary card (app, brand colour + its dark-mode variant, font, concept, first page, files modified). The generated first page follows per-type recipes — e.g. SaaS: Hero + KPI grid + chart + progress + activity list; Social: Hero + stats + feed list + trending carousel.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion, other than the wizard's step sequence (ask one question, wait, apply, next).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Brand palette offered: Purple #721FE5 (default "toss" skin), Blue #2563EB, Green #059669, Orange #EA580C, Red #DC2626, Dark #18181B, or custom hex; each has a fixed dark-mode lightened partner (#721FE5 → #9B5FFF, #2563EB → #60A5FA, #059669 → #34D399, #EA580C → #FB923C, #DC2626 → #F87171, #18181B → #A1A1AA; custom = lighten ~30% in HSL). Style step can fetch a brand's DESIGN.md (Stripe, Linear, Vercel, Notion, Spotify, Supabase, Airbnb) and swap colours only — all layout/type/spacing rules stay StyleSeed's. Fonts: Inter, Pretendard + Inter, Geist, DM Sans. The design lock records: app domain, skin, the ONE accent hex, radius personality (sharp | soft | pill), motion seed (Spring | Silk | Snap | Float | Pulse), type, date. A single removable attribution comment goes on the first scaffolded file only.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed (github.com/bitjaru/styleseed); brand styles fetched from VoltAgent/awesome-design-md on GitHub (raw.githubusercontent.com/VoltAgent/awesome-design-md/main/design-md/<brand>/DESIGN.md).
- **Best for:** Process — the design-lock idea is the keeper: one small file stating the single accent, radius personality, motion seed and type, re-read every session so a long build never drifts. The wizard itself is StyleSeed/React-only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0243⟧

## ⟦S0244⟧ ui-states — PART 12 — MCP Market, by UXKIN
- **What it is:** A completeness skill for the states generated UI forgets: for every screen that loads, lists, searches or saves, enumerate the applicable states (first use, empty, loading, partial, error, offline, validation, permission, success, edge content, busy action), build each properly, then trigger each for real and check it.
- **How it looks:** The unglamorous screens done right: an empty list that says what the place is for with a real next-step button ("Add your first invoice") instead of "No data"; skeleton placeholders shaped like the content while loading (never a whole-screen block for a partial load); an error in plain words with what to do next and the user's typed input still intact; offline keeping already-loaded content visible; long names truncated with the full value reachable; a busy button disabled with progress so it can't double-submit.
- **Frame by frame:** Motion is deliberately minimal: loading placeholders hold the layout steady (shaped skeletons, inline spinners for small areas, progress for long tasks), and success confirms briefly in place — the item appearing in the list, a short message, Undo offered for removals. No numbers for durations are prescribed in this skill.
- **Mechanism & key values:** An 11-row state table, each with its test question ("What if some data loads and some doesn't?"). Rules with teeth: empty-because-of-filter is a different state from empty-because-new, and must offer to clear the filter; validation fires on leaving a field or on submit, never per keystroke, with the message beside the field; errors never show raw codes or stack traces; states are verified by actually forcing them (empty data, throttled/failed requests, offline mode, very long text) at phone and desktop widths, then reported as built / checked / needs-a-decision.
- **Reference / source:** By UXKIN (uxkin.com) — a library of 500,000+ real app screens and 15k+ website design systems; optional MCP connection at uxkin.com/mcp (agent instructed to set it up only when the person asks).
- **Best for:** Any data-touching section — quote/request forms above all (validation, busy, success, error states on a "request a callback" form), plus galleries and lists that can come back empty. Directly relevant to making preview pages feel production-real instead of demo-happy-path.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0244⟧

## ⟦S0245⟧ ui-tokens — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** A token manager: list, add or update StyleSeed design tokens while keeping the JSON source files and the CSS implementation in sync across light and dark modes.
- **How it looks:** No visual output; its product is consistency — change `--success` once and every button, badge and banner that uses it changes together, in both themes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Five token types with fixed homes: colors (tokens/colors.json → css/theme.css `:root` + `@theme inline`), typography (tokens/typography.json → css/fonts.css + css/base.css), spacing (tokens/spacing.json → Tailwind utilities, no custom CSS), radius (tokens/radii.json → theme.css), shadows (tokens/shadows.json → theme.css `:root`). Add/update workflow touches both files every time, plus a `.dark` variant for colours. Naming rule: semantic, never descriptive (`--success`, not `--green-500`). Tailwind v4 / CSS variables only — no Figma or native token systems.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-tokens). No external site named.
- **Best for:** Process reference only — the JSON-source + CSS-implementation dual-write discipline. Little direct use in single-file builds where tokens live as CSS variables in the one file.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0245⟧

## ⟦S0246⟧ ui-update — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** An engine updater: detect a project's installed StyleSeed files, compare them against a pinned upstream revision, report the diff, and update only with explicit approval per item — never touching the project's skin or components.
- **How it looks:** A "StyleSeed Update Report": current state per file (location, found/missing), then recommended updates tagged ✅ safe or ⚠️ review/merge, then a closing summary of what changed and what was explicitly not touched ("Your theme.css (skin) is untouched." / "Your components are untouched.").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Sequence: find files → compare versions → report and ask → execute per-item with approval → summary.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Detection via `find` for DESIGN-LANGUAGE.md, CLAUDE.md, skills (.claude/skills/ss-* current; ui-*/ux-* legacy), theme.css, .cursorrules. Upstream is cloned to a temp dir at one pinned commit — 356ac3aa184595525da3a4e1d9f1c7fe92812da6 of github.com/bitjaru/styleseed — inspected (reject unexpected scripts/hooks/binaries), and its exact commit shown to the user before anything copies. Hard rules: never overwrite theme.css; CLAUDE.md gets the Golden Rules merged, never replaced; clean worktree or approved backup required; diff shown before every write.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed — github.com/bitjaru/styleseed (pinned revision above).
- **Best for:** Process only; not applicable to our builds (no StyleSeed engine installed). Indexed for completeness of the family.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0246⟧

## ⟦S0247⟧ design-spatial — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity)
- **What it is:** A spatial-composition discipline built on one premise: the model cannot see what it made and its first idea is the average. So the skill prescribes a process — render, screenshot, have a fresh judge hunt for what's wrong, measure balance numerically, and pass a hard horizontal-overflow gate — instead of prescribing a look.
- **How it looks:** Nothing directly; its fingerprints on a finished page are: no side-to-side scrollbar at any width, a hero whose visual weight sits at the optical centre (slightly above middle), layouts arranged in the order the user's task runs (orient → work → confirm, with action buttons repeated where the work ends), and compositions that come from the product's own world rather than the two named averages — the "generic-AI mean" (Inter, purple-on-white, centred column, three equal cards) and the "designer-trend mean" (oversized condensed caps, dark + grain, monospace vibe microtext, sticker badges).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. The loop it mandates per iteration: serve the page → screenshot at several widths including narrow → independent judge critiques the image (collisions, tangents, ragged alignment, lopsided weight, no focal point) → fix → re-render → re-judge; plus a live-controls variant (sliders/drag handles) for iterative tuning.
- **Mechanism & key values:** THE overflow gate (blocking, no exceptions): `document.documentElement.scrollWidth − clientWidth` must equal 0, measured at dev width AND ≤1024px AND ~390px, re-armed every time an element joins a horizontal row. Defences: flex rows `flex-wrap: wrap` never `nowrap`; `overflow-x: clip` on body as backstop only; never `100vw` (includes ~15px scrollbar); flex/grid children get `min-width: 0`; edge-pinned nowrap labels anchored inward. Balance measured, not eyeballed: visual weight ≈ area × ink-density (starting coefficients portrait 0.34, h1 0.82, kicker 0.42, lead 0.22, body 0.16, meta 0.5); optical centre x = 0.50, y ≈ 0.46; acceptance |centroid_x − 0.50| < 0.03 and |centroid_y − 0.46| < 0.04 — verified by a pixel oracle over the rendered screenshot (centroid of actual non-background pixels), never by the box model alone, because the box model once reported "balanced" at a pixel-measured 0.93 lopsided. Bundled layout-audit script measures 7 checks: collision (rect intersection ≥ 12%), contrast (WCAG < 4.5, large < 3), tap targets < 44×44 (project heuristic), overflow, alignment near-misses 1–7px, spacing gap coefficient-of-variation, balance — drawn as an SVG overlay on the page so the next screenshot is annotated. Doctrine: overflow/contrast/tap are GATES (real defects, block); balance/alignment/spacing are SIGNALS (convention — obeying them blindly designs the mean; a deliberate asymmetry or brutalist overlap the eye judges good overrules the flag). Optical craft: nudge glyphs ±1–2px when they look off though they measure centred; match icon stroke/size to the text beside it.
- **Reference / source:** PART 12 MCP Market skill; §8 optical craft is from Vercel's Web Interface Guidelines (vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines @ 4e799d4); companion scripts layout-audit.js, analyze.py, asym.html are referenced but not bundled in the bank.
- **Best for:** Every build's composition + QA loop — above all the overflow gate and the screenshot-judge discipline for our section-by-section screenshot approvals, and the balance numbers when a hero "feels off" but nobody can say why. One of the highest-value process entries in this range.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0247⟧

## ⟦S0248⟧ design-token-contrast — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity)
- **What it is:** A token-level contrast checker: a dependency-free Node script (shipped as source inside the skill) that reads a project's CSS colour tokens, pairs text tokens over background tokens in light AND dark themes, measures WCAG 2.2 ratios, and for every failure proposes the nearest same-hue lightness that passes — one value per token that passes against all its backgrounds.
- **How it looks:** A terminal report (in Spanish) per theme: `NO 3.54:1 (mín. 4.5) --color-text #888888 sobre --color-background #ffffff` followed by the suggestion `oklch(56.2% 0.000 89.9) (#757575) → 4.62:1`, plus a closing line for a single unified value ("Un solo valor para --color-text que pasa en sus N fondos"). Exit code 1 if any pair fails, 2 if anything couldn't be measured — an incomplete report never claims all-pass.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Minimums: normal text 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3), large text 3:1 (large = from 24px, or 18.66px bold), UI components/graphics — input borders, icons, focus rings — 3:1 (1.4.11). It parses hex/rgb()/hsl()/oklch(), resolves var() aliases, separates dark blocks (`.dark`, `[data-theme=dark]`, prefers-color-scheme), pairs tokens by name pattern (Spanish names texto/fondo/superficie/tarjeta also recognised), and searches OKLCH lightness in 0.0025–0.005 steps in both directions, reducing chroma only to stay in sRGB gamut, requiring minimum + 0.05 headroom. Explicit pairs can be forced with a `--pares` JSON file; `--todos` measures the full matrix; `--json` writes results (exclusive-create, mode 0600). Run: `node contraste.mjs --tokens src/styles/tokens.css`, Node 18+, no dependencies, no network. Stated limits: regex parsing, not the CSS cascade; it cannot see text over images/gradients/opacity — those need a screen check.
- **Reference / source:** PART 12 MCP Market skill; relates to @wcag-audit-patterns for a full audit. No external site named.
- **Best for:** QA on a build's token palette before sections multiply — fix a failing muted-text token once instead of patching every section; especially the dark-theme pass people forget. Complements ⟦S0236⟧ (which audits rendered components; this one audits the tokens underneath).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0248⟧

## ⟦S0249⟧ uxui-principles — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity)
- **What it is:** A five-skill collection for judging interfaces against 168 research-backed UX/UI principles: evaluate a described interface, detect antipatterns, review AI-powered interfaces, check user flows, or inject UX context into a coding session before implementation.
- **How it looks:** No visual output of its own; it returns structured findings with severity levels and remediation steps for whatever screen or flow was described to it, optionally enriched with full citations via the uxuiprinciples.com API.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The five sub-skills: `uxui-evaluator` (168 principles), `interface-auditor` (antipattern "smell" taxonomy), `ai-interface-reviewer` (44 AI-era principles — trust, transparency, safety), `flow-checker` (decision, error and feedback principles), `vibe-coding-advisor` (pre-implementation UX context). Installed per-skill with `npx skills add uxuiprinciples/agent-skills`. The skill text in the bank is a short hub page — the 168 principles themselves live in the source collection, not in this file.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/uxuiprinciples/agent-skills (named in the skill); API at uxuiprinciples.com.
- **Best for:** A pre-build or audit checklist source — most relevant here is flow-checker thinking for quote/booking flows (decisions, errors, feedback) and the antipattern pass on a finished homepage. Light entry: depth is in the external collection.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0249⟧

## ⟦S0250⟧ ux-audit — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** A UX audit of existing screens against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics plus mobile-specific checks and a dark-pattern sweep, graded A+ to F with issues split Critical / Major / Minor and a code fix for each.
- **How it looks:** No visual output; a graded report. The screens it pushes toward: skeletons instead of spinners, a toast after every action, progress shown on multi-step flows, the active nav item unmistakably lit, destructive buttons visually distinct with confirmation, and an empty state that tells the user what to do next.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed, though it audits other people's: skeleton screens must appear within 300ms, content must not shift after load, and optimistic updates are endorsed only where a failure can be reconciled honestly (never for payments or destructive actions).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Heuristic checks with numbers: spacing on the 6px grid; text hierarchy as a 5-level grayscale system; card density max 4 items; one hero metric per page; key actions reachable within 3 taps; touch targets 44×44px preferred with at least 8px between adjacent targets; form validation on blur, not while typing; skeleton-over-spinner rule; safe-area checks (notch, home indicator, `pb-safe` bottom nav). Dark-pattern list: no forced bottom sheets on entry, no exit-prevention dialogs, every screen dismissible, CTA labels that say what happens. The skill itself flags that several numbers (6px grid, 4-item cards, 3-tap goal) are upstream StyleSeed preferences, not universal laws.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-audit); framework is Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics.
- **Best for:** QA pass on a finished homepage or flow — the status-visibility, error-recovery and dark-pattern checks translate directly to trade-site trust (a roofing page lives or dies on reading as honest). Mobile-first framing; apply the heuristics, not the StyleSeed numbers, to desktop.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0250⟧

## ⟦S0251⟧ ux-copy — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** A microcopy generator for the small words: button labels, error messages, empty states, toasts, form helpers and confirmation dialogs, all in one casual-but-polite voice — active, positively framed, plain, concise.
- **How it looks:** On screen it is the difference between "Submit" and "Save changes": a primary button that names its action in at most 3 words ("Place order", "Get started", "Try again"); an empty state that observes and invites ("No activity yet. Create your first project to get started." — with a relevant 32px icon); an error that says what happened and what to do ("Couldn't load the data. Please try again.") instead of "Error 500"; a toast that confirms in a breath ("Saved!", "Item deleted · Undo", max 2 lines); a form field with a noun label ("Email address"), an example placeholder ("name@example.com") and a format helper ("Must be at least 8 characters").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Toast display durations are treated as design defaults, and the skill warns an essential recovery action must never live only inside a short-lived toast.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Formats are fixed per context: CTA = [action verb] + [object], one primary CTA per screen; empty state = [friendly observation] + [suggested action]; error = [what happened] + [what to do], blame the system never the user, never show technical errors; confirmation dialog = question title + consequence body + action-verb primary ("Delete", "Confirm"), secondary "Cancel" when it cancels a pending action, "Close" only for pure dismissal. Money copy stays calm (from the referenced UX-WRITING rules); one term per concept throughout; security nuance: on public account flows, errors avoid revealing whether an address is registered.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-copy); applies the project's engine/UX-WRITING.md rule set and DESIGN-LANGUAGE microcopy sections (not bundled); Korean/CJK projects pointed to the "Toss feel" rules in §W8.
- **Best for:** Every visible string on a build — most valuable on call/CTA sections and quote forms, where "Request a callback" beats "Submit" and a calm, specific error keeps a homeowner from abandoning the form.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0251⟧

## ⟦S0252⟧ ux-feedback — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** A generator that adds all four feedback states to any data-dependent area of a component or page — loading (skeleton), empty, error, success — following one branching implementation pattern: loading → skeleton, error → retry block, no data → empty state, otherwise content.
- **How it looks:** A card that never sits blank: while loading it shows its own ghost — muted pulsing blocks in the exact shape of the coming content (avatar square, two text bars, a big number block). Empty, it centres a 32px icon over a 14px secondary-colour title and a next action. Failed, it shows a centred alert icon, one plain sentence ("Couldn't load the data") and a small retry button — and if only one card failed, only that card shows it. Success arrives as a toast above the bottom nav ("Changes saved", or "Item deleted" with Undo when undo truly restores).
- **Frame by frame:** Loading: the skeleton's `animate-pulse` breathes on a 1.5s cycle; timing discipline — delay showing the skeleton 300ms (fast loads skip it entirely) and keep it visible at least 300ms once shown (no flash). Success: info toast displays 3s; one toast at a time, new replaces old. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, the pulse is disabled.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Skeleton shapes must match final content dimensions; never a spinner inside a card. Zero values render as "0", never hidden or dashed. Partial failure isolates to the affected card; full-page failure gets the full-screen empty state with retry. Retry offered only when retrying is safe; destructive-action Undo must have a persistent recovery path beyond the toast. Skeleton colours from tokens (`bg-surface-muted`), shapes `rounded` / `rounded-lg`.
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-feedback); reads DESIGN-LANGUAGE sections on loading/empty/error states when present (not bundled).
- **Best for:** Any section that touches data or submission — quote forms, review feeds, galleries. The 300ms delay / 300ms minimum skeleton rule and partial-failure isolation are the portable numbers. Pairs with ⟦S0244⟧ (which enumerates more states; this one implements the core four).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0252⟧

## ⟦S0253⟧ ux-flow — PART 12 — MCP Market, StyleSeed family
- **What it is:** A flow designer: given one user flow, it produces an ASCII flow diagram, a screen inventory with edge cases per screen, and scaffolded pages — structuring navigation as hub-and-spoke, linear, or tab-based before any page is built.
- **How it looks:** The output a visitor eventually feels as an app that never strands them: a dashboard that spokes out to details and back, a checkout/onboarding that steps linearly with progress, 3–5 top-level sections in a bottom tab bar, every screen answering one primary question with its most important metric or action above the fold, composed down an information pyramid (Hero → KPI grid → details → lists).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; loading states inside flows must be skeletons, never spinners in cards.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Laws: Miller's law — chunk to groups of 5–9; Hick's law — fewer choices per screen, faster decisions; progressive disclosure throughout. Hard numbers: maximum 3 taps from home to any key feature; back navigation always available except on root screens; tab navigation 3–5 sections; every flow has a clear entry and exit; every error state has a recovery path (retry, back, contact support). Four section types for composition: Full Card (A), Grid (B), Carousel (C), Hero (D).
- **Reference / source:** StyleSeed family (/ss-flow); composition rules cite DESIGN-LANGUAGE.md sections 13–14 and 19–20 (not bundled).
- **Best for:** Planning multi-step journeys before building — a quote-request journey (landing → service → details → confirm) or a multi-page site's navigation skeleton. The 3-tap and recovery-path rules are the keepers for trade sites where the whole point is one short path to the phone number or form.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0253⟧

## ⟦S0254⟧ code-polish — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity)
- **What it is:** A comments-only cleanup protocol: audit every comment in a file, rewrite the unprofessional ones into clear professional English, do strictly non-semantic tidying — and never, under any circumstances, change what the code does.
- **How it looks:** No visual output. The before/after is textual: "// ugh this took forever… api rate limits us super hard in prod so we have to do exponential backoff here. just leave it alone" becomes "// Uses exponential backoff to handle aggressive API rate-limiting in production."; "count += 1  # increment count by 1" loses its comment entirely; a casual "// careful, this breaks if you call it twice" becomes a precise "Not idempotent: calling this more than once per session corrupts the cache index."
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Five phases in order: full read → comment audit (classify: junk/venting, placeholder, dead code, redundant, outdated, valuable-but-informal, missing) → non-semantic cleanup (indentation, brace style, long-line splits only) → rewrite/add (explain WHY not what, idiomatic doc format, no filler, no invented rationale) → verify the diff is comments-and-whitespace only → report counts and anything flagged.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Prime directive: if a change would alter behaviour it is out of scope, however obviously correct it looks. Renames are NOT treated as safe (reflection/serialization/dynamic lookup); unreachable code is flagged, not deleted; stale comments are corrected AND flagged to the user, not silently fixed; information inside a casual comment must be preserved through its rewrite — deleting a real warning because its tone was casual is a named failure.
- **Reference / source:** PART 12 MCP Market skill, self-contained. No external site named.
- **Best for:** Process only — handover hygiene for generated build files before a client or another developer reads them. No design value; indexed for completeness.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0254⟧

## ⟦S0255⟧ threejs-fundamentals — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The foundation reference for any Three.js scene: scene/camera/renderer setup, the Object3D hierarchy, the right-handed coordinate system, math utilities, the animation loop, resize handling, cleanup, and performance patterns — pinned to Three.js r183.
- **How it looks:** The canonical starter frame: a WebGL canvas filling the window with a lit 3D object (the guide's quick-start is a green cube under ambient + directional light) that keeps rendering smoothly and reframes correctly when the window resizes; richer scenes add fog depth, skybox/environment backgrounds and shadowed ground from the same primitives.
- **Frame by frame:** Continuous render loop via `renderer.setAnimationLoop` (preferred over manual requestAnimationFrame): each tick, delta time is sampled (THREE.Timer in r183, connected to document so it pauses when the tab hides; THREE.Clock is legacy), rotations advance by `delta × speed` so motion is framerate-independent (quick-start cube: rotation.x and rotation.y += 0.01 per frame), controls update, scene renders. On resize: camera aspect updates, projection matrix recomputes, renderer resizes and pixel ratio re-clamps.
- **Mechanism & key values:** PerspectiveCamera(fov 75, aspect, near 0.1, far 1000) in the quick start; OrthographicCamera for isometric/2D; CubeCamera with a 256px cube render target for reflections (updated per frame — flagged expensive). Renderer: `antialias: true`, `setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2))`, ACESFilmicToneMapping with exposure 1.0, outputColorSpace SRGB (r152+), PCFSoftShadowMap. Coordinates: +X right, +Y up, +Z toward viewer. Performance rules: merge static geometries, frustum culling on by default, THREE.LOD levels at distances 0 / 50 / 100 in the example, object pooling, cache getWorldPosition out of loops, full dispose() teardown (geometry, materials, textures, renderer). Also notes the experimental WebGPURenderer in r183, which uses TSL instead of GLSL.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family of skills (PART 12); targets Three.js r183 and the official three/addons module paths.
- **Best for:** The setup layer under any 3D hero or product scene — camera choice, tone mapping and the pixel-ratio cap are what separate a crisp, fast 3D section from a blurry, hot one. Prerequisite reading for ⟦S0256⟧–⟦S0260⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0255⟧

## ⟦S0256⟧ threejs-animation — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The animation-system reference: keyframe clips and tracks, the mixer/action playback model, GLTF animation loading, skeletal (bone) animation, morph targets, blending and crossfades, plus procedural motion patterns (springs, damping, oscillation).
- **How it looks:** A loaded 3D model that moves like it has a skeleton: a character whose Walk clip plays on load, crossfading into Run as speed rises with no pop at the switch; a face whose smile morph weight swells and settles; a head bone that turns to follow, layered over the playing clip; a prop parented to a hand bone riding every gesture.
- **Frame by frame:** Per frame: sample delta once → `mixer.update(delta)` applies all active clips → manual bone overrides apply after the mixer → render. Crossfade: the outgoing action fades out while the incoming fades in over the same window (examples use 0.5s), weights summing through the transition. Speed-blend example: below speed 0.1, idle weight 1; 0.1–5, idle/walk weights trade linearly (t = speed/5); 5–10, walk hands off to run the same way. Morph smile clip: influence 0 → 1 → 0 across keyframes at 0 / 0.5 / 1s. Loop modes: LoopRepeat (default), LoopOnce, LoopPingPong (forward then backward); `clampWhenFinished` holds the last frame instead of snapping back.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Track types: Number, Vector, Quaternion, Color, Boolean, plus morph influences as Number tracks on `.morphTargetInfluences[name]`; interpolation Linear (default) / Smooth (cubic spline) / Discrete (step), plus r183's new BezierInterpolant with tangent control. Action controls: timeScale (negative = reverse), weight 0–1, repetitions, `fadeIn/fadeOut(duration)`, `crossFadeTo(action, duration, warp)`, additive blending via `THREE.AnimationUtils.makeClipAdditive`. Procedural: spring defaults stiffness 100, damping 10; oscillation recipes (sine bob `sin(t×2)×0.5`, bounce `|sin(t×3)|×2`, circular and figure-8 paths); smooth-damp with a smoothTime (example 0.3). GLTF flow: GLTFLoader → mixer on gltf.scene → clips from gltf.animations, `AnimationClip.findByName(clips, "Walk")`. Performance: share clips across mixers, `clip.optimize()`, pause mixers off-screen.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family (PART 12); Three.js r183 API (three/addons GLTFLoader).
- **Best for:** Any animated 3D section — a rotating/exploding product or roof-system model in a hero, scroll- or state-driven model motion, and morph-based before/after 3D. The crossfade and weight-blend numbers are the difference between mechanical and lifelike 3D movement.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0256⟧

## ⟦S0257⟧ threejs-shaders — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The custom-effects reference: writing GLSL for ShaderMaterial/RawShaderMaterial, uniforms and varyings, ready patterns (vertex waves, Fresnel, rim light, dissolve, noise, gradients), extending built-in materials with onBeforeCompile, instanced shaders, and the TSL future direction.
- **How it looks:** Surfaces no stock material can produce: a plane rippling in a continuous wave; an object whose silhouette glows pale blue while its face stays deep navy (Fresnel, edge brightness rising with the cube of the grazing angle); a mesh that burns away edge-first in orange as a progress value climbs, eaten by noise; colours that shade smoothly from one hue at the base to another at the top.
- **Frame by frame:** Continuous, driven by a `time` uniform updated every frame from the clock: the wave pattern displaces each vertex by `sin(pos.x × 5.0 + time) × amplitude` (amplitude 0.5 in the example) on both axes, so the surface undulates without end. The dissolve is state-driven rather than looping: as `progress` goes 0 → 1, fragments whose noise value falls below progress are discarded, and a 0.1-wide smoothstep band at the burn front renders as the glowing edge. Fresnel/rim are view-dependent, changing as the camera or object moves: rim = pow(1 − dot(view, normal), 4.0) added over the base colour.
- **Mechanism & key values:** ShaderMaterial supplies built-in uniforms (modelMatrix, modelViewMatrix, projectionMatrix, viewMatrix, normalMatrix, cameraPosition) and attributes (position, normal, uv); RawShaderMaterial supplies nothing — declare everything. Uniform types map JS → GLSL (Color → vec3, textures → sampler2D/samplerCube, arrays with fixed sizes). Key injection points for onBeforeCompile: `#include <begin_vertex>` (after position), `<project_vertex>`, `<beginnormal_vertex>`, `<color_fragment>`, `<fog_fragment>` — with the cautions to use a shared time-uniform object across material variants and set customProgramCacheKey when patch options vary. GLSL3 requires rewriting texture2D() → texture() and gl_FragColor → an out variable. Debug: print compiled shaders via onBeforeCompile, `renderer.debug.checkShaderErrors = true`. Performance: precalculate on CPU, use textures as lookup tables, limit transparent overdraw, replace if/else with mix/step where profiling supports it. TSL note: node materials (MeshStandardNodeMaterial, colorNode/positionNode) are the WebGPU path; GLSL ShaderMaterial is WebGL-only.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family (PART 12); pinned to Three.js r183 WebGLRenderer unless a snippet is labelled TSL.
- **Best for:** Signature visual effects in 3D sections — a dissolve/wave hero object, Fresnel-glow product renders, shader-driven transitions between section states. Situational for trade sites: powerful as one hero moment, costly to overuse.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0257⟧

## ⟦S0258⟧ threejs-interaction — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The input reference for interactive 3D: raycast picking (click, hover, touch), the six camera-control rigs, drag/transform gizmos, box selection, keyboard input, and world↔screen coordinate conversion.
- **How it looks:** A 3D scene that answers the hand: the cursor turns to a pointer and the hovered part lights orange; a click selects and the piece glows (emissive 0x444444); drag a part and it slides along the ground while the camera locks out until you let go; grab empty space and the whole scene orbits with a soft, damped settle instead of stopping dead; on a configurator-style scene, HTML labels ride exactly on top of their 3D parts as you move.
- **Frame by frame:** Orbit with damping: pointer drag rotates the camera around its target; on release the motion coasts and eases out — `controls.update()` must run every frame with `dampingFactor 0.05`. Auto-rotate (when enabled) turns the scene continuously at autoRotateSpeed 2.0. Hover raycasts are throttled to at most one per 50ms (20fps) so pointer movement stays cheap. Drag: dragstart highlights the object (emissive 0xaaaaaa) and disables OrbitControls; drag moves it (example constrains y to the ground plane, y = 0); dragend restores both. Everything is event/frame driven — no timed keyframe motion of its own.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pointer → NDC conversion from the canvas bounding rect: `x = ((clientX − left) / width) × 2 − 1`, `y = −((clientY − top) / height) × 2 + 1` (guard zero-size rects). Raycaster near/far default 0/Infinity; Line/Points thresholds 0.1; filtering by layers or a clickables list, and cheap invisible box collision meshes for complex models. OrbitControls limits in the examples: minPolarAngle 0, maxPolarAngle π/2 (never under the floor), azimuth ±π/4, distance 2–50. Other rigs: FlyControls movementSpeed 10, rollSpeed π/24; FirstPersonControls lookSpeed 0.1, vertical clamp π/4 to 3π/4; TrackballControls rotate 2.0 / zoom 1.2 / pan 0.8; PointerLockControls for FPS-style (needs a user gesture to lock). TransformControls modes translate/rotate/scale on keys g/r/s, Escape detaches. House rules baked in: canvas-relative coordinates for embedded scenes, dispose listeners/controls on teardown, always provide keyboard/focus alternatives to pointer picking.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family (PART 12); three/addons controls (OrbitControls, FlyControls, FirstPersonControls, PointerLockControls, TrackballControls, MapControls, TransformControls, DragControls, SelectionBox).
- **Best for:** Interactive 3D sections — a rotatable product/system viewer in a hero or work section ("drag to spin" moments), clickable part explorers, and any canvas where hover/selection feedback sells the craft. Overkill for a passive render; this is the entry that makes 3D participatory.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0258⟧

## ⟦S0259⟧ threejs-materials — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The material-system reference: all ten material types with their parameters, PBR and advanced physical features (clearcoat, transmission, sheen, iridescence, anisotropy), environment maps, multi-material groups, and performance rules.
- **How it looks:** The same shape rendered ten different ways, from flat poster colour (Basic — no light at all) through matte Lambert and glossy Phong to true PBR: a metal that mirrors the room, glass you see through with believable refraction, car paint with a wet clear layer over the colour, velvet with a soft sheen rim, a soap-bubble iridescent film, and a cel-shaded toon object banded into three flat tones.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; materials respond to light and camera, so apparent change comes from ⟦S0256⟧/⟦S0258⟧ movement, not from this skill.
- **Mechanism & key values:** MeshStandardMaterial is the default recommendation: roughness 0 (mirror) → 1 (diffuse), metalness 0 (dielectric) → 1 (metal), with map/roughnessMap/metalnessMap/normalMap/aoMap (aoMap UV channel selectable via Texture.channel) /displacement (scale 0.1, bias 0 in the example) and envMapIntensity 1. MeshPhysicalMaterial adds: clearcoat 0–1 with clearcoatRoughness (car-paint recipe: metalness 0.9, roughness 0.5, clearcoat 1, clearcoatRoughness 0.1); transmission 0–1 with thickness 0.5 and ior 1.5 (glass recipe: roughness 0, metalness 0, transmission 1, thickness 0.5, ior 1.5; ior range 1–2.333); attenuation for coloured glass; sheen 1.0 / sheenRoughness 0.5; iridescence with iridescenceIOR 1.3 and thickness range [100, 400]; anisotropy for brushed metal. Phong shininess 0–1000. Toon gradient maps use NearestFilter data textures (example steps 0/128/255). Cost ladder for performance: Basic > Lambert > Phong > Standard > Physical; prefer alphaTest over true transparency; reuse materials via a cache; r183 note — Lambert/Phong now also respond to scene.environment IBL. Environment: HDR via RGBELoader with EquirectangularReflectionMapping set as scene.environment lights every PBR material at once.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family (PART 12); Three.js r183 material API.
- **Best for:** Making 3D read as real material instead of plastic — glass, painted metal, fabric and stone in product/system viewers; the glass and car-paint recipes are copy-ready. Prerequisite companion to ⟦S0260⟧ (lighting is what these surfaces answer to).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0259⟧

## ⟦S0260⟧ threejs-lighting — PART 12 — MCP Market, Three.js family
- **What it is:** The lighting reference: the six light types with costs, full shadow configuration, environment/IBL setup, light probes, three ready-made lighting rigs (three-point, outdoor daylight, indoor studio), light animation, and performance rules.
- **How it looks:** A scene with depth instead of flatness: a warm key light raking across a product from upper right casting a soft-edged shadow onto the ground, a cooler half-strength fill lifting the shadow side, a rim light separating the subject from a dark background; or open daylight — a strong sun with shadows under a blue-sky/brown-ground hemisphere wash; or a studio look from two soft window-like area lights.
- **Frame by frame:** Lights are static unless animated; the skill's animation recipe, per frame from elapsed time: a light orbits the scene (`x = cos(t)×5`, `z = sin(t)×5`), intensity pulses `1 + sin(t×2)×0.5`, and colour cycles hue via `setHSL((t×0.1) % 1, 1, 0.5)` — a full hue rotation every 10 seconds. Helpers update per frame when lights move.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Light table with shadow support and cost: Ambient (no shadow, very low), Hemisphere sky/ground gradient (no shadow, very low), Directional (shadow, low), Point (shadow, medium — distance/decay, physically correct decay = 2), Spot (shadow, medium — angle max π/2, penumbra 0–1), RectAreaLight (no native shadows, high; needs RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init(), works only with Standard/Physical materials). Shadow system: renderer.shadowMap.enabled + type (PCFSoftShadowMap the quality default; Basic fastest, VSM the alternative), light.castShadow, mesh cast/receive; shadow map sizes 512 low / 1024 medium / 2048 high / 4096 very high; directional shadow camera near 0.5 / far 50 with a tight ±10 frustum in the example; acne fixes bias −0.0001 and normalBias 0.02 (point lights bias −0.005). Rigs: three-point = key DirectionalLight 1.0 at (5,5,5), fill 0.5 at (−5,3,5), back 0.3 at (0,5,−5), ambient 0x404040 at 0.3; outdoor = sun 0xffffcc at 1.5 from (50,100,50) with shadows + HemisphereLight(0x87ceeb sky, 0x8b4513 ground, 0.6); studio = RectAreaLights intensity 5 and 3, 2×2 size, aimed at origin + ambient 0.2. IBL: RGBELoader HDR with EquirectangularReflectionMapping → scene.environment (optionally scene.background with backgroundBlurriness 0–1), PMREMGenerator for correct reflections. Explicit warning: there is no verified three/addons ContactShadows — don't import that path; camera layers control visibility, not per-mesh light linking.
- **Reference / source:** Three.js family (PART 12); Three.js r183 lighting API and addons (RectAreaLightUniformsLib, RGBELoader, PMREMGenerator, LightProbeGenerator).
- **Best for:** Any 3D hero or viewer — the three-point rig is the fastest route from "flat render" to "photographed product", and the shadow-map sizing/bias numbers prevent the two classic failures (fuzzy shadows, acne). Pairs with ⟦S0259⟧ materials and ⟦S0255⟧ setup.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0260⟧
## ⟦S0261⟧ threejs-geometry — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity), Three.js family
- **What it is:** The geometry reference for Three.js: every built-in shape, custom BufferGeometry built from raw vertex arrays, and the ways to render many copies cheaply (InstancedMesh, InstancedBufferGeometry, BatchedMesh). A code skill, not a design — it supplies the shapes any WebGL scene is built from.
- **How it looks:** Whatever 3D forms the scene needs on screen: boxes, spheres, cylinders and cones, torus and torus-knot rings, lathe-turned and extruded profiles, beveled 3D text, point clouds (the example scatters 1,000 points through a 10-unit cube), line drawings and white wireframe/edge overlays on solid shapes, and fields of up to 1,000 instanced copies of one shape, each with its own position, rotation, scale and colour.
- **Frame by frame:** Geometry itself is static once built. The one motion it defines is morph targets: a mesh blends continuously from its base shape toward a stored second shape as `morphTargetInfluences[0]` runs 0 → 1 (the worked example stretches a segmented box 2× wider in X and squashes it to 0.5× in Y, shown at a 50% blend). All other motion comes from the scene's animation loop, covered by ⟦S0265⟧.
- **Mechanism & key values:** BufferGeometry with typed arrays (position/normal 3 floats per vertex, UV 2, colour 3–4; Uint16 indices up to 65,535 vertices, Uint32 beyond). Sphere quality steps: 16×16 segments performance, 32×32 good, 64×64 high. EdgesGeometry threshold angle 15°. TextGeometry: curveSegments 12, bevelThickness 0.03, bevelSize 0.02, bevelSegments 5. ExtrudeGeometry example: depth 1, bevelThickness/bevelSize 0.1, bevelSegments 3. TubeGeometry: 64 tubular segments, radius 0.2, 8 radial segments. InstancedMesh example count 1,000 spread over a 20-unit cube; BatchedMesh noted as the r183 multi-geometry alternative. Merging requires identical attribute layouts; dispose geometry when done.
- **Reference / source:** threejs-geometry/references/detailed-guide.md, bundled in full inside the skill; targets Three.js r183 with pinned core/addons versions. Cross-references threejs-fundamentals, threejs-materials, threejs-shaders.
- **Best for:** Supporting skill for any WebGL/3D section — building the actual meshes behind a 3D hero, a product/configurator viewer, or an instanced decorative field. Never the starting point for a design; pair with ⟦S0265⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0261⟧

## ⟦S0262⟧ threejs-postprocessing — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity), Three.js family
- **What it is:** The screen-space effects pipeline for Three.js: an EffectComposer chain of passes (render → effects → output) covering bloom, depth of field, ambient occlusion, anti-aliasing, film grain, vignette, glitch, halftone, pixelation, outlines and custom shaders.
- **How it looks:** The finished 3D image, graded like film: bright objects haloed with soft glow (bloom), backgrounds melting out of focus behind a sharp subject (bokeh depth of field), contact shadows deepened in crevices (SSAO), corners darkened (vignette), a fine grain over everything (film pass), or stylised looks — print-style halftone dots, chunky pixels, RGB-split chromatic aberration at the frame edges, white outline halos around selected objects.
- **Frame by frame:** Every frame of the animation loop runs through `composer.render()` instead of the plain renderer, so effects are continuous: bloom breathes with whatever brightens, the bokeh focus distance can be updated per frame to follow a moving target, and the glitch pass (with `goWild` on) tears the image with continuous random RGB displacement. Passes can be toggled at runtime (`pass.enabled`) to switch looks or quality tiers.
- **Mechanism & key values:** UnrealBloomPass defaults strength 1.5, radius 0.4, threshold 0.85 (a subtler combined stack uses 0.5 / 0.4 / 0.85); selective bloom via Layers (layer 1) plus a second composer and an additive mix shader. SSAOPass kernelRadius 16, minDistance 0.005, maxDistance 0.1. BokehPass focus 10.0, aperture 0.025, maxblur 0.01. FilmPass intensity 0.35. VignetteShader offset ≈ 0.95–1.0, darkness 1.0. RenderPixelatedPass pixel size 6. HalftonePass radius 4, shapes 1 = dot, 2 = ellipse, 3 = line, 4 = square. OutlinePass edgeStrength 3, edgeGlow 0, edgeThickness 1, pulsePeriod 0. Custom chromatic-aberration shader amount 0.005. Ordering rules: OutputPass exactly once after linear-space effects; SMAA before OutputPass, FXAA after it (FXAA resolution uniform = 1 / (size × pixelRatio)); never stack legacy GammaCorrectionShader with OutputPass. WebGPU (r183) uses the node-based RenderPipeline instead — EffectComposer is WebGL-only. Each pass costs a full-screen render; quality gating by measured GPU time is prescribed.
- **Reference / source:** threejs-postprocessing/references/detailed-guide.md, bundled in full inside the skill; Three.js r183 addons (EffectComposer, RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, OutputPass and the other named passes).
- **Best for:** Giving a WebGL hero or 3D showcase its finished, filmed look — glow, focus and grade over a scene built with ⟦S0261⟧/⟦S0264⟧/⟦S0265⟧. Heavy: budget it as a whole-page cost decision, not a per-section extra.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0262⟧

## ⟦S0263⟧ threejs-loaders — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity), Three.js family
- **What it is:** The asset-loading layer for Three.js: GLTF/GLB models, textures, cube and HDR environments, the other model formats (OBJ/MTL, FBX, STL, PLY), LoadingManager progress tracking, promise wrappers, caching, compression decoders and error handling.
- **How it looks:** Mostly invisible plumbing with three visible products: a loading progress readout driven by `onProgress` (loaded ÷ total × 100, formatted to one decimal), a wireframe placeholder box standing where a model will appear and then being swapped for the real model when it lands, and the environment itself — a skybox or HDR backdrop wrapping the scene and lighting the PBR materials.
- **Frame by frame:** Progress events fire asset by asset until `onLoad` fires once when all are complete; failed assets are collected and reported instead of silently missing. Animations baked into a loaded GLTF play through an AnimationMixer that must be updated with the frame delta. Loading itself has no other motion; placeholders and progress UI are the builder's own.
- **Mechanism & key values:** DRACOLoader decoder path pinned to draco 1.5.6 (gstatic); KTX2Loader transcoder path pinned to three@0.183.0 (jsDelivr); MeshoptDecoder supported as the r183 alternative that often beats Draco on animated meshes. FBX models typically scaled 0.01. Loaded models get shadows enabled by traversal and envMapIntensity adjusted (0.5 in the example); models are centred and normalised by their bounding box (scale = 1 ÷ max dimension). Retry helper: up to 3 attempts with backoff of 1000 × (attempt + 1) ms; fetch timeout default 30,000 ms via AbortController. `THREE.Cache.enabled = true` for built-in caching; the custom AssetManager example has no in-flight deduplication (stated honestly in the source). Security rules: allowlist remote origins, bound file/dimension/decode budgets, self-host decoder files where possible.
- **Reference / source:** threejs-loaders/references/detailed-guide.md, bundled in full inside the skill; Three.js r183 addons (GLTFLoader, DRACOLoader, KTX2Loader, RGBELoader, EXRLoader, OBJLoader/MTLLoader, FBXLoader, STLLoader, PLYLoader).
- **Best for:** Any 3D section that loads real assets — a modelled product, a vehicle, a house — and for the loading state in front of a WebGL hero. Pair with ⟦S0264⟧ for what the loaded textures then need.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0263⟧

## ⟦S0264⟧ threejs-textures — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity), Three.js family
- **What it is:** The texture reference for Three.js: loading and configuring image textures, colour space, wrapping and filtering, the full PBR map set, cube/HDR environments, render targets, dynamic CubeCamera reflections, UV channels, atlases and procedural (canvas/data) textures.
- **How it looks:** Surfaces with real material behaviour: a brick or wood image tiled seamlessly across a wall, crisp texture at glancing angles (max anisotropic filtering), a metal panel reflecting a live environment, a television-like plane playing actual video (VideoTexture), a scene background softened by background blur, and fully PBR surfaces where normal, roughness, metalness, ambient-occlusion, emissive and displacement maps combine into lit, tactile material.
- **Frame by frame:** Two texture types move on their own: VideoTexture updates every frame automatically once the video plays (muted autoplay, with a user-gesture fallback required), and a CubeCamera re-renders the whole environment into a cube render target each animation frame so reflections track moving objects — flagged in the source as expensive. Everything else is a static setting applied at setup.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Colour rule: albedo/canvas colour maps get `SRGBColorSpace`; data maps (normal, roughness, metalness, AO) stay in NoColorSpace. Wrapping: ClampToEdge (default), Repeat, MirroredRepeat; repeat/offset in 0–1 units, rotation about `center` (0.5, 0.5). Filters: LinearMipmapLinear minification default, Linear magnification default, Nearest for a pixelated look. Sizes: power-of-two 256–2048, 2048 usually sufficient for web, 1024 suggested for mobile. AO maps read the second UV channel (`uv1`, texture.channel = 1). Displacement example displacementScale 0.1. Render targets 512×512 in the examples, MSAA samples 4; depth texture UnsignedShortType. CubeCamera: near 0.1, far 1000, 256px cube target with mipmaps. Background controls: backgroundBlurriness 0–1, backgroundIntensity, backgroundRotation. KTX2/Basis compression recommended for delivery; r183 note that KTX2Loader now handles BC3 alpha correctly.
- **Reference / source:** threejs-textures/references/detailed-guide.md, bundled in full inside the skill; API references named at the end: threejs.org Texture and MeshStandardMaterial doc pages.
- **Best for:** Material realism in any WebGL section — tiled cladding, timber, stone and metal surfaces for trade-site 3D, environment reflections on a product viewer. Supporting skill for ⟦S0261⟧/⟦S0265⟧ scenes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0264⟧

## ⟦S0265⟧ threejs-skills — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity), Three.js family
- **What it is:** The umbrella Three.js skill: a systematic end-to-end workflow for building an interactive 3D scene — imports, scene/camera/renderer setup, geometry, materials, lighting, animation loop, interaction (orbit controls, raycasting, mouse parallax, scroll), particles, and production optimisation. The entry point to the whole threejs-* family in this part.
- **How it looks:** A live 3D scene in the page: an object (the worked example is a smooth sphere) lit by ambient plus directional light, rotating continuously; the camera swings gently as the visitor moves the mouse; a hovered object swells to 1.2× scale and the cursor turns to a pointer; a field of 1,000 white particles floats in space; soft shadows fall across a ground plane; distance fog fades the far edge of the scene.
- **Frame by frame:** The render loop (`renderer.setAnimationLoop`, preferred over requestAnimationFrame) drives everything: the example increments rotation by 0.01 on X and Y per frame (the guide itself warns to use elapsed seconds for refresh-rate-independent motion); mouse movement re-aims the camera each frame (camera.position.x/y = mouse × 2, lookAt centre); scrolling rotates the object (rotation.y = scrollY × 0.001) and dollies the camera down the page (camera.position.y = −(scrollY ÷ window height) × 10); GSAP, when used, runs property tweens on timelines (a 2 s full rotation with a scale doubling starting 1 s early). Hover raycasting runs inside the loop, resetting all scales then enlarging the hit object.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Import map pinned to three@0.183.0 via jsDelivr; PerspectiveCamera FOV 75 in the template (45–75° called typical), near 0.1, far 1000, camera z = 5; renderer antialias true, ACESFilmicToneMapping at exposure 1.0, outputColorSpace SRGB. Particles: start 1,000–5,000 points spread over a 10-unit cube, PointsMaterial size 0.02, to hold 60 fps. Shadows: PCFSoftShadowMap, directional shadow map 2048×2048, shadow camera near 0.5 / far 50. Custom pointer controls: drag factor 0.005, wheel zoom clamped between 2 and 20 at deltaY × 0.01, single-pointer capture with touchAction none. LOD switch distances 0 / 10 / 50. InstancedMesh example 1,000 instances. Fog: linear near 10 far 50, or FogExp2 density 0.02. r183 notes: THREE.Timer replaces Clock, WebGPURenderer + TSL as the alternative pipeline. Boundaries stated: respect reduced motion, pause offscreen work, cap pixel ratio and asset size, dispose everything on teardown.
- **Reference / source:** threejs-skills/references/detailed-guide.md, bundled in full inside the skill; defers to threejs-postprocessing (⟦S0262⟧) for effects and the sibling threejs-* skills for depth. Recommended production stack named in the source: Three.js r183 + Vite, GSAP, optional React Three Fiber / Drei / Leva.
- **Best for:** Any WebGL hero or interactive 3D moment — a rotating product, a scroll-driven 3D journey, a particle backdrop. This is the scene-level skill; ⟦S0261⟧–⟦S0264⟧ are its specialists.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0265⟧

## ⟦S0266⟧ react-ui-patterns — PART 12 — MCP Market (ECC + Antigravity)
- **What it is:** A pattern set for React UI states: when to show loading indicators, skeletons vs spinners, the error-handling hierarchy, empty states, and button/form submission states. Rules and code shapes, not a visual design.
- **How it looks:** The states a visitor actually meets: skeleton placeholders shaped like the coming list or cards on a first load; no spinner at all when cached data already exists (so refetches never flash); recoverable failures as toast notifications; page-level failures as a banner over still-usable data; a full error state with an exclamation icon, a plain heading ("Something went wrong"), one sentence of explanation and a Try Again button; contextual empty states — a search icon with "No results found / Try different search terms", or a plus-circle with "No items yet" and a Create Item action; submit buttons that disable and show their loading state while a form sends.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The prescribed sequence is a state order, not an animation: error first, then loading-only-when-there-is-no-data, then empty, then content — evaluated in that order on every render.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The golden rule: show a loading indicator only when there is no data to display. Skeleton when the content shape is known (lists, cards, initial page load); spinner when it is not (modal actions, button submissions, inline operations). Error hierarchy, in order: inline field error → toast (recoverable) → error banner (page-level, partial data usable) → full error screen (unrecoverable). Every mutation carries an onError that surfaces a toast; buttons are always disabled during async operations; every collection ships an explicit empty state. Ships with a completion checklist covering UI states and mutation feedback.
- **Reference / source:** The skill itself names no external site; it cross-references sibling skills graphql-schema, testing-patterns and formik-patterns, none of which are this entry's source.
- **Best for:** The state behaviour of any data-driven or form section — quote/contact forms, review feeds, project galleries that load — on trade sites as much as apps. Governs what a form does while sending and after failing, which is where hand-rolled builds most often strand the visitor.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0266⟧

## ⟦S0267⟧ 1weiho/cinematic-shot — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A complete directing and cinematography method for filming software UI like a movie: a sequence of steep, oblique, extreme close-up "hero shots" of a real interface floating on a stage — a black void for dark products, a high-key warm-grey studio for light ones — with a razor-thin focal plane, a slow motivated camera drift, and UI that acts on its own, hard-cut on the action, ending on one line of copy and a still logo. The same method also shoots stills (hero images, key visuals, OG/social cards) with a re-set photographer's camera.
- **How it looks:** The product as a physical slab tilted away from the camera, text running diagonally across the frame and shrinking into the distance, only one line or control sharp while everything near and far melts into bokeh. On the dark stage a soft pool of neutral light lies on the UI plane around the subject and the rest falls to true black (average frame luminance about 7–10%); on the light stage a white slab floats over a warm light-grey ground (#EAE7E2) with a soft cast shadow, nothing falling to black, bokeh reading as pale haze. The only colour anywhere is the product's own.
- **Frame by frame:** Per shot: the cut lands with the subject already arriving; the action starts within 0.3–0.8 s — a nav item highlights itself, a prompt types at 12–13 characters per second with a solid caret, file names turn into inline chips as they complete; on send the composer clears and the message rises into the thread (fade + 12 px rise + blur clearing over 0.35 s); a generated reply streams in line by line, each line condensing out of a fine stipple of dots over about 0.5 s, staggered ~0.1 s per line; all the while the camera tracks 3–10% of the frame width along the reading direction (20–35% for a long pan), pushes in 1–5%, turns 0.5–4°, never stopping; when attention moves, focus racks to the new subject over 0.4–0.8 s and the light pool trails after it, lagging 0.3–0.5 s; the result holds 0.5–1 s, then a hard cut — camera still moving — to the next setup with the diagonal flipped. The single wide shot (whole window, near-frontal) is saved for the payoff. Ending: a 0.4 s blur-and-fade to the empty stage, the copy line un-blurs from ~16 px while fading up over 0.6–1 s, holds 3–5 s, then a cut or 0.3 s dissolve to the motionless logo, held 4–5 s. A full film runs 45–55 s: 8–10 UI shots, process shots 5–9 s alternating with 2–3.5 s punctuation shots, median ~5 s. Sound is foley only — a tick per typed character, a soft click on selection, a whoosh on send, granular hiss under streaming — no music at all.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Camera: pitch (tilt back) 30–50°, in-plane roll ±10–20° (sign flips per shot), yaw ±5–15°, perspective distance 0.6–0.75× frame width (1100–1400 px at 1080p); near text 1.4–1.8× far text. Scales (magnification at the focal point): extreme macro 5–7×, macro 2.5–4×, medium 1.5–2.5×, wide 0.8–1.1× (payoff only, pitch 8–12°, no roll, yaw ±3°). Depth of field: sharp band 4–8% of frame height at extreme macro up to 50–70% on the wide; max blur 24 px down to 6 px; UI must be rasterised at the magnification (e.g. 6×), never upscaled. Light pool: spill radius on screen 0.32–0.38 of frame width (extreme macro) to 0.70–0.80 (wide), core 0.35–0.45 of spill, core offset 8–15% toward the key; a soft flag cuts one side in about a third of shots; the pool grows 20–40% as content streams. Light stage: key darkens at most ~12%, radii 1.6× the dark spill, no flags; slab shadow 0 26px 40px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.18) plus 0 1px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.10), corner radius 14 px. Motion recipes: select pill slides 0.35 s ease-in-out; press scales to 0.97 over 0.08 s and back over 0.2 s; appear = opacity 0→1, translateY 12→0, blur 6→0 over 0.35 s on cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1); diagram connectors draw via stroke-dashoffset over 0.4–0.6 s; scrolling 120–250 px/s. Outro type ~90 px at 1080p, weight 500, tracking −0.02 em; logo mark ~115 px tall. Render: 1920×1080 at 60 fps, motion blur 4+ sub-frames at a 180° shutter, fine luma grain (ffmpeg noise strength ~4 dark stage, ~3 light); preview first at 960×540, 30 fps, 2 sub-frames. Stills change the camera: perspective 2–2.4× frame width, diagonal from a whole-camera roll of 6–10° with the plane level, near:far text only 1.2–1.4×, subject whole and at least 8% of frame height from every edge, rendered at 2× and Lanczos-downsampled, lighter static grain (~2 dark, ~1.5 light), delivered as lossless PNG.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/1weiho/cinematic-shot (skills/cinematic-shot/SKILL.md), with both reference files bundled in full inside the skill: references/look.md (exact camera, DOF, light, grade and still recipes) and references/shot-list-example.md (a complete 52-second, 9-shot example film plus a 5-still set).
- **Best for:** Launch films, product trailers and cinematic hero/key stills of a software interface — for trade-site work, chiefly the stills method applied to a configurator, quote tool or dashboard the client sells. Specialist and heavy; the oblique macro + shallow-focus look is also a strong reference for how a single UI detail should be photographed for a hero image.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0267⟧

## ⟦S0268⟧ aashaexo/humanize ("soundshuman") — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A writing-editor skill that strips AI tells out of prose: a 41-pattern catalog plus statistical checks, run as a draft → audit → final loop, preserving every fact while changing the shape of the writing. Text only — it produces no visuals.
- **How it looks:** The output reads as plain human prose: sentence-case headings instead of Title Case, no em or en dashes anywhere, boldface and emoji decoration removed, inline-header bullet lists collapsed into sentences, paragraph lengths visibly uneven, the same clear word repeated instead of synonym-cycled, and specific facts standing where vague importance claims were.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** 41 numbered patterns in seven groups (content 1–6, language 7–15, style 16–24, communication 25–30, filler/hedging 31–36, rhetoric/cadence 37–41), plus statistical tells: burstiness (sentence-length variation), type-token ratio (human 0.5–0.7 vs AI 0.3–0.5), trigram repetition, paragraph uniformity. Hard rules: the final rewrite contains zero U+2014/U+2013 dashes unless the user's own writing sample uses them (a sample outranks the style rules); never invent a fact, name, number or citation. The bundled `sloplint` CLI measures the four statistical signals — a score above 25 sends the text back for another pass. Four invocation modes: pasted text (deliver draft, audit bullets, final), file (rewrite in place, prose only, git-first), repo audit (rank files, rewrite only chosen ones), embedded (final text only). False-positive guardrails are explicit: clusters of tells, not isolated ones; curly quotes, em dashes or polish alone prove nothing.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/aashaexo/soundshuman (SKILL.md); the catalog merges Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" (via blader/humanizer), Hardik Pandya's Stop Slop structural rules, and brandonwise/humanizer's statistical detection; bundled references include vocabulary.md, phrases.md, structures.md, style-guide.md, checklist.md.
- **Best for:** Humanising the copy on any built page — hero lines, section text, about copy, email drafts — before delivery. Pairs with ⟦S0269⟧: this one has the CLI-verified statistical pass and repo mode; that one has the numeric score and voice profiles.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0268⟧

## ⟦S0269⟧ Aboudjem/humanizer — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A Markdown-only, zero-dependency skill that detects 55 AI writing patterns, optionally scores the text 0–100 for AI-tell density, and rewrites it in one of five voice profiles so it reads like a specific person wrote it. Three modes: detect, rewrite (default), edit (in place).
- **How it looks:** Rewritten prose with a visible pulse: contractions and first person in the casual voice, sentence fragments, paragraphs that vary from four sentences to a single line, specific numbers standing where abstractions were ("cuts p99 latency from 900ms to 40ms"), and — with `--score` — a `[Score: NN/100]` header line above the result. Nothing else visual; it is a text tool.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** 55 patterns P1–P55 across six categories: Content 8, Language & Style 10, Communication 3, Filler & Hedging 9, Emerging 13, Craft & Forensic 12. Voices: casual, professional, technical, warm, blunt; purpose layers: essay, email, marketing, technical, general. Score formula: `score = 4 × patterns_hit + 25 × (1 − burstiness_normalized) + 15 × vocabulary_blacklist_ratio`, clamped 0–100; bands 0–20 pristine, 21–40 mostly human, 41–60 mixed, 61–80 AI-leaning, 81–100 pure AI smell. Burstiness target: mix 3–8, 12–20 and 25–40-word sentences, never 3+ consecutive sentences of similar length. Tiered vocabulary: Tier 1A evidence-grade words (delve, tapestry, testament, multifaceted, realm, interplay, "in today's … landscape") flag alone; Tier 1B wordiness-grade (underscore, leverage as verbs) weigh less; Tier 2 flags at 2+ per paragraph; Tier 3 never flags alone. P13 sets zero tolerance for the em dash (U+2014). Flags: --score, --iterate up to 3 detect-rewrite loops, --aggressive, --purpose, --openings N, --ignore-code, --ignore-quotes. Honest limits stated in the source: under ~40 words there is not enough signal to score; a model grading its own output inflates the result, so the score is a signal, not a verdict. Auto-loads a project `humanizer-context.md` for brand samples and banned phrases when present.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/Aboudjem/humanizer-skill (skills/humanizer/SKILL.md); deep pattern detail in references/patterns.md, a provisional Chinese appendix in references/patterns.zh.md, always-on templates in references/always-on-templates.md. The non-native-English caution cites Liang et al., arXiv:2304.02819.
- **Best for:** Pre-publication copy passes where a number is wanted — blog posts, READMEs, LinkedIn posts, landing-page text — and in-place Markdown edits. Overlaps ⟦S0268⟧; choose this one for the score and voice profiles, that one for CLI measurement and repo audits.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0269⟧

## ⟦S0270⟧ AccessLint/accessibility-diff — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A regression check that diffs a live page's accessibility violations against a baseline — by default your uncommitted changes (stash-based), or a named branch with `--branch` — and reports only what changed: new violations, fixed ones, and the count of pre-existing ones. It locates; it does not fix.
- **How it looks:** A compact terminal-style report: a header line with the target, the comparison and the rule count (the worked example reads "Accessibility diff — http://localhost:3000/ vs main (94 rules, live DOM)" then "2 new · 1 fixed · 4 pre-existing hidden"), new violations grouped by impact with the measured evidence (e.g. "color-contrast — 2.1:1 (needs 4.5:1), #bbb on #fff"), the selector path ("main > p.subtitle"), a concrete fix ("darken to #767676"), and fixed items listed by rule and element. No page visuals are produced.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The run sequence is: warn the user, stash changes, scan and snapshot the baseline, restore, wait ~2 s for hot reload, scan again, compare.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Runs the @accesslint/cli scan over CDP against a debuggable Chrome whose port comes from `@accesslint/chrome ensure` (never hardcode 9222). Baseline snapshot written to /tmp with --update-snapshot; second scan as JSON. Flags pass through to both runs: --selector, --wait-for (the rebuild gate in branch mode, where the CLI opens a fresh tab per run), --include-aaa. CLI exit code 2 means a bad URL/target or a page that never loaded. Caveat stated in the source: a target name only resolves identically in both runs if accesslint.config.json is unchanged across the stash/checkout; large DOM changes cause selector drift, in which case re-run a full scan.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/AccessLint/claude-marketplace (plugins/accesslint/skills/accessibility-diff/SKILL.md); shared conventions in the plugin's shared/methodology.md.
- **Best for:** A pre-merge or pre-launch gate on any build — "did this change break accessibility?" — and CI. The natural companion to ⟦S0271⟧ (find) and ⟦S0275⟧ (fix).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0270⟧

## ⟦S0271⟧ AccessLint/accessibility-scan — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The automated tier of the AccessLint suite: run the @accesslint/core rule engine over a live page's rendered DOM and return a worklist of every mechanically detectable WCAG 2.2 violation, each grounded to its DOM selector and, where source mapping exists, its file:line. It locates; it does not edit.
- **How it looks:** A report that opens with counts by impact, then one entry per violation: the selector verbatim (plus file:line and symbol when source is present; if no violation has source, the report says "source mapping unavailable; located by selector only"), the evidence (a contrast ratio, a missing attribute, an empty accessible name), and a fix — either the mechanical change or the words NEEDS HUMAN.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. One scan run against the loaded page; flags can wait for async content (--wait-for) or scope the run to one component (--selector).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Invocation: `npx @accesslint/cli@latest scan <target> --port <port from chrome ensure> --format json`; the target is a URL, a config target name from accesslint.config.json, or empty for the config default. Optional --include-aaa widens the rule set to AAA; --disable turns named rules off; per-target flags can be pinned in the config. Chrome is torn down afterwards unless ensure reported it unmanaged. Exit code 2 = bad URL/target or page never loaded; an unknown target name makes the CLI list the available targets.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/AccessLint/claude-marketplace (plugins/accesslint/skills/accessibility-scan/SKILL.md); shared conventions in the plugin's shared/methodology.md.
- **Best for:** The first accessibility pass over any single built page — a preview homepage before it is shown or sent. Hands-on checks it cannot decide belong to ⟦S0273⟧; whole-site conformance to ⟦S0272⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0271⟧

## ⟦S0272⟧ AccessLint/audit-and-fix — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Despite the catalog name, the bundled source is the AccessLint **accessibility-audit** skill: a full WCAG 2.2 audit of a whole site or product following the WCAG-EM methodology — scope, explore, sample, evaluate, report — producing one conformance report. It assesses only; fixes belong to ⟦S0275⟧ and regression diffs to ⟦S0270⟧.
- **How it looks:** A structured report: scope (target and boundary, goal level, technologies, the assistive-technology baseline reserved for human testing), the sample (structured pages with reasons, plus a random set), a per-criterion conformance summary (counts and bare SC lists for pass / fail / undetermined / N/A), findings grouped by severity with evidence-basis tags, a human-required handoff section naming the functional ability, the AT and the flow for each item, and recommendations led by root-cause fixes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The evaluation itself is a sequence: each sampled page or state is delegated to its own subagent task, which runs ⟦S0271⟧'s scan first, then the manual inspect tier (⟦S0273⟧) against the same rendered state, deduplicating by success-criterion ownership before checking — the engine owns rule-detectable criteria, inspect owns interaction and judgment criteria, and where both cover the same SC at the same element the scan result wins.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Default goal WCAG 2.2 AA (--level AAA adds AAA criteria). Two axes kept separate on every finding: evidence basis — ● verified (deterministic, cited proof; the only basis that can assert pass/fail), ◐ flagged (evidence captured, a person decides), ○ human-required (needs AT or lived experience; handed off, never emulated) — and severity: critical, serious, moderate, minor. Conformance is per success criterion across the whole sample: one sampled page failing an SC fails it for the scope at that level; every ◐, ○ or not-exercised criterion is reported undetermined, never as a pass. Sampling combines a structured set (entry page, each key flow end to end, every new template or complex widget, important states such as modals, wizards, empty and error states) with a small random set. A one- or two-page scope runs the tiers inline instead of spawning tasks.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/AccessLint/claude-marketplace (plugins/accesslint/skills/accessibility-audit/SKILL.md); doctrine in the plugin's shared/methodology.md; methodology is W3C WCAG-EM.
- **Best for:** A whole-site conformance verdict before handover — the audit a finished homepage-plus-inner-pages build gets when "is it accessible?" must be answered per criterion, with an honest list of what only human AT testing can settle.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0272⟧

## ⟦S0273⟧ AccessLint/contrast-checker — PART 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Despite the catalog name, the bundled source is the AccessLint **accessibility-inspect** skill: the semi-automated manual tier of a WCAG assessment — driving a live page through the checks a rule engine cannot decide (keyboard operation, focus order and visibility, screen-reader names/roles/states from the accessibility tree, reflow and zoom, reduced motion, form errors, target size) and grading every finding by evidence basis and severity. ⟦S0274⟧ and ⟦S0276⟧ bundle this same skill body under other names.
- **How it looks:** A report headed by a compact ledger — severity counts, evidence-basis counts, and bare success-criterion numbers sorted into pass ● / fail ● / flagged ◐○ / engine-owned / N/A / not-exercised buckets — followed by findings grouped by basis: verified items with selector and reproduction (the example: "[serious] Keyboard trap in date picker — SC 2.1.2, where: div.datepicker[role=dialog], repro: Tab into grid, focus never exits via Tab or Esc"), flagged items with their evidence (a focus-ghost screenshot and a measured outline of 1px rgba(0,0,0,.2), with an opinion and what a person should confirm), and human-required handoffs naming the AT and the flow exercised.
- **Frame by frame:** The checking itself is the motion: one full snapshot after the wait gate; then a single batched keyboard walk — one script computes the tabbable sequence and focuses each element in order, recording its selector, role/name, the computed outline/box-shadow it shows on :focus, its bounding box (which settles the 24×24 target-size criterion on the spot) and whether a sticky or overlay element covers it. Real Tab/Esc key presses are spent only at suspect widgets (roving-tabindex composites, aria-activedescendant widgets, handlers that might trap). After any state change, only the changed widget is re-read, never the whole page. Resize passes exercise reflow and 200% zoom.
