## ⟦S0311⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-animation — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The complete three.js animation reference (targets r186): keyframe clips and tracks, the AnimationMixer/Action playback system, playing glTF animations, skeletal posing, morph targets, clip blending and crossfades, procedural motion, and GPU animation with WebGPU/TSL oscillators. The system runs on the CPU and never touches the renderer, so the same clips drive a model identically under WebGLRenderer and WebGPURenderer.
- **How it looks:** Visitor-facing, this is what makes a 3D hero object move: a model spins frame-rate-independently (rotation advanced by delta, not per-frame increments), bobs on absolute time (`position.y = sin(elapsed × 2) × 0.25` in the quick start), a character walks, crossfades into idle, a face smiles as a morph weight rises, a subdivided plane ripples on the GPU. Nothing has a fixed "look" — the look is whatever the clips and curves define.
- **Frame by frame:** Load → clips are parsed (glTF animations arrive as AnimationClips); an action is scheduled with `play()`. Each frame → `timer.update()` first, then `mixer.update(delta)` samples every active action and writes values into ordinary object properties; procedural overrides (e.g. a head bone turning) are applied after the mixer update or the clip overwrites them. Crossfade → `idle.crossFadeTo(walk, 0.4)` ramps weights over 0.4 s (optionally warping both time scales so cycle lengths match); `fadeIn`/`fadeOut` do the same one-sided. Loop end → `finished` / `loop` events fire on the mixer; with LoopOnce + `clampWhenFinished` the model holds its final pose instead of resetting. Scrubbing and reverse are direct: `action.time = 0.5`, `action.timeScale = -1`, `action.paused = true`, `action.halt(0.3)` decelerates to a stop in 0.3 s.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Track name grammar `nodeName.objectName[objectIndex].propertyName[propertyIndex]` (`.position[y]`, `.morphTargetInfluences[smile]`, `Hips.position` for bones). Track types and value sizes: Number 1, Vector 3, Quaternion 4 (quaternions, not Euler angles), Color 3, Boolean (always discrete). `values.length` must equal `times.length × valueSize` or playback samples wrong values / `play()` never returns. Interpolation: InterpolateLinear (default), InterpolateSmooth (cubic), InterpolateDiscrete (step), InterpolateBezier (absolute time/value tangents, two numbers per keyframe per component). Loops: LoopOnce, LoopRepeat (default, Infinity), LoopPingPong. Blending by weight: `setEffectiveWeight` mixes poses (speed 0–5 mapped to run weight 0–1 in the worked example); additive clips are re-based on frame 0 with `AnimationUtils.makeClipAdditive`. Morph targets: full-size position/normal attributes beside the base; influence 0 = base shape, 1 = full target, driven procedurally or by a Number track (never a String track). Procedural motion: exponential approach `MathUtils.damp(current, target, lambda, delta)` — higher lambda snaps faster, frame-rate independent. Performance rules: one clip set can feed any number of mixers (share, don't copy; duplicate characters via `SkeletonUtils.clone`, never `model.clone()`, which shares the skeleton); update only visible/about-to-be-visible mixers; a SkinnedMesh's bounding sphere is computed once, so far-moving clips need `computeBoundingSphere()` after update or `frustumCulled = false`; free a mixer with `stopAllAction()` + `uncacheRoot()`. WebGPU/TSL: `time` and `deltaTime` are renderer-refreshed float uniforms; oscillators `oscSine / oscSquare / oscTriangle / oscSawtooth` return 0–1 waves with a 1-second period; per-vertex motion is built on `positionLocal` (which already carries skinning, morphs, batching and instancing), never `positionGeometry`. Timer discipline throughout: `THREE.Timer` + `timer.connect(document)` replaces the deprecated Clock (r183); call `timer.update()` first each frame or `getDelta()` reads ~0 and the mixer stalls.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-animation/SKILL.md (targets three.js r186). Sibling skills named inside: threejs-fundamentals, threejs-loaders, threejs-shaders.
- **Best for:** Any animated 3D on a homepage: a hero product/model that idles, rotates or reacts, a configurator model that poses or opens, scroll- or hover-driven morphs, character motion in a WebGL scene. The crossfade, additive-blend and morph recipes are the direct tools for "the 3D moves like it's alive" without cartoonish looping.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0311⟧

## ⟦S0312⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-asset-pipeline — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The offline pipeline for shrinking glTF assets before they reach a three.js page, built on gltf-transform: inspect and validate a model, then compress geometry (Draco / meshopt / quantization), compress textures (KTX2 / WebP / AVIF), cut draw calls (weld, simplify, join, instance, dedup, prune), with the exact loader wiring each output then requires, scripted pipelines, and gltfjsx for React.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing design of its own — its visible result is a heavy 3D hero or configurator that loads fast and still looks identical: the same model, at a fraction of the bytes, with `inspect` before/after tables proving which table (meshes, textures, animations) the savings came from.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. It governs the load sequence: `inspect` → `optimize` (or individual passes) → `inspect` again → load with the matching decoders attached, or the load throws.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Core command: `optimize` chains dedup → instance → palette → flatten → join → weld → simplify → resample → prune → sparse, then texture compression, geometry compression last. Defaults: `--compress meshopt`, `--texture-compress auto` (original format), `--texture-size 2048`, simplify ratio 0 / error 0.0001, instance `--min 5`. Codec trade-offs: Draco compresses triangle geometry only (not animation, morphs, textures, points, lines; quantize-position 14 in the worked command) and needs DRACOLoader; meshopt covers point/line/triangle geometry, morphs and animation, decodes very fast, pairs with gzip/brotli, needs MeshoptDecoder; quantize stores floats as 8/16-bit integers (KHR_mesh_quantization) with no runtime decoder. Textures: KTX2 stays compressed in GPU memory (UASTC for normal/occlusion/metallic-roughness slots, ETC1S for everything else — the split `optimize --texture-compress ktx2` applies automatically; `etc1s --quality 128`, `uastc --level 4` for single-bitstream runs; needs the `ktx` CLI from KTX-Software 4.4.0+) while WebP/AVIF (`webp --quality 80`, quality range 1–100) shrink download only and expand 4–8× in GPU memory. Scene passes: `weld` before `simplify` and `meshopt`; `simplify --ratio 0.5 --error 0.001` is lossy, `--lock-border true` preserves open edges; `instance` writes EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing (skips animated files, instances must share materials); `join` can inflate vertex count on heavily reused meshes — instance there instead. Ordering law: geometry compression (draco / meshopt / optimize) is always the last command, because every other rewriting command decodes compressed geometry and writes it back uncompressed. Runtime contract is read from `extensionsRequired` (KHR_draco_mesh_compression, EXT_meshopt_compression, KHR_texture_basisu each map to loader wiring; quantization, GPU instancing, WebP and AVIF textures need none). One shared KTX2Loader per app, `detectSupport(renderer)` mandatory, and under WebGPURenderer only after `await renderer.init()`. `validate` runs the official glTF validator and exits nonzero on errors (CI gate). gltfjsx: `npx gltfjsx model.glb --transform` emits a React component plus a transformed asset with textures capped at 1024 px by default (normal maps JPEG, capped at 2048 px or `--resolution`, whichever is larger).
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-asset-pipeline/SKILL.md (three.js r186; @gltf-transform/cli, KTX-Software, gltfjsx, gltfpack named as the neighbouring tool). Sibling skills: threejs-loaders, threejs-react-three-fiber, threejs-performance.
- **Best for:** Preparing any real 3D model for a trade homepage — a door, roof, window or vehicle configurator model, a hero product GLB — so the 3D earns its place without a multi-megabyte first load. Run it before the loaders skill (⟦S0317⟧) is wired.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0312⟧

## ⟦S0313⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-fundamentals — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The foundation reference for building a three.js scene from scratch (r186): Scene and fog, the four camera types, WebGLRenderer setup and tone mapping, the Timer-driven animation loop, Object3D hierarchies and transforms, core math (Vector3, Matrix4, Quaternion, Color, MathUtils), LoadingManager, cleanup/disposal, and the WebGPURenderer/TSL equivalents of all of it.
- **How it looks:** The scaffold behind every 3D section: a canvas filling its box, a scene with a solid, cube or equirect background (a plain unmapped texture draws as a flat screen-filling quad, not a skybox), linear fog `Fog(color, near, far)` or exponential `FogExp2(color, 0.02)` depth-fading the scene, objects grouped so a parent transform moves the whole subtree, and LOD swaps (full detail at distance 0, lower at 20, lowest at 60 in the worked example) keeping far objects cheap.
- **Frame by frame:** On load → scene, camera and renderer are constructed; under WebGPURenderer nothing renders until `await renderer.init()` completes. Each frame → `timer.update()` first, then transforms advance by `timer.getDelta()` (frame-rate independent), then `renderer.render(scene, camera)` via `renderer.setAnimationLoop` (never a manual requestAnimationFrame loop). On resize → camera aspect is recomputed, `updateProjectionMatrix()` called, renderer resized. On teardown → geometry, materials and their textures are disposed individually (material.dispose() leaves textures alone), `setAnimationLoop(null)`, `renderer.dispose()`, optionally `forceContextLoss()`.
- **Mechanism & key values:** PerspectiveCamera(fov°, aspect, near, far) — worked values 75°, 0.1, 100/1000; OrthographicCamera frustum in world units (frustumHeight 10 example); ArrayCamera renders one viewport per sub-camera (viewports in drawing-buffer pixels under WebGLRenderer — CSS size × pixel ratio; WebGPURenderer scales itself); CubeCamera on a 256-size cube render target for live reflections (hide the reflective mesh while its map updates). Renderer: `setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2))` to cap fill rate; tone mapping ACESFilmic / AgX / Neutral (NoToneMapping default), `toneMappingExposure 1.0`; outputColorSpace is SRGB by default; shadowMap PCFShadowMap default (PCFSoftShadowMap deprecated in r182). Coordinate system: right-handed, +Y up, +Z toward the viewer, an unrotated camera looks down −Z. Object3D: `add()` keeps the child's local transform, `attach()` keeps its world transform; `layers.enable(1)` adds a layer, `set(1)` replaces the mask and removes layer 0 (the classic invisible-mesh bug); `matrixAutoUpdate` true by default. Import maps: WebGL work maps `three` and `three/addons/` to three@0.186.0 on jsDelivr; WebGPU work needs all four keys (`three`, `three/webgpu`, `three/tsl`, `three/addons/`) or the map fails. Disposal law: Object3D.dispose() frees only per-object renderer state — never children, geometry, materials or textures; traverse the subtree. Performance: bounding-sphere frustum culling (recompute after editing positions or moving instances/bones), merge static same-material geometry, InstancedMesh for copies, LOD by distance; WebGLRenderer counters at `renderer.info.render.calls` and `renderer.info.memory` (with `info.autoReset = false` + manual `reset()` for multi-pass frames). WebGPU notes: canvas is transparent by default (set scene.background), built-in materials auto-convert to node versions, anisotropy via `renderer.getMaxAnisotropy()` (no `renderer.capabilities`).
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-fundamentals/SKILL.md (three.js r186). It cross-references every other cloudai-x threejs skill; loaders/textures/lighting/geometry carry the depth per topic.
- **Best for:** The starting scaffold for any WebGL/WebGPU work on a homepage — hero 3D, configurators, interactive scenes — and the checklist (pixel-ratio cap, Timer, disposal, import map) that keeps a hand-built single-file 3D section from leaking memory or stalling.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0313⟧

## ⟦S0314⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-geometry — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The geometry reference (r186): every built-in shape, path-based shapes (lathe, extrude, tube), 3D text, custom BufferGeometry and attributes, interleaved buffers, edges/wireframes, points and lines, and the three draw-call reducers — merging, InstancedMesh and BatchedMesh — plus morph-target geometry, transforms and disposal.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor actually sees in a 3D section is built here: boxes, spheres, cylinders (6 radial segments = a hexagonal prism), cones, tori and torus knots; a profile spun into a lathe solid; a 2D outline extruded with a bevel; text extruded into solid letters; a field of 1,000 points spread over a 10-unit cube; a thousand coloured copies of one small box placed by per-instance matrices in a single draw call.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — geometry itself does not move. Motion built on it (per-frame instance updates, morph influence changes) is flagged honestly in the source: after any batch of `setMatrixAt` calls set `instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true` and call `computeBoundingSphere()` or culling and raycasting go stale; a morph target blends base → target as its influence runs 0 → 1 (0.5 = halfway in the worked example).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Signature values: SphereGeometry(1, 32, 16) — radius, widthSegments, heightSegments, phi/theta start + length (phi sweep π = half sphere, theta length π/2 = dome); CylinderGeometry(radiusTop, radiusBottom, height, radialSegments…); TorusGeometry(1, 0.4, 16, 100); TorusKnotGeometry(1, 0.4, 100, 16, p 2, q 3); CapsuleGeometry(0.5, 1, 4, 8, 1) — its middle-section parameter is `height` (renamed from `length` in r176); polyhedra at detail 0 (icosahedron = 20 faces). Extrude worked values: depth 1, bevelThickness 0.1, bevelSize 0.1, bevelSegments 3. TextGeometry: size 1 world unit, depth 0.2 (renamed from `height` in r163 — an old `height` is ignored and text extrudes the default 50 units), curveSegments 12, bevelThickness 0.03, bevelSize 0.02, from a .typeface.json font via FontLoader. BufferGeometry: attributes are typed arrays with itemSize (position/normal 3, uv 2, color 3); Uint16 indices address vertices 0–65534; Uint8 colours need `normalized = true` or colours blow out to 255; an attribute array cannot grow after first render — allocate the maximum and use `setDrawRange`. EdgesGeometry threshold angle 15° in the example. Points: PointsMaterial size 0.1 with sizeAttenuation (default true) scaling by canvas height / depth. InstancedMesh: one draw call for `count` copies (1,000 in the examples) with per-instance matrix + colour (`setColorAt` creates instanceColor); InstancedBufferGeometry needs `instanceCount` set by hand after `copy()`. BatchedMesh caps in the example: 1,000 instances, 20,000 vertices, 20,000 indices; a geometry renders only through `addInstance` (required since r166); one multi-draw call on WebGLRenderer where WEBGL_multi_draw exists, one draw per instance on the WebGPU backend. Merging: `mergeGeometries` needs matching attributes and uniform index state (else null); `mergeVertices` welds; tangents via `geometry.computeTangents()` (needs index + position + normal + uv) or MikkTSpace for the glTF convention. Pivots: `mesh.pivot` rotates/scales around a local point without touching vertex data. WebGPU differences stated plainly: Points draw at 1 px whatever the size (use an instanced Sprite with PointsNodeMaterial), LineLoop errors and renders nothing (repeat the first point in a Line), per-instance shader data is a TSL node on `positionLocal`. Lines are 1 px on both renderers whatever `linewidth` says — thick lines need Line2/LineGeometry/LineMaterial.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-geometry/SKILL.md (three.js r186; BufferGeometryUtils and MikkTSpace addons named inside).
- **Best for:** Building the actual shapes of a 3D hero or configurator — extruded lettering for a 3D headline, lathed/extruded product forms, instanced fields (shingles, panels, trees, stars) that must stay at one draw call, point-cloud and line accents. The segment-count discipline (sphere 32×16 suits most uses, higher only for close-ups) is the quality/performance dial.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0314⟧

## ⟦S0315⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-interaction — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The interaction reference (r186): raycast picking, dragging on a plane, six camera-control families (Orbit, Map, Fly, FirstPerson, PointerLock, Trackball), TransformControls gizmos, DragControls, click/hover selection and box selection, and screen↔world coordinate conversion — identical under WebGL and WebGPU because controls and the Raycaster are renderer-neutral. Pointer events cover mouse, touch and pen in one listener set.
- **How it looks:** The visitor grabs a 3D hero and orbits it with damping-smoothed motion, scrolls to zoom toward the cursor, clicks an object and it highlights (emissive lifts to 0x444444 in the worked selection code; hover alone flips the cursor to a pointer), drags a part across the ground plane, or drags a rubber-band rectangle that selects everything whose centre falls inside it. In an editor-style scene, a translate/rotate/scale gizmo sits on the selected object with snapping.
- **Frame by frame:** Pointer down/move → the pointer is converted to canvas-relative NDC (`((x − rect.left) / rect.width) × 2 − 1`, `−((y − rect.top) / rect.height) × 2 + 1`) → `raycaster.setFromCamera` casts the ray → hits return sorted, closest first. Drag → while a button is held, each pointermove re-intersects the ray with the ground plane and the mesh follows the hit point (null when the ray is parallel or points away). Orbit with damping → the camera keeps easing after the pointer stops because `controls.update(delta)` runs every frame. Gizmo drag → `dragging-changed` fires and orbit controls are disabled for the duration; `objectChange` fires as the object moves. Box select → pointerdown records the start point, pointermove stretches the helper's rectangle, pointerup runs `select()`.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Intersection record: distance, world point, face {a, b, c, normal, materialIndex}, faceIndex, object, uv, uv1, normal, barycoord, instanceId (InstancedMesh), batchId (BatchedMesh), distanceToRay (Points). Raycaster config: near 0.1 / far 10 in the example; `params.Points.threshold` and `params.Line.threshold` default 1 world unit (0.2 in the example); back faces are not hit unless the material is DoubleSide; invisible meshes ARE raycast (layers are tested, not visibility), so an invisible simple proxy can stand in for a complex model; restrict picking with `raycaster.layers.set(1)` + `mesh.layers.enable(1)`. OrbitControls values: dampingFactor 0.05 (damping requires update every frame), minDistance 2, maxDistance 50, minPolarAngle 0.1, maxPolarAngle π/2 (stop at the horizon), azimuth limits ±π/4 in the example, `zoomToCursor = true`, autoRotateSpeed 2.0 (delta-fed update makes it frame-rate independent); MapControls = OrbitControls tuned for maps (left-drag pans parallel to the ground, screenSpacePanning false). FlyControls: movementSpeed 10, rollSpeed π/24, dragToLook. FirstPersonControls: lookSpeed 0.005 and dampingFactor 0.1 defaults, vertical clamp π/4 to 3π/4 in the example; update() without a delta makes the position NaN. PointerLockControls: pointerSpeed 1.0, lock needs a user gesture, movement eased with `MathUtils.damp(velocity, target, 10, delta)`. TrackballControls: rotateSpeed 2.0, zoomSpeed 1.2, panSpeed 0.8, dynamicDampingFactor 0.2 unless staticMoving. TransformControls: modes translate/rotate/scale (keys g/r/s, Escape detaches), setSize 0.8, translation snap 0.5, rotation snap 15°, scale snap 0.25; the gizmo is added via `getHelper()` — adding the controls themselves only logs an error. DragControls: rotateSpeed 1 default, right-drag rotates, `transformGroup` drags the outermost group. WebGPU caveat: the Raycaster tests CPU geometry, so it never sees `positionNode` displacement — pick against an undisplaced proxy mesh.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-interaction/SKILL.md (three.js r186; controls, TransformControls, DragControls, SelectionBox/SelectionHelper addons).
- **Best for:** Making a 3D section touchable: orbit/zoom on a hero model, click-a-part configurators (door style, roof material, window type), drag interactions, hover feedback on 3D cards. The polar/distance limits and zoomToCursor values are what keep a trade-site 3D hero feeling controlled instead of a free-spinning toy.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0315⟧

## ⟦S0316⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-lighting — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The lighting reference (r186): every light type with its physical units, shadow-map setup and tuning, HDR environment lighting (IBL), light probes and probe grids, common rigs (three-point, outdoor daylight), animating lights, performance costs, and the WebGPU/TSL replacements for the WebGL-only pieces.
- **How it looks:** A 3D scene lit like a photograph: a key directional "sun" raking across a floor with soft PCF shadows, a warm point bulb glowing with real inverse-square falloff, a spot cone with a softened penumbra edge, a window-shaped RectArea glow on PBR surfaces, or a whole scene lit by an HDR sky that also appears behind it — with environment rotation, background blur and intensity independently adjustable. A cheap grounded look is also specified: a 128×128 radial-gradient canvas blob (rgba(0,0,0,0.6) centre → transparent edge) on a 2×2 plane floated 0.001 above the floor instead of a shadow map.
- **Frame by frame:** Static setups dominate. The one animated pattern: a Timer drives a point light on a circular path (`position = (cos t × 4, 3, sin t × 4)`) while its intensity breathes (`100 + sin(t × 2) × 30`) each frame. Shadow maps otherwise re-render every frame unless frozen: `shadow.autoUpdate = false` + `needsUpdate = true` renders a static scene's shadows once (per light, or globally via `renderer.shadowMap.autoUpdate` on WebGLRenderer).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Units are the core discipline: PointLight and SpotLight intensity is candela with decay 2 inverse-square falloff — 1 candela at 5 units contributes 1/25, so useful values run to the hundreds (worked values 100–250; official examples 80–1000); `light.power` sets the same thing in lumens (800 lm example); directional/ambient/hemisphere intensities are plain multipliers (directional 3, hemisphere 0.5–0.6 in the examples); RectAreaLight is nits (5 in the example, 4×10 size) and lights only MeshStandardMaterial/MeshPhysicalMaterial, never casts shadows, and needs RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init() on WebGLRenderer. Spot: angle is the cone half-angle (max π/2), penumbra 0–1 (0.4 example). Shadows need three switches — renderer `shadowMap.enabled`, light `castShadow`, mesh cast/receive. Directional tuning: shadow camera left/right/top/bottom ±10, near 0.5, far 50 in the example, `mapSize` powers of two (2048×2048), `normalBias 0.02`, `bias −0.0001` for acne, `shadow.intensity 0.7` to lighten without fill lights; `shadow.radius` above 1 widens PCF/VSM blur (VSM blurSamples default 8; point lights do not support VSM; every VSM receiver also casts). Spot/point shadow cameras are derived: spot fov = 2 × angle × shadow.focus in degrees, far comes from `light.distance`. SunLight (addon): two cascaded shadow maps fitted to the view automatically, default 1024×1024 per cascade, shadow camera bounds ignored. IBL: assign an equirect HDR directly (renderer prefilters; mapping must be EquirectangularReflectionMapping or a background draws as a flat quad), `scene.environmentIntensity` scales lighting only, `backgroundBlurriness` blurs only the backdrop; PMREMGenerator is kept for generated environments (RoomEnvironment, blur 0.04), not files. Probe grids: 10×4×10 volume = size+1 probes per axis by default, rebake when static lighting changes. Performance: adding/removing a light or toggling castShadow recompiles every lit material (switch via intensity instead); each shadow light adds depth passes — six per point light. WebGPU: register SunLightNode and RectAreaLightTexturesLib, ClusteredLighting for many point lights, per-material light selection via `material.lightsNode`, coloured shadows via `renderer.shadowMap.transmitted`.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-lighting/SKILL.md (three.js r186; SunLight, RectAreaLightUniformsLib, LightProbeGenerator, RoomEnvironment addons named inside).
- **Best for:** Any lit 3D on a homepage — the difference between a flat, gamey hero model and a photographed one. The three-point rig, daylight rig, tight shadow frustum and candela discipline apply directly to product/configurator heroes; the blob contact shadow is the cheap fallback for grounding objects on phones.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0316⟧

## ⟦S0317⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-loaders — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The runtime loading reference (r186): LoadingManager progress and abort, texture loading and configuration, cube textures, HDR/EXR/UltraHDR environments, glTF/GLB with Draco, meshopt and KTX2 decoder wiring, the other model formats (OBJ+MTL, FBX, STL, PLY, USD), async patterns, the shared cache, and correct cloning and disposal of loaded content.
- **How it looks:** Visitor-facing, this is the loading experience of a 3D section: a combined progress readout (`Loading: 42.0%` from loaded/total across every loader on one manager), a placeholder mesh standing in while the real model streams in, then the model appearing lit — glTF PBR materials render black without lights or an environment, so a RoomEnvironment is assigned before the model lands. Textures pop in correctly coloured because colour spaces were set before first render.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: `loadAsync` calls start in parallel (`Promise.all` over model, environment, colour map). During load → the manager fires onStart / onProgress (loaded/total) / onError per item and onLoad when every tracked item finishes; a 30-second timeout example cancels in-flight FileLoader requests via `manager.abort()` (image-element loaders such as TextureLoader ignore abort). TextureLoader returns the texture immediately and fills it when the image decodes — assign it right away; adding a map to an already-rendered material needs `material.needsUpdate = true`. End state → loaded scene added, optionally centred and scaled into a unit box from its Box3 (scale = 1 / max dimension, position offset scaled with it).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Colour-space law: LDR colour images (albedo, emissive) = SRGBColorSpace; scalar maps (normal, bump, roughness, metalness, AO, alpha) keep NoColorSpace; HDR loaders set LinearSRGBColorSpace themselves; a hand-loaded texture for a glTF material needs `flipY = false`. Texture config: wrap modes (ClampToEdge default, Repeat, MirroredRepeat), repeat/offset/rotation/centre apply every frame, while wrap, filters, anisotropy, colourSpace and flipY apply at upload (set before first render or flag needsUpdate); anisotropy from `renderer.capabilities.getMaxAnisotropy()` on WebGLRenderer, `renderer.getMaxAnisotropy()` on WebGPURenderer. Cube textures: six faces in +X, −X, +Y, −Y, +Z, −Z order; the loader sets sRGB itself. HDR/EXR/UltraHDR: set EquirectangularReflectionMapping and assign — both renderers prefilter equirect environments themselves, so a manual PMREM pass on a file only adds code; dim with `scene.environmentIntensity` (material.envMapIntensity does not touch scene.environment). Compression wiring: one GLTFLoader chained with DRACOLoader + MeshoptDecoder + `KTX2Loader().detectSupport(renderer)` covers every compressed output of ⟦S0312⟧; decoders/transcoders load from the three package by default — a path pinned to another release mismatches. Format notes: FBX files are often centimetres (scale 0.01 example); PLY `double` properties arrive as Float64Array attributes WebGLRenderer cannot upload — convert to Float32BufferAttribute, and call `computeVertexNormals()` only when the file has none; USDLoader reads USD/USDA/USDC/USDZ (USDZLoader deprecated r179). Cache: `THREE.Cache.enabled = true` serves repeated URLs from memory. Cloning law: `Object3D.clone()` on a skinned model shares the skeleton — copies follow the original's animation; use `SkeletonUtils.clone()`. Disposal law: traverse the subtree disposing geometry, every material and every texture value, plus per-object `dispose()` — Object3D.dispose() alone frees none of them. Loader renames: HDRLoader replaces RGBELoader (r180); every loader has `loadAsync` — never hand-wrap `load` in a Promise.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-loaders/SKILL.md (three.js r186; GLTFLoader, DRACOLoader, KTX2Loader, MeshoptDecoder, HDRLoader, EXRLoader, UltraHDRLoader, RoomEnvironment addons). Sibling skills: threejs-asset-pipeline (produces the compressed files), threejs-animation, threejs-textures, threejs-materials.
- **Best for:** The load path of every 3D section — model + environment + textures arriving in parallel with honest progress, correct colour, and no black-model or washed-out-texture failures. Pairs with ⟦S0312⟧: that skill compresses, this one loads.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0317⟧

## ⟦S0318⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-materials — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The materials reference (r186): how to choose and configure every three.js material — unlit Basic, diffuse Lambert, specular Phong, PBR Standard, advanced Physical (clearcoat, transmission, sheen, iridescence, anisotropy), Toon, Matcap, Shadow, Points and Line materials, and custom Shader/RawShader — plus shared properties (blending, stencil, alpha), environment response, and the WebGPU node-material/TSL equivalents.
- **How it looks:** The surface of everything in a 3D section: a PBR sphere with roughness 0.35 / metalness 0.1 catching a hemisphere + directional rig; matte Lambert walls; glossy Phong plastic with a shininess-30 highlight; glass that refracts the scene behind it (transmission 1, thickness 0.5, IOR 1.5); car-paint clearcoat; velvet sheen; soap-bubble iridescence shifting over a 100–400 nm film; cel-shaded objects with hard two-step toon bands; a shadow-only plane that shows nothing but the shadow it catches.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — materials define appearance, not motion. The one time-based pattern given is a ShaderMaterial whose `time` uniform is fed from a Timer each frame (`timer.update()` first, then `uniforms.time.value = timer.getElapsed()`), waving vertices by `sin(pos.x × 10 + time) × 0.1` and cycling fragment colour through `0.5 + 0.5 × cos(time + uv.xyx × 3)`. Runtime property changes (colour, roughness) apply with no recompile; compiled-in settings (transparent, side, blending, flatShading, vertexColors, maps added/removed…) need `material.needsUpdate = true`.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Choice ladder, cheapest first: Basic (unlit) → Lambert (diffuse) → Phong (diffuse + specular) → Standard (PBR metal/rough) → Physical (PBR + layers/volume). Standard values: roughness 0 = mirror, 1 = fully diffuse, multiplied by roughnessMap (green channel); metalness 0 = dielectric, 1 = metal, multiplied by metalnessMap (blue); the glTF ORM texture packs AO in red, roughness in green, metalness in blue. UV channels: every texture samples the attribute its `channel` selects (0 = uv default, 1 = uv1, 2 = uv2, 3 = uv3) — aoMap/lightMap need no second UV set unless a separate baked unwrap is used with `channel = 1`. Physical values: clearcoat 0–1 with clearcoatRoughness 0.1 example; transmission 0–1, thickness 0.5, attenuationDistance default Infinity, IOR range 1–2.333 (1.5 glass); sheen 1.0 / sheenRoughness 0.5; iridescenceIOR 1.3, iridescenceThicknessRange [100, 400] nm; anisotropy 1.0 with anisotropyRotation. Toon: gradientMap is a DataTexture with NearestFilter for hard steps (steps [120, 200] = two bands in the example). PointsMaterial size is in world units scaled by sizeAttenuation (default true); alphaTest 0.5 discards fragments below the threshold with a map. Lines: 1 px on both renderers whatever linewidth says; dashed lines (dashSize 0.5, gapSize 0.25) need `computeLineDistances()` or they draw solid; thick lines need Line2. Colour-space law repeats ⟦S0317⟧: colour data textures sRGB, scalar maps default. Blending: Multiply/Subtractive require `premultipliedAlpha = true` or the renderer errors and sets no blend function. Stencil is off by default in both renderers — the renderer must be created with `stencil: true`, then stencilWrite/stencilRef/stencilFunc (EqualStencilFunc, masks 0xff) build mask-and-reveal effects, mask drawn first via renderOrder. Multiple materials per mesh follow geometry groups (BoxGeometry's six in +x, −x, +y, −y, +z, −z order). Performance order: share one material instance across meshes; prefer opaque + alphaTest cutouts over stacked transparent layers (sorted back-to-front, overdraw, misordering); pick the cheapest material that looks right. WebGPU: built-in classes auto-convert to node materials; ShaderMaterial/RawShaderMaterial/Depth/Distance materials have no node equivalent and log "is not compatible" — custom shading is TSL nodes on `three/webgpu` material classes, displacement built on `positionLocal`, never `positionGeometry`.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-materials/SKILL.md (three.js r186). Sibling skills: threejs-textures, threejs-shaders, threejs-lighting.
- **Best for:** Styling every surface in a 3D hero or configurator — realistic PBR for products and materials (wood, metal, glass, painted finishes), toon/matcap for stylised looks, ShadowMaterial for invisible shadow-catcher floors, stencil for mask reveals. The roughness/metalness + ORM discipline is what makes trade materials (timber, uPVC, slate, brushed metal) read as real.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0318⟧

## ⟦S0319⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-performance — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The performance reference (r186): measure first with renderer counters, then cut draw calls (merge, instance, batch, LOD), GPU memory (KTX2, texture size, disposal), fill rate (pixel-ratio cap, overdraw, shadow passes), CPU work per frame (static matrices, raycast scope, zero allocation), and shader compile stalls — plus WebGPU compute particles and the WebGPU counter names.
- **How it looks:** No design of its own; the visitor-visible result is a 3D hero that holds its frame rate on a mid-range phone: no periodic stutters from garbage collection, no first-frame freeze while shaders compile, distant objects quietly dropping detail (LOD levels at distance 0 / 12 / 30 in the worked example) instead of the whole scene slowing down.
- **Frame by frame:** Static as a design entry — it governs per-frame cost. The measured loop it prescribes: render → read the counters for the frame just drawn (they reset at the start of every `render()`) → average frame interval over 60 frames with a Timer (a single frame jitters too much; the interval never drops below one display refresh, 16.7 ms at 60 Hz) and time CPU-in-render with `performance.now()` around the call.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Counters (WebGLRenderer): `info.render.calls / triangles / lines / points`, `info.memory.geometries / textures` (uploads, not bytes), `info.programs.length`; multi-render frames need `info.autoReset = false` + one manual `reset()` per frame. Draw-call multipliers: a transparent DoubleSide material draws each mesh twice (back then front; `forceSinglePass: true` makes it one), and any transmissive MeshPhysicalMaterial in view redraws every opaque object into the transmission buffer. Reducers with worked scales: merge 200 static rocks into one mesh/one call (one bounding sphere — merge per cluster, not per level); InstancedMesh 500 trees in one call (single shared culling sphere; `instanceMatrix.needsUpdate` + `computeBoundingSphere()` after moves); BatchedMesh 500 instances (per-instance culling/sorting on by default; one multi-draw on WebGL where WEBGL_multi_draw exists, one draw per instance on WebGPU); LOD swaps triangle count, not call count. Memory math: RGBA8 = 4 bytes/px, mip chain ×1.333 — a 2048×2048 colour map ≈ 22 MB VRAM; a 1024 texture is a quarter of a 2048; KTX2 stays block-compressed in VRAM (KTX2Loader + detectSupport). Fill rate: shading cost scales with pixel ratio squared (a 3× display shades 9× the pixels of 1×) — cap `setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2))`. Shadow defaults are 512×512 per light; each shadow light re-draws its casters (point light up to six passes; VSM adds receivers + two blur draws); freeze static shadows with `shadowMap.autoUpdate = false` + `needsUpdate = true`. CPU: `matrixAutoUpdate = false` + one `updateMatrix()` for static scenery; raycast an explicit pickables list on a layer (`raycaster.layers.set(1)`, `intersectObjects(pickables, false)`) instead of recursive scene walks on every pointermove; zero allocations in the loop (reuse vectors/matrices declared outside). Compile stalls: `await renderer.compileAsync(scene, camera)` during loading (KHR_parallel_shader_compile) — plain `compile()` returns before programs finish; runtime flips of compiled-in material settings force new programs. WebGPU: counters are `info.render.drawCalls` per frame, `info.render.calls` = render passes since start, `info.memory.total` = byte estimate (compressed textures under-reported at 1 byte); GPU compute example updates 100,000 particles in one dispatch (`instancedArray` storage buffer + `renderer.compute()` before render), no per-particle JS or buffer re-upload.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-performance/SKILL.md (three.js r186; stats-gl and three-mesh-bvh packages and the Chrome DevTools Performance panel named inside). Sibling skills: fundamentals, geometry, materials, loaders, lighting, postprocessing, asset-pipeline.
- **Best for:** Keeping a WebGL hero or configurator smooth on real visitor hardware — the audit to run before a 3D section ships, and the budget discipline (draw calls, pixel-ratio cap, shadow count) to design it against from the start. Essential pairing with ⟦S0320⟧, whose effects are the usual fill-rate cost.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0319⟧

## ⟦S0320⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-postprocessing — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (cloudai-x threejs-skills)
- **What it is:** The post-processing reference (r186): EffectComposer pass chains on WebGLRenderer (bloom, selective bloom, depth of field, SSAO, outline, film, glitch, halftone, vignette, pixelation, custom ShaderPass effects), the composer's MSAA and resize rules, the no-composer `renderer.setEffects()` path, and the WebGPU/TSL RenderPipeline node equivalents.
- **How it looks:** The finishing layer over a rendered 3D scene: a bright emissive object blooms with a soft halo (strength 1.5, radius 0.4, threshold 0.85 in the worked setup — only luminance above the threshold glows); only layer-marked objects bloom in selective bloom while the rest of the scene stays clean; depth of field keeps the focused depth sharp and blurs the rest; SSAO darkens creases and contact corners; a selected object gets a white outline with dark hidden edges; or the whole frame takes film grain, a halftone dot pattern, a vignette, or a pixelated retro render.
- **Frame by frame:** Each frame the composer replaces `renderer.render()`: RenderPass draws the scene into linear HDR buffers → linear-space effects run in chain order (bloom, DOF, SSAO, outline…) → SMAAPass smooths the edges those effects produced → OutputPass applies the renderer's tone mapping and sRGB conversion exactly once → FXAAPass only after OutputPass, because FXAA needs sRGB input. Time-based passes (FilmPass grain) are driven by the composer's own internal delta. Selective bloom runs two composers per frame: darken every non-marked mesh to black and null the background → bloom composer renders off-screen → restore materials and background → final composer renders the clean scene plus a ShaderPass that adds the bloom texture. Under WebGPURenderer the same frame is a node graph: `pass()` renders the scene, effect nodes transform the texture, the result is assigned to `renderPipeline.outputNode` and `renderPipeline.render()` draws it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Chain law: buffers hold linear colours; tone mapping + sRGB happen once, in OutputPass, which ends every chain (GammaCorrectionShader is not a substitute); `pass.enabled = false` skips a pass without rebuilding. Composer setup: it copies the renderer's pixel ratio at construction (set pixel ratio before constructing, or `composer.setPixelRatio()` after); its buffers are not multisampled — pass a WebGLRenderTarget with `type: HalfFloatType, samples: 4` for MSAA; on resize call `composer.setSize(w, h)` and never resize a pass by hand. Bloom: UnrealBloomPass(resolution, strength 1.5, radius 0.4, threshold 0.85); selective bloom marks meshes with `layers.enable(1)` (never `set`, which removes layer 0). DOF: BokehPass focus 10.0 world units, aperture 0.025, maxblur 0.01; refocus at runtime with `camera.position.distanceTo(object)`. SSAO: kernelRadius 16, minDistance 0.005, maxDistance 0.1; it darkens the previous pass's image, so RenderPass must precede it. Outline: edgeStrength 3, visibleEdgeColor white, hiddenEdgeColor 0x190a05. Filters: FilmPass(0.35, false) = (intensity, grayscale) — the old scanline arguments do not exist; HalftonePass takes one params object (shape 1 dot / 2 ellipse / 3 line / 4 square / 5 diamond, radius 4, scatter 0); RenderPixelatedPass(6, scene, camera) with normalEdgeStrength 0.3 and depthEdgeStrength 0.4 replaces RenderPass; ColorCorrectionShader defaults powRGB (2,2,2) darken the image — start from (1,1,1). Custom passes: ShaderPass with `tDiffuse` receiving the previous output, kept before OutputPass while working in linear space. No-composer path: `renderer.setEffects([bloomPass])` requires `outputBufferType: HalfFloatType` (or FloatType), takes no OutputPass/FXAAPass, and gives effects no delta time (FilmPass grain is lost — use the composer for time-driven passes). WebGPU: effects are nodes from three/addons/tsl/display/ (bloom returns only the glow — add it to the scene colour; dof/film/rgbShift/chromaticAberration/afterImage/dotScreen/lut3D/smaa return the finished image; outline returns only edge masks; ssao returns the occlusion factor in .r); `ao()` needs a single-sample pre-pass `pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 })` with an MRT normal attachment; traa needs a velocity MRT and a renderer without antialias; FXAA there needs `outputColorTransform = false` + `renderOutput()` before it; a changed outputNode takes effect only with `renderPipeline.needsUpdate = true`; selective bloom needs no layer trick — bloom the MRT emissive attachment. EffectComposer does not run under WebGPURenderer at all (renamed PostProcessing → RenderPipeline in r183).
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X threejs-skills — https://github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills/blob/main/skills/threejs-postprocessing/SKILL.md (three.js r186; EffectComposer, RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, OutputPass, SMAAPass, FXAAPass, BokehPass, SSAOPass, OutlinePass, FilmPass, GlitchPass, HalftonePass, RenderPixelatedPass addons and the TSL display nodes).
- **Best for:** The cinematic finish on a 3D hero: restrained bloom on lit signage/emissives, DOF focus on a product, SSAO grounding, outline highlights for configurator selection (pairs with ⟦S0315⟧ picking). Powerful but the classic fill-rate trap — budget it with ⟦S0319⟧ and keep chains short on mobile.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0320⟧
## ⟦S0321⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-react-three-fiber — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A reference for building three.js scenes inside React with React Three Fiber (fiber 9.8, React 19, drei 10.7, three.js r186): the whole scene graph written as JSX, with hooks for the frame loop, asset loading and pointer events, adaptive performance tools, and a WebGPU/TSL path.
- **How it looks:** Whatever the JSX scene describes. The worked examples: a dark slate-blue (#111827) full-canvas scene with a warm orange-brown (#d9915b) unit cube spinning above a dark floor plane (#20293a), soft shadows, orbit camera at position [3, 2, 4] with fov 50; a metallic torus knot (color #42699c, roughness 0.2, metalness 0.8); a crowd of 200 coloured capsules sharing one draw call; 3D text and DOM overlays anchored into the scene via drei.
- **Frame by frame:** Continuous render loop by default → `useFrame` callbacks run before each render and mutate objects through refs (rotation.y += delta, so speed is frame-rate independent) → hover on a mesh raycasts and swaps its material colour (#42699c → #e8b4a0) → loading hooks suspend and the Suspense fallback shows until model/textures resolve, then the scene appears → with frameloop="demand" the canvas sits static until a state change or invalidate() requests a frame → dragging OrbitControls orbits with damping; while dragging, "regress" drops the resolution and restores it 200 ms after release.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Canvas props — dpr [1, 2] clamped to devicePixelRatio; shadows filters 'basic' / 'percentage' / 'variance' ('percentage' is the soft filter without the deprecation warning); ACESFilmicToneMapping on by default, `flat` = NoToneMapping; default camera fov 75, near 0.1, far 1000, at z 5. Pointer events raycast CPU geometry, fire nearest first and bubble up parents; the event carries point, distance, face, instanceId and delta. drei values from the examples: OrbitControls dampingFactor 0.1, autoRotateSpeed 0.5, minDistance 2 / maxDistance 12; ContactShadows opacity 0.6, scale 12, blur 2.4, far 4; Detailed LOD distances [0, 15, 40] with hysteresis 0.1; PerformanceMonitor flipflops 3, AdaptiveDpr floor min 0.5 × the first resolved ratio. useGLTF ships with Draco + meshopt decoding on by default (decoder from a pinned gstatic URL). WebGPU: `gl` as an async factory awaiting renderer.init(), extend(THREE) from three/webgpu; drei Text, ContactShadows and Html with occlude="blending" are NOT WebGPU-safe.
- **Reference / source:** cloudai-x/threejs-skills on GitHub (github.com/cloudai-x/threejs-skills); three.js r186, @react-three/fiber 9.8, @react-three/drei 10.7.
- **Best for:** React-based 3D — product configurators, WebGL heroes inside a React app. For single-file vanilla HTML builds there is no React runtime, but the drei helper patterns (contact shadows, LOD distance steps, adaptive DPR) transfer as design targets.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0321⟧

## ⟦S0322⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-shaders — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A reference for writing custom GLSL shaders in three.js r186: ShaderMaterial vs RawShaderMaterial, uniforms and varyings, shader chunks, instanced attributes, extending built-in materials with onBeforeCompile, and the same effects rebuilt as TSL node materials for WebGPU.
- **How it looks:** The quick-start is a flat 2×2 plane whose blue colour pulses in a travelling wave (sin(vUv.x × 10 + time × 2)). The Fresnel example is a shape dark navy (0, 0, 0.5) across its face shading to pale sky blue (0.5, 0.8, 1.0) at the silhouette edges. The dissolve is an image eaten away by a noise pattern with a glowing orange rim (1.0, 0.5, 0) along the burn edge.
- **Frame by frame:** A time uniform advances every frame from a THREE.Timer → the wave brightness sweeps continuously across the surface → vertex displacement (sin(pos.x × 5 + time) × amplitude 0.2) ripples a subdivided 64×64-segment plane like cloth → the dissolve is driven by a progress value 0→1: pixels whose noise value falls below progress are discarded, and the 0.1-wide smoothstep band at the front glows orange → Fresnel/rim shading recomputes per frame from the view direction, so it shifts as the camera moves (rim power 4.0 in view space, Fresnel power 3.0 in world space).
- **Mechanism & key values:** ShaderMaterial always compiles as GLSL ES 3.00; a fragment shader must end with `#include <tonemapping_fragment>` and `#include <colorspace_fragment>` or mid-tones render darker than on built-in materials. RawShaderMaterial needs glslVersion: THREE.GLSL3 plus its own precision and declarations. Built-in matrices must never be passed through uniforms (the renderer sets or overwrites them). Custom instanced attributes are declared by hand (aOffset example via InstancedBufferAttribute; set frustumCulled = false). onBeforeCompile injection points: begin_vertex, beginnormal_vertex, project_vertex (vertex); color_fragment, opaque_fragment, fog_fragment (fragment); variants need customProgramCacheKey(). The final output chunk is opaque_fragment — there is no output_fragment. TSL equivalents: uniform() values, the built-in time node, Fn() compiling to both GLSL and WGSL, positionNode built on positionLocal, .discard(), and renderer.debug.getShaderAsync() for inspection. ShaderMaterial and onBeforeCompile do not run under WebGPURenderer.
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X/threejs-skills on GitHub (github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills); three.js r186.
- **Best for:** The WebGL/3D mechanism family — custom hero effects, dissolve image transitions, rim-lit product/model renders, shader-driven section backgrounds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0322⟧

## ⟦S0323⟧ cloudai-x/threejs-textures — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A reference for three.js textures end to end: loading, colour spaces, UV channels and transforms, filtering and mipmaps, every texture type (image, data, canvas, video, KTX2-compressed, HDR), environment maps, render targets, dynamic reflections and texture memory.
- **How it looks:** The examples: a photo-textured 2×2 plane slowly rotating (rotation.z += 0.01 per frame); an HDR equirectangular photo wrapped around the scene as both background and light source, its blur adjustable 0–1; a mirror-like mesh reflecting the live scene through a 256px cube camera; text drawn on a 256×256 canvas ("Hello" in 48px) appearing as a surface texture; a video playing across a 3D surface.
- **Frame by frame:** Mostly static — a texture is data applied once, and motion comes from the scene. The moving cases the skill defines: VideoTexture re-uploads every frame, so the surface plays the video; dynamic reflections re-render the cube camera every frame (hide the reflective mesh → update → show it again) so reflections track movement; texture offset/repeat/rotation can be animated per frame for scrolling surfaces.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Colour images (map, emissiveMap, specularMap, canvas/video used as colour) get SRGBColorSpace or they render too bright and washed out; scalar maps (normal, bump, displacement, roughness, metalness, AO, alpha) keep NoColorSpace. Channel packing: aoMap reads red, roughnessMap green, metalnessMap blue, alphaMap green — one packed ORM image works. texture.channel 0–3 selects the uv / uv1 / uv2 / uv3 attribute. Tiling needs RepeatWrapping (worked example repeat 4×4, offset 0.5/0.5, rotation π/4 about center 0.5/0.5); anisotropy set to the renderer's maximum for grazing angles; mipmaps are generated whenever generateMipmaps is true, whatever the filter. KTX2 via KTX2Loader.detectSupport(renderer) — flipY stays false and mipmaps must be baked into the file. Render targets: 512×512 examples, MSAA samples 4, MRT count 2 read back through .textures[]. PMREM RoomEnvironment blur sigma 0.04. Scene controls: environmentIntensity, backgroundIntensity, backgroundBlurriness, environment/background rotation. Under WebGPU use CubeRenderTarget (not WebGLCubeRenderTarget) and renderer.getMaxAnisotropy().
- **Reference / source:** CloudAI-X/threejs-skills on GitHub (github.com/CloudAI-X/threejs-skills); three.js r186.
- **Best for:** Any WebGL/3D section — correct colour when photos wrap onto 3D, environment-lit product or model heroes, live reflections, and texture-memory budgeting on heavy pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0323⟧

## ⟦S0324⟧ coldteadotai/agent-skill — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** PR Lens. An agent writes one JSON graph document (lanes, nodes, edges, ordered flows, optional data model and walkthrough) describing a code change or codebase; the PR Lens CLI validates it, renders it as self-contained animated SVGs for pull requests, and can push it to a live web canvas for step-through questions. This file is a discovery stub plus the full bundled operating manual (manual.md) — the live workflow text is served by the CLI itself so it never goes stale.
- **How it looks:** A diagram laid out in horizontal lanes (one lane per runtime, tier or boundary — the reader's mental model, not the folder tree) with component boxes and arrows; changed parts carry delta states (added / changed / removed / unchanged), and one or two "hero" edges are emphasised. On the live canvas a walkthrough steps through the change: the camera flies to each step's diagram, the two or three named elements light up while everything else dims, and clicking a flow step opens a rail showing its sample request/response payload. In a GitHub PR it appears as light/dark SVG pairs in the description; GitLab and Bitbucket get a single neutral-theme render.
- **Frame by frame:** Reader opens the canvas link and presses play / scrolls the walkthrough (2–12 steps, aim 3–7) → step 1 opens on the widest view with no focus, headline change first → each step moves the camera to its stage (an architecture view or a flow), zooms to the focused selection and dims the rest → flow steps animate along the sequence; a click on a step opens its payload rail → questions asked beside the canvas are answered the same way: camera moves step by step, named parts light up, each name is a link. The PR-comment SVG is animated but not interactive.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pipeline: read the diff (git diff --find-renames <base>...<head>, base is the merge base) → write .pr-lens/graph.json → `npx @coldtea/pr-lens-cli@latest validate` (fix every failure; codes include BROKEN_REFERENCE, INVALID_DOCUMENT, DUPLICATE_ID, UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION) → render --theme light by default (neutral for GitLab/Bitbucket) → canvas push prints the view link https://prlens.dev/c/{id}. GitHub attach via gh pr create/edit/comment --attach (needs gh ≥ 2.99; the reference must be a Markdown image and the alt text is the caption). Walkthrough limits: heading ≤48 characters, body ≤140, detail ≤240 with 1–8 cites; payload caps — shape ≤2048 bytes, sample ≤8 levels deep and ≤4096 bytes serialised. Corrections go in a .github/pr-lens.yml overlay (rename / exclude / lane), never by editing the generated document. The `analyze --base <ref>` path is the only one needing an API key.
- **Reference / source:** coldteadotai/pr-lens on GitHub (github.com/coldteadotai/pr-lens); canvas at prlens.dev; JSON Schema published via @coldtea/pr-lens-schema on unpkg.
- **Best for:** Developer-facing explanation — PR descriptions and architecture walkthroughs. Not a visitor-facing page pattern and not for trade homepage sections; relevant only when documenting a build's structure.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0324⟧

## ⟦S0325⟧ coldteadotai/eli5 — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A PR Lens variant that explains a codebase, folder, feature, command or PR to someone who knows nothing about it, as a canvas whose picture grows: start with two boxes and one arrow, add one part at a time, and show the whole diagram only last, when it holds nothing new. Plain words only.
- **How it looks:** A PR Lens canvas that opens nearly empty — the reader themself ("You write the email", kind external) and the first part they touch, with one arrow between them. Each following view adds 1–3 boxes along the one main path, across 2–5 lanes pictured as places ("your browser", "the website", "the mail company", "your reader"). Node labels are three words or fewer saying what the part does; real code names appear once each, in subtitles. The final view — the only one with defaultOpen — shows the whole system, 4–10 nodes total, and a separate data-flow view plays the sequence.
- **Frame by frame:** Reader presses play → walkthrough step 1 stages view 1, heading is the one-sentence answer (under 48 characters, e.g. "When you hit send, it emails everyone."), body introduces the two parts → each next step swaps to the next growing view and focuses only the newly added nodes while the rest dims → 1–2 flow steps follow the sequence, including one matter-of-fact "where things go wrong" step focused on the message just before the failure → the closing step returns to the whole picture, repeats the answer sentence as its heading, and adds one number the reader now understands ("1 email in, 2,000 emails out, 1 request to Postmark."). The reply is just the answer sentence and the canvas link, on two lines.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Same PR Lens CLI pipeline as ⟦S0324⟧ (validate → render --theme light → canvas push). eli5 overrides: the answer sentence is also the document summary; provenance base.sha and head.sha are both the current HEAD; every delta is "unchanged" unless the subject is a pull request; no stats; exactly one hero edge; every edge along the path has animated: true; views are all roots, named by content (you-and-the-editor, plus-the-queue, the-whole-thing), each holding everything the last held plus at most 3 new nodes (codebase view 2 may add up to 5 — the 3–5 things a person does with the product); walkthrough total at most 9 steps. Banned words include leverages, orchestrates, pipeline, abstraction, handler, wrapper, layer, utility, invoke, instantiate.
- **Reference / source:** coldteadotai/pr-lens on GitHub (skills/eli5); canvas at prlens.dev.
- **Best for:** Beginner/onboarding explanations of code. Not a page pattern, but its growing-picture discipline — never show the whole system first, add at most 3 new parts per step — is the transferable lesson for step-by-step process sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0325⟧

## ⟦S0327⟧ cursor/thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** An extremely strict code-review mode that hunts for "code judo" — restructurings that delete whole branches, helpers, modes or layers while behaviour stays identical — and enforces hard rules on file size, spaghetti conditionals, thin abstractions and boundary cleanliness.
- **How it looks:** A text review, not a page: a short list of high-conviction comments in a fixed priority order (structural regressions → missed dramatic simplifications → spaghetti/branching growth → boundary and type-contract problems → file-size concerns → modularity → legibility), in a direct, demanding tone with stock phrasings such as "this pushes the file past 1k lines. can we decompose this first?"
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Hard threshold: do not let a PR push a file from under 1,000 lines to over 1,000 without a very strong reason — decompose first. Presumptive blockers: ad-hoc conditionals bolted onto unrelated flows, feature logic leaking into shared modules, one-off booleans/nullable modes, thin or identity wrappers, unnecessary casts / any / optionality, bespoke duplicates of canonical helpers, sequential orchestration of independent work, non-atomic partial updates. Approval bar: no structural regression and no visible missed code-judo move. Preferred remedies: delete a layer rather than polish it, reframe the state model so conditionals disappear, typed models or explicit dispatchers over condition chains, reuse the canonical helper, move logic to the layer that owns the concept.
- **Reference / source:** Cursor plugins repo on GitHub (cursor/plugins, pstack/skills).
- **Best for:** A QA pass over generated build code — especially single-file HTML builds where one file balloons and conditionals tangle. Process skill, not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0327⟧

## ⟦S0328⟧ cursor/unslop — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A copy-editing rule set (stable numbered rules 3–33, with gaps where rules were removed) for cutting AI tells out of any writing while preserving meaning and the intended tone: scan for the patterns, then rewrite.
- **How it looks:** The same text, plainer. No em dashes at all (periods or commas only — no parentheses or en-dash substitutes), sentence-case headings, straight quotes, no decorative emoji in headings or bullets, no bolded proper nouns, prose instead of bold-label-and-colon list lines, and plain words — "use", "help", "many", "if" — instead of utilize, leverage, numerous, "in the event that".
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Detect-and-fix passes grouped as Content, Language, Style, Communication artifacts, Filler, Jargon and Plain speech. Named bans: AI vocabulary (delve, crucial, pivotal, tapestry, underscore, vibrant, showcase, interplay, intricate, garner, fostering, enduring, enhance); fancy copulas ("serves as", "stands as", "boasts"); "not just X, but Y"; forced rule-of-three groupings; synonym cycling; false ranges; chatbot phrases ("I hope this helps!", "Of course!"); sycophancy; hedging stacks; abstract metaphor nouns (substrate, wedge, vector, locus, nexus, north star, flywheel, scaffolding, "API surface"). Working tests: name the mechanism or a number, not a feeling; a sentence that could appear unchanged in another project's docs says nothing about this one — cut it; one idea per sentence; active voice; cut the adverb or use a stronger verb; write whole sentences, not symbol-speak fragments.
- **Reference / source:** Cursor plugins repo on GitHub (cursor/plugins, pstack/skills/unslop).
- **Best for:** The final copy pass on any section's text — hero headlines, proof, process, CTA — before a build ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0328⟧

## ⟦S0329⟧ Danilaa1/compact-landing — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A workflow for building a small, finished landing page as a compact "product world" rather than a generic marketing template: a fresh design fingerprint is chosen per product (composition, measure, palette, typography, geometry, surface grammar, motif, motion), and one product-native signature artifact — a real demo, data specimen, miniature workflow, comparison or useful control — carries the identity.
- **How it looks:** A compact page, usually 420–720px in measure: an offset-rail, split-pamphlet, framed-console or stacked-specimen silhouette on warm paper, cool fog, monochrome ink or a product tint; grotesk + mono or editorial serif + sans type; one dominant surface grammar (paper rules, inset hairlines, layered rings, tinted panels); 1–3 emoji used as punctuation or tiny stickers; the primary action inside the first viewport. Explicitly not the canonical recipe (centred 440px column, neutral white/zinc, Geist + Geist Mono, 6–10px radii, inset hairline cards) — at least four fingerprint axes must differ from it and from other products.
- **Frame by frame:** One chosen entrance behaviour plus one or two interaction behaviours, all zero-shift → only transform, opacity and filter animate (never transition: all) → a button press is scale(0.96), or 0.98 for wide command controls → alternate labels, icons and panels overlay in the same grid area or fixed box, so nothing reflows → dimensions are reserved before animation (fixed/min heights, aspect-ratio media slots, width-locked labels, tabular numerals for changing numbers) → hover-only effects sit behind (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) → with prefers-reduced-motion the page stays fully usable.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Button scale, applied consistently — compact: 24–28px visual height, 11–12px label; medium: 32–36px, 12.5–13px label; large: 40–44px, 13.5–14px label. Visually tiny controls still get at least a 40px hit area. Visible :focus-visible state and semantic HTML required. Process: ask the button size first, then at most two adaptive questions and only when the answers would change the result; pick the fingerprint with scripts/pick-direction.mjs or references/style-dna.md without taking the first option in every list; never add a dependency for a small effect CSS or the current stack can handle; self-host fonts or use metric-compatible fallbacks.
- **Reference / source:** Danilaa1/compact-landing-skill on GitHub (github.com/Danilaa1/compact-landing-skill).
- **Best for:** Compact landing and small product pages. Its zero-shift motion rules and button scale transfer directly to call/CTA sections and form controls on trade pages, and the anti-template fingerprint discipline fits any hero that must not look generic.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0329⟧

## ⟦S0331⟧ danny/motion-ad — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** Produces a short motion-graphics video ad as a rendered H.264 MP4: one HTML page driven by a paused GSAP timeline, captured frame by frame. All brand and product content sits in a single CONFIG object in the bundled template, which is a finished 15-second 4:5 ad to be re-skinned rather than built from zero.
- **How it looks:** A feed ad (4:5 by default, 9:16 for stories/reels) in the brand's colours, font and logo, with big headlines readable muted (at most ~20 characters per line at 82px). Beats: a hook headline while a phone scrolls a screen capture and a finger taps the input → the tapped card grows into the hero and a scan beam reveals before → after, with benefit pills → the hero shrinks into a tilted 3D wall of output images → a 3-card showcase carousel with an optional "before" inset plus a proof row → a brand-colour circle wipe into the logo, CTA headline, chip and a button tap on the end card. Missing images render as labelled placeholders so the ad previews before real assets exist.
- **Frame by frame:** The GSAP timeline runs the beats at fixed times → 0–2.2s hook, phone scroll and tap → 2.2–5.4s the card grows, the scan beam wipes before to after → 5.5–8.7s the hero shrinks into the 3D wall → 8.7–11.8s carousel and proof row → 11.8–15s circle wipe to the end card. Production flow: render stills first at 0.3, 1.9, 2.7, 3.8, 4.9, 6.6, 9.8, 11.5, 13.6s and review the contact sheet, then the full render (~1 minute for 450 frames = 15s at 30fps); window.seek, window.DURATION and window.ready hooks drive the capture.
- **Mechanism & key values:** GSAP timeline + playwright-core frame capture (render.cjs), ffmpeg for probing/spot-check frames, Python/Pillow contact sheets. CONFIG fields per beat: hook, screen, screenScroll, tap, reveal, before/after + beforeLabel/afterLabel, benefits, scale, scaleChip, gallery, proofHl, showcase, showChip, proof, cta.headline/chip/button/foot. In headlines, *word* marks the accent colour and \n forces a line break. For 9:16, set the stage to 1080×1920 and re-space the vertical positions. Deliverable goes to ~/Downloads/ with a versioned name (<brand>-<topic>-ad-4x5-v2.mp4), never overwriting an earlier version. Hard rules: every claim (prices, counts, speeds, "free") must appear on the destination page the ad links to; only real assets and real proof (proof: null if there is no real number); never fabricate a person — crop or mirror real images instead.
- **Reference / source:** danny.md skills (danny/motion-ad); GSAP; the template and scripts bundled with the skill.
- **Best for:** Video ads and social promos for a product. The deliverable is an MP4, not a page section, but the before/after scan-reveal beat and the tilted 3D wall of outputs are adaptable ideas for work/gallery sections.

## ⟦S0332⟧ danny/screenshot — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** Captures a screenshot of a rendered web page in headless Chrome — full page, viewport, a named section, a single element, or a device rendering — saves the PNG and reads it back so the result is visible inline, for review and motion pipelines.
- **How it looks:** A PNG of the actual rendered page: the whole scrollable page, or the section under a named heading, or one element such as the nav or CTA button, or a mobile/tablet/desktop framing. Default viewport 1280×800 at 2× retina scale.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. A single still capture; the --wait option (milliseconds or a selector) only lets late-loading content settle before the shot.
- **Mechanism & key values:** scripts/screenshot.mjs drives the user's installed Google Chrome through playwright-core (--channel chrome; no bundled-browser download). The core is the intent→flags map: "full page" → --full-page; a named area → --section "pricing" (falls back heading → text → enclosing block); one element → --selector ".hero"; the Nth section → --section 3; an element inside a container → --section plus --container; device presets → --device mobile/tablet/desktop; --scale (default 2), --width/--height, --pad, --wait, --out. Logged-in pages attach to a running Chrome via --cdp (Chrome started with --remote-debugging-port=9222). The PNG path is the last stdout line and must be reported verbatim, full and unabbreviated. Sections are auto-scrolled into view before capture, which usually triggers lazy loads.
- **Reference / source:** danny.md skills (danny/screenshot); Playwright (playwright-core).

## ⟦S0333⟧ DietrichGebert/ponytail — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A persistent "lazy senior developer" mode: solve the whole problem with the least new code, walking a fixed ladder — does it need to exist, is it already in this codebase, does the stdlib/platform do it, is a dependency already installed, can it be one line, otherwise the minimum code that works. Every reply ends with one or two lines naming what was skipped and any risk.
- **How it looks:** No visual output. The visible effect is smaller diffs, no speculative options or wrappers, and the short skipped/risk trailer on replies; a deliberate shortcut carries a code comment in the form `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Levels — lite: build what was asked and name the smaller option in one line; full (default): the ladder, plus one small test or assert-based self-check for any non-trivial new logic; ultra: also question the request and push back before building. The mode stays active for the whole session until "stop ponytail" or "normal mode"; switched with /ponytail lite|full|ultra. Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, real-hardware calibration, and anything the user asked for. Bug fixes grep every caller of the touched function first, then fix the root cause once in shared code. Deletion beats addition; a one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
- **Reference / source:** DietrichGebert/ponytail on GitHub (github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail).
- **Best for:** Keeping generated build code lean — single-file HTML builds especially. A process skill, not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0333⟧

## ⟦S0334⟧ DietrichGebert/ponytail-audit — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** A one-shot audit of a whole repo in the ponytail voice: map the repo and its expected load first, then report findings across six lenses — bug, risk, scale, missing test, speed, lean — ordered correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean. It changes no code.
- **How it looks:** A plain-English report opening with "What this repo does:" in two or three sentences plus the load assumed, then at most 20 findings numbered across three groups (Must fix / Should fix / Nice to have), each in four parts — What this is, Problem, Fix, If we skip it — with file and line references. It closes with a one-line "Verdict:", a "Lean: −N lines, −M dependencies possible." line when lean findings exist, and "Not checked:" for anything unread.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** No finding without a concrete case ("this input or situation leads to this wrong result"). Before calling code unused, grep the whole tree including tests, fixtures, config and string/dynamic references. A `shortcut:` or older `ponytail:` comment naming its limit is a decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it. Lean categories: delete (dead code, unused flags/config), reuse (two helpers doing one job), stdlib/native, yagni (one-implementation interfaces, pass-through wrappers), merge (near-copies), split (one function doing several jobs — split by job, never by line count). Fixes are the smallest that work and prefer deleting code. Simple English throughout; a technical term is explained at first use.
- **Reference / source:** DietrichGebert/ponytail on GitHub (skills/ponytail-audit).
- **Best for:** An audit pass over a finished build or repo before it ships. Process skill, not a design source.

## ⟦S0335⟧ DietrichGebert/ponytail-debt — UI Skills (ui-skills.com catalog)
- **What it is:** Collects every deliberate-shortcut comment in a repo — marked `shortcut:` (older code may say `ponytail:`), each naming its ceiling and upgrade path — into one ledger, so a deferral cannot quietly become permanent.
- **How it looks:** One row per marker, grouped by file: `<file>:<line>, <what was simplified>. ceiling: <the limit named>. upgrade: <the trigger to revisit>.` Rows whose comment names no upgrade path or trigger get a `no-trigger` tag — those are the rot risks. The report ends "<N> markers, <M> with no trigger." or, when clean, "No shortcut debt. Clean ledger."
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scan with `git grep --no-index --exclude-standard -nE '(#|//|/[*]) ?(shortcut|ponytail):'` — this skips .git and everything the .gitignore files ignore; add other comment prefixes for other stacks. A user-supplied marker word (e.g. /ponytail-debt TODO) replaces the default. Hits that are not deferrals (e.g. a note about a keyboard shortcut) are skipped. Adding `git blame -L<line>,<line>` gives an owner per row. Read-and-report only; it writes the ledger to a file (e.g. PONYTAIL-DEBT.md) only when asked.
- **Reference / source:** DietrichGebert/ponytail on GitHub (skills/ponytail-debt).
