Verification loop: `export_video` on the top-level frame (server-side, ~10s to minutes), planned at one frame per phase (usually 4–6 frames; `fps: 5` covers a handful, 10 is the upper bound; start at width constraint 320 low quality, raise to 768+ to judge fine detail), frames extracted locally with `ffmpeg -ss <t> -frames:v 1`, all fixes batched into one pass before re-rendering.
- **Mechanism & key values:** API surface: `node.manualKeyframeTracks`, `applyManualKeyframeTrack(field, track)` / `removeManualKeyframeTrack(field)`, `node.animationStyles`, `applyAnimationStyle(styleId, presetData?)` / `removeAnimationStyle(id)`, `node.animations` (read-only resolved manual tracks), `figma.motion.figmaAnimationStyles()` for discovering first-party styles (including `TextStagger` — discover before applying; if absent, text motion is unavailable, no silent whole-layer substitute), and the custom-style APIs (`figma.getLocalCustomAnimationStylesAsync`, `figma.createCustomAnimationStyle`). Runtime gating: if motion APIs are not enabled for the user, every motion call throws `"<name>" is not a supported API` — bail out immediately, do not retry. The node being animated must not be a top-level frame (direct child of a page) — animate descendants. Authoring new `"figma:motion"` preset module source is out of scope.
- **Reference / source:** figma/mcp-server-guide (GitHub), Figma MCP server guide; references cover motion patterns, custom styles, text animation and easing.
- **Best for:** Prototyping and specifying animation inside Figma — the in-Figma counterpart to ⟦S0372⟧, which implements Figma motion in code. Trade fit is indirect: useful for previewing section motion in Figma, not a source of web mechanisms itself.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0377⟧

## ⟦S0378⟧ figma/figma-use-slides — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The Slides companion to ⟦S0375⟧ figma-use: building and editing Figma Slides decks (`figma.com/slides/...`) with `use_figma` — deck design thinking, a two-phase plan-then-build workflow, slide-grid structure, sections and speaker notes. A separate editor skill, not a duplicate of figma-use. (Where a `generate_deck` tool also exists, pick one approach per deck and commit — never both.)
- **How it looks:** A finished deck: a grid of slides in named rows (sections), each slide a composed frame with a deliberate colour story and type treatment, at least one signature element recognisable out of context, layouts varied from slide to slide rather than repeated two-column templates. New files start from a default light theme that is structural scaffolding — the skill requires overwriting its colour variables and text styles with the deck's own direction. Speaker notes sit in Presenter View only: short scannable bullets that complement the slide (why, transitions, caveats, timing cues), never a repeated copy of the slide text.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Slides are static frames in this skill; its sequences are workflow: Phase 1 plans every slide spatially (purpose, layout in words, background treatment) plus shared constants and a code preamble; Phase 2 builds 3–5 slides per `use_figma` call without re-planning between batches, validates each batch with a deterministic overlap/clipping/bounds script (~3 seconds), and screenshots only at checkpoints (after the first batch and after the final batch, 1–2 representative slides).
- **Mechanism & key values:** The critical Slides bug: newly created nodes are silently auto-parented to a slide context at absolute (240, 240) (the grid's GRID_PADDING), so `appendChild` must come before setting `x`/`y` for every node at every nesting level — setting position first lands the node at (intended − 240, intended − 240), intermittently. `SLIDE_GRID` and `SLIDE_ROW` are opaque (no fills/effects/layout access) except `SLIDE_ROW.name`, which is how sections are renamed — `getSlideGrid()` returns plain arrays, and setting `.name` on those arrays silently no-ops. `get_metadata` does not work on Slides files; `figma.createPage()` throws. Existing slides are never deleted to rebuild them — redesigns modify slides in place. Design process values: read the brief → check for an existing design language → take a position on what's left → give it a signature; for existing decks, run in "inherit" mode and match the file's palette, type and motifs. `slide.speakerNotes` accepts Markdown with lists, bold, italic and strikethrough (no headings, code blocks, inline code or links). Sections: 2–5 per deck typically, names 1–3 concrete words.
- **Reference / source:** figma/mcp-server-guide (GitHub), Figma MCP server guide; references cover slide design principles, lifecycle, grid, content, properties and gotchas.
- **Best for:** Presentation decks in Figma Slides. No homepage-section use and no trade fit — though its design-thinking discipline (position, signature, layout variety) mirrors good page practice.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0378⟧

## ⟦S0379⟧ figma/generate-project-plan — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A workflow skill that turns a PRD (plus optional codebase grounding) into a FigJam project-plan board through an interactive, user-confirmed flow: research → propose candidate sections → per-section deep research → per-section content + block-shape proposal → create the FigJam file → skeleton pass → fill pass → diagrams → final review. The section set is not fixed; the user picks from ~10 catalog candidates, and each section's content and rendering block are confirmed before anything is written. It runs on ⟦S0375⟧ figma-use + ⟦S0376⟧ figma-use-figjam.
- **How it looks:** A two-column board with a strict visual system. Left column: 800px-wide sections, each in a very pale two-tone colour of one hue — pale background with a slightly more saturated matching table-header fill (violet #F8F5FF / #DCCCFF, green #EBFFEE / #CDF4D3, blue #DBF0FF / #C2E5FF, pale blue #F5FBFF / #C2E5FF, orange #FFF7F0 / #FFE0C2, teal #F1FEFD / #C6FAF6, yellow #FFFBF0 / #FFECBD, pink #FFEEF8 / #FFC2EC, red #FFEEE8 / #FFCDC2). Right column: pure-white diagram sections, width max(1200, diagram width + 64). Type is all Inter on charcoal #1E1E1E: H1 board title 40px Medium; H2 section title 40px Medium; H3 at three deliberate sizes chosen by container width — 40px full-width, 32px nested-section headers, 24px column titles; body 16px Medium; table header AND body cells 16px Bold with charcoal text on the light header fill (never white-on-dark). Sections carry no FigJam title-bar label (`section.name = ""`) — the H2 inside is the only title. Architecture diagrams get fixed subgraph colours from `generate_diagram` (client #AFF4C6 rounded-rect, gateway #FFFFFF, service #E4CCFF, datastore #BDE3FF cylinder, external #FFFFFF, async #BDE3FF) that must not be overridden.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The board is built in passes: skeleton sections appear with placeholder shimmer (`placeholder = true`), each fill pass replaces one section's placeholder with real content and clears it, a re-stack pass fixes cumulative Y from actual heights, an outer-wrapper pass wraps the left column, and diagrams are reparented into their sections last (every connector deleted and recreated after reparenting, because long-bend connectors keep stale elbow waypoints; fresh connector labels need fontName + fontSize 14 + characters + fills all set, since default label fills are an empty array = transparent).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Geometry constants: section inner padding 32 on all sides, first child at (32, 32); wrapper inner padding 64; vertical gap between children inside a section 24 everywhere (H2→next, body→H3, H3→next, body→body, list→next — always computed as `prevChild.y + prevChild.height + 24`, never a fixed offset, because H3 height varies by size); last child bottom → section edge 32; vertical gap between sections 64; diagram column starts 64px right of the wrapper, top aligned with the wrapper top. Sections do not auto-grow — height is set manually with `resizeWithoutConstraints(w, maxChildBottom + 32)`. Metadata (Owner / Status / Last updated / Source) is embedded in the outer wrapper under the H1 — H1 at (64, 64), body row 16px below it, 32px between body cells — not a separate section. Operating rules: ≤10 logical operations per `use_figma` call; every write returns created/mutated node IDs; palette colours in hex/255 notation; never write past an unanswered confirmation checkpoint; a failed script is atomic (no changes made). Content blocks each have their own subskill: top-level section, nested section, intro callout, text primitives, table, multi-column text (2–4 columns), sticky column, diagram section, metadata strip. Forbidden defaults are listed explicitly: the saturated FigJam palette (#CDF4D3, #C2E5FF, #874FFF…) for backgrounds/headers, Inter Medium table cells, non-empty section names.
- **Reference / source:** figma/mcp-server-guide (GitHub), workflow skills; conventions derived from a canonical reference board named in the skill; diagrams via `generate_diagram` with `useArchitectureLayoutCode: "FIGMA_DIAGRAM_2026"`.
- **Best for:** Project-plan and planning boards in FigJam. No homepage-section use and no trade fit — but its published constants are a complete, concrete example of a two-tone section system with disciplined type sizes and spacing.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0379⟧

## ⟦S0380⟧ figma/video-interaction-mapper — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A workflow skill that turns a UI screen recording into a static, annotated storyboard inside a Figma Design file: it extracts the important before/after states, infers what triggered each change, and lays out clean screenshots with blue interaction markers and concise annotations. Built on bundled Python scripts (ffmpeg/ffprobe + Pillow) plus the Figma MCP tools.
- **How it looks:** A left-to-right storyboard in Figma: a title block, then rows of Before/After screenshot pairs grouped by moment — moment 1, moment 2, moment 3 across the page — each pair captioned ("Before state", "01 Dropdown menu opens") with annotation text under it. Blue ring/dot overlays sit on the exact target and result locations when coordinates are confident (target on the before frame, result on the after frame); native Figma annotations attach to the marker nodes, or to the screenshot frame when a marker is suppressed. Annotation labels name the UI element or state change in words — never raw coordinate percentages.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion in the output. The motion lives in the source video; the skill samples it into stills. Pipeline: scout pass (extract at 1 fps, frames resized to 640px wide, scene-change scoring, contact sheet) → pick 5–15 key moments (prioritise high scene scores and genuinely different states; raise `--scene-threshold`, e.g. to 0.4, when there are too many) → resolve the chosen before/after frames at higher quality → prepare upload assets (JPEGs 1440px wide for landscape, 900px for portrait, quality 75) → generate self-contained Figma scripts → run the storyboard call, upload assets, run the explicit image-hash fill pass → verify screenshots are visible, markers sit on the intended elements, and no coordinates leak into visible text.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Each key moment records: the visual change (modal, drawer, dropdown, tooltip, snackbar, overlay, navigation, loaded content, selected/validation state, focus, scroll), the inferred trigger (click, tap, keyboard, hover, scroll, swipe, submit, auto/timer — or "Unknown trigger" rather than a guess), and target/result coordinates normalised 0–1 (percent-like values such as 45 are accepted and converted to 0.45). Honesty mechanics: inferred or cursor-only targets are flagged `inferred`/`uncertain`/`visible: false` or confidence "medium"/"low", and the generated script suppresses their markers by default; `show_marker: true` forces one with an alternate style. The generated JavaScript never embeds image bytes and never calls `figma.createImage`; the storyboard script creates all containers, labels, annotations and markers in one call and returns `uploadTargets`, and in a blank file it reuses and renames the default page. Local analysis (key_moments.json, upload_manifest.json, generated scripts) is completed before any Figma file is created, so partial pages are not left behind. The target must be a Design file — FigJam/Slides URLs are refused.
- **Reference / source:** figma/mcp-server-guide (GitHub), workflow skills; requires ffmpeg, ffprobe and Python with Pillow on the machine.
- **Best for:** Documenting app flows and interaction states for handoff, QA or redesign reference. No homepage-section use; trade fit is process-only (e.g. storyboarding a client's existing site behaviour before a rebuild).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0380⟧

## ⟦S0381⟧ filipwojda/regards-art-direction — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A complete art-direction method for marketing pages, landing pages, portfolios and product pages. **Plainly stated: this is a fork of tasteskill v2 — the same underlying skill the catalog holds as ⟦S0095⟧ design-taste-frontend (Part 09).** It keeps tasteskill's subject inventory, idea test, open-collection pictures, real-browser inspector, house rules and look-and-fix critique loop, and replaces one step: instead of dealing one of 20 fixed directions, the direction is derived from a live search of regards.design, a hand-picked index of real website sections searchable by how they look. Same engine, different direction source — read ⟦S0095⟧ for the shared machinery and this entry for what changed.
- **How it looks:** The house style the inspector enforces: flat colour as whole fields — a palette of three to six saturated colours plus ink, sections taking their own field with hard steps between dark and light neighbours, ink type on light fields and white on dark. Type does the visible work at two or three sizes (one very large, one small, nothing between; median headline-to-body ratio 4.3 across the 247 studied sites; largest type median 8.4vw on top sites against 5.0vw on weak ones; display tracking −0.02 to −0.05em, leading 0.85–1.05; running text 16–20px, leading 1.45–1.6, 45–75 characters per line; five sizes per page is the ceiling; one family normal, two the limit; left-aligned by default, centre at most once). Headlines fit two lines or fewer at every width; statements set large stay ≤36px on desktop / 24px on a phone and ~25 words. One grid with tight 16–32px margins, big things running to the edges, section gaps clearly larger than any internal gap (120–220px on desktop), every section a different composition from its neighbours and able to hold the whole screen as a poster. At least four real pictures (usually six to twelve; SVG drawings do not count), one dominant image beating six small ones, consistent crop ratios and square corners. Printed things from the subject's world (ticket, label, ledger, timetable) drawn as paper objects — device-pixel grain, ink catching the tooth, one soft shadow allowed because the object really lifts. Flat square-or-fully-round buttons in one fill colour; navigation is a plain bar (wordmark, 3–5 links, one action); the footer is a designed close, not a sitemap. Banned outright: eyebrows/pill badges, gradients, glass/backdrop blur, icon-topped feature cards and identical card rows, assistant palette (yellow-cream with terracotta, violet/indigo), styled accent words in headlines, emoji, decorative blobs, fake dashboards. Banned-but-earnable by a studied reference (all three conditions: the reference visibly uses it, the specimen line names what it becomes, and on the page it carries real information): monospace, index numbering, hairline rules/outlined boxes, tiny tracked labels, one soft shadow under a physical object, violet/indigo as one whole colour field among several.
- **Frame by frame:** The page is made still first ("a page that needs animation to look finished is not finished"), then the motion layer is added last and is mandatory: the inspector fails a page with fewer than eight elements that really move while it loads and is scrolled. The layer has four parts — the signature move taken from the direction sheet, done well; an entrance for the parts of every section (heading, then text, then picture, staggered 60–90ms, rising 16–32px, playing once); feedback on every control; and one moving picture where an honest clip exists. Transform and opacity only, every move with a `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback. If the signature move comes from a reference, its still capture does not show the motion — the skill directs reading `get_section` for how it moves and opening the live site.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Ten-step run: (1) read the brief and inventory the subject — 8–12 things that belong to this client and no competitor (name, place, numbers, constraints, materials, rituals, printed things) — and establish what imagery truly exists; (2) write the argument: the page as claims with proof, one line per section, deleting any section with no claim; (3) research on regards in three passes — mood (2–3 short Instant searches), components (one Deep search per claim, briefed in full sentences; Deep takes ~half a minute and one credit, failed Deep searches are not charged and same-day repeats are free, ~4 Deep at a time), widen-and-drift (`similar_sections` from the best keys plus one deliberately oblique search; novelty runs 1 template → 5); user-specified site kinds act as a hard filter via `categories`/`exclude_categories`; keep 5–8 references, never more than one from the same site, each with a specimen line (takes / leaves / becomes) in `.taste-skill/references.md`; (4) the idea sentence — "On this page, [something that belongs to the subject] becomes [the device the references point to]" — plus the competitor test and one live thing (a real interaction using the subject's real content, thumb-usable on a phone, with a plain no-script fallback); (5) write the full copy deck before markup (~32 characters is the safe headline length everywhere; proof is never invented — no customers, quotes, reviews, press or statistics); (6) build: tokens first, hero at desktop and phone widths, sections in argument order, imagery in preference order (project's own → generated → open collections via `scripts/assets.mjs` — Openverse, Wikimedia Commons, Art Institute of Chicago, Met; commercial-use licences, credited in the footer → drawn in code → type and colour alone); (7) gate: `lint.mjs` on source, `inspect.mjs` in a real browser at 1440, 768 and 390px — fix every FAIL, treat each WARN as wrong unless defensible in one sentence; (8) look: critique screenshots against the rubric, set each finished section beside the reference it drew on (if a visitor could mistake one for the other, mutate further), fix the top three problems, three rounds at most; (9) motion layer as above; (10) report searches, specimens, exceptions, credits and sample content honestly. Tooling needs Node 22+ and Chrome/Edge/Chromium; scripts install nothing. Fallback when the regards tools are missing or keep failing: deal a direction from the bundled library as tasteskill does, and say in the report that the direction was dealt, not researched.
- **Reference / source:** regards.design (the research index, via its MCP server: `claude mcp add --transport http regards https://mcp.regards.design/mcp`); forked from tasteskill v2 by Leonxlnx (MIT); craft laws cite tasteskill's study of 247 gallery sites.
- **Best for:** Whole public-facing pages end to end — hero, proof, work/gallery, process, pricing, FAQ, call/CTA and footer all carry the idea, never stock blocks after a distinctive first screen. Direct trade fit: this is a page-design method for exactly the client homepage work this bank serves, with trades-relevant disciplines baked in (real pictures of the subject's world, no invented proof, one live thing such as a real price/loan-style calculator, phone-first composition). Not for dashboards or app screens.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0381⟧ (shared machinery: WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0095⟧)

## ⟦S0382⟧ firebenders/sync-figma-token — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A design-token parity workflow: sync tokens between code and Figma variables with strict drift reporting, a mandatory human approval gate, safe delta application and persisted reports. It runs on ⟦S0375⟧ figma-use for every `use_figma` call.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on a page. The visible artefacts are a dry-run drift report (a JSON headline summary plus a detailed per-token list with before/after values) and, after approval, updated Figma variables and/or code token files that match.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The sequence is gated: normalise both sides → validate values → produce the dry-run report → STOP and ask "Apply these changes? (yes/no)" in a normal confirmation question → only on explicit affirmative approval, apply deltas in a fixed order → run a fresh diff; success means unresolved drift is zero or only explicitly approved exceptions remain. Writes never happen in the same turn as the dry-run output, and write calls are never parallelised.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Source preference order: Design Tokens JSON (DTCG-style) → Style Dictionary input JSON → platform theme sources (Compose/Kotlin/TS). Policies are declared before any write: `direction` (`code_to_figma` default, `figma_to_code`, `bidirectional`), `deletePolicy` (default `archive_only` — deletion itself requires explicit user instruction), `conflictPolicy` (`prefer_code` / `prefer_figma` / `manual_review`, which lists conflicts and stops), `namingPolicy`, `modePolicy`. Both sides normalise to canonical rows: key, type (COLOR / FLOAT / STRING / BOOLEAN), modeValues, aliasTarget, scopes, codeSyntax. Value validation is mandatory, not presence-only: COLOR compares RGBA with tolerance epsilon = 0.0001; FLOAT strict unless a tolerance is configured; STRING/BOOLEAN strict equality; aliases compare canonical targets. Nine drift categories: missing_in_figma, missing_in_code, value_mismatch, alias_mismatch, type_mismatch, mode_mismatch, scope_mismatch, code_syntax_mismatch, broken_alias. Dry-run headline counts: create, update, aliasFix, scopeFix, syntaxFix, archive, delete. Apply order: ensure collections/modes → create missing primitives → create/update semantic aliases → value updates → scopes and code syntax → archive stale tokens. Reports persist every run to `/tmp/sync-figma-token-dry-run-{runId}.json` and `/tmp/sync-figma-token-final-{runId}.json`; a persistence failure must be stated explicitly.
- **Reference / source:** firebenders/sync-figma-token-skill (GitHub); DTCG design-token format and Style Dictionary named as the standard sources.
- **Best for:** Design-system maintenance — keeping a token set honest across code and Figma. No homepage-section use and no direct trade fit.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0382⟧

## ⟦S0383⟧ flornkm/prefer-container-queries — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A responsive-design rule skill for Tailwind: components should respond to the space they are in, not to the viewport, so container queries are the default and viewport breakpoints the exception. It covers writing, reviewing and migrating responsive component code.
- **How it looks:** The same component rendering correctly in every context it lands in: a card stacked vertically in a ~300px sidebar stays stacked even on a huge monitor; the identical card in a wide grid cell switches to a horizontal row — image beside text — the moment its own container is wide enough. Concretely from the skill's example: below the container threshold the card is a column with a full-width image; at `@md:` the row becomes `flex-row` with a 6-unit gap, the image fixes at `w-48` (12rem) and the text takes the remaining flex space. A builder uses the table to pick the exact container width at which a gallery card, stat block or form should flip from stacked to side-by-side.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Layout changes are instant flips at container-width thresholds; there is no transition or animation prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Mark the parent `@container`; put `@`-prefixed variants on descendants (an element cannot query its own size; variants answer to the nearest `@container` ancestor). Tailwind v4 container scale: `@3xs` 16rem (256px), `@2xs` 18rem (288px), `@xs` 20rem (320px), `@sm` 24rem (384px), `@md` 28rem (448px), `@lg` 32rem (512px), `@xl` 36rem (576px), `@2xl` 42rem (672px), `@3xl` 48rem (768px), `@4xl` 56rem (896px), `@5xl` 64rem (1024px), `@6xl` 72rem (1152px), `@7xl` 80rem (1280px). Also `@max-md:` for below-a-size styles, `@min-[475px]:` arbitrary values, and named containers (`@container/sidebar` queried as `@md/sidebar:`) for reaching past nested containers. Tailwind v3 needs the `@tailwindcss/container-queries` plugin. Keep viewport breakpoints for: page-level layout (overall grid, whether a sidebar exists, header/navigation behaviour), fixed/sticky elements positioned against the viewport, and the global typography scale. Migration rule: never map `md:` to `@md:` blindly — `md` is 768px of viewport, `@md` is 448px of container; resize the container to find the real flip point, and test in the narrowest real context (sidebar, drawer, small grid cell), not at mobile viewport widths.
- **Reference / source:** flornkm/skills (GitHub); Tailwind CSS container queries documentation (tailwindcss.com/docs/responsive-design).
- **Best for:** Any reused component — work/gallery cards, proof/stat blocks, forms, lists, table-to-list switches — and any section rendered in more than one layout slot. Good trade fit for build discipline: sections that must survive being placed in narrow and wide contexts without breaking.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0383⟧

## ⟦S0384⟧ flornkm/smooth-shadow-ring — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A small craft rule for Tailwind projects with the shadow-plugin installed: elevated surfaces must never pair a `border-*`/`ring-*` with a `shadow-*`; elevation is routed through `smooth-shadow-ring-{size}` utilities instead.
- **How it looks:** A card, dialog, popover, dropdown, menu, tooltip, sheet, toast or command palette whose edge is one continuous stroke: the 1px hairline ring is baked into the final shadow layer, so the outline dissolves into the shadow instead of showing the double edge — a crisp painted line, then a separate soft shadow starting outside it — that makes bordered-and-shadowed surfaces look heavy, greyed and cheap. With no edge stroke wanted at all, plain `smooth-shadow-{size}` gives the shadow alone.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. It is a static styling rule; the utilities carry no `!important` and follow the normal cascade, so a JS animation on `box-shadow` or a later utility overrides them normally (Tailwind's important modifier, e.g. `smooth-shadow-ring-md!`, is the escape when a component library's unlayered `box-shadow` outranks them).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Sizes: `smooth-shadow-ring-xs`, `-sm`, `-md` (also the bare `smooth-shadow-ring`), `-lg`, `-xl`, `-2xl`. Conversions: `border shadow-md` → `smooth-shadow-ring-md`; `ring-1 ring-neutral-200 shadow-lg` → `smooth-shadow-ring-lg`. Ring and shadow tint independently on the same element: `shadow-{color}` tints the shadow, `smooth-ring-{color}` tints the ring (e.g. `smooth-ring-black/10`, `smooth-ring-blue-500/40`). Ring default `rgba(0,0,0,0.05)` in light mode, flipping to `rgba(255,255,255,0.18)` in dark mode — the dark alpha is deliberately much higher because the ring paints outside the surface, so its rendered colour comes from the page behind it; near `neutral-700`-and-lighter dark surfaces need an explicit `smooth-ring-*`. The flip keys off a `.dark` class, `data-theme="dark"`, or a declared `color-scheme: light dark` — never `prefers-color-scheme` alone, so light-only sites keep the light ring for every visitor (a purely media-query dark mode must declare `:root { color-scheme: light dark; }`). Ring width is 1px by default and follows the project's Tailwind ring width automatically (a project with `--default-ring-width: 0.5px` gets a 0.5px hairline); override `--smooth-ring-width` only where it must differ. Never keep a border or ring on an element that already has `smooth-shadow-ring-*` — the ring is already in the shadow.
- **Reference / source:** flornkm/shadow-plugin (GitHub) — the utility set comes from that Tailwind plugin.
- **Best for:** Every floating surface in a page build — cards in work/proof sections, quote-form panels, dropdown navigation, dialogs and toasts. A small but real craft detail for trade pages: one continuous edge reads as quality at screenshot distance.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0384⟧

## ⟦S0385⟧ flornkm/webgl-components — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** An engineering discipline for embedding small, always-on WebGL visuals — identity avatars, ambient orbs, glass and iridescent surfaces, animated textures — inside a normal product UI without wrecking performance, accessibility, SSR or layout. It is written for widgets rendered many times per page (a list of fifty avatars), and its lessons are about cost, correctness and fallback, not about a look to copy.
- **How it looks:** A small shader-driven element — say a glassy identity disc — whose optics are derived rather than painted: from one surface normal, a Fresnel term drives a reflection of a procedural environment, so at grazing angles the rim shows nothing but environment and goes properly opaque, while the clear middle stays premultiplied-transparent and lets the page through; dispersion is physically produced by sampling the interior at multiple wavelengths, so a white emitter inside emerges as a spectrum in the correct order, widening toward the rim where the glass is thick — an effect no hand-authored colour ramp reproduces, since a sphere disperses along its own radius and getting spread perpendicular to a feature needs a wedge (prism) normal, with position computed from the plain normal and only the per-wavelength difference added. Slow ambient drift moves by sampling a precomputed texture at warped positions, not by recomputing the pattern.
- **Frame by frame:** Continuous motion on one module-level `requestAnimationFrame` loop shared by all instances: each frame draws into the single shared offscreen GL canvas and blits each visible instance's region into its own 2D canvas within the same task (blitting from `canvas.height − size`, because GL's origin is bottom-left). Instances agreeing on every visual input are drawn once and blitted to all of them. The loop gates every instance on IntersectionObserver (offscreen instances never draw), pauses entirely when the tab is hidden, stops when nothing visible remains, and is frame-rate capped — slow ambient drift gains nothing above 30fps, and an uncapped loop on a 120Hz display pins a core. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` it renders one still frame at full visual fidelity and never starts the loop. On context loss, or where the strict context refuses to run, every instance flips to its DOM fallback (see below) — the same tint and seed-derived look in plain CSS.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Architecture: never one WebGL context per instance — browsers cap a document at roughly 8–16 live contexts, then silently evict the oldest. Cost model: per-pixel fragment cost × area; aim for one texture tap plus a couple of noise evaluations per pixel; precompute expensive patterns (noise octaves, streaks, grain) into a source texture once; expensive one-time texture generation budgeted to roughly one per frame. UV-perturbing drift needs a negative mip bias in `texture2D(..., bias)` or the widget reads blurry; mipmaps are mandatory and WebGL1 needs power-of-two textures (resample arbitrary images onto a power-of-two canvas). Optics values: disc normal `N = normalize(vec3(p, sqrt(1 − r*r)))`; Fresnel `0.04 + 0.96 × pow(1 − dot(N, V), 5.0)`; the environment can be a direction-to-colour function (one soft key lobe, a vertical gradient, a floor bounce) instead of a cubemap; dispersion needs 8–16 wavelength taps (3 taps only fringe two edges), with everything not varying per wavelength hoisted out of the loop; the index-of-refraction spread is the one number worth pushing well past reality, kept as a named constant. Transparency: output premultiplied `vec4(emitted, coverage)`; drive ambient level from `prefers-color-scheme` as a uniform so a widget on a white page does not grow a black studio ring; WebGL cannot read the pixels behind its canvas — true page refraction needs a DOM `backdrop-filter` layer (an SVG `feDisplacementMap` bends properly but is not portable) and the skill requires saying which option was used. Resolution: let the shader's cost set the device-pixel-ratio cap — around 1.5 for an expensive multi-tap shader, full display density for a cheap one-tap shader; decide the cap after the shader is final. Robustness: `failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat: true` (refuse software rasterisation), bounded texture cache keyed by stable source (each texture ~1 megapixel plus mip chain; evict only keys not in use, via `gl.deleteTexture`), `createImageBitmap` decoding off the main thread with `close()` in a `finally`, luminance clamped in-shader to a mid band with luminosity-preserving tint blends so no input can produce an all-black or blown-out widget. The fallback is a production surface, not an edge case: `fallback` is part of the minimum prop API next to `source` and appears in the first documented example; the clipping frame must be `position: relative` with `overflow: hidden` or an oversized fallback image paints across the surrounding UI; a `forceFallback` prop makes the branch reachable on a healthy GPU for testing. React/SSR: `"use client"` where RSC applies, no browser APIs at module scope under any SSR, object props spread to primitives for effect dependencies. Identity: per-entity variety from a stable hash of the entity id (Knuth multiplicative) into a curated table — never `Math.random()` in the render path; the same entity looks identical across sessions, surfaces and the WebGL-to-fallback boundary. Verification without eyeballs: port the shader math to NumPy/PIL and assert on luminance statistics; the bundled `scripts/gpu-probe.html` measures which branch a machine takes; the checklist ends with fifty instances scrolling at 60fps, tab-hidden CPU near zero, and a production build.
- **Reference / source:** flornkm/skills (GitHub); the skill itself is the reference — hard-won production lessons, with a bundled GPU probe script.
- **Best for:** Small decorative WebGL accents — logos, avatars, orbs, glassy badges — and as cost/fallback discipline for any WebGL used on a page. Trade fit: not a hero system; its value to trade builds is the budget rules (one context, capped frame rate, visibility gating, mandatory fallback) that keep a fancy accent from taxing phones.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0385⟧

## ⟦S0386⟧ github/gh-stack — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Documentation for `gh stack`, a GitHub CLI extension for stacked branches and pull requests: an ordered chain of branches rooted on a trunk, each branch carrying one PR based on the branch below it, so a reviewer sees only that layer's diff. Pure developer tooling — it produces no design of any kind.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual. In a terminal, `gh stack` prints a stack trunk-first, left to right — `(main) <- auth <- api <- frontend` — with the left as the bottom (merges first) and the right as the top (merges last); `up` moves away from trunk, `down` toward it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The working sequence is a command loop: `gh stack init auth` → commit → `gh stack add api` → commit → `gh stack submit --auto` (pushes every branch, opens draft PRs; `--open` for ready-for-review) → `gh stack view --json` to confirm; `gh stack sync` fetches, reconciles, rebases and pushes (`--prune` also deletes local branches for merged PRs, and pruning never happens without the flag non-interactively).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Requires Git 2.36+ and an authenticated GitHub CLI; setup is `gh extension install github/gh-stack`, `git config rerere.enabled true`, and `remote.pushDefault` when the repo has more than one remote (otherwise `push`/`submit`/`sync`/`rebase`/`link` need `--remote <name>`). Non-interactive discipline drives the skill: `gh stack` branches on whether stdout is a TTY, so agents always use `view --json`, `submit --auto`, `merge <target> --yes`, `init <branch>...`, `add <branch>`, `checkout <target>`, and `up`/`down`/`top`/`bottom`; bare `view`, `submit`, `init`, `add`, `checkout`, `switch` and `modify` open prompts or a TUI and block (modify is TUI-only with no non-interactive path — restructure with `unstack` then `init` instead). Merging is scoped and all-or-nothing: a PR number merges that PR plus every unmerged PR below it, a stack number merges the whole stack, with `--squash` / `--merge` / `--rebase` / `--merge-method`; without a method flag the last-used method is reused, and a merge queue overrides the flag with a warning. `view --json` writes JSON to stdout (status messages go to stderr — branch on exit codes, never parse stderr); `branches[].pr.state` is OPEN | MERGED | QUEUED, and `needsRebase` is true when the parent's current tip is no longer an ancestor. Exit codes 0–10 each have a named recovery (3 = rebase conflict: resolve, `git add`, `rebase --continue`; after a failed `sync` the stack is already restored, so re-run `rebase` to recreate the conflict; 8 = stack file locked, retry after ~5s; 9 = stacked PRs not enabled on the repository). Constraints: stacks are strictly linear (one parent, at most one child); rebase/sync update clean worktrees automatically but never auto-stash; PR titles and bodies are auto-generated (edit afterwards with `gh pr edit`). `gh stack <command> --help` is authoritative; `gh stack help <command>` does not work.
- **Reference / source:** github/gh-stack (GitHub), the official GitHub CLI extension; GitHub CLI at cli.github.com.
- **Best for:** Splitting multi-part code work into reviewable stacked PRs. No homepage-section use and no trade fit — included in the catalog as agent tooling.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0386⟧

## ⟦S0387⟧ google-gemini/gemini-api-dev — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The reference skill for writing code against the Gemini API with the current Interactions API — text generation, multi-turn chat, multimodal understanding, image generation and editing, video generation, speech (TTS, voice design, voice replication), transcription, streaming, function calling, structured output, managed agents and deep research — in Python and TypeScript. An API skill, not a design skill. (Its real-time streaming sibling is ⟦S0388⟧ gemini-live-api-dev, a separate skill this one points to.)
- **How it looks:** Nothing prescribed on screen. What an end user ultimately sees depends on the app built with it: generated text, generated or edited images, spoken audio, or generated video inside whatever interface the developer designs. The skill itself specifies models, SDK calls and data shapes only.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. Its one sequence is streaming delivery: an interaction streams as `interaction.created` → (`step.start` → `step.delta`(s) → `step.stop`)+ → `interaction.completed`, with delta types text, audio, image, thought_summary and thought_signature.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Current models as the skill fixes them (1M-token context unless noted): `gemini-4-argon` (most powerful), `gemini-3.8-flash`, `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, `gemini-3.1-flash-lite`, `gemini-3.5-transcribe`; image models `gemini-nano-banana-2.1` (131k/32k, default; multi-image reference fusion with up to 14 reference images), `gemini-3-pro-image` "Nano Banana Pro" (65k/32k), `gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image` "Nano Banana 2 Lite" (65k/32k); TTS `gemini-3.8-flash-tts` and `gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts`; video `gemini-omni-1.1-flash` (first-frame-to-video, first-and-last-frame transitions, extensions up to 40s, editing, reference-guided generation); embeddings `gemini-embedding-2` (multimodal) and `gemini-embedding-001` (text); open Gemma 4 models `gemma-4-31b-it` (31B dense) and `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` (26B total / 4B active MoE). Legacy `gemini-2.5-*`, `2.0-*` and `1.5-*` are deprecated and must never be used — a request for one is answered with `gemini-3.8-flash` and a note. SDKs: Python `google-genai` >= 2.30.1, JS/TS `@google/genai` >= 2.29.1; the old `google-generativeai` / `@google/generative-ai` packages are deprecated. Interactions are stored by default (paid tier retains 55 days, free tier 1 day); `store=False` opts out but disables `previous_interaction_id` and background mode; `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are interaction-scoped and re-specified each turn. Managed agents: `antigravity-preview-09-2026` (sandboxed code execution, files, web; `gemini-3.8-flash` by default, `gemini-4-argon` via agent_config; requires `environment="remote"`), `deep-research-preview-04-2026` and `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` (require `background=True`, polled), and custom agents via `client.agents.create()`. Response helpers: `output_text`, `output_image`, `output_audio`. Hard process rule: fetch the matching hosted documentation page before writing code — the skill's examples are minimal by design.
- **Reference / source:** google-gemini/gemini-skills (GitHub); documentation at ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs (the skill lists ~50 doc pages as the source of truth).
- **Best for:** Building AI-backed features into a site or app — generated imagery, chat, voice, research. No homepage-section design use; trade fit only as an implementation reference if a build ever calls the Gemini API.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0387⟧

## ⟦S0388⟧ google-gemini/gemini-live-api-dev — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The development skill for the Gemini Live API: real-time, bidirectional audio/video/text streaming over WebSockets — live voice agents, background reasoning with spoken fillers, streaming transcription, and live speech-to-speech translation. It is the companion ⟦S0387⟧ points to for everything real-time; a separate skill, not a duplicate.
- **How it looks:** Nothing prescribed visually — the experience is auditory and temporal: a visitor speaks and hears a spoken reply in near-real time; on the extended-thinking model they hear natural conversational fillers ("Checking flight options now…") while tools run in the background; transcripts appear as interim hypotheses that then finalise; with translation, speech comes back spoken in the target language. Any captions or UI around it are the app's own design.
- **Frame by frame:** Not page motion — a session stream: connect over WebSocket with a `LiveConnectConfig` → stream mic audio in via `send_realtime_input` → server events arrive carrying multiple content parts at once (audio chunks plus input/output transcriptions — all parts must be processed or content is lost) → on an `interrupted` signal the client stops playback and clears its audio queue → for extended thinking, turn completion is tracked by `interaction_status` (`IN_PROGRESS` while reasoning/filling/tool-waiting, `IDLE` when ready), never by `turn_complete` alone. Hybrid VAD ends a turn with zero latency: the client sends `audio_stream_end` on detected silence.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Models: `gemini-3.8-live` (default low-latency voice; async function calling `behavior: NON_BLOCKING` by default), `gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking` (background reasoning; all tools must be NON_BLOCKING; thinking levels "minimal" | "low" | "medium" | "high"), `gemini-3.5-transcribe-live` (interim + finalised transcripts; modes `smart` — filler words cleaned, self-corrections resolved, formatting structured — and `verbatim`, the default), `gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview` (70+ languages; `TranslationConfig` with target_language_code and echo_target_language). Audio formats are exact: input raw PCM little-endian 16-bit mono at 16kHz native (`audio/pcm;rate=16000`, other rates resampled); output raw PCM 16-bit mono at 24kHz. Session limits: one response modality per session (TEXT or AUDIO, never both); 15 minutes audio-only and 2 minutes audio+video without compression; connection lifetime ~10 minutes (use session resumption); context window 128k input / 64k output tokens; code execution and URL context not supported. SDKs: `google-genai` >= 2.3.0 (Python), `@google/genai` >= 2.3.0 (JS/TS); legacy SDKs deprecated. Rules: all real-time input goes through `send_realtime_input` with the specific `audio` / `video` / `text` keys (never a generic `media` key); `send_client_content` injects full context turns mid-session with explicit `user`/`model` roles and `turn_complete=true` unconditionally interrupts active generation; ephemeral tokens for client-side auth (never expose API keys in browsers); context compression for sessions over 15 minutes; headphones when testing to prevent echo/self-interruption. Partner WebRTC/WebSocket integrations named: LiveKit, Pipecat by Daily, Fishjam, Vision Agents by Stream, Voximplant, Firebase AI SDK. Documentation discipline: when the Google MCP `search_docs` tool exists it is the only docs source; otherwise fetch the llms.txt index at ai.google.dev.
- **Reference / source:** google-gemini/gemini-skills (GitHub); Live API documentation at ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs.
- **Best for:** Voice agents, live transcription and live translation features. No homepage-section design use and no direct trade fit — an implementation reference only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0388⟧

## ⟦S0389⟧ Graphify-Labs/graphify — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A pipeline skill (`/graphify`) that turns any folder of files — code, docs, papers, images — into a persistent, navigable knowledge graph with community detection and an honest audit trail, built around Andrej Karpathy's /raw folder workflow. Three outputs: interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON (`graphify-out/graph.json`, which survives across sessions), and a plain-language `GRAPH_REPORT.md`; by default it also generates an Obsidian vault.
- **How it looks:** The HTML visualisation is a network graph in the browser (no server needed): nodes coloured by community, clustered into groups, navigable by the reader. The Obsidian output is a vault of one note per node plus `_COMMUNITY_*` overview notes carrying cohesion scores and dataview queries, a graph view with community colours set automatically, and a `graph.canvas` with communities laid out as structured groups. Optional exports render the same graph as SVG (for Notion/GitHub), GraphML (Gephi, yEd) or Neo4j Cypher. The report leads with God Nodes (the most-connected concepts), Surprising Connections (cross-community bridges) and Suggested Questions.
- **Frame by frame:** No prescribed animation — the HTML graph is reader-driven (pan, zoom, click to explore). The skill's own sequence is a nine-step pipeline: install check → detect files and summarise the corpus by type → extract (deterministic AST extraction for code in parallel with semantic extraction by subagents over docs/papers/images) → merge → build graph, cluster, analyse → label communities with 2–5-word plain-language names → regenerate the report → generate the vault + HTML → optional exports → token benchmark (only when the corpus exceeds 5,000 words) → save manifest, update the cost tracker, clean up, and report by pasting only the God Nodes, Surprising Connections and Suggested Questions sections, then offering to trace the single most interesting question.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Corpus guardrails: stop if no supported files; mention (never name) skipped sensitive files; if the corpus exceeds 2,000,000 words or 200 files, show the top 5 subdirectories and ask which subfolder to run on before proceeding. Semantic extraction chunks files 20–25 per subagent (each image gets its own chunk for vision), dispatched all in one message, with a printed estimate (~45s per agent batch); an extraction cache means only new/changed files are re-extracted. Every edge is honesty-tagged with a confidence score: EXTRACTED = 1.0 exactly; INFERRED = 0.4–0.9 (strong structural inference 0.8–0.9, reasonable 0.6–0.7, weak 0.4–0.5); AMBIGUOUS = 0.1–0.3, flagged rather than omitted; cross-cutting `semantically_similar_to` edges score 0.6–0.95 and only for genuinely non-obvious similarity; at most 3 hyperedges per chunk. Visualisation limits: HTML viz is refused above 5,000 nodes (use the Obsidian vault); cohesion scores are always shown as raw numbers. Querying: `/graphify query` BFS explores layer by layer to depth 3 (broad context), `--dfs` follows one chain to depth 6 (tracing); answers use only what the graph contains, cite `source_location`, and are saved back into `graphify-out/memory` so the next `--update` ingests them as nodes; default token budget 2000 at ~4 chars per token. `/graphify path` finds the shortest path between two concepts; `add <url>` ingests Twitter/X (oEmbed), arXiv, PDFs, images and webpages (html2text) into ./raw; `--watch` rebuilds on change with a 3-second debounce (code-only changes rebuild with no LLM; doc/image changes set a needs_update flag); a git post-commit hook and a CLAUDE.md integration (`graphify claude install`) make it always-on. Honesty rules: never invent an edge, never skip the corpus warning, always show token cost.
- **Reference / source:** Graphify-Labs/graphify (GitHub); the /raw folder workflow is credited to Andrej Karpathy.
- **Best for:** Understanding an unfamiliar codebase, a reading list or a research corpus — and querying it weeks later without re-reading everything. No homepage-section use and no trade fit; it is corpus tooling for the agent, not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0389⟧

## ⟦S0394⟧ humanlayer/narrow-react-prop-types — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A code-quality skill that tightens React component prop types so they describe only the states live (non-test, non-Storybook) code paths actually enter.
- **How it looks:** No visual design. The on-screen effect is indirect: UI affordances can no longer render inert — e.g. a menu item that visibly renders must have a real required handler instead of an optional `onRename?.(...)` call.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** 11-step workflow: find live call sites first (live = routes, wired components, providers, hooks, production exports; support = stories/tests/fixtures/mocks); classify each prop Required / Optional / Removed; required-but-empty values become required nullable props (`focusedItem: FocusedItem | null`, not `focusedItem?:`); derive types with `Parameters<typeof fn>[0]`, `ReturnType<typeof fn>`, `Extract<Union, Shape>`; explicit `useState<DialogState>(...)` where inference widens; delete fallback logic (`?? []`, `?? 0`, `items && …`) once props are required; stories/tests adapt to the strict contract, never the reverse. Validate with package typecheck (example: `bun --bun run typecheck --filter <package>`). This skill is the reference pattern ⟦S0391⟧ builds its example loop around.
- **Reference / source:** HumanLayer skills repo on GitHub; ships a sample recurring GitHub Actions workflow (references/agent-narrow-component-props.yml).
- **Best for:** Engineering quality on React builds only — no homepage section, not relevant to single-file HTML trade sites except as a code-review stance.
