## ⟦S0428⟧ mattpocock/codebase-design — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The shared vocabulary for designing deep modules — a lot of behaviour behind a small interface at a clean seam — used when designing/improving a module's interface, finding deepening opportunities, deciding where a seam goes, or making code more testable and AI-navigable. Other skills in the set (tdd, improve-codebase-architecture, ask-matt) pull this vocabulary in.
- **How it looks:** No visual output; in design discussions it produces diagrams of the deep-vs-shallow contrast: a small interface bar over a deep implementation block (good) versus a wide interface bar over a thin pass-through implementation (avoid).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Glossary terms to use exactly (never substitute): Module (anything with an interface + implementation; not "component/service/unit"), Interface (everything a caller must know — signature plus invariants, ordering, error modes, config, performance; not just "API"), Implementation vs Adapter (role at a seam), Depth (leverage at the interface — explicitly NOT Ousterhout's implementation-to-interface line ratio), Seam (Feathers: where behaviour can change without editing there; not "boundary"), Leverage (callers' gain), Locality (maintainers' gain). Tests of depth: the deletion test (delete the module — if complexity reappears across N callers it was earning its keep; if it vanishes it was a pass-through); the interface is the test surface; one adapter = hypothetical seam, two adapters = a real one. Bundled DEEPENING.md: four dependency categories that decide test strategy — 1 in-process (always deepenable, test through the interface), 2 local-substitutable (deepenable with the stand-in, e.g. PGLite), 3 remote-but-owned (define a port; HTTP adapter in prod, in-memory in tests), 4 true external (injected port, mock adapter); internal vs external seams; replace-don't-layer testing (delete old shallow-module unit tests once interface tests exist). Bundled DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md: frame the problem space for the user, spawn 3+ parallel sub-agents with opposed constraints (minimise interface to 1–3 entry points / maximise flexibility / optimise the common caller / ports-and-adapters), each returning interface + usage + what's hidden + dependency strategy + trade-offs, then compare on depth, locality, seam placement and recommend (hybrids allowed). Testability rules: accept dependencies don't create them; return results don't produce side effects; small surface area.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/codebase-design), drawing on Michael Feathers' seam concept and John Ousterhout's "design it twice" / deep modules (with his depth-ratio framing explicitly rejected). Bundled references: DEEPENING.md, DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — architecture vocabulary for code work; the language ⟦S0433⟧'s reports and ⟦S0436⟧'s seam choices are written in.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0428⟧

## ⟦S0429⟧ mattpocock/diagnosing-bugs — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A six-phase discipline for hard bugs and performance regressions, built on one idea: everything depends on first constructing a tight feedback loop — a single command that goes red on this exact bug. Refuses to theorise before that loop exists.
- **How it looks:** No page visuals. Working artefacts: one named red-capable command with its (redacted) output, a minimised repro, a ranked list of 3–5 falsifiable hypotheses shown to the user, tagged debug logs (e.g. [DEBUG-a4f2]), and a regression test written before the fix.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Phase sequence: (1) build the feedback loop — try, in order: failing test, curl/HTTP script, CLI + snapshot diff, headless-browser script, captured-trace replay, throwaway harness, property/fuzz loop (1000 random inputs), bisection harness (git bisect run), differential old-vs-new loop, HITL bash script last; then tighten it (faster, sharper assertion, deterministic — pin time, seed RNG, isolate FS/network); done only when the command is red-capable, deterministic, fast (seconds) and agent-runnable, and has actually been run → (2) reproduce and minimise, cutting one element at a time until every remaining element is load-bearing → (3) 3–5 ranked hypotheses, each in the form "If X is the cause, then changing Y will make it disappear / Z will make it worse", shown to the user before testing → (4) instrument, one variable at a time, debugger before logs, logs tagged with a unique prefix; perf bugs: measure baseline and bisect instead of logging → (5) regression test first at a CORRECT seam (one that exercises the real bug pattern — if none exists, that absence is itself the finding), then fix, then re-run the original un-minimised loop → (6) cleanup checklist: original repro dead, regression test green, all [DEBUG-…] lines grepped out, prototypes deleted/marked, the winning hypothesis stated in the commit/PR message. Secrets are redacted to <REDACTED> in everything shown; non-deterministic bugs are handled by raising the reproduction rate (loop 100×, parallelise, stress — a 50%-flake is debuggable, 1% is not). No loop possible → stop, list what was tried, ask for environment access, a captured artifact (HAR, logs, core dump, recording), or permission for production instrumentation.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/diagnosing-bugs). Reads the project's GLOSSARY.md and area ADRs while exploring.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — debugging discipline for build tooling and site code when something is broken, throwing, failing or slow.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0429⟧

## ⟦S0430⟧ mattpocock/domain-modeling — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The active discipline of building and sharpening a project's domain model during design work: challenging terms against the glossary, resolving overloaded words, stress-testing relationships with invented scenarios, cross-referencing claims against the code, and writing GLOSSARY.md entries and ADRs down inline the moment they crystallise. (Merely reading the glossary for vocabulary is not this skill.)
- **How it looks:** No page visuals. Artefacts: a GLOSSARY.md at the repo root (or GLOSSARY-MAP.md + per-context glossaries in multi-context repos) whose entries are a bold term, a 1–2 sentence definition of what it IS, and an _Avoid_ list of rejected synonyms; and short numbered ADRs in docs/adr/ (0001-slug.md…) that can be a single paragraph — context, decision, why.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. During a session: user uses a term that conflicts with the glossary → call it out immediately ("your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X; you seem to mean Y") → fuzzy/overloaded term → propose a precise canonical term → relationships discussed → invent concrete edge-case scenarios to force precision → user states how something works → check the code and surface contradictions → term resolved → update GLOSSARY.md right there, never batched. Files are created lazily, only when there's something to write; the glossary holds zero implementation details.
- **Mechanism & key values:** ADR gate — offer one only when ALL three hold: hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off; otherwise skip it. Optional ADR sections (Status frontmatter: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN; Considered Options; Consequences) only when they add value. What qualifies: architectural shape, integration patterns between contexts, lock-in technology choices, boundary/scope decisions (the explicit no-s count), deliberate deviations from the obvious path, constraints invisible in code, non-obviously rejected alternatives. Glossary format rules: opinionated (pick one term, list the rest under _Avoid_), tight definitions, project-specific concepts only (no general programming concepts), group under subheadings when clusters emerge. Multi-context signal: GLOSSARY-MAP.md at root lists contexts and their relationships (event flows, shared types).
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/domain-modeling). Bundled references: GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md, ADR-FORMAT.md.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — keeping a project's language and hard decisions straight during planning/grilling; it's the discipline /grill-with-docs (⟦S0432⟧) and /triage (⟦S0439⟧) drive.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0430⟧

## ⟦S0433⟧ mattpocock/improve-codebase-architecture — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Scans a codebase for "deepening opportunities" — refactors that turn shallow modules into deep ones (vocabulary from ⟦S0428⟧) — presents the candidates as a visual HTML report, then grills through whichever candidate the user picks, updating the domain model as decisions land. Aim: testability and AI-navigability.
- **How it looks:** A single self-contained, editorial HTML report page (stone/slate palette, generous whitespace, optional serif headings) opened locally for the user: a compact header with a diagram legend (solid box = module, dashed line = seam, red arrow = leakage, thick dark box = deep module), then one card per candidate — title, a badge row (recommendation strength Strong = emerald / Worth exploring = amber / Speculative = slate, plus a dependency-category tag), a monospaced file list, a side-by-side BEFORE / AFTER diagram (~320px tall), one-sentence Problem and Solution, and ≤6-word Wins bullets; an amber callout where a candidate contradicts an ADR. A final Top Recommendation card closes the page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion (the report is a static page; Mermaid renders its graphs on load). Process: (1) Explore — scope first (YAGNI: weight recently changed hot spots from git log unless the user named a direction), read GLOSSARY.md + ADRs, spawn a sub-agent to walk the code noting friction (bouncing between small modules, shallow interfaces, leaked seams, untestable parts), applying the deletion test → (2) write the report to <tmpdir>/architecture-review-<timestamp>.html (OS temp dir, nothing lands in the repo), open it, ask "Which of these would you like to explore?" — no interfaces proposed yet → (3) grilling loop on the picked candidate via the "grilling" skill, with domain-modeling side effects inline (new/sharpened terms into GLOSSARY.md; a load-bearing rejection can earn an ADR offer; alternative interfaces via ⟦S0428⟧'s design-it-twice).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Report tech: Tailwind via CDN (cdn.tailwindcss.com) + Mermaid 11 ESM (cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@11) initialised theme "neutral", securityLevel "loose"; those are the only scripts. Diagram patterns to mix: Mermaid flowchart/sequence (leakage edges classed red #dc2626), hand-built boxes-and-arrows (absolutely positioned SVG lines over a relative container), cross-section bands (h-12 border-l-4 layer stacks), mass diagrams (interface vs implementation rectangle heights), call-graph collapse. Labels inside diagrams: text-xs uppercase tracking-wider. Language discipline: exactly module/interface/implementation/depth/deep/shallow/seam/adapter/leverage/locality — never component/service/unit, API/signature, boundary, layer/wrapper. ADR conflicts surface only when friction is real enough to reopen, marked clearly in the card.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture). Bundled reference: HTML-REPORT.md (scaffold, diagram patterns, style guidance). Built on ⟦S0428⟧ codebase-design vocabulary and the project's GLOSSARY.md/ADRs.
- **Best for:** No homepage-section use — periodic codebase-health work. Tangential value to the bank: its report is a worked example of a clean one-page editorial HTML document (legend, cards, before/after diagrams) if a "before/after" proof page ever needs a schematic layout.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0433⟧

## ⟦S0434⟧ mattpocock/prototype — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Builds a throwaway prototype that answers ONE design question, in two branches: LOGIC (does this state model/logic feel right?) → a single self-contained HTML file a non-developer can drive; UI (what should this look like?) → several radically different UI variations on one route, switchable in the browser. Throwaway is a constraint on how the code is written, not a promise to destroy it: the answer folds into real code and the prototype is kept as a primary source on a throwaway branch.
- **How it looks:** LOGIC: a clean single page, top to bottom — title + the question in plain domain language, a readable current-state panel (labelled fields, re-rendered after every click, changes called out), free-play buttons (one per action), then tabbed guided walkthroughs whose steps are real buttons; one accent colour, generous spacing, no animations or gimmicks. UI: the real app page (real header, sidebar, data, density) with only the rendering swapped per variant, plus a small high-contrast floating pill bar at bottom-centre that is obviously not part of the design: left arrow, current variant label (e.g. "B (Sidebar layout)"), right arrow.
- **Frame by frame:** LOGIC: click any free-play button → the action dispatches into the pure logic module → the state panel re-renders showing exactly what changed. Open a walkthrough tab → state resets to a known initial state → click step 1's button → the action runs, state updates, the walkthrough advances → repeat through the scenario (happy path, tricky edge case, an action that should be illegal). UI: page loads with ?variant= absent → Variant A renders. Click the bar's right arrow (or press →) → the URL search param updates via the router (shareable, reload-stable) → the page re-renders as Variant B in place, same data; arrows wrap around; arrow keys are ignored while an input/textarea/contenteditable is focused. The switcher is hidden in production builds (NODE_ENV gate).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Shared rules: locate prototype code next to the real module/page but named as a prototype; trivial to run (one task-runner command, or double-click the HTML file); no persistence by default (in-memory; a scratch DB/file must carry a clear "PROTOTYPE, wipe me" name); no tests, no error handling beyond runnability, no abstractions; surface the full relevant state after every action/switch. LOGIC branch: the logic sits in one pure <script> module (reducer (state, action) => state, explicit state machine, pure functions, or a small class — chosen by the question), zero DOM references so it can lift into the real codebase; plain HTML/CSS/JS, no framework/bundler/server. UI branch: default 3 variants, cap 5; variants must disagree about structure (layout, hierarchy, primary affordance), not just colour/copy; sub-shape A (variants on an existing route/host page, only the rendered subtree swaps) is strongly preferred over sub-shape B (a new throwaway route named with "prototype"); each variant a clearly named exported component (VariantA/B/C); shared switcher component reused by both sub-shapes; read-only — mutations point at stubs. Capture: winner folds into real code properly rewritten; the full variant set + switcher go to the throwaway branch, never main.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/prototype). Bundled references: LOGIC.md, UI.md.
- **Best for:** Design exploration before committing — the UI branch's pattern (multiple structurally different variants on one real page behind a switcher) is directly relevant to how homepage section versions can be compared in-browser, and the LOGIC branch suits testing an interactive widget's state model (e.g. a quote-form flow) before building it for real.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0434⟧

## ⟦S0435⟧ mattpocock/setup-matt-pocock-skills — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** One-time, prompt-driven configuration for a repo so the other mattpocock engineering skills can work: it sets up (A) the issue tracker, (B) the triage label vocabulary, and (C) the domain-doc layout, writing an `## Agent skills` block into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md plus seed docs under docs/agents/. Run once before first use of the other engineering skills.
- **How it looks:** No visual output — a conversation (explore → present findings → confirm/edit drafts → write) and three small docs files: docs/agents/issue-tracker.md, docs/agents/domain.md, and (only when triage is installed) docs/agents/triage-labels.md.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Steps: (1) Explore the repo (git remote, existing CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and any `## Agent skills` block, GLOSSARY/GLOSSARY-MAP plus legacy CONTEXT files — offered a git mv rename — docs/adr/, docs/agents/, .scratch/, whether the triage skill is installed, monorepo signals) → (2) present findings, then one section, one answer, each led by the recommended default → (3) show drafts of the block + docs and let the user edit → (4) write (edit CLAUDE.md if it exists, else AGENTS.md, else ask; update an existing block in place; create any missing tracker labels) → (5) report which skills now read these files.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Section A tracker options: GitHub (gh CLI; default when a GitHub remote exists), GitLab (glab CLI), local markdown (.scratch/<feature>/ — spec.md plus issues/<NN>-<slug>.md, state as a `Status:` line), or other (user describes the workflow; recorded as prose). GitHub/GitLab templates carry a "PRs as a request surface" flag defaulted OFF — leave it off. A chosen hosted tracker needs a reachable repo: done when `gh repo view` / `glab repo view` prints the project. GitHub specifics in the seed doc: native issue dependencies for blocking (gh 2.94+: --blocked-by / --add-blocked-by; older gh via API with the blocker's numeric database id), sub-issues, blocked_by count via issue_dependencies_summary; never file into mattpocock/skills unless the user owns it — forks can make gh default upstream, so verify with gh repo view --json nameWithOwner. GitLab: comments are "notes", MRs numbered separately from issues; native blocking links are Premium/Ultimate, fallback is a `Blocked by:` line. Wayfinding operations are defined per tracker (map issue labelled wayfinder:map / .scratch/<effort>/map.md, child tickets, frontier = open + unblocked + unclaimed, claim = first write). Section B defaults (only if triage installed): the five canonical labels equal to their role names — needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-agent, ready-for-human, wontfix — collect overrides only if the user says no. Section C: single-context (root GLOSSARY.md + docs/adr/) by default, written without asking; multi-context (GLOSSARY-MAP.md) offered only on monorepo signals (pnpm-workspace.yaml, package.json workspaces, populated packages/*).
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/setup-matt-pocock-skills). Bundled seed templates: issue-tracker-github.md, issue-tracker-gitlab.md, issue-tracker-local.md, triage-labels.md, domain.md.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — the precondition step for the whole mattpocock set (⟦S0427⟧ names it as such); skills like ⟦S0437⟧, ⟦S0438⟧ and ⟦S0439⟧ refuse to guess the tracker and send the user here.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0435⟧

## ⟦S0436⟧ mattpocock/tdd — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Test-driven development as a reference for the red → green loop: what a good test is, where tests go (pre-agreed seams), the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Consulted before and during every cycle, not after.
- **How it looks:** No page visuals. In the codebase: integration-style tests that read like specifications ("user can checkout with valid cart"), written against public interfaces with independently sourced expected values (a known literal like 15, never a recomputation of the code's own formula).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The loop per cycle: pick one pre-agreed seam → write ONE failing test (red) → write only enough code to pass it (green) → repeat with the next vertical slice, each test a tracer bullet informed by the last cycle. Refactoring is explicitly NOT part of the loop — it belongs to the review stage.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Seams first: before any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user ("What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?", each seam with a one-line catches/misses note); no tests at unconfirmed seams. Anti-patterns: implementation-coupled (mocks internal collaborators, tests privates, verifies via a side channel like querying the DB — tell: breaks on refactor with no behaviour change); tautological (expected value recomputed the way the code computes it, so it can never disagree); horizontal slicing (all tests first, then all implementation — tests imagined behaviour; vertical slices instead). Mocking (bundled mocking.md): mock only at system boundaries — external APIs, time/randomness, sometimes DB (prefer a real test DB) and filesystem; never mock your own classes/modules or internal collaborators; design boundary interfaces SDK-style (one specific function per operation) rather than one generic fetcher, so each mock returns one shape with no conditional logic. When the interface's shape itself is in question, consult ⟦S0428⟧ codebase-design for the seam vocabulary. Tests use the project's GLOSSARY.md language and respect area ADRs.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/tdd). Bundled references: tests.md (good/bad test examples), mocking.md.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — the build engine inside the mattpocock flow: /implement drives this loop per ticket (see ⟦S0427⟧).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0436⟧

## ⟦S0437⟧ mattpocock/to-issues — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Breaks a plan, spec or the current conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, and publishes them to the configured tracker. (Upstream name: "to-tickets" — the skill file lives at skills/engineering/to-tickets; the catalog lists it as to-issues.)
- **How it looks:** A numbered list presented to the user for approval — per ticket: title, "Blocked by", and what it delivers — then published artefacts: locally, one markdown file per ticket under .scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md (never one combined file), each with What to build / Blocked by / Status: ready-for-agent / acceptance-criteria checkboxes; on a real tracker, one issue per ticket with a Parent / What to build / Acceptance criteria / Blocked by structure, native blocking links where the platform has them, and the ready-for-agent label applied.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Process: (1) gather context from the conversation or a referenced spec/issue (read full body + comments) → (2) optionally explore the codebase (glossary vocabulary, ADRs; look for prefactoring — "make the change easy, then make the easy change") → (3) draft vertical slices → (4) quiz the user on granularity, blocking edges, merges/splits until approved → (5) publish in dependency order, blockers first, so edges can reference real identifiers; parent issues are never closed or modified. Work then proceeds along the frontier: any ticket whose blockers are all done.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Vertical-slice rules: each ticket cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests); demoable/verifiable on its own; sized to fit a single fresh context window; prefactoring goes first. Exception — wide refactors (one mechanical change whose blast radius breaks thousands of call sites): sequence as expand (add the new form beside the old) → migrate in blast-radius batches (per package/directory, each its own ticket blocked by the expand, CI green throughout) → contract (delete the old form, blocked by every batch); if batches can't stay green alone, they share an integration branch blocked by a final integrate-and-verify ticket. Tickets avoid file paths and code snippets (they go stale), with one exception: a prototype snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose (state machine, reducer, schema) may be inlined, trimmed to the decision-rich parts. Requires the tracker + label vocabulary from ⟦S0435⟧; without them, send the user there.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/to-tickets/SKILL.md).
- **Best for:** No homepage use — planning a multi-session build into agent-grabbable pieces (step 3 of the flow in ⟦S0427⟧).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0437⟧

## ⟦S0438⟧ mattpocock/to-prd — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Turns the current conversation into a spec and publishes it to the project issue tracker — synthesis only, NO interview (that's what distinguishes it from grilling). Catalog name to-prd; upstream name "to-spec" (skills/engineering/to-spec). The spec it writes follows a fixed template: Problem Statement, Solution, User Stories, Implementation Decisions, Testing Decisions, Out of Scope, Further Notes.
- **How it looks:** One tracker issue written in the project's glossary vocabulary: a user-perspective problem statement and solution, then a LONG numbered list of user stories in the strict format "As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>", then decision lists — no file paths or code snippets anywhere (they go stale), except a prototype snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose, inlined and trimmed.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Process: (1) explore the repo if not already understood (glossary vocabulary throughout, respect ADRs) → (2) sketch the seams the feature will be tested at — prefer existing seams, use the highest seam possible, ideally exactly one across the codebase — and check them with the user → (3) write the spec from the template and publish it to the tracker with the ready-for-agent label (no further triage needed).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Testing Decisions must state what makes a good test (external behaviour only, not implementation details), which modules will be tested, and prior art in the codebase. Implementation Decisions cover modules built/modified, interfaces changed, technical clarifications, architectural decisions, schema changes, API contracts, specific interactions. Requires the tracker + label vocabulary from ⟦S0435⟧; without them, send the user there.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/to-spec/SKILL.md).
- **Best for:** No homepage use — the spec step between grilling and ticket-splitting in the flow mapped by ⟦S0427⟧ (there called /to-spec).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0438⟧

## ⟦S0439⟧ mattpocock/triage — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Moves issues (and, when the tracker config flags them in scope, external PRs — "a PR is an issue with attached code") through a small state machine of triage roles: categorise, verify the claim against the codebase, grill if needed, and write agent-ready briefs. Every comment it posts to the tracker must start with the disclaimer "> *This was generated by AI during triage.*"
- **How it looks:** Tracker-side artefacts: issues carrying exactly one category role + one state role; three attention buckets presented oldest first (Unlabeled / needs-triage / needs-info-with-reporter-activity, external PRs tagged [PR]); needs-info comments in a fixed Triage Notes template (what's established so far / what we still need from you @reporter); ready-for-agent comments as structured Agent Briefs; and a .out-of-scope/ folder in the repo holding one concept file per rejected feature request.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Per-issue flow: (1) gather context — full issue/PR (for a PR, the diff), prior triage notes, codebase exploration, plus two checks: redundancy (search for an existing implementation by domain concept, report where you looked) and prior rejection (read .out-of-scope/*.md) → (2) recommend category + state with reasoning and wait for direction → (3) verify the claim (reproduce the bug from the reporter's steps; for a PR, check it out and run the tests) and report confirmed / failed / insufficient detail → (4) grill if needed (grilling + domain-modeling skills, updating GLOSSARY.md/ADRs inline) → (5) apply the outcome: brief + ready-for-agent, brief-with-reason + ready-for-human, Triage Notes + needs-info, or wontfix + close (already-implemented → point to where it lives, no .out-of-scope write; rejected bug → polite explanation; rejected enhancement → write .out-of-scope file, link it, close). Quick override: "move #42 to ready-for-agent" is trusted and applied directly — confirm, act, skip grilling, ask if they want a brief. Resuming: read prior notes, check which questions got answered, never re-ask resolved ones.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Roles — 2 category (bug, enhancement) + 5 state (needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-agent, ready-for-human, wontfix); canonical names, actual label strings come from the repo mapping set up by ⟦S0435⟧. State machine: unlabeled → needs-triage → needs-info / ready-for-agent / ready-for-human / wontfix; needs-info returns to needs-triage on reporter reply; conflicting state roles → flag and ask before anything else. For PRs the states read against the diff (ready-for-agent = brief attached, an agent takes the next step; ready-for-human = ready for a human to merge). Discovery shows only EXTERNAL PRs; an explicitly named PR is always triaged. Agent briefs (bundled AGENT-BRIEF.md): durability over precision (describe interfaces, types and behavioural contracts; NEVER file paths or line numbers — they go stale), behavioural not procedural, complete testable acceptance criteria, explicit out-of-scope; template fields: Category, Summary, Current behavior, Desired behavior, Key interfaces, Acceptance criteria, Out of scope. Out-of-scope KB (bundled OUT-OF-SCOPE.md): one file per concept (kebab-case), relaxed design-doc style with Decision/Reason/Prior requests, reasons must be durable (scope, technical constraint, strategy — never "too busy"); checked by concept similarity during step 1 ("night theme" matches dark-mode.md); written ONLY for rejected enhancements, never for already-implemented closures (that would poison dedup).
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mattpocock/skills (skills/engineering/triage). Bundled references: AGENT-BRIEF.md, OUT-OF-SCOPE.md.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — the on-ramp that turns raw incoming issues/requests into agent-ready work for the flow in ⟦S0427⟧. Not for tickets produced by ⟦S0437⟧ (already agent-ready).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0439⟧
## ⟦S0440⟧ MengTo/animation-on-scroll — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A small copy-paste system that makes page elements animate in when they scroll into view, using an IntersectionObserver plus CSS keyframes, packaged for Tailwind class-based use.
- **How it looks:** Elements sit invisible, blurred and dropped down the page; as each one scrolls into view it sharpens, fades in and rises into place — the classic soft "fade-up with blur" reveal on cards, text blocks and sections.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: an element crosses the visibility threshold while scrolling → its animation, held paused until now, starts running → it moves from opacity 0, translateY(30px) and blur(8px) to opacity 1, translateY(0) and blur(0) → end state: element fully visible and sharp; by default it never replays.
- **Mechanism & key values:** IntersectionObserver with threshold 0.2 and rootMargin "0px 0px -10% 0px"; the observer adds an `animate` class that flips `animation-play-state` from paused to running, then unobserves (once = true; set false to replay on re-entry). Keyframes `animationIn` as above. Tailwind arbitrary value in the recipe: `[animation:animationIn_0.8s_ease-out_0.1s_both]` — 0.8s duration, ease-out, 0.1s delay, fill both. Tuning knobs: threshold/rootMargin for earlier or later triggers, translateY/blur amounts, duration/delay.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub — github.com/MengTo/Skills, agent-skills/web-design/animation-on-scroll.
- **Best for:** The baseline reveal for any section — proof/reviews cards, process steps, work/gallery items, towns lists. A utility layer under a design rather than a design itself; pair with a stronger hero moment.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0440⟧

## ⟦S0441⟧ MengTo/animation-systems — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A motion-design system in the Stripe / Linear / Apple / Vercel manner: principles, reusable motion primitives, duration and easing defaults, choreography patterns, performance rules and a reduced-motion policy. It designs how a whole site moves, not one effect.
- **How it looks:** Restrained, product-grade motion: one strong hero moment, everything else quiet supporting movement. Text and cards fade and rise a short distance; the primary element moves first and secondary elements follow in a small stagger, so the eye reads the page in order. Hovers lift slightly with a soft shadow increase; nothing bounces.
- **Frame by frame:** Four primitives. A) Fade + rise (default entrance for text blocks, cards, modals): opacity 0 → 1, Y 12–24px → 0, over 300–700ms depending on size. B) Scale + fade (popovers, toasts, selected states): scale 0.98 → 1 with opacity 0 → 1. C) Slide (drawers, step transitions): translate only, no layout animation. D) Morph / shared element (tab indicators, expanding cards): measured geometry morph. Choreography patterns: hero visual first → headline → CTA last; section reveals trigger when the section is ~20–30% visible and play once; hover lift Y −2 to −6px plus subtle shadow/glow; form focus = focus ring + tiny scale/translate.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Durations — micro (hover/press) 120–200ms; UI state change 180–260ms; small transitions (popover, toast) 220–320ms; page-section entrances 400–800ms; hero sequences 800–1600ms with internal beats. Easing: ease-out with a gentle settle for UI and entrances, ease-in (faster) for exits; library equivalents power2.out / expo.out; avoid elastic/bounce unless the brand is playful. Stagger 40–90ms per element (text lines/cards), smaller on mobile. Animate transform and opacity only; clamp canvas DPR to 1–2; keep blur small. Reduced motion: keep content visible, replace motion with instant state + subtle opacity, disable scroll-scrub/pin.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; the style references it names are Stripe, Linear, Apple and Vercel product motion.
- **Best for:** The motion language governing an entire build — hero sequencing, section reveals, hover behaviour on cards and CTAs in every section. Use as the system behind section versions rather than as a section itself.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0441⟧

## ⟦S0442⟧ MengTo/beautiful-shadows — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Three exact, layered, neutral drop-shadow recipes given as Tailwind arbitrary-value classes, replacing the default Tailwind shadow scale with softer, more realistic elevation.
- **How it looks:** White or light surfaces float with a fine 1px edge ring plus a stack of very soft, low-opacity black shadows spreading downward — cards look printed on thick paper rather than stamped with a grey blob. No colour tint anywhere.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Beautiful sm (compact cards, form controls, pills): `0px 2px 3px -1px rgba(0,0,0,0.1), 0px 1px 0px 0px rgba(25,28,33,0.02), 0px 0px 0px 1px rgba(25,28,33,0.08)`. Beautiful md (default for cards, panels, popovers): six layers all at rgba(0,0,0,0.06), from a 0 0 0 1px ring through 1px/1px, 3px/3px, 6px/6px, 12px/12px up to 24px/24px with negative spreads. Beautiful lg (hero media, feature callouts, modal-like containers): six layers rising from 2.8px/2.2px at 0.034 alpha to 100px offset / 80px blur at 0.12 alpha. Rules: one strength per component state; never mix with default Tailwind shadow scales on the same component; never stack two of these utilities on one element; don't use lg on dense lists or tiny controls.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub.
- **Best for:** Every elevated surface in any section — review cards, quote/pricing panels, hero photo frames, CTA cards, form boxes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0442⟧

## ⟦S0443⟧ MengTo/cobejs — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A recipe for an interactive WebGL globe using cobe, a small single-purpose globe library — a dotted world sphere on a canvas with location markers, instead of a full Three.js scene.
- **How it looks:** A softly shaded dotted-map globe, slowly spinning on its own; coloured dots mark locations on the surface, with a gentle glow around the sphere. The visitor can drag to rotate it (interaction level is a setup choice: ambient spin vs drag).
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: page render / requestAnimationFrame loop → the globe rotates continuously (in the recipe, phi increases by 0.01 per frame in onRender) → markers ride the surface as it turns → end state: none, it loops indefinitely until paused with globe.toggle().
- **Mechanism & key values:** `createGlobe(canvas, options)` from the cobe package. Recipe values: theta 0.2, dark 0, diffuse 1.2, scale 1, mapSamples 16000, mapBrightness 6, baseColor [0.2, 0.2, 0.25], glowColor [1, 1, 1], markerColor [0.8, 0.5, 1]; a marker is `{ location: [lat, lon], size }` (example: Singapore [1.3521, 103.8198], size 0.08). Canvas width/height must be set scaled by devicePixelRatio, DPR clamped to 1–2; destroy and recreate the globe on resize.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; library: cobe by shuding — github.com/shuding/cobe (named in its REFERENCES.md).
- **Best for:** Towns/areas-served sections for a firm covering a wide region (markers per service town), or an about/hero ornament. Decorative for most trade sites — earns its place only when geography is part of the pitch.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0443⟧

## ⟦S0444⟧ MengTo/company-logos — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A rule set for rendering brand logos from Iconify's Simple Icons set at a consistent size, instead of typing company names as text or hunting down logo files.
- **How it looks:** A clean row or grid of recognisable brand marks, all in matching 64×64 boxes, monochrome by default, aligned to a shared baseline or centre grid so the strip reads as one composed proof band.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Source: Iconify Simple Icons. Each logo rendered in a 64×64 visual box, the inner SVG scaled to the composition's density. Monochrome by default; brand colour only when recognition matters more than restraint. Guardrails: never mix filled, outline, emoji, bitmap and wordmark styles in one row; never hotlink logo assets from search results; add accessible labels when logos are interactive or carry proof.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; icon source is Iconify Simple Icons (simpleicons.org).
- **Best for:** Proof strips — manufacturer/accreditation logos a firm genuinely holds (for trades: only brands the firm is actually certified or partnered with; never invent affiliations), partner and supplier rows.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0444⟧

## ⟦S0445⟧ MengTo/container-lines — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A layout-detail system: two hairline vertical rules drawn at the exact left and right edges of the content container, running the page's full height, with tiny square markers at section corners — a measured, technical framing device.
- **How it looks:** The whole page reads as if drawn on drafting paper: faint 1px lines bracket the content column from top to bottom, and small 6px solid squares sit precisely on section corners where the lines meet section edges. Quiet, editorial, engineered.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Tokens: --container-max 1120px; --container-pad clamp(20px, 4vw, 48px); --line-color rgba(24,24,27,0.14); --line-strong rgba(24,24,27,0.28); --corner-size 6px (taste range 4–8px). Lines are ::before/::after on the layout shell, positioned with `left/right: max(var(--container-pad), calc((100vw - var(--container-max)) / 2))`, z-index −1, pointer-events none. Corner squares are absolutely positioned spans translated −50%/+50% so they centre exactly on the corner point. Content wrapper must use the same width formula: `width: min(100% - (pad × 2), 1120px)`. Page/major-section level only — never on nested components.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub.
- **Best for:** A whole-page structure system under any section stack; suits heroes and process sections especially, and brands with a technical/industrial register.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0445⟧

## ⟦S0446⟧ MengTo/design-first-ui-prompting — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A prompting method for generating UI with AI tools: write the prompt like a design system spec (goal, format, layout, type system, colour/material, exact copy, constraints, negative prompt) so generated screens come out consistent instead of random. A workflow skill — nothing renders by itself.
- **How it looks:** What it produces, followed well, is disciplined generated UI: one locked layout and hierarchy, exactly one accent colour, copy rendered word-for-word as supplied, and variants that change a single variable (angle/crop, accent, card arrangement, background tone) at a time rather than redesigning the screen each pass.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Prompt skeleton fields: GOAL (what, who, success criteria), FORMAT (size/aspect, safe margins — example 1080×1350 with 90px margins), LAYOUT (grid, placement, hierarchy H1 → subhead → body → CTA), TYPE SYSTEM (font vibe, weights — H1 700 / body 400, leading, tracking), COLOR + MATERIAL (one accent only), IMAGERY/UI STYLE, COPY (render exactly), CONSTRAINTS (change 1–2 things only), NEGATIVE PROMPT (no logos, no watermarks, no extra text, no gibberish type). Supporting playbook rules: screenshots beat prose descriptions (collect references — Mobbin for sections, Bento Grids for cards, Superhero for heroes); lock the hero first, then build section by section; 2-pass workflow when the model misspells type (generate text-free, typeset in Figma); fix weak images manually instead of re-rolling forever; avoid purple gradients and default icon sets (it suggests Iconify Solar for variety and Simple Icons via Iconify for logos).
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; its REFERENCES.md names mobbin.com, bentogrids.com, Figma Community, Iconify icon sets and simpleicons.org; the article also names cta.gallery and H1 Gallery for headlines.
- **Best for:** Process, not a page section: briefing image/UI generation for hero concepts and section variants while keeping a build visually consistent.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0446⟧

## ⟦S0447⟧ MengTo/gsap — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The general GSAP working guide: tweens, timelines, stagger, easing and ScrollTrigger patterns for professional web animation in HTML/CSS/JS or React, with performance rules and fixes for common failures.
- **How it looks:** Whatever the recipes build: hero content arriving in a soft staggered rise on load; sequenced nav → title → CTA entrances; and pinned sections where the page stops scrolling vertically while a panel slides sideways, scrubbed by scroll position.
- **Frame by frame:** Recipe 1, hero entrance (page load): elements start 24px lower and invisible → rise to place and fade in over 0.8s, power2.out, staggered 0.06s apart. Recipe 2, sequenced timeline: nav drops in from y −20 → hero title rises from y 30 → CTA scales up from 0.95, each overlapping the previous by 0.2s, defaults 0.6s power2.out. Recipe 3, scroll-scrub pinned section: trigger reaches top of viewport → section pins → as the user scrolls through 800px of scroll distance the inner panel translates to xPercent −200, scrub smoothing 1 → section unpins and normal scrolling resumes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Core API: gsap.to / from / fromTo; timelines with position parameters (absolute 1.2, relative "+=0.5", overlap "-=0.3", labels); eases named: power2.out, expo.inOut, elastic.out(1, 0.3); stagger 0.05 or object form { each, from: "start|center|end|random", grid }. Animate transforms (x, y, scale, rotation) and autoAlpha only — never top/left/width/height. ScrollTrigger: registerPlugin, trigger/start/end/scrub/pin/snap; call ScrollTrigger.refresh() after images load; in React wrap in gsap.context() and revert on unmount.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; its REFERENCES.md points to gsap.com docs (gsap.to, Timeline, ScrollTrigger).
- **Best for:** The animation engine under any section — hero entrances, pinned process stories, gallery pans, CTA emphasis.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0447⟧

## ⟦S0448⟧ MengTo/gsap-scrolltrigger-storytelling — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A pattern guide for cinematic, scroll-driven product storytelling with GSAP ScrollTrigger: sticky pinned scenes whose interface states change step by step as the visitor scrolls. A companion to ⟦S0447⟧, which covers GSAP generally; this one is the storytelling specialisation.
- **How it looks:** One main artefact — a product frame, device, screenshot or job visual — stays pinned centre-stage while the story moves around it: labels and overlays draw in one at a time, panels slide into place, numbers count up, regions highlight, and at the end of the scene the whole stage scales, masks or blurs into the next section instead of cutting.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: continuous scroll through a pinned section → the scrubbed timeline advances in step with scroll position → scene states reveal progressively (frame draws in → controls fade in → panels slide → values count up → highlights land), each mapped to explicit timeline labels → at the section handoff the current scene transforms (scale / mask / blur / translate) into the next → end state: next section in place, previous scene gone. Supporting entrances and hovers use ordinary tweens; the main narrative is always scrubbed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** GSAP timelines + ScrollTrigger scrub for the narrative; pin: true on long-form story sections; scenes mapped to timeline labels; transform and opacity only; quickSetter/quickTo or lerped values for pointer-following and scroll-reactive details; scrub smoothing for the cinematic feel (direct scrub for precise technical walkthroughs, eased scrub for a product-film feel — the skill gives these as tuning guidance, not fixed numbers); matchMedia() breakpoints so desktop sticky choreography simplifies on small screens; gsap.context() cleanup in React; ScrollTrigger.refresh() after assets load. Avoid: pins that trap the reader too long, effects that cover CTAs or drop text contrast.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub. No external sites named.
- **Best for:** Process sections (a job told step by step around one pinned visual), work/gallery feature stories, hero-to-first-section handoffs.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0448⟧

## ⟦S0449⟧ MengTo/landing-page — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A structure and copy playbook for a single-offer landing page: one offer, one audience, one primary action — the section order, layout types, conversion strategies and copy formulas for a page whose only job is conversion.
- **How it looks:** Above the fold: an outcome headline, a clarifying subheadline, one clear primary CTA, one proof signal (logo strip, stat or short testimonial) and a hero visual. Below: a problem → solution section, 3–5 outcome-driven benefits, a 3-step "how it works", social proof, then objection handling — a 6–12 question FAQ, a risk-reversal offer (trial, guarantee, cancel anytime) — and a final CTA repeating the top one.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four layout types: A) classic hero + sections (product understandable from a hero screenshot); B) long-form story/sales page (education + scepticism to overcome); C) minimal conversion page (high-intent traffic, short offer); D) comparison page ("X vs Y" search intent). Headline formulas: "{Outcome} without {pain}", "The {category} for {audience}", "Ship {result} in {time}". CTA rule: verb + what they get ("Start free trial", "Book a demo"); never "Learn more" / "Submit". Specificity rule: concrete numbers over adjectives ("Cut your weekly reporting from 4 hours to 15 minutes"). Build order: hero → benefits → how it works → proof → FAQ → final CTA, iterated section by section. SEO/AEO: noindex ad-only pages; FAQ in plain Q/A (optional FAQ schema) on indexed evergreen pages.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; REFERENCES.md points to coreyhaines31/marketingskills copywriting skill and Google's FAQ structured-data docs.
- **Best for:** Whole-page structure — directly transferable to a trade homepage or a single-service landing page (one offer → call/quote action), including where proof and FAQ sit.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0449⟧

## ⟦S0450⟧ MengTo/marquee-loop — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The standard recipe for a seamless infinite marquee: a duplicated strip of items (logos, testimonials, screenshots, tags, feature chips) that slides sideways forever with no visible join.
- **How it looks:** A horizontal band of items gliding steadily past, the ends of the band often faded or masked where it enters and leaves the section; the loop point is invisible because the second copy of the sequence is identical to the first.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: page load, runs continuously → the track translates linearly from 0 to −50% of its width → at −50% the duplicated sequence sits exactly where the original began, so the animation resets to 0 with no jump → loops indefinitely. Optional: pause or slow on hover; under prefers-reduced-motion, a static wrap or very slow movement.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Duplicate the item sequence so end and beginning match; animate the track with a linear transform 0 → −50%; keep item widths stable to prevent jumps; mask/fade the edges; no heavy shadows or filters on moving items (CPU cost). The skill prescribes no specific duration — speed is left to the implementer.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub.
- **Best for:** Proof strips (logo bands), testimonial tickers, towns-served tickers, tag/chip rows under a hero. Guardrail from the skill: never put unique content the visitor must read carefully in a marquee.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0450⟧

## ⟦S0451⟧ MengTo/masked-reveal — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A headline reveal in which each word starts hidden below an invisible mask and rises into place one word at a time as the heading scrolls in, built with GSAP ScrollTrigger and a small hand-rolled word splitter (no paid SplitText plugin).
- **How it looks:** A big editorial headline that assembles itself word by word — each word slides up from behind its own overflow-hidden mask in a quick, calm cascade, left to right, until the full line sits still and readable.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: the heading's top reaches 82% of the viewport height while scrolling → word 1 rises from yPercent 110 to 0 → the remaining words follow, staggered → end state: the complete heading at rest. Plays once by default; reduced-motion users see the static heading with no transform.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Defaults: duration 0.7–0.9s (recipe uses 0.8s), stagger 0.025–0.045s per word (recipe 0.035s), offset yPercent 110 → 0, ease power3.out or expo.out, ScrollTrigger start "top 82%", once: true. Each word is wrapped in an inline-block `.word-mask` (overflow hidden) containing a `.word` span (initial translateY(110%)); the full original text is preserved on an aria-label for screen readers and spaces are kept as-is. Taste rules: short headlines and section intros only, never long paragraphs; stagger by word, not letter; do not combine with blur unless the style demands it; don't split text containing links or buttons.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub.
- **Best for:** Hero headlines and section titles — the text-in-motion moment for hero and process/work section openers.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0451⟧

## ⟦S0452⟧ MengTo/matterjs — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A setup and workflow guide for Matter.js, the 2D physics engine: rigid bodies that fall, collide, stack and can be dragged, rendered to a canvas — for playful interactive scenes.
- **How it looks:** Solid shapes drop from above, bounce off a floor and each other, and settle into piles that behave like real objects; with the mouse constraint added, the visitor can grab a shape, drag it around and fling it. In the minimal demo: one 80×80 box falls onto an invisible-ground scene and lands.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: the simulation runs continuously once started (Runner + Render loop) → bodies fall under gravity, collide and come to rest → on pointer drag (optional MouseConstraint) the grabbed body follows the cursor and is released with its throw velocity → end state: none — the simulation keeps running until stopped.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Matter modules: Engine, Render, Runner, Bodies, Composite, Mouse, MouseConstraint. Minimal setup numbers: renderer 800×600, wireframes false; static ground Bodies.rectangle(400, 610, 810, 60, { isStatic: true }); first body Bodies.rectangle(400, 200, 80, 80). Bodies are added with Composite.add(engine.world, [...]); use Runner.run for a simple loop or Engine.update inside a custom loop. SPA cleanup: Runner.stop, remove the canvas, clear engine/world. The skill prescribes no gravity/friction values — engine defaults apply.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; library: Matter.js.
- **Best for:** A playful interactive moment — a footer or hero play-piece where falling/stacking objects are the idea (e.g. trade materials tumbling into a pile). Situational for trades: charming once, gimmicky if repeated; never where the visitor is trying to read or call.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0452⟧

## ⟦S0453⟧ MengTo/pricing-page — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A structure and copy playbook for a pricing page whose job is to reduce uncertainty and help the visitor choose a plan: layout types, plan-table UI checklist, anchoring and risk-reduction strategies, copy templates, SEO/AEO notes.
- **How it looks:** A clear value headline; a monthly/annual toggle with a "Save X%" callout; three plan cards side by side with consistent CTA verbs, the middle one quietly marked Recommended; below, a grouped comparison (Core / Collaboration / Admin-Security / Support), an objection-handling FAQ, proof placed next to decision points, and a final CTA. On mobile the table becomes stacked cards.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed (the billing toggle is an interaction, but the skill gives it no animation values).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four layouts: A) classic 3-card; B) value-metric slider (keep the maths obvious, default to the median customer); C) "pick your path" two columns split by persona; D) enterprise last mile (self-serve + sales-led). Table checklist: at most 3 plans by default; 3–6 key limits and 3–6 included items visible per plan; one recommended plan, styled subtly; consistent CTA verbs across plans ("Start free trial" / "Buy Pro" / "Contact sales"); outcome-written bullets ("Ship unlimited client sites without extra fees", not "Unlimited projects"). FAQ topics: cancel anytime, hitting limits, discounts, who it's for, security/compliance. SEO: title "Pricing — {Product}" + outcome keyword, clean /pricing URL; AEO: plain Q/A FAQ, optional FAQ schema.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; REFERENCES.md points to coreyhaines31/marketingskills copywriting skill and Google's FAQ structured-data docs.

## ⟦S0454⟧ MengTo/progressive-blur — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A CSS technique for a gradient blur band fixed to the top or bottom edge of the viewport: eight stacked backdrop-filter layers, each masked to one band, so content scrolling underneath blurs more and more strongly toward the edge.
- **How it looks:** The top (or bottom) strip of the page is a soft fog: content passing beneath it is sharp at the band's inner edge and melts into heavy blur at the screen edge — the effect Apple-style floating navs and bottom CTA bars sit on.
- **Frame by frame:** The overlay itself is static and fixed; the visible effect happens as the visitor scrolls — page content moves under the band → enters the weakest blur layer → deepens through the steps → is fully blurred at the edge. No animation or transition is prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Eight layers (a ::before, six divs, an ::after) with backdrop-filter blur doubling per step: 0.5px, 1px, 2px, 4px, 8px, 16px, 32px, 64px; each layer's linear-gradient mask is opaque only across its own 12.5% band of the strip (e.g. layer 1 opaque 12.5%–25%, transparent by 37.5%). Container: position fixed, z-index 5, pointer-events none; top version height 12%, bottom version height 65%. Knobs: height %, blur values, layer count, direction (flip `to top` ↔ `to bottom`). Pitfalls: backdrop-filter needs real content behind it (it won't blur a flat background); high blur values are GPU-heavy — reduce steps on low-end devices.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub.
- **Best for:** Under a fixed navigation bar (top), above a sticky mobile call/CTA bar (bottom), or softening a hero's edge into the next section. A finish detail, page-wide.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0454⟧

## ⟦S0455⟧ MengTo/tailwindcss — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The working guide for building UI with Tailwind CSS: utility composition, responsive and state variants, arbitrary values, dark mode, and when to extract components — the styling foundation skill, bundled with three copy-paste recipes.
- **How it looks:** What the recipes produce: a two-column responsive hero (centred max-width container, headline left at 4xl growing to 5xl, a bordered white media card right), and a clean pill CTA button (indigo, rounded-xl) with hover/focus/active colour shifts.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; state variants (hover/focus/active) change colours instantly, with no durations specified.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Utilities compose in the class attribute; responsive variants sm/md/lg/xl; state variants hover/focus/active/disabled/group-hover/peer-checked; arbitrary values sparingly (w-[42rem], bg-[#0b1220]). Recipe values: hero container `mx-auto max-w-6xl px-6 py-16`, grid `gap-10 lg:grid-cols-2 lg:items-center`, headline `text-4xl font-semibold tracking-tight sm:text-5xl`; button `inline-flex rounded-xl px-5 py-3 bg-indigo-600 hover:bg-indigo-500 active:bg-indigo-700 focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-400/60`. Rules: never build class names dynamically ("text-" + color) unless safelisted — map tones through an object instead; prefer components over @apply; content paths must cover all templates or classes vanish in production.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; REFERENCES.md points to tailwindcss.com installation docs.
- **Best for:** The implementation foundation for any section build in a Tailwind stack; no section of its own.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0455⟧

## ⟦S0456⟧ MengTo/threejs — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The working guide for interactive 3D on the web with Three.js: scene/camera/renderer setup, lights and materials, glTF loading, controls, the render loop, disposal and performance discipline.
- **How it looks:** Whatever the scene holds — in the starter recipe, a single violet cube floating in space, lit from above-right, rotating steadily on its Y axis against transparency. In production use: a product model the visitor can orbit, or a lit 3D hero object.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: requestAnimationFrame loop → scene state updates each frame (in the recipe, rotation.y = t × 0.0006 — roughly one full revolution per 10 seconds) → renderer.render draws the frame → loops continuously. Under prefers-reduced-motion: render a still frame instead of running the loop (or slow updates).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Mental model: Scene + Perspective/Orthographic Camera + WebGLRenderer; Mesh = Geometry + Material. Recipe values: PerspectiveCamera(45, aspect, 0.1, 100), camera z = 4; BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); MeshStandardMaterial color 0x7c3aed; AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.8) + DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.8) at (2, 2, 2); setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2)) — the DPR clamp is the mobile survival rule. Loaders: GLTFLoader, DRACOLoader (compressed glTF), TextureLoader; controls: OrbitControls or PointerLockControls. Cleanup is mandatory in SPAs: dispose geometry/material/texture/renderer, cancel RAF, remove listeners.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; REFERENCES.md points to threejs.org/docs.
- **Best for:** Hero 3D moments and product viewers in work/gallery sections — for trades, only where a real 3D object earns it (a model viewer), never as decoration filler.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0456⟧

## ⟦S0457⟧ MengTo/webgl-landing-steering — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A decision framework, used before any code, for steering a WebGL landing page to a chosen outcome: it maps the page's intent to one of four WebGL "lanes" and sets quality gates for conversion clarity, performance and accessibility.
- **How it looks:** The four lanes it chooses between: A) a subtle depth field — soft gradient meshes, slow parallax planes, light bloom behind readable copy; B) data/particle intelligence — particle flows, node networks and vector fields drifting purposefully toward the CTA; C) an object-centric product moment — one central glTF model under a controlled camera orbit with material highlights; D) an immersive cinematic scene — volumetrics, heavy post-processing and scroll-chapter choreography.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; the motion character per lane: A stays low-amplitude and always secondary to copy; B uses directional flow; C is interaction-driven or timeline-based with a short loop; D is a choreographed sequence with scroll chapters and a static/mobile fallback.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pick ONE dominant lane — never mix 3–4 heavy effects in a hero. Steering matrix: waitlist/pre-launch → A or B; product feature page → A or C; pricing/high-intent → mostly A, decorative only; enterprise trust → B with restrained palette; consumer growth → B with playful palette, capped load; campaign microsite → C or D with explicit fallback. Gates: headline + CTA readable in under 3 seconds and WebGL never blocks the offer; pixel-ratio cap Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 1.5–2); stable frame time on common phones; lazy-load heavy assets with an immediate non-WebGL poster/fallback; prefers-reduced-motion still frame or low-motion mode; handle context loss and resize; dispose on route change. Risk tiers: low = CSS + canvas illusion; medium = Three.js with 1–2 meshes and light post FX; high = multi-pass shaders/dense particles. Default to low/medium for conversion pages.
- **Reference / source:** MengTo/Skills (DesignCode) GitHub; REFERENCES.md names threejs.org docs and examples, MDN WebGL API, web.dev rendering performance, and the W3C prefers-reduced-motion spec.
- **Best for:** Planning any WebGL hero — the pre-build decision that keeps a hero in lane A (safe) instead of drifting into lane D weight. Process, not a section.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0457⟧

## ⟦S0458⟧ mickadesign/fluid-functionalism — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Fluid Functionalism: a shadcn/ui component registry (by Mickael Desmedt / mickadesign) plus the motion system and workflow around it — components where every transition makes a state change legible: springs instead of durations, one gliding hover highlight per list, and labels that get heavier without moving their neighbours. Ships each primitive-touching component in two flavours, Radix and Base UI, same API. Requires a React 19 + Tailwind v4 + motion (motion/react) + shadcn project.
- **How it looks:** Calm, precise product UI. In a menu or list, a single highlight pill slides from row to row under the cursor instead of each row blinking its own background on and off. A selected tab's label thickens (weight change) while the row width stays pixel-identical, so nothing shoves sideways. Icon swaps crossfade inside one fixed cell with a touch of blur and scale. Page loads use one reveal class rather than a scatter of fades; slow data shows a Skeleton that crossfades into the real content.
- **Frame by frame:** Hover: pointer enters a list → the shared highlight glides to the row under the cursor and follows row to row without dropping out between rows. State change: label weight animates normal → semibold inside a ghost-span that reserves the bold width, so neighbours never move. Icon swap: old glyph fades/scales/blur slightly out as the new one fades in, same cell, same size. Page reveal: container with reveal-landing / reveal-product (or -subtle) plays the system's single entrance; reveal-items on a skeleton and its loaded replacement hands rows over one by one in a crossfade. Exits use the paired .exit tweens so dismissals read crisp rather than replaying the entrance backwards. Under MotionConfig reducedMotion="user", transforms and layout animation drop out; opacity and colour fades remain.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Three tokenised spring speeds from @/lib/springs: spring.fast 0.08s, spring.moderate 0.16s, spring.slow 0.24s — the bigger the moving thing, the slower the spring; never hand-write a duration, and animate transform/opacity only, never top/left/width/height. Type system: six roles via typeClass(role) (display, title, subtitle, body, caption, micro, each a size + line height); three weights only — normal for text, semibold for headings and selected items, bold for display only; two text colours (foreground, muted), no opacity steps of them; no uppercase, no letter-spacing, no eyebrows; never a raw text-[13px]. Concentric corners: inner radius = max(0, outer radius − inset − border); the shipped shape pair (container 12/24px → bg 8/20px) assumes a 4px total inset; past 24px radius or asymmetric gaps, tune by eye. Inter needs its opsz axis loaded (Inter({ axes: ["opsz"] })) or weight animations widen labels slightly. Install: `npx shadcn@latest registry add @fluid`, then `npx shadcn@latest add @fluid/button` (Radix) or `@fluid/base/button` (Base UI); blocks (sidebar-app, dialog-sidebar, queued-stack) install composed. The skill also prescribes a stack-read script, an evidence-based audit (scripts/audit.mjs measures whether hover glides or blinks, which durations and control heights actually ship), and a diff-based update workflow — never re-install blind with --overwrite over local edits.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/mickadesign/fluid-functionalism; docs and live demos at fluidfunctionalism.com (every component page has a playground and a Copy prompt brief).
- **Best for:** App-like interface behaviour inside a page — navigation menus, service lists, tab strips, accordions/FAQ, dialogs, quote-form states — anywhere hover and selection states must feel engineered. Needs the React/shadcn stack; not a single-file-HTML technique.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0458⟧

## ⟦S0459⟧ microsoft/dev — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Internal maintenance workflows for Microsoft's playwright-cli repository only: how to prepare a release (version bump, Playwright commit-window diff, release notes) and how to roll the Playwright dependency. Not a design or page-building skill.
- **How it looks:** Nothing a website visitor ever sees — the outputs are a GitHub pull request whose body is release notes (emoji-headed Highlights and Fixes sections, plus an Upgrading block) and updated package.json / README / skill files in that repo.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Release flow: bump patch version in package.json, npm install to sync the lockfile; baseline = last `chore: mark v...` commit; list Playwright commits between the two alphas' dates with git log --after/--before (never --since/--until, which silently return empty on a stale ref); keep only CLI-surface commits (src/tools/cli-client/**, cli-daemon/**, mcp/**, CDP paths, fix/feat(cli|mcp) prefixes); write RELEASE_NOTES_v<version>.md with no top-level # header, every highlight title starting with one emoji, highlights ordered by user excitement and worded from the linked issue's problem, not the commit subject. Roll flow: npm info playwright@next version; update playwright, playwright-core and @playwright/test pins; run node scripts/update.js to regenerate skills and README; branch roll_<version>, commit "chore: roll Playwright to <version>".

## ⟦S0460⟧ microsoft/playwright-cli — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The command reference for playwright-cli, Microsoft's CLI for driving a real browser: open pages, snapshot the accessibility tree, click/type/fill by element ref, and capture screenshots, PDFs, traces and videos. A testing and automation tool — it builds nothing on a page.
- **How it looks:** Nothing a site visitor sees. Its visible outputs are for the developer: YAML page snapshots with element refs (e3, e15…), screenshots and PDFs of pages, DevTools console/request logs, recorded videos with optional action callouts naming each step, and an annotation dashboard (show --annotate) where a user draws boxes and comments on the live page for design feedback.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion (the video recording commands capture a page's own motion; the tool prescribes none).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Core loop: playwright-cli open [url] → snapshot → interact by ref (click e15, fill e5 "…" --submit, type, press Enter, drag e2 e8, hover, select, upload, check) → snapshot again → close. Supporting sets: tabs (tab-new/tab-select/tab-close), storage (cookie-*, localstorage-*, sessionstorage-*, state-save/load), emulation (set-color-scheme dark, set-reduced-motion reduce, set-contrast more, set-media print), network mocking (route "**/*.jpg" --status=404, route-list, unroute), DevTools (console, requests, tracing-start/stop, recording-start/stop, video-start/video-chapter/video-stop, video-show-actions --duration=600 --position=top-right). --raw strips output to the bare result value for piping; --json wraps replies as JSON. Sessions: -s=<name> with --persistent/--profile; attach to a running browser via --cdp or --extension. WebMCP: pages that register their own agent tools are listed in the snapshot — prefer webmcp-call over driving the UI when one matches. Falls back to `npx playwright cli` when the global command is absent.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/microsoft/playwright-cli (skills/playwright-cli).
- **Best for:** Build QA process — screenshot and interaction checks of finished sections (the desktop/mobile verification step), never a page section itself.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0460⟧

## ⟦S0461⟧ millionco/budge — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** Budge: a developer-facing tuning widget for Next.js App Router projects. After an agent makes a single-property CSS or Tailwind change, a floating bar appears on the page so the human can fine-tune the exact value with arrow keys before it is persisted.
- **How it looks:** A small floating control bar overlays the (dev) page, the changed element is marked, and the bar shows the property name and current value; the element updates live on the page as the value steps. It is a build-time tool — production visitors never see it.
- **Frame by frame:** Agent edits one CSS value or one Tailwind token → hot module reload applies it → the always-on runtime detects the numeric class/style change, marks the element and mounts the bar → ↑/↓ steps the value with live preview (and audio feedback) → ←/→ moves between "slides" of related properties → Enter copies an edit prompt to the clipboard for the agent to apply → Escape reverts to the original value.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Runtime is a self-contained IIFE loaded from https://www.budge.design/budge.iife.js via next/script (strategy afterInteractive); auto-detects on local/dev hosts by watching HMR-driven class/style mutations; manual element pick with Cmd+E (React Grab primitives); explicit fallback is a hidden `<div data-budge="{slides}">` config element plus data-budge-target on the element. A mechanical gate decides the fallback: exactly one CSS value literal or one Tailwind class token changed in exactly one StrReplace in one file (padding 8px → 16px passes; variables, tokens added/removed, multiple values fail). Slide shape: { label, property, min, max, value, original, unit, type? } — examples: padding-top slide min 0 / max 64, value 16, original 8, unit px; font-size min 8 / max 72; colour slides use type "color" with hue 0–360°. Tailwind resolution: spacing scale × 4 (p-4 = padding 16px, rounded-lg = border-radius 8px); token snapping auto-matches property to --spacing-* / --text-* / --radius-* scales and names the token in the bar (e.g. "16px · md"); colours do not snap yet. In scope: raw CSS values, inline styles, Tailwind classes, SVG fill/stroke. Out of scope: Sass/Less variables, custom-property definitions, CSS-in-JS theme tokens.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/millionco/skills (skills/budge); runtime hosted at budge.design.
- **Best for:** The fine-tuning minute after a build — nudging a hero's padding, a headline size or a gap to the exact value by eye instead of by re-prompting. Process tool for App Router projects only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0461⟧

## ⟦S0462⟧ millionco/interactive-hit-areas — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** One rule, fully worked out: the area that responds to the pointer (hit area) must be separated from the area the visitor sees (visual area) — visual spacing between interactive siblings belongs inside each target, never between them, so hover and click never fall into dead zones.
- **How it looks:** The page looks exactly like the spaced design — airy gaps between bars, rows or tabs — but sweeping the pointer across the component, the highlight never blinks off in the gaps: the whole band responds continuously, and each item's visible shape (a narrower centred bar, a padded row) still reads as separate.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: pointer sweeps horizontally/vertically across the component → the hover/active state hands over from item to item with no dropout anywhere inside the component's bounds → click anywhere in an item's full slot activates that item. Before the fix, the same sweep drops the highlight in every gap (the symptom that diagnoses the bug).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Fix sequence: identify one item's pitch (its full share of the axis) → make the interactive container fill that whole slot, flush against neighbours (remove gap/space-*/margin between siblings; flex-1 or equal grid tracks) → put the handler on the full-slot container → recreate the visual spacing inside it (padding, or a centred child with max-width). Worked example: a bar chart overlay `absolute inset-0 flex items-stretch` with gap-0 columns; each column is flex-1 and full height; the visible bar is a centred child maxWidth 37px; non-hovered bars dim to opacity 0.4. In Tailwind: replace gap-N between interactive items with gap-0 + internal padding; rows take py-* on each row instead of space-y-* between rows; sibling rows that must stay column-aligned (bars and their labels) must share the same gap setting or centres drift. Accessibility tie-in: padding-grown hit areas are how you reach the 24–44px minimum target sizes while keeping glyphs small. Not for genuinely discrete items (cards on a page, unrelated buttons) where the space between is meant to be inert.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/millionco/skills (skills/interactive-hit-areas).
- **Best for:** Navigation bars, tab and segmented controls, service pickers, gallery thumbnail strips, icon-button rows, chart-like selectors — any hover-driven band on hero, work/gallery or navigation sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0462⟧

## ⟦S0463⟧ millionco/paper-flex — Part 13 — UI Skills, rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A workflow for converting layouts inside Paper (the design tool) from absolute positioning to flex/auto-layout without changing a single visible pixel: original nodes are cloned, never redrawn, and spacing is recomputed from their exact coordinates. Design-file surgery, not a web technique. Companion to ⟦S0464⟧ (Paper → code) and ⟦S0466⟧ (verifying the result).
- **How it looks:** Before and after screenshots of the artboard must be identical — same SVGs, image fills, crops, shadows and stacking order — while the node tree underneath becomes a readable flex hierarchy instead of a pile of positioned boxes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; visual identity between source and conversion is the whole point.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Required first pass: read the Paper MCP guide, get_basic_info + get_selection, take the baseline screenshot, get_tree_summary(depth=10) + get_children, and get_computed_styles for the target and every direct visual child (record left/top/width/height, colours, fonts, shadows, filters, radii, image fills) — computed styles, not the screenshot, are the source of truth. Spacing maths: gap = next.top − (current.top + current.height); leftPadding = first.left − container.left; topPadding = first.top − container.top. Preservation rules: complex visuals (SVGs, images, icons, masks, styled shapes) are inserted as <x-paper-clone node-id="…">, never hand-redrawn; after cloning into flow, batch update_styles to left/top "0px" on every flow clone; overlays get their position set by update_styles afterwards (Paper ignores position styles set on the clone element itself, and appends clones after normal divs — so decorative clones are written in an earlier write_html call than content, or z-order breaks). No margins: gap, padding wrappers or spacer frames only. Layered cards: fixed-size non-flex wrapper, back card first child, front card position absolute at 0/0, badges last children. Completion requires screenshot match plus eight get_computed_styles / get_children verifications (clone offsets, overlay positions, clone order, badge order, hidden shadows removed where flex would reveal them, filters on leaf nodes only).
