## ⟦S0509⟧ tjcages/linear-setup — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (tjcages/linear pack)
- **What it is:** The pack's bootstrap skill: the full sequenced procedure for setting up Linear tracking on a project — fresh, or as a careful extension of a project that already exists — ending in a scored done-check.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on a web page. The user sees a new or extended Linear project take shape: milestones mirroring the roadmap's phases, backfilled Done issues with evidence, a small label set, wired dependencies, the README added as a project document, and a tracking protocol written into the repo's agent-instruction file. Chat stays in the pack's numbered, action-first format with one next action at the end.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Step 0: probe Linear MCP; on failure give AUTH.md steps and stop — never invent API calls. Operating order, in sequence: (1) Already tracked? (§1a) — search Linear by repo name AND ask the user; if a project exists, STOP: enumerate issues/milestones/labels/docs/status updates, summarize, get per-category yes/no before any write, extend conservatively, scan the repo for unmirrored roadmap docs (§4 step 7). (2) North Star (§1b) — a README-as-vision is usually enough; say the call out loud; anchoring question 5 (why track at all) picks the project shape. (3–4) Type + structure (§2–§3) — suggested types Product / Tool / Drop / Marketing; milestones 1:1 with real phases; engineering, launch and rollout as separate tracks; dates only with a real signal; §17 shape tree if unclear. (5) Backfill (§4) — source priority CHANGELOG > roadmap > git log; feature-level default, per-release for launched packages; Done only with evidence; a doc's "done" claim is not proof — corroborate (§4 step 8). Ticket writing: titles ≤8 words, descriptions ≤3 sentences or ≤5 bullets, comments ≤3 lines, screenshots over prose (§10). (6) Wire (§4, §10, §11) — real `blockedBy`/`blocks`; surface the UI-only items (Cycles, Project Labels, Initiatives, icons, GitHub integration) early; add README as a Linear project document. (7) Install discipline (§5) — write the protocol into CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / .cursor/rules/ with the real team/project/milestone names; bootstrap is not done without this. (8) Honesty (§6, §9) — status updates at milestone/health moments only; flag `atRisk` before dates slip. (9) Done check (§18, §26) — rubric ≥16/20 with no load-bearing dimension at 0, or run the full §26 self-audit. After setup: point to `linear-finish-install` if always-on is missing. Bundle: all six shared files, identical to S0505's (hash-verified) — full methodology detail under ⟦S0505⟧.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/tjcages/linear, skills/linear-setup/SKILL.md (+ the shared bundle detailed under ⟦S0505⟧).

## ⟦S0510⟧ tjcages/linear-sync — Part 13 — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog (tjcages/linear pack)
- **What it is:** The pack's audit-and-rescue skill: scores an existing Linear project's tracking hygiene against the methodology rubric, gets per-category consent, then fixes it in a set order and re-scores to prove the improvement.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on a web page. The user sees a gap list with a before/after rubric score (e.g. the bundle's worked example runs 8/20 FAIL → 17/20 PASS), then — after consent — a tidied board: orphans assigned, milestone spam collapsed to a few outcome-named milestones, dependencies wired, and one status update recording the cleanup.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Step 0: probe Linear MCP; on failure give AUTH.md steps and stop. Operating order: (1) Identify project — search by name, confirm with the user if several match. (2) Enumerate — open + closed issues, milestones, labels, documents, status updates (§1a). (3) Score — §18 rubric, 10 dimensions × 0–2; PASS ≥16/20 with no load-bearing 0 (dimensions 1–6); emit the gap list. (4) Confirm — explicit per-category yes/no before writes; reorganizing is higher-risk than extending. (5) Fix in §22a order: orphan issues → milestone spam collapse (target 3–6 outcome-named milestones, §23) → missing dependencies (`blockedBy`/`blocks`) → install/update the discipline protocol in agent instructions (§5). (6) Half-tracked? — scan `docs/` for unmirrored roadmaps (§22b) and give each its own milestone set, never folded into an existing one. (7) Backfill-late? — §22c playbook; corroborate doc "done" claims against the user before closing anything (§4 step 8). (8) One status update recording the cleanup, only if health/structure changed (§20). (9) Re-score and show before/after totals; end with one next action. Hard rules: search before every create; never delete or reorganize off-limits or other-owned issues without explicit consent; ticket prose stays terse (§4), chat follows RESPONSE.md. Bundle: all six shared files, identical to S0505's (hash-verified), including EXAMPLES.md's worked rescue example.
- **Reference / source:** github.com/tjcages/linear, skills/linear-sync/SKILL.md (+ the shared bundle detailed under ⟦S0505⟧).
- **Best for:** No homepage section — audit/ops tooling. NOT-FOR-TRADES as a design reference; duplicate of the pack bundle detailed under ⟦S0505⟧, with this skill's own contribution being the score → consent → fix → re-score rescue order.

## ⟦S0511⟧ tt-a1i/archify — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A diagram generator: it turns requirements, Mermaid, or real codebase evidence into validated standalone HTML diagrams — architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, lifecycle/state, ERD, class, tree, timeline and waterfall — or into a one-page "explainer" (conclusion first, structured panels, native diagrams/charts). Not for dashboards.
- **How it looks:** A finished, explorable diagram page in dark or light theme: a system map with components, boundaries and labelled relationships, or an ERD drawn table-first with every physical column, its SQL type and key roles (a junction column is `["pk", "fk"]`, every fk carries `references` like `"orders.id"`), tables grouped into tagged functional domains drawn as solid grid rectangles, one domain per column. Sequence diagrams show call chains and returns; timelines put timestamped events on a proportional clock with source lanes; waterfalls show span durations on a common time axis. Output exports to image/SVG/WebM.
- **Frame by frame:** The rendered viewer's live motion is enabled by default for every diagram (the Viewer's Live/Still button controls playback). The bundled text specifies no motion design of its own — motion and other viewer features defer to a viewer-runtime reference that is not bundled.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The agent authors a `candidate.json` against per-type JSON schemas, then runs `node bin/archify.mjs finalize <type> <candidate.json> <output.html> --quality showcase --json`; a passing receipt proves validate, deliver, strict check and a real-browser browser-check all passed. `meta.quality_profile` is `"showcase"` by default; a dense schema-first ERD (over roughly 8 tables or 50 fields) starts at `"standard"`. Each artifact gets its own `.archify/<type>-<slug>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>/` folder. Mermaid is read for topology only, never rendered mechanically (flowchart → workflow/architecture, sequenceDiagram → sequence, stateDiagram → lifecycle, erDiagram → erd, classDiagram → class). Type choice can be delegated to `node bin/archify.mjs guide "<scenario>" --json`.
- **Reference / source:** The tt-a1i/archify GitHub repository (github.com/tt-a1i/archify). No external design sites named.
- **Best for:** Documentation and explainer pages, system/process diagrams. No homepage-section mechanism and no trade-homepage fit beyond a possible process diagram; this is a tooling skill, not a visual design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0511⟧

## ⟦S0512⟧ tt-a1i/archify-review — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog

- **Mechanism & key values:** Three lenses. Value: the real problem, who benefits, how often it occurs, its consequences, whether it is worth addressing now. Cost: implementation and verification effort plus the future cost of understanding, changing and maintaining the code; prefer existing capabilities, keep the solution proportional. Impact: affected behavior and modules, consequences for users and future development, whether the change improves maintainability or adds coupling. Judgments must be grounded in evidence: verify the target revision and relevant facts, distinguish direct verification from existing evidence and assumptions. Repository-specific requirements come from the repo's REVIEWING.md and CONTRIBUTING.md.

## ⟦S0513⟧ vercel/next-cache-components — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A migration procedure: enable Cache Components on a Next.js App Router app and walk it, feature by feature, to a passing build where every route is prerenderable and navigations are instant. It sequences the work; the per-error recipes live in the dev overlay fix cards and the linked Next.js docs.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor ends up seeing after adoption: a page paints its static shell instantly on load and on navigation, and request-time content streams in behind skeleton/loading fallbacks instead of the whole page blocking on its slowest read. In the build's route table, `○` is fully static, `◐` Partial Prerender (shell prerenders, request-time content streams — the goal state for routes reading cookies/headers/params/searchParams), `ƒ` genuinely dynamic through a documented escape hatch.
- **Frame by frame:** Navigation or load → the layout and static content commit immediately as the shell → each deferred region shows its `<Suspense>` fallback → streamed content replaces the fallbacks as it resolves. Placing a boundary too high (e.g. wrapping the whole page body) empties the shell so everything streams — the build still reports `◐`, so only a browser check catches it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Requires Next.js 16.3+ and App Router (the flag does nothing for `pages/`). The codemod `npx @next/codemod@latest cache-components-instant-false ./app` inserts `export const instant = false` with a `// TODO: Cache Components adoption` comment into every page/layout/default file; opt-outs resolve top-down, first explicit config wins, so they are removed root-first. `cacheComponents: true` errors on any file still exporting `dynamic`, `revalidate` or `fetchCache`; `experimental.dynamicIO` is fatal. Three blocker classes, in usual order: (1) request-time reads — `cookies()`, `headers()`, `await params`, `await searchParams` — pushed into a `<Suspense>`-wrapped child (forward the params promise, don't await at page top); (2) sync-IO at module/render time — `new Date()`, `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `crypto.randomUUID()` — which fail the build even with `instant = false`; (3) `"use cache"` files that read request data. Per-route success bar: dev loop reports no errors AND `next build` passes. Iterating builds use `--debug-build-paths` (file-path globs, not URLs) and `--debug-prerender` (continues past the first blocking route). Runtime verification prefers the `next-dev-loop` skill (cross-checks `/_next/mcp` against a live browser via agent-browser; requires Turbopack), then a self-driven browser, then build-only.
- **Reference / source:** Vercel's next.js repository (canary skills). Canonical reference named: the Next.js "Migrating to Cache Components" guide (nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components), the Caching and Streaming guides, and per-error pages at nextjs.org/docs/messages/<slug>; offline copies ship in node_modules/next/dist/docs/ since Next.js 16.2.
- **Best for:** Next.js engineering migrations and streaming/loading-state behaviour. Adoption comes before ⟦S0514⟧. No direct use for this bank's single-file HTML trade builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0513⟧

## ⟦S0514⟧ vercel/next-cache-components-optimizer — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** The follow-on to ⟦S0513⟧: an agentic optimization loop that drives one Next.js route at a time from "not instant" to "instant" and keeps it there, test-first — the goal is encoded as a failing `@next/playwright` `instant()` test, worked to green, and the test ships as the regression guard. Run once per target route and entry point.
- **How it looks:** The end state a visitor gets: on a click or a load, the destination's meaningful App Shell — layout, headers, existing loading UI — commits immediately, and only genuinely request-time content streams in afterwards. An empty shell does not count: `instant()` alone is satisfied by a blank shell, so the workflow adds a human-judged "non-blank" bar.
- **Frame by frame:** Soft navigation: user clicks a real `<Link>` → the router prefetches and commits the destination's App Shell under the navigation lock → deferred content markers are absent while locked → lock releases and the deferred content streams in. Initial load: `page.goto()` → the document carries the prerendered static shell → shell marker still valid after hydration → deferred parts stream. The shipped test asserts exactly this sequence; no custom timeouts or timing races are allowed — `instant()` is a ruler, not a stopwatch.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Phases P → G, each gated: P prereqs (Next.js 16.3+, `cacheComponents: true`, `@next/playwright` on the same release line as `next`); 0 setup — discover the project's rig once and commit it to `instant-nav.rig.md`; A rig — a production build exposing the testing API via `experimental.exposeTestingApiInProductionBuild` gated on a non-production condition (e.g. `EXPOSE_TESTING_API === '1'`); never measure on `next dev` (no prefetch, unreliable lock, vacuous passes); B unlocked baseline (marker renders for the test user; deleted before the PR); C locked RED plus a VERIFY-RED gate; D fix using the "Optimizing the static shell" guide's four patterns — keep static UI in the shell, push data access down, design loading states, cache reusable work; E parity (the refactor changed only whether the route is instant — same tree, data, redirects, state); F differential (revert the fix → RED, re-apply → GREEN); G PR checklist. Two reference files are bundled in full (rig-template.md, test-template.md); a third, reference/red-test-robustness.md, is cited throughout but is NOT included in the catalog text.
- **Reference / source:** Vercel's next.js repository (canary skills); the Next.js guides "Optimizing the static shell" and "Instant navigation" (nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/…). Hands off to a next-partial-prefetching-optimizer skill when only URL-specific content is missing.
- **Best for:** Next.js performance engineering after ⟦S0513⟧ adoption. Process/testing skill; no section-design use for the single-file trade builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0514⟧

## ⟦S0517⟧ vuejs-ai/create-adaptable-composable — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A Vue code pattern: create a library-grade composable that accepts maybe-reactive inputs (MaybeRef / MaybeRefOrGetter) so callers can pass a plain value, a ref, or a getter, and normalize the inputs with `toValue()`/`toRef()` inside reactive effects to keep behavior predictable.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual of its own — it shapes library code. The visitor-visible result is whatever the composable powers; the worked example `useDocumentTitle` updates `document.title` reactively whenever the passed value, ref or getter changes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Types as given in the source: `MaybeRef<T> = T | Ref<T> | ShallowRef<T> | WritableComputedRef<T>`; `MaybeRefOrGetter<T> = MaybeRef<T> | ComputedRef<T> | (() => T)`. Policy: read-only, computed-friendly inputs use MaybeRefOrGetter; writable/two-way inputs use MaybeRef; a parameter that might be a function value (callback/predicate/comparator) must NOT use MaybeRefOrGetter or it may be invoked as a getter; DOM/element targets may use MaybeRefOrGetter when computed targets are wanted. Resolution: `toRef()` for watcher sources, `toValue()` for plain values. Design steps: confirm purpose/API and expected inputs/outputs → mark which params are MaybeRef/MaybeRefOrGetter → normalize inside watch/watchEffect → implement core logic with Vue reactivity APIs. Examples in full: `useDocumentTitle` (watch(toRef(title), …, { immediate: true })) and two-way `useCounter` (toRef then `countRef.value++`).
- **Reference / source:** The vuejs-ai/skills GitHub repository.
- **Best for:** Vue composable/library authoring. Code-level pattern; no homepage-section use in this bank's single-file vanilla builds.

## ⟦S0526⟧ wheresryan22/anatomy — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A complete production system for building crafted, highly detailed, interactive isometric SVG figures that explain a technical idea as a real physical object — a test rig, a dial gauge, a cabinet of drawers, a plotter, a lock. It ships its own geometry kit, a geometry audit that proves the drawing true, an optional WebGL shader layer that lives inside the drawing in the same isometric perspective, an optional true-3D mode for parts that turn, A4 print sheets, and eight complete examples. At ~324 KB with 8 reference files bundled (3d, craft, kit, motion, react, verify, walkthrough, webgl — all read for this entry) it is by far the largest skill in this range. Same underlying skill as ⟦S0504⟧ — see the duplicate note under Reference / source.
- **How it looks:** A monochrome paper-toned drawing of one recognisable machine built from many small, precise, solid parts: a heavy base plate on feet with corner screws and a label plate, rails with tick rulers, a carriage on bushings, coil springs split around their rod, knurled knobs, a dial gauge whose needle moves. Parts are filled solids shaded in four tones — base and feet `lo`, structure `mid`, the subject `hi`, exactly one part `lit` (white in dark theme, black in light) — with 0.6 px lines, bevels of 0.4–1.6, and a soft halo under the base. The figure sits in a framed card: "Fig n" top left, short title top right, interaction hint bottom left, live readout bottom right (e.g. `120.0 × 32.0 · lean 10.6 px`), legend keys and a true caption under the card, almost no words inside the drawing itself. Dark theme is the kit default; the light theme is the shipping one and is designed for, not converted. At 1× it reads as one clear machine; at 4× every region still has true detail. Dense examples: the desk computer ≈85 solids / 850 paths, the arcade cabinet hero ≈240 solids and 15 cables, the Raptor engine ≈270 solids in 478 depth-sorted items.
- **Frame by frame:** One time-based rAF loop (dt clamped to 1/30 s) drives everything from a single pure model, writing attributes on refs — no re-render per frame. Pointer and keyboard set targets only; parts follow with exponential easing (τ = 0.1–0.3 s; the worked loop uses τ = 0.28 s) or real sub-stepped springs (test rig: press 700/32, hold 540/40, release 320/16 stiffness/drag; exploded views: stiffness 64, drag 14.2, sub-stepped 4× per frame, snapping when error and velocity fall below the settle threshold). Idle: after ~1.4 s untouched, a scripted tour loops the figure's point (test rig loop 7.6 s: rest → press → pull 80 → release → settle); it pauses on hover/focus/press and resumes ~3.6 s after the last interaction. Exploded view: assemblies spring apart staggered 35 ms apart in an order where nothing passes through anything; closing reverses the order; a mid-flight reversal reschedules only the assemblies whose target changed. One-shot events (flash, pop, shock) ride `burst` envelopes: smoothstep attack of 40–120 ms, then exponential decay; every shader uniform rides an envelope the same way, so nothing pops. The loop stops when everything settles or the figure leaves the viewport (IntersectionObserver, rootMargin 120px). Under `prefers-reduced-motion`: targets are jumped to, tours/flow/pulses off, shaders show one still frame — the figure still responds to input. The readout updates live from the same instant of the same model as the moving parts.
- **Mechanism & key values:** World units ≈ 1 px of the real thing (x, y on the floor, z up). Camera: azimuth 45° by default (35–60° to show the long side; test rig 57°, ripple tank elevation 44° vs the default 30°); the figure fills ~55–65% of the card; typical viewBox 600 × 340–380, `fitProjection` pad 24–34. Size tiers named before building: Figure = one mechanism, 40–80 parts, at most one WebGL layer; Hero = 80–150 parts, several WebGL layers or one 3D subject, ~2–4 hours; Epic = 6+ hours, never started unasked. Parts list minimum 40, grouped base/structure/mechanism/controls/subject. Detail values: grooves inset 3–5 from an edge, screws as 0.4–0.55 dots with a ring, ruler ticks every 4–5 units with a major every 5th, label plate with three rule lines. Painter's order is back-to-front by `depthOf`, wrapping parts split into back/front halves; dense figures record every item's true shape into `kit/audit.mjs` (`A.recorder`, `A.settle`, `A.auditOrExit`) which proves clearance (~1.5 radii for pipes/cables), terminals, loose ends, folds, self-overlaps, wobble, seats, supports and depth order at rest, apart and in every replayed explode frame, and fails any recorded shape covering under 60% of its drawing. Pipe radii: main ducts r 5–8, feed lines r 2–4, sense lines r 0.9–1.5, cables r 0.5–0.65; bends ≈2.6×r via `fillet`. Kit: `iso-kit` (camera, solids, parts library, SVG renderer, card/page builders, ISO_CSS), `lathe.mjs` (turned parts on any axis, smooth monotone-Hermite shading), `tube.mjs` (pipes split into depth-sortable chunks with gaps under collars), `gl.mjs` (GLSL_ISO camera contract — `rayOf`, `onFloor`, `onWallX/Y`; device ratio capped at 1.5; light-theme ink solved from the colour paper should show, never a darkened dark-theme glow). 3D turning mode (beta): convex parts only, materials gold/chrome/steel/gunmetal/rubber/brass/copper; live tube bends need R ≥ 2r / sin²(e − θmax) — 8r on a flat plane, 21r on a ±12° hinge; part costs in prism units: prism 1, round 2.5–4, ball with flats 8–10, lathe ~25; small figure weight ≤ ~50, dense ≤ ~230; a full orbit audit takes 15–20 minutes for 30 parts and must end `turn audit passed`. Verification stack: `node build.mjs --audit` to zero, `scripts/lines.mjs` printing `line ends: 0`, 4× close-ups of every junction in both themes, capture/drive scripts in headless Chrome. Also prints A4/Letter sheets (poster, drawing, detailed formats) from the finished figure.
- **Reference / source:** The wheresryan22/anatomy GitHub repository. Eight shipped examples named in the source: dial-indicator (smallest, ~300 lines), desk-computer, arcade-cabinet, raptor-engine (the bar for shader work), ripple-tank, test-rig (the quality bar for the drawing; a production figure from a real React/Next site), spot-plate, turning-dial (the 3D mode). DUPLICATE: ⟦S0504⟧ Teddarific/anatomy-asset is the same underlying skill under another catalog name — its own text calls it "A fork of Anatomy for assets instead of explainers," sharing the kit, the craft rules and eight of the examples, but retargeted from interactive explainers with live readouts to static marketing assets (hero objects, spot illustrations, feature tiles) with calm CSS-only ambient motion, shipping a standalone .svg. This entry (S0526) is the full-detail canonical one for the shared system; S0504's entry carries the asset-specific framing.
- **Best for:** Work/gallery and process sections that need an interactive explainer figure — a mechanism drawn as a real machine the visitor can press, drag and watch (e.g. how a system fits together, shown as a rig) — and hero spot illustration where craft is the point. Its motion discipline (envelopes, springs, tours, reduced-motion behaviour), its WebGL-inside-SVG layering, and its audit/verify workflow also transfer to any rich SVG scene. Cost note from the source itself: a Hero-tier figure is a 2–4 hour build with heavy verification — overkill for small decorative spots, which is the S0504 fork's job.

## ⟦S0527⟧ wshobson/wcag-audit-patterns — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A working guide for auditing a website against WCAG 2.2 and fixing what fails — conformance levels, the common violations ranked by impact, and remediation patterns, with the detailed pattern library in a companion `references/details.md`.
- **How it looks:** Nothing renders from this skill itself; what the visitor ends up seeing is a site that passes the audit — every functional image carrying alt text, every control reachable and operable by keyboard with a visible focus outline, labelled form fields, sufficient colour contrast, a skip link at the top, proper landmarks and heading order, page titles, and no auto-playing media without controls.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. It is an audit-and-remediation process, not a visual effect.
- **Mechanism & key values:** WCAG 2.2 organised by the POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and three conformance levels — A (minimum / legal baseline), AA (standard, most regulations), AAA (enhanced). Violations are triaged Critical (missing alt text on functional images, no keyboard access, missing form labels, auto-play media without controls), Serious (insufficient contrast, missing skip links, inaccessible custom widgets, missing page titles), Moderate (missing language attribute, unclear link text, missing landmarks, improper heading hierarchy). Standing numbers: automated testing catches only 30–50% of issues, so manual testing is mandatory; native HTML before ARIA; never hide focus outlines; never disable zoom; never use colour alone as the only indicator.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/wshobson/agents/blob/main/plugins/accessibility-compliance/skills/wcag-audit-patterns/SKILL.md (wshobson/agents, accessibility-compliance plugin). Named frameworks: WCAG 2.2, ADA, Section 508, VPAT.

## ⟦S0528⟧ zarazhangrui/frontend-slides — UI Skills — rest of the ui-skills.com catalog
- **What it is:** A system for building zero-dependency, animation-rich HTML slide decks as single self-contained files — from scratch, from a style-discovery process, or by converting a PowerPoint file.
- **How it looks:** A polished 16:9 presentation filling the browser window: slides authored on a fixed 1920×1080 stage that scales as one whole canvas (letterboxed if needed, never reflowed), with distinctive display typography (Fontshare/Google Fonts, never Inter/Roboto/Arial/system fonts), a committed palette with sharp accents, layered gradient/pattern backgrounds, and staggered reveal animations. Two density looks: low-density speaker decks (one idea per slide, huge type, 1–3 bullets) or high-density reading decks (grids, tables, 4–8 bullets or 4–6 cards). No generic "AI slop" look — purple gradients on white are named as the cliché to avoid.
- **Frame by frame:** Browsing the deck → arrow keys / space / swipe move between slides; slide visibility swaps via `.active`/`.visible` classes using visibility + opacity + pointer-events (never `display:none`, which later flex rules can override and show every slide at once) → on each slide, elements reveal with staggered animation-delays, one orchestrated load moment rather than scattered micro-interactions → hovering the top-left corner or pressing E enters inline edit mode, click any text to edit, Ctrl+S saves → end state is the edited, still-16:9 deck.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Single HTML file, all CSS/JS inline, no npm or build tools; the full contents of a mandatory `viewport-base.css` are embedded in every deck. Fixed stage 1920×1080, uniform scale, no responsive breakpoints inside slides; `clamp()` allowed only for non-slide UI; `prefers-reduced-motion` support required; never negate CSS functions (`calc(-1 * clamp(...))` instead). Workflow: Phase 1 asks purpose/length/content/density together; Phase 2 generates 3 single-slide style previews (1 safe preset from 12 in STYLE_PRESETS.md, at least 1 bold template, 1 wildcard) for the user to pick visually; Phase 4 converts PPTX via `python scripts/extract-pptx.py` (python-pptx); Phase 6 deploys via `scripts/deploy.sh` (Vercel) or exports PDF via `scripts/export-pdf.sh` — Playwright screenshots each slide at 1920×1080 (~20MB for 18 slides; `--compact` renders 1280×720, cutting size 50–70%). Verification viewports: 1280×720 plus one phone size.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/zarazhangrui/frontend-slides/blob/main/SKILL.md — its own STYLE_PRESETS.md, bold-template-pack, html-template.md, viewport-base.css and animation-patterns.md ship with the skill.
- **Best for:** Pitch decks, talk slides and client presentations — not a homepage-section source, though its fixed-stage discipline and preview-first style selection are a useful model for presenting design options.

## ⟦S0530⟧ google-gemini/gemini-omni-flash-api — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A tooling skill for generating and editing video with Google's Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash model through the official google-genai SDK: text-to-video, first-frame and first/last-frame video, reference-guided generation, extensions and edits, with ffmpeg pre-processing helpers.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor eventually sees is the generated clip itself: a 3–10 second video (16:9 or 9:16) that starts from a supplied still frame or pure text, moves as the prompt directs — including timed events ("after 3 seconds, a woman enters", or timecode blocks like `[0-3s] … [3-6s] …`), on-screen text rendered word by word if asked, and a generated audio track (music, ambience, speech) unless the source audio is kept or stripped for full regeneration. Edits restyle or alter an existing ≤10s clip while "keep everything else the same" holds the rest steady.
- **Frame by frame:** Not a fixed animation: the model generates continuous footage per prompt; the skill's own sequencing is upload media via the Files API → run the generation script → the finished file lands on local disk (e.g. `media/`). Extensions chain: each turn adds up to 10s using the last 10s as context, to a 40s total ceiling.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Model `gemini-omni-1.1-flash` via the Interactions API; requires `google-genai >= 2.19.0`, Python ≥ 3.10, ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH, and a `GEMINI_API_KEY`. Resolutions: 360p (640×360 / 360×640), 720p default (1280×720 / 720×1280), 1080p (1920×1080 / 1080×1920), 4k (3840×2160 / 2160×3840); durations any integer 3–10s; default HTTP timeout 600s (raise to 900–1200 for 4k extensions). Scripts: `upload_file.py` (warns above 25MB), `generate_video.py` (flags `--first-frame`, `--last-frame`, `--image`, `--video-reference`, `--extend`, `--strip-audio`, `--previous-interaction-id`, `--prompts-file`/`--batch` with `--concurrency`), `inspect_video.py`, `prep_video.py` (trims to ≤10s, scales to max 1280×720 landscape / 720×1280 portrait; the model is optimised for 10s at 720p/24fps). Prompt tags: `<FIRST_FRAME>`, `<LAST_FRAME>`, `<IMAGE_REF_N>`, `<VIDEO_REF_N>` (indexes from 0; reference videos ideally ~3s, up to 3 recommended). Recorded restriction: uploading videos for edits/extensions is not available in the EEA, Switzerland, the UK and some US states — an edit returning instantly with empty output (`total_output_tokens: 0`) signals exactly that.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-skills/blob/main/skills/gemini-omni-flash-api/SKILL.md — Google Gemini API docs (Interactions API, Files API) and the companion gemini-api-dev skill.
- **Best for:** Producing video assets rather than page mechanics — an ambient hero background clip, a before/after motion piece, or social cuts for a trade site. Not a section design in itself.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0530⟧

## ⟦S0531⟧ heygen-com/canopy-part-title — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A ready-made HyperFrames video block: a dense canopy of textured leaves sweeps across the frame, parts to reveal a first headline, then a second batch of leaves carries a second headline past the camera.
- **How it looks:** A near-black green frame (#020805) filled with a shallow-depth-of-field thicket of leaves — colour and normal-mapped leaf surfaces, foreground leaves soft and blurred by a bokeh pass. The canopy rushes through, opens over big heavy type (default weight 900, Helvetica; Gelasio is the bundled web font), and after the reveal a few leaves (default 5) remain resting on the letters, stirring slightly in a breeze.
- **Frame by frame:** Composition runs 12s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → the first leaf sweep (default 170 leaves) crosses the frame with shallow focus → the leaves part to uncover headline 1 ("Understory") → a second, depth-lifted batch sweeps through carrying headline 2 ("Move slowly") past the camera → the frame settles with the retained leaves left on the type, moving gently with the breeze → end state holds the second headline under its resting leaves.
- **Mechanism & key values:** HyperFrames block `canopy-part-title`, installed with `npx hyperframes add canopy-part-title`; one paused GSAP timeline (`window.__timelines["canopy-part-title"]`), every frame a closed-form function of time (seeded PRNG only), re-syncing on the `hf-seek` event. Renderer: three.js 0.170.0 + GSAP 3.14.2 + Canvas 2D + post-processing (BokehPass) + shadow maps; runtime budget roughly 350 MB per live instance, one at a time. 11 variables: headline1/headline2, font, fontWeight (default 900, 100–900), fontSize (1 = auto-fit, 0.3–2), letterSpacing (0.01em, −0.2–1), background #020805, leafCount (170; 40–320), stayCount (5; 0–20), sweepSpeed (1; 0.3–3), retainedBreeze (1; 0–2). Assets: leaf-surface colour + normal WebP maps; GSAP and three.js load from jsDelivr CDN.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/canopy-part-title/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A video title card or intro beat; as a borrowed mechanism, the organic-layer-parting reveal suits a hero or section opener where foliage/nature fits the brand. Trade fit: narrow — leaf canopy suits landscapers/garden-adjacent trades more than roofing or HVAC.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0531⟧

## ⟦S0532⟧ heygen-com/captions-overlay — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A doctrine skill for captions in HyperFrames videos: every spoken phrase is classified drop, rail or embed, and captions are treated as an overlay composited on top of the film — never a reserved band the layout must make room for. It supplements the upstream `/hyperframes` skill's captions reference.
- **How it looks:** Ordinary speech appears as one small, clean, word-by-word lower-third line riding in front of the picture, bottom-centred in roughly the bottom 5–8% of the frame, with a punch word optionally popping in an accent colour. Rarely — at a genuine peak — one big word appears composited behind the subject, occluded by their matte, with a designed entrance and exit. The picture itself stays full-bleed and centred on the true frame centre; there is no dead empty band at the bottom.
- **Frame by frame:** Playback → filler (um/uh, stutters, self-corrections) is dropped, never shown → normal phrases roll along the rail line word by word in front of the footage → at a peak beat, a single embed word enters behind the subject, holds as the climax, then exits → the rail resumes. Embeds are rationed: at most 1 per beat/sentence, never two adjacent or co-visible, spaced at least a beat apart, at most one apex; a short clip usually gets one embed, a long explainer about one per section.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Two rules. (1) The caption model — drop / rail (default, verbatim, in front; inline `emphasis` highlight allowed) / embed (scarce, earned, behind the subject via matte occlusion); "rail-first, embed-scarce" for talking-head and explainer work; a pure-cinematic treatment may drop the rail entirely, never for explainer/voiceover. (2) The overlay law — centre the composition on the true vertical centre, y = H/2 (540 landscape, 960 portrait); content may run to the canvas bottom; the only courtesy rule is to keep critical small readable text (URLs, legal lines) out of the bottom ~80px centre span where the caption line sits. No machine keep-out gate exists (the old `captions.mjs keepout` check is retired); legibility over content is judged visually in snapshot review.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/captions-overlay/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills); applies on top of the `/hyperframes` skill's references/captions.md (⟦S0540⟧).
- **Best for:** Any captioned talking-head, launch or explainer video; the drop/rail/embed model is also a sound discipline for on-page text hierarchy — most words quiet, one earned peak.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0532⟧

## ⟦S0533⟧ heygen-com/changelog-video — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** An end-to-end pipeline skill that turns a weekly changelog markdown file into a finished branded changelog video: parse and cut the digest, route each theme to an animated mock-UI visualisation, write a two-layer script, generate a pinned voiceover, build the HyperFrames project and pass its gates.
- **How it looks:** A square 1080×1080 video, about 45–60 seconds: cream background (#f5f6f4) with an animated brand pattern video behind glass cards edged in green-tinted borders; TT Norms Pro text with ABC Solar Display headlines and TT Norms Mono details; one rationed green moment (#5ef17c) per scene; each changelog theme shown as a mock of the actual UI acting out the change rather than bullet text; a low-key 32px caption rail sitting at top:990; a ≤2s title and ≤3.5s outro pointing to the full digest.
- **Frame by frame:** Title beat (≤2s) → four theme scenes of roughly 9–12s each, ordered marquee feature → product surface → performance → reliability, each scene acting out its change in a mock UI with at most 3 spoken items (≤14 spoken beats in the whole video) while the voiceover runs and the caption rail tracks it word by word → seams between scenes are cut-the-curve LEFT by default → outro (≤3.5s) points to the full digest → end state is the branded outro frame.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Self-contained skill (fonts, background, lexicon, scripts ship inside it); the project must be bootstrapped from the skill's own assets — fonts copied to `project/assets/fonts/`, `bgm.mp3`, the background looped/encoded with ffmpeg (`scale=1080:1080, fps=30, saturation=0.72`, black@0.5 fill box, crf 20), and `examples/master-skeleton.html` copied as `index.html` before any scene work. Script is two-layer token lines (`script-tokens.json`): captions show display spelling, the VO reads spoken phonetic forms from `references/lexicon.json` — an unknown term stops the run until the user gives its pronunciation. Voice is pinned: "Annie" via the HeyGen TTS helper, voice id `330290724a1b470fb63153f34d4c0183`, requires heygen CLI ≥0.3.0; word timestamps in `vo-words.json` are a hard gate (empty timestamps → forced-align locally with whisper base.en; captions still use display spelling). Build order: `ledger.json` (seams cut-the-curve LEFT) → seam-stamp → internal beats on VO words → seam-gate verify; gates include a caption-zone check (content stays above the rail; dim text ≥ .66 alpha) and a hard caption-presence check sampling frames across the spoken window. Loads ⟦S0544⟧ motion-doctrine first, plus ⟦S0536⟧, ⟦S0546⟧ and ⟦S0548⟧ as applicable, and ⟦S0532⟧ captions-overlay.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/changelog-video/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills); its references: visualization-registry.md, build-spec.md, script-voice.md, lexicon.json.
- **Best for:** Recurring product-update/changelog videos only; as a pattern it shows a complete branded video pipeline (scaffold-first, audio-as-clock, gated captions) rather than a reusable visual effect.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0533⟧

## ⟦S0534⟧ heygen-com/code-slice-hero — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A HyperFrames video block: a full surface of square tiles carries one seamless headline; an imaginary cursor sweeps across, nearby tiles lift and tilt in its depth field, and only the tiles inside either headline's silhouette flip over to reveal a second headline behind them.
- **How it looks:** A wall of dark square tiles (behind-tile colour #212121) printed as one giant bold Geist headline ("MAKE IT"). A wave of depth passes over the grid — tiles near the invisible cursor bulge toward the viewer and tilt, casting soft projected shadows — and as the wave crosses, individual tiles turn over cell by cell so the rear headline ("MATTER.") appears tiled into the same surface, in the same type, without the grid ever stretching.
- **Frame by frame:** 8s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → the tiled front headline sits composed → the cursor's Gaussian depth field enters from one side (default left-to-right) and travels across over the sweep (default 4.2s): tiles inside its radius lift and tilt as it approaches → each tile whose cell intersects either headline silhouette flips (default 0.75s per flip, slight elastic bounce) as the field reaches it, front face replaced by the rear headline's slice → the sweep exits; the grid settles flat showing the rear headline tiled across the whole surface.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `code-slice-hero` (`npx hyperframes add code-slice-hero`); the whole grid is one instanced WebGL 2 draw with a shared front/rear texture pair plus a batched projected-shadow pass; text size and square cell size are independent variables so tiles never stretch. Runtime: GSAP + Canvas 2D + seeded PRNG, one paused seek-safe timeline, no external runtime dependencies (Geist-Bold.ttf and GSAP 3.14.2 are bundled locally). 18 variables: headline / reverseHeadline (max 32 chars each), direction (left-to-right / right-to-left), sweepDuration (4.2; 2.6–4.5s), sweepEaseStrength (3; 0–3), flipDuration (0.75; 0.65–1.65s), cursorRadius (210; 160–480), cursorFalloff (1.4; 0.4–3.5), cursorDepth (80; −320–320), tiltStrength (55; 0–55), noiseStrength (2; 0–2), flipBounce (0.15; 0–0.8), cellSize (112; 24–120), formationScale (1; 0.94–1), fontSize (310; 160–480), behindColor #212121, shadowStrength (0.19; 0–0.65), shadowSoftness (4; 0.5–4).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/code-slice-hero/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A video hero/title beat with a two-message flip (claim → payoff). As a borrowed mechanism it is a strong hero-version pattern for a homepage: a tile/flip surface where a cursor or scroll sweep swaps one headline for another.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0534⟧

## ⟦S0535⟧ heygen-com/cuboid-carousel — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A HyperFrames video block: a chain of rounded, bevelled 3D cuboids carrying card content rides a travelling wave like a carousel — flying in as one rigid group, cruising with a per-cuboid rotation stagger, holding on a hero card, then exiting.
- **How it looks:** Dark studio backdrop (#0b0d13) lit by a warm three-point rig; a train of chunky dark cards (body #242424, softly bevelled edges, lit faces) sweeps in from the right with a wave running through the chain, each cuboid slightly rotated against its neighbours; the chain decelerates and one hero card (default the 4th) holds centre under a face light while the others recede, then the whole chain exits left. Spacing is computed from cuboid dimensions so cards can never overlap.
- **Frame by frame:** 6.667s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → the cuboid group flies in from the right as one rigid body → cruise phase: the travelling wave passes along the chain with per-cuboid rotation stagger while the camera settles (settle frame 70 of 200) from a narrow 11° FOV toward its 34° target framing → deceleration into the hero hold, hero card lit and centred → the group exits left, the hero spinning out on its exit rotation (default X 288°, Y −234°, Z 198°) → end state clears the frame.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `cuboid-carousel` (`npx hyperframes add cuboid-carousel`); three.js (bundled module builds) + GSAP 3.14.2, WebGL with PMREM environment and shadow maps; one paused seek-safe timeline; ~350 MB per live instance; Inter is the web font. 40 variables (the original DialKit schema): count (8; 1–12), heroCard (4; 1–12), gap (0.01), cuboidWidth 1.7 / Height 2.4 / Depth 0.14, cornerRadius 0.105, bevelSize 0.03, bevelThickness 0.04, smoothness 32, bodyColor #242424, roughness 0.6, metalness 0.4; lights — ambient 0.35 white, top rig 3.1 white, bottom rig 2.15 #ffcaad, key rig 5 #ffe9d6; shadows — mapSize 2048, radius 44.5; camera FOV 11 → target 34, position (−1.65, 8.5, −8.51) → target (−7.25, 1.15, 6.2), handheldStrength 1; cards can also come from a `cardsJson` variable.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/cuboid-carousel/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A video feature/service carousel beat. Borrowed as a page mechanism, the wave-riding card chain suits a work/gallery or services carousel where cards should feel physical rather than slid.
