## ⟦S0536⟧ heygen-com/cut-the-curve — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The technique catalog underneath ⟦S0544⟧'s motion doctrine: five velocity-matched seam techniques (zoom-through, inverse zoom-through, cut-the-curve, waterfall cut, rack-focus blur-cut) plus two in-scene techniques (waterfall entry, nudge curve), each with exact parameters. One principle throughout: cut at peak velocity and match direction and speed on both sides of the cut.
- **How it looks:** Transitions that feel like one continuous camera move rather than a scene change: a headline grows toward the viewer, blurs at its fastest moment and is suddenly a different headline still growing into focus; two scenes hand over mid-slide, the outgoing hero streaking out as the incoming one continues the same direction and settles; a line of words peels away word by word while the next line cascades in on the same wave; occasionally a visible DSLR-style focus pull — the whole frame defocuses, swaps, and snaps sharp.
- **Frame by frame:** Zoom-through (in-scene text swap, total ≈0.4s): outgoing text scales 1→1.2 with blur 0→10px over 0.2s (power3.in; opacity on a separate linear tween to 0.15) → hard swap at peak blur (incoming starts at scale 0.75, blur 10px, opacity 0.15) → incoming grows 0.75→1, blur clears, opacity to 1 over 0.5s (expo.out). Inverse zoom-through (arrival beats, ≈0.7s): outgoing shrinks 1→0.8, incoming arrives oversized at 1.25 and retracts to 1. Cut-the-curve (default scene boundary, ≈0.6s): outgoing hero accelerates ~230px (about 12% of frame) with power4.in, its fade finishing at 25–30% of travel → cut mid-motion → incoming hero starts 230px the other side at ~0.35 opacity and decelerates with power4.out. Waterfall cut: the same at word granularity — exit stagger +0.022s per word in reading order, entry gaps 0.05s shrinking ×0.84 per word. Rack-focus blur-cut: both sides stay opaque, blur spikes to 8–12px peak with ~1.06 lens-breathing scale, swap hidden at peak blur, power2 eases. Waterfall entry (arrivals): elements whip in from below with binary 0→1 opacity, overlapping by 1–2 frames, gaps shrinking across the cascade. Nudge curve (group slides): three chained tweens — power3.in over ~10% of distance in ~20% of time, a linear burst over ~65% in ~18%, then a power4.out tail over the last ~25% in ~62% of the time.
- **Mechanism & key values:** GSAP timelines; code templates in the skill's `examples/gsap-implementation.md`. Load-bearing numbers: partial travel ~12% of frame (≈230px at 1920) — never full off-screen moves; mirrored eases (exit power4.in + entry power4.out = one power4.inOut split at the cut); peak blur 10px for text-scale subjects, 18–20px only for full-frame surfaces, identical on both sides at the swap frame, applied to the wrapper never the children; the Z scale-sign rule — a growing (push) exit must be answered by a growing entry (0.75→1), a shrinking (pull) exit by a shrinking entry (1.25→1), and the incoming scene's own entrances inside the seam window (cut + ~0.5s) must obey the same sign; waterfall entry weights — anchors travel 60–80px over 0.16–0.20s, normal words 40–50px over 0.13–0.16s, light punctuation 30–48px over 0.10–0.13s, ease power4.out (expo.out for snap), never .inOut; rack-focus at most once per ~8s, never mid-caption; nudge tail must be ≥3× the ramp-in in time; the stage ground must be opaque (`#root` background) or mid-window cuts flash white (see ⟦S0548⟧).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/cut-the-curve/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills); seam law lives in ⟦S0544⟧ motion-doctrine.
- **Best for:** Every transition decision — video scene seams first, but the same numbers govern web section-to-section motion, headline swaps, kinetic-type entries and group repositioning on a page. One of the highest-value motion references in this range for homepage work.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0536⟧

## ⟦S0537⟧ heygen-com/figma — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A bridge skill for bringing Figma material into a HyperFrames video: rendered assets, brand tokens and components come over the REST API, while motion, shaders and storyboard frames are reconstructed as animation — frames read as states through time, not as slides.
- **How it looks:** The video ends up wearing the real brand: the actual logo as a crisp SVG, real brand colours and type as composition variables, and a Figma frame rebuilt as editable HTML at its exact geometry. A storyboard's neighbouring frames play as one element tweening between its states — a button that actually moves and changes — instead of a slideshow of stills.
- **Frame by frame:** Storyboard import → every frame-sized node in the section is collected as a scene, ordered by its x position → children are matched across neighbouring frames by name, then by similar size and position → matched elements tween their geometry between the two states; elements whose pixels changed crossfade in place; unmatched children enter or exit at their scene's beat → the sequence plays as continuous motion. Verification compares the reconstruction against Figma's own exported video and fails the translation under 15 dB (faithful ≈ 20+, diverging ≈ 5).
- **Mechanism & key values:** All imports happen at build time and freeze local files with sources recorded under `.media/`; renders never call Figma. Access via `FIGMA_TOKEN` (read-only File content + File metadata scopes, plus Library content for tokens on non-Enterprise plans). Commands: `npx hyperframes figma asset '<url or fileKey:nodeId>' --format svg|png --scale 2` (SVG for vectors/logos, PNG at 2× for raster); `figma tokens <fileKey>` (falls back to published styles without Enterprise); `figma component '<ref>'` packages a frame as editable HTML where a fill bound to a token becomes `var(--slug, #literal)`. Motion path (connector only): fetch motion context in one recursive request, normalise with `motionContextToDocs` from `@hyperframes/core/figma` (never hand-transcribe keyframes; loop-wrap tail keyframes dropped, bezier eases kept), then `motionToGsap` → a paused timeline script; verify with `scripts/verify-motion.mjs`. Storyboard rules: export in batches of about 4 scene frames per call (past ~12 ids the images endpoint times out); text nodes below a frame strip are motion notes, not on-screen copy; Figma's export flattens shaders to their base colour, so shader frames need a native export from the person. The skill text also directs the operator to fire usage-beacon commands (`npx hyperframes events --skill=figma-motion`, and `figma-shaders` / `figma-storyboard` equivalents, with a completion event at the end of those phases) — recorded here as part of the skill's prescribed behaviour.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/figma/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames); Figma REST API.
- **Best for:** Any video that must use a client's real Figma brand, logo or storyboard — and a discipline worth borrowing for web work: treat design frames as states of one element, not separate pictures.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0537⟧

## ⟦S0538⟧ heygen-com/frost-sequence-camera-orbit — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A complete HyperFrames video block: a 22.5-second ice sequence in which an orbiting camera watches a logo made of physical ice break apart, its shards reform into two text moments, and the sequence fades — one particle field carries every transition.
- **How it looks:** Against a near-black backdrop (#050505), a logo and then two lines of Geist type ("Hard to break." / "Easy to remember.") stand as solid ice — clear transmission with pale-blue attenuation (#d5f4ff), frosted patches, fine cracks, crystal and grain bump, inclusions suspended inside. The camera circles slowly, easing into slower front-facing passes while text is meant to be read. Then the form shatters: thousands of ice shards and powder burst outward, tumble and drift, and spring back together into the next shape.
- **Frame by frame:** 22.5s at 30fps, 1920×1080, composition id `frost-sequence-rig` → the ice logo assembles (growth front sweeping from an origin point over the assembly duration, default 3.2s) while the camera orbits → breakup: a diagonal slice (radius 0.6, strength 21.5) then follow-up shatters (radius 0.45, strength 32.5) eject shards and powder (visible shard fraction 0.44) which tumble through curl-noise turbulence → the same field re-forms into headline 1 as shards fly home on springs and align to the surface → breakup and re-formation repeat into headline 2 → final fade. Camera motion is continuous orbit throughout, slower when front-facing for reading.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `frost-sequence-camera-orbit` (`npx hyperframes add frost-sequence-camera-orbit`); WebGPU renderer + GSAP + matcap shading; one paused seek-safe timeline; all code and fonts served locally (frost.js alone is 1.5 MB). 216 variables across material, break, flight, assembly, light and post groups. Key defaults: ice IOR 1.675, base roughness 0.31, materialBacklight 0.27, thicknessScale 2.04, attenuationDistance 6.54, frostScale 0.7 / frostThreshold 0.62 / frostSoftness 0.24, crackWidth 0.0025, particleCount 100k (options to 1M), shape voxel resolution 256, strayDust 24, ejectSpeed 0.91, turbulence 4 at scale 2.65, settleTime 2.2s, returnSpring 29.9 with damping 1.34, returnMaxSpeed 60, refrostTime 10.6s; key light #f0f7ff at intensity 5.05, rim 2.5 #d9f1ff, cool accent #ff5900 / warm accent #75aaff (labels as shipped); ACES tonemap, exposure 1, vignette 0.14; text block width 6.5 (mark is 2.6 wide), line height 0.95, extrusion depth 0.16 of font size. Headlines take `|` as a line break, max 60 chars; logo is a swappable SVG path variable.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/frost-sequence-camera-orbit/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A cinematic brand/logo reveal or launch-film centrepiece. Trade fit: the shatter-and-reform mechanism is the borrowable idea (a mark that breaks and rebuilds); the ice material itself suits cold/frost brands only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0538⟧

## ⟦S0539⟧ heygen-com/glass-shard-title — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A HyperFrames video block: Voronoi-cut glass panes fly in through fog, rotating, and tile themselves exactly into the silhouette of a headline — then fly out past the camera.
- **How it looks:** Out of a foggy depth, translucent glass shards with bevelled edges and matcap reflections converge and lock together like a mosaic, and the assembled panes form the letters of the headline ("Designed in glass") — the type is literally made of glass tiles with hairline gaps (default gap 0.03). After the hold, the panes break away and stream past the camera.
- **Frame by frame:** 12.16s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → shards approach from deep z (−42) through fog (fog distance 36), rotating as they come (fly-in 2.3s, stagger 0.27, strong ease power 10) → each pane lands on its Voronoi cell of the headline silhouette and the tiled title reads complete → hold → panes release and fly out to z +14, past the camera (fly-out 2.4s, rotation 6) → frame clears.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `glass-shard-title` (`npx hyperframes add glass-shard-title`); each shard is a Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a jittered blob against its Voronoi cell (d3-delaunay), so the pieces always cover the type exactly; tile count 1 yields a single pane. Renderer: three.js 0.181.2 (bundled) + GSAP 3.14.2 + GLSL shaders + HDR environment (ferndale_studio_01_1k.hdr) + matcap, per-fragment fog on glass and matcap surfaces, z-flight decoupled from the ease; ~350 MB per live instance. 19 variables: headline (max 40 chars), tileCount (8; 1–400), roundness 0.4, bevel 0.35, meshSmooth 0.6, flyInTime 2.3s (0.2–6), flyOutTime 2.4s, stagger 0.27, flyInRotation 5 (0–60), flyOutRotation 6, chaos 0.25, padding 1, sizeVariance 0.35, gap 0.03 (0–0.3), easePow 10 (1–10), sideDist 3, zDist −42, zOut 14, fog 36 (0–400). Fonts: Geist family + Cormorant Garamond bundled.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/glass-shard-title/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A premium title reveal in video. The fragments-assemble-into-type mechanism is a strong hero/title pattern generally — pieces converging into letterforms reads as craft for glazing, glass and premium trade brands especially.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0539⟧

## ⟦S0540⟧ heygen-com/hyperframes — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The core HyperFrames skill — the gateway for making, editing, animating or rendering any video in HyperFrames, HeyGen's system that renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame so every render is identical. It holds the render contract, the work loop, and what each kind of video needs.
- **How it looks:** The output is a finished video (new projects default to 1920×1080 at 30fps) built as ordinary web pages: an `index.html` root composition declaring variables and mounting one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`, with media and fonts in `assets/` — the same files the person can keep editing in the desktop app's preview.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own. It defines the rules every frame must obey: each timed element is a `.clip` visible over `[start, start + duration)`, and all visible state is a deterministic function of timeline time.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The contract (violations are reported by `npx hyperframes check --json`, most with a `Fix:` line): every timed element carries `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds; the video's length is the root's `data-duration` (overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame); each composition registers one paused timeline as `window.__timelines["<id>"]`; no `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`; never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a clip (animate a child); no CSS transforms on elements GSAP transforms, and animate transforms not left/top/width/height; media is never played/paused/seeked by hand; only bundled fonts resolve by name, anything else needs `@font-face` into `assets/fonts/`; grades/grain/blur on footage go through media-treatment, never CSS filters. Editability rules: content inside the 90% action-safe box, captions and key text inside the 80% title-safe box; copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables. Work loop: `npx hyperframes init <dir>` or `capture <url>` for a website subject; check history before changing an existing project; a narrative film over ~15s gets three storyline options then a SPEC before building, plus music and sound on visible actions unless silence was asked; render only when the person approves the preview or asks for the file. Routes out to ⟦S0541⟧ (CLI), ⟦S0542⟧ (registry), ⟦S0543⟧ (media), ⟦S0549⟧ (slideshow), ⟦S0547⟧ (Remotion import), ⟦S0537⟧ (Figma).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/hyperframes/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames); CLI run as `npx hyperframes <command>`.
- **Best for:** The starting point for any HyperFrames video work — launch films, explainers, title cards, captions and overlays. Read this before any other skill in the S0531–S0550 family.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0540⟧

## ⟦S0541⟧ heygen-com/hyperframes-cli — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The HyperFrames command-line reference organised by job — scaffold, check, inspect frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, publish, and recover from failures — plus how to read its JSON output.
- **How it looks:** No visuals of its own; what the user sees is the workflow's evidence: lint and check reports with `Fix:` lines, snapshot PNGs of frames under `.hyperframes/artifacts/snapshots/`, a live preview URL to approve, and finally the rendered MP4 whose duration is verified against the composition.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The prescribed loop is sequential: write → `lint` → `check --json` and fix every error → `snapshot` and actually look at the frames (a midpoint of every scene) → `preview` and wait for approval → `render` and verify the file.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Run as `npx hyperframes <command>`; requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg; most commands take `--json`; failures print `✗ …` plus a `Fix:` line and exit non-zero. Command groups: start (`init`, `capture`), read (`info`, `compositions`, `timeline --json`, `docs`), check (`lint` while writing, `check --json` as the gate covering lint/runtime/layout/contrast — contrast failures carry a `suggestedColor`; a 3s+ video with no visible change fails `sweep_static`), look (`snapshot --at/--range/--composition/--zoom/--angle/--against`, `keyframes`, `compare`, `audio`), timeline editing (`move/trim/split/set/duplicate/delete/apply/undo` with `--plan` previews and saved receipts; overlaps refused unless `--overwrite`), render (`--quality draft|looks|delivery`; Docker `--docker --strict`; batch from variables; `cloud render`, `lambda`, `cloudrun` for hosted) and upkeep (`doctor`, `browser ensure`, `upgrade`, `skills`, `usage`, `clean`). A 30s film renders locally in a minute or two. Project history is kept per write and can be undone; `.hyperframes` holds that history and must never be deleted. The skill also notes `events` is telemetry for skills' own scripts — recorded here as part of its documentation.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/hyperframes-cli/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames).
- **Best for:** Operating any HyperFrames project day to day — the companion to ⟦S0540⟧; not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0541⟧

## ⟦S0542⟧ heygen-com/hyperframes-registry — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The catalogue skill for roughly 450 ready-made HyperFrames blocks and components — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, map overlays, 3D and camera moves — installed as editable source. Its rule: start from a registry item before hand-building any named visual.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees depends on the item installed — a camcorder HUD overlay, a glitch or CRT-scanline pass, a chart race, a kinetic title card — but always as ordinary source files inside the project that can be restyled, cut down and re-branded, not a black-box effect.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; each installed block or component carries its own timeline behaviour (the block entries in this range, e.g. ⟦S0531⟧, ⟦S0534⟧, ⟦S0535⟧, ⟦S0538⟧, ⟦S0539⟧, ⟦S0545⟧, ⟦S0550⟧, are registry items).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Find with `npx hyperframes catalog --query "<what the beat should do, in English>" --json` — queries are in English regardless of the video's language; the default `words` tier is local, works offline from the cached manifest and sends nothing; the `--on-device` semantic tier ranks by meaning after a one-time ~33 MB download, which the skill says to offer and let the person decide, never enable silently. Narrow with `--type block|component` and `--tag <tag>`. Install with `npx hyperframes add <name> --json` (needs network even for previously installed items; `add <tag>` installs a whole tag, dependencies first). Blocks land in `compositions/<name>.html` and mount via `data-composition-src`; components land in `compositions/components/<name>.html` and are copied into the scene; per-mount values go in `data-variable-values`; beat-synced blocks take hit times from `npx hyperframes beats --json` minus the mount's `data-start`. The skill also prescribes reporting a search miss back (a pre-filled `feedback --search-miss` line) before hand-building — recorded here as its documented behaviour. Example stock: transitions (`beat-freeze-cut`, `chromatic-radial-split`, `cinematic-zoom`), overlays (`camcorder-hud`, `lt-clean-bar`), titles (`canopy-part-title`, `code-slice-hero`), data (`code-diff`, `bar-chart-race`), 3D/backgrounds (`app-showcase`, `aurora`, `blob`); components include `agent-cursor`, `blur-in`, `caption-clip-wipe`, `camera-shake`, `before-after-wipe`, `grain-overlay`.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/hyperframes-registry/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames).
- **Best for:** Sourcing any named effect for a video before building it by hand; for web work it is a reminder that this bank's block entries are the ready-made starting points.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0542⟧

## ⟦S0543⟧ heygen-com/media-use — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The media-sourcing skill for HyperFrames videos: one command finds or makes music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts and colour grades — via HeyGen or free local tools — and lands everything as local files with a ledger record.
- **How it looks:** The finished video carries real media rather than placeholders: catalog music under the film, a presenter or avatar speaking, searched or generated images, true logo files (never redrawn), and footage that has been properly graded — a dark, flat clip lifted with a real treatment instead of a CSS filter.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; it governs where the media in other skills' frames comes from and how placed audio is mixed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** One verb: `npx hyperframes media-use resolve --type <type> --intent "<what you need>" --project <dir>`, printing `resolved <id> → <path>`; list reusable assets first with `--candidates`. Two routes per need: music — HeyGen catalog of 10k+ tracks vs local MusicGen; images/icons — HeyGen asset search 75k+ vs local FLUX (mflux); voiceover — HeyGen voices/voice cloning vs on-device Kokoro TTS via `npx hyperframes tts` (Python 3.10+, kokoro-onnx); presenter — HeyGen avatar video vs local LTX; transcripts — `npx hyperframes transcribe` (Parakeet or whisper); cutouts — `heygen background-removal` vs `npx hyperframes remove-background`; grades/LUTs — `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (never CSS or SVG stand-ins, never a generated .cube just for exposure/warmth). HeyGen access is via the `heygen` CLI with `heygen auth login --oauth` (free allowance on subscription credits; an API key bills API credits); setup checked with `resolve --doctor`. Cost rule: confirm before a paid call you chose to make (an avatar video counts); a call the person asked for just runs. `--local-only` skips every network provider; `--provider <name>` pins a generator. Media gaps in a build (silent cuts, 10s+ with no music, emoji standing in for icons, placeholder images) are offered once as specific fixes, never added silently.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/media-use/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames); HeyGen developer CLI, Openverse, theSVG.
- **Best for:** Any video needing real music, voice, imagery or grading; the "real assets, ledgered locally, renders never fetch" discipline transfers to web builds too.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0543⟧

## ⟦S0544⟧ heygen-com/motion-doctrine — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The gateway motion law for HyperFrames — read first before composing any animation. It decides what happens at every seam and how every scene performs, so a multi-scene video feels like one continuous camera move instead of a stack of independently animated slides. The technique skills (⟦S0536⟧, ⟦S0546⟧, ⟦S0548⟧) implement it; these rules supersede generic motion guidance.
- **How it looks:** A film with momentum: scenes hand over mid-motion in one dominant direction (the "current", house default LEFT), objects visibly carry across cuts, every movement is caused by the previous one (click → squash → spring → flight → impact → recoil → reveal), and no scene ever sits wobbling in place — something meaningful is always mid-flight, with a held breath of stillness just before each climax.
- **Frame by frame:** At any seam: the outgoing scene is still moving at the cut → the incoming scene enters already mid-flight at matched speed (entry initial velocity ≈ exit final velocity, via mirrored eases) on the same axis and direction → it settles into its performance route (staged reveals paying off on narration beats, a camera travelling with intent, UI life ticking forward, an animated sequence, or cursor-led action) → before the climax beat, motion pauses 0.3–0.75s → the result lands → the exit begins at about 75% of the entry's duration and hands its vector to the next seam.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The Vector Law: (1) axis never trades across a cut; (2) direction never mirrors — on Z, direction is the sign of scale change (growing = push, shrinking = pull), and a receding exit answered by a grow-from-small entry is the most common violation; (3) speed matches via mirrored eases (exit `power4.in` + entry `power4.out`, same distance and duration); (4) phase — the cut lands mid-motion on both sides. Reserved vectors spend meaning: upward = elevation/reveal, Z-forward (zoom-through) = deeper into the same thought, Z-backward (inverse zoom) = arrival, scale-burst = leaving a world; never run consecutive seams in opposing directions. Process: write the vector ledger (`ledger.json`) before authoring → stamp master seams from it (`scripts/seam-stamp.mjs`) → verify with `scripts/seam-gate.mjs` (checks ledger consistency, exit still moving, entry mid-flight, zero overlap — one side visible per frame, the Z-sign rule including the incoming scene's own entrances, and carrier continuity). Performance rules: idle wobble (breathe/float/drift/glow pulse) is banned as sustained motion; causes ignite on the same frame, never "shortly after"; single entries ≤ ~800ms; total stagger ≤ 500ms; `bounce.out` / `elastic.out` forbidden, entry overshoot `back.out(1.4–1.7)` allowed; only 2–3 inter-scene transitions per film, repeated; crossfades are banned outright (no carrier). Parameters live in ⟦S0536⟧ cut-the-curve; render mechanics in ⟦S0548⟧ seam-craft.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/motion-doctrine/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills).
- **Best for:** Planning any multi-scene motion — video first, but the vector law, the one-current rule and the no-idle-wobble ban are directly transferable to long scrolling pages and section choreography.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0544⟧

## ⟦S0545⟧ heygen-com/orbit-card — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A HyperFrames video block: a single feature card with a circular cut-out framing a dot sphere, whose camera path and card curves are exported from an approved Blender rig — the card enters, holds, orbits a full turn around the sphere, and exits.
- **How it looks:** One centred feature card (title, description, one accent colour — default #4cc9ff) with a round window in it showing a sphere of dots; the card drifts with a subtle bob and depth shift during its hold, then swings smoothly around the sphere's centre for a full revolution before leaving left. Motion is smooth and physical because it replays real Blender F-curves sampled at 30fps rather than hand-keyed tweens.
- **Frame by frame:** 10s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → the card enters from the right (0.25–1.80s) → hold phase with a gentle bob and depth drift while the dot sphere keeps its own translation and a constant spin → the orbit: one full turn around the sphere's centre, smoothstepped between 4.97s and 5.97s → exit to the left (7.35–8.55s) → frame clears.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `orbit-card` (`npx hyperframes add orbit-card`); camera path and card F-curves exported from the Blender rig at 30fps and interpolated (`orbit-motion.js`, 59 KB); runtime contract lists the renderer as GSAP with one paused seek-safe timeline; three.js builds and Archivo fonts (Regular/SemiBold) are bundled locally, no external dependencies. Only 4 variables: feature1Title (default "Always in sync", max 28 chars), feature1Desc (default "Changes reach every screen the moment they happen.", max 110 chars), feature1Accent (#4cc9ff), cardOrbitDegrees (360; −36000–36000 — 180° and 720° work without touching keys).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/orbit-card/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A single-feature spotlight beat in a video. The borrowed idea — replaying authored (Blender) camera curves instead of easing by hand — suits premium product-card motion generally.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0545⟧

## ⟦S0546⟧ heygen-com/oversized-cursor — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The house technique for an oversized macOS-style cursor in HyperFrames launch videos: a deliberately huge pointer that travels the frame as a visible protagonist — entering physically, walking the viewer's eye to the next point of interest, clicking to cause the next beat, and leaving physically.
- **How it looks:** A big clean arrow (about 134px tall on a 1920 frame — far larger than a real cursor) with a soft drop shadow, gliding up from below the frame to a button or input, tapping it with a quick squash at its tip while the target itself presses in reaction, then drifting aside while the action it started plays out. Where the brand has a recognisable pointer of its own (a Figma-style coloured multiplayer arrow with name tag, a precision crosshair), that motif replaces the macOS arrow at the same scale.
- **Frame by frame:** Resting pose is off-screen below the frame (top ~115%) → the cursor enters on one continuous decelerating glide (0.4–0.92s, power3.out), usually straight up the y-axis → its tip lands exactly on the target's centre → the click tap: scale compresses to 0.84 in 0.1s (power2.in) pivoting on the tip, then releases over 0.22s (power2.out), while a separate parallel tween presses the target (button scale 0.94 plus press colour/shadow) on the same frame → the click ignites the next beat immediately (menu cascade, typing run, morph, play-state flip) → during beats it doesn't own, the cursor drifts aside over 0.5–0.9s (power2.out), never frozen, never wobbling → exit is physical: either accelerate off the nearest edge (0.5–0.7s, power2.in) or a cut-the-curve handoff — it starts accelerating toward the next scene's first click point in the final ~0.3s before the cut and the next composition continues the same journey at matched velocity.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Size `7cqw` for full-frame scenes (≈134px at 1920), 4.6–5.5cqw inside small mocks, never smaller. One SVG arrow geometry everywhere; two proven fills — white body + black stroke, or black body (#1c1c1c) + white stroke at 1.4px; `filter: drop-shadow(0 4px 6px rgba(0,0,0,.3))`, `pointer-events: none`, `will-change: transform`, z-index above all scene content. Tip-targeting: the hot-spot is the arrow tip, with press scaling pivoting at `transformOrigin: '21% 14%'` (house arrow in a 24-unit viewBox). Click asymmetry is 1:2 (0.1s in / 0.22s out) — that ratio is what reads as a real tap. Entry law: always from off-screen (canonical top 115–120%), never an opacity fade or mask reveal at a resting position; a brand-motif name-tag variant travels as one rigid unit. Pairs with `cursor-click-ripple` / `press-release-spring` components for the target side.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/oversized-cursor/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills); the sustained-motion route that calls for it is in ⟦S0544⟧ motion-doctrine.
- **Best for:** Product-demo and UI-walkthrough videos, scene kickoffs, and rescuing static scenes. The same laws (physical entry, tip pivot, click-causes-effect) are the reference standard for custom cursors on interactive web heroes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0546⟧

## ⟦S0547⟧ heygen-com/remotion-to-hyperframes — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** An import skill for bringing existing video work into HyperFrames and verifying it frame by frame against the original — Remotion first, but also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, p5.js, canvas or plain HTML/CSS animation, and rendered output from Manim, After Effects or Blender.
- **How it looks:** The imported video looks like the original — that is the acceptance test: sampled frames from the port sit next to the original's frames at the same times and must match, with any element that arrives late or recoloured treated as a defect to fix.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; it preserves and verifies other works' motion through three import levels: Native (code translated to HTML + GSAP, every element editable afterwards), Hosted (code kept and driven by HyperFrames time via the seek protocol), Media (rendered to a file and used as a clip — cut and layered only). Code depending on wall-clock time, live physics or the network can only come in as media.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Native path for Remotion: lint the source first with `scripts/lint_source.py` — blockers that do not translate (useState/useReducer, useEffect with dependencies, async calculateMetadata, React UI kits such as MUI/Chakra/Mantine/antd/shadcn/Radix/NextUI) must be hosted or refactored out, never approximated; warnings (@remotion/lambda config, delayRender, useMemo, custom hooks) are dropped and noted. Translation maps each Remotion API to its HyperFrames equivalent (per-topic references: parameters, sequencing, timing, media, transitions, lottie, fonts, limitations), converts times from frames to seconds (`frame / fps`), makes props into `data-composition-variables`, and requires Remotion's `* { box-sizing: border-box; }` rule once in the root or every bordered/padded element grows. Verification: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <t,…> --against <original.mp4>` saves side-by-side frames (sample every scene and both sides of every cut); `scripts/render_diff.sh` scores SSIM per frame and `scripts/frame_strip.sh` shows divergent frames (thresholds per complexity tier in references/eval.md) — render the Remotion side with PNG image format and bt709 colour space or the diff measures the encoders (~0.05 SSIM). Losses are written to `TRANSLATION_NOTES.md`. Hosted path: no requestAnimationFrame loop or timer as the time source, seeded randomness only.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/remotion-to-hyperframes/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames); Remotion, Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, p5.js, Manim, After Effects, Blender named as sources.
- **Best for:** Migrating an existing Remotion (or other-tool) video into the HyperFrames workflow without losing editability; its frame-diff verification discipline is the borrowable part.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0547⟧

## ⟦S0548⟧ heygen-com/seam-craft — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The render-correctness doctrine underneath HyperFrames scene transitions: the prerequisites that make any seam composite correctly on the master timeline — above all the opaque stage-ground rule that prevents a white flash at cuts. It contains no transition catalog (that is ⟦S0536⟧); it is the mechanics layer below all of them.
- **How it looks:** Correctly assembled films show nothing at the seam but the intended motion. The failure it prevents is vivid: on a dark film, every cut flashes white for a few frames, because mid-transition the two scene wrappers' opacities sum to less than 1 and the renderer's default white page shows through the dip.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own. At a boundary the injector: extends the outgoing scene wrapper's duration by the transition length so it holds its final frame → pulls the incoming wrapper's start earlier by the same amount, creating the overlap window → reassigns all clip track indexes as a 0/1 ping-pong so the overlapping wrappers never share a track (higher track composites on top) → stamps the transition's GSAP template into the master timeline at the overlap start, and the master tween is seeked and rendered independently of each scene's own paused timeline.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stage-ground prerequisite: the assembled `index.html` must paint `#root { background: var(--canvas-deep, var(--canvas, #000)) }` — the templates that open an opacity window are named (cut-the-curve's mid-window cut, zoom-through's 0.15 opacity floor, a plain crossfade's power-curve dip). The doctrine covers Tier-B transitions only: pure transform/opacity/filter on the two scene clip wrappers (`#el-<sid>`), no injected overlay DOM, no per-scene cooperation; overlay families (staggered blocks, blinds, light leak, grid dissolve, page burn) and shader transitions are deferred in the source. Template tokens the injector substitutes: `__OLD__` / `__NEW__` (outgoing/incoming wrapper selectors), `__T__` (overlap-start seconds), `__DUR__` (transition duration), `__DX__` (−1920 LEFT / +1920 RIGHT), `__DY__` (−1080 UP / +1080 DOWN), `__ORIGIN_OUT__` / `__ORIGIN_IN__` (transformOrigin pair for squeeze). Verified against the runtime and lint sources in the skill's own notes (prototype render dated 2026-05-31).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/.agents/skills/seam-craft/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames agent skills); seam law in ⟦S0544⟧, technique parameters in ⟦S0536⟧.
- **Best for:** Assembling any multi-scene HyperFrames master timeline, and diagnosing seam flashes. The general lesson — a transition's dip reveals whatever is painted behind it, so paint the stage — applies to web page transitions equally.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0548⟧

## ⟦S0549⟧ heygen-com/slideshow — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A skill for building a HyperFrames slideshow to present live — slides, fragment reveals, branching hotspots and presenter mode with speaker notes — served by `hyperframes present`, or for turning an existing page into such a deck. The deliverable is a running deck, not an MP4.
- **How it looks:** A normal HyperFrames composition presented as a deck: full-screen slides the presenter steps through, builds that reveal in fragments at set moments, clickable hotspot regions that branch into side sequences (Back returns to the slide that held the hotspot), a slide counter, and a separate presenter view with editable notes kept per deck. Audience text is set at least 40px at 1920×1080.
- **Frame by frame:** Navigation seeks, it never plays: pressing Next jumps the timeline straight to the next slide or fragment time and the frame must already look right at that exact instant → fragments are absolute timeline times within their slide's `[start, end]` window, each a hold state that reads correctly when seeked to directly → a hotspot click branches into its sequence, Back returns → media stops on slide exit. Nothing auto-plays or loops as a video would.
- **Mechanism & key values:** A slideshow is a normal composition plus one JSON island written in the HTML near the top of `<body>` (`application/hyperframes-slideshow+json` — never generated by script, `present` reads the file statically) listing `slides` (sceneId matching a scene's `data-composition-id`, presenter-only `notes`, `fragments` as absolute times), `hotspots` (`id`, `label`, `target` = a sequence id, `region` as a percentage box — omit for a full-slide button) and `slideSequences` for branch slides (never in the main slides array). Slides are top-level scenes, not wrapped in a master root composition. Hard rule: never render a deck to MP4 — `render` keeps only the first scene and truncates silently; use `snapshot --at` per slide for stills. `npx hyperframes check --json` validates that every sceneId resolves, every hotspot target exists, fragments sit inside their slide and main-line slides don't overlap. Serve with `npx hyperframes present <project-dir>`; the root `index.html` wraps the player in `<hyperframes-slideshow>` which owns Present (P), Prev/Next, counter, global mute, fullscreen, swipe, hotspots and notes. Porting rules for existing pages: scroll/wheel/camera-driven movement becomes a camera move between focal points (never a visibly scrolling page, no reversals the source doesn't make); evidence images keep aspect with `object-fit: contain` and all four edges checked; hidden stacked slides need opacity 0 + visibility hidden + pointer-events none together.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/skills/slideshow/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames); builds on the ⟦S0540⟧ contract.
- **Best for:** Live presentations and decks (contrast ⟦S0528⟧, which builds standalone HTML slide files for a different stack). Screen-sharing note from the skill: in Google Meet share the audience tab; in Zoom give it its own window, since a fully covered window freezes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0549⟧

## ⟦S0550⟧ heygen-com/wireframe-portal-title — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A HyperFrames video block: extruded wireframe letterforms burst through a portal as the title, then the letters swap into a second phrase with a settle glitch.
- **How it looks:** A headline ("BREAKTHROUGH") built as hollow extruded wireframe letters — real 3D letterforms from the Geist typeface, edges outlined, with depth fog softening the far side — erupts through a chaotic portal burst; afterwards the same wireframe letters rearrange into a replacement phrase ("Lets do this sir!"), auto-sized with whole-word wrapping, landing with a small glitch shudder. A subtitle line ("HYPERFRAMES PORTAL TITLE") and one accent colour (#F5C518) complete the card.
- **Frame by frame:** 8s at 30fps, 1920×1080 → the portal bursts open with tunable chaos (default 1 on a 0–2 scale) and the wireframe title comes through it, depth fog fading its early frames → the title holds → the letter-swap beat (default 1.85s, easing snap default 8 on a 1–8 scale): letters stagger into the replacement phrase, auto-laid-out with whole-word wrapping → each letter settles with a glitch (strength default 0.2) → end state holds the second phrase.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Block `wireframe-portal-title` (`npx hyperframes add wireframe-portal-title`); letterforms are built from the bundled Geist TTF with a TTF loader and polygon offsetting (Clipper), extruded as wireframe geometry; renderer three.js 0.181.2 + GSAP 3.14.2 + GLSL shaders + post-processing, ~350 MB per live instance, one paused seek-safe timeline; GSAP and clipper-lib 6.4.2 load from jsDelivr, fonts (Geist Regular/SemiBold/Bold) are local. 9 variables: title (max 18 chars), replacementPhrase, phraseDuration (1.85s; 0.65–2.9), phraseEasing (8; 1 gentle – 8 snap), settleGlitch (0.2; 0–4), depthFog (true; early fade always on), subtitle (max 48 chars), accent (#F5C518), burstChaos (1; 0–2).
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/registry/blocks/wireframe-portal-title/SKILL.md (HeyGen HyperFrames registry block).
- **Best for:** A bold video title card or section-opener beat. The wireframe-letterform mechanism — type as outlined 3D construction — is a distinctive hero-title treatment worth borrowing for tech-leaning brands.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0550⟧

## ⟦S0551⟧ memex-lab/gemini-tts — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A text-to-speech skill using Google Gemini TTS: one Node script generates voiceovers and narration in 70+ languages from single texts or multi-segment scripts, with 30 prebuilt voices and natural-language control of style, pacing and accent. It is the companion voice skill to ⟦S0552⟧ product-launch-video (same repository), whose pipeline consumes its per-scene audio files.
- **How it looks:** Nothing appears on screen — the output is audio: per-segment MP3 (or WAV) files plus a combined full-audio WAV and a JSON report of each segment's duration. What the listener hears is one consistent voice across all segments, performing with the directed tone (a "vocal smile", a whisper, an excited lift on a tagged word) rather than a flat read.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The process: all segments are combined into a single API request with `[3 second pause]` markers → one continuous audio file comes back → silence gaps are detected and the file is split at silence midpoints into per-segment files → residual silence is trimmed, keeping 0.15s of breathing room → the segment files and durations are reported as JSON.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Script `scripts/generate-tts.mjs`; requires Node.js 18+, ffmpeg, the `@google/genai` package and a `GEMINI_API_KEY`. Models: `gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview` (default; most controllable, 200+ audio tags), `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` (fast), `gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts` (highest quality). Voice consistency is engineered, not assumed: because separate requests don't guarantee the same voice, all segments go in ONE call; splitting uses ffmpeg `silencedetect` with adaptive thresholds (starting at noise=-35dB, d=1.5s, progressively relaxed; if a threshold jump yields too few or too many gaps, the audio is regenerated with faster pacing to sharpen the pauses and detection retries). Flags: `--voice` (default Kore), `--director-notes` (style/pacing/accent guidance — beats vague directions with specific ones, e.g. a named place for an accent), `--retries` (3), `--trim` on by default, `--format mp3|wav`. Inline audio tags override locally: `[whispers]`, `[shouting]`, `[excited]`, `[serious]`, `[short pause]`, `[laughs]`, `[very fast]`, `[very slow]`, `[sarcastic]`, creative tags like `[like dracula]` also work. The 30 voices are tabled with gender/character/pitch in the skill (e.g. Kore — female, firm, middle; Puck — male, upbeat, middle; Zephyr — female, bright, higher). Exit codes 0–4 distinguish success, missing args, API failure, ffmpeg failure and file I/O failure.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/memex-lab/product-launch-video-skill/blob/main/skills/gemini-tts/SKILL.md (memex-lab product-launch-video-skill repo); Google Gemini TTS API; companion skill ⟦S0552⟧ in the same repo.
- **Best for:** Voiceover and narration generation for launch videos, explainers and podcasts — the audio half of the ⟦S0552⟧ pipeline.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0551⟧

## ⟦S0552⟧ memex-lab/product-launch-video — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** A complete process skill for designing and building cinematic product launch videos in Remotion (React): gated phases from product understanding and aesthetic direction through a mandatory storyboard contract, voiceover, build standards (motion, choreography, composition, lighting, typography), pre-render review and delivery.
- **How it looks:** A launch film that feels like a product commercial: the product appears within the first 3 seconds; scenes are layered like posters — a drifting gradient or photo background, structural pattern, glow orbs and particles for depth, the content itself entering with weight (opacity + slide + blur sharpening together, springs with overshoot at hero moments), light sweeps polishing elements after they settle, and a whisper of film grain (opacity 0.03–0.05) over everything. Pacing breathes: fast → slow → fast → slow → fast → hold, never one tempo.
- **Frame by frame:** Per the narrative arc (30s spot): Hook (3–5s) poses the problem or strikes visually → Reveal (5–8s) brings the product in as the hero moment (e.g. headline springs from 30px below, scale 0.9→1, blur 8→0 over 0.5s, a diagonal light beam sweeping across at 0.3s delay) → Showcase (12–18s) gives 2–4 features one beat each, no two consecutive scenes sharing a layout or motion pattern, groups choreographed (cards cascade with ~150ms stagger, translateX(40)→0, a 3° rotation settling to 0°) → Climax (3–5s) is the full-screen wow moment, preceded by a breath of stillness → Close (3–5s) lands logo, tagline and CTA; every scene exit is compound (opacity + scale to ~0.96 + blur to ~6px over the last 0.4s), and momentum transfers — an element exiting rightward is answered by the next entering from the right.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Remotion discipline: ALL animation derives from `useCurrentFrame()` — CSS transitions/animations and Tailwind animation classes are forbidden; think in seconds, code in frames (`start * fps`). The storyboard is a contract file, `storyboard.json` (meta with palette by role — background/surface/primary/muted/accent/highlight — fonts, narrative structure; a `voice` profile; scenes with per-element animation mechanics spelled out so two developers would build the same thing). Duration allocations: 15s teaser ≈ 20/50/30 (hook/glimpses/logo); 30s ≈ 15/15/45/15/10; 60s ≈ 8/8/42 features/17 social proof/12 climax/13 close; 90s ≈ 9/8/44/17/11/11. Voiceover is the timing backbone at ~2.5 words/sec; per-scene audio is generated before code (⟦S0551⟧ is the companion TTS skill) and scene durations are corrected to the real audio. Motion density standard (minimum bar): ≥3 simultaneous motion properties per entrance, ≥3 independent layers per scene from a 7-layer stack, ≥1 continuous ambient motion, ≥1 timing-responsive light effect, compound exits only, never linear easing. Numbers: secondary fades 300–500ms, primary springs 400–600ms, stagger 80–200ms, scene transitions 200–400ms (fast 0.2–0.3s / medium 0.3–0.5s / slow cinematic 0.5–0.8s), typewriter 30–60 chars/sec, text minimums 32px headlines / 20px body. Easing Béziers: snappy (0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), smooth glide (0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1), dramatic (0.7, 0, 0.3, 1), gentle drift (0.4, 0, 0.6, 1). Spring configs: precise (damping 200, stiffness 300, mass 1), gentle bounce (10/200/0.5), heavy premium (200/80/2), elastic playful (6/180/0.4); utility defaults fadeIn 0.4s expo-out, springPop damping 12 / stiffness 200 / mass 0.5. Ten named choreography patterns for groups: infinite marquee, counter-scroll lanes, staggered cascade, radial burst, orbital float, grid reveal, perspective wall, fan/spread, converge-to-hero, parallax layers. Aesthetic bans ("AI slop"): purple gradients on dark, Inter/Roboto/system display fonts, uniform timing, emoji icons, flat even lighting, identical card grids, bare fade-in text. Render: `npx remotion render [id] out/video.mp4 --codec h264 --crf 18`; stills audited per scene before the full render.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/memex-lab/product-launch-video-skill/blob/main/skills/product-launch-video/SKILL.md (memex-lab); Remotion; reference admirations it names: Apple keynote style, Nike product films, Stripe developer aesthetic, Notion, luxury watch commercials. Companion: ⟦S0551⟧ gemini-tts (same repo).
- **Best for:** Product launch, promo, demo and brand-reveal videos. Beyond video, its motion-density standard, layer stack and choreography table are a portable quality bar for judging homepage hero and showcase sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0552⟧

## ⟦S0553⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-best-practices — UI Skills — video & motion graphics (HeyGen HyperFrames, Remotion, ...)
- **What it is:** The official Remotion router skill: a short dispatcher that detects what a Remotion task needs and loads the right sub-reference (creating, markup, maps, multimedia, interactivity, Studio, rendering, captions, SaaS, docs, upgrading), plus a few standing behaviour rules.
- **How it looks:** What the user sees is Remotion Studio: an interactive browser preview of the composition, opened as soon as the project can run and kept open while work continues so they can watch progress and steer — not a rendered file, unless they explicitly ask for one.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; it routes to the references that govern the motion and markup of actual Remotion compositions.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Standing rules: preserve user changes (a surprising edit made outside the conversation is intentional — don't overwrite it, ask); creating a video, a new project, markup, maps, multimedia, interactivity, captions, SaaS or upgrade work each load their named `REFERENCE.md` (remotion-create, remotion-markup, remotion-maps, remotion-multimedia, remotion-interactivity, remotion-studio, remotion-render, remotion-captions, remotion-saas, remotion-docs, remotion-upgrade). Preview rule: don't render by default — "make a video" means start Studio (`npx remotion studio`, or `--no-open` plus opening the exact printed URL in an in-app browser, compositions reachable at `/[composition-id]`) and verify Studio and the composition preview actually load; render only on an explicit ask ("Render the video", "Export", "Give me the MP4") via `npx remotion render`. Studio supports WebMCP tools, per the skill's note.
- **Reference / source:** https://github.com/remotion-dev/skills/blob/main/skills/remotion-best-practices/SKILL.md (Remotion's official skills repo).
- **Best for:** The entry point for any Remotion work; pair with ⟦S0552⟧ when the job is specifically a product launch video, and with ⟦S0547⟧ when the job is moving Remotion work into HyperFrames instead.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0553⟧
# Skills chunk S0554–S0567 — Part 14: video & motion graphics (Remotion family, two product-film skills, HyperFrames gateway)

Family note: S0554–S0564 are eleven sibling sub-skills of one Remotion skill set (remotion-dev/skills) — not duplicates: each covers a different job in the same video pipeline (captions, project creation, docs lookup, Studio interactivity, maps, markup/animation/effects, media metadata, rendering, SaaS apps, Studio preview, upgrades). S0559 (remotion-markup) is the family's core animation/effects volume and cross-refers to S0554, S0557 and S0558. S0565 and S0566 are two independent third-party product-film systems that both sit on top of Remotion. S0567 is the gateway skill of a different framework entirely (HeyGen HyperFrames, HTML→video).

## ⟦S0554⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-captions — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** The Remotion workflow for speech captions in code-rendered video: transcribe audio/video to word-timed caption data, display the captions inside the video, or import an existing .srt file.
- **How it looks:** Subtitle text sitting over the video frame, timed word by word to the speech. In the worked example (1920×1080 composition) the caption block is 900px wide, centred (510px from the left edge) and 120px up from the bottom of the frame, rendered by the "Basic Captions" element fetched unchanged from remotion.dev; alternative caption elements exist on the Remotion elements site, but Basic Captions is the default.
- **Frame by frame:** Playback → each caption word/page appears at its recorded startMs and clears at its endMs, so text tracks the voice exactly; a caption carrying `pageBreakAfter: true` ends the current caption page and the next word starts a fresh page. Captions live inside the same `<Sequence>`/`<TransitionSeries.Sequence>` as their clip, sharing its `trimBefore`, `durationInFrames` and `playbackRate`, so trimming or re-speeding the clip moves picture and words together.
- **Mechanism & key values:** All captions are JSON in the `Caption` type {text, startMs, endMs, timestampMs, confidence, pageBreakAfter?}; the `text` field is whitespace-sensitive — a leading space is kept before each word. Transcription runs locally on GPU via `@remotion/whisper-webgpu` `transcribe()` (audio first decoded to a 16kHz mono waveform; model `small.en` recommended for English, multilingual `small` + explicit `language` otherwise; no automatic language detection; needs a compatible GPU, no ONNX on Linux arm64). SRT import via `parseSrt()` from `@remotion/captions`. Timestamps stay relative to the start of each original source file — never flattened into composition-wide times.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub (github.com/remotion-dev/skills); remotion.dev caption docs and the Basic Captions element page.
- **Best for:** Caption/subtitle layers on any Remotion-produced video (launch films, explainers, social cuts); accessibility. Not a web-page section technique — video deliverables only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0554⟧

## ⟦S0555⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-create — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** How to start a new Remotion video project: scaffold it, open the Studio preview before writing the composition, then design the video following the family's layout and interactivity rules.
- **How it looks:** Process skill — the visible output is a Remotion Studio preview of a video frame. Its one layout reference gives video-first framing numbers: for a 1080px-wide composition keep key text at least 80px from the sides and 100px from the top and bottom; rough minimum type sizes at that width are 84px for a main headline and 44px for important supporting text, scaled with composition width; one focal thing per scene.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. (Animation inside the video is covered by ⟦S0559⟧; this skill only routes to it.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scaffold with `npx create-video@latest --yes --blank --no-tailwind` (into the current folder if empty, a named subfolder if not); open Remotion Studio immediately after install and keep it open while building. Tailwind note: never use `transition-*`/`animate-*` classes in Remotion — animate with `useCurrentFrame()`.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub.
- **Best for:** Starting any new Remotion video (pairs with ⟦S0563⟧ remotion-studio and ⟦S0559⟧ remotion-markup). No trade-website use.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0555⟧

## ⟦S0556⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-docs — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** A lookup recipe: how to search the current Remotion documentation instead of relying on memorised API knowledge.
- **How it looks:** No visual output — a documentation-retrieval workflow for whoever is writing Remotion code.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four steps: (1) query the Remotion docs' Algolia search index (the skill text embeds a public search-only API key and application id for that index — an instruction to call a remote search API, recorded here as fact, not executed); (2) pick the most relevant result URLs; (3) fetch each page as Markdown by appending `.md` to the docs URL (e.g. remotion.dev/docs/use-video-config.md); (4) implement from the fetched current docs.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; remotion.dev documentation.
- **Best for:** Any Remotion coding task where an API detail may have changed. Support skill only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0556⟧

## ⟦S0557⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-interactivity — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** The structuring rules that make Remotion markup editable in Remotion Studio: scenes are written so a person can select, move, trim, restyle and keyframe each element in the Studio UI and have the edits written back into the source code.
- **How it looks:** In the rendered video, nothing distinctive — the difference is in the Studio timeline, where every meaningful element appears as a named, independently editable item with its own controls and keyframe diamonds instead of one opaque block of code.
- **Frame by frame:** Animation is written as inline `interpolate()` calls on the property itself, so Studio can keyframe it. Worked values from the skill: a card's scale runs 0→1 over the first second (`[0, fps]`) with `Easing.spring({damping: 200})` and `output: 'perceptual-scale'`; rotation 0deg→20deg across 1s on the same spring; a translate of "0px 0px"→"0px 120px" across the last 30 frames. SVG paths morph via inline `interpolatePaths()` — the example morphs a triangle through three shapes at frames 0/30/60 with `Easing.bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1)`, clamped both sides; `strokeDasharray`/`strokeDashoffset` evolve paths. All ranges/easings/outputs hardcoded inline; only the input range may use `fps`, `durationInFrames`, `width`, `height` from `useVideoConfig()`.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Build elements with `Interactive.*` wrappers (every HTML/SVG element except `<Img>`, already interactive) and `Interactive.create()` for custom components; per-instance schema field types include string, number (keyframable), boolean, color, enum, array, asset, font-family, font-weight, translate/scale/rotation-css/rotation-degrees/transform-origin, uv-coordinate, svg-path, remotion-captions, hidden — each needs a `default` and a `description`. Styles must be plain inline objects (no constants, spreads or math); text stays inline in the element; use the individual CSS `scale`/`translate`/`rotate` properties, never `transform`; composition metadata (`id`, width, height, fps, durationInFrames, defaultProps) inline as literals on `<Composition>`/`<Still>`.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; remotion.dev InteractivitySchema docs.
- **Best for:** Any Remotion video a client or editor will retime/restyle in Studio (templates, product films, caption-driven edits). Companion to ⟦S0559⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0557⟧

## ⟦S0558⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-maps — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** A router skill for animated maps in Remotion video: it names five map techniques and says to load exactly one technique file for the shot you intend. The bank text contains only this menu — the technique files themselves are not reproduced in WEB-SKILLS.md, so no per-technique parameters are recorded here.
- **How it looks:** Depends on the technique chosen: a satellite image mounted in an `<Img>` with animation drawn on top (static map); a Mapbox map that can show a round globe zoomed out and 3D buildings such as the Eiffel Tower; a MapLibre map (no 3D buildings); a MapTiler map with annotations drawn over borders, rivers and labels; or a CesiumJS terrain flythrough with a "flight simulator" perspective.
- **Frame by frame:** Not specified in the bank text (the motion lives in the per-technique files, which are not included).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Static map — needs a grabbed satellite image, animation layered over it. Mapbox — needs a Mapbox API key, nicest default styles. MapLibre — no API key, fully free. MapTiler — MapTiler tiles + annotation overlays. CesiumJS — 3D terrain flythroughs. Each technique directory is self-contained and removable.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; Mapbox, MapLibre, MapTiler, CesiumJS named as the underlying services.
- **Best for:** Map shots inside videos (service-area fly-ins, route stories). For trade sites, a service-area map moment in a promo video — not a page-section technique.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0558⟧

## ⟦S0559⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-markup — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** The core Remotion authoring volume (~107 KB, 31 reference files): how to write the React markup of a video — frame-driven animation, media, timing/sequencing, transitions, a large built-in effects library, 3D, audio and its visualisation, captions routing, fonts, text measurement and highlights, voiceover, and Studio-editable structure.
- **How it looks:** Any video frame built from code: titles fading/scaling in on springs, footage trimmed and layered with captions locked to it, scenes crossfading or wiping into each other, light-leak flares washing over a cut, images with vignette/halftone/blur treatments, spectrum bars or a smooth waveform line pulsing with the soundtrack, hand-drawn-style highlight strokes sweeping behind key words, 3D objects rotating inside the frame.
- **Frame by frame:** Everything is a pure function of the frame counter — CSS transitions/animations and Tailwind animation classes do not render correctly and must be rebuilt on `useCurrentFrame()` + `interpolate()`. Canonical fade: opacity 0→1 over `[0, 2 * fps]` with `Easing.bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`, clamped. Scale animations add `output: 'perceptual-scale'`. Timing model: `from` positions an item, `trimBefore` sets its first internal frame, `durationInFrames` selects its range, `playbackRate` stretches it (the item occupies durationInFrames / playbackRate frames in the parent), `loop` repeats the range. Scene changes: `<TransitionSeries>` transitions (fade, slide with from-left/right/top/bottom, wipe, flip, clockWipe) shorten the timeline by their length — two 60-frame scenes + a 15-frame transition = 105 frames total; overlays (e.g. a light leak) sit on the cut without shortening it. Light leak: `progress` 0→1 across the overlay — the leak reveals during the first half and retracts during the second (options: seed, hueShift 0–360 where 0 = yellow-orange, 120 = green, 240 = blue). Motion blur: `<HtmlInCanvasMotionBlur>` averages fractional-frame captures — shutterAngle default 180 (range 0–360), samples default 8 (integer 1–64). Text annotations (`@remotion/rough-notation` Highlight/Circle/Underline/StrikeThrough/CrossedOff/Box/Bracket) draw on as `progress` interpolates 0→1 (example: frames 15→40). Audio visualisation: spectrum bars from `visualizeAudio()` (numberOfSamples a power of 2 — 32…1024; values 0–1, bass at the left), waveform via `visualizeAudioWaveform()` + `createSmoothSvgPath()`; bass-reactive scale = 1 + bassIntensity × 0.5.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Media via `<Video>`/`<Audio>` from `@remotion/media`, `<CanvasImage>`, `<AnimatedImage>`; assets in `public/` via `staticFile()`. Effects are functions in an `effects` array on media/shape components (or on an `<HtmlInCanvas>` wrapper for plain HTML — needs Chrome 149+ with the canvas-draw-element flag): ~90 built-ins from `@remotion/effects` across colour/tone (brightness, curves, levels, lut, duotone, thermalVision…), blur/trails (blur, lightTrail, progressive blurs, zoomBlur), lighting (glow, lightLeak, shine, starburst, vignette), distortion (fisheye, barrelDistortion, chromaticAberration, wave, mirror…), textures (halftone, paper, noise, scanlines, dotGrid…), edges (outline, tear, roughenEdges) and pixel/transition effects (pixelate, pixelDissolve, venetianBlinds, evolve); custom effects via `createEffect()` (2d / webgl2 / webgpu backends). Cropping via cropLeft/Right/Top/Bottom ratios 0–1 (never combined with clipPath). 3D via `@remotion/three` `<ThreeCanvas>` — rotation driven by frame (example 0.02 rad/frame), `useFrame()` forbidden. Audio: volume 0–1, keyframable; `toneFrequency` 0.01–2 (pitch, render-only); silence detection via FFmpeg loudnorm → silencedetect (d = 0.5s default). Voiceover: ElevenLabs TTS per scene (model eleven_multilingual_v2; stability 0.5, similarity_boost 0.75, style 0.3) with `calculateMetadata()` sizing the composition to the audio. `calculateMetadata` also sets dynamic duration/dimensions/props. Text fitting via `measureText()`/`fitText()`/`fillTextBox()` from `@remotion/layout-utils` after fonts load. Bundled stock SFX URLs on remotion.media (whoosh, whip, page-turn, shutter, ding…) are listed for direct use.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; remotion.dev docs throughout; ElevenLabs named for voiceover.
- **Best for:** The reference volume behind any Remotion video build — promos, explainers, captioned social cuts, product films (⟦S0565⟧/⟦S0566⟧ build on it). Not a web-page section library.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0559⟧

## ⟦S0560⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-multimedia — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** Three tiny Mediabunny helper recipes for reading media metadata — audio duration, video duration, video dimensions — used to size Remotion compositions to their source media.
- **How it looks:** No visual output; the numbers it returns (e.g. duration 10.5s, 1920×1080) drive composition length and canvas size elsewhere.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Mediabunny `Input` with `ALL_FORMATS`; source chosen by environment — `UrlSource` for URLs, `FilePathSource` on disk in Node/Bun (call `input.dispose()` after), `BlobSource` for browser `File` objects; durations from `input.computeDuration()` (seconds), dimensions from the primary video track's `displayWidth`/`displayHeight`; wrap local files in Remotion's `staticFile()`.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; Mediabunny (mediabunny.dev).
- **Best for:** Support step in Remotion builds — pairs with `calculateMetadata` in ⟦S0559⟧ so a composition matches its footage exactly.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0560⟧

## ⟦S0561⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-render — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** How to export a finished Remotion composition: video renders, stills, frame batches, and transparent-background renders.
- **How it looks:** The deliverable files themselves — an .mp4/.mov/.webm video, a single still frame, or a set of frame images (e.g. frames 0, 30, 90 exported as PNGs in one call).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; rendering is a batch export of the timeline built by the other skills.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `npx remotion render` for video, `npx remotion still` for one frame, `render --frames=0,30,90 --image-format=png` for frame sets. Transparent video two ways: ProRes for editing software (`--image-format=png --pixel-format=yuva444p10le --codec=prores --prores-profile=4444`, .mov) or VP9 WebM for browsers (`--pixel-format=yuva420p --codec=vp9`); the same settings can be made a composition's defaults via `calculateMetadata` (defaultCodec / defaultVideoImageFormat / defaultPixelFormat / defaultProResProfile).
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; remotion.dev CLI render/still docs.
- **Best for:** Final delivery step of any Remotion video; transparent renders for overlaying motion graphics onto footage or pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0561⟧

## ⟦S0562⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-saas — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** Guidance for building a product/app around Remotion: pick a template/framework, embed the interactive `<Player>` preview, and choose a programmatic rendering backend.
- **How it looks:** A web app with a form or editor on one side and a live, playable Remotion video preview (the `<Player>` component with controls) on the other; finished videos are rendered on demand by the chosen backend.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; the video content itself comes from ⟦S0559⟧.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Templates: Next.js (Lambda default), Vercel Sandbox, React Router 7 (Lambda default), Express render server (Node default) — clone or use as reference. Player example: 1920×1080, 120 frames at 30 fps, `controls`. Rendering options compared: plain Node APIs (long-running server + headless browser), Remotion Lambda on AWS (described as fastest and most scalable), Vercel Sandbox, GitHub Actions and Azure/Cloudflare only when asked. The Lambda section is a 9-step setup walkthrough that includes creating AWS IAM roles/keys and storing them in a project `.env` — recorded here as the skill's stated procedure; nothing was executed.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub; the four template repos and remotion.dev SSR/Lambda docs.
- **Best for:** Anyone productising video generation (template-video SaaS, in-app editors). Not relevant to trade homepage sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S0562⟧

## ⟦S0563⟧ remotion-dev/remotion-studio — Part 14 — UI Skills — video & motion graphics
- **What it is:** One rule plus flags: start Remotion Studio and open its preview as soon as a project can run, before building or editing the composition, and keep it open so the user watches changes and steers.
- **How it looks:** The Studio browser UI — timeline, canvas preview and props editors — open alongside the code work.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `npx remotion studio` (opens the browser; in clients with an in-app browser use `--no-open` and open the exact printed URL, verifying Studio and then the composition preview load). Flags: `--log=<error|warn|info|verbose>`, `--port=<number>`, `--force-new` for a second instance on the same project/port. If Studio is already running, the command prints the URL and exits.
- **Reference / source:** remotion-dev/skills on GitHub.
- **Best for:** Every Remotion session (companion to ⟦S0555⟧/⟦S0557⟧).
