- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit method: list every form field, storage key, cookie and analytics property → name the feature that reads it → remove or anonymise anything with no consumer; prefer anonymous aggregates, else pseudonymous IDs (example: SHA-256 hash of the email, sliced to 16 chars) in analytics/logs — never raw email/name/phone or full query strings; client storage entries carry `{ value, purpose, expiresAt }` with a defined retention window (example: one week, 7×24×60×60×1000 ms) and are cleared on logout; store a bare user ID, never a whole profile object. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/privacy/data-minimisation ; standards named: GDPR Article 5, ICO data minimisation guidance.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of quote/lead forms and any analytics wiring — directly relevant to trades contact forms, which habitually over-ask; keep the form to what the callback actually needs.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1004⟧

## ⟦S1005⟧ dead-end-pages — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO QA rule requiring every page to link onward — no page may be a dead end with zero outgoing internal links in its body content.
- **How it looks:** Article and service pages carry contextual links inside the prose (a roofing page linking its guttering and repairs pages mid-sentence) and, where inline links don't fit, a closing "Related" / "See also" block of linked cards or list items. Nothing else visual changes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Count `<a href>` to same-domain pages inside `<main>`/`<article>` only — templated header/footer/nav links don't count; flag any page with fewer than 2; fix is 2–3 (fix steps say 2–5) topically related internal links per page, inline preferred, related-content section as fallback; verify by re-crawl (Screaming Frog / Sitebulb) after deployment. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/dead-end-pages ; standards named: Google Search Central links best practices and crawling/indexing docs.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of inner pages and service/town pages in a multi-page build — each service page should hand the visitor (and crawler) to sibling services and the contact page. Little to do on a single homepage.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1005⟧

## ⟦S1006⟧ debounce-throttle — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring high-frequency event handlers (scroll, resize, input, mousemove) to be rate-limited — debounced or throttled — so they don't fire hundreds of times per second.
- **How it looks:** No visual system of its own. The visitor feels it as smoothness: typing in a search or quote field doesn't stutter or spam requests, scrolling stays fluid, the interface keeps up with the pointer instead of janking behind it (INP protection).
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction-timed, not animated: keystrokes fire continuously → a debounced handler waits until typing pauses (300 ms in the search example) → runs once. Scroll fires continuously → a throttled handler runs at most once per interval (100 ms example) throughout the gesture.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Debounce = run after activity stops (search input, form validation), prescribed delays 150–300 ms for user input; throttle = cap the rate (scroll, resize), prescribed 100 ms; reference implementations included (~10-line debounce/throttle helpers); React pattern memoises the debounced function and cancels pending calls on unmount; VueUse `useDebounceFn(…, 300)`; anti-patterns named: creating a new debounced function per render, debouncing inside the handler, never cleaning up. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/debounce-throttle ; standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of any hand-written scroll/pointer/resize machinery — parallax drivers, scroll progress, sticky headers, live form validation on quote forms. Directly relevant to animation-heavy homepage builds where scroll handlers multiply.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1006⟧

## ⟦S1007⟧ decorative-elements — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring purely decorative visuals (divider flourishes, background patterns, bullet icons) to be hidden from assistive technology so screen readers don't announce noise.
- **How it looks:** Identical on screen either way — the ornament still shows. The difference is purely in the screen-reader output: silence where it would otherwise read out "image, decorative-border dot png, image, bullet" between real content.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Decorative `<img>` gets `alt=""` (empty — not `alt="image"`, not missing); decorative SVG and icon fonts get `aria-hidden="true"`; purely decorative visuals preferably delivered as CSS `background-image` (never announced); `role="presentation"` strips semantics from layout tables/lists; the rule's own safe pattern, `<img src="/divider.svg" alt="" aria-hidden="true">`, is explicitly a no-finding, and decorative assets must not be flagged for performance/alt findings without a concrete defect. Charts, product photos and meaning-bearing icons are informative and stay described. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/decorative-elements ; standards named: WAI-ARIA 1.2, MDN ARIA.
- **Best for:** QA sweep on ornament-heavy designs — SVG line-work, texture dividers, icon rows beside text (the icon hides, the text speaks). Frequently triggered on trades homepages with decorative roofline/house illustrations.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1007⟧

## ⟦S1008⟧ defer-async — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring scripts to load with `defer`, `async` or `type="module"` so JavaScript never blocks HTML parsing.
- **How it looks:** No visual system of its own. The visitor sees content render immediately and continuously; the failure it prevents is a frozen blank page while a head script downloads and runs on a slow connection.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The timing diagrams are the content: a plain head script halts parsing for its whole download+execute; `async` downloads in parallel and interrupts parsing the moment it lands; `defer` downloads in parallel and executes once, after parsing completes; `type="module"` behaves as defer with import/export enabled.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Decision order — uses import/export → `type="module"`; depends on DOM or other scripts → `defer` (executes in document order); fully independent (analytics, chat widgets) → `async`; must run before paint (theme anti-flicker) → the one sanctioned inline exception; legacy pairing `<script type="module">` + `<script nomodule>`; dynamic `import()` for on-demand code; scripts found at the end of `<body>` should move to head with defer. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/defer-async ; standards named: MDN HTML, WHATWG HTML Living Standard.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of the page shell on every build; in a single-file homepage, the check that the one big script block sits where it can't block first paint.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1008⟧

## ⟦S1009⟧ definition-list — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule on definition-list structure: a `<dl>` may contain only `<dt>`, `<dd>` (or `<script>`/`<template>`, and HTML5 `<div>` wrappers around term/description pairs) — nothing else.
- **How it looks:** No visual change; a spec or glossary list looks the same. What changes is the announced structure: the screen reader can group each term with its definition(s) and offer list navigation, instead of losing the relationship.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Headings and paragraphs must live outside the `<dl>`; every `<dt>` should have at least one associated `<dd>`; `<div class="row">` wrapping a dt/dd pair is the valid way to get grid/flex styling hooks; validated with the W3C Markup Validation Service. Companion rule ⟦S1014⟧ covers the reverse direction (dt/dd must be inside a dl); together they mirror axe-core's `definition-list` and `dlitem` checks. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/definition-list ; references named: MDN `<dl>` element, WCAG overview.
- **Best for:** QA sweep wherever a build uses definition lists — spec tables, glossary blocks, key/value detail lists on service pages (licence numbers, coverage figures, warranty terms).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1009⟧

## ⟦S1010⟧ dependency-audit — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A security QA rule requiring dependencies to be scanned continuously for known vulnerabilities (CVEs), with critical/high findings treated as release blockers.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on any page. Its visible artifacts are in the pipeline: an audit report table (severity, package, patched-in version, dependency path) and CI runs that go red on high/critical findings.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `pnpm audit` / `npm audit` (severity filter `--audit-level=high`; `--json` for scripting); severity ladder — Critical: block deployment, fix immediately · High: fix before next release · Moderate: current sprint · Low: next update cycle; fixes by upgrade, `pnpm.overrides` for transitive pins (examples: lodash `>=4.17.21`, semver `>=7.5.2`), or `audit --fix`; CI gate on push/PR plus a weekly scheduled run (example cron Mondays 09:00 UTC); Dependabot weekly grouped minor/patch PRs, majors ignored for manual review; Snyk for reachability + licence checks; lockfile committed and installed `--frozen-lockfile`. Incidents motivating it: Log4Shell (2021), node-ipc (2022). Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/dependency-audit .
- **Best for:** Project-level QA for any build with a package.json — a pre-deployment gate, not a page check. Marginal for a single static HTML file with no dependencies.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1010⟧

## ⟦S1011⟧ dimensions — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring explicit `width` and `height` attributes on every content `<img>`, matching the image's intrinsic dimensions, so the browser reserves the right space before the file downloads.
- **How it looks:** Image slots sit at their final size from first paint — a photo rectangle of the correct proportions that the picture fills when it arrives. The failure it prevents: a 0-height gap that suddenly expands and shoves all the text below it down the page as each image loads.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own. Sequence with the rule: parse → browser derives the aspect ratio from the attributes and reserves the box → image loads into it → nothing else moves. Without it: parse → 0-height placeholder → load → layout jump (see ⟦S1000⟧, the CLS rule this one feeds).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Attributes carry the intrinsic ratio (examples: `width="600" height="400"`, picture fallback `width="1600" height="900"`) and sit on the `<img>`, never on `<source>`; CSS pairs `max-width: 100%; height: auto` so the reserved ratio scales fluidly; browsers derive `aspect-ratio` from the attributes pre-CSS (Chrome 79+, Firefox 71+, Safari 15+); dynamic images use a known-ratio map (`16/9 → 1600×900`, `4/3 → 800×600`, `1/1 → 800×800`) or a container with `aspect-ratio` (hero example 21/9); CLS context thresholds 0.1 / 0.25; explicit exemptions — SVG icons under 32 px, decorative micro-ornaments with stable CSS sizing, CSS background images, images in fixed-height overflow-hidden containers. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/dimensions .
- **Best for:** QA sweep on every image-bearing section — hero, project gallery, before/after pairs, team and review avatars. One of the highest-value checks for a photo-led trades homepage.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1011⟧

## ⟦S1012⟧ direction-attribute — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring correct text direction markup — `dir="rtl"` for right-to-left languages, `dir="auto"` and bidi isolation for mixed-direction user content — so RTL text and mirrored UI render in reading order.
- **How it looks:** On an Arabic/Hebrew/Persian/Urdu page the whole layout mirrors: text right-aligned and reading right-to-left, navigation order reversed, sidebar on the opposite side, directional icons (arrows, breadcrumb separators) flipped; phone numbers and emails inside RTL prose stay left-to-right and readable instead of scrambling.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Direction is set at parse/render; the rule's JS pattern re-sets the `dir` attribute on `<html>` at language switch, and the layout mirrors in one step.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `dir` on `<html>` paired with `lang` (RTL codes: ar, he, fa, ur, yi); `dir="auto"` lets the first strongly directional character decide (detection regex covers U+0590–U+083F, U+08A0–U+08FF, U+FB1D–U+FDFF, U+FE70–U+FEFF); `<bdi>` isolates inline mixed-direction names/handles; CSS logical properties preferred over physical ones (`margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end`, `text-align: start`, `border-inline-start`); directional icons flipped with `transform: scaleX(-1)` under `[dir="rtl"]`; flex/grid either follow direction automatically or get explicit row-reverse/column swaps. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/direction-attribute .
- **Best for:** QA sweep only for multilingual or user-generated-content builds; for the current English-only trades sites it is a dormant check — relevant the moment a testimonials feed or a second language appears.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1012⟧

## ⟦S1013⟧ disclaimers — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO/trust QA rule requiring visible, specific disclaimers on sensitive (YMYL) content — medical, financial, legal, safety — and FTC-style disclosure before the first affiliate link.
- **How it looks:** A visually distinct boxed note (the rule's markup: an `<aside class="disclaimer" role="note">`, set apart by background/italics) sitting at the top of the article, before the advice begins — not buried in the footer, not in tiny type, not hidden behind a "read more" toggle. Affiliate posts open with an italic disclosure paragraph above the headline content.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Placement law: before the relevant content, prominent, linked to a fuller policy page when the inline note is insufficient; prescribed copy patterns per category — medical ("for informational purposes only… consult a qualified healthcare professional"), financial ("not financial advice. Past performance is not indicative of future results"), legal ("general in nature… consult a licensed attorney"), affiliate ("contains affiliate links… we may earn a commission… at no extra cost to you"), plus AI-generated content in the required-disclaimer table; check procedure scans for YMYL topic keywords, then verifies a disclaimer near the top of `<main>`/`<article>` and disclosure before the first referral `<a>`. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/disclaimers ; standards named: Google Search Quality Rater Guidelines, FTC .com Disclosures.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of advice-style content — cost guides, finance explainers, safety guidance on trades sites (e.g. a pricing/financing page needs the financial pattern). Not a homepage-section concern.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1013⟧

## ⟦S1014⟧ dlitem — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring every `<dt>` and `<dd>` to be a child of a `<dl>` — orphaned definition items outside a list are invalid and lose their term↔definition association. Companion to ⟦S1009⟧, which governs what may go inside the `<dl>`; this one governs the items' parentage (the axe-core `dlitem` rule).
- **How it looks:** No visual change; term/definition pairs render identically. The difference is structural: assistive technology exposes the group as a list and can navigate it, instead of meeting two unconnected text elements.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Fix is a single wrap — collect the orphaned `<dt>`/`<dd>` run into one `<dl>`; term normally precedes its description(s); one `<dt>` may legitimately carry multiple `<dd>`; using `<dt>` inside a `<ul>/<li>` or purely for styling is called out as invalid; validated with the W3C HTML Validator and axe. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/dlitem ; tool named: axe-core rule dlitem (dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.7/dlitem).
- **Best for:** QA sweep of the same surfaces as ⟦S1009⟧ — spec lists, key/value detail blocks — checked together in one pass.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1014⟧

## ⟦S1015⟧ doctype — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring `<!DOCTYPE html>` as the absolute first line of every HTML document, switching browsers into Standards Mode. The only critical-priority rule in this range.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible when correct — the whole page simply renders to the modern CSS box model identically in every browser. When missing, the page falls into Quirks Mode and the same CSS produces subtly wrong layouts (padding inflating widths, broken vertical centring, odd table rendering) that differ per browser.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. A parse-time switch, decided by the first bytes of the response.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Exact string `<!DOCTYPE html>` (case-insensitive, uppercase DOCTYPE conventional), with nothing before it — no whitespace, comments or BOM, any of which can trip Quirks Mode; old HTML4/XHTML PUBLIC doctypes must be removed (some trigger "Almost Standards" with minor table quirks); check the raw HTTP response / view-source, not the DOM; frameworks (Next.js, Nuxt, Remix, Astro, CRA, Rails) include it automatically but SSR setups can drop it, so the rendered output is what gets verified. Priority critical · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/doctype ; standards named: HTML Living Standard (DOCTYPE), MDN Quirks/Standards Mode.
- **Best for:** First line of the QA sweep for any hand-written single-file build — a five-second check that the file starts correctly before anything else is judged.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference (its own priority inside that sweep is critical).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1015⟧

## ⟦S1016⟧ dom-performance — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring DOM reads and writes to be batched separately — never interleaved — to avoid layout thrashing (forced synchronous reflow in a loop).
- **How it looks:** No visual system of its own. The visitor feels it in animation and interaction: scroll-driven effects and resizes stay smooth instead of freezing for hundreds of milliseconds while the browser recomputes layout over and over.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction-driven: a loop that reads `offsetHeight` then writes a style per element forces a full reflow on every iteration; batched, the sequence is read-all → write-all → one reflow. Visual updates are scheduled on `requestAnimationFrame` so they land once per paint, replacing `setTimeout(…, 16)` loops.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Read/write batching (measure everything into an array, then mutate); `DocumentFragment` for bulk insertion (1,000 items = one DOM insertion, one reflow); one class toggle instead of several inline style writes; `contain: layout style` isolates a widget's internal layout cost; scroll/touch/wheel listeners marked `{ passive: true }` when they never call `preventDefault()`; repeated rAF-driven React state updates across many mounted components flagged as a smell where a CSS or lower-frequency approach would do. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/dom-performance ; standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of the animation engine in an immersive build — parallax, pinned scenes, marquees, counters all read and write layout; this is the check that the frame loop is built read-then-write. Core relevance to animation-heavy homepages.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1016⟧

## ⟦S1017⟧ dom-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance QA rule capping DOM size and depth — fewer, shallower nodes — because every style recalculation, layout pass and interaction gets slower as the tree grows.
- **How it looks:** No direct visual change; flattening wrapper divs leaves the design identical. The felt difference is responsiveness on low-end phones: scrolling, filtering and expanding stay responsive instead of lagging, and memory pressure (tab crashes) drops.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Budgets: total nodes below ~1,500, maximum depth below ~32; any view rendering more than ~100–200 repeated items is a candidate for pagination or virtualization (react-window pattern: render the visible window plus a small overscan); remediation order — flatten wrapper nesting first → unmount hidden panels/tabs/drawers instead of keeping them in the tree → defer optional sections until needed → virtualize what remains; diagnosis first (confirm traces show Recalculate Style / Layout dominating before optimising); quick count via `document.querySelectorAll('*').length`, audited by Lighthouse's DOM-size audit. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/dom-size ; standards named: web.dev Learn Performance, Lighthouse overview, Patterns.dev list virtualization.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of long single-file homepages with many sections ×3 switchable versions — the variant copies multiply node count fast, so this budget is a real constraint on the three-version pattern; also galleries and long town lists.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1017⟧

## ⟦S1018⟧ draggable-accessibility — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring drag-and-drop interfaces to be fully operable without a mouse — keyboard alternative, ARIA state and spoken announcements — since native HTML5 drag and drop is keyboard-inaccessible by itself.
- **How it looks:** A sortable list or kanban board of cards, each with a visible grip handle (⋮⋮); the focused card shows a strong outline (example CSS: `2px solid #0066cc`, offset 2px); a grabbed card lifts visually — light blue fill, blue border, drop shadow `0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.15)`, cursor switching grab → grabbing. Screen-reader-only instruction text sits beside the list.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: keyboard focus on an item. Tab moves between items → Space/Enter picks the item up (`aria-grabbed` flips true, live region announces "grabbed — use arrow keys to move, Space to drop, Escape to cancel") → each Arrow press swaps the item one position and announces its new position number → Space/Enter drops it and announces the final position → Escape cancels and restores. Mouse drag runs in parallel with the same state.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Key table — Tab navigate · Space/Enter pick up & drop · ArrowUp/Down (or Left/Right across kanban columns) move · Escape cancel; `aria-grabbed` on items, assertive `aria-live` region for every state change, `aria-describedby` pointing at the hidden instructions; kanban variant: Space selects, Left/Right move the card between columns with an announcement per move. Priority medium · Difficulty advanced · Time 35 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/draggable-accessibility .
- **Best for:** QA sweep only if a build includes drag interaction (sortable configurators, reorderable galleries) — not present on a standard trades homepage; decisive when a before/after or planner widget uses drag.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1018⟧

## ⟦S1019⟧ duplicate-description — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO QA rule requiring a unique meta description per page — the same description pasted across pages makes Google discard it and auto-generate a worse snippet.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page itself. The visible surface is the search-results listing: each page's snippet under its title describes that page specifically (homepage vs products vs contact in the rule's examples) instead of one identical tagline repeated under every result.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Length target 50–160 characters, written for the page's specific content; detection by crawling and grouping identical `content` values (Screaming Frog / Sitebulb / Search Console Page Indexing report); also flag descriptions equal to the homepage's, to the site tagline, or left as a CMS placeholder; fix by dynamic per-route metadata (Next.js `metadata` export, Nuxt `useHead`, SEO-component prop) or per-post CMS fields with the site-wide fallback disabled. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/duplicate-description ; standards named: Google Search Central snippet guidance, MDN meta description reference.
- **Best for:** QA sweep when a build grows inner pages (services, towns, guides) from one template — the classic way every page ships the homepage's description. Nothing to check on a single page.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1019⟧

## ⟦S1020⟧ duplicate-id-active — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring unique `id` values on all focusable/active elements (links, buttons, inputs) — duplicate IDs break focus tracking and corrupt the screen reader's map of the controls. The axe-core `duplicate-id-active` rule as a skill.
- **How it looks:** No visual change. The defect it prevents is behavioural: clicking a label focuses the wrong field, keyboard focus lands on the first of two same-ID buttons, a control becomes unreachable.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Every interactive element's id unique within the rendered document; component systems must namespace or generate IDs (prefixes, React `useId`) because the same component mounted twice is the usual collision source; label `for` attributes must resolve to the one matching input id; validated with the W3C validator and axe. Companion rule ⟦S1021⟧ covers IDs that ARIA attributes point at. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/duplicate-id-active ; tool named: axe-core rule duplicate-id-active (dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.7/duplicate-id-active).
- **Best for:** QA sweep of forms and repeated components — quote forms with repeated field blocks, multiple CTA buttons, section switchers rendered per version. A real risk in copy-pasted section markup.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1020⟧

## ⟦S1021⟧ duplicate-id-aria — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring IDs referenced by ARIA attributes (`aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`) to be unique — a duplicated target ID resolves to the first match only, so controls get labelled/described by the wrong element. The axe-core `duplicate-id-aria` rule as a skill; companion to ⟦S1020⟧.
- **How it looks:** No visual change. The defect is spoken: in the rule's example, two shipping options both point `aria-describedby` at `id="desc"`, so the "Express shipping" button is announced with the "Standard shipping" description.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Every label/description source element carries a globally unique ID and every ARIA reference is re-pointed after renaming; dynamic content must mint unique IDs (React `useId` named); verification inspects the accessibility tree (not just source) plus axe / Accessibility Insights. The entry also records the collection's standing caution: prefer native semantics over ARIA, and don't add ARIA just to satisfy the rule. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/duplicate-id-aria ; tools named: axe-core rule duplicate-id-aria, Accessibility Insights for Web; standards: WAI-ARIA 1.2, MDN ARIA.
- **Best for:** QA sweep wherever dialogs, accordions, tabs or described buttons repeat on one page — modals and FAQ accordions on a homepage are the usual collision site. Run together with ⟦S1020⟧.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1021⟧

## ⟦S1022⟧ duplicate-js — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance QA rule requiring duplicate JavaScript libraries — the same library loaded twice, or two versions of it — to be detected and consolidated to a single version.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible on the page; the cost shows up as page weight and load time, and occasionally as bizarre behaviour when two versions of one library fight over the same global.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Detection: `npm ls <pkg>` / `pnpm why <pkg>` for the dependency tree, bundle analysers (webpack-bundle-analyzer, rollup-plugin-visualizer) for what's actually shipped, Lighthouse's duplicate-modules flag; consolidation via package-manager `overrides` (example pins lodash `^4.17.21`) and `npm dedupe` / `pnpm dedupe`; audit third-party tags/GTM, which often smuggle in their own copies; check Bundlephobia before adding anything new; libraries should declare `peerDependencies` rather than bundle their own copy. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/duplicate-js ; tools named: Bundlephobia, Webpack Bundle Analyzer, Lighthouse, JSHint.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of bundled builds; for a hand-written single-file homepage its analogue is checking the file doesn't embed two animation libraries doing the same job.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1022⟧

## ⟦S1023⟧ e2e-testing — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring end-to-end tests (Playwright or Cypress) over the critical user journeys, run in CI, so integration failures are caught from the user's point of view rather than unit by unit.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the site. Its artifacts are test runs: scripted browser sessions walking login → dashboard, product → cart → checkout → confirmation, with an HTML report uploaded as a CI artifact when a run fails.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The journeys it scripts are sequences: arrive at /login → fill email/password → submit → land on /dashboard with "Welcome back" visible; and the negative path — wrong credentials → error text visible, URL unchanged.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Journeys to cover: authentication (login/logout/registration), core business flow (checkout/booking/submission), navigation/routing, form validation, error states and recovery; selectors by `data-testid` (never styling classes like `btn btn-primary mt-4`); Page Object Model for reusable page drivers; test isolation via state reset per test and stored auth state (`playwright/.auth/user.json`); CI on push/PR with report artifact on failure; Agent QA (vostride/agent-qa) named as a natural-language black-box complement, not a replacement. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/e2e-testing ; standards named: Playwright Docs, Testing Library Guiding Principles.
- **Best for:** Project-level QA for apps with real flows (booking, checkout, account areas). For a static trades homepage its scope shrinks to: the quote form submits, the phone links work, navigation lands — usually covered by the build's own checks.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1023⟧

## ⟦S1024⟧ editorial-policy — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO/trust QA rule requiring a published editorial policy page documenting how content is researched, written, reviewed and corrected — direct E-E-A-T evidence for Google's quality raters.
- **How it looks:** A plain, well-structured policy page (mission, author qualifications, corrections policy as headed sections) reachable from the footer nav and the About page, and referenced from article bylines — the rule's byline example names a credentialed author and reviewer ("By Dr Jane Smith, MD · Reviewed by Dr Robert Jones, PhD · Editorial standards") instead of a generic "Editorial Team".
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Canonical URL /editorial-policy (or /about/editorial-standards); six required contents — editorial mission, author standards, research methodology, review process, update policy, conflict-of-interest/funding disclosure; the sample corrections commitment is correction within 24 hours of notification, noted at the top of the article; checks: the URL returns 200, is linked from footer + About + bylines, and carries substantive content rather than a boilerplate paragraph. Companion trust rules: ⟦S1013⟧ (page-level disclaimers) and the About-page rule earlier in this collection. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/editorial-policy ; standards named: Google Search Quality Rater Guidelines, Search Central E-E-A-T / helpful-content guidance.
- **Best for:** QA sweep for content-led or YMYL sites; for a trades business site the analogue is a real About/process page with named people and credentials — the policy page itself is a publisher pattern, not a trades-homepage section.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1024⟧

## ⟦S1025⟧ element-hiding — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring legitimate UI elements to avoid class names and IDs that adblocker filter lists (EasyList/EasyPrivacy) hide — so real content isn't silently deleted for users with blockers. The rule's own text notes roughly 30–40% of desktop users run one.
- **How it looks:** The defect is an absence: with uBlock Origin active, a cookie-consent bar, announcement strip or promo section simply isn't there — an empty gap or a missing dialog — while the same page looks complete in the developer's browser. GDPR consent that never renders is the named worst case.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Filter rules apply `display: none` at page render; the element never appears.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Blocked patterns named: classes `.ad .ads .ad-block .ad-container .advertisement .advert .advertising .banner .sponsor .sponsored .promotion .promo .cookie-banner .cookie-notice .gdpr-banner .consent-banner .tracking-notice` and IDs `#ad #ads #advertisement #banner #cookie-banner #consent-popup`, including substring/attribute filters like `##[class*="banner"]`; sanctioned renames — `.cookie-banner → .privacy-controls`, `#consent-popup → #privacy-preferences`, `.promotion → .featured-offer`, `.banner → .headline-ticker`, `.ad-bar → .site-notice`, `#sidebar-ads → #sidebar-recommendations`; test with uBlock Origin (EasyList + EasyPrivacy + uBlock filters) and a computed-style probe for `display: none` on critical elements; real ads/trackers keep blockable names on purpose — only legitimate UI gets renamed. Priority low · Difficulty intermediate · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/element-hiding ; sources named: EasyList filter rules, uBlock Origin static filter syntax, MDN class attribute.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of banners and consent UI — an announcement bar, a promo strip or a cookie notice on a trades homepage must not be named `.banner`/`.promotion`. A quick, concrete naming check.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1025⟧

## ⟦S1026⟧ embedded-or-inline-css — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring styles to live in external stylesheets (cacheable, reusable, lower specificity) rather than `style=""` attributes or scattered `<style>` blocks — with named exceptions.
- **How it looks:** No visual difference when done right — the same design, organised differently. The costs it removes are invisible until maintenance or repeat visits: uncached styles re-downloaded with every page, identical declarations repeated element by element, inline specificity overriding the design system.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Sanctioned inline uses, exactly three: (1) critical above-the-fold CSS inlined in `<head>` (with the rest preloaded async — the pattern cross-referenced by ⟦S0997⟧; extraction example uses a 1300×900 viewport), (2) genuinely dynamic values (progress width %, data-driven colour, user theme via inline CSS custom properties like `--user-theme-color`), (3) CSS-in-JS with proper abstraction; component patterns endorsed: CSS Modules, Vue scoped styles, styled-components with static parts extracted and dynamic parts via custom properties; enforcement via ESLint `react/forbid-component-props`/`forbid-dom-props` warnings on `style`, and stylelint (BEM class pattern, max-nesting-depth 3 in the example config). Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/embedded-or-inline-css .
- **Best for:** QA sweep of codebase organisation rather than of a single delivered file — for the one-file homepage format the whole file is technically embedded CSS, so the rule applies to multi-file/app builds, and its critical-CSS exception is the part that transfers.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1026⟧

## ⟦S1027⟧ empty-heading — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring every heading (h1–h6) to contain perceivable text — empty or whitespace-only headings are "ghost stops" in the document outline.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible changes; the defect is an outline entry with no words — a screen-reader user jumping heading-to-heading lands on silence, and the heading list shows a blank rung. An icon-only heading (just a font-awesome glyph) is named as the same failure unless it gains a label or screen-reader-only text.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Check = find h1–h6 whose content is empty or whitespace-only; fix = add descriptive text or remove the tag; screen-reader-only text class is the sanctioned fallback for a genuinely visual-only heading; don't use a heading tag just to borrow its font size — style with CSS instead; checked with Heading Map extension / WAVE / axe. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/empty-heading ; tools named: HeadingsMap extension, WAVE; standards: WCAG overview, MDN Accessibility.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of section markup — decorative heading slots and icon-headed cards in a designed homepage are exactly where empty headings creep in.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1027⟧

## ⟦S1028⟧ empty-links — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility QA rule requiring every link to have an accessible name — visible text, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or a linked image's alt — and a working destination.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual changes for sighted users. The defect is spoken: an empty or icon-only link is announced as just "link" with no destination or purpose, making navigation by ear impossible.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Icon-only pattern: `<a aria-label="Account settings">` wrapping an `aria-hidden="true"` SVG; social icons labelled ("Follow us on Twitter"); visually-hidden span pattern (`.sr-only`: 1×1 px, clipped, `white-space: nowrap`) for names like "Shopping cart (3 items)"; external links announce "(opens in new tab)" via hidden text alongside `rel="noopener noreferrer"`; detection snippet iterates all anchors and flags any with no text, no aria-label and no img alt; broken destinations in scope as well as empty names. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/empty-links ; standards: WCAG overview, MDN Accessibility.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of navigation, social-icon rows, logo links and image-card links — a homepage's header/footer and gallery cards are dense with icon and image links. High practical value for trades sites whose social/contact icons are links.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1028⟧

## ⟦S1029⟧ error-handling — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring proper JavaScript error handling — try-catch around async work, checked response statuses, React error boundaries, global handlers — with errors logged and never silently swallowed.
- **How it looks:** When something fails, the visitor sees a designed fallback instead of a frozen or half-broken page: the rule's boundary fallback is a `role="alert"` panel ("Something went wrong") with a Try again button that resets the boundary; data failures offer a cached fallback or a plain-language "Unable to load… please try again" message.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The sequence it specifies: async call throws or returns non-OK → catch logs with context → fallback data or user-facing error state renders → the rest of the page keeps working (an error boundary contains the crash to one component subtree).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Check `response.ok` and throw on HTTP error status before parsing; `.catch()` on every promise chain; class Error Boundary with `getDerivedStateFromError` + `componentDidCatch` reporting to a tracking service; global nets — `window.addEventListener('error', …)` and `'unhandledrejection'` (with `preventDefault` where appropriate); fallback ladder: live data → cached copy (localStorage) → friendly error; always re-throw or handle after logging. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/error-handling ; services named: Sentry, LogRocket; standards: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of any script that fetches or computes — quote-form submission, live data widgets; for a mostly static homepage its weight falls on the form path and any dynamic section.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1029⟧

## ⟦S1030⟧ error-images — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring image load failures to degrade gracefully — a fallback image, placeholder or initials block replaces the broken-image icon.
- **How it looks:** Where a photo fails, the layout keeps a styled placeholder: a neutral grey block (example CSS: `min-height: 100px`, background `#f5f5f5`) with the alt text centred in 14px grey type via `img::after`, or a swapped-in placeholder image; avatars fall back to a coloured circle carrying the person's initials (up to 2 letters, 48 px default size). While loading, a skeleton block shows and the image fades in (opacity 0 → 1 on load).
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: image request fails or is still in flight. Loading → skeleton/placeholder holds the box → on error the fallback source or initials block replaces it in place (no layout change) → on success the real image fades to full opacity. The swap is guarded (`this.onerror = null` / a hasError flag) so a broken fallback can't loop error events forever.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Inline pattern `onerror="this.src='/images/placeholder.png'; this.onerror=null;"`; React `ImageWithFallback` / `SmartImage` components with loading/loaded/error states; CSS background-colour fallback behind background-images; failures logged (console + analytics "Image Load Error" event with src and page path); verified by blocking the image URL in DevTools and by requesting invalid URLs. Priority low · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/error-images .
- **Best for:** QA sweep of image-heavy sections — project galleries, before/after pairs, review avatars on a trades homepage, where one dead image URL otherwise breaks the grid's polish.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1030⟧

## ⟦S1031⟧ error-monitoring — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring real-time production error monitoring (Sentry-class) — capturing, grouping and alerting on unhandled exceptions, promise rejections, framework boundary errors, failed requests and Web-Vitals regressions. Note the behaviour it prescribes: the SDK transmits error events, breadcrumbs and (opaque-ID) user context to the vendor's service; the entry records that factually — nothing here was executed.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the site. Its surfaces are the monitoring dashboard (grouped issues with stack traces, release tags, breadcrumbs) and the alert messages that land in Slack/PagerDuty when a new error appears.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Runtime sequence: error occurs in production → SDK captures with release/environment/user context (PII filtered by a `beforeSend` hook) → service groups it → threshold rules fire alerts.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Initialise in the app entry point, production only (`enabled: NODE_ENV === 'production'`); sample rates from the reference config — errors `sampleRate: 1.0`, performance `tracesSampleRate: 0.1` client / 0.05 server, session replay 0.1 of sessions and 1.0 of errored sessions (with `maskAllText`/`blockAllMedia`); every event tagged with release + environment; user context is an opaque ID + plan only, never email/name; alert table — new error: immediate (Slack) · rate spike +200% vs previous hour: PagerDuty · any critical unhandled exception: Slack + email · regression of a fixed issue: immediate · LCP/INP sustained regression and failed-request spikes: routed to owners; RUM capture of LCP/CLS/INP and non-OK fetch responses; acceptance test: a deliberate staging error must appear in the dashboard within 30 seconds, with source-mapped stack traces. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/error-monitoring ; services named: Sentry, Datadog, Bugsnag; standards: Sentry JS getting-started, web.dev monitoring guidance.
- **Best for:** Project-level observability for live apps; for a static trades homepage the transferable core is the global-handler + failed-request capture feeding ⟦S1029⟧'s handling — full SDK monitoring is an app-scale step.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1031⟧

## ⟦S1032⟧ es-modules — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A QA rule requiring native ES module syntax (`import`/`export`) instead of CommonJS `require()`/`module.exports`, enabling static analysis and tree-shaking.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible on the page. The effect is in the shipped bundle: only the functions actually imported are included, so pages download and parse less JavaScript.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Named exports preferred (better autocompletion, finer tree-shaking); default exports acceptable for single-concept modules; in the browser, `<script type="module">` — module scripts are deferred by default, run in strict mode, and keep their own scope; dynamic `import()` for code splitting (heavy module loaded on first click); barrel files re-export from a central index; conversion check = any remaining `require(`, `module.exports` or `exports.` in source. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/es-modules ; standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** QA sweep of bundled JavaScript projects; for a hand-written single-file homepage the transferable part is the dynamic-import pattern — load a heavy module only when the visitor reaches for it.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-sweep check, not a design reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1032⟧
# Skills S1033–S1072 — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills

All 40 entries in this chunk are rule-skills from thedaviddias/front-end-checklist, expressed in WEB-SKILLS.md as `## RULE-SKILL:` blocks. Each is a single checkable rule with a Check / Fix / Explain / Code Review brief plus a bundled `references/rule.md` carrying priority, difficulty and time. They are QA/audit rules, not design systems: "How it looks" below describes what a visitor (or an assistive-technology user) actually experiences when the rule is followed, and "Frame by frame" is "Static — no motion" except where the rule governs load order or interaction state. Tiers grade value as a build-QA reference for trade homepages, from each rule's own stated priority.

**Duplicate / overlap findings in this range (stated plainly):**
- **S1065 heading-order is a short restatement of S1064 heading-hierarchy** — the same underlying rule (sequential h1–h6 order, no skipped levels) at lower priority with no parameters S1064 lacks. Full detail under S1064; S1065 is a pointer entry.
- **S1036 favicon (SEO) and S1037 favicons (HTML) cover the same favicon stack from two category angles** — S1036 is the Google-search-display angle (≥48×48, robots-accessible), S1037 the full all-devices set (complete size matrix, manifest, dynamic favicon controller). Both carry distinct material, so both are indexed in full and cross-pointed.
- S1053 (exactly one label per field) and S1055 (every field has an associated label) are companion rules, not duplicates. S1062 (single descriptive H1) overlaps S1064/S1065 on the one-H1 point only; its subject is SEO topic signalling.

## ⟦S1033⟧ event-delegation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A JavaScript performance rule: attach one click listener to a stable parent container and resolve the intended child with `event.target.closest()`, instead of one listener per list item or table row.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual changes for the visitor — lists, galleries and toolbars behave identically, but long lists and dynamically loaded items (AJAX-loaded rows, infinite-scroll cards) respond to clicks immediately, including items added after page load.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Interaction sequence: user clicks any child (even a nested SVG icon) → the event bubbles to the parent listener → `closest()` walks up to the matching item → the handler runs on that item.
- **Mechanism & key values:** DOM event bubbling + `closest()`; one listener per container regardless of item count (the source contrasts 1,000 items = 1,000 listeners vs 1). Do NOT use for high-frequency events (mousemove, scroll) or non-bubbling events (focus, blur — use capture phase or focusin/focusout instead). Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, JavaScript category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/event-delegation. Standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** Work/gallery grids, towns/areas lists and any filterable or dynamically extended list on a homepage; a build-hygiene rule behind interactive sections rather than a section design itself.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium-priority rule; matters once a page has large or dynamic lists.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1033⟧

## ⟦S1034⟧ external-links — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO/content rule: back factual claims with inline links to authoritative external sources, and set correct `rel` attributes on every outbound link.
- **How it looks:** Body copy where statistics and claims carry visible inline links to the study, official documentation or government source behind them; paid/affiliate links are indistinguishable visually but carry `rel="sponsored"` in the markup.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `rel` table from the source: regular external link = `noopener noreferrer`; paid/sponsored = `sponsored noopener noreferrer`; user-generated or unvouched = `nofollow noopener noreferrer`. Audit trigger: long-form pages (>500 words) with factual claims and zero external links get flagged. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/external-links. Worked example cites the WebAIM Million report (over 96% of home pages have detectable WCAG failures).
- **Best for:** Proof/credibility copy on any section making claims (review counts, guarantees, certifications) — the citation habit behind trustworthy trade copy; not a layout reference.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium-priority content rule; supports proof sections but designs nothing.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1034⟧

## ⟦S1035⟧ faq — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO rule: any page with a visible FAQ section must carry matching `FAQPage` JSON-LD structured data so Google can show expandable Q&A rich results.
- **How it looks:** On the page, an ordinary FAQ section of questions with visible answers; in Google results, the listing expands to show the question-and-answer pairs directly under the snippet, taking more SERP space.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** JSON-LD with `"@type": "FAQPage"`, `mainEntity` array of `Question` objects, each with `name` and `acceptedAnswer` (`"@type": "Answer"`, non-empty `text`). Hard constraints from the source: schema questions must exactly match visible page content; no FAQPage on pages where Q&A is hidden behind tabs/accordions at load; validate with Google's Rich Results Test. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/faq. Standards named: Google Search Central FAQPage documentation, Schema.org FAQPage.
- **Best for:** The FAQ section of a homepage (already a standard trade-homepage section) — pairs the visible Q&A with its search-result expansion.
- **Tier:** STRONG — directly serves the FAQ section every trade homepage ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1035⟧

## ⟦S1036⟧ favicon — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The SEO angle on favicons: declare a `<link rel="icon">` favicon Google can fetch and display next to the site's name in mobile search results. Overlaps S1037 (the HTML-category full device set) — see the chunk header.
- **How it looks:** The firm's small brand icon sitting beside its name in Google mobile results, in browser tabs and in bookmarks, instead of a generic globe placeholder.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Google's requirements as stated: favicon publicly accessible over HTTPS, not blocked by robots.txt, at least 48×48px (Google scales it to 16×16 for display); recommended stack is favicon.ico (16×16 + 32×32) + favicon.svg + apple-touch-icon.png (180×180). A new favicon can take several weeks to appear in search. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/favicon.
- **Best for:** Every page's `<head>`; brand recognition in search results for the firm's name searches.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — small but universal head item; the build detail lives in S1037.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1036⟧

## ⟦S1037⟧ favicons — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The full all-devices favicon implementation: the complete ICO/PNG/SVG/Apple/Android/Microsoft size set plus web app manifest, so the brand icon renders correctly in every tab, home screen and pinned surface. Same favicon stack as S1036, from the HTML category — S1036 holds the Google-display requirements, this entry holds the build matrix.
- **How it looks:** One consistent brand mark at every surface: 16px browser tab, 180px iOS home-screen icon, 192/512px Android icons, Microsoft tiles — plus an optional animated SVG spinner favicon and JS-swappable state favicons (notification badge with count, error, success, loading) described in the source.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion, except the source's optional animated SVG favicon (a 2s linear infinite spin) and the dynamic controller's state swaps (success state auto-resets to default after 3 seconds; notification badge drawn on a 32×32 canvas, badge 60% of icon size, "99+" cap).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Minimum set per the source: favicon.ico (32×32) + apple-touch-icon.png (180×180); full matrix adds PNG 16/32, Apple 76/120/152/180, Android 192/512, MS tiles 70/144/150/310; SVG favicon with `prefers-color-scheme` dark-mode swap; manifest.json icons with maskable/any purposes; tools named: RealFaviconGenerator, favicons npm package, sharp + to-ico generation script; favicon.ico cache header `public, immutable, max-age=31536000`. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, HTML category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/favicons.
- **Best for:** The `<head>` of every build; the size matrix is the copy-paste reference when generating a client's icon set.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium-priority production detail; needed once per site, not a design source.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1037⟧

## ⟦S1038⟧ fetchpriority-attribute — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance rule: mark the LCP (usually hero) image `fetchpriority="high"`, below-fold images `fetchpriority="low"`, so the browser's network queue loads what the visitor sees first.
- **How it looks:** The hero image arrives visibly earlier — the source cites 5–30% LCP reduction in real-world tests from this one attribute — while below-fold gallery images stream in afterwards instead of competing.
- **Frame by frame:** Load sequence, not animation: HTML parses → the `fetchpriority="high"` hero image and high-priority preloads jump the queue ahead of same-type default resources → hero paints → low-priority below-fold images fetch last.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Values `high` / `low` / `auto` (default). Applies to `<img>`, preload `<link>` and `<script>`. Hard rule from the source: never mark more than one or two resources high — it defeats the hint. Browser defaults table included (HTML/CSS = Highest, fonts/head scripts = High, deferred scripts = Low). Support: Chromium 101+, Safari 17.2+, ignored gracefully elsewhere; Next.js `priority={true}` sets it automatically; JSX uses camelCase `fetchPriority`. Rule metadata: priority medium, beginner, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Performance category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/fetchpriority-attribute. Standards named: web.dev Fetch Priority API, MDN fetchpriority.
- **Best for:** Hero sections first (the LCP image), then work/gallery images below the fold — a one-attribute win on every homepage build.
- **Tier:** STRONG — cheapest recorded LCP lever for image-led heroes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1038⟧

## ⟦S1039⟧ figure-figcaption — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A semantic-markup rule: any image with a visible caption is wrapped in `<figure>` with the caption in a `<figcaption>`, so the caption is machine-readably tied to the image.
- **How it looks:** A project photo with its caption line directly under it (the source's example style: 0.875rem, grey #666, italic, 0.5rem above) — visually identical to a plain caption paragraph, but screen readers announce the caption as part of the figure and search engines read it as describing the image.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<figcaption>` must be the first or last child of `<figure>`; alt and figcaption must not duplicate — alt is the invisible text alternative, figcaption is the visible description/credit (the source's chart example keeps a data-describing alt and a "Figure 1: … Source:" caption). `<figure>` also suits code blocks, diagrams and charts; hero images without captions stay plain `<img>`. Rule metadata: priority medium, beginner, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Images category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/figure-figcaption.
- **Best for:** Work/gallery sections where each job photo carries a location or job-type caption; before/after pairs with labels.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium-priority markup detail for captioned imagery.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1039⟧

## ⟦S1040⟧ file-upload-accessibility — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule for file-upload components: labelled inputs, stated file types/size limits, keyboard-operable drag-and-drop zones, and ARIA live feedback for progress and errors.
- **How it looks:** An upload box with a visible label and hint line ("Accepted formats: PDF, DOC, DOCX. Max size: 10MB."), a dashed 2px dropzone (2rem padding) that highlights on hover/drag-over/focus, a progress bar (8px high) filling as the upload runs, and an error line in #dc3545 when a file is rejected.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction sequence: user tabs to the zone or input → picker opens → files selected or dropped → each file validated (type, size) → progress bar advances with sr-only percentage announcements → completion announced in the polite live region, or the error appears in a `role="alert"` span tied to the input by `aria-describedby`.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<label>` + `accept` attribute + visible restriction text; dropzone as `tabIndex={0}` `role="button"`; progress as `role="progressbar"` with aria-valuenow/min/max; default max size in the reference component 10MB (10 × 1024 × 1024 bytes); the native input may be visually hidden with sr-only styles but never `display: none` (must stay focusable). Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 25 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, HTML category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/file-upload-accessibility.
- **Best for:** Quote/inspection forms that let a homeowner attach damage photos — the upload pattern for call/CTA and form sections.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority; relevant only where a form takes uploads.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1040⟧

## ⟦S1041⟧ filename-quality — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An image-SEO rule: name image files descriptively in lowercase hyphenated words (`homepage-hero-team-meeting.jpg`) instead of camera defaults or generic names (`IMG_4532.jpg`, `image1.jpg`) — Google uses the filename as an image-search relevance signal.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen changes; the effect shows in image-search discoverability and in an asset folder a developer can read without opening files.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules from the source: lowercase only; hyphens as separators (underscores are not word separators to Google); 3–5 meaningful words, no filler ("final", "v2"); no spaces (they become %20). Always rename camera defaults and generic names; leave hashed build output and third-party CDN names alone. Includes a bash batch-rename script and a server-side upload filename sanitiser. Rule metadata: priority low, beginner, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Images category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/filename-quality. Cites Google's Image SEO best practices.
- **Best for:** Asset preparation for work/gallery and hero imagery on every build — a prep-stage habit, not a page pattern.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — the corpus's own low priority; cheap hygiene for image-heavy trade pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1041⟧

## ⟦S1042⟧ find-npm-packages — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A maintenance skill for the Front-End Checklist repository itself — not a website rule. It finds, validates and records the 2–3 npm packages that implement or enforce a given checklist rule, writing them into the rule's `npmPackages` frontmatter. (Described factually as data; nothing in it was executed.)
- **How it looks:** No page output at all. The visible product is an edited rule file whose frontmatter gains a package list (example given: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe-core, @testing-library/jest-dom for the form-labels rule).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Workflow: read the rule file → identify detector/fixer/tester candidates → verify each against the npm registry → select 2–3 → insert frontmatter after `tools:` → run the repo's validation script.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Mandatory quality thresholds: >10,000 weekly downloads, last published within 18 months, listed on registry.npmjs.org; maximum 3 packages per rule, names only (versions fetched at build time); validation via `pnpm validate:packages`.
- **Reference / source:** Part 20 collection in WEB-SKILLS.md; it names the npm registry and npmjs.com search as its sources. No rule page of its own.
- **Best for:** Nothing in a homepage build — it exists to maintain the checklist corpus that the other rules in this chunk come from.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — repo-maintenance meta skill with no build application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1042⟧

## ⟦S1043⟧ first-contentful-paint — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance rule: get the first text or image painted fast — FCP target under 1.8 seconds — by removing render-blocking resources, inlining critical CSS and preconnecting to third-party origins.
- **How it looks:** The visitor sees the page's first words and hero begin rendering almost immediately instead of staring at a blank white screen; content above the fold appears in the site's real styling because the critical CSS was inlined in the document.
- **Frame by frame:** Load sequence: HTML arrives → render tree builds from inlined critical CSS (no blocking stylesheet wait) → first content paints (FCP) → deferred full CSS and JS stream in behind it → fonts swap in without hiding text.
- **Mechanism & key values:** FCP thresholds from the source: 0–1.8s good, 1.8–3s needs improvement, >3s poor. Techniques with values: preload-pattern for deferred CSS (`rel="preload" as="style"` + onload swap, noscript fallback), `defer` on scripts, preconnect/dns-prefetch for font and CDN origins, `font-display: swap`, Next.js cache header example `s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400`, critical-CSS extraction sized 1300×900 in the example. Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Performance category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/first-contentful-paint. Tools named: Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, web-vitals (onFCP).
- **Best for:** Whole-page load behaviour, hero first impression above all — a gate every homepage build should pass.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority rule; the first-paint budget behind every hero.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1043⟧

## ⟦S1044⟧ flashing-content — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A safety rule (WCAG 2.3.1, Level A): nothing on the page may flash more than 3 times per second — flashing between 3–60 Hz can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.
- **How it looks:** Attention effects are slow pulses and fades instead of strobes: the source's safe pattern fades opacity 1 → 0.7 over a 2s ease-in-out cycle (0.5 flashes/sec); warning indicators use amber #ff9800 rather than flashing red.
- **Frame by frame:** Motion constraint, stated as limits: any loop's full flash cycle must take at least ~0.34s (the reference React component clamps duration to a 0.34s minimum); faster cycles — the source's banned examples run at 0.1s (10 flashes/sec) and 0.2s (5 Hz) — are seizure risks and fail.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Thresholds: ≤3 flashes/sec; above that, allowed only if the flashing area is under 25% of 10 degrees of visual field (roughly 341×256px at typical viewing distance) and flash contrast is under 10% of maximum brightness. Saturated red flashing is banned outright. Unavoidable flashing video gets a pre-play warning dialog (`role="alert"`) the viewer must acknowledge. Test tools named: PEAT, Harding Test. Rule metadata: priority critical, beginner, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/flashing-content. Standards named: WCAG 2.3.1, MDN accessibility guidance.
- **Best for:** Any animated section — a hard ceiling on strobe-like effects, GIF/video content and alert animations across all sections.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the corpus's critical safety limit on motion; binds every animated version.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1044⟧

## ⟦S1045⟧ flexbox-patterns — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A CSS rule: use Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts with correct shorthand values, `gap` spacing and the `min-width: 0` fix, avoiding the classic flex overflow bugs.
- **How it looks:** Rows and columns that behave as drawn: a fixed 280px sidebar beside a fluid main column, equal-width nav items, card titles that truncate with an ellipsis instead of blowing out the card, tag lists that wrap cleanly.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Layout states only: items grow/shrink per their flex values as the viewport narrows; wrapped rows re-flow via `gap` without margin hacks.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Shorthand table from the source: `flex: 0 0 auto` (default, fixed), `flex: 1` = `1 1 0` (equal fill), `1 1 auto` (grow from content), `none` = `0 0 auto`. The two named fixes: `min-width: 0` on text-bearing flex children (flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which blocks truncation) and `gap` instead of sibling margins (works with wrapping). Centering = align-items + justify-content center; push-to-end = `margin-left: auto`. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, CSS category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/flexbox-patterns.
- **Best for:** Navigation bars, card rows, sidebar+content layouts — the everyday layout substrate of hero, services and gallery sections.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium-priority craft rule; prevents layout breakage rather than supplying a design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1045⟧

## ⟦S1046⟧ focus-management — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule: when content changes dynamically — modal opens, route changes, item deleted, form submitted — focus must be moved deliberately to the new context and returned afterwards, so keyboard and screen-reader users are never stranded.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual for mouse users. For keyboard users: opening a dialog puts them inside it, closing returns them to the exact button they pressed; after a page change they start at the new main content; after deleting a list item they land on the next item, not at the top of the page.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction sequences per scenario from the source's table: modal opens → focus moves to the modal/first focusable element inside; modal closes → focus returns to the triggering element; SPA navigation → focus moves to the main heading/container (`tabIndex={-1}` target); content deleted → focus moves to the next/previous item or the parent container; form submitted → focus moves to the success message or error summary.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Programmatic focus via refs and `focus()`, `tabindex="-1"` to make containers script-focusable, stored trigger element restored on close, status regions with `role="status"`/`role="alert"`. Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 25 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/focus-management. Standards named: W3C WAI WCAG, MDN Accessibility.
- **Best for:** Modals and quote-form dialogs, SPA-style section switching (directly relevant to 1·2·3 version switchers), and any dynamic homepage interaction.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority rule governing every interactive overlay a build ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1046⟧

## ⟦S1047⟧ focus-not-obscured — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A WCAG focus-visibility rule: sticky headers, footers, cookie banners and chat widgets must never fully cover the element that currently has keyboard focus.
- **How it looks:** As a keyboard user tabs down the page, each focused control scrolls fully into the clear — never sliding underneath the sticky header or disappearing behind the cookie banner at the bottom.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction sequence: user tabs → browser scrolls the newly focused element into view → scroll-padding holds it clear of the fixed chrome → both the control and its focus ring stay visible; repeat with banners/chat open and at 200–400% zoom.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Worked values from the source's example: a 72px sticky header and an 88px-min-height fixed cookie banner are fixed by `scroll-padding-top: 80px; scroll-padding-bottom: 96px` on the html element and capping the banner at `max-height: 96px`. Test matrix mandated: all transient UI active (consent bars, chat launchers, promo bars, sticky mobile toolbars) and zoomed/narrow layouts. Explicitly not a fix: removing focus outlines. Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/focus-not-obscured. Standard named: WCAG Focus Not Obscured (2.4.11/2.4.12 family).
- **Best for:** Navigation (sticky headers) and footer/consent bars on every page; a pass/fail check for the sticky call bar common on trade sites.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority; sticky call/CTA bars are standard on trade homepages and are exactly the obscuring chrome named.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1047⟧

## ⟦S1048⟧ focus-order — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule: tab order must follow the visual reading order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom), which means DOM order must match the visual layout and positive `tabindex` values are banned.
- **How it looks:** Tabbing moves the focus ring steadily across the screen in the order the eye reads — header left to right, then down the page — with no jumps to distant corners; CSS-reordered layouts (flex `order`) are called out because they change the picture but not the tab sequence.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Sequence is the tab walk itself: focus advances in DOM order through nav, hero actions, sections, footer, predictably at every step.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `tabindex="0"` adds a custom element in DOM position; `tabindex="-1"` is script-focus only; `tabindex="1+"` never. Form example from the source: two-column DOM (first → city → last → state) breaks reading; row-grouped DOM (first → last → city → state) matches the eye. Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/focus-order. Standards named: W3C WAI WCAG, MDN Accessibility.
