- **Best for:** Every section — most sharply forms and navigation where multi-column layouts tempt DOM/visual mismatch.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — high priority in the corpus, but it is a verification pass over layouts other rules design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1048⟧

## ⟦S1049⟧ focus-styles — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A CSS rule: never remove the focus outline without a visible replacement — use `:focus-visible` so a clear ring appears for keyboard navigation but not on mouse clicks (WCAG 2.4.7, with 2.4.13 as the stronger target).
- **How it looks:** Tab through the page and every button, link and input wears a crisp ring — the source's reference style is a 2px solid outline in the primary colour with a 2–3px offset (optionally radius-matched); click the same elements with a mouse and no ring appears. Inputs may swap the ring for a border colour change plus a 3px soft shadow (example: `0 0 0 3px rgb(37 99 235 / 0.25)`); a skip link sits hidden above the page until focused, when it drops into view at the top-left.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction states: keyboard focus lands → ring draws around the control; mouse press → no ring (`:focus` outline suppressed, `:focus-visible` not triggered); focus leaves → ring gone. No timed motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** WCAG 2.2 focus-appearance numbers from the source: indicator area at least the component's perimeter × 2 CSS pixels; ≥3:1 contrast between focused and unfocused states and ≥3:1 against adjacent colours; at least a 2px solid outline with offset as the quality bar. Cautions carried: pseudo-element rings must be anchored to the positioned element and not clipped by `overflow: hidden`; stretched-link cards must ring the real interactive element. Rule metadata: priority high, beginner, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, CSS category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/focus-styles. Standards named: WCAG 2.4.7 and 2.4.13/2.4.11.
- **Best for:** Every interactive element in every section — the focus ring is part of the design system of any build, nav and forms first.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority, beginner-cost; a visible quality marker of a cared-for build.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1049⟧

## ⟦S1050⟧ font-loading — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance rule: load webfonts so text is never invisible and never jumps — `font-display: swap`, WOFF2, preloaded critical fonts, subsetting and self-hosting.
- **How it looks:** Page text renders immediately in a fallback system font, then swaps once into the brand font when it lands — no blank gaps where headlines should be (no FOIT) and minimal layout shift when the swap happens.
- **Frame by frame:** Load sequence: HTML parses → preloaded WOFF2 font fetch starts in parallel (discovered from the `<link rel="preload">`, not late from CSS) → text paints in fallback → font arrives → text re-paints in the brand face.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `font-display: swap` in every `@font-face`; preload the critical font with `as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin`; WOFF2 as the format; subset to needed character sets; prefer variable fonts over many weight files; self-host to skip third-party DNS/TLS; never base64-inline fonts into CSS (breaks separate caching). Verification named: Lighthouse "All text remains visible during webfont loads". Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Performance category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/font-loading. Tools named: FontSubsetter, Wakamai Fondue, Google Fonts Helper.
- **Best for:** Typography-led heroes and headings on every build — the display face is usually the heaviest late-discovered asset on a trade homepage.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority; governs the font behaviour behind every headline.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1050⟧

## ⟦S1051⟧ font-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A CSS/accessibility rule: body text at least 16px on mobile, expressed in rem/em so it honours the visitor's browser font-size setting, and resizable to 200% without breaking (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4).
- **How it looks:** Comfortable reading without pinch-zoom: 1rem body text, 0.875rem captions, 2rem+ H1s; a user who has set a larger browser font size sees the whole page scale up proportionally instead of being locked to the designer's pixels; form inputs at 1rem never trigger iOS Safari's jarring auto-zoom on focus.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. States: at 200% browser zoom/text resize, text grows and layout reflows without loss of content or function.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Numbers from the source's table: body minimum/recommended 1rem (16px); small text minimum 0.75rem (12px), recommended 0.875rem; nav labels 0.875–1rem; H1 minimum 1.5rem, recommended 2rem+; inputs exactly 1rem to prevent iOS zoom-on-focus. Below 12px, iOS Safari auto-inflates text and shifts layout. Banned pattern: `html { font-size: 10px }` reset (a 62.5% base is the tolerated form); conversion is px ÷ 16 = rem. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, CSS category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/font-size. Standard named: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4 Resize Text.
- **Best for:** All body copy — decisive for the older homeowner audience trade sites serve, and for form usability on phones.
- **Tier:** STRONG — medium priority in the corpus, but the 16px/input rules are hard usability gates for the trade audience.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1051⟧

## ⟦S1052⟧ form-captcha — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A security rule: every public form (contact, registration, login, password reset, comment) needs bot protection — invisible CAPTCHA preferred — with the token always validated server-side. (The prescribed integrations are described as data; none were executed.)
- **How it looks:** To a genuine visitor, nothing: Turnstile/reCAPTCHA v3/hCaptcha run invisibly in the background, so the quote form looks like a plain form. Bots meet a silent rejection — and a honeypot build adds one off-screen field (positioned at left:-9999px, `tabindex="-1"`) that only bots fill.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction sequence: visitor submits → widget/script produces a token → form posts with the token → server verifies it with the provider before processing → submission accepted, or rejected (reCAPTCHA v3 score < 0.5 treated as bot in the source's example); a filled honeypot short-circuits to a fake success so the trap stays hidden.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Providers named: Cloudflare Turnstile (recommended, siteverify endpoint), Google reCAPTCHA v3 (score 0.0 bot – 1.0 human, reject under 0.5), hCaptcha. Client-side-only validation is stated to provide no protection. Defence-in-depth example: sliding-window rate limit of 5 requests/minute/IP returning 429 with `Retry-After: 60`. Risk table: login/registration/password-reset = high priority, contact/newsletter/comment = medium, search = low. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Security category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/form-captcha. Standards named: OWASP automated-threats and credential-stuffing guidance.
- **Best for:** Forms and call/CTA sections — the quote-request form is the highest-value public form on a trade homepage.
- **Tier:** STRONG — protects the one form the whole page exists to submit.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1052⟧

## ⟦S1053⟧ form-field-multiple-labels — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule: each form field gets exactly one `<label>`; where several text fragments must name one field, they are combined with `aria-labelledby` instead of stacking label elements. Companion to S1055 (which requires the label to exist at all).
- **How it looks:** No visual difference — each field shows one clear label. The difference is heard: a screen reader announces one unambiguous name per field, and a voice-control user can say that one name to focus the field.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** 1:1 label-to-input mapping; `for`/`id` association preferred; supplemental text ("Password must be 8 characters") goes in `aria-describedby`, never a second label; the source's worked `aria-labelledby` example joins two spans ("Phone Number" + "(Include area code)"). Detection: axe-core rule `form-field-multiple-labels`. Rule metadata: priority medium, beginner, 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/form-field-multiple-labels. Named: WebAIM Creating Accessible Forms, Deque axe rule page.
- **Best for:** Forms — a five-minute lint-level check inside the quote-form build.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority, tiny scope; folds into the form QA pass beside S1055/S1056.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1053⟧

## ⟦S1054⟧ form-https — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A security rule: every form must submit over HTTPS — every `action` URL, every fetch/XHR endpoint — because HTTP posts send the visitor's details as readable plain text.
- **How it looks:** The padlock stays clean in the address bar on form pages and the browser's autofill works; on an HTTP form the visitor instead sees a "Not Secure" warning and, for password fields, Chrome disables autofill.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Submission sequence: form posts → data travels TLS-encrypted → server receives it; the source's counter-example shows the raw readable HTTP request body (`username=alice&password=hunter2`) anyone on the network path can read.
- **Mechanism & key values:** All form actions `https://` or relative (relative inherits the page scheme, safe only when the page itself is HTTPS with an HTTP→HTTPS 301 redirect + HSTS behind it). Key subtlety stated in the source: redirecting an HTTP POST to HTTPS does not protect it — the plaintext request already happened, so the form must start secure. Browser-behaviour table: password field on HTTP = autofill disabled from Chrome 86+. Audit greps for `action="http://` and `fetch('http://` are given. Rule metadata: priority critical, beginner, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Security category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/form-https. Standards named: OWASP Transport Layer Protection cheat sheet, MDN form-sending guidance, web.dev why-HTTPS.
- **Best for:** Quote/contact forms and any data collection — the transport guarantee under the form every homepage ends with.
- **Tier:** STRONG — critical-priority baseline; in practice a one-line audit on static trade sites.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1054⟧

## ⟦S1055⟧ form-labels — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule: every form control (input, select, textarea) must have a programmatically associated `<label>` — placeholder text is not a label. Grouped controls (radios, checkboxes) share a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`.
- **How it looks:** Each field carries a persistent visible label above it that stays put while the visitor types (where placeholder-only fields go blank); tapping or clicking the label text itself focuses the field, giving mouse and touch users a bigger target.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Heard sequence for screen-reader users: focus lands on a field → its label is announced; entering a radio group → the legend question is announced first, then the focused option's own label.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Association by `for` + matching `id` (most robust) or by nesting the input inside the label; placeholder-only labelling explicitly banned; fieldset/legend pattern given for grouped choices. Detection is the baseline axe/Lighthouse label checks. Rule metadata: priority critical, beginner, 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/form-labels. Standards named: MDN `<label>` reference, WCAG form guidance.
- **Best for:** Forms — the quote form first; the single most common accessibility failure class on lead-gen pages.
- **Tier:** STRONG — critical priority and five-minute cost; non-negotiable on the conversion form.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1055⟧

## ⟦S1056⟧ form-validation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule for form validation: errors are written next to the field, tied to it with `aria-describedby`, state is exposed with `aria-invalid`, required is programmatic, and colour is never the only error signal.
- **How it looks:** Submit with a bad email and the field gains a red border (#dc3545 in the reference styling) plus a written message under it with a warning icon — "Please enter a valid email address" — while an optional summary box at the top lists every error as anchor links; the help text under the field ("We'll never share your email") stays in place before and after the error.
- **Frame by frame:** Interaction sequence: submit → validation runs → focus moves to the first invalid field → its error text (in a `role="alert"` span referenced by `aria-describedby`, alongside the help-text id) is announced → visitor corrects the field → its error clears as they type. Grouped choices announce the fieldset legend before the option.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Attribute kit from the source: `aria-describedby` carrying BOTH help and error ids, `aria-invalid="true"` on error, `required` or `aria-required="true"`, error span `role="alert"`, focus-first-error on submit, error colour #dc3545 with icon so meaning is not colour-only. Review caveat stated in the source: do not flag client-handled React forms for missing `method`/`action`. Native fallback pattern included (`type="email"`, `minlength="8"`, `pattern`, `title`). Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 25 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, HTML category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/form-validation.
- **Best for:** Forms — the error behaviour of the quote form decides whether a confused visitor recovers or abandons.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority; the complete pattern for the page's money form.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1056⟧

## ⟦S1057⟧ frame-title — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility rule: every `<iframe>` (and legacy `<frame>`) carries a descriptive `title` attribute naming what's embedded, so screen-reader users can identify and skip embeds without entering them.
- **How it looks:** Visually nothing changes — a map or video embed looks the same. In a screen reader's frame list the embeds read as "Map of our office location" and "Tutorial video: How to use our product" instead of anonymous frames.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Non-empty, content-describing `title` on every iframe; keep it concise, no redundant words like "iframe"; the `name` attribute is explicitly not a substitute. Rule metadata: priority medium, beginner, 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/frame-title. Standard named: WCAG guidance.
- **Best for:** Towns/areas and call/CTA sections embedding Google Maps, and any video embed — the two iframe cases trade homepages actually have.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority, five-minute fix, but applies to the map embeds most trade pages ship.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1057⟧

## ⟦S1058⟧ freshness — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO rule: publish consistent freshness signals — `Last-Modified` header, `dateModified` in Article JSON-LD, and a visible "Last updated" date — so Google's Query Deserves Freshness system credits genuinely updated content.
- **How it looks:** An article byline reading "Published June 1, 2022 · Last updated November 15, 2024" (the source's worked dates), with matching machine-readable dates behind it in the head and response headers.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Signal hierarchy as Google reads it, per the source: 1) `dateModified` in Article/BlogPosting JSON-LD (ISO 8601), 2) `Last-Modified` HTTP header, 3) `article:modified_time` Open Graph tag, 4) visible date text (least reliable). Discipline: update `dateModified` only on substantive change — blanket deploy-time refreshes can be penalised; all three signals must agree. Server snippets: Nginx `add_header Last-Modified $date_gmt;`, Next.js frontmatter `updatedAt` passed into JSON-LD and `<time datetime>`. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/freshness. Standards named: Google ranking systems guide, Schema.org dateModified.
- **Best for:** Advice/guide content and news-style sections; minor for a static homepage, relevant if the firm publishes articles.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority; a content-site rule more than a homepage rule.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1058⟧

## ⟦S1059⟧ frontend-checklist-global — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The umbrella skill for the whole Front-End Checklist corpus: one entry point that routes an audit to all 386 rules through the checklist's MCP tools (`review_code`, `audit_url`, `search_rules`, `get_rule`, `fix_rule`, `explain_rule`, `get_checklist_rules`, `get_workflow`, `get_quick_reference`) instead of recalling rules from memory. Nearly every other entry in this chunk (S1033–S1072, and the wider S0902–S1292 block) is one of the rules it routes to. (Its workflow is described as data; no tools were invoked.)
- **How it looks:** No page output. Its visible product is an audit report: a short list of evidence-backed findings per file or page, critical and high first, each tied to an exact file, selector or snippet — deliberately conservative, preferring silence over weak nitpicks.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Workflow: review pasted code or audit a URL → narrow with search/categories → pull the exact rule → report only findings the shown code directly supports.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Corpus coverage as stated: 386 rules — accessibility 89 (9 critical, 25 high), seo 93 (19 high), performance 43 (1 critical, 22 high), html 34 (3 critical, 12 high), css 31 (10 high), javascript 26 (1 critical, 12 high), images 25 (1 critical, 15 high), security 22 (4 critical, 10 high), testing 13 (7 high), i18n 5, privacy 5 (2 high). Doctrine worth carrying: known-safe patterns that must NOT be flagged — decorative images with `alt="" aria-hidden="true"`, client-handled React forms without method/action, Next.js metadata-API files without literal head tags, aspect-ratio wrappers reserving media space; conflict rule: decorative-image guidance beats dimension guidance absent real layout-shift evidence. Rule-derived highlights restate several sibling rules (transform/opacity-only animation, ≤3 flashes/sec, focus ring ≥2px at 3:1, batched DOM reads/writes).
- **Reference / source:** Part 20 collection in WEB-SKILLS.md; MCP documentation at https://frontendchecklist.io/mcp, rules browser at https://frontendchecklist.io/rules.
- **Best for:** The QA gate over a finished homepage build — the routing layer that turns this whole rule block into one audit pass before sign-off.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the entry point to the corpus; the audit stance (evidence-only findings, safe-pattern exemptions) is itself reusable doctrine.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1059⟧

## ⟦S1060⟧ geo-meta — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO rule: add geo meta tags (`geo.region`, `geo.placename`, `geo.position`, ICBM) as a supplementary regional signal — read by Bing, explicitly not used by Google.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible on the page; the tags live in the `<head>`. The visitor-facing local signals remain the address, map and LocalBusiness data elsewhere on the page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Formats from the source: `geo.region` = ISO 3166-2 code (e.g. `US-CA`, `GB-ENG` — never the spelled-out country name); `geo.position` = `latitude;longitude` with a SEMICOLON separator (`37.7749;-122.4194`); ICBM repeats the coordinates with a comma. The source's own ranking of effort: hreflang and LocalBusiness JSON-LD (with geo coordinates) are the impactful Google signals; geo meta is a Bing-only extra. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/geo-meta. Standards named: Bing Webmaster Guidelines, Google international targeting.
- **Best for:** Towns/areas pages at most — and only as a footnote to the LocalBusiness schema; never invent addresses or coordinates to satisfy it (the source's exceptions say accuracy overrides completeness).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — weak, Bing-only signal; the local-SEO value for trades sits in LocalBusiness markup, not here.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1060⟧

## ⟦S1061⟧ gtm-present — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance rule: keep Google Tag Manager lean — audit and prune tags, delay non-critical ones, consider server-side GTM — because every tag executes JavaScript on the visitor's main thread.
- **How it looks:** No visual change; the difference is felt as snappier first paint and response, since fewer third-party scripts (pixels, chat widgets, heatmaps) compete with the page's own content at load.
- **Frame by frame:** Load sequence: GTM container loads async from the head → tags fire per their triggers — the rule pushes non-critical tags from "All Pages" (immediate) to "Window Loaded" or custom `app_ready` events so they run after the page is usable.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Practices from the source: async snippet only, never synchronous; consolidate tags; remove expired-campaign tags; server-side GTM to offload processing; a faulty custom HTML tag can break the whole site. Measurement named: Lighthouse "Reduce the impact of third-party code", Tag Assistant, DevTools long-task tracing; GTM is called out as a direct drag on LCP and INP. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Performance category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/gtm-present.
- **Best for:** Whole-page performance hygiene on marketing builds that carry analytics and tracking pixels (the tracking-pixel pages in this practice included).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority; relevant where tag containers exist, invisible where they don't.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1061⟧

## ⟦S1062⟧ h1 — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO rule: exactly one `<h1>` per page, descriptive of the page's specific topic with its primary keyword — not empty, not duplicated, not just the brand name.
- **How it looks:** The page's largest headline names what the page is about — the source's worked fix turns `<h1>Acme Corp</h1>` into `<h1>Project Management Software for Enterprise Teams</h1>`; the H1 and the title tag agree on topic without being identical, and the H1 is genuinely visible (never CSS-hidden).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit checks five failure modes: zero H1s, multiple H1s, empty H1, brand-only H1, H1 off-topic; plus placement traps — the H1 belongs in the page component, not the shared layout/header (the logo-in-header H1 anti-pattern). Demote extra H1 candidates to H2. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/h1. Named: Google heading guidance, MDN heading elements; John Mueller cited on H1s aiding structure understanding.
- **Best for:** Hero sections — the hero headline choice and the page's H1 are the same decision on a homepage.
- **Tier:** STRONG — small rule, but it arbitrates the single most-read line on the page.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1062⟧

## ⟦S1063⟧ has-selector — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A CSS rule: use the `:has()` relational pseudo-class — the "parent selector" — to style elements based on what they contain, deleting the JavaScript class-toggling that used to do the job.
- **How it looks:** Interface states that react to content with zero scripting: a form group whose label and border turn error-red only while its input is invalid and non-empty; a card that switches to a two-column grid only when it contains an image, and gains top padding when it carries a badge; a nav item highlighted because its link is the current page; a whole page that flips to a dark theme when a radio is checked (`html:has(#theme-dark:checked)`).
- **Frame by frame:** State changes, no timed motion: a descendant's state flips (input becomes invalid, checkbox checks, image is added) → the browser re-matches `:has()` → the parent's styles apply or drop instantly.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Full selector grammar inside `:has()` including combinators (`>`, `+`, `~`); support baseline late 2023 — Chrome/Edge 105+, Firefox 121+, Safari 15.4+, with `@supports selector(:has(*))` as the fallback gate. Performance caution stated in the source: avoid broad or deeply nested `:has()` on frequently repainting elements; scope it to a subtree (`.card:has(img)`, not a root-level selector). Rule metadata: priority low, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, CSS category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/has-selector. Named: MDN `:has()`, web.dev CSS :has() guide, Can I Use.
- **Best for:** Forms (state-driven field styling), work/gallery cards (layout by content), navigation active states — anywhere a build currently spends JS on styling state.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — the corpus grades it low priority, but it is a genuine modern technique for state-driven section styling.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1063⟧

## ⟦S1064⟧ heading-hierarchy — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The corpus's full heading-structure rule: one h1 for the page title, then h2 sections and h3 subsections in strict sequence — never skipping a level, never choosing a heading for its font size. This is the canonical entry for the rule that S1065 restates in short form.
- **How it looks:** Visually, headings sized by CSS classes rather than by level, so the design's type scale stays free; structurally, the page reads as a clean table of contents — the source's model outline runs h1 "Web Accessibility Guide" → h2 "Getting Started" → h3 "Prerequisites" / "Tools" → h2 "Core Principles".
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Heard sequence: a screen-reader user jumps heading to heading (H key) and hears the outline in order, each level nesting predictably under the last.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Failure catalogue from the source: multiple h1s, skipped levels (h1 → h3), headings used purely for styling, non-descriptive headings ("Section 1", "Click Here"). Verification: HeadingsMap outline check + exactly-one-h1 count. Rule metadata: priority critical, beginner, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/heading-hierarchy. Standards named: W3C WAI WCAG, MDN Accessibility.
- **Best for:** Every section's heading stack — the outline discipline behind hero → services → process → reviews → FAQ flow.
- **Tier:** STRONG — critical priority; the structural skeleton every homepage is audited against.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1064⟧

## ⟦S1065⟧ heading-order — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Pointer entry — the same underlying rule as S1064 heading-hierarchy (sequential h1–h6 order, no skipped levels), restated as a short 5-minute rule at medium priority. Read S1064 for the full treatment; this entry records only what this cataloguing adds.
- **How it looks:** Identical outcome to S1064: a page whose headings nest h1 → h2 → h3 without gaps, styled by CSS rather than by level.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Deltas versus S1064: priority medium (vs critical), beginner, 5 min (vs 15); its one-line fix example — change an `<h3>` that follows an `<h1>` into an `<h2>`; it explicitly cross-references the heading-hierarchy rule as its broader companion. No parameters beyond S1064's.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/heading-order.
- **Best for:** Same use as S1064 — do not read both as two designs; this is the quick-check version.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — duplicate restatement; value sits in S1064.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1065⟧ (canonical: ⟦S1064⟧)

## ⟦S1066⟧ horizontal-scroll — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A CSS rule: no horizontal scrolling at any standard viewport — content must reflow to a 320px CSS width (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10 Reflow, the equivalent of 400% zoom on a 1280px screen) without two-dimensional scrolling.
- **How it looks:** On a phone or a zoomed desktop, every line of text, image and form field fits the screen width; the visitor scrolls only downward. The classic failures it names: a 1200px fixed-width container hanging off the right edge, an unshrinkable image, a long URL bursting its column, a `100vw` hero overflowing by exactly the scrollbar's width.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Layout behaviour as the viewport narrows: fluid containers shrink (`max-width` + `width: 100%`), media caps at `max-width: 100%`, long strings wrap, multi-column layouts wrap — the horizontal scrollbar never appears. (Data tables are the named exception: they scroll inside their own `overflow-x: auto` wrapper, not the page.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Six fixes with values from the source: fixed `width` → `max-width` + `width: 100%`; `img, video, iframe, embed, object { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }`; `overflow-wrap: break-word` (plus `word-break` fallback) for long strings; `width: 100vw` → `width: 100%`; Grid/Flexbox with wrapping; tables in scrollable regions. Test protocol: 320px viewport and 400% zoom. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, CSS category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/horizontal-scroll. Standard named: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow, Level AA).
- **Best for:** Responsive QA over every section — a pass/fail gate for mobile, where most trade traffic arrives.
- **Tier:** STRONG — medium priority in the corpus, but a hard AA requirement and a common real-world failure on image-heavy pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1066⟧

## ⟦S1067⟧ hreflang — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An i18n/SEO rule: multilingual or multi-region pages declare their language versions with reciprocal `hreflang` links (plus an `x-default`), so searchers get the version written for them.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page itself; the effect is which URL a searcher in each country lands on — the Spanish speaker gets /es/, the British searcher /en-GB/, everyone else the x-default.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Codes: ISO 639-1 language + optional ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 region (`en`, `en-US`, `en-GB`, `es-MX`); every variant page must list ALL variants including itself (non-reciprocal sets are ignored); `x-default` points at the fallback/language-selector page; implementable in `<head>` links or in the XML sitemap via `xhtml:link`. Rule metadata: priority medium, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, i18n category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/i18n/hreflang. Verification named: Google Search Console International Targeting report.
- **Best for:** Only genuinely multilingual/multi-region sites — a single-market trade homepage has no use for it beyond its towns/areas pages staying in one language.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — correct and complete, but out of scope for single-region trade builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1067⟧

## ⟦S1068⟧ hsts — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A security rule: serve the `Strict-Transport-Security` header on all HTTPS responses so browsers refuse to ever load the site over plain HTTP, closing the SSL-stripping window that redirects leave open.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible — the visitor simply never reaches an insecure version: after the first HTTPS visit, even a typed `http://` address is upgraded inside the browser before any network request leaves it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Sequence: first HTTPS response carries the header → browser caches the policy for max-age → all later HTTP navigations are rewritten to HTTPS internally, so an attacker never sees plaintext traffic.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Header value from the source: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` — max-age 31,536,000 seconds (1 year) minimum, `includeSubDomains` recommended, `preload` optional and hard to reverse (weeks-to-months removal; requires every subdomain on valid HTTPS first). Never send the header over HTTP (ignored, and dangerous if cached). Server snippets given for Nginx, Apache, Next.js headers and Express/Helmet. Defined in RFC 6797. Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Security category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/hsts. Standards named: MDN Strict-Transport-Security, OWASP HSTS cheat sheet.
- **Best for:** Server/hosting configuration for the whole site rather than any section — the transport companion to S1054's form rule.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — high priority, but a one-time host setting rather than build material.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1068⟧

## ⟦S1069⟧ html-resource-hints — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance rule: give the browser advance notice with resource hints — `preload` for current-page criticals, `preconnect`/`dns-prefetch` for early third-party origins, `prefetch` for likely next pages — so late-discovered resources start fetching in parallel with parsing.
- **How it looks:** The hero image and headline font arrive with the first paint instead of stuttering in afterwards; the source quantifies the font case — one preload for a critical font can eliminate a 100–300ms flash of invisible text.
- **Frame by frame:** Load sequence: HTML head parses → preload directives fire immediately at high priority (font, hero image, critical CSS/JS) while preconnect completes DNS+TCP+TLS handshakes with third-party origins → parser reaches the stylesheet/body already holding the critical assets → first paint includes font and hero; prefetches trickle in at low priority behind everything.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Hint semantics from the source: preload = fetch now, high priority, this page; prefetch = low priority, next navigation; preconnect = DNS+TCP+TLS; dns-prefetch = DNS only (sufficient for analytics/tag origins). Responsive hero preload pattern given (`imagesrcset`/`imagesizes` on the preload link). Three named mistakes: over-preloading (each preload competes for bandwidth — only what the first ~2 seconds need), missing `as` attribute (wrong priority, cache not reused), missing `crossorigin` on font preloads (causes double-fetch). Rule metadata: priority high, intermediate, 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, HTML category — https://frontendchecklist.io/en/rules/html/html-resource-hints.
- **Best for:** Hero sections (LCP image + display font) and head architecture on every build — pairs with S1038 (fetchpriority) and S1050 (font loading).
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority; the head-level half of hero load performance.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1069⟧

## ⟦S1070⟧ html-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO/crawl rule: keep the HTML document small — Googlebot parses only roughly the first 15MB of a document, and oversized HTML (usually inline JSON dumps, inlined SVGs or base64 images) wastes crawl budget and delays rendering.
- **How it looks:** No direct visual effect; the symptom it prevents is tail content silently missing from Google's index and slow first paint on data-heavy pages.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Numbers from the source: ~15MB Googlebot parse ceiling; targets — under 100KB excellent, 100KB–2MB acceptable, 2MB–5MB needs optimisation (investigate anything over 2MB), over 5MB critical. Cause table: inline `__NEXT_DATA__` JSON 100KB–5MB, inline SVG 10–500KB each, base64 images +33% over binary, unminified scripts 50KB–1MB, massive inline utility CSS 50–300KB; flag any single JSON block over 500KB. Fixes: pass only rendered data to the page, externalise SVGs (sprites for icons), serve images by URL from a CDN, minify, gzip/Brotli. Measurement: `curl -so /dev/null -w '%{size_download}'`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, SEO category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/html-size.
- **Best for:** Whole-document budget discipline — a real watch-item for single-file builds that inline large SVG artwork, where the inline-SVG line of the cause table applies directly.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — medium priority; the inline-SVG caution is the trade-relevant slice of it.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1070⟧

## ⟦S1071⟧ html-xml-lang-mismatch — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An accessibility/i18n rule: if `<html>` carries both `lang` and `xml:lang`, their values must be identical valid BCP 47 codes — HTML parsers read one, XML parsers the other, and a disagreement makes assistive tech pronounce the page in the wrong language.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible. Heard effect when wrong: a screen reader voicing French content with an English speech profile — unintelligible output. When right (or when `xml:lang` is simply omitted on a normal HTML5 page), pronunciation follows the content.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Attribute matrix from the source: standard HTML5 (`text/html`) = `lang` required, `xml:lang` unnecessary; XHTML (`application/xhtml+xml`) = `xml:lang` required; polyglot = both, identical including subtags (`en` vs `en-US` counts as a mismatch, as does an invalid tag like `lang="english"`). Tied to WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.1 (Language of Page) and BCP 47 / RFC 5646. Rule metadata: priority medium, beginner, 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, Accessibility category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/html-xml-lang-mismatch. Standards named: HTML Living Standard, W3C language-declaration guidance.
- **Best for:** Nothing in ordinary HTML5 trade builds beyond confirming `lang` is set correctly — it only bites XHTML/polyglot documents and EPUB-style pipelines.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — narrow-scope rule; a one-line check, not build material.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1071⟧

## ⟦S1072⟧ html5-semantic-elements — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A markup rule: build page structure from semantic HTML5 elements — `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<figure>`, `<time>`, `<address>` — instead of div soup, so landmarks, outlines and search engines all read the page's structure.
- **How it looks:** Visually identical to the div version — the difference is structural: a screen-reader user jumps straight to `<main>` or by landmark to the nav, and the document outline (site header with nav list, article with its own header/time/address, sections per topic, footer with copyright and footer nav) exists as machine-readable skeleton under the design. The source's worked structures cover a blog page, an e-commerce product page (article product + figure gallery + reviews as nested articles + related-products aside) and a news homepage.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Cardinality from the source: exactly one `<main>` per page; multiple `<header>`/`<footer>` allowed (page-level and article-level); `<article>` for self-contained content, `<section>` for thematic grouping, `<aside>` for tangential content. Pattern support: skip link to `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">`, aria-labels distinguishing multiple navs ("Main navigation", "Footer navigation"), schema.org microdata riding on the same elements (`itemscope` Article with headline/datePublished/author). Rule metadata: priority high, beginner, 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, HTML category — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/html5-semantic-elements. Tools named: HTML5 Outliner, WAVE, axe DevTools, Lighthouse, W3C Markup Validator.
- **Best for:** The skeleton of every section of every build — the element vocabulary the homepage's header/hero/services/reviews/footer structure is written in.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority and foundational; not a visual design, but the structure every visual design is hung on.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1072⟧
# Skills S1073–S1108 — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills

All 36 entries in this chunk are individual rules from the Front-End Checklist
(thedaviddias/front-end-checklist), each a short checkable rule-skill with the same
shape: a "When to use" trigger, the rule, Quick Reference, Check / Fix / Explain /
Code Review prompts, and a bundled `references/rule.md` carrying the rule's priority,
difficulty, estimated time, code examples and verification steps. None of them is a
design or motion reference: they are QA gates a finished page is audited against.
"How it looks" therefore describes what the visitor experiences when the rule holds
(usually: nothing to see — the page simply loads fast, stays secure, is findable and
is operable), and "Frame by frame" is "Static — no motion" except where the rule
governs an interaction sequence, which is then written out as trigger → steps →
end state.

Family notes (no two skills in this range are the same underlying skill — each has
its own rule page in the source):
- **HTTPS pair:** ⟦S1074⟧ http-to-https (the redirect itself) and ⟦S1076⟧ https
  (site-wide HTTPS + certificate validity) overlap on redirect configuration; both
  are indexed in full because their checks differ. ⟦S1077⟧ is the companion
  link-level rule.
- **Image family:** ⟦S1080⟧ image-cdn (delivery), ⟦S1081⟧ image-compression
  (technique), ⟦S1082⟧ image-file-size (byte budgets), ⟦S1083⟧ image-optimization
  (the umbrella rule that combines format, compression, srcset and loading). Four
  distinct rules, cross-referenced in their entries.
- **Indexability pair:** ⟦S1090⟧ indexability and ⟦S1091⟧ indexability-conflicts
  are companions — the second audits clashes between the signals the first checks.
- **Deferral pair:** ⟦S1086⟧ import-on-interaction and ⟦S1087⟧
  import-on-visibility are sibling loading patterns (intent-triggered vs
  viewport-triggered).
- ⟦S1088⟧ improve-rule is a meta-skill about editing the checklist's own rule
  files; it has no page application and is marked NOT-FOR-TRADES.

## ⟦S1073⟧ http-requests — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: minimise the number of HTTP requests a page makes on initial load, because each request pays DNS, TCP and TLS setup latency before any bytes move.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible in itself — the visitor's page simply assembles faster: hero, type and icons arrive in few round trips instead of dozens of small staggered downloads.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Load sequence only: browser requests the document → bundled CSS/JS, one SVG sprite and subset fonts follow in parallel → first paint without a long tail of icon/font requests.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Target **under 50 requests for initial page load**. Per-request overhead table from the rule: DNS lookup 20–120 ms, TCP connection 20–100 ms, TLS handshake 30–100 ms, time to first byte 50–500 ms. HTTP/1.1 allows 6 connections per domain vs HTTP/2's single multiplexed connection. Techniques: bundle critical CSS/JS (Vite `manualChunks` vendor/utils split), inline critical above-fold CSS and load the rest via `rel=preload` + onload stylesheet swap, one inline SVG `<symbol>` sprite for all icons, data URIs for tiny assets, font subsetting with `unicode-range: U+0000-007F` (Basic Latin). Priority: high · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/http-requests
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Whole-page load budget on every section; the bank's single-file builds satisfy it by construction, but it is the audit to run on any multi-asset page (hero first).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1073⟧

## ⟦S1074⟧ http-to-https — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Security rule: every HTTP request must be permanently redirected to HTTPS at the server or CDN edge, preserving path and query string.
- **How it looks:** Invisible when right — a visitor who types the bare domain or follows an old link lands straight on the padlocked HTTPS page in one hop, with no insecure version ever rendered.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Navigation sequence: browser requests `http://…` → server answers 301 with `Location: https://$host$request_uri` → browser loads the HTTPS page; on later visits the cached 301 and then HSTS skip the HTTP request entirely.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Use **301, never 302** (301 is cached by browsers and transfers link equity; 302 is re-requested every time). Nginx: `return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`. Consolidate www/non-www and protocol into a **single hop** — redirect chains are a fail. Never do the redirect in JavaScript (`window.location` runs after the insecure request already happened). After HTTPS is verified, add HSTS: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. Platform notes: Cloudflare "Always Use HTTPS" toggle, Vercel automatic, CloudFront Viewer Protocol Policy "Redirect HTTP to HTTPS", Caddy automatic. Priority: **critical** · beginner · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/http-to-https (companion: ⟦S1076⟧ covers site-wide HTTPS and certificates; the redirect configuration is shared ground between the two.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Launch gate for every page and preview deployment — hosting-level, section-independent.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1074⟧

## ⟦S1075⟧ http2 — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: serve the site over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 so many resources share one connection with compressed headers instead of queueing over HTTP/1.1.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible — assets for image-heavy sections stream in parallel over a single connection, so galleries and below-fold sections populate together rather than in six-at-a-time batches.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** HTTP/2 multiplexing (many streams, one TCP connection, no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer), HPACK header compression (QPACK in HTTP/3), HTTP/3 over QUIC for faster connection setup and better packet-loss handling. Requires HTTPS in browsers. Nginx: `listen 443 ssl http2;`. Practice changes the rule prescribes: stop concatenating files (small files cache better under multiplexing), **never domain-shard** (splitting across static1/static2 subdomains breaks multiplexing), still avoid thousands of tiny files, use `preload`/`preconnect` for critical assets. Verify in DevTools Network "Protocol" column (`h2`/`h3`) on the real CDN/edge path, not just origin config. Priority: high · intermediate · 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/http2 (tools named: KeyCDN HTTP/2 Test, http3check.net, Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Hosting/CDN configuration check at launch; no design input, but it changes how asset-splitting decisions (see ⟦S1073⟧) should be made.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1075⟧

## ⟦S1076⟧ https — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Security rule: every page and resource on the site is served over HTTPS with a valid, unexpired certificate covering all hostnames.
- **How it looks:** The padlock state on every page — no browser security warnings, no blocked content; forms, phone links and quote flows all sit inside the secure context.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication. Certificate must cover `www` as well as the bare domain (SAN certificate); free certificates via Let's Encrypt/Certbot (`certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com`, auto-renewal on); managed TLS on Vercel/Netlify/CloudFront/Cloudflare (Cloudflare minimum TLS version 1.2). Verify the chain with SSL Labs — aim for **A or A+**. HTTP→HTTPS 301 site-wide (see ⟦S1074⟧). HTTPS is the prerequisite for service workers, push notifications, geolocation, getUserMedia, Web Crypto, Payment Request API, HSTS and HTTP/2/3. Mixed content fails the rule: active mixed content (scripts, iframes over HTTP) is blocked outright. Named pitfalls: expired certificate, certificate missing `www`, 302 instead of 301, HTTPS only on login pages. Priority: **critical** · beginner · 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/https (references web.dev "Why HTTPS matters", MDN Transport Layer Security, OWASP Transport Layer Protection cheat sheet.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Launch gate for every deliverable; also the precondition for several richer homepage features (service-worker caching, geolocation for towns/areas features).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1076⟧

## ⟦S1077⟧ https-downgrade — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO/security rule: an HTTPS page must never link to or load from `http://` URLs — no downgrade links in anchors, images, scripts or styles.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible when right; when wrong, visitors hit browser mixed-content warnings, blocked scripts/styles (page renders broken or unstyled), and every internal click pays an extra redirect hop before the page starts loading.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Failure sequence: HTTPS page loads → browser meets an `http://` script or stylesheet → blocks it silently → dependent behaviour/styling missing.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit all `<a href>`, `<img src>`, `<script src>`, `<link href>` (and `fetch()`/router calls) for values starting `http://`. Risk table from the rule: `<script src>` HTTP = critical, blocked silently; `<link href>` CSS = critical, blocked silently; `<img src>` HTTP = warning, blocked in strict mode; `<a href>` HTTP = warning, redirected if the target supports HTTPS. Fixes: internal links as relative paths (`/about`) or absolute HTTPS; external links upgraded after checking the destination supports HTTPS; CMS/database search-and-replace of stored HTTP URLs; server-level HTTP→HTTPS redirect as the safety net. Audit commands: `grep -rn 'href="http://' ./src/templates/`, or in DevTools console `document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="http://"]')`. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/https-downgrade (references Google's HTTPS-as-ranking-signal post and MDN's mixed-content guide.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Post-migration and pre-launch link audit across all sections; matters most for call/CTA and towns/areas pages full of outbound and internal links.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1077⟧

## ⟦S1078⟧ hyphens — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: separate words in URL paths with hyphens, never underscores or spaces, because Google tokenises hyphens as word boundaries and underscores as word joiners.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page itself — it is the address bar and the shared link: `/roof-repair-springboro` reads as separate searchable words; `/roof_repair_springboro` is read by Google as one compound token.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `/best-seo-practices` matches queries for the individual words; `/best_seo_practices` matches only the joined token (John Mueller, quoted in the rule). Slug generator prescribed: lowercase → strip non-word characters → `replace(/[\s_]+/g, '-')` → trim leading/trailing hyphens. Changing existing URLs requires per-URL **301 redirects** (Nginx `rewrite … permanent;` or Next.js `redirects()` with `permanent: true`), internal-link updates, sitemap regeneration, Search Console re-indexing, and 3–4 weeks of 404 monitoring. Flag categories: underscores as separators, `%20`/`+` in paths, mixed separators in one URL. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/hyphens
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** URL scheme decisions for towns/areas and service pages before a site structure is fixed; a one-time migration rule thereafter.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1078⟧

## ⟦S1079⟧ identical-links-same-purpose — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: links with identical text must lead to the same destination; where destinations differ, the link text (or its accessible name) must differ.
- **How it looks:** No visual change for sighted scanning — the difference is heard: a screen-reader user pulling up the page's link list hears "Download 2022 Report" and "Download 2023 Report" as two predictable entries instead of two indistinguishable "Download Report" entries pointing at different files.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Check = find same-text/different-URL link pairs in the rendered page. Fixes: make the text unique per destination, or unify the destination; where the visual design needs short text, extend the accessible name only — `aria-label="Read more about Product Alpha"` on a visible "Read more". Generic text ("Click here", repeated "Read more") is named as the major barrier. Grounded in WCAG link-purpose-in-context and WebAIM link-text guidance. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/identical-links-same-purpose
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Work/gallery grids and proof sections where repeated card links ("See this project", "Read review") are the natural design — each card's link needs a distinguishing accessible name.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1079⟧

## ⟦S1080⟧ image-cdn — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Images rule: serve images through an image CDN that resizes, converts format and edge-caches on the fly via URL parameters, instead of hand-processed static files.
- **How it looks:** The same photography, delivered sized to the visitor's actual slot: a phone gets a small WebP/AVIF, a retina desktop a 2× variant, both from a nearby edge cache — galleries and hero imagery arrive fast without the builder pre-generating every size.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Request sequence: browser asks the CDN URL with width/format parameters → CDN transforms or serves its cached variant → smallest suitable bytes returned.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** URL-parameter transforms: Cloudinary `w_400,h_300,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto`; Imgix `?w=400&h=300&fit=crop&auto=format,compress`; Cloudflare Images variants; Next.js Image with `formats: ['image/avif','image/webp']`, `deviceSizes: [640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920]`, `imageSizes: [16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384]`. Claimed benefit: **40–80% smaller files** plus edge caching; no build step. Providers named: Cloudinary, Imgix, Cloudflare Images, Vercel/Next.js Image, Bunny.net. Priority: high · intermediate · 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/image-cdn (image family: delivery — see also ⟦S1081⟧ compression, ⟦S1082⟧ file-size budgets, ⟦S1083⟧ the umbrella optimization rule.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Work/gallery and hero imagery on hosted builds with many photo sizes; less relevant to the bank's self-contained single-file previews, where images are embedded instead — the sizing discipline still applies.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1080⟧

## ⟦S1081⟧ image-compression — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Images rule: compress every image with the right lossy/lossless setting per image type — most uncompressed images are 5–10× larger than they need to be.
- **How it looks:** Visually identical pages at a fraction of the weight: photographs stay rich, screenshots stay crisp, icons stay exact — the visitor notices only that sections paint sooner.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Recommended quality table: photos JPEG/WebP **70–85%**, product images **80–90%**, screenshots PNG/WebP lossless or 90%+, icons/logos SVG/PNG lossless, thumbnails **60–75%**. Expected saving **60–80%** with no visible loss. Tool commands given: ImageMagick `convert input.jpg -quality 80`, Sharp CLI to WebP at quality 80, `pngquant --quality=65-80`, `svgo` for SVG. Automation examples: Sharp batch scripts, image-minimizer-webpack-plugin (jpeg/webp/png quality 80, avif 60), vite-imagemin (mozjpeg 80, optipng level 5, gifsicle level 3), calibreapp/image-actions in GitHub Actions at 80/80/80. Verify side-by-side for artefacts; Lighthouse "Efficiently encode images". Priority: high · beginner · 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/image-compression (references MDN responsive images and web.dev image performance; image family — technique; see ⟦S1082⟧ for the byte budgets this achieves.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Every photographic section — hero, work/gallery, before/after pairs — before any file is embedded or shipped.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1081⟧

## ⟦S1082⟧ image-file-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Images rule: keep each image file under a byte budget matched to its role on the page, audited file by file.
- **How it looks:** Nothing to see directly — the effect is the LCP image (usually the hero) arriving inside the budget on mobile data instead of stalling the first screen; HTTP Archive data quoted in the rule puts images at over 50% of average page weight.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Budget table from the rule: hero/full-bleed **≤400 KB**, content photo **≤200 KB**, product image **≤150 KB**, thumbnail **≤30 KB**, icon/logo **≤10 KB** (SVG or WebP), transparent PNG **≤100 KB**. Audit flags: photo >200 KB, graphic/icon >100 KB, hero >400 KB, thumbnail (<200 px wide) >30 KB. Format maths: WebP ≈25–35% smaller than equivalent JPEG, AVIF ≈40–50% smaller (web.dev figures). Sharp settings given: WebP quality 80, AVIF quality 60 effort 6, progressive mozjpeg quality 80, PNG compressionLevel 9. Strip EXIF/IPTC metadata. Lighthouse CI assertions prescribed: `uses-optimized-images` and `uses-responsive-images` at minScore 0.9 (flags any image reducible by >4 KB). Source-cited stakes: 1 s of mobile load delay can cut conversions by up to 20% (Google research, as quoted). Priority: high · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/image-file-size (image family — budgets; technique in ⟦S1081⟧, delivery in ⟦S1080⟧, umbrella in ⟦S1083⟧.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Hero image sign-off and gallery batch checks — the concrete per-file numbers a build is held to before delivery.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1082⟧

## ⟦S1083⟧ image-optimization — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Images rule (the umbrella of the image family): every image uses the right format, compression, responsive sizes, dimensions and loading strategy as one complete pass.
- **How it looks:** A photo-led page where each image is exactly as big as its slot: sharp on retina, light on mobile, no layout jump as images land (width/height declared), below-fold galleries loading only as the visitor approaches.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Optional pattern the rule's framework examples include: blur-up progressive image — blurred placeholder shown → full image swaps in with a 300 ms opacity/blur transition once loaded.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Format order **AVIF > WebP > JPEG/PNG**, SVG for icons/logos, PNG only for transparency. Quality: photos 80%, AVIF 60%; below ~60% quality artefacts appear. Responsive pattern: `srcset` at **400w, 800w, 1200w, 1600w** with a `sizes` attribute per layout; `<picture>` for format fallback and for art direction (square crop ≤600 px, 4:3 ≤1024 px, wide banner on desktop). Always width/height attributes (CLS), `loading="lazy"` below the fold only, `decoding="async"`. Named mistakes: desktop-size images served to mobile, missing dimensions, over-compression, no format fallback, no lazy loading, huge hero images. Animated GIFs should become MP4/WebM; sub-1 KB images may be inlined as data URIs. Target: page weight down 50–80%; LCP < 2.5 s. Priority: high · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/image-optimization (umbrella rule — sub-rules ⟦S1080⟧, ⟦S1081⟧, ⟦S1082⟧ carry the delivery, compression and budget detail.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** The single image checklist applied to hero, work/gallery, proof and towns/areas sections of any image-led homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1083⟧

## ⟦S1084⟧ image-redundant-alt — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: alt text must not repeat what assistive technology already announces — no "image of" / "photo of" openers, and no alt that duplicates the adjacent caption.
- **How it looks:** No visual difference; the difference is in the screen-reader stream: "Golden Retriever playing in the park" instead of "Graphic, image of a Golden Retriever playing in the park", and a captioned photo gets `alt=""` so it is not read twice.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scan alt attributes for "image of", "photo of" and caption-identical text; never use the filename as alt. Decorative or caption-described images take null alt (`alt=""`). Priority: **low** · beginner · 5 min — the smallest rule in this range, but a named failure in the alt-text pass.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/image-redundant-alt (references the WAI images tutorial decision tree and the MDN `<img>` reference.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Alt-text pass over work/gallery and before/after imagery, where captions and alt text naturally collide.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1084⟧

## ⟦S1085⟧ immutable-patterns — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: never mutate shared objects or arrays in place — produce updated copies (spread, `map`/`filter`) so state changes are detectable by reference and debuggable.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — it is a code pattern. Its visible effect is indirect: UI that re-renders exactly when data changes (reference comparison works), with no stale or half-updated widgets.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Copy-on-write: `{ ...user, ...changes }` for objects, `[...todos, newTodo]` for arrays. Mutation→alternative table from the rule: `push` → `[...array, item]`, `pop` → `slice(0, -1)`, `shift` → `slice(1)`, `unshift` → `[item, ...array]`, `splice(i,1)` → `filter`, `sort`/`reverse` → copy first (`[...array].sort(fn)`). `Object.freeze()` for configuration objects — with the caveat that freeze is shallow (nested objects stay mutable). Immer `produce()` for complex nested updates. Especially prescribed inside state management (Redux, Zustand, Signals). Priority: medium · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/immutable-patterns (standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Code hygiene inside interactive sections — version switchers, configurators, before/after state — where shared state bugs show up as UI that will not update.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1085⟧

## ⟦S1086⟧ import-on-interaction — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: code for features the visitor may never use must not be in the initial bundle — it loads by dynamic `import()` only when a click, focus or hover signals intent.
- **How it looks:** A page that paints its content immediately, with heavy extras absent; tap "Configure" or "Open chat" and the control answers at once with a skeleton or "Loading…" state, then the full feature opens a beat later, already cached on the second use.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: visitor clicks/focuses/hovers the feature's control → immediate UI feedback appears (skeleton, disabled button, loading label) → the deferred chunk is fetched and executed → the feature (configurator, chat, editor, map) opens fully → repeat interactions reuse the cached chunk with no new download.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dynamic `import()` inside the event handler; the module must be verifiably absent from the initial route bundle (DevTools Coverage / waterfall). Loading feedback should show within roughly **100 ms** of the interaction; the triggered flow must not create new long tasks above **50 ms** before loading starts. Named candidates: chat widgets, rich text editors, map embeds, export/print flows, advanced filters, configurators, comparison tools. Named exclusions: first-screen navigation, the primary purchase/sign-in action, LCP content, anything the first interaction depends on. Priority: high · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/import-on-interaction (sibling pattern: ⟦S1087⟧ import-on-visibility.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Heavy optional homepage machinery — quote calculators/configurators, chat, map embeds — anywhere a feature's code would otherwise tax every visitor for the few who open it.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1086⟧

## ⟦S1087⟧ import-on-visibility — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: code for offscreen sections loads when the section approaches the viewport (Intersection Observer), not at first paint and not only when it is already on screen.
- **How it looks:** A long page whose first screen is light, while heavy lower sections — reviews, charts, embeds — are simply *ready* when the visitor scrolls to them: a reserved-height placeholder holds the space, then the real content is there with no jump and no spinner-wait.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: visitor scrolls → a section crosses the pre-load margin (hundreds of pixels before it becomes visible) → its module is fetched and mounted into the reserved placeholder → visitor arrives to a finished section; the observer disconnects so it loads exactly once.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `IntersectionObserver` with `rootMargin` — prescribed starting range **300–1000 px** for heavier modules (worked examples use `'400px 0px'` and `'500px 0px'`), tuned against asset weight and scroll speed. Placeholder/skeleton must reserve the final height (example: `minHeight: 320`) so loading causes **no CLS**; headings, landmarks and focus order must already make sense before hydration. Named candidates: charts, reviews sections, related products, embeds, offscreen dashboards. Priority: high · intermediate · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/import-on-visibility (references patterns.dev's import-on-visibility pattern and MDN's Intersection Observer API; sibling: ⟦S1086⟧.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Long homepages with expensive below-fold sections — proof/reviews, work/gallery, towns/areas — keeping the hero's load clean without making later sections feel unfinished.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1087⟧

## ⟦S1088⟧ improve-rule — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Meta-skill for the checklist project itself: how to review and raise the quality score of a Front-End Checklist rule MDX file — fixing stub prompts, adding missing fields, enriching with real code examples. It governs the corpus the rest of this range is drawn from; it is not a website rule.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on any page — its output is a better rule document: specific audit prompts instead of "Verify if the project adheres to…", ✅/❌ example pairs, and a structure that passes the project's own validator.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scoring rubric (bundled `references/scoring-rubric.md`): prompts 30 pts (check 10, fix 10, explain 10 — a stub pattern scores 3), metadata 20 (tldr 5 — needs 3+ bullets; whyItMatters 5 — >40 characters of user impact; aiContext 5; relatedRules 5 — 2+ entries), body 20 (codeExamples 10 — 3+ fenced blocks; bodyDepth 10 — 300+ words), bonus 10 (resources 5, codeReview prompt 5). Rubric maximum 80; grades A ≥68, B ≥56, C ≥44; **minimum passing score 50**, enforced in CI. Tool commands named: `pnpm score:rules packages/content/rules/en/{category}/{slug}.mdx` and `pnpm validate:rule-structure …`. Required body order: intro → `## Code Example(s)` → `## Why It Matters` → optional guidance (Exceptions, Standards, Browser Support) → `## Verification` last, with Automated/Manual subsections.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist project — https://frontendchecklist.io (no per-rule page; the skill's reference is its own scoring-rubric.md.)
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES
- **Best for:** Maintaining this checklist corpus only — no section, page or trade application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1088⟧

## ⟦S1089⟧ inclusive-language — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility/content rule: all user-facing language — copy, labels, error messages, placeholders, even code identifiers — avoids ableist, gendered and culture-bound wording.
- **How it looks:** The words on the page: error messages that guide instead of blame ("Please enter a valid email address (example: name@domain.com)" rather than "You entered an invalid email"), forms that ask for a full name once instead of assuming first/last structure, success text with no idioms ("Complete! Your changes are saved." rather than "Home run!").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Substitution table from the rule: crazy/insane → unexpected/surprising; lame → uninteresting/ineffective; blind to / turn a blind eye → unaware of / ignore; deaf to → unresponsive to; dumb → silent; cripple → disable/impair; sanity check → confidence check / validation; dummy → placeholder/sample. Gender-neutral default (they/users/people); gender fields optional with "Prefer not to say", non-binary and other options; titles optional (Mx. named). Placeholders generic or international (`+1 555 123 4567` with country-code help text). Ships with a four-part review checklist (ableist terms, gender, tone, names & identity). Priority: medium · beginner · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/inclusive-language (standards named: W3C WAI WCAG overview, MDN Accessibility.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Copy pass over hero, process and form text on any homepage — especially form labels, error states and quote-form wording, where blaming or assumptive language costs conversions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1089⟧

## ⟦S1090⟧ indexability — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: pages meant to rank must not be blocked from indexing by any of the three independent blocking mechanisms — meta robots `noindex`, the `X-Robots-Tag` header, or robots.txt.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page — the failure this prevents is absence: the homepage or a town page silently missing from Google results while looking perfectly fine to its owner.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Three-mechanism table from the rule: `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` (single page, read by crawlers that fetched it), `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` header (single resource), robots.txt `Disallow` (URL pattern, read before fetching). Audit per important page: check the meta tag, `curl -I … | grep -i 'x-robots'`, `curl -s … | grep -i 'robots'`, robots.txt, then confirm in Search Console URL Inspection ("URL is on Google"). Named accident sources: staging promoted to production, CMS default noindex (Next.js `robots: { index: false }` in metadata is the worked example), overly broad Disallow. Legitimate use is conditional only — drafts/previews noindexed, published pages not. Fixes are per-mechanism, followed by Request Indexing and Coverage monitoring. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/indexability (companion: ⟦S1091⟧ audits conflicts between these same signals.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Launch gate for the homepage and every towns/areas page — checked once per deployment, catastrophic if missed.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1090⟧

## ⟦S1091⟧ indexability-conflicts — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: the crawl/index signals on a page must agree — robots.txt, meta robots, `X-Robots-Tag` and canonical tags giving contradictory instructions leave pages in indexing limbo.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible on the page; the symptom lives in Search Console — URLs stuck as "Blocked by robots.txt" yet known to Google, or canonicalised pages that never settle into the index.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The core distinction: robots.txt is a *crawl* directive, `noindex` an *indexing* directive — a robots-blocked page is never fetched, so its `noindex` is never read. Conflict table from the rule: robots block + on-page `noindex` → noindex never read; `noindex` in meta + `index` in X-Robots-Tag → most restrictive wins (noindex); canonical → a noindexed page → undefined behaviour, canonical may be ignored; sitemap listing noindexed URLs → conflicting inclusion/exclusion. Fixes: to exclude a page, remove the robots block and keep a readable `noindex, follow`; canonical targets must be indexable; resolve duplicated meta/header signals to one intent; verify per page in URL Inspection. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/indexability-conflicts (companion to ⟦S1090⟧; references Google's robots-meta and robots.txt documentation.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Post-launch and post-migration SEO audits, especially where preview/staging copies of a homepage coexist with the live one.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1091⟧

## ⟦S1092⟧ input-image-alt — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: an `<input type="image">` used as a form button must carry a non-empty `alt` that names the action it performs.
- **How it looks:** Visually unchanged — an image submit button (a magnifier-glass search button, a graphic "submit" button). The difference is functional: a screen reader announces "Search" or "Submit Registration"; without alt it may read the raw filename ("go.png") and the button is unusable, and if the image fails to load the alt text is what remains to click.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rule: every `<input type="image">` has a non-empty alt describing the *action*, not the picture — correct: `alt="Search"`, `alt="Submit Registration"`; wrong: `alt="Magnifying glass"`, or no alt at all. One or two words is the prescribed length. Unlike decorative images, a functional image button must never take empty alt. WCAG 1.1.1 (non-text content) is the cited basis. Priority: **critical** · beginner · 5 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/input-image-alt (references WCAG 1.1.1 and MDN's `<input type="image">` reference.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Forms — only where a quote/contact form still uses image submit buttons (rare in modern builds, but a critical-severity fail when present).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1092⟧

## ⟦S1093⟧ input-types — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** HTML rule: every form field uses the semantic input `type` (plus `inputmode` and `autocomplete`) that matches its data, instead of `type="text"` for everything.
- **How it looks:** On a phone, the keyboard itself changes per field: the email field shows `@` and `.com` keys, the phone field opens the numeric dial pad, a date field opens the native picker — and returning visitors get correct one-tap autofill for name, address and phone.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: visitor taps a field → the keyboard/picker matching that field's type appears (email layout, dial pad, date wheel) → entry is validated in the browser's own format → autofill offers the stored value for the field's `autocomplete` token.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Type set prescribed: `email`, `tel`, `url`, `search`, `password`, `number`, `range`, `date` (returns YYYY-MM-DD), `time`, `datetime-local`, `month`, `week`, `color`, `file`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `hidden`. `inputmode` decouples keyboard from validation: numeric-looking text (postcodes, card numbers) uses `type="text" inputmode="numeric"`; `decimal` for decimal pads. Autocomplete tokens named: `name`, `given-name`, `family-name`, `email`, `tel`, `street-address`, `address-level2`, `postal-code`, `country-name`, `cc-name`, `cc-number`, `cc-exp`, `cc-csc`, `username`, `current-password`, `new-password`. The rule cites up to **40% faster form completion** for returning users when types and autocomplete combine. Priority: high · beginner · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/input-types (standards named: MDN HTML, WHATWG HTML Living Standard.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
