- **Best for:** Forms — the quote/contact form is the conversion point of every trade homepage; phone and email fields are exactly where this rule pays.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1093⟧

## ⟦S1094⟧ integration-testing — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Testing rule: key workflows are covered by integration tests that exercise units wired together (API route + database, form + submission + feedback), because wiring bugs are invisible to unit tests.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on any page — its product is a CI suite that fails the build when a connected flow breaks, e.g. a profile form that submits, persists and shows its success message.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Worked patterns: Supertest against the real app with a migrated, seeded test database (happy path asserts the 201 response *and* the saved row; duplicate email asserts 400); React Testing Library + user-event driving form → API → state → rendered feedback, with mocked 422s for the error path. High-value targets listed: API routes + queries, form submission flows, authentication (login → session → protected route), cart + checkout + order creation, upload + processing + display, search → results. Explicitly skip: pure utilities, simple transforms, dependency-free components. Verified by running the suite and confirming it fails when the rule is violated — warnings alone do not count. Priority: high · intermediate · 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/integration-testing (references Playwright documentation and Testing Library guiding principles.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Project QA on form-handling and lead-capture flows behind a homepage; no design or section application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1094⟧

## ⟦S1095⟧ interaction-to-next-paint — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: optimise Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — every tap, click and keypress on the page must produce a visible response within 200 ms, across the whole session, not just the first interaction.
- **How it looks:** Controls that answer instantly: a filter chip, accordion or gallery control visibly reacts the moment it is tapped — no dead beat between press and paint, even on a mid-range phone, even after the page has been open for minutes.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: visitor taps/clicks/keys → handler runs; if its work is chunked or deferred, the pressed/loading state paints immediately → heavy processing continues in slices (yielding between chunks) or in a worker → the final result paints. Failure shape the rule targets: one long synchronous handler → nothing paints until it finishes → the interaction feels frozen.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Thresholds: **0–200 ms good, 200–500 ms needs improvement, >500 ms poor**; any task over **50 ms** is a long task. INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in 2024 and covers all interactions, worst-case representative. Techniques: yield to the main thread periodically (`setTimeout` yield, or `scheduler.yield()`), web workers for heavy computation, `startTransition`/`requestIdleCallback` to defer non-urgent work after immediate feedback, batch DOM reads before writes (no layout thrashing), debounce frequent events (300 ms search example). Measure with the web-vitals `onINP` callback, DevTools Performance, PageSpeed field data; test under 6× CPU throttling. Priority: high · advanced · 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/interaction-to-next-paint
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Every interactive element on an animated homepage — version switchers, accordions, galleries, configurators — where rich motion code competes with input response.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1095⟧

## ⟦S1096⟧ internal-links — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: key pages must receive multiple internal links with descriptive anchor text from topically related pages, because internal links are how PageRank and crawler discovery flow through a site.
- **How it looks:** Nothing stylistic — it is the link fabric inside the copy: body text that links its subject ("our guide to CSS Grid" style descriptive anchors), a "Related articles" block closing a page, and a pillar page that lists its cluster pages. Pages nobody links to become orphans found only via the sitemap.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit method: crawl → build the internal link graph → compute in-degree per page → flag important pages with **0–2 incoming links**. Link-value table from the rule: contextual inline (body) highest, related-articles sections high, top navigation medium (sitewide), sidebar medium, footer lower. Prescribed fixes: list the top 10–20 pages by business value, add contextual links from 3–5 related pages each, descriptive keyword-bearing anchor text (never "click here"), pillar ↔ cluster linking both directions, top navigation carrying the 5–10 most important commercial pages. Anchor text is itself a topic signal to Google. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/internal-links (references Google's crawlable-links guidance and the SEO Starter Guide's anchor-text section.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Multi-page sites — service pages and towns/areas pages linking into each other and into the homepage's key offers; minor for a single-page preview.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1096⟧

## ⟦S1097⟧ interstitials — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** CSS/SEO/accessibility rule: no intrusive interstitials — full-screen pop-ups, overlays and banners that cover the main content, above all on mobile immediately after arrival from search.
- **How it looks:** The bad shape: the page lands and a full-viewport overlay (100% × 100%, dark backdrop, z-index 9999) buries the content until dismissed. The prescribed shape: content fully visible on arrival, with any notice docked as a slim sticky banner along the bottom edge occupying at most about 15% of the viewport height.
- **Frame by frame:** Bad path — trigger: page load (or a few seconds after) → overlay fades/covers the whole screen → visitor must find and work a close control before reaching any content; keyboard focus is lost behind the overlay. Good path — trigger: page load → page renders unobstructed → a small sticky banner sits at the bottom edge → visitor reads the page and dismisses the banner at leisure. Modal path (when a dialog is genuinely needed): trigger opens it → focus moves into the dialog and is trapped there → Escape or close dismisses it → focus returns to the element that opened it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Google demotes mobile pages showing content-covering interstitials after a search click (Intrusive Interstitials update, January 2017). Acceptable: age verification, legally required notices (cookie consent), login walls for private content; delayed, easily dismissed newsletter dialogs only with caution. Replacement shapes: sticky banner `max-height: 15vh` (fix text says 10–15% of viewport), inline content blocks, slide-in panels that do not cover main content. Required dialog mechanics: `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, `aria-labelledby`/`aria-describedby`, focus trap, Escape to close, focus return — WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) and SC 4.1.3 (Status Messages) cited. Detect via `position: fixed`/absolute + high z-index covering the viewport at <600 px widths. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/interstitials
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Call/CTA and forms — governs cookie notices, offer banners and any pop-up quote prompt on a homepage; a full-screen load-time pop-up is a named ranking and accessibility failure.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1097⟧

## ⟦S1098⟧ invalid-links — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: every navigational link must be a real `<a href>` with a valid URL — empty hrefs, `javascript:void(0)`, missing hrefs and click-handler divs are invisible to crawlers.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visually different — a "Products" item that is secretly a `<div onclick>` looks identical to a real link, but Googlebot cannot follow it, the destination gets no PageRank, and keyboard/screen-reader navigation degrades with it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Crawlable = an `<a>` element + an `href` attribute + a valid relative or absolute URL (Google's crawlable-links definition). Flag list: absent href, `href=""`, bare `href="#"`, `href` starting `javascript:` or `void`, plus `<div>`/`<span>`/`<button>` elements carrying navigation `onclick` with no corresponding anchor. `mailto:`/`tel:` are valid but not crawlable for discovery — counted separately. Fix pattern: keep the real URL in the href and let JavaScript *enhance* it (`onclick` may open a modal after `preventDefault`, the href still carries the route); action-only controls become `<button>`; fragment links must point at an `id` that exists. Manual check query given: `document.querySelectorAll('a:not([href]), a[href=""], a[href^="javascript:"]')`. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/invalid-links (references Google Search Central's crawlable-links documentation and MDN's anchor element reference.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Navigation and section links in JS-heavy builds — framework routers and custom switchers must still render real anchors underneath (tel: links for call CTAs are the legitimate exception).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1098⟧

## ⟦S1099⟧ javascript-inline — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: no behaviour inline in the HTML — no `onclick`/`onmouseover` attributes, no `javascript:` URLs, no scattered inline script blocks; behaviour lives in external files wired with `addEventListener` and `data-*` attributes.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — the visitor sees the same buttons and hovers. The difference is underneath: the same external script is cached once and reused across pages, and the page still works under a strict Content Security Policy that would silently disable inline code.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Failure list the rule enumerates: no caching (JS re-downloaded with every page), CSP violations and XSS surface, no minification, blocked HTML parsing, untestable scattered code. Prescribed shape: external `<script src … defer>` files; event delegation from one document-level listener dispatching on `data-action`; CSP header shown: `script-src 'self'` (with `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`). The rule's own stated exception: critical above-the-fold JavaScript may be inlined. Priority: high · beginner · 15 min. Honest trade note for this bank: the portfolio deliverable format is a single self-contained HTML file, which is inline by construction — treat the rule as applying to multi-file production sites, and the single-file preview format as a deliberate, documented deviation in the spirit of the rule's own critical-code exception.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/javascript-inline (references MDN's `<script>` element and `addEventListener` documentation.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Production multi-page builds and CSP-governed hosting; a structural check when a design graduates from preview file to a real site.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1099⟧

## ⟦S1100⟧ javascript-linter — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: the codebase is linted (ESLint, or Biome) in the editor, in build tooling and in CI, so syntax errors, dangerous patterns and style drift are caught before runtime.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on any page — its surface is the developer's editor underlines and a CI check that blocks a bad merge; visitors only benefit indirectly through fewer shipped bugs.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Setup: `pnpm dlx eslint --init`; shared configs `eslint:recommended`, airbnb-base, `@typescript-eslint`, framework plugins (react + react-hooks + jsx-a11y, vue). Core error rules prescribed as `error`: `no-debugger`, `no-alert`, `no-unused-vars`, `no-undef`, `no-unreachable`, `eqeqeq`, `no-eval`, `no-implied-eval`, `no-new-func`, `no-script-url`, `prefer-const`, `no-var`. Security plugin set: `security/detect-eval-with-expression`, `detect-object-injection`, `detect-unsafe-regex`, plus `no-secrets`. Complexity caps in the advanced config: complexity max 10, max-depth 4, max-lines 300 (skipComments), max-lines-per-function 50, max-params 5, max-statements 20. Workflow: husky + lint-staged running `eslint --fix` on staged files, GitHub Actions lint job with annotated reports. Priority: medium · beginner · 20 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/javascript-linter (tools named: ESLint, Biome, typescript-eslint.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Build-pipeline hygiene for any coded deliverable; no section or design application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1100⟧

## ⟦S1101⟧ javascript-minification — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: all production JavaScript is minified — whitespace, comments and long identifiers removed and dead code eliminated by the build tool, never by hand.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible — the same scripts arrive as a single dense line of code; the visitor's gain is download and parse time, largest on mobile networks.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Typical saving **50–70%**; the rule's worked example shrinks an auth module from ~2.1 KB to ~0.32 KB (**~85%**). Toolchain: Terser (webpack TerserPlugin, Vite `minify: 'terser'` or `'esbuild'`, Rollup terser plugin; Next.js SWC minify; CRA/Vue CLI minimizer overrides). Prescribed compress flags: `drop_console`, `drop_debugger`, `dead_code`, `unused`, `conditionals`, `evaluate`, `booleans`, `loops`, `passes: 2`; mangle `toplevel: true`, property mangling only for `^_`-prefixed names; `comments: false`. Safety rails: keep `keep_fnames`/`keep_fargs` where error reporting or libraries need them, reserve dynamic names (`$`, `jQuery`) from mangling, ship `hidden-source-map` for production debugging, and pair minification with tree-shaking (`usedExports`, `sideEffects: false`) and code splitting. Priority: high · beginner · 15 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/javascript-minification
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Delivery step for scripted sections on hosted builds; inside the bank's single-file previews the equivalent discipline is keeping the embedded script lean rather than running a minifier over the file.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1101⟧

## ⟦S1102⟧ js-file-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: keep individual JavaScript bundles under a compressed size budget; oversized bundles are paid for three times — download, parse/compile, execute — all on the main thread.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible when held; when broken, the page looks loaded but ignores taps — the device disparity the rule cites: a 1 MB script parses in ~1 s on a flagship phone but ~10 s on a budget device, which is the visitor's frozen first screen.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Budget: **individual JS bundles under 200 KB compressed (gzip/brotli)**. Levers: code splitting (dynamic `import()` / Next.js `dynamic()` with a loading fallback), tree-shaking via named ES-module imports (the rule's example: `import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` instead of the whole library), dependency audits, gzip/brotli always on. Tools named: webpack-bundle-analyzer, Lighthouse, BundlePhobia, DevTools Coverage tab. Knock-on metric: slow FID/INP feeds Core Web Vitals rankings. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/js-file-size (companion loading patterns: ⟦S1086⟧, ⟦S1087⟧; minification in ⟦S1101⟧.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Whole-page budget on animation-heavy homepages — the check that keeps GSAP/3D machinery from silently taxing every mobile visitor.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1102⟧

## ⟦S1103⟧ js-libraries — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance/security rule: JavaScript dependencies are audited for known vulnerabilities and outdated or bloated packages are updated or swapped for lightweight or native alternatives.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — the library list behind the page: current, patched and tree-shakable, instead of an old monolith carrying redundant polyfills and known XSS vectors.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit commands: `npm audit` / `pnpm audit` / `yarn audit`, wired into CI; Snyk and Dependabot named for continuous scanning; BundlePhobia checked before any library is added. The rule's worked swap: Moment.js (**280 KB+**, whole-library import) → date-fns modular imports (`format(new Date(), 'MMMM do yyyy')`), and native APIs (`Intl` for formatting, `fetch` for requests) preferred where they cover the need. Selection criteria: ES modules + tree-shaking support, pinned versions, reliable CDN or self-hosting. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/js-libraries
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Dependency decisions when a build reaches for an animation or utility library — the audit that precedes adding anything heavy to a homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1103⟧

## ⟦S1104⟧ js-redirects — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: never redirect with JavaScript (`window.location`) — redirects belong at the server or edge as real 301/302 responses.
- **How it looks:** The failure is a visible hiccup: the visitor briefly sees the original page flash, then is thrown to the destination after the script finally runs. Done right, the browser never renders the wrong page at all — the redirect happens before any HTML arrives.
- **Frame by frame:** Bad path — trigger: visitor requests a URL → full HTML downloads → browser parses and executes the script → `window.location` fires → a second full request/round trip → destination paints (with a flash of the first page in between). Good path — trigger: request → server/edge answers 301/302 immediately → browser requests the destination → it paints once.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Cost named: at least one full extra round trip versus a server redirect, plus unreliable link-equity transfer (301s are the reliable vehicle). Prescribed: web-server config (nginx/Apache), edge configuration (Cloudflare, Vercel), edge functions for state-dependent redirects, Next.js server-side `redirect: { destination, permanent }` as the worked example. `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` is rated "avoid if possible, but better than JS". Verify with `curl -I` and the DevTools Network 3xx chain; Ahrefs Redirect Checker and httpstatus.io named. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/js-redirects (references web.dev Learn Performance and the Lighthouse overview.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Site-structure work — moved pages, campaign landers, www/protocol consolidation (with ⟦S1074⟧); rarely a homepage-design concern, costly when it appears.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1104⟧

## ⟦S1105⟧ json-ld-valid — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: every JSON-LD structured-data block must be syntactically valid JSON, use `@context` `https://schema.org`, a real schema.org `@type`, and all required properties for that type.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page itself — the payoff is in Google's results: star ratings, FAQ expansions and breadcrumb trails attached to the listing. The failure is silent: one trailing comma and the whole block is ignored, with no error anywhere a visitor or owner would see.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Validation sequence: `JSON.parse()` the block (trailing commas, single quotes and missing brackets are the named killers) → `@context` exactly `"https://schema.org"` → `@type` against schema.org → required properties per type: Article needs `headline`, `author`, `datePublished`; Product needs `name`; FAQPage needs `mainEntity` (Question/acceptedAnswer); BreadcrumbList needs `itemListElement` (ListItem with position, name, item). Generate programmatically with `JSON.stringify` — never hand-write JSON-LD strings. Validate in Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema Markup Validator; monitor via Search Console's rich-results report. Only mark up what the visible page content truthfully supports. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/json-ld-valid (references Google's structured-data introduction and the schema.org specification.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Every trade homepage's invisible layer — LocalBusiness with aggregate rating, FAQ and breadcrumb schema is what turns the proof/reviews content into starred search listings; pair with the FAQ and reviews sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1105⟧

## ⟦S1106⟧ json-safety — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: every `JSON.parse()` is wrapped in try/catch with a fallback, and the parsed shape is validated before any property is read — malformed JSON from APIs, localStorage or users must never crash the page.
- **How it looks:** Nothing when right; when wrong, one corrupt stored value or one non-JSON API response throws an uncaught SyntaxError and the widget (or page) dies silently mid-interaction.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Runtime sequence the rule prescribes: raw string arrives → parse inside try/catch → shape check (types / schema) → data used; on any failure → fallback value or null, error logged, page continues.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pattern given: `safeParse(json, fallback = null)` returning the fallback on throw. Shape validation before deep access (`typeof data?.user?.profile?.name !== 'string'` → reject), escalating to schema libraries — Zod/Valibot (`UserSchema.parse` / `safeParse` returning `{ success, data, error }`). `JSON.stringify` edge cases catalogued: `undefined` and functions are dropped from objects, `stringify(undefined)` returns `undefined` (not a string), `Date` serialises to a string, `Map` serialises to `{}` — guard with `result ?? fallback`. For fetch: check `response.ok` and that `content-type` includes `application/json` before `response.json()`. Priority: medium · beginner · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/json-safety (standards named: MDN JavaScript Guide, web.dev Learn JavaScript.)
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Best for:** Any scripted section reading stored or fetched data — saved form state, configurator presets, review feeds — inside the page's own JavaScript.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1106⟧

## ⟦S1107⟧ keyboard-navigation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: every interactive element is reachable and operable by keyboard alone, in a focus order that matches the visual reading order, with hidden content removed from the tab sequence.
- **How it looks:** A visible focus indicator travelling the page in reading order — top to bottom, left to right — landing on every button, link, card control and form field in the order the eye meets them; nothing focusable hides off-screen, and a modal holds focus inside itself until Escape releases it back to what opened it.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: visitor presses Tab → focus advances to the next interactive element in DOM/visual order (Shift+Tab reverses) → Enter activates links/buttons, Space activates buttons and toggles checkboxes, arrow keys move inside widgets (menus, tabs, sliders) → Escape closes modals, menus and dropdowns → focus returns to the trigger.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The rule's figure: **15% of users rely on keyboard navigation**. Laws: never use positive `tabindex` (it breaks natural flow — the worked anti-example reorders buttons 3/1/2); hidden or closed content takes `tabindex="-1"` / `display: none` so it cannot receive focus; a `<div onclick>` is not keyboard-accessible — use a native `<button>`, or as a fallback `role="button" tabindex="0"` with Enter/Space key handlers. Focus trapping is legitimate **only** inside an active modal/popover with a working Escape path — trapping in drawers, carousels, chat widgets or sticky banners is a keyboard trap (failure). Test prescribed: unplug the mouse and traverse the whole page. Priority: **critical** · intermediate · 30 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/keyboard-navigation (standards named: W3C WAI WCAG overview, MDN Accessibility; dialog behaviour pairs with ⟦S1097⟧.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** All interactive sections — navigation, version switchers, galleries, accordions, forms and footer — the operability gate every control must pass, especially custom-built ones.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1107⟧

## ⟦S1108⟧ keyword-stuffing — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: write copy naturally with topical variation — never repeat target phrases at manipulative density in body text, titles, headings, meta descriptions or alt text.
- **How it looks:** The difference is readable on the page: natural copy that varies its terms ("search engine optimisation", "ranking strategies", "organic search tips" for one topic) versus a paragraph that chants the same phrase in every sentence, a heading that repeats it three times, and alt text that is a comma-separated keyword list instead of a description.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit thresholds from the rule: flag any keyword/phrase above **~3% density** of total word count (target primary-keyword density **under 2–3%**), any keyword appearing **more than 3× in the `<title>`**, context-free keyword lists, keyword-list alt text, and hidden text (white-on-white, 1 px, `display:none` stuffing — a serious violation). Prescribed placement: keyword once in the title (near the front), once naturally in the H1, once in the meta description if natural. Detection: tokenise stripped body text, compute word/bigram/trigram frequencies, check title/meta/alt separately, sanity-check with Flesch Reading Ease. Enforcement named: Google's Panda (now core) and SpamBrain demote or remove stuffed pages. Priority: medium · intermediate · 10 min.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule — https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/keyword-stuffing (references Google's keyword-stuffing spam policy.)
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Best for:** Copy pass over hero, service and towns/areas text — town-listing pages are the classic stuffing trap (blocks of place names without substance are named in Google's definition, quoted in the rule).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1108⟧
# Skills chunk — S1109–S1151 (43 entries)

All 43 are individual rule-skills from **The Front-End Checklist** (thedaviddias/front-end-checklist), Part "MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills". Each is one checkable rule packaged the same way: a when-to-use trigger, the rule, Quick Reference, Check / Fix / Explain / Code Review actions, a rule page at frontendchecklist.io, and a bundled `references/rule.md` carrying priority · difficulty · time, code examples and verification steps. These are audit/QA rules, not visual designs — "How it looks" describes the visitor-facing end state when the rule is followed, and most are static.

**Duplicate check:** no two skills in this range are the same underlying skill under different names. Three related families are distinct rules with distinct rule pages and are indexed in full separately: landmarks (S1110 one-main / S1111 regions / S1147 navigation), lazy loading (S1114 never above the fold / S1115 always below it — complementary halves, not copies), lists (S1122 list children / S1124 list-item parents — opposite directions of the same structure rule).

## ⟦S1109⟧ label-content-name-mismatch — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: a control's accessible name must contain its visible label text, so voice-control users can activate it by speaking the words they see (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name). Rule page carries Check/Fix/Explain plus a bundled rule.md (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** Nothing changes visually — buttons and links keep their printed words ("Submit", "Add item"). The difference is invisible: the name a screen reader or voice assistant uses for the button is those same printed words.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Interaction: a voice user says "click Submit" → the control whose accessible name starts with "Submit" activates; if the aria-label said "Send feedback" instead, the command fails.
- **Mechanism & key values:** If `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` is used at all, it must begin with the exact visible label string; preferred fix is no aria-label — rely on the visible text content. Verify in the browser accessibility tree; axe/Lighthouse flag mismatches.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/label-content-name-mismatch; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.3.
- **Best for:** Every interactive element on a homepage — call/CTA buttons, nav links, form submit buttons. Direct trade fit: the "Get my quote" and tap-to-call buttons must be speakable by their printed words.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a hard accessibility requirement on every CTA a build ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1109⟧

## ⟦S1110⟧ landmark-one-main — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: each page has exactly one main landmark — one `<main>` element and no extra `role="main"` containers (priority medium · beginner · 5 min).
- **How it looks:** Visually identical either way — header, nav, page content, footer in their usual stacked layout. The landmark exists only in the accessibility tree: one clearly bounded "primary content" region between the global header/nav and the footer.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Interaction: a screen-reader user presses the main-landmark shortcut → focus lands directly at the start of the page's unique content, skipping all repeated navigation.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Count of `<main>` + `[role="main"]` must equal exactly 1; `<main>` is never nested inside `<article>`, `<aside>` or `<nav>`; only page-unique content goes inside; it is the normal target of "Skip to content" links.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/landmark-one-main; MDN `<main>` element; WAI-ARIA 1.2 main role.
- **Best for:** Page skeleton of every build — the structural wrapper the whole homepage sits in.
- **Tier:** STRONG — basic page-structure law for every section stack.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1110⟧

## ⟦S1111⟧ landmark-regions — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: build page structure from HTML5 landmark elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`) instead of generic `<div>` containers, and label repeated landmarks of the same type (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** The familiar page frame — banner header with title and nav on top, main article content in the middle, footer at the bottom — but each zone is a real semantic region a screen reader can list and jump between, not an anonymous div.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Interaction: screen-reader landmark navigation moves the user header → nav → main → footer in single keystrokes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** One `<main>`; multiple `<nav>` elements distinguished with `aria-label` (e.g. "Main navigation"); replace div containers with the semantic elements; also an SEO structure signal.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/landmark-regions; MDN Accessibility; W3C WAI WCAG overview.
- **Best for:** Navigation, footer and the overall homepage skeleton; pairs with S1110 (one main) and S1147 (nav regions in detail).
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational structure rule for every build.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1111⟧

## ⟦S1112⟧ lang-attribute — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (html)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: the `<html>` element must carry a valid, non-empty BCP 47 `lang` attribute matching the page's language, with `lang` repeated on elements where the language changes inline (priority high · beginner · 5 min; WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.1 Level A, SC 3.1.2 Level AA).
- **How it looks:** No visual change on screen. What the visitor gets: a screen reader pronounces the page with the correct voice (French text is not read in an English accent), the browser offers translation correctly, hyphenation and spell-check use the right dictionary.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<html lang="en">` / `en-US` / `en-GB` / `fr` / `zh-Hans` / `zh-Hant` / `ar` (with `dir="rtl"`); empty `lang=""` counts as missing; full names like `lang="english"` are invalid; codes validated against the IANA Language Subtag Registry; nested `lang` only where language actually changes.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/lang-attribute; WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.1 / 3.1.2; HTML Living Standard lang attribute.
- **Best for:** The root element of every page a build ships — a five-minute, Level A requirement.
- **Tier:** STRONG — mandatory baseline, zero cost.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1112⟧

## ⟦S1113⟧ largest-contentful-paint — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: the page's largest visible element (usually the hero image or hero heading) must render within 2.5 seconds — LCP, the Core Web Vital for perceived load speed (priority critical · intermediate · 25 min).
- **How it looks:** The hero arrives essentially complete on first paint: full-width hero photo (or the big headline, or a video poster) visible almost immediately instead of a blank or half-built first screen that fills in late.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: navigation → server returns HTML fast (TTFB) → the browser discovers the hero resource in the initial scan → it downloads at high priority → the hero paints, complete, at or under the 2.5s mark; failure modes are late discovery, heavy transfer, or the hero being held back by client-side rendering until after fetches/hydration.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Thresholds: ≤2.5s good · 2.5–4s needs improvement · >4s poor. Techniques: `<link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high">` on the route's actual LCP asset, server-render the LCP candidate, responsive image sizes/formats, CDN/edge delivery, `font-display: swap` + preloaded fonts for text LCP; anti-patterns: lazy-loading the LCP element, multiple `fetchpriority="high"` images, preloading the wrong variant. Measured with Lighthouse / PageSpeed Insights / web-vitals.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/largest-contentful-paint; web.dev Learn Performance; PageSpeed Insights.
- **Best for:** Hero sections above all — the single metric that decides whether a trade homepage feels instant; also any full-width lead image or poster.
- **Tier:** CROWN — the bank's governing load-speed rule for heroes; every hero version lives or dies by it.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1113⟧

## ⟦S1114⟧ lazy-above-fold — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: never put `loading="lazy"` on images in the initial viewport — lazy loading the hero delays LCP because the browser deprioritises the download until it confirms the image is visible (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** The first screen's imagery (hero photo, lead product shot) is simply there as the page paints — no hero-shaped hole that pops in a beat after the text.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; it governs load order: page request → above-fold images start downloading immediately at full priority alongside CSS/fonts → they paint with the first screen instead of after a visibility check.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Remove `loading="lazy"` from initial-viewport images; add `fetchpriority="high"` to the LCP image; rule of thumb — do not lazy-load the first 2–3 images on the page; test mobile viewports separately, because fold position differs from desktop; in Next.js use the Image `priority` prop on the hero.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/lazy-above-fold; web.dev Learn Performance; Lighthouse.
- **Best for:** Hero and any first-screen gallery imagery. The necessary counterweight to S1115.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a one-attribute fix that protects the hero on every build.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1114⟧

## ⟦S1115⟧ lazy-loading — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: defer below-the-fold images, iframes, videos and heavy sections until the visitor approaches them, so initial load spends its bandwidth on the first screen (priority high · beginner · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** A long homepage that loads fast at the top; as the visitor scrolls, gallery photos, testimonial videos and embeds are already in place when reached — each deferred block sits in a reserved, correctly-sized space so nothing jumps.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: page load → only critical CSS, fonts and hero media download → visitor scrolls → an offscreen image enters the browser's lazy-load margin (or an Intersection Observer threshold, rootMargin ~200–400px) → it downloads and fades/paints into its reserved box before or as it enters the viewport → end state: full page rendered with no blank sections.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Native `loading="lazy"` on `<img>`/`<iframe>` is the default tool; Intersection Observer only for section-level deferral/custom placeholders, starting rootMargin 200px–400px (worked example uses 300px); exclude the first visible row of grids — roughly the first 2–4 images; always reserve dimensions/placeholders to keep CLS low; never lazy the LCP image (see S1114).
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/lazy-loading; web.dev Learn Performance; Lighthouse.
- **Best for:** Work/gallery grids, review videos, map and video embeds, long process sections — the weight-saving half of image strategy on media-heavy trade homepages.
- **Tier:** STRONG — standard practice on every media-heavy build.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1115⟧

## ⟦S1116⟧ leaked-secrets — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (security)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: no API keys, tokens or credentials may exist in client-side code, HTML or committed files — anything shipped to a browser is public, and found secrets must be rotated immediately (priority critical · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — the page looks identical. What the visitor (and any attacker with DevTools) cannot find in the page source or JS bundle is a working credential.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scan for key patterns — AWS `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}`, Stripe secret `sk_live_` + 24 chars (publishable `pk_live_` is safe to expose), GitHub PAT `ghp_` + 36, Google API key `AIza` + 35 chars, JWT `eyJ…`; framework trap: Next.js `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables are inlined into the browser bundle, so secrets must never use that prefix; hunt history with `git log -S 'keyword' --all` and `git grep`; prevention via GitLeaks / TruffleHog / GitHub Secret Scanning / git-secrets pre-commit hooks and `.env*` in .gitignore; architecture: browser → your server-side API proxy → third-party API. If leaked: rotate → revoke → purge history (git filter-repo/BFG) → audit logs.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/leaked-secrets; OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet; OWASP Top 10 A02:2021; GitHub Secret Scanning docs.
- **Best for:** Any build embedding third-party services (maps, forms, analytics, chat) — a pre-launch sweep for single-file homepages and their form endpoints.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — critical when a page carries keys/endpoints; nothing to apply on a purely static page with none.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1116⟧

## ⟦S1117⟧ legacy-js — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: stop serving transpiled ES5 and blanket polyfills to modern browsers — use differential serving so modern browsers get smaller, native ES6+ code (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** No visual difference; the visitor's browser simply downloads and parses less JavaScript, so interactive pieces (switchers, sliders, forms) start working sooner.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Load sequence: browser parses the HTML → a `type="module"` script loads only in modern browsers, the `nomodule` fallback only in legacy ones → each audience gets one bundle, not both.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<script type="module" src="modern.js">` + `<script nomodule src="legacy.js">`; Vite `build.target: 'esnext'` (or es2020/es2022); browserslist recipe "defaults and supports es6-module / last 2 versions / not dead"; core-js with `useBuiltIns: 'usage'` so only used polyfills ship; Lighthouse `legacy-javascript` audit names the waste.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/legacy-js; web.dev Learn Performance; Lighthouse.
- **Best for:** The JS payload of animation-heavy single-file builds — GSAP/Three bundles and custom interaction code aimed at modern phones and desktops.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — applies where a build pipeline transpiles; a hand-written single file already targets modern browsers.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1117⟧

## ⟦S1118⟧ length — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule ("Keep URLs concise"): page paths should be short, flat and descriptive — under 100 characters, few segments, no stop words, no dates on evergreen content (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** Clean addresses a visitor can read, copy and share: `/blog/css-grid-guide` instead of `/blog/2024/03/15/technology/a-comprehensive-step-by-step-guide-to-the-basics-of-css-grid-layout-for-beginners`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Path length table: <60 chars ideal · 60–100 acceptable · 100–150 consider shortening · >150 shorten; flag more than 4 path segments; slug generation strips a stop-word set (a, an, the, and, or, but, in, on, at, to, for, of, with, how, what, your, is); dates only where the date is the identifier (news/events); every shortening ships with 301 redirects from the old URL, plus sitemap and internal-link updates.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/length; Google URL structure guidance; Google SEO Starter Guide. Companion rule S1131 (lowercase).
- **Best for:** Preview-page and service/town page URLs on trade sites — short slugs for towns and services pages; structural hygiene for any multi-page build.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — matters once a build has real URL structure beyond a single homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1118⟧

## ⟦S1119⟧ link-checker — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (html)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every internal, external, anchor, mailto, tel and file link on the site must resolve to its intended destination — checked automatically and continuously, not by hand (priority medium · beginner · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** Invisible when it passes: every link a visitor taps lands where its text promised — no 404 pages, no stale redirects, no dead PDF or phone links.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Tools: lychee (Rust; worked config: max_concurrency 8, timeout 30s, follow_redirects true, max_redirects 5), linkchecker (`--recursive --threads=10 --timeout=30`), broken-link-checker (`blc --recursive --ordered`); wire into CI (GitHub Actions example runs on push/PR plus a weekly cron `0 0 * * 0` to catch external rot) and into webpack/Vite builds with failOnError in production; redirect chains over 3 hops flagged excessive; monitor services re-check on a schedule (example: every 6 hours) and alert on breakage.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/link-checker; lychee, linkchecker and broken-link-checker project docs.
- **Best for:** Pre-launch and maintenance QA on multi-page builds — town/service page matrices and footer link blocks are where dead links accumulate.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a QA-pass tool, most valuable on larger page sets.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1119⟧

## ⟦S1120⟧ link-in-text-block — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: links inside paragraphs must be identifiable by more than colour alone — keep the underline, or meet strict contrast-plus-hover-cue conditions (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color, Level A; priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** In body copy, links read as links at a glance: underlined words inside the paragraph (the default), so a visitor with red-green colour blindness (about 8% of men, 0.5% of women) can still spot them; in the no-underline variant the link colour is visibly far from the text colour and an underline/outline appears on hover and focus.
- **Frame by frame:** Static at rest. On hover/focus in the no-underline design: a non-colour cue appears (underline draws in, outline or background change) — that state change is part of the rule, not decoration.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Option 1: `text-decoration: underline` — satisfies the rule on its own. Option 2 (technique G183) requires all three at once: link colour ≥3:1 contrast against surrounding body text AND ≥4.5:1 against the background AND a non-colour hover/focus change. Colour-only difference is documented failure F73.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/link-in-text-block; WCAG 1.4.1; Technique G183; WebAIM link guidance.
- **Best for:** Any prose with inline links — service descriptions, process copy, review text; the rule that stops a "clean minimal" redesign quietly breaking body links.
- **Tier:** STRONG — Level A law for every text block a build ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1120⟧

## ⟦S1121⟧ link-text — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: link text must describe its destination out of context — no bare "click here", "read more" or "learn more" (priority high · beginner · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** Links that read as real phrases inside the copy — "View pricing plans", "Read the React introduction guide", "Download annual report (PDF, 2.4 MB)" — so a screen-reader user listing all links on the page hears a meaningful menu instead of ten identical "Read more"s.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Each link's purpose clear from its text alone; where the visual design needs short text, extend it with `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` or a visually hidden span ("Read more" + sr-only "about Getting Started with React"); download links state file type and size; external links note "(opens in new tab)"; links navigate, actions (menus, toggles, submits) use `<button>`.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/link-text.
- **Best for:** Card grids, blog/preview teasers, "read more" patterns and CTA rows — anywhere a template repeats generic link text; also an SEO anchor-text signal.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority, beginner-cost fix on every content section.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1121⟧

## ⟦S1122⟧ list-structure — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: `<ul>` and `<ol>` may contain only `<li>` elements (plus `<script>`/`<template>`) as direct children — no wrapper `<div>` or `<p>` between the list and its items (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** Ordinary bulleted or numbered lists on screen — services lists, process steps, checklists. The rule changes nothing visible; it guarantees the screen reader announces "list of 3 items" and the visitor's position instead of miscounting or ignoring the list.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Direct children of `ul`/`ol` = `li` only; nested lists must sit inside an `<li>`; fix is to remove or relocate the offending wrapper element. Companion rule S1124 covers the opposite direction (every `<li>` needs a list parent).
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/list-structure; HTML standard (ul element content model); MDN Accessibility.
- **Best for:** Services lists, process/step sections, credential and checklist blocks — the list patterns every trade homepage repeats.
- **Tier:** STRONG — cheap structural correctness for ubiquitous components.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1122⟧

## ⟦S1123⟧ list-virtualization — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: very long lists, tables and feeds should render only the visible rows plus a small overscan buffer (windowing) instead of mounting the entire dataset (priority high · intermediate · 25 min).
- **How it looks:** A huge scrolling collection — hundreds of rows of a table, gallery or feed — that scrolls smoothly with no jank, because the DOM holds tens of row elements at a time instead of thousands; rows swap in and out as the visitor scrolls.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: scroll → rows leaving the viewport unmount → new rows entering mount just ahead of the visible edge (overscan) so fast scrolling never shows blank gaps → end state unchanged: the visitor perceives one continuous long list.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Consider virtualization when a view renders more than roughly 100–200 repeated items or total DOM approaches/exceeds ~1,500 nodes; library pattern: react-window (web.dev guidance); must preserve item sizing, keyboard navigation, selection and screen-reader semantics; avoid when SEO or find-in-page needs everything mounted, or the list is small.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/list-virtualization; Patterns.dev list virtualization; web.dev "Virtualize large lists with react-window".
- **Best for:** Towns/areas served grids, large project galleries, review walls and data tables — only when the item count is genuinely large; a normal homepage section never needs it.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — powerful but only above the item-count thresholds it names.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1123⟧

## ⟦S1124⟧ listitem — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every `<li>` must be a direct child of `<ul>`, `<ol>` or `<menu>` — orphan list items are invalid HTML and lose all list context in assistive technology (priority medium · beginner · 5 min).
- **How it looks:** Plain lists, same as S1122 — the difference is in what the screen reader announces: with a real parent it says "list, 3 items, item 2 of 3"; an orphan `<li>` inside a `<div>` is read as bare text with no count or position.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Direct parent of every `li` ∈ {ul, ol, menu}; ARIA mirror rule: `role="listitem"` must be owned by `role="list"`; fixes: wrap siblings in the right container, or replace styling-only `<li>`s with `<div>`/`<p>` + CSS; gotcha recorded in the source: `list-style: none` can strip list semantics in Safari/VoiceOver — restore them with `role="list"` on the `<ul>` (common in nav menus).
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/listitem; HTML Living Standard (li element); WAI-ARIA 1.2 listitem role; MDN.
- **Best for:** Navigation markup and any component-split templating where list pieces are generated separately — the usual orphan source.
- **Tier:** STRONG — five-minute structural check; companion to S1122.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1124⟧

## ⟦S1125⟧ llm-parsability — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: structure content so AI answer engines (Google AI Overviews, Bing Copilot, Perplexity) can extract and cite it accurately — semantic HTML, server-rendered text, self-contained sections, JSON-LD annotation (priority medium · intermediate · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** A page whose answers read as clean, standalone blocks: real heading hierarchy (h1→h2→h3), lead sentences that answer the section's question in full, explicit Q&A blocks — instead of "div soup" or content that only appears after JavaScript runs or a tab is clicked.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Content in semantic tags (`<article>`, `<section>`, headings, lists, tables) and present in the initial HTML response, not injected by JS/effects; headings descriptive enough to stand alone; sentences written context-free (no "as mentioned above"); FAQPage, HowTo and Article JSON-LD supplied alongside the visible text; content hidden behind modals/tabs/accordions counts against it.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/llm-parsability; Google AI Overviews documentation.
- **Best for:** FAQ sections, process/how-it-works copy, service explainers — the extractable content blocks of a trade homepage that can win AI-answer citations.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — valuable for content-rich pages; little to apply on a pure visual landing page.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1125⟧

## ⟦S1126⟧ llms-txt — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: documentation-heavy sites should publish a curated `/llms.txt` at the domain root giving AI tools a clean entry point to the highest-value docs pages (priority medium · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** Not a page design — a plain-text/Markdown file at `https://site/llms.txt`: an H1 title, a one-paragraph summary, then short sections of links with one-sentence descriptions (Getting Started, Concepts, API Reference, Examples), optionally pointing to a fuller `llms-full.txt`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** File must live at exactly `/llms.txt` and return HTTP 200; every listed URL absolute, public, stable and returning 200; link only task-oriented docs, never marketing/pricing/login pages; `llms-full.txt` is an optional companion, linked from llms.txt (worked route example serves it with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`); it never replaces robots.txt, sitemaps or structured data, and is not a ranking requirement; small brochure/landing sites are explicitly told to skip it.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/llms-txt; the llms.txt convention at llmstxt.org; Google Search Central AI-features guidance.
- **Best for:** Docs portals, API references and help centres only — not trade homepages or preview pages.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — no application to a local firm's homepage; recorded for completeness of the checklist.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1126⟧

## ⟦S1127⟧ loading-indicators — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (performance)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every asynchronous operation must show immediate visual feedback — skeletons for content, spinners for actions, progress bars for long processes — with ARIA state so screen readers announce it too (priority high · beginner · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** Tap "Get my quote" and the button swaps its label for a small spinning ring while it works; a loading gallery first appears as grey placeholder blocks in the exact shape of the finished cards, a soft light band sweeping across them, then the real photos land in the same boxes with no layout jump.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: async action starts → spinner appears and rotates continuously (one full turn per second, linear) / skeleton blocks render instantly with the shimmer band travelling left→right across them on a 1.5s loop / a progress bar's fill advances with its percentage → operation completes → indicator is replaced by content in pre-reserved space (min-height set) → end state: loaded UI, focus and layout unmoved.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Indicator choice by duration: skeleton 1–5s, spinner 0.5–3s, progress bar 5s+, shimmer cards 1–3s. Reference build: SVG spinner (`animate-spin`, keyframes rotate 360°, 1s linear infinite), skeleton gradient `linear-gradient(90deg,#f0f0f0 25%,#e0e0e0 50%,#f0f0f0 75%)` at `background-size: 200% 100%` with a 1.5s shimmer animation; accessibility contract: `aria-busy`, `aria-live="polite"`, `role="status"`/`role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuenow/min/max`, button disabled + `aria-busy` while loading, space reserved to prevent CLS.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/loading-indicators.
- **Best for:** Quote/contact form submission states, gallery and review loading, any fetch-driven section — the perceived-performance layer of forms and galleries on trade homepages.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the standard feedback pattern for every form and async section a build ships.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1127⟧

## ⟦S1128⟧ local-business — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: a business serving a physical location must carry LocalBusiness JSON-LD structured data so Google can show its name, address, phone, hours and rating in search results, the local pack and Maps (priority medium · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** Invisible in the page itself; visible in Google: the firm's Knowledge Panel and map-pack listing populated with correct address, phone, opening hours and a photo — the details a homeowner sees before ever clicking.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Required: `@type` (use the most specific subtype — Restaurant, DentalClinic, AutoRepair, Store…), `name`, `address` as PostalAddress (streetAddress, addressLocality, addressRegion, postalCode, addressCountry), `telephone`, `url`. Recommended: `openingHours` (e.g. "Mo-Fr 11:00-22:00"), `geo` (latitude/longitude), `image`, `priceRange`, `areaServed`, `hasMap`. Schema values must match the visible on-page address exactly (see S1146); validate with Google's Rich Results Test.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/local-business; Schema.org LocalBusiness; Google local business structured data docs.
- **Best for:** Homepage + contact page of every local trade firm — roofers, remodelers, HVAC: this is the schema block that feeds their map presence. Pairs with S1146 (NAP consistency).
- **Tier:** CROWN — for local-service homepages this is the single highest-value structured-data rule in the range.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1128⟧

## ⟦S1129⟧ locale-images — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (i18n)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: default to culture-neutral imagery (abstract/geometric icons), and where an image's meaning genuinely differs by culture, serve a locale variant through one central lookup with a neutral fallback (priority low · beginner · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** The same interface with different pictures per region only where meaning demands it — e.g. an approval badge that is a star in the default locale and a circle in Japan, where a standalone checkmark reads as "wrong"; everywhere else the icon set is abstract (envelope, padlock, magnifier, arrows) and identical worldwide.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Resolution logic per image: exact locale match (ar-SA) → language-only match (ar) → default asset.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Recorded meaning clashes: thumbs-up = offensive gesture in parts of the Middle East, West Africa, Greece, Iran; checkmark ✓ = "wrong/no" in Japan and parts of East Asia; owl = wisdom in the West, bad omen in parts of South Asia/Africa; white = mourning in China, South Korea, Japan; red = luck/prosperity in China, mourning in South Africa; OK hand = vulgar in Brazil/Turkey/parts of Europe; flag icons must never stand for languages (French is spoken in 29 countries — use the language's own name or a globe icon). Hard rule: never bake text into raster images; SVG text stays in translatable `<text>`/props. Implementation: a LocaleImage component with an assetKey → locale → path map plus neutral fallback; audit the map each release and shrink it over time.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/i18n/locale-images; W3C Internationalization cultural considerations; MDN Internationalization.
- **Best for:** Iconography choices on any page (approval/success badges, gesture imagery, colour-coded status); single-market trade homepages mostly just inherit the "prefer abstract icons, no text in images" half.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — the override machinery is for multi-locale products; the neutral-default principle is universal.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1129⟧

## ⟦S1130⟧ logical-properties — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (css)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: write direction-sensitive CSS with logical properties (inline/block) instead of physical ones (left/right), so the same stylesheet mirrors itself correctly for RTL languages and vertical writing modes (priority medium · intermediate · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** In an Arabic or Hebrew version of the page, the whole layout flips correctly with zero extra CSS: the nav item spacing, the quote's accent border and the icon's gap all move to the reading-start side automatically, instead of a broken LTR layout with Hebrew text poured into it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; the mapping is resolved by the browser from the document's writing direction at layout time.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Conversion table (physical → logical): margin-left → margin-inline-start; margin-right → margin-inline-end; margin-top → margin-block-start; margin-bottom → margin-block-end; padding-left/right → padding-inline-start/end; border-left/right → border-inline-start/end; left/right (position) → inset-inline-start/end; width → inline-size; height → block-size; min-width → min-inline-size; text-align:left → text-align:start. Shorthands: `margin-inline: 1rem 2rem` (start|end), `padding-block`, and `inset: 0` for full-cover overlays. Canonical example: `blockquote { border-inline-start: 4px solid; padding-inline-start: 1.5rem; }`.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/logical-properties; MDN CSS logical properties.
- **Best for:** Any design system or component CSS that might ever be localised; on single-locale trade builds it mainly future-proofs spacing/border code.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — no visible effect on an English-only page; decisive the day RTL is needed.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1130⟧

## ⟦S1131⟧ lowercase — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: all URL paths lowercase — because paths are case-sensitive (RFC 3986), `/Products` and `/products` are two different pages that split link equity (priority medium · beginner · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** Every address on the site in one clean form — `https://example.com/products/running-shoes` — and typing the capitalised variant lands the visitor on the lowercase page via a permanent redirect instead of a duplicate copy.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Request flow for a mixed-case URL: server compares the path with its lowercase form → replies 301 → browser loads the canonical lowercase URL.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Enforce at the server/framework layer, not ad hoc: Nginx `if ($uri != $uri_lower) { rewrite ^(.*)$ $uri_lower permanent; }`, Apache `RewriteMap lc int:tolower` + 301 rule, Next.js redirects config, or an Express middleware 301; then audit sitemap `<loc>` entries, internal links and canonical tags for stray capitals (Screaming Frog); redirect first, never just delete indexed uppercase URLs.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/lowercase; RFC 3986 §6.2.2.1; Google URL structure best practices. Companion rule S1118 (URL length).
- **Best for:** Routing hygiene on any multi-page build — service and town page matrices where slug casing drifts.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — set once at the server level, then invisible.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1131⟧

## ⟦S1132⟧ memory-leaks — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (javascript)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: hunt and fix the four classic JavaScript leak patterns — unremoved event listeners, uncleared timers, retained references to detached DOM, and closures capturing large data — especially in SPAs where nothing reloads (priority high · intermediate · 25 min).
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible at first — the symptom is temporal: a tab that starts fast and gets slower and jankier over a long session (the source's benchmark: an app can become unusable after ~30 minutes of in-app navigation) until it crashes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Leak cycle per component mount: listener/timer/reference registered → component removed → registration survives → repeats each mount, memory climbing stepwise.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Cleanup patterns with exact shapes: keep a stable handler reference so `removeEventListener` can work; group listeners under an `AbortController` and `controller.abort()` on teardown (`{ signal }` option); store interval IDs and `clearInterval` in the returned cleanup; cancel fetches with AbortController so stale responses can't update dead UI; hold DOM metadata in `WeakMap`/`WeakSet` so nodes can be collected; restructure closures so only the small result is captured, not the large source array; React: unsubscribe + clear timers in the useEffect cleanup; Vue: onUnmounted removal.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/memory-leaks; MDN JavaScript Guide; web.dev Learn JavaScript.
- **Best for:** Long-lived interactive pages — single-file homepages with scroll listeners, resize handlers, carousels and timers that stay open on a homeowner's phone; audit target whenever a build adds global listeners.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — matters in proportion to how much long-lived JS a build runs.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1132⟧

## ⟦S1133⟧ meta-description — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every indexable page carries a unique meta description of 120–160 characters, written as organic ad copy — not a ranking factor, but the text that wins or loses the click in search results (priority high · beginner · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** In Google results, under the blue title: one or two clean lines that summarise the page's value with a natural call to action — instead of a truncated fragment, the same boilerplate sentence on every page, or nothing (Google then improvises from page text).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Length table: <70 chars too short · 120–160 ideal for desktop SERPs · >160 truncated with "…" (Google measures ~920px, so character counts are approximate); must be present, non-empty, unique per page, plain text with no HTML inside the content attribute; in Next.js set per-route via metadata (`post.excerpt.slice(0, 155)` pattern) with a site-wide default in the root layout; verify in Search Console's duplicate/missing reports and a SERP simulator.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/meta-description.
- **Best for:** Every page of a build — homepage, service pages, town pages each get their own description.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high-priority, ten-minute rule with direct click-through payoff.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1133⟧

## ⟦S1134⟧ meta-in-body — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: no `<meta>` tags (or canonical links) may appear inside `<body>` — crawlers and browsers only honour metadata in `<head>`, so a body-placed noindex, description or OG tag is silently ineffective (priority high · beginner · 5 min).
- **How it looks:** The page renders identically either way — the failure is invisible on screen and shows up in outcomes: a page the owner believes is noindexed gets indexed, or social shares pull no Open Graph title because the og: tags sat in the body.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Detection: walk every `<meta>` element's ancestor chain — any with a `<body>` ancestor, or appearing after `</head>` in source, is flagged; pay special attention to `name="robots"`, `name="description"`, `property="og:*"` and `rel="canonical"`. Usual causes: CMS plugins and JS injecting into document.body — fix by targeting `document.head.appendChild(meta)`; WordPress must use the `wp_head` hook, never wp_footer/manual injection.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/meta-in-body; HTML Living Standard (meta element); MDN.
- **Best for:** Template assembly QA on any build — a five-minute parse check that protects every other metadata rule in this range.
- **Tier:** STRONG — cheap insurance for all SEO metadata work.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1134⟧

## ⟦S1135⟧ meta-refresh — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (accessibility)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: never redirect or refresh with `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` — use server-side 301/302 redirects, or a plain user-clicked link (priority medium · intermediate · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** The failure on screen: a visitor is mid-paragraph when the page suddenly vanishes and a new one loads — a screen reader restarts reading from the top and a slow reader simply loses the content. Done right, a moved page just arrives at the new URL instantly via the server, or says "this page has moved" with a link.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: the `content` timer (the source's example: `content="5; url=…"` — five seconds) expires → the browser navigates without any user action → reading position, focus and context are destroyed → end state: new page from the top.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Detection is a single search for `http-equiv="refresh"` in the HTML; fix ranking: server-side redirect (best) > clear manual link (acceptable) > meta refresh (never); grounded in WCAG timing-adjustable guidance — users must control when context changes.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/meta-refresh; MDN meta element; WCAG timing-adjustable understanding doc.
- **Best for:** Redirect handling on relaunches and URL migrations (with S1118/S1131 changes); a one-line check in any page audit.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — only appears on sites that inherited the pattern, but disqualifying when present.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1135⟧

## ⟦S1136⟧ meta-title — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every page has exactly one unique, descriptive `<title>` of 10–60 characters with the primary keyword in the first half — the clickable headline in search results and the browser tab label (priority high · beginner · 10 min).
- **How it looks:** In search results and tabs: "Sourdough Bread Recipe — Step-by-Step Guide | BakeCo" (~55 chars, keyword first) instead of "Page", a bare brand name repeated on every page, or a keyword-stuffed string.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Length table: <10 too short · 10–60 ideal (target 50–60) · 61–70 may truncate · >70 truncated (Google measures ~600px); patterns by page type: homepage = brand + tagline, post = topic + brand, product = name + key attribute, category = name + brand; Next.js: per-route `title` plus a root-layout template `'%s | Brand'` with a default; check for duplicates in Search Console coverage.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/meta-title.
- **Best for:** Every page; on trade sites the pattern is service + town + brand across the town/service matrix — each page's title unique by construction.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the most important on-page SEO element, per the source itself.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1136⟧

## ⟦S1137⟧ mime-type — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (seo)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every response's Content-Type header must match its actual file type, with charset declared on text — a stylesheet served as text/plain simply won't apply once nosniff is on (priority medium · intermediate · 15 min).
- **How it looks:** The failure is dramatic and visible: a page that renders unstyled, or scripts that never run, because the browser blocked a CSS/JS file whose header lied about its type. Correctly served, nothing is noticeable at all.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Correct types: HTML `text/html; charset=utf-8` · CSS `text/css` · JS `text/javascript` · JSON `application/json` · SVG `image/svg+xml` · JPEG/PNG/WebP `image/jpeg|png|webp` · WOFF2 `font/woff2` · PDF `application/pdf`. Check with `curl -I` on the page plus its CSS/JS; always set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (and fix the server config rather than removing it — sniffing is itself an upload-attack vector); Nginx: `include mime.types` + `charset utf-8`.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/mime-type; MDN MIME types (IANA registry); MDN X-Content-Type-Options.
- **Best for:** Server/hosting setup for self-hosted builds and preview hosting — one header audit per deployment.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a hosting-configuration check, not a design decision.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1137⟧

## ⟦S1138⟧ mixed-content — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (security)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: an HTTPS page must load zero resources over plain HTTP — active mixed content is blocked outright by browsers and gives a network attacker script-level control of the secure page (priority high · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** The failure on screen: missing images, dead embeds, an unstyled or partly broken page and a browser security warning, on a page whose address bar claims to be secure. Fixed, the padlock state is clean and every asset loads.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Load sequence when violated: HTTPS document arrives → browser requests an `http://` sub-resource → active types (script, stylesheet, iframe, fetch/XHR, object) are refused before execution; passive types (img, audio, video) are auto-upgraded to HTTPS in Chrome 81+ and blocked if no HTTPS version exists.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit every `src`/`href`/`url()` in HTML, CSS, JS and CMS-stored content for `http://` (grep recipe: `src="http://|href="http://|url\(http://`); fix at the source by rewriting to https://, self-hosting, or replacing the resource; `Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests` (header, Nginx add_header, or Next.js headers config) is a safety net for legacy content, not a fix — resources without an HTTPS version still fail; detection via DevTools console ("Mixed Content: … this request has been blocked") and Lighthouse best-practices.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/mixed-content; MDN mixed content; web.dev fixing mixed content.
- **Best for:** Any page embedding third-party assets — maps, videos, fonts, review widgets — and older content migrated to HTTPS; a launch checklist item for trade homepages with embeds.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a hard browser-enforced failure mode, cheap to sweep for.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1138⟧

## ⟦S1139⟧ mobile-testing — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (testing)
- **What it is:** Audit rule: key flows must be tested on real mobile devices and standard mobile viewports, not only desktop emulation — touch behaviour, keyboards, notches and memory limits only exist on real hardware (priority high · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** What it protects: a page that works in a phone's hand — no horizontal scroll at 375px, tap targets that hit first time, a form input that stays visible when the virtual keyboard opens, sticky elements that clear the notch/home indicator.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; it verifies other motion: animations must hold 60fps on throttled hardware, swipe gestures on carousels/drawers must track the finger, hover-dependent UI must not stick on touch.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Context number: >55% of global web traffic is mobile. Viewport test set: 375×667 (iPhone SE), 390×844 (iPhone 14), 430×932 (iPhone 14 Plus), 768×1024 (iPad Mini), 1024×1366 (iPad Pro); tap targets at least 44×44px; checks include correct keyboard type per input, autocomplete, no content overflow (`scrollWidth ≤ clientWidth` assertion), usability on throttled 3G. Tooling: Playwright device presets as CI projects (Pixel 7 / Mobile Chrome, iPhone 14 / Mobile Safari, iPad Pro 11 / Tablet), using `tap()` not `click()`; real-device priority order: iOS Safari → Android Chrome → DevTools emulation → Samsung Internet; BrowserStack for devices not owned.
- **Reference / source:** https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/mobile-testing; Playwright device emulation docs.
- **Best for:** The verification half of every build — the desktop+mobile (375px) screenshot/QA pass a homepage must pass before it is shown or shipped.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source and the rule behind mobile QA on every build.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1139⟧

## ⟦S1140⟧ mock-best-practices — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (testing)
- **What it is:** Audit rule for test suites: mock external dependencies (APIs, databases, file system, time, network) but never the business logic under test, clean every mock up, and assert behaviour rather than implementation (priority medium · intermediate · 20 min).
- **How it looks:** Nothing on any screen — this governs the test suite behind a build, not a page. Its visitor-facing effect is indirect: tests that pass for real reasons, so production behaviour matches what CI promised.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Mock / don't-mock table: mock external APIs, DB calls, FS, time/date, network requests; don't mock pure functions, business logic, data transforms, simple utilities, usually components.
