- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "Publish high-quality content", https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/quality; cites Google's people-first content guidance and the Search Quality Rater Guidelines.
- **Best for:** Every content-bearing section — service pages, towns/areas pages, proof stories. Trade fit: STRONG — the anti-templating rule is exactly what separates a real local firm's pages from spun location pages; pairs with ⟦S1187⟧ (reading level).
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1186⟧

## ⟦S1187⟧ reading-level — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (SEO)
- **What it is:** A readability rule: page copy is measured (Flesch-Kincaid) and rewritten to the audience's level — for general audiences a Flesch Reading Ease of 60–70, i.e. Grade 8–9.
- **How it looks:** Short sentences and short paragraphs with subheadings breaking the text every 200–300 words, key terms bolded, conclusion first — a page a visitor can scan (the source cites Nielsen Norman Group: 79% of users scan rather than read).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rule.md priority medium · intermediate · 15 min. Numbers from the source: Flesch scale — 90–100 very easy (5th grade), 60–70 standard (8th–9th grade, the target), 50–60 fairly difficult, under 30 professional/academic. Sentences 15–20 words on average; flag anything over 25 words; paragraphs 2–4 sentences (6+ hurts); active voice over passive; common words over 3+ syllable jargon. Audience calibration: consumer products/blogs Grade 6–8, medical/legal/technical Grade 10–12, academic Grade 12+. Tools: Hemingway App, Yoast, Grammarly, Word. The accessibility twin of this rule is ⟦S1179⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "Write at a clear reading level", https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/reading-level.
- **Best for:** All homepage copy, measured after writing. Trade fit: STRONG — pairs with ⟦S1179⟧; homeowner-facing copy should sit at the easy end (Grade 6–8 consumer band).
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1187⟧

## ⟦S1188⟧ redirect-chain — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (SEO)
- **What it is:** The server-side redirect rule: no URL may redirect to another URL that itself redirects — chains are flattened so the first redirect points directly at the final destination. Companion to ⟦S1189⟧, not a duplicate of it: this rule fixes the redirect map; ⟦S1189⟧ fixes the links that point into it.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible on the page; following an old URL costs one 301 hop and lands on the final page instead of two or three hops of latency — or, in a redirect loop, an error page that never loads at all.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (The audited sequence: request A → 301 to B → 301 to C → 200; after the fix: request A → 301 to C → 200.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rule.md priority high · intermediate · 15 min. Values from the source: Googlebot reportedly follows about 5 hops before abandoning a chain; severity table — 2 hops moderate (acceptable in transition), 3 hops significant (fix promptly), 4+ hops severe (Googlebot may abandon), a loop is critical. Fix pattern: a flat redirect map (every source → final target) rather than stacked rewrite rules. Security note carried in the source: destinations built from user input (`?next=`, `?redirect=`) must be allow-listed to internal paths, or the cleanup leaves an open-redirect hole. Detection: `curl -L -I` hop traces or Screaming Frog's Redirect Chains report; audit after every migration.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "Avoid multi-hop redirect chains", https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/redirect-chain; cites Google's redirect guidance. Cross-references ⟦S1189⟧ in its own text.
- **Best for:** Post-migration QA sweep. Trade fit: SITUATIONAL — only bites after URL changes, but a homepage rebuild (the core business here) is exactly such a change.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1188⟧

## ⟦S1189⟧ redirect-chains — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (SEO)
- **What it is:** The internal-linking redirect rule: internal links (and sitemap entries) must point directly at final destination URLs, never at URLs that redirect. Companion to ⟦S1188⟧, not a duplicate: ⟦S1188⟧ flattens the chains themselves; this rule removes the site's own links into them. The 301s stay in place for external links and bookmarks.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visibly different; every menu item, body link and footer link resolves in a single 200 response instead of detouring through a redirect.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (The audited sequence per link: click/crawl → href returns 301 → second request → 200; after the fix: href returns 200 directly.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rule.md priority medium · intermediate · 15 min. Process from the source: (1) inventory all current 301 rules, (2) crawl and find internal links pointing at any redirect source URL (Screaming Frog: filter Response Code 3xx, then the Inlinks tab), (3) rewrite each href to the destination, (4) re-crawl to verify none remain, (5) keep the redirects themselves. Rationale values: each hop adds latency, spends crawl budget on an extra request, and passes less PageRank (Google confirms some loss per hop but publishes no figure — the entry invents none). Sitemap corollary: only final URLs belong in the sitemap (see also ⟦S1152⟧).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "Link directly to final destination URLs", https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/redirect-chains; cites Google's redirect and crawlable-link guidance. Cross-references ⟦S1188⟧ in its own text.
- **Best for:** Post-migration QA sweep — navigation, footer and towns/service links after any rebuild. Trade fit: SITUATIONAL — same trigger as ⟦S1188⟧: it matters precisely when a site has been rebuilt or moved.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1189⟧

## ⟦S1190⟧ reduced-motion — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (Accessibility)
- **What it is:** The general motion-safety rule: all animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion` — non-essential animation is disabled or replaced with opacity/colour transitions, nothing flashes more than 3 times per second, and immersive experiences carry motion warnings and pause controls.
- **How it looks:** With reduced motion set, cards no longer scale or slide on hover — they simply change opacity; smooth scrolling becomes instant; content is all present, just still. With motion allowed, the same components animate normally (the source's example: a card scaling to 1.05 on hover over 0.3s).
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: any animation start, with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` set → the global pattern collapses every animation/transition duration to 0.01ms, iteration count to 1, and scroll-behavior to auto → end state: the final visual state, reached instantly, with no intermediate movement. Flash law at all times: ≤ 3 flashes per second (seizure threshold).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rule.md priority high · beginner · 15 min. Safe vs dangerous table from the source: safe = opacity transitions, colour changes, border changes, subtle scale under 1.1; dangerous = spinning/rotating, parallax scrolling (see ⟦S1169⟧), zooming, bouncing. JS side: a `useReducedMotion` hook over `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` with a change listener; Framer Motion's useReducedMotion zeroes durations and drops hover scale. Verify by enabling Reduce Motion in the OS (macOS Accessibility → Display; Windows Ease of Access → Display; iOS Accessibility → Motion) and re-checking every animated section.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "Respect reduced motion preferences", https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/reduced-motion.
- **Best for:** A hard gate on every animated section — heroes, scroll stories, marquees, parallax (⟦S1169⟧). Trade fit: STRONG — this bank's immersive builds are motion-heavy by design, so this fallback is part of "done", not an extra.
- **Tier:** STRONG
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1190⟧
# Skills S1191–S1231 — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills

All 41 skills in this range are single-rule audit/fix skills from the Front-End Checklist
(thedaviddias/front-end-checklist), each bundling its full rule.md reference. They are
QA-sweep skills, not design systems: "How it looks" below describes what a visitor
experiences when the rule holds on a finished page.

Duplicate in range: ⟦S1225⟧ skip-navigation is the same underlying rule as ⟦S1224⟧
skip-link (a "Skip to main content" link as first focusable element) under a second
catalog name — full detail in S1224, pointer + genuine deltas in S1225.

## ⟦S1191⟧ redundant-entry — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule for multi-step flows (checkout, signup, onboarding, support): information a user already entered earlier in the same process must be auto-populated or selectable later, never retyped. Maps to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.7 Redundant Entry. Rule priority high, difficulty intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** On step 2 of a checkout the shipping fields arrive already filled from the billing step, or a "Same as billing address" checkbox sits above empty fields; a review step shows the earlier email/phone as read-only text with an Edit link instead of blank "confirm your email" inputs.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The behaviour is state carried across steps: enter once → value reappears prefilled or selectable at every later step → review screens display the data for checking, not re-entry.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Three allowed mechanisms — auto-populate the repeat field, offer a selection mechanism ("same as" toggle), or show the prior value on a review screen. Pass = previously entered non-exempt data is prefilled/selectable later in the same flow; fail = manual re-entry of the same contact/address/profile data. Only three narrow re-entry exceptions: essential to the activity, required for security (e.g. confirming a new password), or the earlier value is no longer valid.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "redundant-entry" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/redundant-entry); standard named: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7.
- **Best for:** Forms and any multi-step call/CTA or quote flow on a trade homepage (address, phone, job details asked once and carried through); a final QA sweep item for checkout-style funnels.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1191⟧

## ⟦S1192⟧ referrer-policy — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Security-header rule: set a Referrer-Policy on all responses so the Referer header sent to third-party sites cannot leak sensitive URL parts (e.g. a `/reset?token=abc123` path). Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min. Invisible plumbing — nothing renders differently.
- **How it looks:** Static — no motion, no visual change. The effect is only in outbound request headers: same-origin clicks carry the full URL, cross-origin HTTPS clicks carry only the origin, HTTPS→HTTP carries nothing.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Recommended value `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (browser default since Chrome 85+/Firefox 87+, set explicitly anyway). Full 8-value table in the source: no-referrer, no-referrer-when-downgrade, origin, origin-when-cross-origin, same-origin, strict-origin, strict-origin-when-cross-origin, unsafe-url (never use — sends full URL everywhere). Set via server header (Nginx `add_header ... always`, Apache `Header always set`, Next.js headers(), Helmet referrerPolicy), or `<meta name="referrer">`, or per-element `referrerpolicy` attribute on `<a>`/`<img>`. For especially sensitive pages use no-referrer or same-origin. Baseline browser minimums named: Chrome/Edge 115, Firefox 116, Safari 16.4.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "referrer-policy" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/referrer-policy); MDN Referrer-Policy header doc named.
- **Best for:** Site-wide hardening on any build; matters most on pages carrying tokens/IDs in query strings (quote confirmations, account links). Not a section design — a launch checklist item.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1192⟧

## ⟦S1193⟧ render-blocking — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: eliminate CSS/JS that blocks first paint — anything the browser must fetch, parse and apply before it can paint causes the "white screen" delay and hurts First Contentful Paint. Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** The first screen — hero layout and headline type — paints immediately instead of a blank white page; below-the-fold widgets (chat, reviews, carousels) appear afterwards without holding up the hero.
- **Frame by frame:** Page request → only minimal above-the-fold CSS (inlined) and the LCP asset load → first paint of the hero → non-critical CSS/JS stream in after (deferred scripts execute in order after parsing).
- **Mechanism & key values:** `defer` for ordered application JS, `async` for independent scripts (analytics); inline only critical above-the-fold CSS in a `<style>` block; load the rest with the `media="print" onload="this.media='all'"` swap pattern; never use CSS `@import` (serial request chains); never preload non-critical assets (chat-widget.js, reviews.js named as anti-pattern preloads). Pass bar: blocking third-party scripts = 0 on normal content routes; nested-`@import` CSS on the critical path = fail. Verify in Lighthouse ("eliminate-render-blocking-resources"), PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest waterfall.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "render-blocking" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/render-blocking); Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights named as tools.
- **Best for:** Every page, but decisive for the hero/LCP: single-file trade homepages must keep the first paint path to critical CSS + hero media only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1193⟧

## ⟦S1194⟧ reset-css — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** CSS foundation rule: ship a reset or normalize stylesheet (loaded before all custom styles) so browser default styling differences disappear across Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge. Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min. The bundled reference reproduces four full reset sources.
- **How it looks:** Identical starting rendering in every browser: body margin 0, headings at deliberate sizes rather than UA defaults, form controls inheriting the page font, images block-level and capped at 100% width, border-box sizing everywhere.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own. One motion clause: modern resets include a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block that collapses all animation/transition durations to 0.01ms with iteration count 1 and disables smooth scroll.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Options with full source in the entry — Meyer reset v2.0 (strips everything: margin/padding/border 0, font inherit); normalize.css v8.0.1 (preserves useful defaults, targeted fixes only: html line-height 1.15, h1 2em/0.67em inside section/article, small 80%, sub/sup 75%); Andy Bell's modern reset (`* { margin: 0 }`, border-box, body min-height 100vh / line-height 1.5, list-style none only on role="list", img/picture max-width 100% display block, font: inherit on form controls); CSS Remedy (border-box, tab-size 4, svg:not([fill]) fill currentColor). Packages: `pnpm add normalize.css` / `modern-css-reset` / `@csstools/css-remedy` / `sanitize.css`. Framework note: Tailwind's Preflight and Bootstrap's Reboot already are resets — do not double up.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "reset-css" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/reset-css); sources named: necolas/normalize.css, jensimmons (mozdevs) CSS Remedy, Meyer reset (meyerweb.com), Andy Bell modern reset (piccalil.li).
- **Best for:** The base layer of any build — first stylesheet in a single-file homepage; also the reference for writing a small hand-rolled reset when no framework is used.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1194⟧

## ⟦S1195⟧ resource-hints — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: use preload / prefetch / preconnect / dns-prefetch so the browser discovers critical assets earlier; the source claims 100–300ms average LCP improvement when used correctly. Priority high, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** The hero image and headline font are already downloaded when the parser reaches them — the hero paints complete, with no late font swap or image pop-in; the next page in a funnel feels pre-loaded.
- **Frame by frame:** HTML head parsed → hinted assets start fetching immediately at high priority (preload) or the socket to a needed origin is already open (preconnect) → page renders with those assets in hand → idle-time prefetch quietly downloads the likely next route.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Decision table with practical limits — preload: current-route late-discovered critical assets only (hero image with `fetchpriority="high"`, route font), usually ≤3–5 per route; prefetch: next likely navigation only, never current-route critical CSS; preconnect: origins definitely used immediately (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com with crossorigin, image CDN), usually ≤2–4 origins; dns-prefetch: low-confidence speculative origins. Fonts preloaded without `as="font"` + `crossorigin` cause duplicate requests. Anti-pattern named: preloading many fonts/widgets and preconnecting chat/ads/social origins steals bandwidth and sockets from the LCP path.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "resource-hints" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/resource-hints); web.dev Learn Performance and Patterns.dev preload/prefetch guidance named.
- **Best for:** Hero performance on any homepage (hero image + display font), and multi-page funnels (prefetch the quote/next-step page).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1195⟧

## ⟦S1196⟧ responsive-images — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Image-delivery rule: serve each image at the size the device actually needs via `srcset` + `sizes`, instead of shipping one desktop file to every screen; source cites 50–70% bandwidth savings on mobile. Priority high, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** A gallery or hero photo is equally sharp on phone and desktop, but the phone downloads a 400–800px file while the desktop gets 1200–1600px; art-directed crops differ per breakpoint when `<picture>` is used (tighter mobile crop, wide desktop crop).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Selection happens once at load: browser reads viewport width × device pixel ratio against the `sizes` result and downloads the smallest adequate `srcset` candidate.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Width-descriptor pattern: `srcset` at 400w/800w/1200w/1600w with `sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, (max-width: 1200px) 50vw, 33vw"`; worked example — 400px viewport at 2x DPR with sizes 100vw needs 800px of image → browser picks image-800. Fixed-size images (logos/icons) use density descriptors 1x/2x/3x instead. `<picture>` with media queries handles art direction and format (WebP) switching. Always include width/height attributes. Warning carried in the source: a wrong `sizes` negates a correct `srcset` — without `sizes` the browser assumes 100vw. Variant generation example uses Sharp at quality 80 WebP.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "responsive-images" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/responsive-images); Sharp named for variant generation.
- **Best for:** Hero images, work/gallery photos, before/after pairs, review avatars — every raster image on a trade homepage; pairs with ⟦S1197⟧ (the oversizing audit) and ⟦S1199⟧ (density variants).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1196⟧

## ⟦S1197⟧ responsive-size — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The audit companion to ⟦S1196⟧: images must not be significantly larger than their rendered display size — the Lighthouse "Properly size images" audit. Priority high, intermediate, ~20 min. Distinct rule page and check procedure (intrinsic-vs-rendered comparison), not a duplicate of S1196.
- **How it looks:** No visual difference when fixed — the same photo at the same sharpness, only the download shrinks (source example: a 2000×1500 image shown at 400×300 downloads ~25× the needed pixels; an 800KB file becomes ~50KB at 400w).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Audit procedure: for each `<img>` compare intrinsic width to rendered CSS width; flag any image whose intrinsic width is more than 2× the rendered width at any common viewport; images over 200px wide should carry srcset variants (400w/800w/1200w/1600w); `sizes` must describe real layout widths per breakpoint (fallback `src` = medium 800w); a DevTools console script in the source lists every image with ratio >2. Bandwidth scales with pixel count, not linear size: 1600px into a 400px slot ≈ 16× waste; 2000px into 300px ≈ 44×.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "responsive-size" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/responsive-size); Lighthouse "Properly size images" audit named as the primary signal.
- **Best for:** QA pass over hero and gallery imagery on image-heavy trade pages (project photos, before/after sets) before launch.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1197⟧

## ⟦S1198⟧ responsive-units — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** CSS rule: build layouts with relative units (rem, em, %, vw/vh, clamp()) instead of fixed px, so pages respect the user's browser font-size preference and adapt without extra breakpoints. Priority high, beginner, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** Text and spacing scale smoothly as the window resizes (fluid headlines via clamp), and the whole layout grows proportionally when a low-vision user raises their default font size instead of breaking or staying fixed.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Continuous behaviour: viewport or root-font changes re-flow sizes immediately with no breakpoint jumps inside clamp ranges.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Unit table — rem (root font size; fonts and consistent spacing), em (parent font size; component-scoped padding/radius), % (parent dimension; widths), vw/vh (viewport; full-bleed sections, heroes), ch (width of "0"; text containers), clamp() (fluid type). Rules: never fix the root (`html { font-size: 100% }`); 1rem = browser default (0.875rem ≈ 14px, 1.125rem ≈ 18px, 2rem ≈ 32px at 16px base); fluid-type example `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw + 0.5rem, 1.5rem)`; button padding in em (0.5em 1em) so variants scale with their own font size; hero `min-height: 100svh` (small-viewport-height, safer than vh on mobile); container `width: 90%; max-width: 1200px`; card `width: min(100%, 400px)`. px stays correct for 1px borders, shadows and fixed icon/avatar sizes.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "responsive-units" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/responsive-units).
- **Best for:** Typography and spacing systems across all sections; the fluid-type mechanism for hero/section headlines that must scale between phone and desktop without stepped breakpoints.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1198⟧

## ⟦S1199⟧ retina-display — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Image rule: provide 2x (and optionally 3x) resolution assets so images stay sharp on high-DPI/Retina screens. Priority medium, intermediate, ~15 min.
- **How it looks:** Logos, hero photos and product shots render crisp on phones and Retina laptops instead of slightly blurred; standard displays download only the 1x file and pay nothing.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The browser picks the density candidate matching the device pixel ratio at load.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Fixed-size images use density descriptors (`srcset="logo.png 1x, logo@2x.png 2x, logo@3x.png 3x"` with explicit width/height); responsive images prefer w descriptors + sizes (browser multiplies by DPR itself). CSS backgrounds: `image-set()` with 1x/2x/3x, or media-query fallback at `min-resolution: 192dpi` (2x) / `288dpi` (3x) with background-size set back to the 1x dimensions. Density table: 1x standard, 2x most phones (200px file for a 100px slot), 3x iPhone Pro/high-end Android. Cost warning in the source: 3x = 9× the pixels of 1x — 2x is often enough. SVG is named as the resolution-independent answer for logos/icons.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "retina-display" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/retina-display); Sharp named for generating the density set.
- **Best for:** Logos and credential badges in navigation/footer, hero imagery, gallery photos; complements ⟦S1196⟧/⟦S1197⟧ (same srcset machinery, density angle).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1199⟧

## ⟦S1200⟧ review — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO structured-data rule: add Review / AggregateRating JSON-LD to product, service and local-business pages to earn star-rating rich results; source cites up to 35% CTR uplift from stars in results. Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing changes on the page itself; in Google results the listing gains a row of gold stars, the numeric average and a review count under the title — the visual difference is in the SERP, next to competitors without stars.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** AggregateRating nests inside the main entity (Product, LocalBusiness…). Required: `ratingValue`, `ratingCount` or `reviewCount`; recommended `bestRating` (default 5) / `worstRating` (default 1). Individual Review requires `author`, `reviewRating`, `itemReviewed`. Eligible entity types named: Product, Recipe, Movie, Book, Software, LocalBusiness, Course, Event. Hard policy lines: ratings must come from genuine user reviews — no self-authored reviews, no `reviewCount: 0`, no markup on pages that don't visibly show review content. Validate with Google's Rich Results Test.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "review" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/review); Google Review snippet structured-data docs and Schema.org AggregateRating named as standards.
- **Best for:** Proof/reviews sections of trade homepages — marking up the firm's real aggregate Google rating (count + average exactly as published) so the SERP listing shows stars; never for invented ratings.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1200⟧

## ⟦S1201⟧ right-to-erasure — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Privacy rule: provide a user-facing "Delete my account and data" flow that honours GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure) — clearing all client-side storage and triggering server-side deletion. Priority medium, intermediate, ~60 min. Non-compliance fines cited: up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
- **How it looks:** In account settings, a clearly labelled Privacy/Your-data section with a delete button; tapping it opens a confirmation dialog ("Delete your account and all data? This action cannot be undone"), then a status message confirming receipt, the 30-day removal deadline and that the user has been signed out.
- **Frame by frame:** Idle → user taps delete → confirmation alertdialog (role="alertdialog", labelled heading, "Yes, delete my data" / Cancel) → on confirm: client storage cleared immediately, deletion POST sent → done state shows the confirmation + 30-day timeline; error state if the server call fails (local data stays cleared).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Deletion must cover every store — localStorage (`localStorage.clear()`), sessionStorage, IndexedDB (`indexedDB.databases()` + `deleteDatabase` each), cookies (re-set each with `Max-Age=0; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970`), Service Worker caches (`caches.delete`), plus a server deletion request; server queues deletion within the GDPR 30-day window and sends a confirmation email before the address is deleted; requests must also be forwarded to third-party processors (analytics, CRM, email tools). Clear client storage before awaiting the server response.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "right-to-erasure" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/privacy/right-to-erasure); GDPR Article 17 and ICO right-to-erasure guidance named as standards.
- **Best for:** Account/privacy pages on apps; rarely relevant to a static trade homepage — a compliance checklist item only if the site has accounts or dashboards.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1201⟧

## ⟦S1202⟧ robots-meta — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: audit the per-page `<meta name="robots">` directive on every page — an accidental `noindex` (classically left over from staging) silently removes a page from search results. Priority high, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No on-page visual change. The visible symptom is in search: a key landing page either appears in Google results or has vanished from them.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Directive table — index/noindex (appear in results or not), follow/nofollow (link equity flow), noarchive, nosnippet, max-snippet:-1, max-image-preview:large, noimageindex. Correct patterns: public pages `index, follow` (or no tag); thank-you/utility pages `noindex, nofollow`; deindex-but-keep-equity `noindex, follow`; snippet-limited `index, follow, max-snippet:150`. Crawler-specific tags (`googlebot`, `bingbot`) override the generic `robots` tag for that crawler. Key distinction: robots.txt blocks fetching (page never seen, so its noindex is never read); meta noindex blocks indexing after fetch — to deindex, use noindex without a robots.txt block (see ⟦S1203⟧).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "robots-meta" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/robots-meta); Google's robots meta tag documentation named.
- **Best for:** Launch QA on every page of a build — the staging-to-production parity check; thank-you pages after quote forms are the intended noindex candidates.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1202⟧

## ⟦S1203⟧ robots-meta-conflict — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO conflict rule: a page that is both Disallowed in robots.txt and tagged `noindex` can never be deindexed properly — crawlers never fetch it, so they never read the noindex, and Google may still list the URL from backlink anchor text. Priority high, intermediate, ~10 min. Companion to ⟦S1202⟧ (directive correctness) — this one is specifically the robots.txt × meta interaction.
- **How it looks:** No on-page change; the symptom is a supposedly removed page still surfacing in Google results as a bare URL listing with no snippet.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Decision table — index normally: no Disallow + `index, follow`; deindex with link equity kept: no Disallow + `noindex, follow`; block crawling only (no deindex guarantee): Disallow, meta irrelevant; full staging block: `Disallow: /` on the staging host. Fix procedure: to deindex, remove the Disallow for that path and keep noindex; to merely uncrawl, keep Disallow and drop the tag. Verify with Search Console URL Inspection + the robots.txt tester.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "robots-meta-conflict" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/robots-meta-conflict); Google "Remove a page from Google" and robots meta docs named.
- **Best for:** Site migrations and cleanup of old preview/landing pages; launch QA wherever robots.txt and templates are edited by different hands.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1203⟧

## ⟦S1204⟧ robots-txt — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO foundation rule: publish a valid robots.txt at exactly `/robots.txt` on the production domain — the first file crawlers fetch; a stray `Disallow: /` can delist the whole site. Priority high, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No visual change on the site; the file itself is plain text: User-agent groups with Disallow/Allow path rules and a Sitemap line.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Must return HTTP 200 at `/robots.txt` (4xx = Google treats as "no restrictions"; 5xx blocks crawling). Required shape: `User-agent: *` rules, Disallow only admin/cart/checkout/internal paths, never CSS/JS asset paths (Googlebot must render), and `Sitemap: <absolute sitemap URL>`. Empty `Disallow:` = allow everything. Crawler-specific groups (e.g. Googlebot-Image) allowed. Verify with `curl -I` on the live host and the Search Console robots.txt tester.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "robots-txt" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/robots-txt); Google's robots.txt introduction and RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol) named as standards.
- **Best for:** Every site launch; pairs with ⟦S1202⟧/⟦S1203⟧ and the sitemap rules ⟦S1219⟧–⟦S1223⟧ as the crawl-control set.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1204⟧

## ⟦S1205⟧ runtime-validation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript rule: validate all external data at runtime with a schema library (Zod or Valibot) at trust boundaries — TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so an API returning `price: "12.99"` passes type-checking and produces NaN in the UI. Priority high, intermediate, ~30 min.
- **How it looks:** No intended visual change; the user-facing difference is failure behaviour — a malformed API response produces a handled error state / fallback instead of a crashed or garbage-rendered page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Data flow: raw JSON enters at fetch/form/storage/env boundary → schema parse validates and coerces → typed value propagates; invalid data throws a ZodError (`.parse()`) or returns a handled failure (`.safeParse()`).
- **Mechanism & key values:** One schema = validation + inferred type (`z.infer<typeof Schema>`, no duplicated interfaces). Validate once at the edge only: API responses, form submissions, localStorage reads, environment variables at startup (example env rules: API_SECRET min 32 chars, PORT coerced positive int default 3000). Form schema examples carry real constraints (name min 2, message min 10 / max 1000, enum subjects). `.parse()` for fail-fast boundaries, `.safeParse()` where the UI must degrade gracefully. Valibot named as the smaller tree-shakeable alternative.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "runtime-validation" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/runtime-validation); Zod (zod.dev) and Valibot (valibot.dev) named.
- **Best for:** Any page consuming API/CMS data or handling form submissions (quote forms, configurators); engineering QA, not a design mechanism.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1205⟧

## ⟦S1206⟧ scheduler-yield — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** JavaScript performance rule: break up main-thread tasks longer than 50ms with `scheduler.yield()` (MessageChannel fallback) so clicks, keys and rendering stay responsive — the 50ms figure is the RAIL/INP long-task budget. Priority medium, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** During heavy on-page work (rendering hundreds of result cards, processing a big list) the page keeps responding — taps register and animations keep moving instead of the UI freezing until the loop finishes.
- **Frame by frame:** Long loop starts → after each chunk the task suspends → browser processes queued input/paint → task resumes where it left off → completes with no single task over ~50ms and no red "Long Task" bars in the Performance panel.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `scheduler.yield()` is Promise-based and preserves task priority (unlike setTimeout 0); supported Chrome/Edge 115+, fallback is a MessageChannel port post (faster than the 4ms-clamped timer). Default chunk size 50 items for light per-item work, 10–20 for heavy items; yield at chunk end, never per item. Dev detection: PerformanceObserver on `longtask` entries > 50ms. Boundary rule: DOM-touching loops and one-off init → yield; pure CPU work (image processing, crypto, big parses) → Web Worker instead.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "scheduler-yield" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/scheduler-yield); web.dev RAIL model and long-tasks guidance named.
- **Best for:** Interaction-heavy sections — filterable galleries, big project/town lists, configurators — on single-file builds where a large DOM build-up could jank the first interaction (INP).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1206⟧

## ⟦S1207⟧ schema-noindex-conflict — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO conflict rule: rich-result schema (Product, Recipe, Review/AggregateRating…) on a page Google cannot index is dead weight — Google does not process structured data on noindexed or blocked pages. Priority high, intermediate, ~10 min. Companion to ⟦S1200⟧ (the Review schema itself) and ⟦S1203⟧ (the robots conflict family).
- **How it looks:** No on-page change; the symptom is a page with valid-looking JSON-LD that never earns stars/FAQ rich results in Google.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Three conflict types — (1) meta `noindex` + schema: parsed but no rich result; (2) robots.txt Disallow + schema: never fetched, never seen; (3) non-self canonical + schema: rich results attributed to the canonical URL, which needs its own schema. Audit procedure: crawl all JSON-LD/Microdata pages → check meta robots for noindex → check path against robots.txt Disallows → check canonical is self-referencing → flag. Fix: make the page indexable (remove noindex, unblock, self-canonical) or delete the pointless schema. Verify in Search Console Rich Results + Rich Results Test ("not indexable" = no rich result).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "schema-noindex-conflict" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/schema-noindex-conflict); Google structured-data policies named.
- **Best for:** QA on any page carrying Review/LocalBusiness schema (proof sections, service pages) — confirms the schema in ⟦S1200⟧ can actually pay off.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1207⟧

## ⟦S1208⟧ screen-reader-testing — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility testing rule: manually test pages with real screen readers — automated scanners catch only ~30–40% of issues and cannot judge announcements, reading order or focus behaviour. Priority high, intermediate, ~60 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual; the "view" is the spoken/braille stream: headings, landmarks and controls announced with name + role + state in DOM order, dynamic updates spoken via live regions, modal focus trapped and returned to its trigger on close.
- **Frame by frame:** Tester opens the flow → navigates by Tab, heading key (H), landmark keys (D/R), links list (NVDA Insert+F7) → each control announces name/role/state → a modal opens, focus moves inside and is trapped → modal closes, focus returns to the trigger → form submitted with an error: focus moves to the error summary and each error is tied to its field via aria-describedby.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pairings table with estimated share — JAWS + Chrome/Edge ~40%, NVDA + Chrome/Firefox ~41%, VoiceOver + Safari ~10% desktop / ~70% iOS mobile, TalkBack + Chrome (most Android), Narrator + Edge. Minimum coverage: NVDA + Chrome and VoiceOver + Safari. Checklist groups: navigation (all content Tab-reachable, skip link works), interactive (APG keyboard patterns — roving tabindex in menus, arrow keys in tabs), forms (labels announced, required announced, errors associated), dynamic (aria-live polite for non-critical, assertive for critical alerts). Standards named: ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, WebAIM screen-reader testing guide.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "screen-reader-testing" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/screen-reader-testing); WebAIM, NVDA and VoiceOver user guides named.
- **Best for:** Final accessibility QA on interactive sections — navigation menus, quote forms, before/after sliders, version switchers — before any launch.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1208⟧

## ⟦S1209⟧ scrolljacking — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: never hijack native scrolling — no modified scroll speed/direction, no wheel-event section-snapping, no scroll-driven navigation without consent. Priority medium, beginner, ~15 min. Directly relevant to immersive builds: it bans the hijack pattern, not scroll-triggered animation itself.
- **How it looks:** The page scrolls exactly as the user's wheel/trackpad expects — continuous, proportional, same direction — while reveal animations may play as sections enter, without ever blocking or redirecting the scroll. The footer stays reachable.
- **Frame by frame:** User scrolls → content moves natively at the user's own pace → IntersectionObserver-triggered animations fire as elements enter (threshold 0.1 in the source example) but scrolling never pauses, snaps or reroutes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Banned patterns shown in source: `wheel` handler with preventDefault driving section jumps; scroll handler rescaling scrollY (×0.5 half-speed); vertical wheel input converted to horizontal scrollLeft. Allowed: CSS scroll-snap (`scroll-snap-type: y mandatory` + `scroll-snap-align: start` — user stays in control) and non-blocking scroll-triggered animation. If custom scroll is truly required: respect prefers-reduced-motion and ship an opt-out toggle. Infinite scroll must keep a fallback (Load-more button + pagination links) so the footer is reachable. A console self-test for defaultPrevented wheel events is included in the source.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "scrolljacking" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/scrolljacking).
- **Best for:** A governing constraint on hero/pinned-scroll/process sections of immersive trade builds: parallax and reveals are fine, taking over the wheel is not — use it as the audit line when a version leans on scroll effects.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1209⟧

## ⟦S1210⟧ search-input — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** HTML/accessibility rule: build site search accessibly — `type="search"` input, a real label, `role="search"` on the form, keyboard-navigable autocomplete and screen-reader-announced result counts. Priority medium, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** A search box with a visible (or accessibly named) "Search" label and a magnifier submit button; typing opens a suggestion dropdown under the field where the highlighted suggestion is visibly marked; the results area states "N results for '…'" as a status line.
- **Frame by frame:** User types (suggestions fetched after a 300ms debounce once ≥2 characters) → dropdown opens and an aria-live region announces "N suggestions available" → ArrowDown/ArrowUp move the active suggestion (wrapping), Enter selects it, Escape closes → submit → the results count is announced via role="status" and rendered as text.
- **Mechanism & key values:** ARIA combobox pattern on the input: role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls → listbox id, aria-activedescendant pointing at the active option, aria-autocomplete="list"; options are role="option" with aria-selected. Never rely on placeholder as the label. Clear button must be keyboard-reachable with its own aria-label. Focus styling in the source example: 3px rgba(0,102,204,0.2) ring; dropdown z-index 100, 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.1) shadow.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "search-input" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/search-input).
- **Best for:** Navigation/header search where a site has one; the autocomplete pattern also transfers to town/service pickers in quote flows.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1210⟧

## ⟦S1211⟧ select-name — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: every `<select>` must have an accessible name — a `<label for>` matching its id, or aria-label/aria-labelledby when no visible label is possible. Maps to WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value). Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** Each dropdown sits next to its visible label text ("Choose your country:"); the first option may read "Please select…" but never serves as the label. Clicking the label text also opens the dropdown, enlarging the tap target.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. On focus, the screen reader announces the label + role, so the user knows what the dropdown asks before opening it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Preferred: `<label for="country-select">` + `<select id="country-select">`. Fallback: `aria-label="Select theme"` on the select itself. Anti-pattern named: an unlabelled `<select name="sort">` whose first option ("Price") is doing label duty. Verify in the browser accessibility tree / axe / Lighthouse.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "select-name" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/select-name); W3C WAI WCAG overview and MDN Accessibility named as standards.
- **Best for:** Forms — service/town dropdowns in quote and call-back forms; a one-line item in any form QA sweep.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1211⟧

## ⟦S1212⟧ semantic-lists — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** HTML semantics rule: groups of related items must use real list elements — `<ul>` unordered, `<ol>` ordered, `<dl>` term/definition — not styled divs, so screen readers announce the grouping and item count. Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** Visually identical either way (bullets can be removed with `list-style: none` and custom markers added via `li::before`, e.g. a green "✓"); the difference is announced structure: "list with 5 items", position within ordered steps.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Element choice by content — ul: navigation, features, bullets; ol: steps, rankings, instructions (never hand-numbered divs); dl with dt/dd: glossaries and FAQs (question as dt, answer as dd). Nav pattern: `<nav aria-label>` wrapping a ul of links. Verify by screen reader: the announced item count must match the visible count.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "semantic-lists" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/semantic-lists).
- **Best for:** Navigation menus, feature/benefit lists in proof sections, numbered process steps, FAQ blocks — everywhere a trade homepage groups items.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1212⟧

## ⟦S1213⟧ sensory-instructions — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility content rule: instructions must never rely on a single sensory channel — not colour alone ("click the red button"), shape ("the round icon"), location ("the menu on the right") or sound ("when you hear the beep"). Priority high, beginner, ~15 min.
- **How it looks:** Instructions name the control by its text label with the sensory cue as backup ("Click the 'Submit' button (green)"); required fields carry an asterisk plus visually-hidden "(required)" text, not just red labels; error states stack three cues — red border/background, an icon, and bold text.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Notification pattern in the source: a cue event fires sound + a visible toast + a page-title change ("(1) New message") together, so no user group misses it.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Fix pattern per channel — colour: add text/icon indicators; location: reference the element's name, location optional in parentheses; shape: aria-label on icon buttons ("Settings" for the gear); sound: pair every audio cue with a visual alternative. Error-field recipe: aria-invalid + aria-describedby to the error text, error colour #d32f2f with 2px border and #ffebee background plus ⚠ icon. Source stat: colour-only references exclude ~8% of men. Audit method: read instructions without looking at the screen; view in grayscale; mute audio.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sensory-instructions" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/sensory-instructions).
- **Best for:** Forms and process instructions on quote/call flows; any "look for the…" copy in hero or gallery sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1213⟧

## ⟦S1214⟧ service-area — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Local-SEO rule: a business serving several towns gets a dedicated page per service area with genuinely unique local content, plus LocalBusiness schema with `areaServed` — thin city-name-swapped clones are doorway pages under Google's spam policy. Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** One page per town ("Plumber in Austin") with its own title, H1 and body: local specifics a template can't fake — area regulations, a testimonial or case study from that town, neighbourhood/landmark references, area-specific FAQs and a local number.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Per-page checklist from the source: unique title `[Service] in [City, State] | [Brand]`; unique H1; at least 300 words of unique body content; at least one local-specific detail; LocalBusiness JSON-LD with an `areaServed` array of City entries; internal links to the main service page and homepage. URL pattern: `/services/plumbing/austin-tx`. Hard honesty line in the source: never invent addresses, categories or geographic claims to satisfy the rule.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "service-area" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/service-area); Google doorway-pages spam policy and Schema.org areaServed named.
- **Best for:** Towns/areas sections of trade sites — the rule that decides whether a town list becomes real per-town pages with local proof or stays one honest coverage section; central to multi-town roofer/siding/remodeling builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1214⟧

## ⟦S1215⟧ service-worker — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance/PWA rule: register a service worker that pre-caches critical assets and intercepts fetches with per-resource caching strategies; source claims 50–90% faster repeat visits plus offline function. Priority medium, intermediate, ~60 min.
- **How it looks:** Repeat visits load near-instantly from cache; on a flaky connection the app still opens, and a navigation that can't be served shows a designed offline page instead of a browser error.
- **Frame by frame:** First visit: page loads from network → worker registers (deferred until window load so it doesn't compete with critical resources) → install event pre-caches the shell → activate deletes old caches and claims clients. Later visits: each GET is intercepted → static assets served cache-first, navigations network-first with offline fallback, everything else stale-while-revalidate (cached copy instantly, fresh copy fetched behind it).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Lifecycle: registration → download → install (pre-cache) → activate (cleanup) → fetch (intercept). Strategy routing by request type — cache-first for hashed static assets (js/css/woff2/images/svg), network-first for navigations, stale-while-revalidate for the rest; only same-origin GETs are intercepted. Versioning: bump CACHE_VERSION per deploy (or build-timestamp BUILD_ID). Workbox named as the production route (example: static assets CacheFirst with 30-day maxAgeSeconds = 30×24×60×60 expiration; APIs NetworkFirst; navigations StaleWhileRevalidate); next-pwa for Next.js. Safety line: never cache user-specific or mutation responses (shared-device data leaks). Baseline minimums: Chrome/Edge 115, Firefox 116, Safari 16.4.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "service-worker" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/service-worker); MDN Service Worker API, web.dev service-worker overview and Offline Cookbook, Workbox named.
- **Best for:** App-like sites and repeat-visit funnels; marginal for a static single-page trade homepage — a launch-checklist consideration, not a section mechanism.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1215⟧

## ⟦S1216⟧ session-cookie-flags — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Security rule: every session/auth cookie must carry Secure, HttpOnly and an explicit SameSite flag — each flag blocks a distinct attack (network capture, XSS token theft, CSRF). Priority high, beginner, ~15 min.
- **How it looks:** Invisible to visitors; visible in DevTools' Cookies panel as ticked HttpOnly/Secure boxes and a SameSite value, and in the raw header: `Set-Cookie: session_id=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=86400`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Behaviour: the cookie travels only over HTTPS, is unreadable from `document.cookie`, and is withheld from cross-site requests per the SameSite mode.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Flag table — Secure: never omit in production; HttpOnly: omit only for cookies JS must read (e.g. a CSRF token); SameSite=Strict blocks all cross-site sending (breaks OAuth-return logins — use Lax there, which allows top-level cross-site GET navigation but blocks cross-site POST/PUT/DELETE); SameSite=None requires Secure and gives no CSRF protection (third-party embeds only). Cookie prefixes enforce by name: `__Host-` forces Secure + Path=/ + no Domain; `__Secure-` forces Secure. Session-cookie example lifetimes: 24h general, 7 days scoped to /api/auth, 10-minute PKCE state cookie. Rename framework defaults (e.g. Express `connect.sid` → `__session`). Audit with `curl -I` on the login endpoint or Mozilla Observatory.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "session-cookie-flags" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/session-cookie-flags); MDN Set-Cookie and OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet named.
- **Best for:** Any build with login/accounts or form backends; a server-config checklist item, invisible in page design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1216⟧

## ⟦S1217⟧ session-timeout-recovery — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: authenticated flows must not silently erase work at session timeout — warn before expiry, let users extend, autosave/preserve drafts, and restore route + step + data after re-authentication. Priority high, advanced, ~30 min; grounded in WCAG timing-adjustable and re-authenticating guidance.
- **How it looks:** During a long form, a dialog appears before sign-out: "Your session is about to expire — you will be signed out in 60 seconds. Select 'Stay signed in' to keep working without losing your draft", with Stay signed in / Sign out now buttons; after a forced re-login the user lands back on the same step with fields still filled.
- **Frame by frame:** Inactivity timer runs (source example: warn at 14 min, logout at 15 min) → warning dialog opens with a live countdown (60s), focus moves to the Stay-signed-in button → extend: session refreshes, dialog closes, work untouched → or expiry: draft is preserved server-side, user is sent to login with a resume token (`?resume=<draftId>`) → after login the draft is fetched and route, step, field values, error context and focus are all restored.
- **Mechanism & key values:** WCAG-aligned thresholds — warn at least 20 seconds before the loss-causing action; extension by one simple action, repeatable where the limit is content-controlled. Warning UI must be role="alertdialog" when blocking (or role="status"/live region when passive), keyboard-operable, focus-managed. Recovery pattern is WCAG Technique G105 (save state server-side; client sessionStorage drafts only for non-sensitive fields). Pass/fail in the source is strict: fail if re-authentication loses previously entered data.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "session-timeout-recovery" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/session-timeout-recovery); WCAG 2.2 Timing Adjustable + Re-authenticating understanding docs and Technique G105 named.
- **Best for:** Long quote forms, multi-step applications and account flows; the dialog pattern transfers to any "about to lose your work" moment in a form-heavy section.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1217⟧

## ⟦S1218⟧ share-buttons — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO/distribution rule: put social share buttons on content pages (articles, posts, tutorials) built as plain share-URL links — no third-party share SDKs. Priority low, beginner, ~10 min. Share buttons don't rank directly; they drive traffic that can earn backlinks.
- **How it looks:** A row of labelled platform links (X, LinkedIn, Facebook, WhatsApp) on the article; clicking one opens the platform's share dialog pre-filled with the article title and URL, and the shared post renders a rich preview (title, description, cover image) from the page's Open Graph tags.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion on the page itself; the sequence is click → new tab with the platform composer pre-populated → post.
- **Mechanism & key values:** URL schemes copied in the source — X: `https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=<title>&url=<url>`; LinkedIn: `https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=<url>`; Facebook: `https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=<url>`; WhatsApp: `https://wa.me/?text=<text + url>`; all with target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer", values URL-encoded from the canonical URL + document title. Why no widgets: third-party share scripts (AddThis, ShareThis, FB SDK) add 50–300 KB of JS, set third-party cookies and create privacy obligations. Prerequisite: og:title / og:description / og:image / og:url on the shared page. Platform fit table: X = tech/news, LinkedIn = B2B, Facebook = consumer/local, WhatsApp = mobile-first/international, Reddit = technical communities.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "share-buttons" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/share-buttons); X/Twitter Tweet Button docs named.
- **Best for:** Blog/article pages only — the source itself marks it less relevant for product, service and home pages; at most a footer/article-end row on content-led builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1218⟧

## ⟦S1219⟧ sitemap — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** SEO rule: publish a valid XML sitemap at /sitemap.xml listing all important pages, reference it in robots.txt, and submit it to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. Priority high, beginner, ~15 min.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing change; the sitemap itself is an XML list of URLs with lastmod dates. Its effect shows as faster, more complete indexing of new pages.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<urlset>` with the sitemaps.org namespace; per-URL elements — `loc` (required, absolute), `lastmod` (recommended), `changefreq` and `priority` (optional). Priority guidelines from the source: homepage 1.0, main categories 0.8–0.9, product/service pages 0.7–0.8, blog posts 0.5–0.7, legal 0.3–0.5, archives/tags 0.3–0.4. Large sites split into a `<sitemapindex>` of per-section files. Exclude: noindex pages, duplicates, 404s, login-gated pages, parameter variants. The validity, coverage, status-code and domain details are separate rules — ⟦S1220⟧–⟦S1223⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sitemap" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/sitemap); sitemaps.org protocol implied throughout.
- **Best for:** Every launched site, especially multi-page builds (service + town pages) where link discovery alone is slow.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1219⟧

## ⟦S1220⟧ sitemap-4xx — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Sitemap-hygiene rule: the sitemap must contain only live URLs — any entry returning 4XX wastes crawl budget and floods Search Console with errors that mask real problems. Priority high, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing change; health shows in Search Console's Coverage report as the absence of "Submitted URL not found (404)" errors.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Status-action table — page exists and is indexable (200): include; permanently moved (301): update `<loc>` to the new URL; deleted (410 Gone or 404): remove from sitemap; temporarily down (503): keep but fix fast. Migration procedure: map old→new URLs, implement 301s, regenerate the sitemap with only new URLs, resubmit. Prevention: generate the sitemap from the live-content database (published and not-deleted rows only). Verify by crawling all sitemap URLs (Screaming Frog/Sitebulb) and filtering Search Console Coverage by "Submitted in sitemap".
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sitemap-4xx" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/sitemap-4xx); Google sitemap best practices and HTTP-status-code SEO docs named.
- **Best for:** Post-migration and post-redesign QA; any site where pages get deleted (old previews, retired service pages).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1220⟧

## ⟦S1221⟧ sitemap-coverage — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Sitemap-completeness rule, the inverse of ⟦S1220⟧: every canonical, indexable page should be in the sitemap, and nothing non-indexable should be — missing pages rely on link discovery and index slowly. Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing change; the effect is indexing speed and completeness for new or deep pages (new town/service pages especially).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Include: HTTP-200 canonical pages with self-referencing canonicals and no noindex — new pages from the last 7 days flagged high-priority. Exclude: noindex pages (a sitemap entry contradicting a noindex tag is the named anti-pattern), robots.txt-blocked pages, non-self-canonical pages, 3XX redirects, faceted/filtered duplicates, login/checkout/private pages; paginated subpages excluded unless uniquely indexable. Gap-finding method: Search Console Coverage ("Discovered – currently not indexed"), a full crawl diffed against sitemap URLs, and server-log analysis for Googlebot-visited URLs missing from the sitemap. Fix by automating generation from published, indexable content.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sitemap-coverage" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/sitemap-coverage); Google sitemap best practices named.
- **Best for:** Launch QA on multi-page trade builds (service × town matrices) and ongoing publishing.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1221⟧

## ⟦S1222⟧ sitemap-domain — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Sitemap rule: every `<loc>` must use the same protocol and hostname as the sitemap file itself — Google silently ignores cross-domain entries, and http/https or www/non-www mixing signals a canonicalization problem underneath. Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing change; a broken version shows up as mysteriously low sitemap coverage in Search Console after a migration or rebrand.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Check = parse all `<loc>` values, extract protocol + host, flag any mismatch with the sitemap's own URL. Usual causes named: stale static sitemap after an HTTP→HTTPS migration, www/non-www drift (sitemap must use the final canonical host that redirects resolve to), old domain left in the generator config after a rebrand. Prevention: build sitemaps from one explicit base-URL env value (`NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://www.example.com`) rather than relative paths; regenerate and resubmit after any domain change, and remove the old property's sitemap in Search Console.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sitemap-domain" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/sitemap-domain); Google sitemap best practices and the Sitemaps XML format named.
- **Best for:** Migration/rebrand QA; one checklist line for any launch on a fresh domain.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1222⟧

## ⟦S1223⟧ sitemap-valid — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Sitemap rule: the XML must validate against the sitemaps.org protocol — a malformed sitemap is silently ignored, leaving new and orphaned pages undiscovered. Priority high, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** No visitor-facing change; validity is visible in Search Console's Sitemaps report (processed vs error) and via `xmllint --noout`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Hard limits: max 50,000 URLs and 50 MB per file (split into a sitemap index beyond that); `<loc>` absolute URL, max 2,048 chars; root `<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">`. Element table: loc required; lastmod in W3C datetime; changefreq one of always/hourly/daily/weekly/monthly/yearly/never; priority 0.0–1.0 (default 0.5) — with the source's note that Google ignores changefreq and priority but does use lastmod for crawl scheduling. Classic errors: missing/wrong namespace, relative `<loc>`, unencoded `&` in a URL (must be `&amp;`; also `&lt; &gt; &quot; &apos;`). Generate with a validated library, never string templates.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "sitemap-valid" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/sitemap-valid); sitemaps.org protocol and Google Search Console named.
- **Best for:** Any hand-rolled or CMS-generated sitemap; part of the launch QA set with ⟦S1219⟧–⟦S1222⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1223⟧

## ⟦S1224⟧ skip-link — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Accessibility rule: a "Skip to main content" link as the first focusable element of the page, hidden until focused, jumping keyboard and screen-reader users past the navigation straight to `<main>`. Meets WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.1 (Bypass Blocks). Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min. (Same underlying rule as ⟦S1225⟧ — see its pointer entry.)
- **How it looks:** Invisible on load. The moment a keyboard user presses Tab, a small solid bar appears at the top-left of the viewport — black background, white text, "Skip to main content" — floating above the header; it vanishes again once focus moves on.
- **Frame by frame:** Page loads (link parked off-screen) → first Tab press: link slides/fades into view at the top-left → Enter: viewport jumps to the main content and focus lands there → subsequent Tabs walk the content, not the 50+ nav links.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Markup: `<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">` as the body's first element, targeting `<main id="main-content">`. Source CSS values: position absolute, top −40px parked, left 0, background #000, color #fff, padding 8px, z-index 100; `:focus` sets top 0. Verify: Tab once after load shows it; Enter moves focus to main; screen reader announces the main region.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "skip-link" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/skip-link); WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.1 named.
- **Best for:** Navigation/header of every page — a one-element addition that is also the standard opener of the accessibility QA sweep (⟦S1208⟧ tests it).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1224⟧

## ⟦S1225⟧ skip-navigation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** DUPLICATE of ⟦S1224⟧ skip-link — the same underlying rule ("Skip to main content" link as first focusable element, hidden until focus, targeting the main landmark) catalogued a second time in the Front-End Checklist rule set. Full mechanism, CSS values and verification are in the S1224 entry; do not read this as a second design.
- **How it looks:** As ⟦S1224⟧: a hidden-until-Tab bar at the top-left that jumps focus to the content.
- **Frame by frame:** As ⟦S1224⟧.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Genuine deltas in this version only: it rates the rule priority high (S1224 says medium) and difficulty beginner; its CSS adds `transition: top 0.3s` so the bar animates down on focus instead of snapping, padding 8px 16px; its target main carries `tabindex="-1"` so focus (not just scroll) moves in all browsers; and it adds a React/Tailwind variant using sr-only + focus:not-sr-only / focus:absolute utilities. Everything else restates S1224.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "skip-navigation" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/skip-navigation).
- **Best for:** Same as ⟦S1224⟧ — navigation of every page.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1225⟧ (canonical detail: ⟦S1224⟧)

## ⟦S1226⟧ slug-keywords — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** URL rule: page slugs carry the page's primary keyword in plain words — `/buy-running-shoes-women` instead of `/products/4832` — so users can judge relevance before clicking and search engines get a weak relevance signal. Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** Browser bars, search results and shared links show readable paths: `/blog/how-to-train-for-a-marathon`, `/services/web-design-london`. Anti-patterns named: `/p?id=48392`, `/blog/post-1`, `/products/SKU-A4B9X`, date-only paths, and stuffed slugs (a 12-word example is given as too long).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Guidelines table — always lowercase; hyphens as separators (underscores join words in Google's reading, so `running_shoes` = one word); 3–5 words typical; primary keyword early; drop stop words (a, the, of, in) where possible; no `% # ? & +` or spaces. Safe-change procedure: new slug → 301 redirect from the old URL → update internal links, canonical and sitemap → monitor Search Console; weigh link-equity risk on high-traffic pages before renaming. WordPress: permalink structure `/%postname%/`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "slug-keywords" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/slug-keywords); Google's URL-structure guidance named. Companion to ⟦S1229⟧ (character legality in URLs).
- **Best for:** URL architecture for multi-page builds — service and town page paths (`/roof-repair/springboro` style), blog slugs; set once at build time.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1226⟧

## ⟦S1227⟧ social-profiles — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Entity/E-E-A-T rule: link the site's footer or About page to the organisation's official social profiles and list them in Organization/Person schema `sameAs`, so Google can verify identity and connect the entity across the web. Priority low, beginner, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** A footer row of labelled social links (LinkedIn, X, Facebook…) going to the firm's real, current profiles; the schema itself is invisible JSON-LD carrying the same URLs in a `sameAs` array.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** JSON-LD pattern: Organization (or Person for personal brands) with name, url, logo and `sameAs` array of profile URLs; footer implementation uses a `<nav aria-label="Social media profiles">` with rel="noopener" target="_blank" links. Quality bar from the source: only profiles that are regularly updated (at least monthly), correctly branded and official — abandoned accounts, ex-employee personal accounts and fan pages actively harm trust and must not be linked. Platform-priority table: LinkedIn = B2B/professional services, Facebook = consumer/local business, YouTube = video-forward, Instagram = visual products, X = tech/media, GitHub = developer tools.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "social-profiles" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/social-profiles); Schema.org sameAs and Google Organization structured-data docs named.
- **Best for:** Footer of every trade homepage — link only the firm's genuinely active profiles (e.g. its Google/Facebook presence); never fabricate profile URLs to fill the row.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1227⟧

## ⟦S1228⟧ source-maps — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Build rule: generate source maps for production JS/CSS so minified code debugs back to original source — but keep the maps out of public reach by uploading them to the error tracker instead of the web server. Priority medium, intermediate, ~10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visitor-facing. In the error tracker (Sentry/LogRocket), a production crash shows the original file, line and column instead of minified gibberish; in DevTools' Sources panel the original files appear.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Pipeline: build emits bundle + .map → deploy serves the bundle only → maps uploaded to the tracker → a live error's stack trace is de-minified against the uploaded map.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Webpack `devtool: 'source-map'`; the link comment `//# sourceMappingURL=app.min.js.map` at the end of the minified file is what the browser follows — so Vite's `sourcemap: 'hidden'` (maps generated, comment omitted) is the recommended production posture, equivalently Webpack's hidden-source-map. Always generate in build; verify the tracker actually de-minifies a test error. Not a performance rule despite its catalog placement — it lives in the performance part of the Checklist.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "source-maps" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/source-maps); Sentry source-map docs and Webpack/Vite docs named.
- **Best for:** Any bundled build's error monitoring; irrelevant to a plain single-file HTML homepage with no bundler — checklist item only where a build pipeline exists.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1228⟧

## ⟦S1229⟧ special-chars — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** URL rule: paths must use only unreserved characters (RFC 3986) — special characters, spaces and inconsistent percent-encoding cause broken shared links, crawl inconsistencies and duplicate-URL canonicalization failures. Priority medium, beginner, ~10 min. Companion to ⟦S1226⟧ (keywords in slugs) — this one governs character legality.
- **How it looks:** URLs stay clean and copy-paste-safe: `/blog/my-post-title`, `/cafe-parisien` (accent transliterated), `/products/cpp-tips` — instead of `/blog/my post title`, `/café-parisien` or `/products/C++ tips`, which break or fork into duplicate addresses.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Unreserved set: `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . ~`. Reserved characters and their encodings: ? %3F, # %23, & %26, = %3D, + %2B in paths (a `+` means space only in query strings), / %2F if literal, % %25; spaces are %20, never `+`, and should become hyphens in slugs. Non-ASCII: browsers display decoded but transmit percent-encoded, and servers may treat `/über-uns` and `/%C3%BCber-uns` as different URLs — transliterate to ASCII or normalize encodings server-side to one canonical form. The source includes a slugify() recipe: lowercase → NFD-decompose → strip combining marks U+0300–U+036F → drop non [a-z0-9\s-] → spaces to hyphens → collapse repeats ("Café & Restaurant — Paris!" → `cafe-restaurant-paris`). Redirect old problem URLs to the clean slugs.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "special-chars" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/special-chars); RFC 3986 and MDN's percent-encoding glossary named.
- **Best for:** CMS slug generation and any hand-built URL set (town/service pages with punctuation-prone names); a crawl-audit filter: flag any path character outside `[A-Za-z0-9\-_./~]`.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1229⟧

## ⟦S1230⟧ specificity-management — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** CSS architecture rule: keep specificity low and flat — single classes, nesting ≤3 levels, no ID styling selectors, no !important except true utilities — so overrides stay predictable instead of escalating. Priority high, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** No direct visual signature; the visible symptom of failure is a page where a small style change "doesn't take" until someone adds !important, and themes/variants (e.g. the 1·2·3 section-version switcher) fight each other unpredictably.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Specificity ladder as printed: inline styles 1,0,0,0; ID 0,1,0,0; class/pseudo-class 0,0,1,0; element/pseudo-element 0,0,0,1; universal 0,0,0,0. Worked escalation: `#sidebar .nav-item` (0,1,1,0) → overridden only by `#sidebar #main-nav .nav-item` (0,2,1,0) → then !important chaos. Flat alternative: `.nav-link` + `.nav-link--active` modifier (BEM-style, both 0,0,1,0). Tools: `:where()` wraps base/reset styles at zero specificity so any class wins regardless of order; `:is()` groups selectors at the specificity of its most specific argument; a 4-level nested selector (0,0,4,0) flattens to one class (0,0,1,0). The one sanctioned !important: utility classes that must always win (.sr-only, .hidden).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "specificity-management" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/specificity-management).
- **Best for:** The stylesheet discipline behind multi-version sections — three switchable variants per section only stay manageable if their styles are flat, single-class and order-predictable.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1230⟧

## ⟦S1231⟧ speculation-rules — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Performance rule: use the Speculation Rules API (`<script type="speculationrules">`) to prefetch or fully prerender likely next pages, making multi-page navigation feel instant; source cites prerendered pages appearing in under 100ms. Priority low, intermediate, ~20 min.
- **How it looks:** Clicking the obvious next step (next wizard step, product page, checkout confirm) opens it instantly — no spinner, no blank gap — because the page was already downloaded and rendered in a hidden tab while the user read the current one.
- **Frame by frame:** Rule parsed → at the chosen eagerness trigger the browser fetches (prefetch: HTML only) or downloads + renders (prerender) the target in the background → user clicks → the prerendered page is activated with ~0ms navigation latency; a prefetched page still renders on click but with TTFB already paid.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Eagerness levels — immediate/eager: fire as soon as the rule parses; moderate: user hovers the link ~200ms; conservative: fires on mousedown/touchstart. Preferred form is document rules with CSS-selector targeting (`href_matches`, `selector_matches`, `and`/`not` combinators) over explicit URL lists; exclude `/logout`, `/admin/*`, `/api/*` and give individual links a `data-no-prefetch` opt-out. Strategy: start with prefetch (low cost), graduate to prerender only for high-confidence next steps. Never speculate: logout/destructive actions, authenticated/personalised pages, heavy server operations, cross-origin URLs (blocked anyway), POST flows. Caveat in the source: prerendered pages execute JS and analytics — confirm the analytics library suppresses never-viewed pageviews (GA4/Plausible handle visibilitychange). Support: Chromium 109+, ignored gracefully elsewhere; debug in DevTools → Application → Background services → Speculative loads (targets should read "Ready"; network shows "(prefetch cache)").
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist rule "speculation-rules" (frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/speculation-rules); MDN Speculation Rules API named.
