- **Best for:** Multi-page funnels and section-to-inner-page navigation (homepage → service page → quote step) on plain MPA builds; the modern successor to rel=prefetch habits in ⟦S1195⟧.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1231⟧

Duplicate check: no two skills in this range are the same underlying skill under different names — every rule is a distinct check. There are sibling clusters worth knowing before shortlisting: the four table-accessibility rules S1244 (unique table names), S1245 (th + scope), S1254 (every th has data cells) and S1247 (td headers attribute for complex tables) are four separate checks on one element family — the sources themselves say to resolve the header-cell relationship first; S1241 (inline-SVG size policy) and S1242 (SVGO optimisation) overlap on SVGO but check different things, and S1232 (sprites) points at SVG sprites as its modern alternative; S1250 (coverage thresholds) and S1269 (writing unit tests) are complementary testing rules; S1251 (text expansion) and S1261 (translation strings) are the i18n pair; S1265/S1266/S1267 are three distinct JavaScript/TypeScript rules. ## ⟦S1232⟧ sprite-generation — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: many small images/icons should be combined into one sprite (one HTTP request), or — the modern default the rule itself recommends — replaced by an SVG icon system. Priority: low · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing changes visually when done right: the same rows of small icons (home, settings, user, search) render identically, but they are windows into a single combined image, each icon shown by shifting the sprite's background position behind a fixed-size frame. In the SVG form, icons are crisp symbols referenced by ID.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** CSS sprite: `.icon` fixed 24×24px, `background-image: url('icons.png')`, each icon offset by negative `background-position` (−24px steps on the grid). SVG sprite: one hidden `<svg>` of `<symbol id="icon-…">` elements, used via `<use href="icons.svg#icon-home">`. Retina: 2× sprite file with `background-size` set to half the real size (200px for a 400px sprite) at `min-device-pixel-ratio: 2` / 192dpi. Generation automated with spritesmith (glob icons, emit sprite.png + generated CSS coordinates). Decision table: UI/social icons → SVG sprite; small decorative images → CSS sprite; complex illustrations and photo thumbnails → individual files with lazy loading. HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces the request-count benefit.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist (thedaviddias/front-end-checklist); rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/sprite-generation
- **Best for:** Icon delivery on any section (navigation, proof badges, footer socials). Trade fit: minor for single-file trades builds — the takeaway is "one SVG sprite for all icons" rather than many small image requests.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1232⟧

## ⟦S1233⟧ srcset — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every image wider than ~100px must offer multiple resolution variants via `srcset` + `sizes` so each device downloads only the size it needs. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** The page looks identical on every device — the difference is invisible: a phone shows the same hero photo as a desktop monitor but fetched a file a quarter of the size, so the image arrives and sharpens fast instead of trickling in.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Width descriptors for variable-size images: variants typically 400w, 800w, 1200w (add 1600w for full-bleed), `src` fallback at a mid-range 800w. `sizes` is mandatory with w descriptors — without it the browser assumes 100vw and downloads the largest file; sizes must mirror the real CSS layout (e.g. full-width banner `100vw`; 2-column grid `(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw`; 3-column grid `calc(33.33vw - 16px)` on desktop). Density descriptors (1x/2x/3x) only for fixed-size images like a 48px avatar. Browser picks the candidate closest to display width × device pixel ratio. Claimed saving: 50–80% bandwidth on mobile; a 1600px hero on a 375px screen otherwise downloads 4× the needed data. Combine with `<picture>` for AVIF/WebP format variants. Check flags: <img> >100px without srcset, srcset without sizes, density-only where width descriptors fit, single-candidate srcset.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/srcset
- **Best for:** Hero, work/gallery and before/after imagery on every build — the main image-weight lever for photo-heavy trades pages. Trade fit: direct; gallery and hero photos are the largest payloads on a roofer/remodeler homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1233⟧

## ⟦S1234⟧ stack-trace-exposure — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: production error responses must never contain stack traces, file paths or framework internals — full detail goes to server logs, the client gets a generic message plus a correlation ID (OWASP A09). Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** When something breaks, the visitor sees a plain, friendly failure — "An unexpected error occurred." with a short reference code — instead of a screen of code showing server file paths like `/app/config/secrets.yml` and library line numbers.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The React error-boundary fallback swaps the crashed subtree for a generic "Something went wrong — please refresh" panel.
- **Mechanism & key values:** One central error handler for all routes: log full error (message, stack, code, method, URL, status) server-side / to Sentry keyed by requestId; return `{ error: <generic>, requestId }`. Generic message table by status: 400 "Invalid request.", 401 "Authentication required.", 403 "You do not have permission…", 404 "The requested resource was not found.", 429 "Too many requests…", else the unexpected-error line. Operational errors (validation, 404) may pass their message through; unexpected errors never do in production. Also: `app.disable('x-powered-by')`, production env suppresses framework debug handlers, `productionBrowserSourceMaps: false`. Verify by forcing a 500 in staging and by grepping for `res.json(error)` / `res.send(err.stack)` patterns.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/stack-trace-exposure (cites OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet, OWASP Top 10 A09)
- **Best for:** Any build with form handlers, APIs or a quote endpoint. Trade fit: process/security gate for the contact/quote form backend rather than a page-design input.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1234⟧

## ⟦S1235⟧ stop-words — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: strip stop words (a, an, the, of, in, to…) from URL slugs on NEW content pages so slugs stay short and keyword-focused; never rewrite established URLs just for this. Priority: low · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page itself changes — the difference is in the address bar and shared links: `/blog/best-ways-improve-website-performance` instead of `/blog/the-best-ways-to-improve-the-performance-of-your-website`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stop-word list given in full: a, an, the, and, or, but, of, in, on, at, to, for, with, by, from, is, are, was, were, be, been, being, have, has, had. Decision table: new content → strip; existing page with backlinks or ranking well → leave it (redirect risk outweighs the gain); site-wide cleanup → only with full 301 coverage. WordPress route: a `sanitize_title` filter that removes stop words with a fallback if every word is stripped. Caveats stated in the source: a minor factor, not a cited Google ranking signal (Mueller: URL structure is a very lightweight signal), and some stop words carry meaning (`/how-to-cook-pasta` ≠ `/cook-pasta`).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/stop-words
- **Best for:** Towns/areas and service-page URL conventions when a multi-page site is first structured. Trade fit: small hygiene item for location pages (e.g. /roof-repair-springboro over /roof-repair-in-springboro).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1235⟧

## ⟦S1236⟧ streaming-html — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: server rendering must stream HTML in chunks (shell first, slow sections as their data resolves) instead of buffering the whole page until the slowest query finishes. Priority: medium · Difficulty: advanced · Time: 45 min.
- **How it looks:** The visitor sees the page arrive in stages: header, headline and above-fold skeleton paint almost immediately, then slower sections (stats, lists) swap in as their data lands — instead of a blank white screen held until everything is ready.
- **Frame by frame:** Request starts → server flushes the shell chunk (head, nav, hero skeleton, preload hints) at ~10ms in the worked example → browser immediately fetches CSS and the LCP image while the server still works → each slow component's HTML streams in and replaces its skeleton as its query completes (~300ms in the example) → full page painted (FCP 380ms) versus the buffered timeline where the first byte waits for all queries (TTFB 820ms, FCP 900ms).
- **Mechanism & key values:** React `renderToPipeableStream` with `onShellReady` flush; Next.js App Router streams by default — the discipline is granular `<Suspense>` boundaries around each independently fetched section (one page-wide boundary = buffered SSR). Non-React: Web `ReadableStream` with the shell enqueued first. Abort the stream after 10s. Put `<link rel="preload">` for the LCP image and critical fonts in the first chunk. Defeat proxy buffering with `X-Accel-Buffering: no` (Nginx) / CDN streaming pass-through. Diagnostic numbers: TTFB above 600ms suggests no streaming; targets TTFB under 200ms on WebPageTest's waterfall and FCP under 1.8s in Lighthouse.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/streaming-html
- **Best for:** Server-rendered lead pages and dashboards; background knowledge for judging any SSR framework's first paint. Trade fit: low for the single static-file homepage builds; relevant if a preview/quote app is server-rendered.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1236⟧

## ⟦S1237⟧ structured-data — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: pages must carry Schema.org structured data (JSON-LD) matching their content type, so search results can show rich snippets — stars, prices, FAQ dropdowns. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 25 min.
- **How it looks:** Invisible on the page itself; the visible result is in Google: the listing gains star ratings, a price, or expandable FAQ questions under the title instead of a plain blue link.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Format: JSON-LD in a `<script type="application/ld+json">` block (Google's recommended format). Type table from the source: Article → author/date/image; Product → price, rating, availability; FAQPage → expandable questions; HowTo → step-by-step; LocalBusiness → map, hours, reviews; Organization → logo, social profiles; BreadcrumbList → breadcrumb trail. Worked Product example: name/description/image plus Offer price "49.99", priceCurrency USD, availability InStock; Product component adds aggregateRating (ratingValue + reviewCount) only when both exist. React pattern: small schema components (Article/Product/FAQ/Breadcrumb/Organization) rendered per page; in Next.js App Router the schema component sits alongside the page component. Validate with Google Rich Results Test, the Schema Markup Validator and Search Console.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/structured-data (judged against Google Search Central Search Essentials)
- **Best for:** Every trades homepage — LocalBusiness (hours, phone, reviews aggregate) is the single highest-value schema for a local firm; FAQ schema fits the FAQ section. Trade fit: direct and high — this is how the 4.9★/295-reviews proof becomes visible in search results.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1237⟧

## ⟦S1238⟧ styles-lint — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: all CSS/SCSS must be linted with Stylelint in the editor, pre-commit and CI, catching syntax errors and enforcing one house style. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a code-quality rule. Its visible effect is indirect: stylesheets that behave consistently across breakpoints and states instead of drifting into specificity and ordering surprises.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stack: `stylelint` + `stylelint-config-standard` (+ `stylelint-config-standard-scss`, `stylelint-order`, `stylelint-scss`). Sample house rules copied from the source config: indentation 2, string-quotes double, color-hex-case lower, color-hex-length short, color-named never, `no-duplicate-selectors`, `property-no-unknown`, `no-descending-specificity`, `max-nesting-depth` 3, `selector-max-id` 0, `selector-no-qualifying-type`, unit allow-list px/rem/em/%/vh/vw/deg/s/ms, alphabetical or grouped property order (Positioning → Box Model → Typography → Visual → Animation → Misc). Framework variants: Tailwind (ignore @tailwind/@apply/@layer at-rules), CSS Modules (ignore :global/:local), styled-components processor. Enforcement: VS Code `source.fixAll.stylelint` on save, husky + lint-staged (`stylelint --fix` on staged css/scss), GitHub Actions lint job with a PR comment report; `--cache` for large projects.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/styles-lint
- **Best for:** Build process QA for hand-written single-file builds. Trade fit: process rule — useful discipline when one large hand-built stylesheet carries a whole homepage.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1238⟧

## ⟦S1239⟧ subgrid — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: where card grids need titles, bodies and footers to line up across cards of different content lengths, use CSS subgrid so cards inherit the parent grid's tracks — no JavaScript height matching, no fixed heights. Priority: low · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 25 min.
- **How it looks:** A row of cards whose headings all start at the same height, whose body text blocks stretch to a shared depth, and whose price/CTA footers sit on one perfectly level line — even though one card's text is twice as long as its neighbour's.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Alignment is resolved by the layout engine at render and reflows automatically when content or viewport changes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Parent defines the row tracks: `grid-template-rows: repeat(auto-fill, auto 1fr auto)` (title / content / footer). Each card spans them and inherits: `grid-row: span 3; display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid`. Full product-card example: columns `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr))`, four tracks per card `200px auto 1fr auto` (image/title/description/footer), card `grid-row: span 4`, gap 1.5rem 1rem. Works on columns too (named lines like [content-start] are inherited). Caveat from the source: gap is NOT inherited — use padding inside card items for internal spacing. Support: Firefox 71+, Safari 16+, Chrome/Edge 117+; `@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid)` fallback is a flex-column card. Flag JS height-matching, fixed heights and display:contents workarounds as violations.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/subgrid (references MDN subgrid guide, web.dev subgrid article)
- **Best for:** Work/gallery cards, services grids, reviews cards and pricing tiers — anywhere cards sit in a row. Trade fit: strong — service and project cards are core homepage sections, and level CTA footers are a visible quality marker.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1239⟧

## ⟦S1240⟧ subresource-integrity — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every externally hosted (CDN) script or stylesheet tag must carry a Subresource Integrity hash plus `crossorigin="anonymous"`, so the browser refuses to run a tampered file. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen when it works — the page loads exactly as designed. The visible difference only appears in the attack case: a compromised CDN's malicious script is silently blocked instead of executing in every visitor's browser.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Attribute form: `integrity="sha384-<base64 hash>"` (sha512 also used; multiple hashes may be listed and the browser accepts the file if any supported hash matches, preferring the strongest algorithm). `crossorigin="anonymous"` is required — SRI needs CORS. Generate: `cat library.min.js | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A` (or curl the URL through the same pipeline); major CDNs (cdnjs, jsDelivr) publish ready-made hashes in their embed snippets. Limits stated in the source: only stable, versioned file URLs (never `latest`), not dynamically generated scripts; any CDN-side change, even whitespace, breaks the hash. Self-hosted alternative: CSP `script-src 'self' 'sha384-…'`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/subresource-integrity (standards: MDN HTML, WHATWG HTML Living Standard)
- **Best for:** Any page pulling libraries (GSAP, Lenis, fonts) from a CDN. Trade fit: applies directly to the single-file builds when they reference CDN scripts rather than inlining them.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1240⟧

## ⟦S1241⟧ svg-inline — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: inline SVG is only for graphics that need CSS/JS control of individual paths; keep inlined SVGs tiny, extract large ones to files, and never paste the same icon inline repeatedly. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** The graphics look the same either way — the rule governs where the SVG lives, not how it renders. Done right, pages still show crisp icons and illustrations, but the HTML stays lean and the big illustration is a cached file instead of markup re-sent with every page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed (though CSS/GSAP animation of individual paths is one of the two legitimate reasons to inline).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Size ceiling: inline SVG under 1KB, ideally under 500 bytes after SVGO; a design-tool illustration export typically runs 50–200KB of markup and must not be inlined. Decision table: icon with hover/focus colour change → inline or component; animated illustration → inline; static illustration or unthemed logo → `<img src="file.svg">` (cacheable, doesn't block the parser); repeated icon → SVG sprite or component; background decoration → CSS `background-image`. React route: SVGR imports (tree-shaken, SVGO applied). Accessibility forms given: decorative inline SVG gets `aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"`; informative gets `role="img"` + `<title>`; icon buttons put the label on the button. Check method: measure each inline SVG's character count (~1000 chars = the flag line), look for editor artefacts/generator comments and un-SVGO'd output.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/svg-inline
- **Best for:** Icon systems and the animated-SVG artwork the portfolio builds rely on — this rule is the size discipline behind "rich animated SVG" without bloating the single HTML file. Trade fit: direct; pairs with S1242 (optimisation) and S1232 (sprites).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1241⟧

## ⟦S1242⟧ svg-optimization — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every SVG must be run through SVGO (or equivalent) to strip editor metadata, comments and redundant attributes before it ships. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Visually identical graphics at a fraction of the bytes — an icon that was a wall of Illustrator export markup (XML prolog, generator comment, layer IDs, inline enable-background styles) becomes a two-line file with the same circle in it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Animated SVGs need a gentler SVGO config, noted below, so optimisation doesn't strip animation parts.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Expected reduction 50–80%; worked example in the source: 15KB icon → 3KB (80%). Safe config (preset-default with overrides): `removeViewBox: false` (keep for scaling), `removeTitle: false`, `removeDesc: false` (keep for accessibility). What SVGO removes: editor metadata/generator comments, empty groups, unused defs, redundant default attributes, comments, unused IDs. Routes: CLI (`svgo input.svg -o output.svg`, `svgo -f ./icons -o ./icons-optimized`), build integration via @svgr/webpack or vite-plugin-svgr with svgo on, or the SVGOMG web tool for one-offs. For animated SVGs additionally disable removeHiddenElems / removeUselessDefs / removeUnknownsAndDefaults. Always compare visually after optimising — aggressive settings can break filters, masks and animations.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/svg-optimization
- **Best for:** Every SVG asset in every section (icons, logos, decorative artwork). Trade fit: direct — the portfolio builds are SVG-heavy, so this is a standing pre-ship step; companion to S1241's placement policy.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1242⟧

## ⟦S1243⟧ tabindex — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: tabindex values are only ever 0 or −1; positive values (1, 2, 3…) are banned because they tear the tab order away from the visual order. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visual changes — the effect is felt by keyboard users: pressing Tab walks focus down the page in the same order the eye reads it, never leaping to a "tabindex=1" element stranded elsewhere on the page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Focus movement itself follows the DOM/visual order; `tabindex="-1"` elements receive focus only when script calls .focus() (e.g. a modal opening).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Exactly two legal values: `tabindex="0"` puts a custom interactive element (e.g. a div with role="button") into the natural tab order; `tabindex="-1"` makes an element script-focusable only — the modal/overlay pattern. Any positive value is a violation. Judged in the rendered interaction, not just static markup, per the source's exceptions.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/tabindex (standards: W3C WAI WCAG, MDN Accessibility)
- **Best for:** Navigation, custom buttons, modals and any hand-built interactive widget. Trade fit: a standing check for the custom cursor/switcher/gallery controls in the portfolio builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1243⟧

## ⟦S1244⟧ table-duplicate-name — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: when a page has more than one data table, every table needs its own unique accessible name — a `<caption>` or `aria-label` — never a generic or repeated one. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Visually, good captions double as visible table titles ("Monthly Sales Data (2023)", "Employee Directory") above each table; with aria-label the name exists only for assistive technology. Either way, a screen-reader user pulling up the list of tables hears distinct names and can jump straight to the right one.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Name via `<caption>` (visible) or `aria-label` (programmatic); must be unique per page and descriptive — "Table 1" style names are called out as a failure. Source exceptions: fix header relationships before caption-level polish, and don't convert layout structures into data tables just to satisfy the rule.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/table-duplicate-name
- **Best for:** Pricing/comparison tables and spec tables. Trade fit: situational — matters when a services or price-band table appears; sibling checks are S1245 (headers), S1247 (headers attribute) and S1254 (headers with data cells).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1244⟧

## ⟦S1245⟧ table-headers — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: data tables must mark header cells with `<th>` and a `scope` attribute so screen readers can announce each cell's context. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Headers render bold and centred by default browser styling, so a correct table reads visually as a labelled grid; the programmatic win is invisible — a screen reader moving through cells announces "Monday, Alice, 9:00–5:00" style context instead of bare values.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<th scope="col">` for column headers, `<th scope="row">` for row headers; every `<td>` must be associated with at least one header. Using styled `<td>` cells as headers is the violation. The source's ordering advice: on simple tables, a missing `scope="col"` on the header row is the clearest first fix, ahead of caption-level enhancements.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/table-headers
- **Best for:** Pricing tables, comparison tables, opening-hours or coverage tables. Trade fit: situational; the canonical table-markup pattern when a trades page uses real tables.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1245⟧

## ⟦S1246⟧ tabs-accessibility — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: tab components must implement the full ARIA tabs pattern — roles, states, and arrow-key navigation with a roving tabindex. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 25 min.
- **How it looks:** A familiar tab strip: a row of labels with the active one marked by a coloured underline, and its panel below. The rule governs behaviour, not styling — but the reference CSS shows the expected shape: tabs at 0.75rem 1.5rem padding, active tab in #0066cc with a 2px bottom border, panels padded 1.5rem.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no animated motion is prescribed. The interaction sequence: Tab moves focus into the strip (landing on the active tab only) → Arrow Left/Right move between tabs, wrapping at the ends → Home/End jump to first/last → Tab again moves into the panel. With automatic activation the panel swaps as focus moves; with manual activation, Enter/Space performs the swap.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Structure: container `role="tablist"` with aria-label; tabs `role="tab"` with `aria-selected` and `aria-controls`; panels `role="tabpanel"` with `aria-labelledby` and `tabindex="0"`, inactive panels `hidden`. Roving tabindex: active tab `tabindex="0"`, all others `tabindex="-1"`. Vertical variant: `aria-orientation="vertical"`, Arrow Up/Down replace Left/Right. Focus-visible outline 2px solid #0066cc. Verify by keyboard-walking the strip and checking the screen reader announces roles/states.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/tabs-accessibility
- **Best for:** Any tabbed section — service categories, before/after galleries, version switchers. Trade fit: directly relevant to the 1·2·3 section-version switchers on the portfolio builds; this is their accessibility contract.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1246⟧

## ⟦S1247⟧ td-headers-attr — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: in complex tables where `scope` can't express the relationships, each `<td>` must carry a `headers` attribute listing the IDs of its header cells — and those IDs must exist. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible changes; the table renders as a normal multi-level grid. The association is purely programmatic: a screen reader entering a cell announces both its row and column headers ("North, Q1, $10k") even where headers span or nest.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Headers get IDs (`<th id="h-q1">`); data cells reference them space-separated (`<td headers="r-north h-q1">`). Row headers can themselves carry `headers` pointing at the column group. The check is referential integrity: every ID named in a `headers` attribute must be an existing `<th>` id. Use only when scope is insufficient — multi-level or spanning headers; simple tables belong to S1245.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/td-headers-attr
- **Best for:** Complex pricing/spec matrices only. Trade fit: situational — rare on a trades homepage; part of the table cluster with S1244/S1245/S1254.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1247⟧

## ⟦S1248⟧ tel-mailto — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every displayed phone number must be a `tel:` link and every email a `mailto:` link, with tel values in E.164 format — plain-text contact details are a conversion defect. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Contact details look unchanged — "(555) 123-4567" in the header, footer and contact section — but on a phone each number is a live tap target that opens the dialler with the number filled in, and each email opens a compose window. On desktop they behave as normal links.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. One tap on mobile hands off to the native dialler/mail app.
- **Mechanism & key values:** E.164: `+` + country code + subscriber number, no spaces, dashes or parentheses in the href, max 15 digits (`tel:+15551234567`, `tel:+442071234567`); the visible text stays human-readable. mailto may prefill `?subject=…&body=…` (URL-encoded) and take comma-separated recipients. Visible links must match the LocalBusiness schema's telephone/email values. Screen-reader refinement from the source: keep readable text, optionally aria-label the spoken form ("Call us at 1 555 123 4567").
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/tel-mailto (standards: IETF RFC 3966, MDN tel URI scheme)
- **Best for:** Call/CTA, navigation (sticky call button), footer and contact sections — everywhere a number appears. Trade fit: direct and high — click-to-call is the primary conversion action on a trades homepage, especially mobile.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1248⟧

## ⟦S1249⟧ terms-of-service — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: a Terms of Service page must exist at a stable URL and be linked from the footer of every page; for account-based services, acceptance must be explicit (clickwrap), not just linked (browsewrap). Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** A "Legal" link group in the footer of every page — Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, Cookie Policy — above the copyright line. On signup forms, an unticked-by-default "I agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy" checkbox gates the Create account button.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stable URL conventions: /terms, /terms-of-service or /legal/terms, linked site-wide including interior pages. Clickwrap enforcement: server rejects registration without `terms_accepted`, and stores the acceptance timestamp plus the terms version (e.g. "2025-01-15") per user so changed terms can trigger re-consent. When ToS is needed (source table): accounts → yes; e-commerce → yes (payment processors require it); SaaS → yes; UGC platform → yes; app stores → required; purely informational site → optional. Key clauses listed: acceptance, user conduct, IP, liability limitation, dispute resolution, termination, changes, contact. Review terms annually and on any practice change — terms describing dead features create liability.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/terms-of-service
- **Best for:** Footer completeness and legal hygiene. Trade fit: low for a trades homepage (no accounts), beyond shipping the footer legal links; relevant if a client site ever adds accounts or payments.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1249⟧

## ⟦S1250⟧ test-coverage — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: minimum code-coverage thresholds must be configured and enforced in CI so the build fails when coverage drops. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a CI/test-infrastructure rule; its output is a coverage report and a red build when a change drops a metric under its floor.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Prescribed global thresholds: 70% branches, 80% functions, 80% lines, 80% statements (Jest `coverageThreshold.global`). Stricter per-folder tier for critical utilities: 90% branches, 95% functions/lines/statements. The source's calibration table — statements 60% minimum / 80% good / 90%+ excellent; branches 60/75/85+; functions 70/85/95+; lines 60/80/90+. Exclude generated code, type definitions (*.d.ts), stories and config from collection. Vitest form: v8 provider with the same thresholds under `test.coverage.thresholds`. CI: run coverage in GitHub Actions and upload to Codecov or Coveralls. Doctrine: thresholds guard behaviour testing, not line-hitting — assertions required.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/test-coverage
- **Best for:** Build QA process. Trade fit: process rule, pairs with S1269 (unit tests) — thresholds are the enforcement half, test-writing the substance half.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1250⟧

## ⟦S1251⟧ text-expansion — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: components must be sized so translated text — typically 30–50% longer than English — never overflows, clips or wraps destructively; verified with pseudo-locale testing before real translations arrive. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Buttons, nav items and labels with room to breathe: a button labelled "Submit" in English keeps its shape and padding when it becomes "Abschicken" in German — the box grows wider instead of squeezing the word into an ellipsis.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The change is in layout behaviour: flexible boxes reflow and grow with longer strings instead of truncating them.
- **Mechanism & key values:** W3C expansion factors by English string length: up to 10 chars → 100–200% longer; 11–20 → 80–100%; 21–30 → 60–80%; over 70 chars → ~30%. Language norms: German/Dutch ≈ +30%, Finnish/Hungarian ≈ +50%; design rule: plan at least 30% expansion in every text-bearing component. Technique: `min-inline-size` instead of fixed width (worked button: `min-inline-size: 7.5rem`, padding-inline 1rem, no nowrap/ellipsis); flex-wrap label rows; badges with no width at all. Logical properties (inline-size, padding-inline-start, text-align: start) so the same flexibility works in RTL. Pseudo-locale: accent-map every character and pad ~40% (`[…~~~~]`), run in dev/CI via an env flag (e.g. NEXT_PUBLIC_PSEUDO_LOCALE=true) plus visual-regression snapshots. Truncation only as a last resort (e.g. table cells) and then with title + aria-label carrying the full text.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/i18n/text-expansion
- **Best for:** Navigation, call/CTA buttons and form labels on any site that might be localised. Trade fit: situational for single-language trades sites, but the underlying discipline — never fixed-width text boxes — also protects long English service names.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1251⟧

## ⟦S1252⟧ text-in-images — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: meaningful text must be real HTML text, not baked into an image; images of text are allowed only for logos, decorative typography, or where the exact rendering is essential. Priority: low · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** The headline on the banner is actual text — it stays razor-sharp at any zoom, can be selected, translated and restyled — even when it wears fancy styling: gradient-filled letters, an outline stroke, or a soft shadow, all done in CSS instead of Photoshop.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Replace the text image with a styled heading; the source's effect recipes: gradient text (`background: linear-gradient(…)`, `background-clip: text`, transparent fill), `text-shadow: 2px 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.3)`, outline via `-webkit-text-stroke: 2px`. Why images fail (source table): can't resize, can't reflow, can't translate, can't be user-restyled, can't be found with Ctrl+F, heavier to load. Exceptions with their required handling: logo (alt = company name), purely decorative calligraphy (alt="" + role="presentation"), documentation screenshot (alt describes the shown text). If a text image is unavoidable: alt carries the image's complete wording, or wrap it in a `role="img"` container whose aria-label carries the full text while the img itself gets alt="". SVG `<text>` is the scalable middle path. Detection heuristic from the source: filenames containing banner/header/title/text/quote/testimonial are suspects.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/text-in-images
- **Best for:** Hero headlines and testimonial/proof sections. Trade fit: direct — review quotes and offer banners on trades pages must stay real text (also what keeps them selectable, translatable and cheap to change).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1252⟧

## ⟦S1253⟧ text-resizing — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: text must resize to 200% via browser settings with no loss of content or function (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text) — relative units and containers that grow. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** A low-vision visitor doubles the text size and the page simply breathes: cards get taller, paragraphs get longer, nothing is clipped, overlapped or pushed off-screen, and every button and label still works.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Layout reflows live as the text scale changes.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Units: rem/em for font sizes off a `:root { font-size: 100% }` base (body 1rem, h1 2rem, small 0.875rem in the example); px font sizes are the violation. Containers: `min-height` instead of fixed `height` + `overflow: hidden`; buttons get `min-width` + padding instead of fixed widths with nowrap/ellipsis. Unitless line-height 1.5 and em-based spacing/margins so rhythm scales too. Fluid type with a floor: `clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3rem)` — raw vw-only sizing is flagged. Breakpoints in em (e.g. 40em) or container queries so layout responds to text size, not just screen size. Testing method matters: text-only zoom (Firefox) or browser font-size settings — Ctrl+Plus scales everything and does not test this rule.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/text-resizing (standard: WCAG 1.4.4)
- **Best for:** All typography and card layout on every section. Trade fit: standing QA item for the portfolio builds — fixed-height cards and clipped text are exactly the failure this catches.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1253⟧

## ⟦S1254⟧ th-has-data-cells — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every `<th>` in a data table must actually head at least one data cell; empty or orphaned headers are removed. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** A clean table with no blank header cell sitting over a column of nothing — every bold header visibly labels the data beneath or beside it.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The association can come from position/scope or explicit linking; the failure shape shown in the source is an empty `<th scope="col"></th>` left in the header row. Rationale given: less screen-reader noise, no dead ends in table navigation, visual and programmatic structure matching. Completes the table cluster: names (S1244), headers + scope (S1245), cell linking (S1247), header-data association (this rule) — fix the header relationship first when several overlap.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/th-has-data-cells
- **Best for:** Pricing/spec tables. Trade fit: situational, same table contexts as S1244/S1245.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1254⟧

## ⟦S1255⟧ third-party-cookies — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: avoid third-party cookies — audit what external scripts set, replace cross-site tracking with first-party/privacy-preserving analytics, and gate anything non-essential behind prior consent (GDPR/CCPA/PECR). Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible in the page design; the visitor-facing difference is a consent banner that actually works — no trackers fire before the visitor agrees — and embeds (e.g. YouTube) that don't track until played.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stakes figure from the source: GDPR penalties up to 4% of global annual turnover. Browser state: Safari ITP blocks third-party cookies by default since 2017; Firefox ETP blocks most; Chrome is phasing them out via Privacy Sandbox. Common sources table: GA4, Facebook Pixel, Google Ads, Hotjar/FullStory — all consent-required; support chat may be essential; YouTube embeds → use `youtube-nocookie.com`. Own-cookie discipline: `SameSite=Strict` (never sent cross-site), `Lax` (top-level GET navigations only), `None` (always, requires Secure), always with Secure + HttpOnly for sessions. Replacements named: Plausible and Fathom (no cookies, no cross-site tracking). Consent law as stated: before setting, as easy to withdraw as to give, no pre-ticked boxes, refusal must not block core functionality — a banner that loads trackers before acceptance is non-compliant. Audit method: DevTools Application → Cookies, compare domains to the page origin; Network tab third-party filter.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/privacy/third-party-cookies (references: MDN third-party cookies, web.dev end-of-third-party-cookies guidance)
- **Best for:** Any page with analytics, embeds or chat widgets; privacy/consent setup. Trade fit: situational — relevant when a trades page embeds YouTube job videos or adds analytics; keep the tracking pixel/embeds consent-aware.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1255⟧

## ⟦S1256⟧ third-party-scripts — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: third-party scripts must never block the initial render — load them async/defer, on idle, on visibility, or on interaction, and remove the ones that earn nothing. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 20 min.
- **How it looks:** The page paints at full speed as if the chat widget, review embed and video player weren't there; tap "Chat with support" or the video thumbnail and that one tool loads on demand, in a reserved space so nothing jumps.
- **Frame by frame:** Initial load: only critical resources compete; first paint and LCP complete without vendor code → on idle (requestIdleCallback, ~1500ms setTimeout fallback) or first interaction/visibility, the optional script is injected and its widget appears.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Cost framing from the source: unoptimised third parties add 2–5 seconds. Strategy by criticality: bot detection/consent/fraud → early only if truly required; analytics/tag managers → async, defer or framework afterInteractive; chat, reviews, social, maps, video → idle/visibility/interaction loading or a facade (thumbnail button swapped for the iframe on click); ads/experiments → after critical content only. Budgets: 0 blocking third-party scripts on normal content pages; any single script above roughly 100KB transferred, or any long task above ~50ms, is a defer/facade/remove candidate. async alone is not a fix — execution cost remains; reserve dimensions for deferred embeds to avoid CLS; Next.js route: next/script strategies.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/third-party-scripts
- **Best for:** Any section with embeds or widgets — reviews widgets, chat, maps, video. Trade fit: direct — review-platform widgets and map embeds are standard on trades pages and are exactly the scripts this rule defers.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1256⟧

## ⟦S1257⟧ title-unique — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every page's `<title>` must be unique across the whole site and describe that page — duplicates make Google pick arbitrarily between competing pages. Priority: high · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Invisible on the page; visible in search results and browser tabs: each page announces its own topic — "Women's Trail Running Shoes | ShoeShop" on the category page, the product's own name on the product page — instead of a dozen pages all titled "Category" or "Home".
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pattern: `[Specific Topic] | [Brand]` (post title for articles; product name + differentiator for products; category + context for listings). Length 50–60 characters (truncation at ~580px in results); primary keyword near the start; no stuffing. Violation shapes: template titles with no unique element, CMS defaults ("Untitled", "Home" used on 12 pages). Generation: per-page metadata (Next.js generateMetadata example) or SEO-plugin templates in WordPress. Detection: full crawl (Screaming Frog), group titles, COUNTIF duplicates; Search Console's "Duplicate, Google chose different canonical" filter.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/title-unique (standard: Google title-link guidance)
- **Best for:** Towns/areas and service pages on multi-page builds — each location page needs its own title. Trade fit: direct for the inner pages that follow a homepage (town pages are the classic duplicate-title trap).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1257⟧

## ⟦S1258⟧ token-storage-security — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: session tokens and JWTs live in httpOnly cookies, never in localStorage/sessionStorage where any script (including an XSS payload) can read them; state-changing requests additionally need CSRF protection (OWASP A07). Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — an architecture rule. The user-visible flow is an ordinary login that stays logged in across tabs and refreshes, then logs out cleanly; the tokens enabling it are simply never visible to page JavaScript.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The lifecycle the source specifies: login → server sets the cookie pair → requests carry them automatically → refresh endpoint rotates both tokens and invalidates the old refresh token → logout clears both with maxAge 0.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Cookie recipe from the worked example: access token httpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict, maxAge 60×15 (15 minutes); refresh token same flags, maxAge 7 days, path-scoped to /api/auth only, rotated on every use with server-side invalidation of the predecessor. Storage comparison table: localStorage/sessionStorage/document.cookie = JS-readable, high XSS risk; httpOnly cookie = not JS-readable, low risk; in-memory variable = medium. localStorage remains acceptable only for non-credentials: short-lived CSRF token, OAuth state, UI preferences, analytics IDs. CSRF pairing: a JS-readable csrf_token cookie (httpOnly false, 1-hour maxAge) echoed back as an `X-CSRF-Token` header, plus server-side Origin/Referer validation. Verify: `document.cookie` in the console must not show the session token; a mutation without the CSRF header must be rejected.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/token-storage-security (standards: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, OWASP A07:2021, MDN HTTP cookies)
- **Best for:** Any authenticated app or portal. Trade fit: low for brochure homepages; relevant only if a build gains logins (client portal, quote dashboard).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1258⟧

## ⟦S1259⟧ touch-targets — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: interactive elements must be big enough to tap reliably — at least 24×24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2 AA), with 44×44 as the practical target (AAA / Apple) and 48×48 Material's recommendation. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Buttons, icon buttons and menu rows with generous invisible padding around them: a small × close icon that still catches a thumb reliably, a phone-number button a gloved or shaky hand can hit first try, and enough clear space between neighbouring actions that the wrong one never fires.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The rule is about the size of the hit area at the moment of the tap.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Thresholds table from the source: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA) = 24×24px minimum OR 24px of spacing offset from other targets; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5 (AAA) = 44×44px; Apple HIG = 44×44pt; Material = 48×48dp. Human factors given: fingertip ≈10mm; tremor can deviate a tap by 20–30px. Techniques: padding grows the target without changing the glyph (20px icon + 12px padding = 44×44 total); min-width/min-height 44px floors; invisible extension via `::before { position: absolute; inset: -12px; }` on a relatively positioned control; stretched-link pattern makes a whole card the target. Failure example: a 16×16px close icon fails both thresholds. Inline text links are exempt from 2.5.8. Check = rendered bounding box including padding, for every button/link/input/role=button.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/touch-targets (standards: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8, WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5, Apple HIG, Material Design)
- **Best for:** Navigation, call/CTA buttons, gallery controls, form inputs — everything tappable, mobile first. Trade fit: direct and high — trades traffic is heavily mobile, and the tap-to-call button, hamburger and switcher controls all live or die by this rule.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1259⟧

## ⟦S1260⟧ trailing-slash — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: pick one trailing-slash convention and enforce it site-wide with 301 redirects — `/page` and `/page/` must never both return 200 with the same content. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page changes; the difference is in the address bar: whichever form a visitor (or a sloppy internal link) uses, they land on the one canonical form, so the site never appears twice in Google's index under two spellings.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The non-preferred variant answers with a 301 and the browser continues to the preferred URL.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Preferred variant → 200; alternate → 301 → preferred. Canonical tag points at the preferred form on every page; internal links, sitemap `<loc>` values and canonicals must all use the same spelling (mixed conventions = a redirect on every navigation). Implementations given: Next.js `trailingSlash: false` (or true); Nginx `rewrite ^/(.*)/$ /$1 permanent;`; Apache `RewriteRule ^(.*)/$ /$1 [R=301,L]` guarded by `RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d`. Verification: `curl -I` both variants — exactly one may return 200.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/trailing-slash (standards: Google trailing-slash and duplicate-URL consolidation guidance)
- **Best for:** Site-wide URL hygiene on multi-page builds (towns/areas, services). Trade fit: situational — set it once at site configuration; not a section-design input.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1260⟧

## ⟦S1261⟧ translation-strings — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: user-visible strings must be built as message templates with named placeholders and ICU MessageFormat plurals/selects — never by concatenating translated fragments in code. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing differs in the source language; the difference appears in translation: "Found 3 results" reorders correctly in Arabic or Japanese, and a cart label picks the grammatically right noun form for 1, 2 or 5 items in every language instead of a broken word salad.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Core rule: `t('search.resultsFound', { count, query })` with `"Found {{count}} results for \"{{query}}\""` in the locale file; concatenation like `t('found') + ' ' + count + ' ' + t('results')` is the violation. Plurals via ICU: `{count, plural, =0 {No items} one {# item} other {# items}}` — English needs 2 forms, Arabic 6 (zero/one/two/few/many/other); never branch plurals in JS conditionals. Gender via `{gender, select, …}`. Values formatted with Intl.NumberFormat / Intl.DateTimeFormat (the source's example: "$12.50" in en-US renders "12,50 $US" in fr-FR). Keys scoped and descriptive (`checkout.orderSummary.totalItems`), never generic (`title`, `error`). No HTML inside translation strings — use rich-text/Trans components so tags stay in code. Verify: grep for `t('…') +` patterns, check every count uses a plural pattern, run pseudo-locale (+30% length) and an RTL locale.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/translation-strings (references: ICU MessageFormat, Intl.PluralRules)
- **Best for:** Any localised app UI; pairs with S1251 (text expansion — the layout half of the same problem). Trade fit: low for single-language trades homepages; the placeholder discipline still applies to dynamic strings like review counts.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1261⟧

## ⟦S1262⟧ trust-signals — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: key conversion pages must show genuine, verifiable trust evidence — review ratings, certifications, named testimonials, security badges — placed near the calls to action; fake badges actively damage credibility. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Beside the quote form: a "256-bit SSL encryption" line and the firm's real Google rating with its star row and a link to read the reviews; on the homepage, a strip of client logos and certification badges that click through to the certifying body's verification page; testimonials carrying a real name, photo and job title rather than anonymous praise.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Placement table from the source: homepage → client logos, overall review rating, key certifications; pricing/services → guarantee language, testimonials, security badge; contact/lead form → security badge, response-time commitment, privacy statement; checkout → payment icons, SSL badge, returns policy; about → team credentials, history, awards; YMYL pages → author credentials, citations, disclaimers. Worked shapes: review block ("4.8/5 from 312 Google Reviews" + link to the review profile), certification badges wrapped in verification links with rel="noopener", blockquote testimonials with photo + name/company cite. E-E-A-T mapping: Experience = first-hand accounts/case studies; Expertise = qualifications; Authoritativeness = third-party recognition; Trustworthiness = accuracy, authorship, security signals. Anti-patterns listed: unlinked generic badge images, anonymous testimonials, stale review counts, lapsed certifications, guarantees without terms.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/trust-signals (standard: Google Quality Rater Guidelines / E-E-A-T guidance)
- **Best for:** Proof/reviews, call/CTA and forms — the trust layer of the whole homepage. Trade fit: direct and central — this rule is the checklist form of the portfolio builds' proof doctrine (aggregate ratings, accreditations and guarantees next to the phone number and form).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1262⟧

## ⟦S1263⟧ ttfb — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: measure and optimise Time to First Byte — the server's response start — because every later load stage waits on it. Priority: medium · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing distinctive on screen; the felt difference is the blank-screen interval after tapping a link shrinking from a long white pause to a near-instant first paint.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. TTFB is the first step of the load sequence: request → (DNS/connect + server processing) → first byte → parsing, subresource fetches and rendering can begin.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Target used by the source's verification: TTFB under 800ms for key pages, checked on cache-hit and cache-miss responses and from multiple regions. Levers: edge caching (CDN) so most requests never hit origin; long-lived cache headers for static assets (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`); database discipline (select only needed columns, indexed predicates — the `SELECT *` anti-pattern); trimming synchronous work before the first byte; SSG for content that rarely changes. Measurement tools named: Lighthouse "server-response-time", PageSpeed Insights, DevTools Network timing breakdown, WebPageTest, KeyCDN TTFB checker; distinguish origin compute from network latency and cache misses before fixing.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/ttfb
- **Best for:** Hosting/server configuration for any deployed page. Trade fit: situational — the single static-file previews make TTFB mostly a hosting/CDN question; pairs with S1236 (streaming) for server-rendered work.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1263⟧

## ⟦S1264⟧ twitter-cards — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: pages meant to be shared on X must carry Twitter Card meta tags so shared links render as rich cards instead of bare URLs. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** The visible artefact is off-site: paste the page's link into X and the post shows a large landscape image with the page's title and a short description under it, instead of a plain blue text link.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Minimum tags: `twitter:card`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`; full set adds `twitter:site` (@brand), `twitter:creator`, `twitter:image` and `twitter:image:alt`. Card types: `summary_large_image` (articles/sharable pages) and `summary` (square thumbnail). Image specs: summary_large_image minimum 300×157px, recommended 1200×630px; summary minimum 144×144px, recommended 400×400px; max 5MB; JPG/PNG/WebP/GIF; the image URL must be absolute HTTPS. X falls back to Open Graph (og:title/og:description/og:image) when twitter: tags are missing — the source still prescribes shipping both. Common mistakes listed: missing twitter:card entirely, relative image URL, invalid card type string.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/twitter-cards
- **Best for:** Head metadata on every page, especially sharable proof/case-study content. Trade fit: minor but free — one head block per page template; pairs with the Open Graph tags a build ships anyway.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1264⟧

## ⟦S1265⟧ type-coercion — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: JavaScript must compare and convert types explicitly — `===`/`!==` always, explicit Number()/String()/Boolean() conversions — because implicit coercion silently produces wrong results. Priority: medium · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a code-correctness rule; its absence shows up as intermittent logic bugs (a filter that matches the wrong items, a total computed as a string) rather than a visual defect.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The trap table from the source: `0 == false`, `'' == false`, `null == undefined`, `'5' == 5`, `[] == false`, `[] == ![]` all evaluate true under `==` and false (where applicable) under `===`. The `+` trap: `'5' + 3` is '53' (concatenation wins when either side is a string); force numeric with Number() or unary +. parseInt always with radix 10. Type checks: `typeof null` is 'object' (historical bug) and `typeof []` is 'object' — use Array.isArray, `value === null`, instanceof for dates. Falsy set to memorise: false, 0, −0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN — so a count of 0 fails a bare `if (count)`; empty array/object are truthy. Enforcement: ESLint `eqeqeq: ["error", "always"]` and `no-implicit-coercion: warn`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/type-coercion
- **Best for:** All hand-written page JavaScript (calculators, form logic, switchers). Trade fit: situational — relevant to interactive bits like price estimators on trades pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1265⟧

## ⟦S1266⟧ type-only-imports — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: imports used only as TypeScript types must be written `import type`, so they are erased at compile time with zero runtime cost. Priority: low · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a bundle/compiler rule. Its measurable effect is in the shipped JavaScript: modules that were only type sources simply do not appear in the output.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** A regular import evaluates the module at runtime (bundle weight, side effects, possible circular-dependency trouble) even when only an interface was needed; `import type` guarantees erasure. Mixed imports: inline `type` modifiers on individual names (TS 4.5+), or split into two import statements. Automatic enforcement: `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` (TypeScript 5) turns a value-import of a type-only binding into a compile error (and replaces the older importsNotUsedAsValues/preserveValueImports options — don't set both). Lint route: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` (prefer type-imports), auto-fixable with `eslint --fix`. Boundary case from the source: a class is both a type and a runtime value — importing it with `import type` then calling `new` is a compile error; keep a regular import whenever the binding is constructed, called, or its statics are touched. Same pattern for re-exports (`export type`).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/type-only-imports (references: TypeScript 3.8 type-only imports notes, typescript-eslint consistent-type-imports)
- **Best for:** TypeScript codebases' bundle hygiene. Trade fit: none for the single-file HTML builds; process knowledge only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1266⟧

## ⟦S1267⟧ typescript-strict-mode — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: `"strict": true` must be on in tsconfig.json (and actually enforced by CI) so the whole strict family of type checks catches null/implicit-any bugs at compile time. Priority: high · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a project-configuration rule; its output is type errors at build time where a non-strict project would have shipped a runtime crash (the source's example: reading `.name` of a possibly-null user).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The strict umbrella switches on eight flags: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, useUnknownInCatchVariables, alwaysStrict. Recommended additions beyond strict: noUncheckedIndexedAccess (index access yields T | undefined), noImplicitOverride, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noFallthroughCasesInSwitch. Retrofit path for legacy codebases: phase 1 strictNullChecks alone, phase 2 add noImplicitAny, phase 3 full strict — and fix errors rather than suppressing with @ts-ignore/@ts-expect-error. Verification includes a subtle one from the source: confirm no later tsconfig line silently re-disables a strict flag (e.g. `"strictNullChecks": false` after `"strict": true`), and that CI runs `tsc --noEmit`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/typescript-strict-mode (standard: TSConfig strict reference)
- **Best for:** TypeScript project setup. Trade fit: none for the HTML builds; general process knowledge.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1267⟧

## ⟦S1268⟧ unique-id — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: every `id` attribute on a page must be unique — duplicates break label association, ARIA relationships and getElementById. Priority: high · Difficulty: beginner · Time: 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing distinctive visually; the failures it prevents are behavioural: clicking a label that focuses the wrong form field, a menu button that opens the wrong menu, a script that updates the first of two same-ID blocks and leaves the other stale.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** One occurrence per document, full stop; classes are for repeated styling, IDs for unique anchors and references (labels' `for`, aria-labelledby/aria-controls, fragment links, getElementById — which returns only the first match). Repeated-component route from the source: React `useId()` per instance, suffixing field IDs from it (instances render as :r1:-name, :r2:-name…); equivalent prefix-per-instance counters in Vue/vanilla JS. Naming guidance: descriptive kebab-case and namespaced groups (modal-login, modal-login-title, modal-login-close), not div1/box/input1. Verification routes: W3C validator, a console duplicate scan over `[id]` elements, or an automated test asserting id count equals unique-id count.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/unique-id (standards: MDN HTML, WHATWG HTML Living Standard)
- **Best for:** Forms and any page rendering repeated components (cards, accordions, switchers). Trade fit: direct — a single-file homepage with repeated section versions and form fields is exactly where duplicate IDs creep in and silently break labels.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1268⟧

## ⟦S1269⟧ unit-tests — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: critical functionality must have unit tests — behaviour-focused, with external dependencies mocked — running in CI on every pull request. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on screen — a development-process rule; its artefact is the test suite itself: descriptively named cases ("formats other currencies", "does not call onClick when disabled") that read as documentation of expected behaviour.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Coverage aim stated up front: 80%+ on critical paths; the source's own Vitest config example enforces 80% branches/functions/lines/statements as global thresholds (the enforcement mechanism is S1250's subject). Test-worthiness table: payment calculations critical; form validation and authentication logic high; data transformations and utilities medium; simple getters low. Stack in the examples: Vitest + jsdom + Testing Library (render/screen/userEvent/renderHook), tests structured describe → describe → it, AAA (Arrange, Act, Assert) pattern. Mocking doctrine: mock external modules, fetch and timers (vi.mock, vi.stubGlobal, fake timers) — not internal modules. Checklist from the source: happy path, edge cases (empty/null/boundary), error conditions, async states, accessibility attributes, user interactions, CI on every PR — with the closing caveat that high coverage ≠ high quality; test behaviour, not implementation.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/unit-tests (standards: Playwright docs, Testing Library guiding principles)
- **Best for:** Build QA process for any coded deliverable. Trade fit: process rule; pairs with S1250 (thresholds) and S0904 (accessibility testing).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1269⟧

## ⟦S1270⟧ unused-css — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** Audit rule: unused CSS must be identified and removed from production stylesheets (PurgeCSS/UnCSS/DevTools Coverage), with dynamic and state classes safelisted so nothing live is stripped. Priority: high · Difficulty: intermediate · Time: 25 min.
- **How it looks:** The page looks exactly the same — that is the point and the risk. Done right, every visual is untouched while the stylesheet shrinks dramatically; done carelessly, a JS-toggled state (an open menu, an active tab) loses its styling, which is why the source insists on thorough post-purge testing.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Unused @keyframes are one of the things purged when the keyframes option is on.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Scale of the problem from the source: projects typically use only 10–25% of their CSS; worked example: Bootstrap ≈160KB minified with ≈120KB (75%) unused when only grid/buttons/utilities are used. Expected reduction: 50–90% for framework users. Tooling: PurgeCSS (content globs over html/js/tsx/vue + `defaultExtractor` regex `[\w-/:]+`, options keyframes/fontFace/variables all true), UnCSS, or Chrome DevTools Coverage for manual audit. Safelist discipline: standard patterns like /^btn-/, /^carousel-/, deep/greedy lists for component families, plus raw-content injection for state classes JS adds at runtime (dark-mode, is-mobile); run the purge in production builds only (PostCSS plugin gated on NODE_ENV). Dynamic-class pitfall: template-built class names (`btn-${type}`) are invisible to the extractor — safelist the pattern or enumerate full class names in a lookup object.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist; rule page https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/unused-css
- **Best for:** Stylesheet weight on framework-based builds; for hand-written single-file builds it is the audit habit (Coverage tab) rather than the tooling. Trade fit: situational — the portfolio builds hand-write their CSS, but a coverage audit before shipping still finds dead rules.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1270⟧
# Skills S1271–S1293

**Collections in this range:** ⟦S1271⟧–⟦S1292⟧ are Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills (thedaviddias/front-end-checklist): short audit rules, each with a main rule text plus a bundled `references/rule.md` carrying priority / difficulty / time, code examples and verification steps. All 22 were read in full, rule.md included. These are QA/audit rules, not design systems — "How it looks" describes what the visitor (or a search engine / assistive tech) experiences when the rule is applied, and "Frame by frame" is "Static — no motion" except where a rule itself prescribes motion (⟦S1276⟧, and one font-loading detail in ⟦S1284⟧). ⟦S1293⟧ is Part 21 — MCP Market — shadcn and n8n UI skills.

**Relationships inside the range (stated plainly, not duplicates):** ⟦S1273⟧ video-captions is the captions-only deep dive inside ⟦S1272⟧ video-accessibility's wider checklist (captions + audio descriptions + transcripts + pause controls + autoplay) — two distinct rules, both given full entries, cross-pointed. ⟦S1278⟧ viewport-zoom is the zoom companion to ⟦S1277⟧ viewport (one sets the tag, the other forbids disabling zoom in it). ⟦S1275⟧ is the dedicated poster rule for one of ⟦S1274⟧'s five checks.

**Duplicate finding:** ⟦S1293⟧ shadcn-ui/shadcn is the SAME underlying skill as ⟦S0498⟧ shadcn-ui/shadcn in Part 13 (identical heading, "When to use" text, Principles and Critical Rules — verified against the source). The difference is packaging only: ⟦S0498⟧'s copy inlines 6 reference files and links the six `rules/*.md` files; ⟦S1293⟧'s copy inlines all 12. ⟦S1293⟧ is therefore written as a pointer entry to ⟦S0498⟧ plus the deltas that exist in full text only here.

## ⟦S1271⟧ video — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO audit rule: every page embedding or hosting video (YouTube, Vimeo, self-hosted) should carry VideoObject JSON-LD schema so the video is eligible for Google video carousels, the Video tab and Discover. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/video. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing changes on the page itself. What changes is the search result: the video can appear in a video carousel / rich result with its thumbnail, title, description and duration instead of a plain link.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** A `<script type="application/ld+json">` block with `"@type": "VideoObject"`. Required properties: `name`, `description`, `thumbnailUrl` (absolute URL, min 60×30 px), `uploadDate` (ISO 8601). Recommended: `contentUrl` (direct file) or `embedUrl` (iframe URL), `duration` (ISO 8601, e.g. `PT12M30S`), `expires`, `interactionStatistic`, `author`. YouTube thumbnails follow `https://img.youtube.com/vi/{VIDEO_ID}/maxresdefault.jpg`. Validate with Google's Rich Results Test; monitor in Search Console → Rich Results → Video. Exception stated in the source: only add schema the page can truthfully support — a valid block whose claims the visible page doesn't back up is worse than none.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist (thedaviddias/front-end-checklist), rule "video"; Google Rich Results Test and schema.org VideoObject named as the standards.
- **Best for:** Any page with a real video on it — hero films, testimonial videos, project walk-throughs on trade sites. No visual-design content; it is a search-visibility gate for video pages.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — applies only where a page actually hosts/embeds video (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1271⟧

## ⟦S1272⟧ video-accessibility — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The broad video-accessibility audit rule: videos must ship with accurate captions, audio descriptions, transcripts and keyboard-usable pause controls, and must never autoplay with sound. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/video-accessibility. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** A video player with visible controls; a caption line rendered over the picture in sync with speech (short lines, speaker names, bracketed sounds like [door closes]); a "Show Transcript" toggle under the player opening a text panel (the source's styling: max-height 300px, scrollable, light-grey box); a written description line under the video.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. (Playback behaviour rules only: no autoplay with sound; autoplay at all is gated on `prefers-reduced-motion` in the source's responsive example — muted + loop only when the user has NOT requested reduced motion.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<track kind="captions">` (reviewed, never raw auto-generated), `<track kind="descriptions">` for audio description, WebVTT caption files with timestamps, caption best practice: lines of 32–40 characters, include speaker ID and non-speech audio, never all-caps. Spacebar on the focused video must pause without scrolling the page. Embeds keep the duty: YouTube via `youtube-nocookie.com/embed/{id}?cc_load_policy=1`, Vimeo via `?texttrack=en`. Responsive embed wrapper: `padding-bottom: 56.25%` (16:9). Focus style in the source's CSS: 2px solid #0066cc outline, 2px offset.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "video-accessibility"; WCAG media requirements as the underlying standard.
- **Best for:** Every video used anywhere on a homepage — hero films, review/testimonial videos, before/after walk-throughs. The captions half of this rule is deep-dived separately in ⟦S1273⟧.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; governs any section that plays video (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1272⟧

## ⟦S1273⟧ video-captions — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The captions-only rule: prerecorded video with audio must have synchronized captions (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.2.2, Level AA) and live video must have real-time captions (SC 1.2.4). It is the deep dive on one requirement of ⟦S1272⟧, not a restatement of the whole rule — audio descriptions, transcripts-as-alternative and controls live in ⟦S1272⟧. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/video-captions. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Caption text appears over the video in sync with the audio, carrying everything the audio carries: dialogue, who is speaking ([Speaker 2]), and relevant non-speech sound ([upbeat music playing], [applause]).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `<track kind="captions" srclang label src="….vtt" default>` inside `<video>`; at least one track carries `default` so captions are on. Captions ≠ subtitles: `kind="subtitles"` is translation-only and does NOT satisfy SC 1.2.2 because non-speech audio may be omitted; transcripts are unsynchronized and satisfy SC 1.2.1 for audio-only content instead. Auto-generated captions average ~80% accuracy and must be reviewed/corrected before publishing (worst on proper nouns, technical terms, accented speech). Live streams need a real-time service / CART. Source stat: ~15% of adults have some degree of hearing loss.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "video-captions"; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.2.2 / 1.2.4, MDN `<track>` element and WebAIM caption guidance named.
- **Best for:** Any spoken-word video on a trade homepage — testimonial clips, the owner talking through a finished job, process explainers.
