- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; a legal-compliance requirement wherever video with audio ships (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1273⟧

## ⟦S1274⟧ video-optimization — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The video-weight audit rule: re-encode web video instead of shipping camera/screen-recorder output, match resolution to the rendered player size, prefer efficient codecs, strip audio from silent loops. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/performance/video-optimization. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 20 min.
- **How it looks:** The same video, visually indistinguishable at its displayed size — the difference is invisible: the hero film simply arrives fast instead of stalling the page's Largest Contentful Paint.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed (it governs the file, not the animation).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Resolution matched to player: full-bleed desktop hero 1080p, inline article video 720p, thumbnail/preview 480p or a static poster. Codec order in `<source>`: AV1 (WebM/MP4, best compression) → VP9 (WebM) → HEVC/H.265 (MP4, Safari) → H.264 (MP4, universal fallback). Source FFmpeg values: H.264 `-crf 23 -preset slow`, audio AAC 128k; VP9 `-crf 32 -b:v 0`; strip audio with `-an`. `preload="metadata"` (or "none") below the fold, never "auto"; a poster on every video; hero/background files kept under a few MB. Recorded limitation: native `<video>` cannot pick resolution per breakpoint like `<picture>` does — the source's fix is an SSR `<picture>` placeholder swapped for the right-resolution `<video>` by JS media query.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "video-optimization"; FFmpeg as the encoding tool.
- **Best for:** Hero background films and any embedded job/testimonial video — the single heaviest asset class on the immersive homepages this bank builds.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; hero video is a core device of these builds (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1274⟧

## ⟦S1275⟧ video-thumbnail — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The poster rule: every `<video>` gets a `poster` image so the player shows a representative still before load/play instead of a blank black rectangle. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/video-thumbnail. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Before anyone presses play, the video frame shows a real still from the video (or a branded title card) at the video's own aspect ratio, with the play control over it — on slow connections and wherever autoplay is blocked, that still IS the section's visual.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `poster` attribute with a non-empty, resolving URL; poster dimensions 1280×720 px minimum for HD, 640×360 acceptable for small embeds; aspect ratio matching the video (typically 16:9); file under 100 KB; JPEG for photos, WebP with JPEG fallback; host on a CDN-cached URL. Pair with explicit `width`/`height` (or CSS `aspect-ratio: 16/9`) so the reserved box prevents Cumulative Layout Shift. Deceptive/clickbait posters are an explicit violation. This is the dedicated rule for one check inside ⟦S1274⟧, and the poster behaviour pairs with `preload="none"/"metadata"` — with no frames downloaded, the poster is the only visual shown.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "video-thumbnail".
- **Best for:** Hero films, work/gallery video tiles, testimonial players — anywhere a video sits unplayed in the layout, which on a trade homepage is most of the page's video.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the unplayed state is the state most visitors actually see (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1275⟧

## ⟦S1276⟧ view-transitions — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The one true motion mechanism in this range: use the native View Transitions API to animate between page states/navigations instead of hard cuts or a JS animation library. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/view-transitions. Priority low (checklist urgency) · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Navigating no longer snaps: the old page fades/slides away as the new one fades/slides in, and an element that exists on both views — a project photo on a gallery tile and the same photo large on its detail view — visibly grows/morphs from its old position and size into the new one (the "magic move").
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger: a navigation or DOM change wrapped in `document.startViewTransition(callback)` (same-document), or a plain page load with `@view-transition { navigation: auto }` in CSS (cross-document, Chrome 126+). Step 1: the browser screenshots the current state ("old"). Step 2: the callback swaps the DOM. Step 3: the browser animates old → new through `::view-transition-old(root)` / `::view-transition-new(root)`. Default: a cross-fade. The source's custom example: old view runs 200ms ease-out fade-out + slide-out to translateX(−30px); new view runs 300ms ease-in fade-in + slide-in from translateX(30px). End state: screenshots discarded, live DOM takes over. Elements sharing a `view-transition-name` animate as one unit between states instead of fading.
- **Mechanism & key values:** `view-transition-name` must be unique per snapshot — duplicates throw and skip the transition entirely (for lists, generate per-item names, e.g. `product-${id}`). Feature-detect `'startViewTransition' in document` and fall back to an instant update. Reduced motion is mandatory handling: inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` set both pseudo-elements' `animation: none` (the source's guarded example uses 250ms ease-out/ease-in fade-and-slide outside the media query). Next.js App Router has no native exposure — the source injects the `@view-transition` opt-in globally in the root layout. Support notes recorded: cross-document needs Chrome 126+; baseline minimums listed as Chrome 115 / Edge 115 / Firefox 116 / Safari 16.4.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "view-transitions"; MDN View Transitions API and the Chrome web-platform guide named.
- **Best for:** Navigation and view-switching motion — page-to-page transitions on multi-page sites, and gallery tile → full-view shared-element moves. In a single-file homepage it is the native way to morph between the 1·2·3 section versions or between gallery states without a library.
- **Tier:** STRONG — trade-fit call: the only mechanism-grade motion entry in this range; the source's "low" is checklist priority, not design value.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1276⟧

## ⟦S1277⟧ viewport — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The foundational responsive rule: every HTML document declares `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`, or mobile browsers render the page at desktop width (~980px) and shrink it to unreadable size. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/viewport. Priority critical · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **How it looks:** On a phone the page renders at the phone's real width — text at readable size with no pinch-zoom needed, media queries responding to the actual device width.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The one tag, in `<head>`: `width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0`. Never `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no` (that half of the topic is ⟦S1278⟧'s whole rule). Property table in the source: `width`, `initial-scale`, `maximum-scale`, `minimum-scale`, `user-scalable`, with an "allow limited zoom" example of `maximum-scale=3.0, minimum-scale=0.5`. Media queries keyed off it (source example breakpoint 768px). Framework placements given for Next.js (metadata export / _document), React Helmet and Nuxt config. Mobile-friendliness is a Google ranking factor.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "viewport".
- **Best for:** Every page, unconditionally — the precondition for all responsive/mobile work in this bank.
- **Tier:** STRONG — critical priority in the source; a missing tag breaks the entire mobile experience (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1277⟧

## ⟦S1278⟧ viewport-zoom — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The zoom companion to ⟦S1277⟧: the viewport tag must never disable pinch-to-zoom — no `user-scalable=no`/`0`, no `maximum-scale=1` (or anything below 2; the rule's quick reference says never below 5). Disabling zoom violates WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4 (Resize Text, AA). Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/viewport-zoom. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **How it looks:** A low-vision visitor pinches and the page enlarges — text, fine print, map and chart labels all grow until readable. With the violation, the page sits fixed at 1× and that visitor is simply locked out.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Correct tag: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`; `maximum-scale=5` recorded as acceptable. Also check CSS for `touch-action: none` / `user-zoom: fixed`. Browser behaviour table in the source: iOS Safari 10+ ignores `user-scalable=no`, but Chrome for iOS, Chrome for Android and Samsung Internet still honor it — removal is required regardless. The usual reason developers disable zoom (iOS auto-zoom on input focus) has a different correct fix: form inputs at `font-size: 1rem` (16px), since iOS only auto-zooms below 16px.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "viewport-zoom"; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4.
- **Best for:** Every page's `<head>` — a one-line check in the launch QA of any homepage, especially form-heavy quote pages where the input-zoom temptation appears.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; one of the most harmful and most easily prevented accessibility failures, per the source (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1278⟧

## ⟦S1279⟧ visual-regression — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A testing-strategy rule: run visual regression testing — screenshot components/pages and diff them against approved baselines in CI — because functional tests cannot see a broken layout. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/testing/visual-regression. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the live page. What the team sees is a CI failure with a pixel-diff image when a CSS change makes text overlap an image, a button vanish or a colour shift — before it ships.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Playwright `toHaveScreenshot` with a pixel-difference tolerance — the source's example allows `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01` (1%, for anti-aliasing noise); baselines created/updated with `--update-snapshots`; component-level coverage via Storybook + Chromatic (`onlyChanged: true` in CI). Dynamic content (timestamps, chart data, avatars) is masked with `visibility: hidden` before screenshotting. Failures upload diff artifacts and must block merges, not just warn. Thresholds live in version control.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "visual-regression"; Playwright and Chromatic named as the tooling.
- **Best for:** The build QA loop itself — section-by-section screenshot approval on portfolio/preview builds is exactly this discipline done by hand; this rule is its automated form. No page-design content.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — process tooling, valuable in the pipeline but not a design reference (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1279⟧

## ⟦S1280⟧ w3c-compliant — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The markup-validity rule: validate HTML against W3C standards (validator.w3.org / html-validate in CI) and fix errors before warnings, because invalid HTML renders unpredictably across browsers and breaks accessibility tools. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/w3c-compliant. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible when it passes — the page simply renders the same in every browser, with no parser error-correction reshaping the layout.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The common error set, each with a fix in the source: unclosed tags, missing required attributes (`img` without `alt`, `input` without `name`/`id`), invalid nesting (block element inside `<p>`), duplicate IDs, missing DOCTYPE, missing `lang`. Automation: `html-validate` CLI with the `html-validate:recommended` config (rules such as `close-order`, `doctype-html`, `element-required-attributes` as errors), wired into webpack/Gulp/Grunt, GitHub Actions/GitLab CI, pre-commit hooks, and Jest/Cypress checks of the rendered output.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "w3c-compliant"; W3C Markup Validator, MDN HTML and the WHATWG HTML Living Standard named as the standards.
- **Best for:** Final QA on any hand-built single-file homepage before it ships — the last gate after the visual audit.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; a cheap gate that protects every other rule in this range (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1280⟧

## ⟦S1281⟧ weak-internal-links — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO architecture rule for sites over ~20 pages: find pages receiving 0–1 dofollow internal links (orphans and near-orphans) and link them properly, because internal links are how search engines discover pages and how PageRank flows. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/weak-internal-links. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Invisible on any single page; visible in the site's shape — important pages gain contextual links from inside the body copy of relevant, well-linked pages (not just footer/nav links, which the source weights less).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Inlink thresholds from the source: 0 = orphan (may never be crawled), 1 = very weak, 2–4 = moderate (fine for supporting content), 5+ = good, 10+ = strong (key money pages); important pages should have at least 3–5 internal links. Only dofollow links pass ranking signals — `rel="nofollow"` internal links pass none. Method: crawl, build the inlink graph, filter indexable pages with inlinks ≤ 1, cross-reference Search Console, prioritise pages ranking on page 2–3. Strategy: pick 5–10 cornerstone pages and link to them systematically from related pages (hub-and-spoke), with descriptive keyword-relevant anchor text in body content.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "weak-internal-links"; Google's crawlable-links guidance named.
- **Best for:** Multi-page structure — service pages and town/area pages on a trade site, where a town page nobody links to is a page Google never finds. Little to do on a single homepage alone.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — bites only once a site has real inner-page depth (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1281⟧

## ⟦S1282⟧ web-app-manifest — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The installability rule: link a Web App Manifest (`<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">`) so the site can be installed as a PWA / home-screen app with its own window and launch experience. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/web-app-manifest. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 20 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing in the browser tab. On install, the site launches in its own chrome-free window (`display: standalone`), appears in the app switcher with its own icon, and the address bar / taskbar takes the manifest's `theme_color`.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Required for installability: `name`, `short_name`, `start_url`, icons at 192×192 (Android home screen) and 512×512 (splash/high-DPI), plus a maskable 512 icon recommended; `theme_color` and `background_color`; display modes `browser` / `minimal-ui` / `standalone` / `fullscreen`. Richer fields in the source: `scope`, `orientation`, `categories`, `screenshots` (with `form_factor: "wide"`), `shortcuts`. Safari ignores the manifest for its pieces — pair with `<meta name="theme-color">`, `apple-mobile-web-app-capable` and `apple-touch-icon`.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "web-app-manifest"; MDN / WHATWG HTML named as the standards.
- **Best for:** Any site that wants a home-screen presence; on a trade homepage its value is mostly the theme-colour and icon polish around bookmarks/share dialogs rather than full PWA behaviour.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — metadata, invisible unless a visitor installs or bookmarks (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1282⟧

## ⟦S1283⟧ web-storage — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A JavaScript safety rule: use the Web Storage API defensively — wrap every localStorage/sessionStorage access in try/catch, serialize with JSON, and never store sensitive data in it. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/javascript/web-storage. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible — the difference is that a preference (theme, a dismissed banner, a saved draft) is still there after the browser restarts, and the app keeps working instead of silently crashing when storage is full or disabled.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Quota is 5–10 MB per origin and any write can throw `QuotaExceededError`; some private-browsing modes throw on all writes. The source's pattern: a wrapper with `get`/`set`/`remove`, `JSON.parse` in a try with a fallback value, `JSON.stringify` on write, and eviction of oldest `cache:`-prefixed keys on quota failure. localStorage persists across sessions; sessionStorage is per-tab and dies with the tab. Never store auth tokens, passwords or PII — any XSS can read localStorage; tokens belong in httpOnly cookies. Safe cargo: UI preferences, feature flags, non-sensitive cache.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "web-storage".
- **Best for:** Any persisted UI state in a build — e.g. remembering which of the 1·2·3 section versions a returning visitor picked, theme or banner-dismissal state.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a code-safety rule, relevant only where a build persists state (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1283⟧

## ⟦S1284⟧ webfont-format — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The font-delivery rule: serve web fonts as WOFF2 (WOFF fallback), with `font-display`, preloading and subsetting, instead of legacy formats. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/css/webfont-format. Priority medium · Difficulty intermediate · Time 20 min.
- **How it looks:** Text arrives in the real typeface almost immediately; with `font-display: swap` the visitor first sees the fallback font, then the text swaps into the brand face when it lands — versus a blank gap (block) or a permanently wrong font.
- **Frame by frame:** Mostly static — no prescribed page motion. One prescribed micro-motion in the source's examples: a variable font's weight animates on hover (`transition: font-weight 0.3s ease`, e.g. 400 → 600), and a "font loaded" state fades content in with a 0.3s ease-in fadeIn keyframe.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Format ladder: WOFF2 ~30% smaller than WOFF; the source's worked sizes — TTF 180 KB → WOFF 120 KB (−33%) → WOFF2 95 KB (−47% vs TTF). `font-display` values and their behaviour: `swap` (fallback immediately, swap on load — the recommended default), `optional` (use only if loaded within ~100ms), `fallback` (~100ms invisible, ~3s swap window), `block` (~3s invisible). Variable fonts: one file for a 100–900 weight range. Preload only critical above-the-fold faces; `preconnect` to fonts.googleapis.com / fonts.gstatic.com; subset with fonttools `pyftsubset` (source example: Latin ranges U+0020–007F, U+00A0–00FF, keep `kern,liga`). Browser support recorded: WOFF2 96%+, WOFF 98%+; EOT/SVG fonts are dead weight.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "webfont-format"; fonttools/pyftsubset and the CSS Font Loading API named.
- **Best for:** Typography on every build — display faces are half the look of these homepages, and this rule is what keeps them from also being half the page weight.
- **Tier:** STRONG — fonts are a core visual and weight decision on every homepage (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1284⟧

## ⟦S1285⟧ webp-format — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The image-format rule: serve images as WebP with JPEG/PNG fallbacks via `<picture>`, instead of shipping only legacy formats. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/images/webp-format. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 15 min.
- **How it looks:** Identical pictures on screen — same photos, same quality at a glance; the visitor just gets them sooner, especially on mobile connections.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** WebP is 25–35% smaller than JPEG/PNG at similar quality, with 97%+ browser support, transparency (like PNG) and animation (like GIF). Pattern: `<picture>` with `<source type="image/webp" srcset="…400w, 800w, 1200w">` over an `<img>` JPEG fallback carrying `width`/`height`, `sizes` and `loading="lazy"` (eager for priority images). Conversion: `cwebp -q 80`, Sharp `.webp({ quality: 80 })` (alphaQuality 90 for PNG sources), or build-time generation (image-minimizer-webpack-plugin); Next.js via `images.formats: ['image/webp']`; servers can negotiate on the `Accept` header with `Vary: Accept`. Verify in the Network tab that WebP is actually served and is 25–35% smaller.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "webp-format".
- **Best for:** Every photographic section — heroes, work galleries, before/after pairs — the dominant bytes on a trade homepage.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; image weight is the homepage's main cost (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1285⟧

## ⟦S1286⟧ webpagetest — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A performance-audit method rule: analyse pages with WebPageTest (webpagetest.org) — real browsers, real locations, throttled connections, filmstrip + waterfall — not only synthetic local tools. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/html/webpagetest. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the page. The analyst sees a filmstrip of the page painting frame by frame and a waterfall of every request, exposing render-blocking chains and slow third parties that lab scores hide.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Run 3–9 runs (3 minimum) from a location near the users, on a realistic connection (the source's examples use 3G/4G/Cable), first view and repeat view. Budgets/thresholds used throughout: LCP good < 2.5s (poor > 4.0s), FID < 100ms (poor > 300ms), CLS < 0.1 (poor > 0.25), FCP target ≤ 1800ms, TTFB flag > 500ms, request-count flag > 100, uncompressed text resources > 1 KB flagged. Regression thresholds in the source's detector: TTFB 20%, FCP/LCP 15%, CLS 10%, Speed Index 20% change vs baseline. API/CI integration patterns included (test → poll every 10s → analyse → budget-check, PR comments, scheduled runs every 6 hours in the dashboard example).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "webpagetest"; WebPageTest (www.webpagetest.org) as the tool.
- **Best for:** Pre-launch and post-launch performance QA of a finished homepage — the independent check on the weight budgets the bank sets (hero media, single-file size).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a measurement method, not a design input; high source priority but nothing to adapt visually (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1286⟧

## ⟦S1287⟧ website-search — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** An SEO schema rule: add `WebSite` JSON-LD with a `SearchAction` to the homepage so Google can show a Sitelinks Searchbox under the brand's search result. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/website-search. Priority low · Difficulty beginner · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the site. In Google, a branded search for the firm can gain a small search box inside the result itself ("Search <site>") that jumps straight into the site's own search results.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** JSON-LD on the canonical homepage only: `"@type": "WebSite"` with `name`, `url`, and `potentialAction` → `"@type": "SearchAction"`, `target` as an EntryPoint `urlTemplate` containing the literal placeholder `{search_term_string}` (e.g. `https://www.example.com/search?q={search_term_string}`), and `query-input` exactly `"required name=search_term_string"`. Recorded common failures: omitting `query-input`, writing it as `name=q`, or placing the schema on an inner page. The source is explicit that the box is a signal, not a guarantee — Google shows it at its discretion, typically only for brands with strong branded-query volume, and suppresses it if the site search itself is poor.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "website-search"; Google's Sitelinks Searchbox documentation and schema.org SearchAction named.
- **Best for:** Larger multi-page sites with real internal search and brand demand; a typical trade homepage has neither site search nor branded volume, so this rarely fires there.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — low priority in the source and conditional on having site search at all (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1287⟧

## ⟦S1288⟧ word-count — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A content-depth rule: key pages must not be thin — judged against user intent and competitor depth, not a magic number. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/word-count. Priority medium · Difficulty beginner · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** A service or town page that actually answers the visitor: a real description, features explained as benefits, who it's for, FAQs — instead of a heading over a bare grid or a manufacturer's paragraph.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Flag pages under ~200 words of unique body content (excluding nav/header/footer), then compare against the top 3 ranking pages for the query. The source's depth guidelines: homepage 100–300 words, product page 200–400, category page 200–400, informational blog post 500–1,500, long-form guide 1,500+, FAQ answer 50–200. Thin patterns per Google's spam policy: auto-generated/template-filled text, affiliate pages with only the manufacturer's description, doorway pages, scraped content. A short page that fully answers a simple query is explicitly NOT thin. Remedies in order: expand (FAQs, examples, comparisons, how-to steps, data) → merge with a sibling thin page → 301 to a stronger page → `noindex` if it must exist but shouldn't rank.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "word-count"; Google's helpful-content guidance and thin-content spam policy named.
- **Best for:** Service pages, town/area pages and any landing page targeting a competitive query — the templated town page is exactly the thin-content risk in trade sites.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — matters per page type; a homepage's job is conversion, not word count (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1288⟧

## ⟦S1289⟧ x-content-type — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A server-hardening rule: send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on all responses so browsers cannot MIME-sniff a file away from its declared Content-Type. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/x-content-type. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing visible. The attack it removes: a file uploaded as `photo.png` but containing script gets sniffed and executed as HTML/JS in the site's origin — full XSS. With `nosniff`, an `image/png` response is only ever treated as an image, and scripts/stylesheets with the wrong MIME type are blocked outright.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** One header, one legal value: `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` — there are no other directives. Set it on HTML, scripts, stylesheets and API responses alike, at server level (Nginx `add_header … always;`, Apache `Header always set`, Next.js `headers()`, or Helmet, where noSniff is on by default). Verify against the live response (`curl -I`), including CDN-served static assets, not just the config file. The source bundles it with the usual set: X-Frame-Options DENY (⟦S1290⟧), Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin, HSTS max-age=31536000 includeSubDomains, Permissions-Policy camera/microphone/geolocation off. Older browsers may ignore it, so correct Content-Type headers remain the primary defence.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "x-content-type"; MDN header reference, the Fetch standard's MIME-blocking rules and OWASP's header cheat sheet named.
- **Best for:** The launch checklist of any hosted site — a 5-minute server/CDN setting, no design content.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; part of the non-negotiable launch-hardening set (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1289⟧

## ⟦S1290⟧ x-frame-options — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The clickjacking rule: control whether the page may be framed, via `X-Frame-Options` and/or CSP `frame-ancestors`, so an attacker can't lay the page invisibly over a decoy and harvest the victim's clicks. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/security/x-frame-options. Priority high · Difficulty beginner · Time 5 min.
- **How it looks:** Nothing on the real site. On an attacker's page, the framed copy of the site simply refuses to render — the invisible-iframe trick (the source's diagram: a transparent bank page floated over a "Click here to win a prize!" button) fails.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Values: `DENY` (never frameable — the default recommendation), `SAMEORIGIN` (frameable only by the same origin), `ALLOW-FROM` (obsolete, unsupported in Chrome/Firefox). Modern equivalent: `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (= DENY) or `'self'` (= SAMEORIGIN); frame-ancestors additionally allows named trusted domains, which X-Frame-Options cannot. Browsers that support both give frame-ancestors precedence; the source's recommendation is to send both headers. Set at server level or via Helmet `frameguard({ action: 'deny' })`. Legitimate-embed exceptions (payment widgets, dashboards, video players) are carved out deliberately, not left open by default.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "x-frame-options"; MDN (header + CSP frame-ancestors) and OWASP's Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet named.
- **Best for:** Every hosted page, doubly so any page with forms or authenticated actions — a quote form is exactly the kind of action worth protecting. Launch-checklist item; no design content.
- **Tier:** STRONG — high priority in the source; pairs with ⟦S1289⟧ in the hardening set (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1290⟧

## ⟦S1291⟧ ymyl-detection — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** A content-quality rule: identify YMYL ("Your Money or Your Life") pages — health, finance, legal, safety, news/civics, high-value shopping — because Google's Quality Raters hold them to the highest E-E-A-T bar, and a YMYL page without visible expertise rates low regardless of technical SEO. Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/seo/ymyl-detection. Priority high · Difficulty intermediate · Time 10 min.
- **How it looks:** The page wears its credentials: an author block with photo, name, qualifications and a link to a full bio; claims cited inline to primary sources (government data, peer-reviewed studies); a footer strip reading "Reviewed by: <name, credential>" and "Last reviewed: <date>", with a references section.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The audit checklist from the source: named author with relevant credentials displayed prominently; author bio page with qualifications/experience/affiliations; "Reviewed by" credit when the author isn't the expert; visible last-reviewed date; in-text citations to primary sources; a references section; a linked editorial policy; no misleading or exaggerated claims. Structured data pattern given: `MedicalWebPage` JSON-LD with `author` (Person + honorificSuffix + medicalSpecialty), `reviewedBy`, `dateModified`. Categories with examples are tabulated in the source (health & medical, financial, legal, safety, news & civics, shopping, other incl. parenting/nutrition/housing).
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "ymyl-detection"; Google's Quality Rater Guidelines and helpful-content documentation named.
- **Best for:** Trust-signal design on any page making health/safety/money claims — for trade sites this is the discipline behind showing licences, certifications, review aggregates and who stands behind a guarantee, though the trades are not classic YMYL.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — high priority in the source but only where content enters YMYL territory (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1291⟧

## ⟦S1292⟧ zoom-reflow — Part 20 — MCP Market — Front-End Checklist rule-skills
- **What it is:** The reflow rule: at 400% browser zoom, content must reflow to a single column with no horizontal scrolling and no loss of content or function (WCAG reflow requirement). Rule page: https://frontendchecklist.io/rules/accessibility/zoom-reflow. Priority critical · Difficulty intermediate · Time 30 min.
- **How it looks:** Zoomed to 400%, the multi-column page stacks into one readable column — grid cards one per row, the nav wraps vertical, tables turn into stacked label/value blocks, images shrink to fit — and everything still works. With the violation: fixed-width boxes overflow, text runs off-screen, and every line needs a sideways scroll.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (The "frames" are layout states: at 400% zoom on a 1280px viewport the effective width is 320 CSS px, and the layout must already be in its narrow form.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** The equivalence from the source: 400% at 1280px = 320px-wide layout. Build fluid: `width: 100%; max-width: 1200px` instead of fixed `width: 1200px`; grids as `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))`; flex rows with `flex-wrap: wrap` (sidebar `flex: 1 1 250px`, main `flex: 2 1 300px`); images `max-width: 100%; height: auto`; inputs `width: 100%; max-width: 400px`. Tables under 600px become block rows with `td::before { content: attr(data-label) }`; nav switches to column under 400px. Test protocol: set the browser to 1280px, zoom to 400%, verify no horizontal scrollbar, no overlap, all interactions live. Recorded exceptions: genuinely two-dimensional content (maps, data tables, diagrams) may keep 2D scrolling, with alternatives where possible.
- **Reference / source:** Front-End Checklist, rule "zoom-reflow"; WCAG reflow criterion as the underlying standard.
- **Best for:** The layout system of every section — it is the rule that forbids the fixed-width, desktop-only composition and forces the fluid grids the mobile versions of these homepages already need.
- **Tier:** STRONG — critical priority in the source; it constrains every layout decision, not just mobile (trade-fit call).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1292⟧

## ⟦S1295⟧ n8n/ui-design — MCP Market — shadcn and n8n UI skills
- **What it is:** n8n's internal UI design-and-build guidelines: how to style and animate components inside n8n's `editor-ui` and design-system packages — always build from the design system's tokens and existing components, plus two bundled rule files (web animation guidelines; web interface guidelines).
- **How it looks:** The output is n8n's own product UI built from its design system: every length, colour, font-size and duration comes from CSS variables in `_tokens.scss` / `_primitives.scss` (spacing scale starts at 2px — `--spacing--5xs: 0.125rem` — with the px value carried in a comment on each token), existing `N8n*` components preferred over custom ones (`N8nDialog`, `N8nDropdown`/`N8nSelect`, `N8nButton` with `variant="destructive"`, `N8nTooltip`, `N8nIcon`), hover/active alpha via `color-mix()` with explicit percentages, surface colour via `var(--background--surface)`.
- **Frame by frame:** The skill prescribes micro-motion, all short and purposeful. Title entering: `fade-in-up` mixin over `var(--duration--base)`. Button press: `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active`. Element appearing: starts at `scale(0.95)`, never `scale(0)`; dialogs fade opacity and scale from ~0.8, never 0 → 1. Popovers scale from the trigger point (`transform-origin` set to the trigger). Sequential tooltips skip delay/animation after the first. Exits run ~20% faster than entrances. Theme switches trigger no transitions at all.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Duration table — micro-interactions 100–150ms; standard UI (tooltips, dropdowns) 150–250ms; modals/drawers 200–300ms; hard rule: UI animations stay under 300ms, larger elements slower, duration matched to travel distance (the bundled interface guidelines separately cap interaction animation at 200ms to feel immediate). Frequency rule: seen 100+ times/day → no animation (Raycast cited as the example); occasional → standard; rare/first-time → may be special. Easing decision flowchart: entering/exiting viewport → ease-out; moving/morphing on screen → ease-in-out; hover change → ease; constant motion → linear; default ease-out. Performance: animate `transform` and `opacity` only (GPU, skip layout/paint); avoid animating padding/margin/height/width, blur filters above 20px, CSS variables in deep trees; `will-change: transform` as a last resort. Practical values: 44px minimum hit area (via pseudo-element), subtle blur under 20px to mask jank, hover gated behind `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, input font-size ≥ 16px to prevent iOS zoom, dropdowns open on `mousedown` not `click`, fluid type via `clamp()` (e.g. `clamp(48px, 5vw, 72px)`), `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for tables/timers.
- **Reference / source:** n8n repository (`packages/frontend/@n8n/design-system`); the interface-guidelines reference credits https://github.com/raunofreiberg/interfaces.
- **Best for:** The motion discipline transfers directly to trade homepages — nav dropdowns, quote-form micro-interactions, modal/drawer timing, button press feedback, FAQ/tooltip behaviour — anywhere small UI motion must feel instant rather than decorative. The token/component rules themselves are n8n-internal and do not transfer. Pairs with ⟦S1296⟧ (the copy that goes inside these components).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL (basis: duration ladder, easing flowchart and press/appear values are reusable craft; the design-system tokens and N8n* components are one company's internal kit).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1295⟧

## ⟦S1296⟧ n8n/content-design — MCP Market — shadcn and n8n UI skills
- **What it is:** A senior content-designer persona and rulebook for writing n8n's UI copy — labels, buttons, errors, empty states, tooltips, confirmations — in three modes (Write new copy with 1–3 ranked options, Review existing copy against every rule, Audit files with grep patterns). Copy skill: it produces words, not layouts.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor reads inside a SaaS UI: short, direct, sentence-case text everywhere. Verb-first specific buttons ("Add connection", "Save workflow", "Delete credential" — never "New", "Submit", "OK"); destructive confirmations that name the thing ("Delete workflow?" / "This will permanently delete 'My Workflow'… This can't be undone." / buttons "Delete workflow" / "Cancel"); errors structured as what happened + what to do ("Connection failed. Check that the API key is correct and try again." — never "Error 403", never blaming the user); empty states that guide ("No executions yet. Run this workflow to see results here." — never "No data"); loading states short with an ellipsis and no period ("Loading workflows…"); status labels sentence case ("Active", "Running" — never "ACTIVE").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The only behaviour prescribed is textual: truncated names show the full text on hover/tooltip (names truncate from the end, file paths from the middle).
- **Mechanism & key values:** ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (short sentences, active voice, one approved word per meaning); US English always; contractions used; Oxford comma always; no Latin abbreviations (e.g. → "for example", i.e. → "that is", via → "through", vs → "compared to"); dates US format with months spelled out ("Apr 2", "February 14, 2025" — never "02/14/2025"); times 24-hour with leading zero (13:34, 07:52); numbers with comma thousands and period decimals (23,456 / 346.65); one "please" per surface maximum; humour only in low-stakes surfaces, never in errors or warnings. i18n key convention: hierarchical dot-notation (`generic.*`, `featureArea.subArea.element`, `_reusableBaseText.*`, `_reusableDynamicText.*`), copy edited in `en.json` in preference to hardcoded Vue strings. Fixed terminology glossary: workflow (not flow/automation), node (not block/step), trigger, execution, credential, canvas, connection, input/output, pin; "n8n" always lowercase, node names capitalised proper nouns ("Slack Node"). Audit greps supplied with expected hit counts (Latin abbreviations 50+ typical, missing contractions 20+ typical).
- **Reference / source:** n8n's own content guidelines (self-contained in the skill; no external site named beyond the n8n codebase paths).
- **Best for:** Microcopy discipline for a trade homepage's forms, call/CTA buttons, error and empty states — the verb-first button rule, name-the-thing destructive labels, and what-happened-plus-what-to-do error structure transfer directly to quote forms. The n8n terminology glossary and i18n mechanics do not transfer. Pairs with ⟦S1295⟧ (the UI these words sit in).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL (basis: copy rules transfer to form/CTA microcopy; it carries no visual, layout or motion design).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1296⟧

## ⟦S1299⟧ beautiful-article — User's installed catalog (AI design-slop prevention & taste)
- **What it is:** An editorial harness that turns raw source material (web URL / PDF / DOCX / Markdown / plain text / screenshots / pasted text) into a beautiful, offline-openable, single-file HTML article. Articles are assembled with the `reacticle` component protocol — semantic prose components plus a theme-constrained `Raw` free layer — never hand-written bare HTML/CSS, through an 8-phase workflow with three hard user checkpoints. It generates articles only: no dashboards, forms, prototypes or general web apps (it stops and clarifies if asked for one).
- **How it looks:** A publication-grade long-form reading page. On top, an optional book-cover-style cover: a 3:4 image-and-type composition sitting above everything, width capped at `min(100%, 48rem, calc((100vh - 8rem) * 3 / 4))` so the whole cover fits one screen. Below it, a left-hand table of contents (auto-derived from sections, up to three levels, with scroll highlighting; collapses to a single column under 1000px) beside a reading column in one of four widths — narrow ~34rem, regular ~46rem (default), wide ~58rem, full ~78rem. The article opens with a Hero (title, subtitle, meta), a Lead, an optional Summary, then prose sections mixing semantic components (`Summary`, `Aside`, `Quote`, `Table`, `CodeBlock`, `Formula`, `Image`) with bespoke Raw blocks (inline SVG sparklines, canvas, small interactive sliders/steppers/calculators, custom layouts) written fresh for the paragraph they sit beside. One of 11 themes dresses the whole page through `--ra-*` tokens: tufte (old-style serif ~16px/1.6, data-ink discipline, hairline rules, no cards/shadows/rounded corners), press (Stripe Press book feel — Newsreader serif ~17px/1.7, h1 ≈ 3rem, one oxide-blood-red accent carrying structure), bodoni (black-and-white broadsheet — Playfair Display weight 900 at huge sizes over Source Serif body ~17px/1.62, drop caps, small-caps kickers, hairline column rules), vignelli (Swiss — one grotesque family, cold neutrals, hairline grid, a single Swiss red), bayer (Bauhaus — Josefin/Poppins ~17px/1.65, red/blue/yellow as structural colour, blue circle section numbers, lowercase kickers), sottsass (Memphis — Space Grotesk/Hanken ~17px/1.65, clashing pastels, black outlines with hard offset shadows, slight rotations, cobalt blue reserved for links/numbers), freddie (Mailchimp warmth — Fraunces headings, Hanken body ~17px/1.65, Cavendish yellow used only as highlighter/block, never as text), andy (Headspace calm — Quicksand/Nunito ~17px/1.7, warm cream, pumpkin orange, big rounded corners and soft warm shadows), fuller (blueprint — deep-blue ground with faint grid paper, IBM Plex Sans/Mono ~17px/1.62, cyan hairlines and dimension annotations, warm orange reserved for risk), knuth (arXiv preprint — Computer Modern ~16.5px/1.58 justified, numbered sections/figures/formulas), shannon (dark engineering — warm graphite ground, IBM Plex with mono raised for numbers/timestamps, one amber signal colour). A small low-contrast colophon ("Made with beautiful-article · \<theme\> theme") closes every article and may not be removed.
- **Frame by frame:** Essentially a static reading page — motion is deliberately near-zero and theme-bound. Default themes prescribe no animation at all (tufte, bodoni: near-static, no loops, no bounce); where motion exists it is a single short one-shot transition (press: brief soft one-time transitions; vignelli: ~120ms crisp one-shots; shannon: instant response or ≤120ms, no decorative loops; freddie allows a short transition with slight bounce; sottsass bouncy pop-ins; andy permits a slow calming loop such as a breathing guide). The exception is the `interactive-explainer` article type, where Raw blocks are the main carrier: the reader drags sliders / steps parameters and sees values and visualisations update live, with state always visible and a reset for every interaction. Print/PDF freezes all Raw at its first frame, so first frames must stand alone.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript scaffold (`scripts/scaffold.sh ./my-article --theme=<id> [--no-cover]`), consuming the npm `reacticle` package; build inlines all CSS+JS via vite-plugin-singlefile into one self-contained `article/article.html`. Workflow: Phase 0 Intake → 1 Source→Markdown (MarkItDown script primary, lightweight fallback script; optional idiomatic translation draft `source/source.<lang>.md` when the target language differs) → 2 Editorial Planning (single `plan/plan.md`: Brief / Outline / Theme / Assets) → 3 Plan Checkpoint → 4 First Spread (cover + Hero + first section + one representative visual block) → Checkpoint 2 → 5 Full Build → 6 Final Review (Editorial / Visual / Technical) → 7 Repair (smallest-slice only) → Checkpoint 3 → 8 Delivery. **Checkpoint law:** at each of the three checkpoints every decision is confirmed as its own separate question (AskQuestion tool preferred, else a numbered list and a full stop) — bundling into one "all OK?" yes/no is forbidden, and the agent may recommend but never silently decide. Checkpoint 1 confirms exactly 5 items: article type, theme, layout width, image mode, cover on/off. Article types carry bundled information-retention ratios: longform ~100% (default), tutorial ~90% (80–100), full-report ~80%, explainer ~80%, dialogue ~80%, review ~70% (60–80), essay ~70% (60–80), briefing ~50% (40–60, 3–5 minute read), visual-essay ~40% (20–60), interactive-explainer ~25% verbatim excerpt + 75% AI reconstruction around the excerpts. Component law: prose-first (body text is the bulk; semantic components only when content truly is that structure — a litmus test is prescribed), missing required props render an explicit `⚠ unspecified` marker rather than being fabricated, one section = one file (`article/sections/NN-*.tsx`; `Article.tsx` is assembler only, section numbering owned and calibrated by the main agent), Raw blocks must use only `--ra-*` theme tokens (no wild colours/fonts) and are written per-article, never reused as a widget library. Cover law: 3:4 shell locked, must combine a visual subject with a title layer, five composition templates (A text-over-image split, B big type over full image, C split screen, D full collage, E minimal frame), no remote images ever, base64 raster only under user-assets/ai-generated image modes. Image policy is orthogonal to Raw: Raw always exists; `Image` use is a separate checkpoint choice among none / user-assets / placeholders / ai-generated (AI images never generated unasked). QA protocol is fixed per node: Source and Plan checked inline by the main agent (sub-agents and review files forbidden there), First Spread and Final Review use reviewer sub-agents writing `review/first-spread-review.md` / `review/final-review.md`, per-section reviewers return pass/fail by message only; failures are fixed before anything is reported. Optional PDF: `scripts/html-to-pdf.sh` (headless system Chromium, zero npm dependencies, `--virtual-time-budget=5000`) injects print CSS that stacks the TOC above the body on its own first page(s), gives the cover its own first page (`break-after: always`), sets orphans/widows 3 and keeps figures/tables/code/Raw unbroken where possible.
- **Reference / source:** ConardLi — skill `beautiful-article`, component library `reacticle` (github.com/ConardLi/reacticle, npm `reacticle`, docs https://rearticle.mmh1.top/); live example articles at mmh1.top/#/ai-article and the theme gallery at rearticle.mmh1.top/#/gallery. MIT licensed.
- **Best for:** Long-form article, report, explainer and case-study pages — the layout system (cover + TOC + reading column), the 11 theme contracts and the retention-ratio article typing are a complete model for a guides/resources article page. Not a homepage builder by its own explicit boundary: it refuses landing pages, dashboards and apps, so it has no hero/proof/gallery section use for the trade homepages themselves.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL (basis: first-class for article-type pages and a strong discipline reference — checkpoints, prose-first, token-only free layer; out of scope for homepage sections).

## ⟦S1300⟧ gpt-image-2 — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (ConardLi)
- **What it is:** A focused image-generation and image-editing skill for GPT Image 2 (any OpenAI-compatible image API). It does exactly two operations — `POST /images/generations` and `POST /images/edits` — wrapped in a large prompt-engineering library: 93 ready-made JSON prompt templates in 17 category folders, plus a methodology master doc (`references/prompt-writing.md`) and a Chinese README, 95 reference files in total. (SKILL.md claims "18 categories / 80+ templates"; README.zh-CN.md says 79 templates and 160+ cases; the bundled reality is 93 template files in 17 folders.)
- **How it looks:** The deliverable is a finished still PNG image, not a page. Used well, the output looks like a professionally art-directed graphic whose genre the chosen template fixes in advance: a dark engineering diagram on deep-slate `#0F172A` with a 32px grid and mono type; a white-background academic figure in a low-saturation blue/slate palette; a parchment-and-gold vintage travel poster; a glossy dark e-commerce sales board with gold Chinese display type; a photorealistic studio product shot with one dramatic key light. Every template pins its own composition numerically — hero element scale (%), panel counts, gaps in px, font sizes in pt, exact hex palettes — so results read as designed artefacts with strict internal consistency (same character / same product / same palette across every panel) rather than loose AI pictures.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. The skill produces still images only; nothing animates. (Its workflow is sequential — mode check → template pick → argument fill → prompt render → generate/edit → save — but that is process, not on-screen motion.)
- **Mechanism & key values:**
  - **Three run modes, decided first** by `scripts/check-mode.js`. **A · Garden local:** `ENABLE_GARDEN_IMAGEGEN` truthy (1/true/yes/on) AND `OPENAI_API_KEY` present → the skill runs end-to-end via `scripts/generate.js` / `scripts/edit.js` (shared code in `shared.js`); prompts are saved to `garden-gpt-image-2/prompt/`, images to `garden-gpt-image-2/image/`, files named `<task-slug>-<timestamp>` with timestamp `YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS`. **B · Host-Native:** Garden off but the host agent has its own image tool → the skill degrades to pure prompt engineering and hands the rendered prompt to the host tool; it never calls generate.js. **C · Advisor:** no image tool anywhere → it prints the finished prompt and saves it, and explicitly never pretends an image was produced. If Mode A fails mid-run (401 / network / quota) it reports and asks about switching to B/C; if B-vs-C is unclear it asks the user one question.
  - **Environment resolution order:** CLI args → `process.env` → `<cwd>/.env` → `<cwd>/.gateway.env` → `~/.gateway.env`. `OPENAI_BASE_URL` defaults to `https://api.openai.com/v1`; `OPENAI_IMAGE_MODEL` defaults to `gpt-image-2` (gpt-image-1 / dall-e-3 possible). Mode A sends generations as a JSON body and edits as multipart form data; the result is parsed from `data[0].b64_json` or `data[0].url`.
  - **Template system:** `references/` is a two-level tree (category folder → one .md per template). Every template file follows one fixed anatomy: 适用范围 (scope) / 何时使用 + 不要使用 (when to use, and which sibling template to use instead) / 缺失信息优先提问顺序 (ordered list of what to ask first) / 主模板 (a 📖 prose description + a 📝 JSON prompt) / 参数策略 / 自动补全策略 / 变体 (variants, written as small JSON `modify` patches on the main template, never replacements) / 避免事项 (avoid list) — the last three may not be omitted. Placeholders are `{argument name="…" default="…"}`: user values fill directly, defaults apply silently, and the agent asks only when a missing field would significantly change the result; "你随机生成" ("generate randomly") licenses in-range randomisation. Asking doctrine is precise per-field questions (for live-commerce: who is the host — real photo / celebrity name / description / random; product name; is the price fixed?; auto-fill comments and gifts?) — never a generic "what style do you want?".
  - **prompt-writing.md (the methodology master doc, 1 of the 95 files):** when JSON templates beat free text (many elements, multiple regions, UI/cards/legends, variants, reuse); the recommended JSON skeleton `{type, goal, subject, scene, layout, style, details, constraints}`; category field extensions (UI mockups: `ui_overlay` with top_header/chat_area/gift_area/product_card/bottom_bar; product: header/centerpiece/callout_labels/footer/component_layers; maps & infographics: title_section/sections/legend/centerpiece/extras; slides: page_type/information_density/headline_system/visual_blocks/annotation_style; cinematic storyboard grids need row-major `sections` + a mandatory `continuity` field, TVC boards need header.product_name_subtitle + a `timestamp` per shot, process boards need a fixed `subject.character` + `number_badges`; catalog/lineup posters need a distinct `theme_color` per panel and 12–36 SKUs with a legend; day-trip itinerary posters need a mandatory `alignment_rule` and 5–7 stops each with left vignette + right scene; multi-grid ad banners need narratively INDEPENDENT panels with per-quadrant theme+style; the full mascot doc is a 3×6 grid of 18 sections with two-digit ids 01–18); parameter classes （必问 must-ask / 可默认 defaultable / 可随机 randomisable); question priority (subject source → purpose → core object/theme → auto-fill permission → must-keep/must-avoid); auto-fill must never break subject consistency or contradict given info; an 8-step case→template extraction method; file naming (lowercase-hyphen, topical, never source names or numbers); a 12-item single-file checklist; and the Phase 1–8 build-out history of the library itself.

- **Reference / source:** ConardLi's gpt-image-2 skill (the SKILL.md + README inside the bundle name the origin; MIT licence). Companion case library: GitHub repo ConardLi/gpt-image-2-101, with an online case browser at gpt-image2.mmh1.top (160+ cases). Collection: Part 22 — User's installed catalog. The skill's own machinery (described, never run by this index): `scripts/check-mode.js`, `scripts/generate.js`, `scripts/edit.js`, `scripts/shared.js`, hitting `POST /images/generations` and `POST /images/edits` on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`OPENAI_BASE_URL`, default `https://api.openai.com/v1`; model default `gpt-image-2`).
- **Best for:** Asset production for pages, not page mechanisms: directed imagery briefs for hero and product sections (premium-studio-product, lifestyle-product-scene, white-background-product), an exploded-view poster for a process/how-it-works section, banner-hero and product-card-overlay as composition briefs for hero/CTA areas, bento-grid and kpi-dashboard infographics for proof/stats sections, bilingual-layout and title-safe posters for campaign graphics, and the landing-page-case-study template as a full-page layout reference. Hard limits for trade work: outputs are AI-generated stills — they cannot substitute a firm's real project photography, real before/after pairs or real review data (and the library's own no-fabricated-data rule agrees); most categories (anime, VTuber, mascot, comics, maps) are off-brief for contractor homepages.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL (basis: a still-image prompt library with no page layout, motion or interaction mechanisms of its own; a minority of templates — banner-hero, premium-studio-product, lifestyle-product-scene, exploded-view-poster, landing-page-case-study — double as strong composition briefs for hero/product/proof sections, while the bulk of the 93 templates serve illustration, social and print use outside trade homepages).
