- **Mechanism & key values:** Prescribed defaults: 5–8 participants per user segment (recruit with buffer); 5–8 tasks, each with clear success criteria and an expected time; metrics recorded are task success rate, time on task, error count and type, a SUS questionnaire at session end and a Single Ease Question after each task; session structure runs welcome and consent → pre-session questions → tasks → post-session questionnaire → debrief; a pilot session is run and the plan revised before the real sessions; sessions are recorded with consent.
- **Reference / source:** Rocket Surgery Made Easy (Steve Krug) and Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert), named in the source's further reading.
- **Best for:** Testing a quote/booking flow or a new page design with real users before launch.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1403⟧

## ⟦S1404⟧ user-persona — UX research & discovery
- **What it is:** A method skill for creating research-based user personas — composite archetypes built from behavioral clusters, not demographic stereotypes — for use in design decisions and stakeholder communication.
- **How it looks:** The output is 2–4 persona profiles, each carrying a name, a photo description, a mindset quote, demographics, goals (split into life goals, experience goals and end goals), frustrations, behaviors, a day-in-the-life scenario and explicit design implications; one persona is designated primary, and assumptions and research gaps are stated openly.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. (Research document output.)
- **Mechanism & key values:** Method: Alan Cooper's goal-directed personas. Rules: base personas on research (interviews, surveys, analytics) — never create from assumptions alone; cluster users by goals and behaviors rather than demographics; keep the set to 2–4 so it stays memorable; design for the primary persona first while others inform edge cases; a persona that never changes a decision is decoration. Input gate: if the research basis is thin (2–3 data points), the source requires saying so and sketching what research would strengthen the set.
- **Reference / source:** About Face (Alan Cooper), Lean UX (Gothelf & Seiden) and Just Enough Research (Erika Hall), named in the source's further reading.
- **Best for:** Fixing the homeowner archetypes a build must serve (e.g. emergency-repair vs planned-renovation) before design starts.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1404⟧
# Skills chunk — ⟦S1405⟧–⟦S1504⟧ (User's installed catalog, Owl-Listener designer-skills)

All 100 skills sit in **Part 22 — User's installed catalog** (the Owl-Listener designer-skills set), organised in the source by CATEGORY: UX strategy (S1405–S1416), UI design fundamentals (S1417–S1435), Interaction design (S1436–S1457), Design systems (S1458–S1468), Prototyping & testing (S1469–S1478), Design ops & team process (S1479–S1487), Designer toolkit (S1488–S1494), Visual critique (S1495–S1501), Priority skills added in v10.1 (S1502–S1504). Most are principle, process or document skills rather than page mechanisms; entries say so honestly — "How it looks" describes the artifact produced or what a visitor sees when the principle is applied, and "Frame by frame" is "Static — no motion" except where the skill itself prescribes motion values.

**Duplicate / name notes:** ⟦S1504⟧ playwright-cli shares its name and subject with the earlier catalogued ⟦S0460⟧ playwright-cli — S1504 is description-only in the bank, so treat S0460 as the full entry and this one as a pointer. ⟦S1408⟧ design-brief (project brief document) is a different artifact from ⟦S0608⟧ design-brief (brief→design-token tables) despite the shared name. The seven critique skills ⟦S1495⟧–⟦S1501⟧ are siblings sharing one output format (per-dimension Observation / Problem / Fix, rated pass / minor issue / major issue), not duplicates. ⟦S1502⟧–⟦S1504⟧ are **description-only** in the bank — the catalog itself records that their full instructions were not in the uploaded catalog or any public repo; their entries index only what the description states and invent nothing beyond it.

## ⟦S1405⟧ business-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** A process skill for reading a business commercially — P&L, competitive landscape, KPI alignment — so design decisions can be argued in the language of value to PMs and CFOs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. The artifact is a framing: each design decision stated as a bet ("reducing friction at this step will increase completion rate, which moves [metric]"), anchored to research, analytics, support tickets or NPS comments.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Revenue drivers (conversion, retention, average order value, referral) vs cost drivers (support volume, onboarding failure, churn). KPI map given: onboarding redesign → activation rate / time-to-value; error-state improvement → support ticket volume / retry rate; navigation restructure → task completion / session depth; empty states → feature discovery; search & filter UX → conversion / bounce. Pre-work rule: map any significant design effort to at least one metric before starting.
- **Reference / source:** Alen Faljic, Mini Design MBA / d.MBA (https://d.mba) — named in the skill as its underpinning framework.
- **Best for:** No section use — stakeholder defence of preview/proposal work and pricing conversations; pairs with design-negotiation ⟦S1489⟧ for the live conversation.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — business framing only, no design mechanism.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1405⟧

## ⟦S1406⟧ competitive-analysis — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** A framework for systematically comparing rival products' UX — patterns, features, strengths and gaps — across direct competitors, indirect competitors and aspirational benchmarks from adjacent domains.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Deliverable is a summary overview, a feature comparison matrix (per key task: support level, steps required, UX quality scored 1–5, unique approaches), competitor profiles, an opportunity map and annotated references.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Evaluation dimensions fixed: information architecture, interaction patterns, visual design, content strategy, performance, accessibility, mobile experience. Rules: judge UX quality not feature presence; analyse full journeys, not isolated screens.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Research stage before a build — the competitor half of picking a proven reference; for deliberately adopting rivals' conventions use jakobs-law ⟦S1446⟧.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — research method, not a page reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1406⟧

## ⟦S1407⟧ content-strategy — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Defines what content a product needs, how it is structured and modelled, who owns it, and the voice/tone framework the words follow.
- **How it looks:** No page output directly; its visible consequence is a page whose content hierarchy reads primary (the main thing users come to do/read) over secondary (supporting context, labels, help) over tertiary (metadata, timestamps, attribution), with design reflecting that order.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Components: content audit (inventory by type/location/owner/age/performance; classify keep / revise / consolidate / remove), content model (content types with attributes and relationships, built for reuse across contexts), voice (consistent personality) vs tone (register adjusted per context — reassuring in errors, celebratory in success, neutral in legal), governance (creator, reviewer, review cadence, source of truth, deprecation), revisited quarterly.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Cross-points: ux-writing ⟦S1494⟧ executes at component level; information-architecture ⟦S1411⟧ structures where content lives.
- **Best for:** Planning a homepage's copy structure and proof inventory before design; content model drives component/form fields.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — planning discipline behind copy, not a visual reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1407⟧

## ⟦S1408⟧ design-brief — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** A template for the project brief written at kickoff — problem space, audience, constraints, success criteria — for one specific project. (Different artifact from ⟦S0608⟧ design-brief, which turns a brief into design tokens.)
- **How it looks:** No page output. A seven-part document: 1 Project Overview, 2 Problem Statement (what, who, evidence, consequences), 3 Target Audience, 4 Goals and Success Criteria (metrics + qualitative indicators), 5 Scope and Constraints (in/out, technical/brand/timeline/legal), 6 Context and Inputs, 7 Deliverables and Timeline.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules: focus on the problem, not a predetermined solution; include measurable success criteria; stakeholder sign-off before starting; reference the brief throughout the project.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Kickoff document for a build; the success criteria written here are what concept-selection ⟦S1472⟧ later judges versions against.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — process document.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1408⟧

## ⟦S1409⟧ design-principles — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** A method for writing team design principles that actually resolve trade-offs when decisions are relitigated — opinionated, actionable, memorable, distinctive, testable, and ranked for conflicts.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Each principle is recorded as: title (3–6 words), statement, rationale, application example, counter-example, trade-off.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Six-step process: gather inputs → workshop candidates → draft and debate ("Would anyone disagree?") → prioritise for conflicts → test against past decisions → socialise. Referenced in design reviews and revisited as the product evolves.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Standing decision rules for a build programme (e.g. the criteria a plan is confirmed against); for one project's framing use design-brief ⟦S1408⟧.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — process document.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1409⟧

## ⟦S1410⟧ experience-map — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** A systems-level map of a whole service ecosystem — every touchpoint, channel and relationship across time — for experiences spanning more than one product.
- **How it looks:** A wide grid diagram: horizontal axis = phases (awareness, evaluation, onboarding, regular use, advanced use, advocacy/departure); vertical layers = user actions, touchpoints, channels, emotions, pain points, opportunities; plus the connections and data flow between channels and human/automated handoffs.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Map current state before future state; include digital and physical touchpoints; validate with research, not assumptions. For one persona's linear journey the skill points to journey-map; for backstage operations to service-blueprint ⟦S1415⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Omnichannel services; on a trade homepage its nearest use is mapping the full enquiry journey (search → preview → call → quote visit → job → review) before designing the call/CTA path.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — research artifact.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1410⟧

## ⟦S1411⟧ information-architecture — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Designs the underlying structure of a site — how content and features are categorised, labelled and connected — and produces the sitemap, navigation model, taxonomy and content model that communicate it.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: a header with global navigation present everywhere, local navigation inside a section (sidebar, tabs, breadcrumbs), utility navigation (account, help) kept visually separate, and labels in the user's own vocabulary that accurately predict what is inside each section.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Heuristics with numbers: findability — any item reachable in under 3 clicks from any entry point; depth — prefer shallow hierarchies, 3 levels max for primary content; wayfinding — user always knows where they are, how they got there, how to get back. Validation: open card sorts for new structures, closed to validate, tree testing before building navigation. Named mistakes: building IA around org structure, designing from the homepage outward, assuming search substitutes for IA.
- **Reference / source:** None named. UI that exposes the structure: navigation-patterns ⟦S1450⟧.
- **Best for:** Navigation and overall site structure on every build; service/town page architecture.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governing structure reference for navigation and page organisation.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1411⟧

## ⟦S1412⟧ metrics-definition — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Defines the UX metrics and KPIs that connect design decisions to measurable outcomes — what to measure, before anyone reports results.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A metric set recorded per metric as: name, definition, method, data source, target, frequency, owner.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four categories — behavioural (task completion, time on task, error rate, adoption), attitudinal (SUS, NPS, CSAT), business (conversion, retention, support volume), engagement (DAU/MAU, session duration, discovery). HEART framework: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success. Rules: choose 3–5 primary metrics, balance behavioural and attitudinal, set baselines before measuring change.
- **Reference / source:** HEART framework (Google) — named in the skill. Presenting results afterwards: design-impact-reporting ⟦S1481⟧.
- **Best for:** Deciding what a preview/build is trying to move (calls, quote-form completions) before it ships.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — measurement planning.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1412⟧

## ⟦S1413⟧ north-star-vision — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Articulates a long-horizon product vision — one sentence of who/what/why — that aligns teams and anchors strategy when direction is contested or absent.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Components: vision statement (one sentence), 3–5 design pillars (strategic focus areas), vision scenarios (concrete narrative stories of the future experience), success criteria (qualitative signals, quantitative metrics, milestones).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Time horizons: near-term 1 year (tangible improvements), mid-term 2–3 years (major experience shifts), long-term 5+ years (aspirational transformation). Process: research synthesis → aspiration workshop → narrative writing → validation → communication.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Near-term project scope belongs to design-brief ⟦S1408⟧.
- **Best for:** Direction-setting documents only; no homepage application.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — strategy document.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1413⟧

## ⟦S1414⟧ opportunity-framework — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Identifies, scores and prioritises design opportunities against impact and effort when there are more ideas than capacity.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Output is a ranked list with rationale, theme groupings, dependencies and confidence levels.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four scoring frames: Impact–Effort 2×2 (quick wins / strategic bets / fill-ins / deprioritise); RICE — Reach, Impact (scored 1–3), Confidence (%), Effort (person-weeks); Kano (must-be, one-dimensional, attractive, indifferent, reverse); Value vs Complexity (user value 1–10, complexity 1–10). Rule: use multiple frameworks to triangulate; document the "why" behind every decision.
- **Reference / source:** RICE and Kano models — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Prioritising a fix/improvement backlog across sites; framing the chosen one is design-brief ⟦S1408⟧.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — prioritisation method.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1414⟧

## ⟦S1415⟧ service-blueprint — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Maps how a service is actually delivered — frontstage actions, backstage processes and supporting systems — so operational gaps behind the user-facing layer become visible.
- **How it looks:** A swim-lane diagram with five horizontal lanes: 1 physical evidence (screens, emails, receipts the user receives), 2 user actions, 3 frontstage actions (visible: support replies, onboarding calls), 4 backstage actions (invisible: order processing, fraud checks, fulfilment), 5 support processes (databases, third-party services, policies) — divided by the line of interaction, line of visibility, and line of internal interaction.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Nine-step process from scoping one scenario ("first-time user completes onboarding") to validating with operations/engineering/support. Reading rules: gaps between lanes = promises backstage can't keep; long stretches without user touchpoints = the user is waiting, is it communicated?
- **Reference / source:** None named. Customer-visible layer only: experience-map ⟦S1410⟧.
- **Best for:** Service businesses' enquiry-to-job pipeline (quote request → callback → survey → install → aftercare) when designing what the site must promise and capture.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — service-design artifact.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1415⟧

## ⟦S1416⟧ stakeholder-alignment — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UX strategy
- **What it is:** Builds alignment artifacts — stakeholder maps, RACI matrices, decision frameworks, communication plans, feedback protocols — for when unclear ownership stalls decisions.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Documents only: influence-vs-interest stakeholder map, RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) per decision, decision rights and disagreement route, communication cadence/channels, feedback format and timing.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules: map stakeholders at kickoff; establish decision rights before conflict; document decisions and rationale; revisit as projects evolve. Named challenges: stakeholders designing solutions, conflicting priorities, late-stage scope changes, missing stakeholders.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Persuading in the moment: design-negotiation ⟦S1489⟧.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — team/process organisation.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — internal process artifact, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1416⟧

## ⟦S1417⟧ aesthetic-usability — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Aesthetic-Usability Effect: users perceive a polished, consistent interface as easier to use before they interact with it, and forgive minor friction in it — consistency is the signal of quality.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: even spacing, aligned elements, one consistent type scale, similar actions carrying the same visual weight, and error/empty/loading states finished to the same standard as the hero — the page reads as well-considered at first glance.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Applies most at first impressions (landing pages, onboarding, empty states), error states, and trust-critical contexts (payment flows, health, legal) where aesthetics affect willingness to proceed. Application steps: enforce a consistent spacing/type scale, align to grid, keep visual weight consistent across similar actions, design secondary states with equal care, audit for visual inconsistency before launch — one rough screen lowers perceived quality of its neighbours. Stated limit: the effect masks usability problems only briefly; it never substitutes for sound IA or interaction design.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Emotional resonance specifically: interfaces-that-feel ⟦S1445⟧.
- **Best for:** Every section — the justification for finish-level polish on heroes, proof and forms alike, especially trust-critical call/CTA moments.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a judging lens for polish across all sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1417⟧

## ⟦S1418⟧ color-system — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Builds a product colour system in layers — raw tonal palettes, a neutral scale, semantic colours and extended palettes — with accessibility compliance built in.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: one brand hue family in graded tints and shades, calm neutrals carrying text/surfaces/borders, and success (green), warning (amber), error (red), info (blue) used consistently, each with background, foreground, border and icon variants.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Layers: 1 brand palette with full tonal scales (50–950 or equivalent), 2 neutral palette, 3 semantic colours with four variants each, 4 extended (data-viz, illustration, gradients). Contrast law: text on backgrounds ≥4.5:1 (AA) or 7:1 (AAA); large text ≥3:1; UI components ≥3:1 against adjacent colours; never colour alone to convey meaning. Rules: generate full scales not single swatches, test every foreground/background pair, design for colour blindness, include dark-mode mappings from the start.
- **Reference / source:** WCAG contrast thresholds — named in the skill. Dark adaptation: dark-mode-design ⟦S1419⟧; chart ramps: data-visualization ⟦S1420⟧; token architecture: theming-system ⟦S1468⟧.
- **Best for:** Foundations of any build — palette for hero, sections, forms and footer.
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational palette reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1418⟧

## ⟦S1419⟧ dark-mode-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Adapts an existing light palette to dark mode properly — surface elevation by lightness instead of shadow, contrast rebalancing and desaturation — rather than simple inversion.
- **How it looks:** A dark page where the background is the darkest layer (e.g. #121212), cards sit one shade lighter, modals/dropdowns lighter again, tooltips lightest; text is off-white, borders are low-opacity white, and brand colours look slightly muted rather than neon.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; the skill asks for smooth transitions between modes but gives no durations.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Surface hierarchy: background darkest → Surface 1 (elevated cards) → Surface 2 (modals, dropdowns) → Surface 3 (tooltips, menus). Colour adaptation: reduce primary saturation 10–20%; text #E0E0E0, never pure #FFFFFF; body text still ≥4.5:1. Media: dim images slightly, provide dark-variant illustrations and light-on-dark logos. Respect prefers-color-scheme and provide a manual toggle; use semantic tokens so switching is effortless.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Base palette first: color-system ⟦S1418⟧.
- **Best for:** Any dark-themed section or full dark build (several portfolio directions are dark); hero and footer treatments.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the dark-surface ruleset when a version goes dark.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1419⟧

## ⟦S1420⟧ data-visualization — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Selects chart types and designs data encodings — marks, axes, labels, accessible styling — for presenting data graphically. Owns chart selection and encoding; the categorical colour ramp itself belongs to color-system ⟦S1418⟧.
- **How it looks:** Charts a visitor can read at a glance: bar charts for category comparison, lines for trends, sparklines inline in text, donut only for few categories, direct labels on the chart instead of a legend, y-axis starting at zero on bar charts.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Selection table: comparison → bar / grouped bar / bullet (target vs actual); trend → line / area / sparkline; part-of-whole → pie-donut (few), stacked bar (many), treemap (hierarchical); distribution → histogram, box plot, scatter; relationship → scatter, bubble, heat map. Colour: sequential light→dark for ordered data, diverging two-hue for above/below midpoint, categorical distinct hues, colourblind-safe (avoid red-green only). Accessibility: never colour alone (patterns/labels/shapes too), text alternatives, keyboard-navigable interactive charts. Responsive: simplify at small sizes; table instead of chart on mobile where needed.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Proof/stats sections — review counts, project counts, savings figures — where numbers are shown as charts rather than big numerals.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — only where a section genuinely charts data.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1420⟧

## ⟦S1421⟧ illustration-style — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Defines an illustration style guide — visual language, colour usage and application rules — so illustration stays consistent across a product.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees when it works: illustrations in one recognisable hand everywhere — same geometry (geometric or organic), same dimensionality (flat 2D, 2.5D isometric or 3D), same line style (stroke weight, corners, endpoints), same detail level — in spots inline with text, large hero pieces, empty states, onboarding and error states.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; the guide includes animation guidelines for illustrated elements but prescribes no values.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Style axes to fix: geometric vs organic; flat vs dimensional; detailed vs minimal; abstract vs representational; line style. Colour: a subset of the product palette with primary/secondary/accent illustration colours, gradient and shadow rules, dark-mode variants. Character design (if any): proportions, face detail level, diversity guidelines, pose/expression library. Application rules: when to use vs not, size constraints per context, grid alignment; never convey information only through illustration.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Icons belong to icon-system ⟦S1463⟧.
- **Best for:** Hero and spot illustration direction on builds that use drawn artwork (e.g. SVG renders); empty-state and error-state art.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — only for builds with a real illustration programme.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1421⟧

## ⟦S1422⟧ law-of-closure — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Gestalt Law of Closure — the mind completes implied shapes from partial forms — to cut visual weight: drop borders and let negative space suggest structure.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: icons drawn with gaps that still read whole (a ring with a missing segment reads as a progress circle), sections bounded by a single top rule or corner accents instead of a full box, a fading section background whose edge the mind closes, and a carousel item clipped at the screen edge that signals "more this way".
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Techniques: single-edge dividers, corner accents implying a bounding rectangle, fading backgrounds, partial rules; alignment alone implies grid lines (consistently left-aligned elements imply a vertical grid). Depends on generous negative space — clutter defeats it. Use explicit full borders instead when the boundary is the primary grouping signal, defines a hit area, or the layout may collapse (email, dense tables). Test icons at 16px and 20px — the shape must still close; re-validate in dark mode where negative-space relationships shift.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology — named in the skill. Explicit containers: law-of-common-region ⟦S1423⟧.
- **Best for:** Lightening cards, icon sets, section dividers and gallery edges across all sections.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a core layout-lightening principle for section design.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1422⟧

## ⟦S1423⟧ law-of-common-region — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Law of Common Region — elements inside a shared container, background or border are perceived as a group regardless of spacing — the strongest grouping signal, used when grouping must survive a tight layout.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: cards that clearly delimit one item each, a sidebar set off by background from content, a modal surface isolating one task, form sections divided by background or rule inside a long form, table rows that light up as a unit on hover, pill backgrounds making each tag a discrete object.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Use proximity first; add common region when proximity is insufficient or the boundary must be explicit. Strength ladder: background before border, border before card surface — use the weakest container that works. Limits: nesting depth ≤2 levels; cards for everything flattens hierarchy. Containers keep consistent corner radius, padding and shadow within a system, and must survive low-contrast and dark-mode contexts.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology — named in the skill. Grouping by spacing alone: law-of-proximity ⟦S1426⟧.
- **Best for:** Work/gallery cards, proof cards, form sections, pricing/offer panels.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the card/panel grouping rule behind gallery and proof sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1423⟧

## ⟦S1424⟧ law-of-continuity — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Law of Continuity — the eye follows alignment and unbroken paths — to sequence steps, align content, and design carousels and timelines.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a clean left edge running down a form or list that the eye rides without reorienting, step indicators joined by a line that makes a process read as one sequence, carousel arrows and dot indicators that extend the path, and a deliberate larger gap or divider where one group ends and another begins.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed; it governs the paths that scroll and swipe gestures follow.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Alignment is the fundamental application — even a few pixels of misalignment interrupt the eye's path and signal a boundary or error. Directional indicators (arrows, chevrons) add no information; they make the implied path explicit. Interrupted continuity separates: bigger gap = new section, divider = category boundary, indentation = sub-hierarchy on a secondary axis. Audit alignment at every breakpoint.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology — named in the skill. Grouping rather than sequencing: law-of-proximity ⟦S1426⟧.
- **Best for:** Process sections (step sequences, timelines), forms, carousels and galleries.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governs process sequences and reading paths.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1424⟧

## ⟦S1425⟧ law-of-figure-ground — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Law of Figure-Ground — the mind reflexively separates a bounded, higher-contrast foreground figure from an unbounded, receding ground — to modals, overlays and depth.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a card lifted off the page by its shadow, a modal sitting unambiguous over a dimmed page, a selected nav item filled while its neighbours recede, and headline text kept legible over photography by a colour overlay, blur or gradient layer between image and type.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Figure traits: in front, bounded, focus of attention, higher contrast/richer detail, typically smaller area; ground is the reverse. Tools: elevation/shadow (primary), scrims (a modal on a white page without a scrim is a named failure — always provide background dimming), contrast, selected-state fills. Named failures: nested elevation without luminance difference, text directly on photography, flat design with no surface differentiation. Define the surface stack in tokens: base, raised, overlay, modal. In dark mode shadows vanish — use light borders or reduced-luminance fills. Test by removing colour: foreground must still read from shape and contrast alone.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology (Rubin vase cited as the ambiguity example) — named in the skill. Emphasising one element among peers: von-restorff-effect ⟦S1435⟧.
- **Best for:** Layered/parallax heroes, modals and quote-form overlays, selected states in navigation and switchers.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the depth-layering rule for heroes and overlays.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1425⟧

## ⟦S1426⟧ law-of-proximity — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Law of Proximity — spatial closeness groups elements more strongly than any other cue — so spacing alone carries grouping, without labels or borders.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a label hugging its input, a heading sitting closer to the content below it than to the section above, card title/body/metadata tight together with clear air between cards, related buttons clustered and the destructive action set apart.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The signal is the ratio of within-group spacing to between-group spacing — no fixed pixel value; apply one consistent scale (the skill's example: 4px, 8px, 16px, 24px, 32px…). Pattern rules: section headers get less space below than above; row padding tighter than row gap; icon+label tight, pairs separated. Check by squinting — groups must be legible without reading content. Never use a border to do work spacing can do.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology — named in the skill. Containers: law-of-common-region ⟦S1423⟧; shared appearance: law-of-similarity ⟦S1427⟧.
- **Best for:** Every section's internal spacing — forms, cards, proof blocks, footer columns.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the fundamental grouping rule for all layout work.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1426⟧

## ⟦S1427⟧ law-of-similarity — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Law of Similarity — elements sharing colour, shape, size or style are perceived as one category even across distance — to signal relationships and keep interactive elements recognisable as a set.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: every clickable thing sharing one treatment (fill, underline, cursor) that static content lacks; status colours meaning the same thing everywhere (green success, amber warning, red error); all buttons the same shape, all icons the same stroke weight — and one red element inside a blue group reading instantly as different.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Carriers: colour, shape, size, style. Similarity can override proximity — a differently-coloured element inside a close group reads as a separate sub-group; use deliberately for category boundaries. Any unintended deviation (two buttons with slightly different corner radii) reads as a categorical difference — treat as a bug. Never code categories by colour alone: use redundant coding (shape + colour) so the signal survives colourblind viewing and monochrome rendering. Define the similarity vocabulary in design tokens.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt psychology — named in the skill. Grouping by position: law-of-proximity ⟦S1426⟧.
- **Best for:** Interactive-state consistency across a whole page; status/proof coding; version-switcher and nav coherence.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governs category coding and component coherence.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1427⟧

## ⟦S1428⟧ layout-grid — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Defines a responsive grid — columns, gutters, margins and breakpoint behaviour — that page structure is built on.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: content aligned to consistent columns with even gutters, page margins that widen on desktop, card grids that drop columns gracefully on smaller screens, and the occasional deliberate grid-break for emphasis.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Anatomy: columns typically 4 (mobile), 8 (tablet), 12 (desktop); gutters 16px, 24px or 32px; margins 16px mobile, 24–48px desktop; example breakpoints 375, 768, 1024, 1440px. Grid types: column, modular (columns + rows), baseline (4px or 8px vertical rhythm), compound. Responsive behaviour: fluid stretch, fixed max-width container, adaptive per-breakpoint layouts, column dropping. Patterns: full-bleed, contained, asymmetric sidebar + main, auto-fill card grids.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Spacing inside components: spacing-system ⟦S1432⟧; cross-device behaviour: responsive-design ⟦S1431⟧.
- **Best for:** Page structure of every build — hero composition, gallery grids, section alignment.
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational layout reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1428⟧

## ⟦S1429⟧ platform-conventions — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** A reference of iOS Human Interface Guidelines vs Android Material Design 3 conventions — what each OS mandates, where they diverge, and when to unify — for native apps.
- **How it looks:** No web page output; it describes native-app screens: iOS bottom tab bars (up to 5 tabs, labels optional) vs Android navigation bars (3–5 tabs, labels required), iOS action sheets vs Android dialogs for destructive confirmation, wheel pickers vs calendar-plus-text-input date pickers.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion values prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Hard rules with values: iOS reserves swipe-from-left-edge for back — never suppress it; Android system back is a predictive gesture from either edge; both platforms require respecting system font scaling (Dynamic Type / sp) — fixed text sizes are an accessibility failure on both; SF Pro vs Roboto/Google Sans; SF Symbols vs Material Symbols; iOS uses larger "squircle" corner radii, Material 3 prominent rounding; no FAB on iOS without justification. Hybrid default: unified visual language, platform-specific navigation, system controls and gesture handling.
- **Reference / source:** Apple iOS Human Interface Guidelines and Google Material Design 3 — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Native apps only; on web builds its transferable residue is respecting user font-size settings and not fighting platform gestures. Breakpoint adaptation: responsive-design ⟦S1431⟧.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — native-app reference; marginal for trade homepages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1429⟧

## ⟦S1430⟧ readable-measure — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Sets line length (measure) for comfortable reading across type sizes and breakpoints. Covers measure only; the full size/weight scale is typography-scale ⟦S1433⟧.
- **How it looks:** Body text columns that neither sprawl edge-to-edge on desktop nor chop into ribbon-thin lines: a paragraph block visibly narrower than its container, with leading that grows slightly as the column widens.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Optimal range 45–75 characters per line including spaces; 66 often cited as ideal; below 45 the eye jumps lines too often, above 75 it loses the return. Targets by context: long-form articles/docs 55–70; UI body copy 45–65; captions/helper text 40–60; pull quotes/callouts 30–45. Practice: use the CSS ch unit as proxy (max-width: 65ch) but validate by counting real characters; wide faces (Georgia) need narrower columns, condensed faces allow wider. Mobile single column at 16px+ rarely exceeds 70 characters; tablet/desktop must constrain width explicitly.
- **Reference / source:** Classic typographic measure guidance — no specific source named.
- **Best for:** Every text-bearing section — hero subcopy, proof/review text, process descriptions, town pages.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the line-length law for all body copy.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1430⟧

## ⟦S1431⟧ responsive-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Designs layouts and interactions that adapt across screen sizes, pixel densities and input methods, so one design serves many viewports.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: multi-column layouts on desktop reflowing to a single stack on a phone, secondary content moving behind a toggle, fluid type that steps down on small screens, and appropriately cropped/resolved images per breakpoint.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion values prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Strategies: fluid (percentage widths), adaptive (distinct layouts per breakpoint), mobile-first, content-first (content needs drive breakpoints). Common breakpoints: Small 375–639px (phones), Medium 640–1023px (tablets), Large 1024–1439px (laptops), Extra large 1440px+ (desktops). Patterns: column drop, reflow, off-canvas, priority+ (show most important, overflow the rest). Input adaptation: touch targets 44px minimum with gesture support; mouse hover states; keyboard focus indicators and logical tab order; voice needs clear labels. Test on real devices, in landscape and portrait, on slow connections, with accessibility tools at each breakpoint.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Underlying grid: layout-grid ⟦S1428⟧; OS patterns: platform-conventions ⟦S1429⟧.
- **Best for:** Every build — the adaptation discipline behind desktop + 375px mobile presentations of each section.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governing responsive reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1431⟧

## ⟦S1432⟧ spacing-system — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Creates a spacing scale from a single base unit, with rules for when each step applies, so padding and margins are systematic rather than arbitrary.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: rhythm — related items sitting close, sections clearly separated, components with consistent internal padding, page margins steady per breakpoint.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Base unit typically 4px or 8px; example scale: 2xs 2px, xs 4px, sm 8px, md 16px, lg 24px, xl 32px, 2xl 48px, 3xl 64px. Four spacing types: inset (padding inside containers), stack (vertical between stacked elements), inline (horizontal between inline elements), grid gap. Application: related items sm/md, distinct sections lg/xl, page margins consistent per breakpoint. Density modes shift one step: compact (−1 step, data-heavy), comfortable (default), spacious (+1 step, reading-focused). Never use values off the scale.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Page-level columns/gutters: layout-grid ⟦S1428⟧.
- **Best for:** All sections — the spacing tokens underneath cards, forms, heroes and footers.
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational spacing reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1432⟧

## ⟦S1433⟧ typography-scale — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Creates a modular type scale — size steps from a mathematical ratio, with weight, line-height and letter-spacing relationships — for harmonious, consistent text.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a clear ladder from caption to display where each level is visibly distinct, headings set tight, body text open and readable, uppercase labels slightly letterspaced.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Ratios: 1.25 (major third) or 1.333 (perfect fourth). Example scale: Caption 12px, Body small 14px, Body 16px (base), Subheading 20px, H3 24px, H2 32px, H1 40px, Display 48–64px. Weights: 400 / 500 / 600 / 700. Line height: tight 1.2 (headings), normal 1.5 (body), relaxed 1.75 (long-form). Letter spacing: tight −0.02em (large headings), normal 0 (body), wide 0.05em (uppercase labels, captions). Rules: limit to 4–5 sizes in regular use; body minimum 16px; headings scale down on mobile while body holds; line length 45–75 characters (see readable-measure ⟦S1430⟧).
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Type system of every build — hero display sizes, section headings, proof and body text.
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational typography reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1433⟧

## ⟦S1434⟧ visual-hierarchy — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Establishes hierarchy through size, weight, colour, spacing and position so the visitor's eye lands in the intended order on new work.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: one dominant element first (page title or primary CTA), section headings and key content second, supporting text third, fine print last — a hero reads large type + image + single CTA; a card reads image > title > description > action.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Tools with values: size differences of at least 1.5× for clear distinction; weight (bold/filled over light); colour and contrast reserved for CTAs, status, emphasis; whitespace around an element raises its importance; position — top-left first in LTR, F-pattern and Z-pattern scanning. Four levels: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary. Tests: the squint test (blur your eyes — hierarchy must survive), one primary action per view. Judging an existing screen instead: critique-visual-hierarchy ⟦S1501⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Composing every section — hero above all, then proof, work and CTA ordering.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the composition-order reference for all sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1434⟧

## ⟦S1435⟧ von-restorff-effect — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · UI design fundamentals
- **What it is:** Applies the Von Restorff (Isolation) Effect — the one element that differs from its neighbours is the one noticed and remembered — so a single action can dominate.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: one filled button in a row of ghost buttons, one highlighted pricing tier among quieter ones, the active nav state distinct from inactive, a badge or accent colour that appears only on the actionable item.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** The effect needs contrast with context: one (or very few) deviants, surrounding items visually consistent, deviation meaningful not decorative. Applications table: CTA (one filled/primary), pricing (highlight one recommended tier, reduce others' weight), navigation (active state), data tables (highlight the key record), notifications (accent reserved for actionable), onboarding (one isolated step at a time). Avoid: multiple competing highlights ("isolation inflation" — every feature requesting highlight degrades the system), decorative pops, colour-only differentiation (pair with shape, size or weight; must survive grayscale and colourblind simulation, and hold across hover/focus/disabled states).
- **Reference / source:** Von Restorff effect — named in the skill. Overall ordering: visual-hierarchy ⟦S1434⟧.
- **Best for:** Call/CTA sections and pricing — making the call button or the recommended tier the single remembered element.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the single-emphasis rule for CTAs and pricing.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1435⟧

## ⟦S1436⟧ animation-principles — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies classic animation principles — easing, staging, follow-through — to one specific UI motion, tuning how that animation feels. (Product-wide tokens belong to motion-system ⟦S1465⟧; a full interaction spec to micro-interaction-spec ⟦S1448⟧.)
- **How it looks:** Elements enter decelerating, leave accelerating, move between positions with ease-in-out; related items arrive in a choreographed stagger led by the most important; loading shows as skeleton shimmer, spinner or progress.
- **Frame by frame:** Trigger (load / state change / interaction) → the element eases out into place (entering) or eases in away (exiting), related items following at 30–50ms stagger intervals → sequence settles in under 700ms total; any animation can be cancelled mid-flight (interruptible).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Easing law: ease-out = entering, ease-in = exiting, ease-in-out = moving between positions, linear only for continuous animation (progress bars). Duration ladder: Micro 50–100ms (button states, toggles), Short 150–250ms (tooltips, fades, small movements), Medium 250–400ms (page transitions, modals), Long 400–700ms (complex choreography). Principles: purposeful, quick, natural physics, choreographed, interruptible. Types: entrance (fade/slide/scale), exit, emphasis (pulse, shake, bounce), transition (morph, crossfade, shared element), loading. Keep under 400ms for responsive feel; support prefers-reduced-motion; animate transform/will-change for performance.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Tuning any single motion in any section — reveals, switcher swaps, hover responses.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the per-animation tuning reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1436⟧

## ⟦S1437⟧ conversational-ux — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs voice and conversational interfaces — dialog flows, turn logic, error recovery and persona — for when the interface speaks and listens rather than being tapped.
- **How it looks:** No visual page of its own; in text chat it surfaces as message turns with quick-reply chips, a persistent menu, a typing indicator while the system processes, and structured cards (flight details, product results) inside the chat stream instead of raw prose.
- **Frame by frame:** Turn loop: system prompt (one clear thing, signals the expected response) → user speaks/types → system acknowledgement + next prompt. Error ladder: first error rephrases with more context → second error offers explicit examples or constrained choices → third error offers a graceful exit (live agent, other channel); the same prompt is never looped unchanged.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Confirmation strategies: explicit for high-stakes/easily confused inputs, implicit for low-stakes recoverable, none when misrecognition is rare. Voice rules: short sentences, active voice, spell out abbreviations on first use, lists no longer than 3 items, system responses under 8 seconds, earcons for state transitions. Persona: consistent name/register, stays in voice during failures, never claims to be human when sincerely asked. Warning: do not force conversation onto tasks better served by a form, table or menu.
- **Reference / source:** Alexa Show / Google Nest Hub named as multimodal examples.
- **Best for:** Chat widgets or voice assistants only — marginal on a trade homepage beyond a chat-based quote helper.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — narrow fit (chat/voice surfaces).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1437⟧

## ⟦S1438⟧ doherty-threshold — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies the Doherty Threshold — keep system response under 400ms — to diagnose perceived slowness and set performance budgets that preserve user flow.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: taps and toggles that respond instantly, search results beginning to appear as they type, and — when a wait is unavoidable — an immediate state change on the pressed element, then a skeleton that holds the layout's shape instead of a blank screen.
- **Frame by frame:** User acts → within 100ms the element visually acknowledges (state change) → if completion takes 400ms–3s a loading indicator runs → if over 3s, progress (not just a spinner) → result lands; optimistic UI shows the expected result immediately and reconciles when the server answers.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Perception bands: 0–100ms instant; 100–300ms fast; 300–400ms approaching the boundary; 400ms–1s slow (indicator needed); 1s+ definitely slow (progress feedback required, flow broken); 10s+ task-level disruption. Hard numbers: button feedback within 100ms regardless of completion; autocomplete first suggestions within 300ms; view transitions complete under 400ms. Never flash a spinner for actions completing under 400ms. Skeleton screens preferred over spinners for known layouts. The threshold governs perceived wait, not deliberate motion (a 250ms entrance animation is fine).
- **Reference / source:** Walter Doherty & Ahrvind Thadani, IBM, 1982 — named in the skill. What to show during waits: loading-states ⟦S1447⟧.
- **Best for:** Performance feel of every interactive element — switchers, forms, filters, search.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the responsiveness budget behind all interactions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1438⟧

## ⟦S1439⟧ error-handling-ux — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs error prevention, detection, communication and recovery across a whole product — message content, placement and escape routes — where errors span multiple flows. (Validation inside one form: form-design ⟦S1442⟧.)
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees when something goes wrong: an inline message directly beside the field that failed, in plain language, saying what happened and exactly what to do — with everything they already typed still in place; network failures arrive as a toast/banner with a retry action rather than a dead page.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. The sequence it designs: input → detection (real-time field check, submit check, network/timeout/permission check) → message placed near the source at the right severity (error / warning / info) → recovery path (retry, alternative path, auto-retry with backoff, undo) with user input preserved throughout.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four-layer hierarchy: 1 Prevention (inline validation, smart defaults, confirmations for destructive actions, constraint inputs like date pickers, auto-save), 2 Detection, 3 Communication, 4 Recovery. Message format fixed: what happened / why (if helpful) / what to do next. Placement by context: forms = inline per-field + summary at top; pages = full-page error with retry/back; network = toast/banner with retry; empty results = helpful empty state; permissions = explain what access is needed and how to get it. Never blame the user; never clear the form on error.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Quote forms and contact flows above all — the error system behind forms and call/CTA paths.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governs error states across forms and flows.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1439⟧

## ⟦S1440⟧ feedback-patterns — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs the confirmations, status updates and notifications that tell users an action registered — success, progress and change. (Waiting states: loading-states ⟦S1447⟧; failures: error-handling-ux ⟦S1439⟧.)
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a button that visibly changes the instant it is clicked, a success toast with a checkmark animation after submitting, status badges (pending / active / complete), a badge count on unread items, a banner for system-wide messages.
- **Frame by frame:** User acts → immediate feedback at the closest level available (button state change, inline validation, toggle response, drag position update) → confirmation feedback on completion (toast/snackbar, checkmark, summary of what was done, undo offered for reversible actions) → toast auto-dismisses after 3–5 seconds; errors instead persist until resolved or dismissed; status persists while relevant.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four feedback types: immediate, confirmation, status, notification. Four channels: visual (colour, icon, animation, badge), text, audio (click, chime, alert), haptic (tap, success vibration, warning buzz). Hierarchy of placement: inline/contextual (preferred) → component-level → page-level banner/toast → system-level notification. Rules: acknowledge every action; match intensity to importance; undo rather than "Are you sure?"; never colour-only (accessibility).
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Form submissions, switcher interactions, any tap/click response on the page.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the acknowledgement system for all interactions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1440⟧

## ⟦S1441⟧ fitts-law — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies Fitts's Law — target acquisition time depends on target size and distance — when sizing and positioning controls, especially for touch.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: a big call button sitting in the thumb zone at the bottom of a phone screen, card actions on the card itself rather than across the screen, modal confirm buttons near the bottom of the modal, and the destructive action kept small and distant so it is hard to hit by accident.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Formula: MT = a + b × log₂(2D / W) — movement time grows with distance D and shrinks with target width W; the interactive area counts, not the visual icon (a 16px icon can carry a 44px tap area — expand with padding). Minimums: touch 44×44pt (Apple HIG) / 48×48dp (Material); pointer 24×24px minimum. Screen edges and corners are effectively infinite-size targets (the pointer cannot overshoot) — use them for persistent navigation on desktop; on mobile, bottom placement shortens thumb reach. Limits: the law models motor time, not decision time or label clarity.
- **Reference / source:** Fitts's Law; Apple HIG and Material Design target minimums — named in the skill. How many controls at once: hicks-law ⟦S1444⟧.
- **Best for:** Call/CTA buttons, sticky mobile call bars, navigation, form submit placement.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the target sizing/placement law for CTAs and nav.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1441⟧

## ⟦S1442⟧ form-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs a form end to end — field order, grouping, labels, input types, validation and completion — to reduce abandonment and prevent errors.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: one single column of fields, each with a persistent label above it, field widths that hint at the expected answer (narrow postcode, wide bio), related fields grouped under section headings, helper text under the label, errors appearing directly below the offending field saying how to fix them, and a checkmark on fields whose correctness isn't obvious.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. Interaction sequence: user fills field → validation fires on blur (leaving the field), never per keystroke → error renders below that field (e.g. "Email address must include @" — not "Invalid email") → server errors surface inline where possible, summarised at top if several fields fail → multi-step forms show a step indicator, allow back without data loss, and save progress.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Layout law: single column almost always; top-aligned labels; mark optional fields, not required ones (when most are required). Input-type table: short text → text input; long text → textarea; one from ≤5 options → radio buttons (all visible); one from 6+ → select/combobox; multiple from few → checkboxes; date → picker or segmented day/month/year, never freeform; phone/card → formatted masked input; password → input with show/hide toggle. Character counts shown always, not only near the limit. Accessibility: programmatic label per field, errors tied via aria-describedby, focus order = visual order, error summary keyboard-focusable with links to fields, never colour alone for required/error. High-stakes forms (payments, medical, legal) add a review step before submission. Measure field-level abandonment to target fixes.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Product-wide error strategy: error-handling-ux ⟦S1439⟧; signup first-run: onboarding-design ⟦S1451⟧.
- **Best for:** Forms — the quote/estimate form is the conversion core of a trade homepage; also contact forms.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the governing reference for quote forms.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1442⟧

## ⟦S1443⟧ gesture-patterns — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs gesture interactions for touch and pointer — swipe, drag, long-press, pinch, pull — and makes them discoverable.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: a swipe that starts responding the moment the finger moves, a threshold indicator or rubber-band as it nears the snap point, a pull-to-refresh that follows an implied vertical path, and always a visible button or menu alternative for anything a gesture can do.
- **Frame by frame:** Finger lands → after a 10–15px minimum travel the gesture activates and direction locks (horizontal vs vertical) → progress feedback tracks the finger, with snap-point/rubber-band cues → passing the velocity/distance threshold completes the action with confirmation; returning to the start cancels (cancel zone). System gestures (back swipe, notification pull) always take priority.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Gesture set: tap (select), double tap (zoom/like), long press (context menu, reorder, preview), swipe (navigate, dismiss, reveal actions), pinch (zoom), rotate, drag (move, reorder, adjust), pull (refresh). Conflict resolution: tap vs long-press by time threshold (500ms typical); pinch vs drag by touch-point count. Accessibility law: every gesture must have a non-gesture alternative; support switch and voice control; respect reduced-motion for gesture animations. Keep gestures to one or two fingers; provide undo for destructive gesture actions.
- **Reference / source:** None named. OS-standard gestures: platform-conventions ⟦S1429⟧.
- **Best for:** Mobile galleries, before/after sliders, carousels and swipeable proof on touch devices.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — applies where a section is gesture-driven (galleries, sliders).
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1443⟧

## ⟦S1444⟧ hicks-law — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies Hick's Law — decision time grows logarithmically with the number of simultaneous choices — when a screen offers too many options at once.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a short top-level menu with the rest grouped or tucked into overflow, one decision per onboarding step, the most common actions surfaced and the rest behind "more", results arriving in pages rather than one overwhelming list.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Formula: RT = a + b × log₂(n + 1). Levers: reduce simultaneous choices, group related options (categorisation reduces apparent complexity more than removal), progressive disclosure, smart defaults that skip the choice entirely. Named sweet spot: three pricing tiers; more creates analysis paralysis. Mistakes: confusing fewer options with less functionality; hiding frequently needed options; ignoring choice quality (five clear distinct options beat three vague ones).
- **Reference / source:** Hick's Law — named in the skill. How much survives in memory afterwards: millers-law ⟦S1449⟧.
- **Best for:** Navigation menus, service pickers, pricing tiers, filter sets.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the choice-count law for nav, services and pricing.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1444⟧

## ⟦S1445⟧ interfaces-that-feel — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** An emotional-resonance lens for a UI that is technically correct but lands cold: start from the state the person is in, find a physical analogue for that feeling, extract its behavioural property, and apply it at the copy, motion or interaction layer.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: a loading message that reads "Getting your data" instead of "Loading...", an error that owns the fault and gives one specific next step, a small win acknowledged warmly and briefly, heavy news arriving slowly and good news instantly.
- **Frame by frame:** State change occurs → the interface matches its timing to the feeling: after an error it holds 300–600ms of recovery space before the next prompt → copy speaks in the state's voice (loading calm, empty invitational, system error apologetic with a path forward, success warm and brief) → motion eases like the physical analogue (ease-out = something soft landing; linear reads mechanical and is avoided for anything touching feeling).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Translation process: name the felt state → physical analogue → behavioural property (weight, resistance, speed, recovery arc, rhythm) → apply to easing curve, delay, copy tone, colour temperature, spacing, duration. Durations: 150–300ms for UI response; 400–600ms for transitions that carry meaning; never longer than the user's patience for the task. Springs: stiff = snappy/confident, loose = playful/forgiving. Review test: strip all colour and imagery — the emotional signal must survive.
- **Reference / source:** Reference products named: How We Feel, Headspace, Gentler Streak, Amie, Arc Browser. Polish-perception argument: aesthetic-usability ⟦S1417⟧.
- **Best for:** Final feel pass on heroes, form success/error moments and CTA confirmations.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the emotional-timing layer for key moments.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1445⟧

## ⟦S1446⟧ jakobs-law — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies Jakob's Law — users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know — to decide deliberately when to follow a familiar pattern and when a departure is worth its learning cost.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: the logo top-left taking them home, a magnifying glass meaning search, an X closing the modal, a hamburger hiding mobile navigation — everything where their habits from other sites say it should be.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Strongest conventions listed: logo top-left → home; cart icon → checkout; hamburger → hidden navigation; search icon → search field; X → close; blue underlined text → link (weakening but active). Cost model of departing: users must discover the pattern doesn't apply, work out the new one, and hold both in memory — paid on every visit until learned. Deviation is justified only when convention fails the use case, a domain convention supersedes it, testing shows convention performs measurably worse, or the category is genuinely new — never for differentiation or taste alone. Practice: audit 3–5 comparable products first; weight by task frequency; name the convention before departing from it.
- **Reference / source:** Jakob Nielsen — named in the skill. OS-mandated conventions: platform-conventions ⟦S1429⟧; adopting rivals' patterns deliberately: competitive-analysis ⟦S1406⟧.
- **Best for:** Navigation, header and CTA conventions on every build — the counterweight that keeps invention usable.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the convention check applied to every pattern choice.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1446⟧

## ⟦S1447⟧ loading-states — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs waiting experiences — skeleton screens, spinners, progressive loading, optimistic updates, blur-up images — so content arriving slowly never means a blank screen.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: the page's layout shape present immediately as a subtly shimmering skeleton, images resolving from a low-res blur to full sharpness, list items fading in one after another, and content fading in rather than popping.
- **Frame by frame:** Load starts → under 100ms, nothing shown (no indicator); 100ms–1s, a subtle indicator or skeleton appears matched to the real content's shape → 1–10s, a clear loading state with progress if measurable; over 10s, detailed progress with a time estimate and a background/cancel option → content fades in, list items staggered at 30–50ms intervals, with no layout shift and scroll position maintained on refresh.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Patterns: skeleton screens (known structure), indeterminate spinner (unknown duration), determinate progress bar (measurable), progressive loading (critical first, below-fold lazy), optimistic UI (show expected result, reconcile, roll back on failure), placeholder content with realistic proportions. Rules: show something immediately; match skeleton shapes to actual content; avoid multiple competing indicators; respect reduced-motion for shimmer.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Latency budget itself: doherty-threshold ⟦S1438⟧; success confirmation: feedback-patterns ⟦S1440⟧.
- **Best for:** Image-heavy galleries, review feeds, any section fed by slow assets.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the waiting-state system for asset-heavy sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1447⟧

## ⟦S1448⟧ micro-interaction-spec — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Specifies one micro-interaction completely — trigger, rules, feedback, loops and modes — in the structured format engineering needs to build it exactly.
- **How it looks:** The spec'd behaviours it produces: a toggle that animates between states, pull-to-refresh with progress indication, a like button with a celebratory burst, a button press with a depth/scale response, a long-press filling a radial progress ring.
- **Frame by frame:** Written per interaction as: trigger fires (user action, system event, or condition) → rules execute (logic, sequence, branching) → feedback lands across visual (colour/size/position), motion, audio and haptic channels → loop/mode behaviour applies (repeat? first-time vs repeat differences, progressive disclosure).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Four-part framework: 1 Trigger, 2 Rules, 3 Feedback, 4 Loops and Modes. Spec format per interaction: name, trigger, rules (sequence), feedback (visual/audio/haptic), duration/easing, loop behaviour, accessibility considerations. Durations: keep most at 100–500ms; immediate feedback for user actions; respect reduced-motion.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Motion craft alone: animation-principles ⟦S1436⟧; multi-state components: state-machine ⟦S1455⟧.
- **Best for:** Handing over the signature interactions — version switchers, cursor responses, button presses — without ambiguity.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — a specification format, used per interaction.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1448⟧

## ⟦S1449⟧ millers-law — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies Miller's Law correctly — chunk information into meaningful groups — using the modern working-memory figure rather than the folklore "7 items" rule.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: menus grouped into a few labelled categories instead of one flat list of ten, long forms broken into headed sections that each feel completable, phone numbers and verification codes formatted in chunks (555-867-5309, XXXX-XXXX), pricing tiers with a handful of bullets each.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Miller (1956) proposed 7 ± 2 items; Cowan (2001) puts meaningful chunks closer to 4 ± 1 — and the unit is the chunk (whatever has meaning to the person), not the raw item. Applications with numbers: onboarding progress shown as 3–5 named phases rather than a raw count of 12; feature lists and pricing at 3–5 bullet points per tier (beyond that users stop reading); navigation grouped (3 groups of 3–4 scan better than a flat 10+). Misapplications named: menus of exactly 7 "because Miller", applying it to colours/icons, ignoring that experts chunk more than novices. Test recall, not just comprehension.
- **Reference / source:** George Miller (1956); Nelson Cowan (2001) — named in the skill. Reducing choices offered: hicks-law ⟦S1444⟧.
- **Best for:** Menu grouping, form sectioning, pricing bullet counts, step displays.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the chunking law for lists, menus and tiers.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1449⟧

## ⟦S1450⟧ navigation-patterns — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Selects and designs the navigation pattern — tabs, drawer, sidebar, breadcrumbs, hub — matched to the product's structure and the user's tasks.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: on a phone, a bottom tab bar with 3–5 labelled destinations always visible; on desktop, a header bar for a simple site or a sidebar for a deep one; breadcrumbs showing the path in deep hierarchies; the current destination clearly marked by weight, underline or indicator bar — never colour alone.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Pattern table: mobile with 3–5 primary destinations → tab bar; desktop app with many/nested destinations → side navigation; simple marketing site or docs → top nav bar (works for 4–7 destinations); deep hierarchy → breadcrumbs + local sidebar; parallel views → tabs or segmented control (2–4 views); occasional access → utility nav or overflow. Global / local / utility / contextual nav kept as separate layers, never mixed in one component. Principles: orientation (always know where you are), wayfinding (predict the destination), reachability (primary destinations in thumb reach on mobile), consistency, scent (labels tested with first-click tests). Hard limit: more than 7 top-level destinations creates choice paralysis — fix the IA (⟦S1411⟧) before adding nav items. Hamburger for primary desktop navigation is a named mistake.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Navigation on every build — header, mobile bar, footer and in-section movement.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the navigation pattern reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1450⟧

## ⟦S1451⟧ onboarding-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs the first-run experience — activation path, progressive disclosure, time to first value — for a user's very first session with a product.
- **How it looks:** What a new user sees: an empty state that explains what belongs there and offers one clear first action (with a preview of the populated state), features taught by tooltips at the moment of first use, or a short setup sequence with visible progress and skippable optional steps.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. Flow logic: sign-up → collect only what's needed now → first meaningful action (the "aha moment") as directly as possible → remaining setup deferred and resurfaced later in-product.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Goals in priority order: get to value fast; orient, don't educate; build confidence with early wins; reduce setup friction. Four patterns: progressive onboarding (in-context teaching), setup wizard (minimal steps, progress shown, skipping allowed), sample data/demo mode (clearly labelled, easy to clear, realistic content), interactive product tour (3–5 core concepts only, dismissable at any point, never locking). Metrics: activation rate, time to activation, onboarding completion rate, day-7/day-30 retention, drop-off by step. Named mistakes: feature tour before context, collecting profile/billing/preferences before value, neglecting empty states (new users spend more time in them than any other state).
- **Reference / source:** None named. Signup form mechanics: form-design ⟦S1442⟧.
- **Best for:** Product onboarding — on a trade homepage its transferable piece is the empty-state/first-action discipline; limited direct fit.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — app first-run design; partial transfer to homepages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1451⟧

## ⟦S1452⟧ peak-end-rule — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies the Peak-End Rule — an experience is remembered by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by its average — to completion, celebration and cancellation moments.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor remembers: the moment the result lands (order confirmed and visualised, first output delivered, milestone reached) made genuinely satisfying, and a final screen that is a warm, clear confirmation with next steps — never an administrative screen, a confusing status page, or an unresolved error.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed. The designed arc: ordinary middle (duration is neglected) → engineered peak at the natural payoff moment → deliberate end at a moment of visible value or confirmed resolution.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Kahneman's finding: retrospective judgement = peak + end; duration and average quality contribute far less ("duration neglect" — a 10-minute experience ending well outrates a 5-minute one ending poorly). If the peak is unavoidably negative (long wait, rejection), set expectations before it, give something useful during it, and make the recovery the new peak. Applications table covers checkout, onboarding, signup, data-heavy tasks, error recovery. Practice: map each key flow's emotional arc, mark the highest-intensity and final moments, invest disproportionately there; test by asking users to describe the experience afterwards.
- **Reference / source:** Daniel Kahneman — named in the skill. Sustaining engagement mid-flow: zeigarnik-effect ⟦S1457⟧.
- **Best for:** Form-submit confirmations, quote-request completions, the closing section of a page.
- **Tier:** STRONG — shapes endings and payoff moments on conversion flows.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1452⟧

## ⟦S1453⟧ search-ux — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Designs search end to end — query input, autocomplete, results, filtering and the zero-results state — for when users retrieve rather than browse.
