- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a search box whose placeholder names what can be searched, suggestions appearing after a few characters with the typed portion bolded, results with the matching terms highlighted and a count ("142 results for 'onboarding'"), applied filters shown as removable chips — and a zero-results page that confirms the query, suggests corrections and offers alternatives instead of a blank.
- **Frame by frame:** User types 2–3 characters → suggestions appear (recent searches first, then trending, then predicted completions; 5–8 maximum, keyboard navigable) → submit on Enter → results render (list for most content, grid for visual content, grouped by type for mixed) with matched fields highlighted → refinement via faceted filters with counts → zero results triggers the correction/alternatives state, never a blank page.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Input width should suggest expected query length; auto-focus on open; clear/reset button once a query exists; query persists in the field for refinement. Search-as-navigation: include destinations ("settings", "invoices") in suggestions and surface exact-match pages first. Analytics to mine: top queries, zero-results queries, refinement rate, click position, search abandonment. Tolerance required: typos, synonyms, plurals, partial matches. Never remove search from mobile to save space.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Browse structure: navigation-patterns ⟦S1450⟧.
- **Best for:** Sites with real search (large service/town catalogues); the zero-results discipline transfers to empty states generally.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — only where the site carries genuine search.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1453⟧

## ⟦S1454⟧ serial-position-effect — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies the Serial Position Effect — first and last items in a sequence are recalled best, the middle is a dead zone — when ordering menus, lists and steps.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor remembers: the first menu item and the last, the outer two pricing options, the opening and closing steps of a flow — while positions 3–5 of a seven-item menu quietly drop out of recall.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Primacy (beginning items encoded into long-term memory) + recency (end items still in short-term memory) = the "serial position valley" in the middle. Rules: critical navigation first or last (global actions first; account/settings/logout last — convention reinforces it); strongest choices first and last in curated lists; in a three-item set the middle is the comparison anchor and the recalled items are the outer two — never put the primary CTA in the middle of three; bury tedious required steps (permissions, legal, fields) mid-flow and make the last step resolution/confirmation. A trapped important item is rescued by visual distinction (von-restorff ⟦S1435⟧). Reinforces the peak-end rule ⟦S1452⟧ at sequence close.
- **Reference / source:** Hermann Ebbinghaus's memory research — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Menu order, pricing-tier order, service list order, step sequences.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the ordering law for lists, menus and tiers.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1454⟧

## ⟦S1455⟧ state-machine — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Models a component's or flow's behaviour as explicit states, events, transitions, actions and guards, so impossible states are eliminated and behaviour is exhaustively specified.
- **How it looks:** No page output of its own; its visible product is a component that can never show loading and error at once, a form that moves idle → editing → validating → submitting → success/error without dead ends, a wizard that always offers a way out of every step.
- **Frame by frame:** Written as transition chains per concern — form: idle → editing → validating → submitting → success/error → idle; data fetching: idle → loading → success/error, error → retrying → success/error; authentication: logged-out → authenticating → logged-in → logging-out → logged-out; wizard: step1 → step2 → step3 → review → submitting → complete. Each transition names its event, guard condition (isValid, hasPermission) and side-effect actions (fetch, toast, log).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Components: states, events, transitions, actions, guards. Method: list all states → list all events → define valid transitions → identify impossible states to prevent → add guards → define entry/exit actions; map every state to a UI representation. Start with the happy path, then error states; one machine per concern; document with visual diagrams.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Feel of a single interaction: micro-interaction-spec ⟦S1448⟧.
- **Best for:** Complex components — multi-step quote forms, configurators, switchers with many interacting states.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — modelling discipline for stateful components.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1455⟧

## ⟦S1456⟧ teslers-law — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies Tesler's Law (conservation of complexity) — every process has irreducible complexity that someone must absorb — to decide deliberately whether the product or the user carries it.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: a date field that accepts the format they type or offers a picker, a country choice that fills in the region automatically, sensible defaults already set with the options still reachable — instead of twelve settings demanded before starting.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Distinguish inherent complexity (from the task itself — removing it removes capability) from extraneous complexity (from the design — eliminate it). Absorption table: user typing dates in one exact format → product accepts multiple formats or provides a picker; user re-entering region after country → product detects and populates; user following a file-naming convention → product enforces/generates names; user reading an error then hunting the fix → product suggests the correction directly. Over-simplification warnings: hiding options makes power users hunt; over-defaulting critical decisions removes control; verify where removed complexity went (it may reappear as support load). Measure complexity by outcomes — error rate, time-on-task, abandonment, support volume — not by counting visible elements.
- **Reference / source:** Larry Tesler — named in the skill. Reducing apparent choice: hicks-law ⟦S1444⟧.
- **Best for:** Quote-form and configurator design — deciding what the form asks vs what it works out itself.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the complexity-placement law for forms and flows.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1456⟧

## ⟦S1457⟧ zeigarnik-effect — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Interaction design
- **What it is:** Applies the Zeigarnik Effect — incomplete tasks stay mentally active as open loops — to progress indicators, saved drafts and return hooks, without abusing it.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: a progress bar on a multi-step form ("You're 60% done" rather than a bare "complete your profile"), a checklist with named steps and a clear endpoint, and on return, "You have an unsaved draft" pointing at the exact step where they stopped.
- **Frame by frame:** User starts a task → the product shows progress made and finite distance remaining → if interrupted, state is auto-saved without user action and resumability is signalled clearly → on return, context is restored exactly where they left it → completion closes the loop with resolution.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Limits: surface one or two open loops at a time — more than two or three competing incomplete states overwhelm rather than motivate; never show a progress bar with no clear completion path (anxiety, not motivation); only surface incompleteness for tasks the user genuinely started. Re-engagement copies the real state ("one step away from completing setup"), and tone must read as a helpful reminder, not guilt.
- **Reference / source:** Bluma Zeigarnik — named in the skill. Emotional shape of the ending: peak-end-rule ⟦S1452⟧.
- **Best for:** Multi-step quote forms (progress + resume), profile/setup completion meters.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — applies to multi-step flows and return visits.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1457⟧

## ⟦S1458⟧ accessibility-audit — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Audits an existing interface against WCAG, producing findings with severity ratings and remediation steps. (Planning future sessions with AT users is accessibility-test-plan ⟦S1470⟧.)
- **How it looks:** No page output. The deliverable is an issue list, each item recorded as: description, location, WCAG criterion, severity, impact, remediation steps, code examples.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Framework: WCAG 2.2 POUR — Perceivable (text alternatives, captions, contrast), Operable (keyboard, time limits, no seizures, navigation), Understandable (readable, predictable, input assistance), Robust (assistive-tech compatibility, semantic markup, ARIA). Severity scale: 1 Critical (blocks access entirely), 2 Major (significant difficulty), 3 Minor (inconvenience with workarounds), 4 Enhancement (beyond compliance). Method: test with real assistive technologies, include users with disabilities where possible, audit static and interactive states across devices and browsers, prioritise by severity × user impact.
- **Reference / source:** WCAG 2.2 — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Final QA sweep on a finished build before screenshots go for approval.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the accessibility QA gate for completed pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1458⟧

## ⟦S1459⟧ component-spec — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Specifies one library component completely — anatomy, props, variants, states, behaviour and accessibility — so it can be implemented without guessing.
- **How it looks:** No page output. An eight-part document: 1 Overview (name, when to use / not use), 2 Anatomy (required vs optional elements), 3 Variants (size sm/md/lg, style primary/secondary/ghost, layout), 4 Props/API (name, type, default, description, required), 5 States (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error), 6 Behavior (interactions, animations, responsive behaviour, edge cases), 7 Accessibility (ARIA roles, keyboard nav, screen reader, focus management), 8 Usage Guidelines (do/don't examples, content rules, related components).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; animations are specified inside the Behavior section, with no values prescribed by the skill itself.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules: write for designers and developers; include examples for every variant and state; specify behaviour, not just appearance; consider all input methods; document edge cases explicitly. Reusable doc scaffold: documentation-template ⟦S1462⟧; problem-solution patterns: pattern-library ⟦S1467⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Speccing reusable components (buttons, cards, form fields) shared across the portfolio builds.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — specification format for component libraries.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1459⟧

## ⟦S1460⟧ design-system-governance — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Defines how a design system evolves — ownership, contribution model, versioning, deprecation and breaking-change policy — when multiple teams contribute.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Process documents: contribution lifecycle (request → triage → design → review → build/test → release → communication), changelog, migration guides.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Ownership models: centralized (core team builds all; consistent but bottleneck), federated (any team contributes under review; fast but needs strong standards), hybrid (core owns foundations, teams own domain components — most common). Versioning is semantic: Patch (fixes/docs, no API change), Minor (new components/variants, backwards compatible), Major (breaking: renamed props, removed components, changed behaviour) — major bumps rare and flagged "BREAKING:" with a migration guide. Deprecation: announced with the release that introduces the replacement, migration guide with code examples, deprecated items stay functional for at least one minor version cycle, in-product warnings surface it. Quality gate for entry: documented props/variants/states, WCAG AA accessibility review, responsive behaviour specified, token usage only (no hardcoded values), usage guidance, design file synced with code.
- **Reference / source:** Semantic versioning — named in the skill. Driving uptake: design-system-adoption ⟦S1491⟧.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — running a shared component library across teams.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — organisational process, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1460⟧

## ⟦S1461⟧ design-token — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Defines and organises design tokens — the atomic values for colour, spacing, type, elevation, border and motion — in a three-tier architecture with naming and usage rules.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees is its consequence: every surface drawing from the same values, so the same action colour, radius and spacing recur identically across hero, cards, forms and footer.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion values of its own; motion durations/easings are one of its token categories (see motion-system ⟦S1465⟧ for the worked scale).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Tiers: 1 Global tokens (raw values, e.g. blue-500: #3B82F6), 2 Alias tokens (semantic references, e.g. color-action-primary), 3 Component tokens (scoped, e.g. button-color-primary). Naming pattern: {category}-{property}-{variant}-{state}. Categories: colour (palette/alias/component), spacing (4px/8px base, xs–3xl, inset/stack/inline), typography (families, size scale, weights, line heights), elevation (shadow levels, z-index scale), border (radius, width, style), motion (durations, easings). Laws: components never reference raw values; keep alias tokens abstract so theming works; version tokens alongside the system. Auditing existing usage: design-token-audit ⟦S1492⟧; multi-brand mapping: theming-system ⟦S1468⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Foundations of any single-file build — the token layer its CSS variables implement.
- **Tier:** STRONG — foundational token architecture for builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1461⟧

## ⟦S1462⟧ documentation-template — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Generates a reusable documentation scaffold for components, patterns or guidelines, standardising how a design system is documented.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Three template types: Component Docs (title, status, when to use, example, anatomy, variants, props, states, accessibility, content guidelines, tokens, related, changelog); Pattern Docs (problem, context, solution, behaviour, good/bad examples, accessibility, related patterns); Foundation Docs (purpose, principles, rules/specs, examples, exceptions, resources).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Standards: consistent heading hierarchy, table of contents for long pages, tables for comparisons, code alongside visuals, status indicators for maturity. Practice: audit freshness quarterly, generate from code where possible, test with new team members, write in second person, lead with the important information. Content of one component's spec: component-spec ⟦S1459⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — documenting a design system.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — documentation scaffolding, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1462⟧

## ⟦S1463⟧ icon-system — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Specifies an icon system — grid, sizing, stroke weight, naming, categories and delivery — so iconography stays consistent and manageable.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: icons drawn on one grid with one stroke weight and corner treatment, in a stepped size ladder, reading as a single family across nav, cards and footer.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Foundations: base grid 24×24px with keylines, stroke width and corner radius fixed; sizes XS 12–16px, S 20px, M 24px, L 32px, XL 48px+; styles stroke / filled / duotone with rules for each. Naming: icon-[category]-[name]-[variant]; categories: action, navigation, content, communication, social, status, file, device. Delivery: SVG source, sprite sheets, component wrappers, Figma library. Accessibility: every icon labelled or aria-hidden, critical actions paired with text, sufficient contrast, 44×44px minimum touch targets. Audit and remove unused icons; version alongside the system; test at every supported size.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Broader illustration: illustration-style ⟦S1421⟧.
- **Best for:** Icon sets for services, proof points and navigation in any build.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the iconography standard for section artwork.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1463⟧

## ⟦S1464⟧ localization-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Designs UI that survives multiple languages, writing directions and cultural contexts — text expansion, RTL mirroring, non-Latin typography and locale formats — without per-locale redesigns.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees in another locale: buttons that grow instead of clipping, a layout that mirrors fully in Arabic or Hebrew (sidebar, nav and reading order flipped) while logos, clocks and numbers stay put, dates and currency formatted the local way.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Text expansion vs English: German +20–35%, French +15–25%, Finnish +30–40%, Arabic −20–30% (but RTL, different script), Japanese/Chinese often shorter with different type rules. Design law: never size containers to English copy; flexible heights/widths; buttons min-width not fixed; test all nav items together at 130% length. RTL: use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-block-end) and text-align: start; directional icons mirror, non-directional (camera, settings) do not; logos, clocks, maths and usually images do not mirror. Type: Arabic/Hebrew minimum 16px+; never fake-bold or fake-italic non-Latin scripts. Culture: colour meanings vary (red = luck in China, mourning in South Africa; white = mourning in many East Asian cultures); avoid hand-gesture icons; use Intl.DateTimeFormat and locale-aware address forms. Pre-launch: pseudo-localization test string; test with one RTL and one long-expansion locale.
- **Reference / source:** Intl.DateTimeFormat — named in the skill. The words themselves: ux-writing ⟦S1494⟧.
- **Best for:** Any build expected to serve more than one language/region; otherwise a robustness check on flexible layout.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — essential for multilingual sites, peripheral for single-locale trade pages.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1464⟧

## ⟦S1465⟧ motion-system — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Defines motion as a token layer — a small duration scale, named easing curves, choreography rules and system-level reduced-motion handling — so animation is consistent product-wide instead of one-off per component.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor experiences: every transition across the page sharing the same handful of speeds and curves — instant state ticks, quick tooltip appearances, a default-feeling 200ms for most movement, slower deliberate pacing reserved for high-emphasis reveals — and, under reduced-motion settings, slides and scales replaced by simple fades.
- **Frame by frame:** Any transition draws its duration + easing from the tokens: entering elements use ease-decelerate, leaving elements ease-accelerate, state-to-state movement ease-standard, playful/tactile moments ease-spring; grouped elements stagger 30–50ms leading with the most important, the whole sequence capped at 500ms, directions consistent (in from right ⇒ out to left). Under prefers-reduced-motion, all duration tokens collapse to an instant override (0ms or 1ms) applied globally at :root.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Duration tokens (example scale): duration-instant 50ms (checkbox tick, toggle), duration-fast 100ms (tooltip appear, chip dismiss), duration-normal 200ms (default — dropdown open, focus ring), duration-moderate 300ms (modal entry, panel slide), duration-slow 400ms (page-level transitions, complex choreography), duration-deliberate 600ms (onboarding reveal). Easing tokens: ease-standard cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1); ease-decelerate cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1); ease-accelerate cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 0.3); ease-spring spring / cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); ease-linear for looping only (spinners, shimmer). Keep 4–6 duration values maximum. Reduced motion: disable sliding/scaling/rotation, replace with instant changes or opacity fades, preserve state-essential animation (spinners, progress). Ship tokens as CSS custom properties in the same export pipeline as colour and spacing, each documented with name, value, use case and live example.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Crafting one specific animation: animation-principles ⟦S1436⟧.
- **Best for:** The motion token layer of every build — the consistency standard all section animation is tuned against.
- **Tier:** STRONG — governing motion-token reference.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1465⟧

## ⟦S1466⟧ naming-convention — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Establishes naming rules for components, tokens, files and layers — patterns with worked examples — so a design system stays predictable, searchable and maintainable.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Naming patterns: Components [category]/[name]/[variant]/[state]; Tokens {category}-{property}-{concept}-{variant}-{state}; Files [type]-[name]-[variant].[ext]; Assets icon-[name]-[size], illust-[scene]-[variant]; Code kebab-case CSS, PascalCase React components, camelCase props.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Principles: predictable, consistent, scalable, scannable, unambiguous. Pitfalls: abbreviations only the author understands, inconsistent separators, names based on visual properties instead of purpose. Practice: one reference page for the rules, automated name linting, prefixes for sorting/grouping, names reviewed in critiques. What tokens contain: design-token ⟦S1461⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — internal organisation of design files and code.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — internal naming hygiene, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1466⟧

## ⟦S1467⟧ pattern-library — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Structures a pattern-library entry — problem context, solution, examples, related patterns — for documenting a recurring solution rather than a single component.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Entry structure: Problem Statement, Solution (principles + visual/interaction description), Anatomy (components, layout, required vs optional), Variants (context-specific, responsive), Behavior (user flow, state changes, error handling), Examples (good implementations and anti-patterns, explained), Accessibility, Related Patterns. Categories: navigation, input, display, feedback, onboarding.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; behaviour is described inside the entry's Behavior field.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules: problem first, solution second; include real examples and anti-patterns; connect patterns into a knowledge graph (similar, commonly combined, builds upon); update as research reveals new insights. A single component's API belongs to component-spec ⟦S1459⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — documenting reusable solutions across builds.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — documentation format, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1467⟧

## ⟦S1468⟧ theming-system — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design systems
- **What it is:** Designs theming architecture — brand variants, dark mode, high contrast, density — mapped through token layers so one component library serves multiple themes.
- **How it looks:** What the visitor sees: the same components re-skinned per brand or mode — a dark theme where elevation comes from lighter surfaces rather than shadows and colours are desaturated, a white-label variant with a different palette — without any component changing shape.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion values prescribed; runtime theme switching is the implementation mechanism (CSS custom properties, per-theme token files, Figma variable modes).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Three layers: Layer 1 global tokens (raw palette), Layer 2 semantic tokens (purpose-driven aliases — themes override here), Layer 3 component tokens (scoped). Theme types: colour modes (light, dark, high contrast, dimmed), brand themes (primary, sub-brands, white-label, seasonal), density (comfortable, compact, spacious). Dark-mode rules repeated: don't invert, reduce brightness thoughtfully, lighter surfaces for elevation, desaturate, provide image/illustration variants. Practice: tokens-first (themes emerge from overrides), test every component in every theme, respect OS theme preferences, document themeable vs fixed tokens.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Single palette: color-system ⟦S1418⟧; dark-mode craft: dark-mode-design ⟦S1419⟧.
- **Best for:** Multi-brand or light/dark builds; the override layer behind section variant systems.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — needed when one build must carry multiple themes/modes.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1468⟧

## ⟦S1469⟧ a-b-test-design — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Designs a rigorous A/B experiment — hypothesis, isolated variants, one primary metric, sample size and duration — for changes that can be measured quantitatively at scale.
- **How it looks:** No page output. An experiment plan: hypothesis in the form "If we [change], then [outcome] will [improve/decrease] because [rationale]"; control A vs treatment B with one variable changed; primary metric plus secondary/guardrail metrics.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Sample size from minimum detectable effect, baseline conversion rate, significance typically 95%, power typically 80%. Duration: run until sample size is reached, in full weeks to cover weekly cycles, minimum 1–2 weeks typically. Pitfalls: peeking before completion, too many variants, insensitive metric, novelty effects, ignoring segmentation. Do not test when traffic is too low, when withholding an improvement is unethical, for foundational changes, or when qualitative insight is more valuable.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Qualitative observation: test-scenario ⟦S1476⟧.
- **Best for:** Post-launch optimisation of live pages (headline/CTA variants) where traffic exists.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — live-traffic experiments only.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1469⟧

## ⟦S1470⟧ accessibility-test-plan — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Plans accessibility testing — assistive technologies, participant criteria, WCAG coverage and session protocol — for testing with real AT users. (Evaluating a design yourself: accessibility-audit ⟦S1458⟧.)
- **How it looks:** No page output. A four-layer test plan plus a matrix: every key flow tested across keyboard only, VoiceOver, NVDA, zoom 200%, high contrast, reduced motion; issues reported with description, WCAG criterion, severity, AT affected, reproduction steps, remediation.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Layers: 1 Automated (Axe, Lighthouse, WAVE — catches approximately 30–40% of issues; run on every page/state, integrate into CI/CD), 2 Manual (keyboard-only navigation, screen-reader walkthrough, zoom to 200% and 400%, high contrast, reduced motion), 3 Assistive technology (VoiceOver Mac/iOS, NVDA Windows, TalkBack Android, voice control, switch control, magnification), 4 User testing with disabled participants on their own devices and settings, focused on real tasks. WCAG checklist organised by POUR principle and A/AA/AAA level. Include accessibility in the definition of done; prioritise by user impact over compliance level.
- **Reference / source:** Axe, Lighthouse, WAVE, VoiceOver, NVDA, TalkBack — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Pre-launch verification programme for finished builds.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — testing programme, supports the QA gate.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1470⟧

## ⟦S1471⟧ click-test-plan — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Designs first-click and click tests that measure findability — whether users can locate things — plus click-path, navigation and five-second tests.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Deliverables: first-click success rate, time to first click, confidence ratings, and a click-distribution heat map over the tested screen.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Plan structure: objective → stimuli (screens/states) → tasks (goal-oriented, no UI hints — "Where would you click to change your email address?") → success criteria (correct first click against pre-defined target areas, time, confidence) → participants (typically 20–50 for quantitative). Benchmark: first-click success above 65% generally indicates good findability; hesitation indicates confusion. Rules: one task per screen, define target areas before testing, realistic content (not lorem ipsum), compare alternative designs on identical tasks.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Full task-based observation: test-scenario ⟦S1476⟧.
- **Best for:** Testing navigation labels and CTA placement on a homepage design before build.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — findability testing method.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1471⟧

## ⟦S1472⟧ concept-selection — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Runs the decision that ends a parallel exploration: criteria fixed in advance, applied to every concept, one winner chosen, and what each rejected concept was testing recorded.
- **How it looks:** No page output. The deliverable is a decision record — criteria, the choice, what the winner sacrificed, and for each rejected concept: what it was testing, what it lost on, and what would bring it back.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Order is the mechanism: criteria are written before the options are compared (criteria written afterwards merely describe the preferred option). Every criterion must be capable of failing a concept — "feels modern" fails nothing; "completes the core task in three steps or fewer" and "holds at 400 items without pagination" can fail. Each criterion is marked threshold (fail = out) or trade-off (weighed) — mixing them silently keeps constraint-breaking concepts alive. Rules: evidence over volume in the room; name the winner's cost; a split set is a priority conflict to escalate, not an average to blend; never graft losers onto the winner; apply the criteria to the incumbent too; keep rejected concepts retrievable. Criteria come from the brief's success criteria (⟦S1408⟧) and the product's principles (⟦S1409⟧), not from the room.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Picking which problem to work on: opportunity-framework ⟦S1414⟧; deciding by live traffic: a-b-test-design ⟦S1469⟧; the written defence afterwards: design-rationale ⟦S1490⟧.
- **Best for:** Choosing between the wholly-different section versions a build produces — the decision discipline behind version approval.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the selection method for competing design versions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1472⟧

## ⟦S1473⟧ heuristic-evaluation — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Runs an expert review against Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, with severity ratings — findings without recruiting participants.
- **How it looks:** No page output. An issue list: for each issue, the heuristic violated, description, location, severity (0–4), screenshot/reference, recommendation.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Nielsen's 10: visibility of system status; match with the real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise/diagnose/recover from errors; help and documentation. Severity scale: 0 not a problem, 1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major (important to fix), 4 catastrophe (must fix before release). Process: scope → walk through as a new user → as an experienced user → through each task flow → document → rate → prioritise. Use 3–5 evaluators working independently before comparing; suggest solutions, not just problems; combine with real user testing. Facilitated team session instead: design-critique ⟦S1479⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristics — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Solo expert QA pass on a built page before user testing or approval screenshots.
- **Tier:** STRONG — a standard expert-review gate for finished sections.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1473⟧

## ⟦S1474⟧ parallel-concepts — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Builds several genuinely different solutions to the same problem at once — differing in what the user does, not how it looks — held at equal effort until evidence chooses between them.
- **How it looks:** No page output; it produces the set itself: multiple versions of the same section or flow, in one constant visual language, each testing a different behavioural idea.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Distinctness is behavioural, tested on five dimensions: sequence (what is asked first), unit of interaction (one item / batch / continuous stream), division of labour (person decides vs system decides), entry point, commitment point (how far before irreversible). Two concepts with the same steps in the same order and different visual treatment are one concept rendered twice — cut one. Sizing: the count follows cost and stakes; three cheap sketches beat two polished mockups at equal total effort; every concept must sit at comparable fidelity (a rendered option beats a rough one on presentation alone); every concept must be one the team would actually ship. Evidence cited: Stanford parallel prototyping research (Dow, Glienke & Klemmer, 2010) — parallel producers outperformed serial iterators on real audience response; critique also lands as information about options rather than a verdict on the designer. Choosing afterwards: concept-selection ⟦S1472⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Dow, Glienke & Klemmer (2010), Stanford — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** The multi-version method itself — generating the genuinely different versions each homepage section must offer.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the divergence discipline behind section versions.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1474⟧

## ⟦S1475⟧ prototype-strategy — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Chooses prototype fidelity and method to match the design question and the decision at stake, before anything is built.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A fidelity decision: low (paper sketches, sticky notes, rough wireframes — exploration, IA, flow validation), medium (digital wireframes, clickable prototypes, grey-box layouts — interaction patterns, navigation testing, stakeholder alignment), high (pixel-perfect mockups, coded prototypes, motion prototypes — visual validation, micro-interaction testing, handoff, usability testing).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; motion prototypes are one of the high-fidelity methods.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Methods: paper prototyping, clickable wireframes, interactive (stateful) prototypes, coded prototypes (HTML/CSS/JS), Wizard of Oz (fake backend, real frontend), video prototypes (walkthrough animations). Choice questions: what question is being answered, who is the audience, how much time, how many iterations expected, what decisions will it inform. Rules: match fidelity to the question, not the deadline; prototype the riskiest assumption first; signal clearly that it is a prototype; build to throw away.
- **Reference / source:** None named. What to test once it exists: test-scenario ⟦S1476⟧.
- **Best for:** Deciding how much to build before approval at each build stage (proof-first sections vs full page).
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — planning method for prototype effort.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1475⟧

## ⟦S1476⟧ test-scenario — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Writes realistic usability task scenarios with success criteria and facilitation notes for a study that already exists.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Scenario documents: a brief realistic context (motivation without leading), one action-oriented task in the participant's language (no UI terminology that hints at the answer), and an observation guide.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Success criteria measured per task: completion (yes/no), time to complete, number of errors or wrong paths, assistance requests, self-reported difficulty (1–5 scale). Task types: exploratory (find information), specific (complete a goal), comparative (choose between options), open-ended (multiple valid paths). Writing rules: one goal per task, give motivation not instructions, never reveal the UI path in the wording, order easy → hard with a warm-up task first, pilot the scenarios before real sessions, write more scenarios than needed. Surrounding study design: usability-test-plan (design-research collection).
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Usability sessions on built pages — e.g. can a homeowner find the phone number and complete the quote form.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — test-session authoring.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1476⟧

## ⟦S1477⟧ user-flow-diagram — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Diagrams screen-level paths, decision points and branch logic for how a feature is traversed.
- **How it looks:** A flow diagram in standard notation: entry/end points as circles (end double-bordered), screens as rectangles, decisions as diamonds, user actions as rounded rectangles, system processes as rectangles with side bars, arrows labelled with the trigger or action.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion. Construction order: define the goal → identify entry points → map the happy path first → add decision points and branches → map error paths and recovery → mark exit points → note background system actions.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Flow types: task flow (single path), user flow (multiple paths by user type/choice), wire flow (flow combined with wireframe thumbnails). Annotations: screen names and key content, decision criteria at each branch, error conditions and handling, system events and notifications, time delays/async processes. Rules: one flow per user goal; keep branch counts readable on one diagram; consistent notation; label every arrow.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Emotional end-to-end arc: journey-map (design-research collection).
- **Best for:** Specifying multi-step flows — quote form steps, switcher journeys — before build.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — flow documentation.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1477⟧

## ⟦S1478⟧ wireframe-spec — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Prototyping & testing
- **What it is:** Specifies wireframe layout — content priority, component placement, behaviour annotation and responsive notes — defining structure before visual design.
- **How it looks:** Grey/black/white-only layouts: X-boxes for images, wavy lines for text blocks, real labels for navigation and buttons, content blocks ordered by priority numbers, with annotations for what happens on click/hover and how each block behaves at other breakpoints.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; interaction behaviour is written as annotations, not animated.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Fidelity levels: sketch (hand-drawn) → low-fi (grey boxes with content labels) → mid-fi (realistic layout, placeholder content) → annotated (mid-fi plus detailed behaviour specs). Content specs per block: heading hierarchy (H1, H2, H3), approximate text lengths/character counts, image aspect ratios and sizing, required vs optional content, content source (static, CMS, API). Rules: focus on content hierarchy not visual design; annotate behaviour, not just layout; show multiple states (empty, loading, populated, error); include responsive breakpoint versions; get content strategy input early. Grid mechanics: layout-grid ⟦S1428⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Structure-first passes for a new section before visual treatment.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — early-structure specification.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1478⟧

## ⟦S1479⟧ design-critique — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Structures a design critique session — rules, feedback formats, facilitation and follow-up — so feedback is specific, actionable and depersonalised.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Session agenda with timed sections: Present (5 min), Clarify (5 min), individual feedback rounds, Discuss, Capture action items — plus written notes, decisions and follow-up actions as outputs.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Format statements: "I notice…", "I wonder…", "What if…", "I think… because…", "Have you considered…". Principles: critique the design not the designer; be specific not vague; ask before telling; suggest don't prescribe; ground feedback in user needs and business goals; presenter sets context and scope first ("I'm looking for feedback specifically on the checkout flow, not the visual design"). Running rules: designated facilitator, all context up front, note-taker assigned, criticism of alternatives welcomed, parking lot for tangents, decisions and actions recorded at the close. Self-running visual verdicts on screenshots instead: the critique-* family ⟦S1495⟧–⟦S1501⟧; choosing between the presented options afterwards: concept-selection ⟦S1472⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — review sessions for design work.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — team process, no page application.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1479⟧

## ⟦S1480⟧ design-debt-audit — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Audits accumulated design debt — inconsistencies, outdated patterns, accessibility gaps, dead documentation, code drift — and prioritises the paydown.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A live register: each item has a title, debt category, severity, user impact, effort estimate, age and owner — reviewed quarterly.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Five categories: Visual (inconsistent spacing, mixed icon styles, one-off colours), Structural (redundant components/patterns), Accessibility (WCAG failures, keyboard gaps, contrast failures), Documentation (missing guidelines, outdated examples), Implementation (code out of sync with design, hardcoded values). Priority score = Severity × Frequency / Effort. Rules: quantify user impact in numbers where possible, batch small fixes, address high-impact accessibility debt first, communicate the value of paydown to stakeholders, never let debt accumulation outpace paydown. The token-specific sweep: design-token-audit ⟦S1492⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Periodic cleanup of an ageing multi-version build.
- **Tier:** SITUATIONAL — maintenance audit for mature projects.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1480⟧

## ⟦S1481⟧ design-impact-reporting — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Measures and reports design impact — a metrics framework connecting design work to user, product and business outcomes, with a scorecard and stakeholder reporting cadence.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A Design Scorecard (baseline / current / target per metric) and before/after case studies; reporting formats: quarterly design review, release summaries, case studies, annual assessment.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Metric levels: User (satisfaction NPS/CSAT, task success, time on task, error rates, accessibility compliance), Product (adoption, retention, feature usage, support volume, conversion), Business (revenue impact, cost savings, time to market, dev efficiency, customer acquisition). Results are framed in a five-part narrative: context → intervention → evidence → business value → what's next. Rules: measure from project start (baseline), attribute honestly (contribution, not sole credit), one metric set per audience (executives vs product teams vs design teams), celebrate wins and analyse losses, make reporting routine.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — stakeholder reporting.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — reporting process, no page application.

## ⟦S1482⟧ design-qa-checklist — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** A QA checklist verifying an implementation against the design spec — visual accuracy, states, content, accessibility behaviour, cross-platform — used before a design ships.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A pass/fail checklist worked across six categories: Visual Accuracy, Layout & Structure, Interaction, Content, Accessibility, Cross-Platform.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; motion is checked inside the Interaction category (durations, easing, reduced-motion behaviour) against the spec.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Check values named: hover/active/pressed/focus/loading/empty/error states all present; hit targets at least 44px; keyboard navigation complete with visible focus; colour contrast meets WCAG AA; alt text on meaningful images; prefers-reduced-motion respected; no horizontal scroll; checked across breakpoints (mobile, tablet, desktop, wide) and browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge); long/short/empty content; images load with fallbacks. Process: designer self-review → design QA pass (design vs implementation side by side) → file bugs with screenshots and expected-vs-actual → prioritise by impact → verify fixes. Giving the implementer the spec: handoff-spec ⟦S1485⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** The final verification pass on a built homepage before screenshots and approval.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the implementation-QA gate for builds.

## ⟦S1483⟧ design-review-process — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Defines formal design review gates with checklists and approval criteria — the gates a design passes through from concept to implementation QA.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Four gates: 1 Concept Review (problem understood, aligned with strategy, scope defined, success criteria established), 2 Design Review (solution addresses the problem, meets UX standards, edge cases covered, accessibility considered), 3 Pre-Handoff Review (all states designed, assets ready, specs written, responsive behaviour defined), 4 Implementation QA (matches specs, interactions work, accessibility requirements met, performance acceptable) — each with criteria, reviewers, decision options and SLA.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Principles: reviews are gates, not roadblocks; checklists make criteria objective; feedback is specific and actionable; decisions are documented with rationale; escalations are defined. Quality standards inside gates: accessibility compliance, performance impact, consistency with the system, user-centredness. Running the critique conversation inside a gate: design-critique ⟦S1479⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — structuring review and sign-off.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — process design, no page application.

## ⟦S1484⟧ design-sprint-plan — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Plans a one-to-five-day design sprint answering a business question with a prototype and user feedback.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A day-by-day plan: Day 1 Understand (problem, goals, expert interviews, target moment), Day 2 Diverge (sketch solutions, review, vote on concepts), Day 3 Decide (pick one, storyboard the prototype), Day 4 Prototype (fake it fast, realistic enough for testing), Day 5 Test (five 1:1 interviews, observe, pattern-find, next steps).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Team 5–7 (decider, facilitator, designer, engineer, domain expert, marketer, customer support); decider holds final say on scope and decisions; sprint question and long-term goal written up front; recruit test users before starting; every day ends with decisions documented. Post-sprint: summarise insights, share findings, define next actions, archive artefacts.
- **Reference / source:** The classic five-day sprint (Google Ventures format) — implied by structure; not named in the skill.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — workshop planning.

## ⟦S1485⟧ handoff-spec — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Design ops & team process
- **What it is:** Creates a handoff specification — visual specs, interaction specs, design tokens and asset delivery — so developers implement the design without interpreting it.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Four spec parts: Visual Spec (token-based colour, spacing/layout, typography scale — developers should use tokens, not raw values), Interaction Spec (animations with duration/easing, gesture behaviour, error and empty states), Assets (SVG icons, optimised images, illustrated assets), Implementation Notes (breakpoint table, component patterns, browser support, third-party dependencies).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion of its own; animation durations and easings are written into the Interaction Spec.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Edge cases required: long content, no content (empty state), error content, loading state, offline state, permission-denied. Rules: annotate in the design file (Figma comments) and export tokens; include responsive specs for every component; flag new patterns vs components; provide asset exports at every needed size. Verifying the result afterwards: design-qa-checklist ⟦S1482⟧; the component-level counterpart: component-spec ⟦S1459⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Handing a finished design to a builder with zero ambiguity.

## ⟦S1489⟧ design-negotiation — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Designer toolkit
- **What it is:** Prepares evidence-based negotiation for the four recurring design conflicts — compressed timelines, reduced scope, stakeholder overrides, headcount requests — each with several distinct approaches.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A preparation playbook: for each context, several named approaches with the evidence to assemble (e.g. for scope reduction: map cuts to risk by user impact, propose a phased delivery, propose dropping features rather than the review steps); plus general principles (understand their constraints, bring data, propose alternatives, know your walk-away, build alliances, document outcomes in writing).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Contexts and example approaches: Timeline compression (show the cost of rushed timelines, offer phased delivery, ask what specifically ships sooner); Scope reduction without review (map proposed cuts to risks, suggest dropping low-impact features instead, propose async review); Stakeholder override (present the evidence, ask what data they hold that you don't, propose testing both); Headcount requests (quantify the bottleneck, compare contracting vs hiring). Meta-rule: prepare before the meeting, not in it; win the argument with evidence or escalate — never quietly absorb a harmful decision.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** No homepage use — stakeholder negotiation preparation.
- **Tier:** NOT-FOR-TRADES — interpersonal process, no page application.

## ⟦S1490⟧ design-rationale — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Designer toolkit
- **What it is:** Documents why a design decision was made — context, options considered, evidence, trade-offs — in a record that survives staff changes and future redesigns.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A seven-part record: 1 Decision (what was decided), 2 Context (problem, constraints, timing, who was affected), 3 Options Considered (description, pros, cons, effort estimate each), 4 Evidence (user research, analytics, test results, expert review), 5 Reasoning (why this option best met the criteria), 6 Trade-offs (what was consciously given up), 7 Validation Plan (how success will be measured, when to revisit).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Rules: write it at decision time, from notes, not from memory later; include rejected options (more valuable than the choice itself); attach the evidence, don't summarise it away; revisit rationales when conditions change; store in one searchable place linked to the design files. The decision meeting itself: concept-selection ⟦S1472⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Recording why one version won over others on a build.

## ⟦S1492⟧ design-token-audit — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Designer toolkit
- **What it is:** Audits how tokens are actually used across a codebase — inventory, duplicates, hardcoded values, naming compliance — and reports an adoption percentage with a migration path.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A six-step audit producing a report that leads with one number (e.g. "64% of colour values use approved tokens; 847 hardcoded values remain"), then a findings/recommendations table (severity, effort, impact) and a prioritised migration roadmap.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Steps: 1 Inventory (extract all tokens from source files; scan design files for raw values), 2 Categorize (type: colour/spacing/type/etc.; tier: global/alias/component), 3 Map (usage counts per token; identical values under multiple names), 4 Flag (duplicates, unused tokens, hardcoded values, naming violations, deprecated tokens still in use), 5 Prioritize (group by remediation effort and consistency impact), 6 Recommend (specific actions with expected outcomes). Tooling named: token extraction via Style Dictionary or custom scripts; Figma plugins for raw-value scans; grep/scripts for codebase analysis. Token architecture being audited: design-token ⟦S1461⟧; the wider debt picture: design-debt-audit ⟦S1480⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Style Dictionary — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Cleaning up token drift in a mature build.

## ⟦S1493⟧ presentation-deck — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Designer toolkit
- **What it is:** Structures a design presentation deck around a narrative arc — Hook → Context → Journey → Solution → Evidence → Ask — adapted by audience (executives, engineers, whole company).
- **How it looks:** A slide narrative: the hook opens on a user story or striking insight; context states the problem and why it matters now; journey walks the process through key decisions; solution presents the design with a walkthrough; evidence shows research/testing/impact; the ask closes with specific next steps and the decisions needed.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion prescribed (slide sequencing is the only order mechanism).
- **Mechanism & key values:** Slide law: one idea per slide; visuals over text (show, don't tell); consistent hierarchy (title, visual, caption); section dividers for long decks; appendix for detail questions; rehearse with a timer and cut to fit. Audience adaptations: executives (business impact first, less process), engineers (technical feasibility and constraints), whole company (story and vision). Deck narrative vs written record: case-study ⟦S1488⟧ (long-form), design-rationale ⟦S1490⟧ (one decision).
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Presenting design work to clients or stakeholders.

## ⟦S1494⟧ ux-writing — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Designer toolkit
- **What it is:** UX writing guidance for interface text — buttons, errors, empty states, confirmations, onboarding, CTAs — with voice principles and per-category rules.
- **How it looks:** The words on the page: error messages that state what happened and the exact fix in plain language; empty states that explain the value of filling them with one clear next step; destructive confirmations that name the consequence (never a bare "Are you sure?"); buttons that start with a verb and say what happens ("Save changes", never "Submit" or "OK").
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Voice principles, each a forced choice: clear over clever; concise over comprehensive; helpful over promotional; consistent over creative; inclusive over casual. Category rules: Microcopy — front-load important words, active voice, sentence case, no jargon without definitions. Errors — what happened + why + the specific fix, no blame, no error codes as the primary message, link to help for complex ones. Empty states — explain what belongs there and why it matters, one clear CTA, never blame the user for emptiness. Confirmations — describe the consequence, label buttons with the action itself. Onboarding — one concept per screen, benefit-first, short sentences, skippable where possible. CTAs — 2–5 words, specific outcomes, consistent primary/secondary hierarchy. Tone flexes by situation (celebration, error) without changing the underlying voice.
- **Reference / source:** None named. Voice definition: voice-and-tone ⟦S1435⟧.
- **Best for:** Every label, error and CTA on a trade homepage — especially form copy.
- **Tier:** STRONG — the interface-copy standard for builds.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1494⟧

## ⟦S1495⟧ critique-affordance — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates whether elements look interactive and interactive elements look their state — affordance, feedback and control clarity — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. A critique report: per dimension, an Observation (what is there), a Problem (why it harms usability or perception), and a Fix (the concrete change) — each dimension rated pass / minor issue / major issue, closing with an overall verdict and top fixes. Shared output format of the critique family ⟦S1495⟧–⟦S1501⟧.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion; hover/press behaviour is assessed from the states shown, not animated.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions: Clickability cues (buttons need visible boundaries, fill or shadow; text links need underline or strong colour differentiation — if it looks like body text, users will not test it; cards acting as links need a hover state or chevron), State visibility (selected vs unselected must differ clearly; disabled controls must be visibly dimmed AND non-interactive), CTA clarity (one primary action per view, visually dominant; secondary actions present but subordinate), Action discoverability (touch targets at least 44×44px; actions hidden behind hover or long-press with no visible alternative are flagged).
- **Reference / source:** None named. Lens family: composition ⟦S1498⟧, hierarchy ⟦S1501⟧, the rest ⟦S1496⟧–⟦S1500⟧.
- **Best for:** CTA and control QA on section screenshots — is the call button obviously the call button.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1495⟧

## ⟦S1496⟧ critique-brand-consistency — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates a design against the project's own brand documents — checking colour, typography, voice, spacing and component rules against what the brand actually specifies.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format — per dimension: Observation, Divergence (this lens's middle field, not "Problem"), Fix — rated pass / minor issue / major issue, with an overall verdict and top fixes.
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Source documents, read from the project root before critiquing: mood.md (visual direction, feeling, references), voice.md (tone, vocabulary, phrasing rules for copy), tokens.md (approved colour values, type scale, spacing scale, component definitions). Dimensions: Colour fidelity (every colour traceable to tokens.md; off-palette values flagged even if close), Type fidelity (families, weights and scale steps against tokens.md), Voice consistency (headlines, CTAs and body checked against voice.md — adjective choices, sentence length, banned words), Spacing & layout rules (grid and spacing scale as specified), Component consistency (same component in two places must render identically). Discipline: if a brand file is missing, that dimension is skipped and the gap stated — brand rules are never invented.
- **Reference / source:** The project's own mood.md / voice.md / tokens.md — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Checking a build stays on the client's real brand (colours, type, tone) across sections.
- **Tier:** STRONG — brand-fidelity lens for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1496⟧

## ⟦S1497⟧ critique-color — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates colour usage — contrast, semantic meaning, palette cohesion and colour-only signification — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format (Observation / Problem / Fix per dimension; pass / minor issue / major issue; overall verdict and top fixes).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions with named failure patterns: Contrast ratios (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 body text, 3:1 large text 18pt+/14pt bold+, 3:1 UI components and meaningful graphics; placeholder text rendered at 40% opacity is a named failure; text over images needs a scrim or solid background), Semantic consistency (error/success/warning colours applied consistently; a green success and a green CTA on the same screen confuse state with action), Palette discipline (primary actions one colour — three different blues used for links, buttons and selected states reads as incoherence; neutrals must share one temperature — warm greys and cool greys mixed looks accidental), Colour-only signification (status by coloured dot alone fails for colour-blind users — always pair with an icon or text label; required-field asterisks in red alone fail, add "(required)" text). Supporting laws pulled in: palette construction color-system ⟦S1418⟧.
- **Reference / source:** WCAG AA contrast values — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Colour QA on section screenshots — contrast failures and palette drift.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1497⟧

## ⟦S1498⟧ critique-composition — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates layout composition — balance, whitespace distribution, rhythm and gestalt grouping — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format (Observation / Problem / Fix per dimension; pass / minor issue / major issue; overall verdict and top fixes).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions: Balance (visual weight distributed intentionally; a heavy element on one side with nothing countering it reads as a mistake), Whitespace distribution (breathing room consistent; related elements closer together than unrelated ones — proximity is the primary grouping signal; crowded sections with no rest areas increase cognitive load), Rhythm & repetition (spacing follows a consistent scale — alternating 16px and 20/24px section padding with no pattern breaks the rhythm; repeated elements must share size, spacing and alignment), Gestalt grouping (elements grouped by proximity, similarity or enclosure read as units; items that belong together but sit closer to unrelated items are flagged; borders and background tints creating false groups are flagged). Craft behind it: spacing-system ⟦S1433⟧, layout-grid ⟦S1428⟧.
- **Reference / source:** Gestalt principles — named in the skill.
- **Best for:** Layout QA on section screenshots — spacing rhythm and grouping defects.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1498⟧

## ⟦S1499⟧ critique-information-density — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates content volume and cognitive load — too much, too little, or wrongly organised information — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format (Observation / Problem / Fix per dimension; pass / minor issue / major issue; overall verdict and top fixes).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions: Cognitive load (count the decisions demanded in one view; elements competing for attention at equal weight are flagged; working-memory rule of thumb — grouping into chunks of 3–5 beats 9 competing items), Content priority (the most important content must get the most space and prominence; a long unbroken list with no headings, grouping or visual breaks is flagged — users need entry points), Scanning pattern (designs are scanned in F or Z patterns depending on layout; key content placed outside the natural scan path gets missed), Progressive disclosure (advanced options visible alongside the basics, with no show/hide or expand mechanism, overwhelm new users; summary views should carry expandable detail, not everything inline). Named example: tables with 10+ columns where three columns do 90% of the work — the rest should hide behind a column toggle or detail view.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Density QA on content-heavy sections (services lists, pricing, proof) — cutting overload before approval.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1499⟧

## ⟦S1500⟧ critique-typography — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates typography — hierarchy, readability, scale consistency and line length — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format (Observation / Problem / Fix per dimension; pass / minor issue / major issue; overall verdict and top fixes).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions with values: Scale consistency (sizes must come from a defined scale, steps at least ~1.25× apart — ad-hoc sizes a few px apart like 15px/17px read as accidents), Readability (body text minimum 16px desktop / 14px mobile; line-height 1.4–1.6 for body, 1.1–1.3 for headings; line length 45–75 characters — longer lines tire the eye, shorter break flow), Weight & style discipline (more than 3 weights or styles on one screen is noise; italics reserved for emphasis, not whole paragraphs; all-caps only for short labels), Alignment (mixed left/centre alignment without pattern confuses the reading path; justified text creates uneven word spacing and should be avoided on screen). Type system behind it: typography-system ⟦S1434⟧.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Type QA on section screenshots — scale drift and readability failures.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1500⟧

## ⟦S1501⟧ critique-visual-hierarchy — Part 22 — User's installed catalog (Owl-Listener designer-skills) · Visual critique
- **What it is:** A single-dimension visual critique lens: evaluates whether the eye lands where the design intends — entry point, scanning flow, weight distribution and emphasis — from design screenshots or specs.
- **How it looks:** No page output. Same family format (Observation / Problem / Fix per dimension; pass / minor issue / major issue; overall verdict and top fixes).
- **Frame by frame:** Static — no motion.
- **Mechanism & key values:** Dimensions: Entry point (the first thing the eye hits must be the most important element — if the eye goes to a decorative image or secondary nav first, hierarchy has failed), Eye flow (F-pattern for text-heavy layouts, Z-pattern for sparse ones; interruptions and dead ends in the path are flagged), Weight distribution (size differentials between levels at least 1.5×; colour weight intentional; elements at nearby sizes compete — the squint test: at a blur, the intended hierarchy should still read), Emphasis discipline (exactly one primary emphasis zone per view; multiple bold/high-contrast elements competing flatten the hierarchy; the primary CTA must be the strongest element in its region). Squint-test and scale values double as the pass bar for hero screenshots.
- **Reference / source:** None named.
- **Best for:** Hero and section QA — does the eye land on the headline and CTA first.
- **Tier:** STRONG — one of the seven screenshot-critique lenses for build QA.
- **Deep read:** WEB-SKILLS.md ⟦S1501⟧
